entries.description: SI units, gas law derivations, latent heat, specific heat capacity, and laws of thermodynamics
entries.text:
# SI Units & Thermodynamics SI units, gas law derivations, latent heat, specific heat capacity, and laws of thermodynamics Système International (SI) defines seven base units from which all other units are derived. In anaesthesia, the most commonly encountered derived units are the (pressure = N/m²), (energy = N·m), and (power = J/s). Temperature in gas calculations must always be in (K = °C + 273.15). 1 atmosphere = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg ≈ 1033 cmH₂O = 14.7 psi = 1.013 bar . (The cmH₂O equivalence comes from P = ρgh with ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².) Understanding these conversions is essential for interpreting arterial blood gases, ventilator settings, and gas cylinder pressures. The SI unit of pressure is the Pascal, though mmHg and cmH₂O remain in widespread clinical use. Celsius scale defines 0 °C as the freezing point and 100 °C as the boiling point of water at 1 atmosphere. The Fahrenheit scale sets water's freezing point at 32 °F and boiling at 212 °F. Conversions: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32 °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9 . Normal body temperature (37 °C = 98.6 °F). Kelvin scale is the SI unit of temperature and is an — its zero point (0 K = −273.15 °C) represents the theoretical minimum where molecular motion ceases. The Kelvin scale has no negative values , which is why it must be used in all gas law calculations. Using Celsius in PV = nRT would give nonsensical results because a "doubling" of temperature from 10 °C to 20 °C is not a doubling of absolute temperature (283 K to 293 K is only a 3.5% increase). Why Kelvin matters for gas laws: Charles' law states V ∝ T (at constant P). If you plot volume against temperature in °C and extrapolate to zero volume, the line crosses the x-axis at −273.15 °C — this is absolute zero. Spirometry readings taken at room temperature (20 °C = 293 K) corrected to body temperature (37 °C = 310 K) increase by 310/293 = 5.8%. Quick Conversion Reference Celsius → Kelvin: K = °C + 273.15 (e.g., 37 °C = 310.15 K) Celsius → Fahrenheit: °F = (°C × 1.8) + 32 (e.g., 37 °C = 98.6 °F) Fahrenheit → Celsius: °C = (°F − 32) / 1.8 (e.g., 104 °F = 40 °C) Key landmarks: 0 °C = 273 K = 32 °F | 37 °C = 310 K = 98.6 °F | 100 °C = 373 K = 212 °F zeroth law of thermodynamics : the measuring device must reach thermal equilibrium with the tissue being measured. Core temperature is best reflected by the pulmonary artery catheter (gold standard), distal oesophageal probe (lower third, near the heart), and nasopharyngeal probe Tympanic membrane thermometry uses infrared detection (shared blood supply with hypothalamus via the internal carotid artery) for a rapid, non-invasive estimate of core temperature. Peripheral sites (axillary, skin) are 0.5–1 °C lower than core. The core-peripheral gradient Thermometry Devices — Physical Principles Seebeck effect — voltage at junction of two dissimilar metals (copper–constantan). Fast, used in PA catheters Semiconductor whose resistance falls exponentially with temperature (NTC). Sensitive, used in oesophageal/rectal probes RTD (platinum): Resistance increases linearly with temperature. Very accurate laboratory standard — slower than thermistors Infrared tympanic: Detects IR radiation whose intensity is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature (Stefan–Boltzmann law: j* = σT⁴); peak wavelength shifts with T per Wien's displacement law. Non-contact, <2 s, but accuracy affected by cerumen/positioning Liquid crystal: Cholesteric crystals change colour with T. Forehead strips — convenient but inaccurate (±1–2 °C) Perioperative temperature management: Hypothermia (<36 °C) prolongs neuromuscular blockade, reduces MAC, impairs platelet function, increases wound infection rates, and triggers shivering (↑VO₂ 200–400%). Current UK guidance is NICE (Perioperative care in adults, 2020), which superseded the earlier CG65 (2008/2016). NG180 defines inadvertent perioperative hypothermia as a core temperature <36.0 °C, requires induction not to begin unless the patient is ≥36.0 °C, and instructs that forced-air warming devices be set to maintain a patient temperature of at least 36.5 °C . The superseded CG65 is retained on the NICE site for archival reference only ideal gas equation PV = nRT (R = 8.314 J/mol/K) describes a hypothetical gas with no intermolecular forces and negligible molecular volume. All individual gas laws are special cases when certain variables are held constant: Boyle's law Charles' law (constant P, n → V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂), and Gay-Lussac's law (constant V, n → P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂). Dalton's law (total pressure = sum of partial pressures) underpins the alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = FiO₂(P − PH₂O) − PaCO₂/RQ. Henry's law (amount dissolved ∝ partial pressure × solubility) explains nitrogen narcosis, decompression sickness, and blood gas analysis. high pressures low temperatures (near the critical point). N₂O in cylinders is a real gas (stored as liquid), while O₂ behaves close to an ideal gas at clinical temperatures. The van der Waals equation Specific heat capacity (c) is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K. Water has an exceptionally high c ( 4.18 kJ/kg/K ), providing thermal stability to the body (60% water) and making water an effective warming/cooling medium. Q = m × c × ΔT calculates the heat energy transferred. Latent heat is the energy required for a phase change at constant temperature. The latent heat of vaporisation of water ( 2260 kJ/kg ) is very large — evaporation is therefore extremely effective at cooling, explaining why evaporative loss is the dominant mechanism of intraoperative heat loss from exposed surgical surfaces, and why sweating is so effective. zeroth law establishes thermal equilibrium as transitive — if two systems are each in equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. This is the fundamental basis of temperature measurement. first law (conservation of energy: ΔU = Q − W) states energy cannot be created or destroyed. In an adiabatic process Joule-Thomson coefficient is positive for most gases at room temperature but negative for hydrogen and helium. second law states heat flows spontaneously hot → cold and entropy of an isolated system always increases. This explains perioperative heat loss to the cold theatre. UK-focused reviews (BJA Education 2016) cite typical proportions of radiation ≈ 40–60% convection ≈ 30% , and evaporation up to 20% , with conduction contributing only a small share; an older, widely-quoted breakdown from Sessler (Anesthesiology 2008) gives radiation ≈ 40%, convection ≈ 30%, evaporation ≈ 25% and conduction ≈ 5%. Both data sets vary considerably with exposed surface area, ambient airflow, surgical irrigation and whether the patient is awake or anaesthetised. The third law Heat to warm 1 L of crystalloid from 20 °C to 37 °C Approximately 71 kJ. Each litre of 20 °C fluid effectively cools the patient by transferring this much heat away from them if not warmed. Spirometry temperature correction (BTPS) ≈4.23 L (an increase of ~5.8%), illustrating why temperatures in gas law calculations must always be converted to Kelvin. SI Units & Thermodynamics SI base and derived units, gas law derivations, latent heat, specific heat capacity, and the laws of thermodynamics There are 7 SI base units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd) Key derived units: Pascal (N/m²), Joule (N·m), Watt (J/s). Pressure conversions: 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg ≈ 1033 cmH₂O All individual gas laws (Boyle's, Charles', Gay-Lussac's, Avogadro's) derive from the ideal gas equation PV = nRT Specific heat capacity (c): energy to raise 1 kg by 1 K; water's high c (4.18 kJ/kg/K) provides thermal stability Latent heat of vaporisation (2260 kJ/kg for water): energy for phase change without temperature change — drives evaporative heat loss First law: energy conservation (ΔU = Q − W); adiabatic gas expansion causes cooling (pressure regulators, cryotherapy) Second law: heat flows hot → cold spontaneously; entropy always increases — explains perioperative hypothermia mechanisms Introduction SI Units Temperature Scales Clinical Thermometry Principles Gas Law Derivations Heat & Specific Heat Capacity Laws of Thermodynamics Metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (electric current), kelvin (thermodynamic temperature), mole (amount of substance), candela (luminous intensity). All other units are derived from these (e.g. pascal = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻², joule = kg·m²·s⁻²). State the first and second laws of thermodynamics with one anaesthetic example. First law — energy is conserved; ΔU = Q − W. Example: heat lost by patient (Q) = heat absorbed by cold IV fluids + heat lost by evaporation from open body cavity. Second law — entropy of an isolated system always increases; heat flows from hot to cold. Example: warming a patient requires an active energy input (forced-air warmer), it does not happen spontaneously. What is the triple point of water and why is it important? The unique temperature and pressure (273.16 K, 611.657 Pa) at which solid, liquid and vapour water coexist in equilibrium. It defines the kelvin scale: 1 K = 1/273.16 of the temperature of the triple point. Used as the primary calibration point for thermometers because it is highly reproducible. List the 7 SI base units and the most relevant derived units (Pa, J, W) Convert between Celsius, Kelvin and Fahrenheit and justify use of Kelvin in gas law calculations s laws from the ideal gas equation PV = nRT Define specific heat capacity and latent heat and apply them to vaporiser physics and perioperative heat loss State the four laws of thermodynamics and apply the first/second laws to clinical scenarios How much energy (kJ) is required to warm 1 L of normal saline from room temperature (20 °C) to body temperature (37 °C)? (c ≈ 4.18 kJ/kg/K, density ≈ 1 kg/L) Q = m × c × ΔT m = 1 kg, c = 4.18 kJ/kg/K, ΔT = 17 K Q = 1 × 4.18 × 17 = 71.1 kJ This is the basis for fluid warmers — significant energy is needed, hence the need for high-power countercurrent or dry-heat warming devices to keep up at infusion rates >500 ml/min. A patient exhales a measured volume of 4.00 L at room temperature 20 °C, ambient pressure. Using Charles law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (T in Kelvin) T₁ = 293 K, T₂ = 310 K V₂ = V₁ × (T₂/T₁) = 4.00 × (310/293) = 4.23 L This ~5.8% expansion is why pulmonary function values must be reported BTPS (body temperature, ambient pressure, saturated). ], }, ]; const SIUnitsThermodynamicsTopic = () => { return ( A solid understanding of SI units, gas laws, and thermodynamic principles underpins much of the physics examined in the Primary FRCA. The SI system provides a coherent framework for all physical measurements in medicine. The gas laws — all derivable from the ideal gas equation PV = nRT — have direct clinical applications from altitude physiology to anaesthetic vaporiser function. Thermodynamics governs heat transfer, phase changes, and energy conservation, with immediate relevance to perioperative temperature management, vaporiser physics, and cryotherapy.

°F = (°C × 9/5) + 32 and °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9. Normal body temperature (37 °C = 98.6 °F).

The Kelvin scale is the SI unit of temperature and is an absolute scale — its zero point (0 K = −273.15 °C) represents the theoretical minimum where molecular motion ceases. The Kelvin scale has no negative values, which is why it must be used in all gas law calculations. Using Celsius in PV = nRT would give nonsensical results because a of temperature from 10 °C to 20 °C is not a doubling of absolute temperature (283 K to 293 K is only a 3.5% increase).

Why Kelvin matters for gas laws: Charles s law (constant T, n → P₁V₁ = P₂V₂), Charles s law (constant V, n → P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂).

Dalton s law (amount dissolved ∝ partial pressure × solubility) explains nitrogen narcosis, decompression sickness, and blood gas analysis.

Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressures and low temperatures (near the critical point). N₂O in cylinders is a real gas (stored as liquid), while O₂ behaves close to an ideal gas at clinical temperatures. The van der Waals equation accounts for intermolecular forces and molecular volume in real gases.

Defines inadvertent perioperative hypothermia as core temperature <36.0 °C; forced-air warming devices to maintain ≥36.5 °C; induction not to begin unless ≥36.0 °C.
references.excerpt: Induction of anaesthesia should not begin unless the patient's temperature is 36.0°C or above (unless there is a need to expedite surgery because of clinical urgency). The temperature setting on forced-air warming devices should be set at maximum and then adjusted to maintain a patient temperature of at least 36.5°C. Hypothermia is defined as a core temperature below 36.0°C.

entries.description: Graph shapes, exponentials, logarithms, sigmoid curves and their physiological and pharmacokinetic applications
entries.text:
# Mathematical Concepts Graph shapes, exponentials, logarithms, sigmoid curves and their physiological and pharmacokinetic applications First order Elimination rate is proportional to concentration, so a constant is removed per unit time. Half-life is constant. Concentration falls exponentially on an arithmetic plot and forms a straight line on a semi-log plot. Zero order The elimination pathway is saturated, so a constant is removed per unit time independently of concentration. Half-life is not constant and becomes shorter as concentration falls. The arithmetic concentration–time plot is linear; the semi-log plot is curved. Categorical data are nominal (unordered groups, such as blood group) or ordinal (ordered categories, such as pain score). Numerical data are discrete counts or continuous measurements. The mean uses every value and suits approximately normal continuous data but is sensitive to outliers. The median is the middle ranked value and is preferred for skewed or ordinal data. The mode is the most frequent value and can describe categorical data. Spread and precision Variance is the mean squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation (SD) is its square root and describes spread of individual observations. Interquartile range (IQR) spans the 25th–75th centiles and suits skewed data. Standard error of the mean (SEM = SD/√n) describes precision of the sample mean, not population variability. normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, with mean = median = mode; approximately 95% of observations lie within 1.96 SD of the mean. Positive skew has a long right tail and usually mean > median; negative skew has a long left tail and usually mean < median. A 95% confidence interval gives a range generated by a method that would contain the true population parameter in 95% of repeated samples; its width communicates estimate precision t½ = τ × ln(2) = 0.693 × τ . The empirical Hill equation is fractional occupancy = [A]ⁿ/(K ⁿ + [A]ⁿ), where the Hill coefficient n is an index of cooperativity and curve steepness. When n > 1, binding is positively cooperative: one ligand increases affinity for the next (oxygen binding to haemoglobin; n ≈ 2.7). When n = 1, sites behave independently with no cooperativity (for example myoglobin or a simple drug–receptor interaction). When n < 1, binding is negatively cooperative: one ligand reduces affinity for subsequent ligand. The coefficient is not necessarily the number of binding sites ; it is an empirical summary of interaction. In pharmacology, plotting dose on a logarithmic axis converts the hyperbolic dose-response into its familiar sigmoid shape, with EC₅₀ at the midpoint. The central portion can be linearised using a probit or logit transformation Pre-oxygenation wash-in time End-tidal O₂ reaches ~95% after roughly one minute (3 time constants). This underpins the Association of Anaesthetists' recommendation (Recommendations for standards of monitoring during anaesthesia and recovery 2021) for ≥3 minutes of tidal-volume pre-oxygenation, which provides a comfortable safety margin to ≥99% (5τ). Why a single time constant fails for remifentanil Equating CSHT to a first-order t½ is a fundamental pharmacokinetic error: remifentanil's offset is multi-exponential and its CSHT (~3–4 min) stays short only because rapid metabolism by non-specific esterases dominates redistribution. Use single-τ models only for genuine single-compartment processes such as nitrogen wash-out or capacitor discharge. Mathematical Concepts Graph shapes, exponentials, logarithms and sigmoid curves underpinning physiology and pharmacokinetics Linear (y = kx): Ohm's law, laminar flow, Beer-Lambert — direct proportionality Exponential decay (e⁻ᵏˣ): First-order drug elimination, nitrogen washout, capacitor discharge Negative exponential rise (1 − e⁻ᵏˣ): Preoxygenation wash-in, volatile agent uptake, capacitor charging Sigmoid: ODC (cooperative binding), dose-response curves — Hill coefficient determines steepness; central portion linearised by probit/logit transformation One time constant (τ) = 63% change; t½ = 0.693 × τ; after 5τ ≈ 99.3% complete Logarithmic scales (pH, dB, pKa) compress large ranges — 1 pH unit = 10× change in [H⁺] Multi-compartment PK is multi-exponential — a single τ or t½ is inadequate, hence context-sensitive half-time (e.g. remifentanil) Introduction First-Order and Zero-Order Kinetics Statistical Concepts for Data Interpretation Graph Types & Clinical Examples Time Constants (τ) 63.2% complete 86.5% complete 95.0% complete 99.3% complete τ for wash-in τ = Volume / Flow rate τ for RC circuit τ = R × C Half-Life vs Time Constant Logarithmic Scales in Medicine pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]. A change of 1 pH unit = 10-fold change in [H⁺]. pH 7.4 → [H⁺] = 40 nmol/L; pH 7.1 → [H⁺] = 80 nmol/L. dB = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀). A 10 dB increase = 10× intensity. Used in ultrasound attenuation and noise measurement. pKa = −log₁₀(Ka). Describes acid strength. At pH = pKa, 50% of drug is ionised. MAC values are often plotted on log scales when comparing agents. Plotting dose on a log axis gives a dose-response curve its familiar sigmoid shape; the central portion can then be linearised with a probit or logit transformation for analysis. The Sigmoid Curve & Cooperativity What is a time constant and how many are needed for completion? Time constant (τ) = volume / flow (in compartment kinetics) or R × C (electrical). It is the time taken for an exponential process to reach 63 % of its final value. 3τ reaches 95 %, 5τ reaches 99 % (clinically ). Example: with FRC 3 L and alveolar ventilation 4 L/min, τ ≈ 0.75 min → wash-in/wash-out ≈ 4 min. Distinguish zero-order and first-order kinetics with an example. First-order kinetics eliminate a constant fraction per unit time, producing an exponential concentration–time curve and a straight line on a semi-log plot; half-life is constant. Zero-order kinetics occur when elimination is saturated: a constant amount is removed per unit time regardless of concentration, producing a straight concentration–time line and a curved semi-log plot; half-life is not constant and decreases as concentration falls. Examples include ethanol, phenytoin at high concentration and salicylate overdose. What is the difference between mean, median and mode, and when is each preferred? Mean — arithmetic average; appropriate for normally distributed data. Median — middle value; preferred for skewed or ordinal data (e.g. pain scores, length of stay). Mode — most frequent value; used for categorical data. Reporting median (IQR) is more honest than mean (SD) for ICU length-of-stay because of long-tailed distributions. Recognise the canonical graph shapes (linear, exponential decay/rise, sigmoid, hyperbolic) and the equations behind them Apply the time constant (τ) and half-life (t½) to first-order processes such as drug elimination and pre-oxygenation wash-in Convert between time constants and half-lives (t½ = 0.693 × τ) and predict completion at 1τ, 3τ and 5τ Use logarithmic scales (pH, pKa, decibels) to interpret order-of-magnitude changes in clinical variables Explain why cooperative binding produces a sigmoid curve (Hill coefficient) and recognise it in the ODC and dose-response relationships A 70 kg adult has an FRC of 2.5 L and is pre-oxygenated at 8 L/min via a tight-fitting mask. Estimate when end-tidal O₂ will reach 95%. τ = Volume / Flow = 2.5 L / 8 L·min⁻¹ = 0.31 min ≈ 19 s. Wash-in is a negative exponential rise: 1 τ → 63%, 3 τ → 95%, 5 τ → 99%. Time to ~95% ≈ 3 τ = 3 × 19 s ≈ 57 s. End-tidal O₂ reaches ~95% after roughly one minute (3 time constants). This underpins the Association of Anaesthetists s offset by taking its context-sensitive half-time (CSHT) of ~3 min after a 4-hour infusion (Ultiva SmPC) and converting it to a single time constant. Critique this approach and contrast it with a true single-compartment example. Naïve calculation: τ = t½ / 0.693 = 3 / 0.693 ≈ 4.3 min, predicting ~95% decline at 3τ ≈ 13 min. Why this is wrong: remifentanil is described by a 3-compartment PK model. Plasma concentration after stopping an infusion is a sum of exponentials (rapid, slow and terminal phases), not a single first-order decay. A true single-compartment exponential — and therefore a setting where one τ is appropriate — is nitrogen wash-out during pre-oxygenation (τ = FRC / alveolar ventilation), or the discharge of a defibrillator capacitor (τ = RC). Recognising the shape of a graph — linear, exponential, sigmoid, hyperbolic — allows you to predict how a system will behave when variables change. This topic covers the key mathematical relationships encountered in anaesthesia and intensive care, with clinical examples for each.

First order

Elimination rate is proportional to concentration, so a constant fraction is removed per unit time. Half-life is constant. Concentration falls exponentially on an arithmetic plot and forms a straight line on a semi-log plot.

Zero order

The elimination pathway is saturated, so a constant amount is removed per unit time independently of concentration. Half-life is not constant and becomes shorter as concentration falls. The arithmetic concentration–time plot is linear; the semi-log plot is curved.

# Gas Laws Boyle's, Charles', Dalton's, Henry's laws and their clinical applications Step-by-step reasoning Pick the right relationship. Reversible adiabatic process for an ideal gas: T₂ = T₁ × (P₂ / P₁) Compute the exponent. T₂ = 293 × (1 / 138) 78 K (≈ −195 °C) Reality check. True adiabatic conditions never hold — heat conducts in from the cylinder wall and ambient air, so observed surface cooling is only ~30–50 °C. Frost on the cylinder body is the visual sign. Common traps Using °C in T₁ — the relation is only valid in Confusing this with Joule–Thomson cooling — adiabatic expansion does external work; J–T throttling is isenthalpic with no external work. Forgetting that for a real cylinder the process is not reversible, so the prediction over-estimates cooling. Two-phase storage. N₂O at 20 °C is below its Tc (36.5 °C) — the cylinder contains liquid + vapour at the saturated vapour pressure (~52 bar). Latent heat of vaporisation. ~376 kJ/kg is taken from the liquid and cylinder wall as withdrawn vapour is replaced by evaporation, cooling the cylinder. Joule–Thomson cooling at the regulator. ΔT ≈ μ × ΔP ≈ 0.25 × (52 − 4) ≈ 12 °C drop across the regulator. Frost forms at the liquid–vapour interface. The wall there is coldest because that is where evaporation is occurring; ambient water vapour deposits as frost. The height of the frost line ≈ remaining liquid contents. Estimating N₂O contents from the pressure gauge — pressure stays at SVP until the very last liquid evaporates. Forgetting that delivered pressure during fast discharge (cylinder cools → SVP drops). Thinking the cylinder cools because of work done against the regulator — the dominant mechanism in heavy use is latent heat, with J–T cooling on top. Apply Dalton's law to derive the alveolar gas equation. PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (Patm − PH₂O) − PaCO₂ / R. PAO₂ = 0.21 × (460 − 47) − 40 / 0.8 = 0.21 × 413 − 50. ~37 mmHg . (Sea level for comparison: 0.21 × 713 − 50 ≈ 100 mmHg.) Clinical implication. A PAO₂ of 37 mmHg sits on the steep part of the haemoglobin dissociation curve — significant desaturation. Supplemental O₂ is essential at altitude. Forgetting to subtract PH₂O 47 mmHg — fully saturated alveolar gas is humidified at body temperature. Using barometric pressure in kPa with PaCO₂ in mmHg — keep units consistent. Assuming hyperventilation alone fully compensates — even with PaCO₂ down to 25, PAO₂ rises only to ~55 mmHg at 4000 m on FiO₂ 0.21. Boyle's law , increasing ambient pressure compresses gas-filled spaces, so an untreated pneumothorax is dangerous and failure to equalise the middle ear or sinuses causes barotrauma. Gas density also rises, increasing airway and ventilator resistance Dalton's law predicts the marked rise in inspired and arterial oxygen partial pressure. Henry's law predicts that more oxygen dissolves directly in plasma as its partial pressure rises, increasing oxygen carriage independently of haemoglobin. Hyperoxia causes vasoconstriction while preserving tissue oxygen delivery and supports angiogenesis/neovascularisation and oxygen-dependent antimicrobial function. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ ). This is clinically relevant to the function of bellows ventilators, compression of gas in closed spaces (e.g., pneumothorax, air emboli), and the behaviour of gas cylinders. Clinical Application V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ ). Temperature must be measured in Kelvin. This explains why gas volumes measured at room temperature differ from those at body temperature. P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ ). As temperature rises, gas molecules move faster and strike the rigid container walls more frequently and forcefully, raising the measured pressure. Constant T → P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (Boyle's law) Constant P → V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (Charles' law) Constant V → P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ (Gay-Lussac's law) Pₜₒₜₐₗ = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + ... ). The partial pressure of each gas is proportional to its fractional concentration. oxygen partial pressure (not the arterial PaO₂). Understanding partial pressures is essential for calculating safe FiO₂ at altitude and during hyperbaric therapy. PV = nRT unifies Boyle's, Charles', Gay-Lussac's critical temperature of a substance is the temperature above which it cannot be liquefied by the application of pressure alone, no matter how great. The critical pressure Key values for anaesthetic gases critical temperature −118 °C, critical pressure 50 bar Nitrous oxide: critical temperature 36.5 °C, critical pressure 72 bar Carbon dioxide: critical temperature 31 °C, critical pressure 74 bar critical temperature −141 °C (pseudo-critical, as it is a mixture) Why N₂O cylinder pressure is constant its critical temperature of 36.5 °C. When it is compressed into a cylinder it partially liquefies, so the cylinder contains a two-phase system: a pool of liquid N₂O at the bottom in equilibrium with N₂O vapour above it. The pressure of the vapour phase is the saturated vapour pressure (SVP) of N₂O, which depends only on temperature — taken as ~52 bar at 20 °C in UK anaesthetic teaching (equation-of-state models give 52–53 bar, which is what the interactive isotherm below displays). (full weight − tare weight), not by the pressure gauge. Cylinders are filled to a filling ratio (mass of N₂O / mass of water that would fill the cylinder) of 0.75 in temperate climates and 0.67 in the tropics, to leave vapour headspace and prevent dangerous pressure rises if the cylinder warms. As N₂O vaporises, latent heat of vaporisation cools the cylinder and the vapour pressure (and hence delivered pressure) actually during heavy use — frost may form on the outside of the cylinder. How to read the diagram Sub-critical isotherms (T < Tc). Starting from large volume (right) and compressing the gas, pressure rises along the vapour branch until it meets the dashed dome at the saturated-vapour point. Further compression occurs at constant pressure (the horizontal tie-line) as vapour condenses to liquid — this is the two-phase region. Once all the vapour is liquid, pressure rises almost vertically because liquids are nearly incompressible. The critical isotherm (T = Tc, 36.5 °C for N₂O). The horizontal tie-line shrinks to a single point — the critical point — where the densities of liquid and vapour become equal and the meniscus disappears (critical opalescence). The isotherm has a point of inflection here with (∂P/∂V) = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²) Super-critical isotherms (T > Tc). No phase change is possible at any pressure. The substance exists as a single fluid phase whose density rises smoothly with pressure. At high T the curve tends to PV = constant (Boyle's law). The dashed dome is the locus of all saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour points; its apex is the critical point. Inside the dome, liquid and vapour coexist; outside it, only one phase exists. Pseudo-critical temperature is defined: the temperature below which the components of the mixture may separate into two phases. Two clinically important examples: Air (≈79 % N₂, 21 % O₂): pseudo-critical temperature −141 °C — the temperature below which air, if compressed, can be liquefied as a single mixed fluid. This is exploited industrially in the fractional distillation of liquid air to separate its components such as oxygen and nitrogen for medical use. Entonox (50 % N₂O / 50 % O₂): −5.5 °C at 137 bar (the cylinder pressure). Below this, the N₂O can liquefy out and pool at the bottom of the cylinder, leaving an O₂-rich gas to be delivered first and a hypoxic N₂O-rich mixture later — the so-called Poynting effect failure . Cylinders left in cold environments must be re-warmed (≥10 °C for at least 2 h, or 24 h with inversion) and inverted three times before clinical use. adiabatic expansion (work done by the gas as it pushes back its surroundings, no heat exchange) and the Joule–Thomson effect (isenthalpic throttling through a restriction with no external work). Both produce cooling on cylinder discharge but for different physical reasons. process exchanges no heat with the surroundings (Q = 0). For an ideal gas the first law gives ΔU = −W; the gas does work at the expense of its own internal energy, so its temperature falls. For a reversible adiabatic process: = constant    and    T₁V₁ = T₂V₂ cryotherapy probes (rapid expansion of high-pressure gas at the probe tip cools tissue to −70 °C or below for ablation of tumours, arrhythmic foci or skin lesions), and the cooling of an O₂ cylinder during fast discharge The Joule–Thomson (throttling) effect (H = constant). For an ideal gas H depends only on T, so there is no temperature change. For a gas there is, because of the work done against (or by) intermolecular forces: = (∂T/∂P) > 0: gas on expansion. μ < 0: gas > 0). At very high temperatures, repulsive forces dominate; the gas warms on expansion (μ < 0). The temperature at which μ = 0 — the dividing line between cooling and warming — is the inversion temperature Inversion T (max) Behaviour at room T (293 K) on throttling ~1500 K Cools strongly (~0.25 K per bar) Cools strongly — used in cryotherapy ~620 K Cools modestly ~760 K Cools modestly (~0.31 K per bar) ~205 K — must be pre-cooled below 205 K to liquefy ~45 K — must be pre-cooled to liquefy (key to MRI cryostat design) Clinical Application — H₂ and He on throttling at 20 °C. To liquefy them they must first be pre-cooled below the inversion temperature. This is why MRI cryostats use liquid helium pre-cooled through a multi-stage cascade — and why a sudden quench of an MRI magnet vents enormous volumes of warming He gas rather than a self-cooling jet. states that, at constant temperature, the amount of a given gas that dissolves in a given type and volume of liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas in equilibrium with the liquid (C = k·P, where k is the gas- and solvent-specific solubility coefficient). It underpins oxygen and carbon dioxide transport in blood, alveolar uptake of volatile anaesthetic agents, and the behaviour of dissolved gases under altered ambient pressure. nitrogen narcosis during deep diving reflects increased PN₂ driving more nitrogen into neural tissue; pulmonary oxygen toxicity at prolonged high FiO₂ or under hyperbaric conditions reflects the elevated dissolved O₂ load; and decompression illness occurs when dissolved N₂ comes out of solution as bubbles when ambient pressure falls too rapidly. Anaesthetic Application Adiabatic emptying of an O₂ cylinder The reversible-adiabatic prediction is ~78 K (−195 °C). In practice heat conduction limits surface cooling to ~30–50 °C, but it explains the frost on a rapidly discharged O₂ cylinder. Frost line on an N₂O cylinder during heavy use Latent heat of vaporisation cools the cylinder where evaporation occurs (the liquid–vapour interface), and J–T cooling at the regulator adds ~12 °C drop. The frost line marks the level of remaining liquid — the only reliable visual gauge of N₂O contents. Alveolar oxygen tension at altitude PAO₂ ≈ 37 mmHg, well below the safe lower limit. Supplemental oxygen, hyperventilation, or descent are required. The gas laws describe the relationships between pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas under defined conditions.

This is clinically relevant to the function of bellows ventilators, compression of gas in closed spaces (e.g., pneumothorax, air emboli), and the behaviour of gas cylinders.

    Clinical Application

    A pneumothorax at altitude: as atmospheric pressure decreases, Boyle > At constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂). Temperature must be measured in Kelvin. This explains why gas volumes measured at room temperature differ from those at body temperature.

    Spirometry measurements taken at room temperature (ATPS) must be corrected to body conditions (BTPS) using Charles > At constant volume, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂). As temperature rises, gas molecules move faster and strike the rigid container walls more frequently and forcefully, raising the measured pressure.

    The pressure inside a full oxygen cylinder rises if the cylinder is stored in a hot environment, and falls if it is cooled. This is why cylinder pressures should be interpreted in the context of ambient temperature, and why cylinders must be protected from fire — a heated cylinder can develop dangerously high internal pressures and rupture.

    (P₁ × V₁) / T₁ = (P₂ × V₂) / T₂

    Each individual gas law is a special case in which one of the three variables is held constant:

      The combined gas law is the practical bridge to the ideal gas equation (PV = nRT): when the amount of gas (n) is also allowed to vary, the constant of proportionality becomes nR. Temperature must always be in Kelvin, and pressures must be absolute (not gauge) for the relationship to hold.

      Converting a measured gas volume between conditions — for example, expired gas volumes measured at ATPS being corrected to BTPS or STPD for metabolic calculations — relies directly on the combined gas law.

      In a mixture of gases, the total pressure equals the sum of the partial pressures of each constituent gas (Pₜₒₜₐₗ = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + ...). The partial pressure of each gas is proportional to its fractional concentration.

      Calculating alveolar oxygen tension using the alveolar gas equation depends on Dalton > The ideal gas equation PV = nRT unifies Boyle s laws (V ∝ n at constant T and P, which supplies the molar term n) into a single expression, where P = pressure, V = volume, n = number of moles, R = universal gas constant (8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹), and T = absolute temperature. Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressures and low temperatures, described by the van der Waals equation.

      The critical temperature of a substance is the temperature above which it cannot be liquefied by the application of pressure alone, no matter how great. The critical pressure is the pressure required to liquefy the gas at exactly its critical temperature. Above the critical temperature, the substance can only exist as a gas; below it, gas and liquid phases can coexist if the pressure is high enough.

      Key values for anaesthetic gases

        Why N₂O cylinder pressure is constant

        At a typical room temperature of 20 °C, N₂O is below its critical temperature of 36.5 °C. When it is compressed into a cylinder it partially liquefies, so the cylinder contains a two-phase system: a pool of liquid N₂O at the bottom in equilibrium with N₂O vapour above it. The pressure of the vapour phase is the saturated vapour pressure (SVP) of N₂O, which depends only on temperature — taken as ~52 bar at 20 °C in UK anaesthetic teaching (equation-of-state models give 52–53 bar, which is what the interactive isotherm below displays).

        As gas is drawn off, more liquid evaporates to replace it and the vapour pressure stays constant. The gauge therefore continues to read ~52 bar throughout the working life of the cylinder, even as the contents progressively diminish. Only once the very last drop of liquid has evaporated does the cylinder behave as a simple gas reservoir — and at that point the pressure falls rapidly as the remaining vapour is consumed (typically when ~20% of the original mass remains).

        By contrast, O₂ has a critical temperature of −118 °C, far below room temperature. It cannot be liquefied by pressure alone at 20 °C and is stored as a compressed gas only. The cylinder pressure therefore obeys Boyle > The contents of an N₂O cylinder are determined by weighing (full weight − tare weight), not by the pressure gauge. Cylinders are filled to a filling ratio (mass of N₂O / mass of water that would fill the cylinder) of 0.75 in temperate climates and 0.67 in the tropics, to leave vapour headspace and prevent dangerous pressure rises if the cylinder warms. As N₂O vaporises, latent heat of vaporisation cools the cylinder and the vapour pressure (and hence delivered pressure) actually falls during heavy use — frost may form on the outside of the cylinder.

      How to read the diagram

      • Sub-critical isotherms (T < Tc). Starting from large volume (right) and compressing the gas, pressure rises along the vapour branch until it meets the dashed dome at the saturated-vapour point. Further compression occurs at constant pressure (the horizontal tie-line) as vapour condenses to liquid — this is the two-phase region. Once all the vapour is liquid, pressure rises almost vertically because liquids are nearly incompressible.
      • The critical isotherm (T = Tc, 36.5 °C for N₂O). The horizontal tie-line shrinks to a single point — the critical point — where the densities of liquid and vapour become equal and the meniscus disappears (critical opalescence). The isotherm has a point of inflection here with (∂P/∂V)T = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)T = 0.
      • Super-critical isotherms (T > Tc). No phase change is possible at any pressure. The substance exists as a single fluid phase whose density rises smoothly with pressure. case_bank.title: Diathermy, a pacing wire and an electrical alarm
case_bank.text:
Case: Diathermy, a pacing wire and an electrical alarm (Equipment safety, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with a temporary transvenous pacing wire is having emergency abdominal surgery. The line isolation monitor alarms as monopolar diathermy is used.
Presentation: The theatre team asks whether surgery can continue. The patient is haemodynamically dependent on pacing and the return electrode is on the contralateral thigh.
Stage 1 — Define the hazard
  Question: Why is this patient a class CF/microshock risk?
  Model answer: A conductor in direct contact with myocardium concentrates current over a tiny area, so currents as small as around 50–100 µA can cause ventricular fibrillation.
  Model answer: Macroshock thresholds are far higher (mains-frequency current of about 50–100 mA), so ordinary body protection is not enough.
  Model answer: Only class CF equipment, with an isolated and current-limited patient circuit, should be connected to intracardiac conductors.
Stage 2 — Interpret the alarm
  Question: What does the line isolation monitor actually indicate?
  Model answer: An isolated power supply has no deliberate connection to earth, so a single fault does not create a shock path.
  Model answer: The monitor warns that leakage current to earth has risen — the isolation is degraded, not that a shock is occurring.
  Model answer: Response is to identify and remove the most recently connected or faulty device rather than to silence the alarm.
Stage 3 — Make the operation safe
  Question: How do you proceed?
  Model answer: Prefer bipolar diathermy, keep the return plate large, well applied and positioned so current does not traverse the heart, and use short bursts.
  Model answer: Insulate exposed pacing terminals, avoid touching them, and have the pacing box, external pacing and defibrillation immediately available.
  Model answer: Monitor rhythm continuously, anticipate diathermy interference with the ECG, and plan for pacing inhibition or reprogramming needs with cardiology.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Electrical injury depends on current density, duration, frequency and pathway. Mains frequency (50 Hz) is the most arrhythmogenic; diathermy uses radiofrequency currents around 0.3–3 MHz, which do not stimulate excitable tissue but generate heat at high current density. An intracardiac conductor bypasses skin impedance entirely, converting a trivial leakage current into a lethal one.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Combine equipment measures (class CF devices, isolated supply, residual current devices where used, regular electrical testing) with technique (bipolar diathermy, correct plate siting, avoiding a heart-crossing current path). Keep defibrillation and external pacing at hand, and document rhythm and pacing thresholds before and after. Investigate the alarm with the theatre team and biomedical engineering rather than continuing blindly.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not confuse macroshock and microshock thresholds, and do not describe an isolated power supply as preventing all shock. Explain that isolation converts a first fault into a warning rather than an injury.
Take-home: An intracardiac conductor turns microamps into a lethal risk: use class CF equipment, bipolar diathermy and a current path away from the heart, and treat an isolation alarm as a fault to find.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: electrical safety (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx035)

case_bank.title: Anaesthesia in the MRI scanner
case_bank.text:
Case: Anaesthesia in the MRI scanner (Imaging & radiation, Intermediate)
Patient: A child needs general anaesthesia for a 3 T MRI brain scan. A non-MR-conditional syringe pump has been brought to the scanner door and the patient has an unlabelled implant.
Presentation: The radiographer asks you to proceed quickly because the list is delayed.
Stage 1 — Name the physical hazards
  Question: Which fields cause which risks?
  Model answer: The always-on static field causes projectile injury, implant torque and displacement, and disables non-MR-safe equipment.
  Model answer: Radiofrequency pulses deposit energy, quantified as specific absorption rate, and can heat tissue, loops of wire and ECG leads, causing burns.
  Model answer: Rapidly switching gradients generate acoustic noise (often over 100 dB) and peripheral nerve stimulation; cryogen loss during a quench causes asphyxiation risk from displaced oxygen.
Stage 2 — Apply the safety system
  Question: How is access controlled and screening performed?
  Model answer: Zones I–IV restrict access, with the scanner room (zone IV) entered only after checklist-based screening by trained staff.
  Model answer: Every implant and device must be documented as MR safe, MR conditional or MR unsafe; unlabelled implants are treated as unsafe until identified.
  Model answer: Only MR-conditional monitoring, pumps and airway equipment enter zone IV, with long extension lines for infusions and remote-controlled ventilation.
Stage 3 — Plan the anaesthetic
  Question: What practical anaesthetic issues follow?
  Model answer: Remote and partly obscured patient access means secured airway, capnography, reliable IV access and a clear evacuation plan to a resuscitation area outside zone IV.
  Model answer: Provide ear protection, temperature care and dose-appropriate depth for immobility, and remove loops from cables and leads.
  Model answer: Rehearse quench and cardiac arrest responses; resuscitation takes place outside the scanner room.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: MRI safety follows directly from physics: a permanent superconducting static field, pulsed radiofrequency excitation and switched gradients each create a distinct hazard. Field strength increases signal but also projectile force and radiofrequency energy deposition, so 3 T scanning demands stricter screening than 1.5 T. Contrast agents raise separate concerns, with gadolinium-based agent choice restricted by renal function.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use a documented screening checklist for patient, staff and equipment; never rely on verbal assurance under time pressure. Anaesthetise where possible outside the magnet or use MR-conditional systems with waveguide-passed lines. Monitor temperature and depth, protect hearing, keep the resuscitation trolley outside zone IV and know who holds the quench button and evacuation responsibility.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not say the magnet is 'switched off between scans' — the static field is permanent. Distinguish MR safe, MR conditional and MR unsafe precisely, and mention SAR heating as a burn mechanism, not just projectile risk.
Take-home: The static field is always on: screen every person, implant and device, use only MR-conditional equipment in zone IV, and resuscitate outside the scanner room.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: MRI physics and safety (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.04.004); Assoc Anaesth 2021: MRI (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.15517)

case_bank.title: Diathermy, a pacing wire and an electrical alarm
case_bank.text:
Case: Diathermy, a pacing wire and an electrical alarm (Equipment safety, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with a temporary transvenous pacing wire is having emergency abdominal surgery. The line isolation monitor alarms as monopolar diathermy is used.
Presentation: The theatre team asks whether surgery can continue. The patient is haemodynamically dependent on pacing and the return electrode is on the contralateral thigh.
Stage 1 — Define the hazard
  Question: Why is this patient a class CF/microshock risk?
  Model answer: A conductor in direct contact with myocardium concentrates current over a tiny area, so currents as small as around 50–100 µA can cause ventricular fibrillation.
  Model answer: Macroshock thresholds are far higher (mains-frequency current of about 50–100 mA), so ordinary body protection is not enough.
  Model answer: Only class CF equipment, with an isolated and current-limited patient circuit, should be connected to intracardiac conductors.
Stage 2 — Interpret the alarm
  Question: What does the line isolation monitor actually indicate?
  Model answer: An isolated power supply has no deliberate connection to earth, so a single fault does not create a shock path.
  Model answer: The monitor warns that leakage current to earth has risen — the isolation is degraded, not that a shock is occurring.
  Model answer: Response is to identify and remove the most recently connected or faulty device rather than to silence the alarm.
Stage 3 — Make the operation safe
  Question: How do you proceed?
  Model answer: Prefer bipolar diathermy, keep the return plate large, well applied and positioned so current does not traverse the heart, and use short bursts.
  Model answer: Insulate exposed pacing terminals, avoid touching them, and have the pacing box, external pacing and defibrillation immediately available.
  Model answer: Monitor rhythm continuously, anticipate diathermy interference with the ECG, and plan for pacing inhibition or reprogramming needs with cardiology.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Electrical injury depends on current density, duration, frequency and pathway. Mains frequency (50 Hz) is the most arrhythmogenic; diathermy uses radiofrequency currents around 0.3–3 MHz, which do not stimulate excitable tissue but generate heat at high current density. An intracardiac conductor bypasses skin impedance entirely, converting a trivial leakage current into a lethal one.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Combine equipment measures (class CF devices, isolated supply, residual current devices where used, regular electrical testing) with technique (bipolar diathermy, correct plate siting, avoiding a heart-crossing current path). Keep defibrillation and external pacing at hand, and document rhythm and pacing thresholds before and after. Investigate the alarm with the theatre team and biomedical engineering rather than continuing blindly.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not confuse macroshock and microshock thresholds, and do not describe an isolated power supply as preventing all shock. Explain that isolation converts a first fault into a warning rather than an injury.
Take-home: An intracardiac conductor turns microamps into a lethal risk: use class CF equipment, bipolar diathermy and a current path away from the heart, and treat an isolation alarm as a fault to find.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: electrical safety (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx035)

# Defibrillation & Pacing Monophasic vs biphasic waveforms, transthoracic impedance, pacemaker modes, and EMI Monophasic damped sinusoidal (MDS) waveforms deliver current in a single direction. They require higher energies (up to 360 J for VF) and do not compensate for varying transthoracic impedance. They have been largely superseded by biphasic technology. Biphasic waveforms reverse polarity during the shock, delivering current first in one direction then the other. Two subtypes exist: biphasic truncated exponential (BTE) rectilinear biphasic (RLB) . Both achieve equivalent or superior defibrillation success at lower energies (120–200 J), causing less myocardial injury and post-shock ST changes. impedance compensation — the waveform automatically adjusts its duration and voltage based on measured transthoracic impedance, ensuring consistent current delivery regardless of patient characteristics. devices — manufacturer guidance always takes precedence. For monophasic devices, use 200 J for AF and consider 360 J early; double the listed biphasic dose as a rough guide for other rhythms. First shock (biphasic) Atrial fibrillation 120–150 J synchronised Escalate to maximum (typically 200 J), then consider AP pad position Atrial flutter / SVT 70–120 J synchronised Lower thresholds — many flutters cardiovert at 50–100 J Stable VT with pulse Escalate stepwise to maximum biphasic output Polymorphic VT (pulse) / unsynchronised Treat as VF — defibrillate 120–200 J first shock, then 150–360 J per device guidance VF / pulseless VT 120–150 J unsynchronised Subsequent shocks 150–200 J (or up to 360 J biphasic per manufacturer) Paediatric (synch or defib) 1 J/kg synch; 4 J/kg defib Synchronised cardioversion may be escalated to 2 J/kg Practical points: sedate or anaesthetise the conscious patient (propofol ± fentanyl, or short-acting induction with airway support). Confirm the marker is on the R wave — re-enable sync after every shock (most devices revert to unsynchronised mode automatically). For refractory AF, consider anteroposterior pad position , ensure full expiration, firm pad pressure (~8 kg), and exclude reversible factors (electrolytes, hypoxia, thyroid). Anticoagulation status must be confirmed for AF >48 h or unknown duration before elective DCCV. but ranging from 15–150 Ω. Only approximately 4% of delivered current actually traverses the heart — the remainder follows alternative pathways through chest wall muscle, lung, and other structures. increase impedance include obesity, hyperinflated lungs (COPD, inspiration), poor pad-skin contact, small pad size, and excessive chest hair. Factors that reduce impedance include self-adhesive gel pads, firm application pressure (~25 lb), defibrillation during expiration, larger pad surface area, and successive shocks (transthoracic impedance falls with repeated defibrillation). position: one pad below the right clavicle (right sternal edge) and one at the left mid-axillary line (V6 position). Alternative positions include anteroposterior, which may be preferred in certain circumstances. NASPE/BPEG Generic (NBG) code , a five-position system describing chamber paced (I), chamber sensed (II), response to sensing (III), rate modulation (IV), and multisite pacing (V). Letters used include A (atrium), V (ventricle), D (dual), O (none), I (inhibited), T (triggered), and R (rate-responsive). (ventricular demand) is the most common single-chamber mode — it paces and senses the ventricle, inhibiting output when intrinsic activity is detected. Its main limitation is pacemaker syndrome : ventricular pacing without AV synchrony permits atrial contraction against closed mitral and tricuspid valves, reducing cardiac output and producing fatigue, dizziness, syncope, hypotension and prominent neck pulsations (cannon waves in the JVP). Upgrading to a dual-chamber system restores AV synchrony and usually resolves it. is the most physiological mode, pacing and sensing both chambers to maintain AV synchrony, and is the mode of choice for complete heart block. asynchronous mode (VOO or DOO) — fixed-rate pacing without sensing. This eliminates the risk of EMI-induced inhibition during surgery. The magnet rate also provides information about battery status (rate decreases as battery depletes). include haemodynamically significant symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to drugs, high-grade AV block after myocardial infarction, drug toxicity, and a bridge to recovery or permanent pacing. Transcutaneous pacing Apply anterolateral or anteroposterior multifunction pads, select demand mode and a rate around 60–80 min⁻¹, then increase current from about 50 mA until electrical and mechanical capture occurs (often 50–100 mA). Confirm a pulse for every paced complex; provide sedation and analgesia because skeletal-muscle contraction is painful. Limitations are discomfort, artefact and failure to capture. Transvenous pacing Insert via the internal jugular or subclavian vein and advance the electrode to the right-ventricular apex under fluoroscopy, intracavitary ECG or pressure-waveform guidance. A typical initial mode is VVI at 70 min⁻¹; set output above the measured capture threshold and sensitivity below the sensed R-wave amplitude. Complications include arrhythmia, failure to sense/capture, pneumothorax, cardiac perforation/tamponade, infection and venous thrombosis. Transcutaneous pacing is a rapid bridge, not a substitute for prompt definitive planning when ongoing pacing is required Surgical diathermy is the most significant source of EMI in the operating theatre. Monopolar diathermy poses the greatest risk as current passes through the body between the active electrode and return pad. EMI can cause inappropriate (pacemaker interprets diathermy as cardiac activity and withholds pacing) or inappropriate tracking (device interprets EMI as atrial activity and paces the ventricle rapidly). , anti-tachycardia therapies must be disabled intra-operatively (via magnet application or reprogramming) to prevent inappropriate shock delivery triggered by diathermy artefact. External defibrillation pads must be applied before disabling the ICD. bipolar diathermy first; consider a harmonic scalpel when monopolar energy is otherwise required; if conventional monopolar diathermy is essential, use the lowest effective energy in short intermittent bursts. Position the return pad so the current path does not cross the CIED and keep the active electrode and cables away from the generator temporary, device-specific intervention , not a universal off switch. Many pacemakers pace asynchronously, some have a programmable or absent response, while an ICD magnet usually suspends anti-tachycardia therapy without changing bradycardia pacing. Pre-operative identification, interrogation and a documented pacing-team plan are therefore essential; reprogram when the magnet response is unknown or unreliable. mechanical capture while diathermy obscures the ECG. External pacing/defibrillation must be immediately available, and all altered therapies must be restored with post-operative interrogation. Energy delivered by a defibrillator capacitor Stored energy is 400 J. The 'selected energy' on the front panel (e.g. 200 J) is the energy actually delivered into a 50 Ω test load — only a small fraction (≈4%) reaches the heart, which is why pad contact, expiration phase and gel use matter so much. Pacemaker patient for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy Pre-op interrogation, intra-op magnet (DOO), bipolar diathermy where feasible with the return pad on the thigh, defib pads attached, plethysmographic confirmation of perfusion, and post-op reinterrogation. ICD patients additionally need anti-tachycardia therapies disabled before incision. Transcutaneous pacing

Apply anterolateral or anteroposterior multifunction pads, select demand mode and a rate around 60–80 min⁻¹, then increase current from about 50 mA until electrical and mechanical capture occurs (often 50–100 mA). Confirm a pulse for every paced complex; provide sedation and analgesia because skeletal-muscle contraction is painful. Limitations are discomfort, artefact and failure to capture.

Insert via the internal jugular or subclavian vein and advance the electrode to the right-ventricular apex under fluoroscopy, intracavitary ECG or pressure-waveform guidance. A typical initial mode is VVI at 70 min⁻¹; set output above the measured capture threshold and sensitivity below the sensed R-wave amplitude. Complications include arrhythmia, failure to sense/capture, pneumothorax, cardiac perforation/tamponade, infection and venous thrombosis.

case_bank.title: Diathermy, a pacing wire and an electrical alarm
case_bank.text:
Case: Diathermy, a pacing wire and an electrical alarm (Equipment safety, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with a temporary transvenous pacing wire is having emergency abdominal surgery. The line isolation monitor alarms as monopolar diathermy is used.
Presentation: The theatre team asks whether surgery can continue. The patient is haemodynamically dependent on pacing and the return electrode is on the contralateral thigh.
Stage 1 — Define the hazard
  Question: Why is this patient a class CF/microshock risk?
  Model answer: A conductor in direct contact with myocardium concentrates current over a tiny area, so currents as small as around 50–100 µA can cause ventricular fibrillation.
  Model answer: Macroshock thresholds are far higher (mains-frequency current of about 50–100 mA), so ordinary body protection is not enough.
  Model answer: Only class CF equipment, with an isolated and current-limited patient circuit, should be connected to intracardiac conductors.
Stage 2 — Interpret the alarm
  Question: What does the line isolation monitor actually indicate?
  Model answer: An isolated power supply has no deliberate connection to earth, so a single fault does not create a shock path.
  Model answer: The monitor warns that leakage current to earth has risen — the isolation is degraded, not that a shock is occurring.
  Model answer: Response is to identify and remove the most recently connected or faulty device rather than to silence the alarm.
Stage 3 — Make the operation safe
  Question: How do you proceed?
  Model answer: Prefer bipolar diathermy, keep the return plate large, well applied and positioned so current does not traverse the heart, and use short bursts.
  Model answer: Insulate exposed pacing terminals, avoid touching them, and have the pacing box, external pacing and defibrillation immediately available.
  Model answer: Monitor rhythm continuously, anticipate diathermy interference with the ECG, and plan for pacing inhibition or reprogramming needs with cardiology.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Electrical injury depends on current density, duration, frequency and pathway. Mains frequency (50 Hz) is the most arrhythmogenic; diathermy uses radiofrequency currents around 0.3–3 MHz, which do not stimulate excitable tissue but generate heat at high current density. An intracardiac conductor bypasses skin impedance entirely, converting a trivial leakage current into a lethal one.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Combine equipment measures (class CF devices, isolated supply, residual current devices where used, regular electrical testing) with technique (bipolar diathermy, correct plate siting, avoiding a heart-crossing current path). Keep defibrillation and external pacing at hand, and document rhythm and pacing thresholds before and after. Investigate the alarm with the theatre team and biomedical engineering rather than continuing blindly.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not confuse macroshock and microshock thresholds, and do not describe an isolated power supply as preventing all shock. Explain that isolation converts a first fault into a warning rather than an injury.
Take-home: An intracardiac conductor turns microamps into a lethal risk: use class CF equipment, bipolar diathermy and a current path away from the heart, and treat an isolation alarm as a fault to find.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: electrical safety (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx035)

The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane. Specular reflection occurs at smooth surfaces (mirrors) where parallel rays remain parallel; diffuse reflection occurs at rough surfaces where rays scatter in all directions. reflectance pulse oximetry uses reflected rather than transmitted light — the LED and photodetector are on the same side of the tissue. This allows measurement at sites where transmission is impractical (forehead, oesophagus). The principles are identical to transmission oximetry, but the optical path is different. is the bending of light as it passes between media of different optical density. Snell's law (n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂) quantifies this: light bends toward the normal when entering a denser medium (higher refractive index n). The refractive index is defined as n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium. critical angle total internal reflection (TIR) . At this wavelength, absorption depends only on total haemoglobin concentration, independent of oxygenation — it is used for calibration and total Hb estimation. Pulse oximeter reading in carbon monoxide poisoning SpO₂ is falsely reassuring because the ratio of COHb absorbances at 660 nm and 940 nm mimics that of HbO₂, so the two-wavelength algorithm reports COHb as oxyhaemoglobin. case_bank.title: Airway fire during laser laryngeal surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Airway fire during laser laryngeal surgery (Equipment safety, Advanced)
Patient: During CO₂ laser resection of a laryngeal lesion, a flash and smoke appear in the surgical field while the patient is ventilated with 60% oxygen.
Presentation: The tube is in situ. The surgeon has stopped lasing and the team looks to you.
Stage 1 — Prevent it first
  Question: What reduces the risk before the laser is fired?
  Model answer: Minimise the oxidiser: use the lowest tolerated FiO₂, ideally under 30%, and avoid nitrous oxide, which supports combustion.
  Model answer: Use laser-resistant tubes or jet ventilation, saline-filled cuffs, wet swabs and matt instruments to limit reflection.
  Model answer: Apply theatre-wide laser controls: signage, restricted access, wavelength-specific eye protection, smoke evacuation and a trained laser safety officer.
Stage 2 — Manage the fire
  Question: What is the immediate sequence?
  Model answer: Stop lasing, stop gas flow and disconnect the circuit, remove the burning tube and any flammable material, and flood the field with saline.
  Model answer: Re-establish ventilation on air, then reintubate and inspect the airway with bronchoscopy for thermal injury and debris.
  Model answer: Continue with humidified oxygen as required, consider critical care admission, and treat inhalational injury and oedema.
Stage 3 — Close the loop
  Question: What follows the immediate management?
  Model answer: Document the event, retain equipment for examination and report through local governance and national incident systems.
  Model answer: Debrief the team and inform the patient and family openly about what happened and the follow-up plan.
  Model answer: Review protocols: FiO₂ limits, tube choice, cuff protection and communication before lasing.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Laser output combines high irradiance with a specific wavelength. CO₂ lasers (10.6 µm) are absorbed by water and cut superficially, while Nd:YAG (1064 µm) penetrates deeper — determining both tissue effect and eye-protection requirements. A fire needs fuel (tube, swabs, drapes), an oxidiser (oxygen or nitrous oxide) and an ignition source (the laser); anaesthetic control is mainly over the oxidiser and the fuel.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Rehearse the fire drill so the sequence is automatic: stop laser, stop gases, remove fuel, extinguish with saline, then reassess airway and ventilation. After the fire, expect airway oedema, mucosal burn and carbonaceous debris; plan bronchoscopy, consider corticosteroids case-by-case and secure critical care support. Non-technical skills — a pre-lasing brief and clear shared FiO₂ target — prevent most events.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not begin with 'remove the tube' without stopping the oxygen supply, and do not omit the wider laser-safety framework (eye protection, controlled area, smoke evacuation) which examiners expect alongside fire management.
Take-home: Control the oxidiser and the fuel before lasing; if fire occurs, stop the laser and gases, remove the burning tube, flood with saline, then reassess the airway.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: lasers in surgery (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx009); Assoc Anaesth: airway fire (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.15941)

# Lasers & Fibreoptics LASER principles, fibreoptic light transmission, total internal reflection, clinical applications stimulated emission . An incoming photon interacts with an atom in an excited (metastable) state, causing it to emit an identical photon — same wavelength, phase, and direction. This requires population inversion : more atoms must be in the excited state than the ground state, achieved by external energy input (pumping) — optical, electrical, or chemical. optical cavity bounded by two mirrors. The total mirror reflects all light back; the partial mirror allows a fraction to escape as the laser beam. Multiple passes through the gain medium amplify the light exponentially. The resulting beam is (single wavelength), (waves in phase), and (parallel, minimal divergence). Laser / active medium Chromophore and tissue effect Clinical uses Fibre transmission CO₂/N₂/He gas mixture; 10,600 nm Water; very shallow penetration gives precise cutting and vaporisation with limited coagulation. Laryngeal and airway lesions, skin resurfacing and microsurgery. Not through conventional silica fibre; delivered by articulated mirrors or specialised hollow fibres. Neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet crystal; 1,064 nm Relatively weak water/haemoglobin absorption permits deep penetration and strong coagulation, with greater collateral injury. Endoscopic tumour debulking, haemostasis and posterior capsulotomy. Yes — readily transmitted through flexible silica fibre. Frequency-doubled Nd:YAG through potassium titanyl phosphate; 532 nm Oxyhaemoglobin; selective superficial photocoagulation with little tissue penetration. Vocal-cord papilloma/vascular lesions, nasal and dermatological vascular lesions. Yes — transmitted through fibre. Ionised argon gas; 488/514 nm Haemoglobin and melanin; superficial photocoagulation. Retinal photocoagulation and superficial vascular lesions. Excited halide dimer, commonly ArF; 193 nm ultraviolet Proteins/nucleic acids; photoablation breaks molecular bonds with minimal thermal spread. Corneal refractive surgery (PRK/LASIK) and angioplasty. Not through standard silica fibre; UV-compatible delivery systems are required. Total internal reflection (TIR) occurs when light travelling from a medium of higher refractive index (n₁, core) to one of lower refractive index (n₂, cladding) strikes the interface at an angle greater than the critical angle : sin θc = n₂/n₁. All light is reflected back into the core with zero transmission loss. numerical aperture (NA) of a fibre defines the cone of light it can accept: NA = √(n₁² − n₂²). A larger NA accepts more light but provides lower image resolution. Clinical fibreoptic bundles contain thousands of individual fibres, each 8–12 μm in diameter. Coherent bundles maintain the spatial arrangement of fibres from one end to the other, allowing image transmission (viewing channel of bronchoscope). Incoherent bundles have random fibre arrangement and transmit light only (illumination channel). Modern video bronchoscopes use a CCD chip at the tip instead of a coherent bundle, providing superior image quality. Airway fire is the most feared complication of airway laser surgery. The CO₂ laser can ignite standard PVC or rubber endotracheal tubes. Prevention — as set out in the Association of Anaesthetists 2023 guideline Management of complications of airway management — requires: laser-resistant tubes (metal shaft, e.g. Laser-Flex); the lowest clinically appropriate FiO₂ , titrated to SpO₂ (commonly ≤ 0.30 when tolerated); avoidance of N₂O (acts as an oxidiser at laser temperatures); a saline-filled cuff (± methylene blue as a leak indicator); and saline-soaked pledgets around the cuff. If ignition occurs, the guideline drill is: simultaneously stop the airway gases and remove the burning tracheal tube; extinguish the fire with saline; re-establish ventilation with air, titrating FiO₂ upward only as needed; re-intubate and perform bronchoscopy to assess thermal and inhalational injury and remove debris Eye protection is mandatory for all theatre personnel. The goggles must be specific to the laser wavelength in use and have an optical density sufficient to reduce exposure below the maximum permissible level (CO₂ goggles do not protect against Nd:YAG). The patient's eyes are taped shut and covered with wet gauze. Warning signs must be displayed on all theatre doors, and the laser should be key-operated with a designated laser safety officer. Laser Classification Class 1: safe under all conditions of normal use, including enclosed higher-power systems. Class 2: visible light only; momentary viewing for less than 0.25 s is normally limited by the blink reflex (for example barcode scanners). Class 3R: direct viewing is potentially hazardous, although risk is lower than Class 3B. Class 3B can injure the eye after brief direct exposure; diffuse reflections are usually safer. Class 4: high-power beams hazardous to eyes and skin, with hazardous diffuse reflections, smoke and fire risk. Most surgical lasers are Class 4. Airway fire risk during CO₂ laser laryngeal surgery Decline the original plan. Use a laser-resistant ETT, deliver the lowest FiO₂ that maintains adequate SpO₂ (commonly ≤ 0.30) with N₂O omitted, fill the cuff with saline + dye, and follow the Association of Anaesthetists 2023 airway-fire drill if ignition occurs: simultaneously stop airway gases and remove the burning tracheal tube, extinguish the fire with saline, then re-establish ventilation with air (titrating FiO₂ up only as needed), re-intubate and perform bronchoscopy to assess thermal/inhalational injury. Numerical aperture of a fibreoptic bronchoscope NA ≈ 0.56, giving an acceptance half-angle of ~34° in air. Light entering within this cone undergoes total internal reflection (above the 69.8° critical angle) and propagates with negligible loss along the fibre. Lasers & Fibreoptics LASER principles, fibreoptic light transmission, total internal reflection, and clinical applications LASER = Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation — requires population inversion in a gain medium Laser light is monochromatic (single wavelength), coherent (waves in phase), and collimated (parallel beam) CO₂ laser (10,600 nm) is absorbed by water and cuts tissue; it ignites PVC ETTs — use laser-safe tubes with saline-filled cuffs Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from high to low refractive index at angle > critical angle (sin θc = n₂/n₁) Coherent fibre bundles transmit images (fibres maintain spatial position); incoherent bundles transmit light only Numerical aperture NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) defines the acceptance cone angle of the fibre Use the lowest clinically appropriate FiO₂ (typically ≤30%) during airway laser surgery and avoid N₂O — per current Association of Anaesthetists / DAS shared-airway guidance and the published airway-fire algorithm Introduction Interactive Diagrams LASER Physics Fibreoptics & Total Internal Reflection Laser Safety in Anaesthesia What are the key safety measures for airway laser surgery? FiO₂ ≤30 %, avoid N₂O (supports combustion), use a laser-resistant ETT (red-rubber wrapped with metallic foil, or purpose-built Mallinckrodt Laser-Flex), saline-filled cuff with methylene blue indicator, eye protection for staff and patient (wavelength-specific goggles), warning signs on theatre doors, smoke evacuation, and immediate access to saline and a backup tube. What is the management of an airway fire? Stop ventilation and disconnect O₂. Remove the burning tube. Pour saline into the airway to extinguish. Re-mask ventilate on air. Re-intubate (often with a smaller tube), then perform flexible or rigid bronchoscopy to assess thermal and inhalational injury and remove debris. Administer humidified O₂ and admit to critical care for observation of progressive airway oedema. How does an optical fibre transmit light? Total internal reflection. The core (high refractive index) is surrounded by a cladding (lower refractive index). Light entering within the acceptance cone reflects off the core–cladding boundary at angles greater than the critical angle and propagates along the fibre with minimal loss. Bundles are coherent (image transmission — fibrescope) or non-coherent (light transmission only). Define LASER and explain the requirement for population inversion in a gain medium Describe the three defining properties of laser light: monochromaticity, coherence and collimation Match common surgical lasers (CO₂, Nd:YAG, KTP) to their wavelengths, target chromophores and clinical applications s law and total internal reflection to explain image transmission through fibreoptic bundles (NA = √(n₁² − n₂²)) Plan an anaesthetic for airway laser surgery, including FiO₂ minimisation, laser-safe ETT selection and eye protection A 55-year-old smoker is listed for CO₂ laser excision of a vocal cord papilloma. The surgeon asks for FiO₂ 0.4 with N₂O supplementation through a standard PVC microlaryngeal tube. What changes are required? CO₂ laser (10,600 nm) is fully absorbed by water → ignites PVC at low energies. Fire triangle = oxidiser + fuel + ignition. PVC = fuel; CO₂ laser = ignition; O₂ ± N₂O = oxidiser (N₂O behaves as an oxidiser at temperatures generated by the laser). Key mitigations (per the Association of Anaesthetists 2023 guideline): laser-resistant (metal-bodied, e.g. Laser-Flex) ETT; lowest clinically appropriate FiO₂ — typically ≤ 0.30 in air, titrated to SpO₂ — with N₂O omitted; cuff filled with saline ± methylene blue; saline-soaked pledgets around the cuff; surgeon to use the lowest effective laser power; saline, a spare circuit and a bronchoscope immediately to hand. A coherent fibre bundle uses a glass core (n₁ = 1.62) and cladding (n₂ = 1.52). Calculate the numerical aperture and the maximum acceptance half-angle in air. NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = √(1.62² − 1.52²) = √(2.6244 − 2.3104) = √0.314 ≈ 0.56. NA = n₀ sin θ_max with n₀ (air) = 1 → sin θ_max = 0.56 → θ_max ≈ 34°. Critical angle inside the fibre: sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.52/1.62 = 0.938 → θc ≈ 69.8° (measured from the normal). ], }, ]; const LaserFibreopticsTopic = () => { return ( Lasers and fibreoptics are fundamental to modern anaesthetic and surgical practice. Understanding laser physics is essential for safe airway laser surgery, while fibreoptic principles underpin the fibreoptic bronchoscope — a cornerstone of difficult airway management. Both topics appear regularly in the Primary FRCA physics examination.

references.excerpt: If an airway fire occurs, immediately and simultaneously: stop the flow of all airway gases and remove the tracheal tube. Extinguish any burning material with saline. Re-establish ventilation using air, avoiding nitrous oxide and supplemental oxygen until certain the fire is out. Inspect the airway by bronchoscopy and treat thermal/inhalational injury. Prevention includes a laser-resistant tube, lowest clinically acceptable FiO₂ (typically ≤0.30), avoidance of N₂O, and a saline-filled cuff (± methylene blue) protected by saline-soaked pledgets.
