# Pressure Measurement Transducers, manometers, and invasive monitoring principles 1, sluggish); 2–3 decreasing oscillations (under-damped, ζ Clinical Application aneroid gauge uses an evacuated flexible metal capsule or bellows that expands or contracts with pressure and drives a dial through linkages. A Bourdon gauge uses a curved, flattened hollow metal tube open to the pressure source; rising pressure makes it straighten, and a lever-and-gear mechanism amplifies movement of the free end to turn a pointer. Its robust high-pressure range suits gas cylinders and regulators Monro–Kellie doctrine treats brain, CSF and intracranial blood as a fixed-volume compartment; compensation initially buffers added volume, then ICP rises steeply as compliance is exhausted. An external ventricular drain (EVD) is the clinical reference standard because it measures ventricular pressure and permits CSF sampling and drainage. Level its fluid transducer to the tragus/external auditory meatus as a practical surrogate for the foramen of Monro and re-level after position changes. tidal/compliance and dicrotic components. Normally P1 > P2; P2 exceeding P1 suggests reduced intracranial compliance Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is sustained/repeated IAP ≥12 mmHg; grades are I 12–15, II 16–20, III 21–25 and IV >25 mmHg. Abdominal compartment syndrome is sustained IAP >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction 25 mL sterile saline , connect to a pressure transducer zeroed at the mid-axillary line at the iliac crest, and read at end-expiration with the patient supine and abdominal muscles relaxed. Raised IAP reduces renal perfusion and urine output, raises diaphragm and airway pressures, impairs venous return and cardiac output, and compromises splanchnic perfusion; it is independently associated with acute kidney injury Wheatstone bridge strain gauge transducer. A diaphragm deflects under pressure, changing the resistance of strain gauge elements arranged in a Wheatstone bridge circuit. The voltage change is amplified and displayed as a pressure waveform. (opened to atmosphere at the level of interest — typically the phlebostatic axis at the right atrium) and . A 13 cm height error produces approximately 10 mmHg error. natural (resonant) frequency which must exceed the highest significant harmonic of the arterial waveform (around the 10th harmonic). At a heart rate of 120 bpm the fundamental is 2 Hz, so the 10th harmonic is 20 Hz and a system with a natural frequency >24 Hz is sufficient for accurate waveform reproduction. The damping coefficient (ζ) describes how quickly oscillations decay after a step change. Optimal damping (ζ = 0.64) provides the best balance between bandwidth and overshoot. Over-damping vs Under-damping (air bubbles, clot, kink, compliant tubing): sluggish waveform, underestimates systolic, overestimates diastolic. (long stiff tubing): resonant artefact, overestimates systolic, underestimates diastolic. Mean arterial pressure is least affected by damping artefact. oscillometric method detects oscillations in cuff pressure during deflation. Maximum oscillation amplitude corresponds to MAP. Systolic and diastolic are calculated algorithmically. Cuff width should be ~40% of arm circumference — too narrow overestimates, too wide underestimates. Limitations of oscillometry — atrial fibrillation or marked rhythm irregularity disrupts the oscillometric envelope, producing unreliable or absent readings. Severe hypotension / shock — low pulse pressure and peripheral vasoconstriction reduce cuff oscillations, causing overestimation or failure to measure. Patient movement / shivering — motion artefact is interpreted as pressure oscillations and distorts the algorithmically derived systolic and diastolic values. Vasoconstriction / vasopressor infusion — reduced arterial pulsatility alters the oscillation amplitude versus pressure relationship. Morbid obesity — incorrect cuff size or shape can make a standard adult cuff too small (overestimates BP) or the arm too conical for even pressure distribution. Cuffless blood pressure measurement Pulse transit time (PTT) — estimates BP from the interval between an ECG R-wave and the corresponding pulse wave arrival at a peripheral site (e.g. pulse oximeter fingertip or wrist PPG). PTT is influenced by arterial stiffness and preload, so it generally requires periodic cuff calibration. Pulse wave analysis (PWA) — extracts features from the photoplethysmography waveform shape (amplitude, area, reflection indices). Like PTT, it usually needs calibration to an oscillometric device for absolute BP values. Von Recklinghausen oscillotonometer uses two cuffs (occluding and sensing) and was the precursor to modern automated oscillometry. Finapres (FINger Arterial PRESsure) Penáz principle (volume-clamp method). A small finger cuff contains an infrared plethysmograph and a fast servo-controlled pressure system. The cuff pressure is continuously adjusted to keep the arterial wall in a state of constant diameter (the "unloaded" state), matching intra-arterial pressure beat-to-beat. Physiocal algorithm : periodically recalibrates the volume-clamp set-point to account for smooth muscle tone changes : beat-to-beat BP waveform without arterial cannulation; allows pulse contour analysis for stroke volume variation (SVV) and cardiac output estimation : inaccurate in vasoconstriction, Raynaud's, poor peripheral perfusion; finger pressure ≠ aortic pressure (transfer function correction applied in modern devices e.g. ClearSight/CNAP) Clinical use : perioperative haemodynamic monitoring, autonomic function testing, research Levelling error in arterial monitoring True MAP ≈ 52 + 19 ≈ 71 mmHg. The displayed hypotension was an artefact of levelling. Always zero AND level to the phlebostatic axis (4th ICS, mid-axillary line) — every 13 cm of height error gives ~10 mmHg. Damping diagnosis from a fast-flush test Optimal damping (ζ ≈ 0.64). The trace is reliable: SBP, DBP and MAP can all be trusted. Over-damping under-reads SBP and over-reads DBP; under-damping does the opposite. MAP is least affected by damping artefact in either direction. Pressure Measurement Transducers, manometers and the principles of invasive and non-invasive monitoring Pressure = Force/Area. SI unit is Pascal. Clinical units: mmHg, cmH₂O, kPa, bar. Wheatstone bridge strain gauge transducers convert diaphragm deflection to voltage via resistance change. Transducers must be zeroed to atmosphere and levelled to the phlebostatic axis. 13 cm error ≈ 10 mmHg. Natural frequency must exceed the highest significant harmonic of the arterial waveform (≈10th harmonic, so typically >24 Hz at clinical heart rates). Optimal damping coefficient ζ = 0.64. Over-damping underestimates systolic; under-damping overestimates systolic. MAP is least affected. NIBP oscillometric method: maximum oscillation amplitude = MAP; systolic and diastolic are derived algorithmically. Introduction Units of Pressure Manometers Intracranial Pressure Measurement Intra-Abdominal Pressure Measurement Pressure Transducers Invasive Arterial Monitoring Dynamic Response & Damping Non-Invasive Blood Pressure (NIBP) What is the natural frequency of an arterial line and why must it exceed 40 Hz? Natural frequency f₀ = (1/2π) × √(πd²E / 4ρLV) — depends on tubing diameter, stiffness, length and fluid density. The pulse pressure waveform contains harmonics up to ~10× heart rate (~25 Hz at HR 150). To reproduce these without resonance distortion, f₀ should exceed 40 Hz. Short, stiff, wide-bore, bubble-free tubing maximises f₀. What is optimal damping and how is it measured? Damping coefficient 0.6–0.7 is optimal — fast response without overshoot. Measured by the fast-flush (square-wave) test: count oscillations after release. ≥2 oscillations = under-damped (overshoots, overestimates SBP); ≤1 oscillation = over-damped (underestimates SBP). MAP is reliable in both cases. How does a strain-gauge transducer convert pressure into an electrical signal? A flexible diaphragm deforms under pressure, stretching wires arranged in a Wheatstone bridge configuration. The resistance change unbalances the bridge, producing a small voltage proportional to applied pressure. The transducer is zeroed at the level of the right atrium (phlebostatic axis) to remove the effect of hydrostatic column. The system ], }, ]; const PressureMeasurementTopic = () => { return ( Accurate pressure measurement is fundamental to anaesthetic monitoring. Pressures encountered in clinical practice range from atmospheric (101.3 kPa) to intracranial (0.7–2 kPa). Understanding the physics behind transducers, manometers, and invasive monitoring is essential for safe practice and FRCA examinations.

Pressure = Force / Area. The SI unit is the Pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². In clinical practice, pressures are commonly expressed in mmHg (arterial BP), cmH₂O (CVP, airway pressure), kPa (gas partial pressures), and bar (gas cylinders). Key conversions: 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg = 1033 cmH₂O.

Clinical Application

CVP was historically measured using a water manometer (cmH₂O). A 20 cmH₂O column equates to approximately 15 mmHg. Modern practice uses electronic transducers, but understanding the principle remains essential. Bourdon gauges remain ubiquitous on cylinder yokes and pipeline regulators.

An aneroid gauge uses an evacuated flexible metal capsule or bellows that expands or contracts with pressure and drives a dial through linkages. A Bourdon gauge uses a curved, flattened hollow metal tube open to the pressure source; rising pressure makes it straighten, and a lever-and-gear mechanism amplifies movement of the free end to turn a pointer. Its robust high-pressure range suits gas cylinders and regulators Modern invasive pressure monitoring uses a Wheatstone bridge strain gauge transducer. A diaphragm deflects under pressure, changing the resistance of strain gauge elements arranged in a Wheatstone bridge circuit. The voltage change is amplified and displayed as a pressure waveform.

The transducer must be zeroed (opened to atmosphere at the level of interest — typically the phlebostatic axis at the right atrium) and levelled. A 13 cm height error produces approximately 10 mmHg error.

The arterial line system consists of an intra-arterial cannula, fluid-filled non-compliant tubing, a three-way tap, a flush device (300 mmHg pressure bag with heparinised saline delivering 3–4 ml/hr), and the transducer. The system must faithfully reproduce the arterial waveform.

The monitoring system has a natural (resonant) frequency which must exceed the highest significant harmonic of the arterial waveform (around the 10th harmonic). At a heart rate of 120 bpm the fundamental is 2 Hz, so the 10th harmonic is 20 Hz and a system with a natural frequency >24 Hz is sufficient for accurate waveform reproduction. The damping coefficient (ζ) describes how quickly oscillations decay after a step change. Optimal damping (ζ = 0.64) provides the best balance between bandwidth and overshoot.

Over-damping vs Under-damping

Over-damped (air bubbles, clot, kink, compliant tubing): sluggish waveform, underestimates systolic, overestimates diastolic. Under-damped (long stiff tubing): resonant artefact, overestimates systolic, underestimates diastolic. Mean arterial pressure is least affected by damping artefact.

The oscillometric method detects oscillations in cuff pressure during deflation. Maximum oscillation amplitude corresponds to MAP. Systolic and diastolic are calculated algorithmically. Cuff width should be ~40% of arm circumference — too narrow overestimates, too wide underestimates.

Limitations of oscillometry

    These technologies are promising for longitudinal trends and hypertension screening, but at present automated cuff-based NIBP remains the standard for perioperative and critical-care measurement.

Von Recklinghausen oscillotonometer uses two cuffs (occluding and sensing) and was the precursor to modern automated oscillometry.

case_bank.title: The arterial line that under-reads
case_bank.text:
Case: The arterial line that under-reads (Monitoring artefact, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient in theatre has a radial arterial line. The trace looks rounded, the systolic reading is 30 mmHg lower than a cuff measurement, and vasopressor is being escalated.
Presentation: The flush test shows a slow return to baseline without oscillation. There is a long compliant extension and an air bubble near the transducer.
Stage 1 — Interpret the flush test
  Question: What does the square-wave test tell you?
  Model answer: Optimal damping gives one or two brisk oscillations before the trace settles.
  Model answer: Overdamping — a sluggish return with no oscillation — under-reads systolic and over-reads diastolic pressure while mean pressure stays comparatively reliable.
  Model answer: Underdamping (resonance) produces prolonged ringing and falsely high systolic values.
Stage 2 — Find the physical cause
  Question: Which components produce this pattern?
  Model answer: Air bubbles, clot, kinks, compliant tubing, excessive tubing length, a partially open tap or arterial spasm all add damping.
  Model answer: Zeroing at the wrong height changes mean pressure by roughly 7.5 mmHg for every 10 cm of height error.
  Model answer: Transducer natural frequency must be well above the pressure waveform harmonics for faithful reproduction.
Stage 3 — Correct before you treat
  Question: What action do you take?
  Model answer: Aspirate and flush, remove bubbles, shorten and stiffen the tubing, and re-zero at the phlebostatic axis.
  Model answer: Base decisions on mean arterial pressure and perfusion while the trace is unreliable, cross-checked with a cuff.
  Model answer: Do not escalate vasopressor for an artefact; document the corrected values.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: The catheter–tubing–transducer assembly is a second-order system whose behaviour depends on natural frequency and damping coefficient. Because the arterial waveform contains harmonics up to about 20 Hz, a low natural frequency or excessive damping distorts systolic and diastolic peaks. Mean pressure is the most robust derived value, which is why it guides therapy when the trace quality is uncertain.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Perform and document a square-wave test at set-up and whenever readings look implausible. Keep tubing short, stiff and bubble-free, avoid multiple taps and extensions, re-zero after any patient or transducer movement, and reconcile with non-invasive measurement. Persistent damping despite optimisation suggests thrombus or spasm and may need a new line.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not say 'the arterial line is wrong' without a systematic answer: state zeroing and levelling, the flush test result, the direction of error for over- and underdamping, and which derived value remains usable.
Take-home: Test damping before treating a number: overdamped traces under-read systolic pressure, and mean pressure is the value to trust while you fix the system.
Cited sources: BJA: arterial pressure measurement (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.06.047); Assoc Anaesth monitoring standards (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.13316)

Understanding laminar and turbulent flow, and the devices used to measure gas and liquid flow, is essential for anaesthetic equipment design and clinical practice.

Use the interactive diagram below to explore the differences between laminar and turbulent flow, including the velocity profiles and key equations governing each.

For laminar flow through a tube: Q = πΔPr⁴ / 8ηl, where Q = flow, ΔP = pressure gradient, r = radius, η = viscosity, l = length. Flow is proportional to the fourth power of radius — halving the radius reduces flow 16-fold.

Clinical Application

A 4.0 mm ETT has only 1/16 the flow of an 8.0 mm tube at the same driving pressure. This explains why small tubes produce significant resistance and why even a small reduction in airway calibre (e.g., subglottic oedema) dramatically increases work of breathing.

Re = ρvd / η, where ρ = density, v = velocity, d = diameter, η = viscosity. Laminar flow occurs when Re < 2000; turbulent flow when Re > 4000. Between 2000–4000 is the transition zone. Turbulent flow depends on gas density (not viscosity), which is why heliox (low density) reduces resistance in upper airway obstruction.

A rotameter is a tapered glass tube with a bobbin. As flow increases, the bobbin rises. At low flows, the annular gap is narrow (tube-like) — flow is laminar and depends on viscosity. At high flows, the gap is wide (orifice-like) — flow is turbulent and depends on density.

Rotameters are calibrated for specific gases at specific temperatures and pressures, and are read at the top of the bobbin (ball floats read at centre). O₂ rotameter is placed downstream to prevent hypoxic mixtures if an upstream tube leaks.

Pneumotachograph: measures pressure drop across a known resistance (Fleisch — bundle of tubes; Lilly — fine mesh screen). Integrating flow over time gives volume — the basis of many ventilator spirometers.

Wright respirometer: a turbine vane flowmeter. Under-reads at low flows and over-reads at high flows. Measures expired tidal and minute volumes.

Venturi effect exploits this — a jet of gas through a constriction entrains surrounding gas through side ports. Used in Venturi masks (fixed FiO₂), jet ventilation, and suction devices.

A 28% Venturi mask uses an entrainment ratio of ~10:1 (air:oxygen). The total flow (~40 L/min) exceeds peak inspiratory flow, ensuring accurate FiO₂ delivery regardless of breathing pattern.

The Coandă effect is the tendency of a fluid jet to follow a nearby convex surface rather than continue in a straight line. Entrainment of surrounding fluid is restricted on the wall side of the jet, lowering pressure there; the resulting pressure gradient deflects the jet onto the surface, where it remains attached until the curvature becomes too sharp.

It is closely related to Bernoulli >

Anaesthetic relevance

  • Maldistribution of gas or blood at airway and vascular bifurcations (one daughter branch preferentially the jet)
  • Historic fluidic ventilators used Coandă-based bistable switches with no moving parts
  • During jet ventilation, the jet may hug the tracheal wall, altering entrainment and delivered FiO₂
  • Echocardiography: regurgitant jets (e.g. eccentric MR) tracking along an atrial wall appear smaller than they are — Coandă-related underestimation
 Both effects share the same underlying physics — the conservation of energy expressed by Bernoulli > Geometry Fluid confined inside a tube that narrows then widens Free (or semi-free) jet emerging next to a curved surface Cause of low pressure Velocity ↑ at the throat (continuity: A·v = constant) → static pressure ↓ Entrainment is blocked on the wall side → pressure between jet and wall ↓ Effect on the flow Drives entrainment of a second fluid through a side port Deflects the jet so it adheres to the surface Direction of jet Stays axial — straight through the tube Bends toward the wall, may follow significant curvature Predictability Highly predictable — used for fixed entrainment ratios Bistable / can flip between branches — exploited in fluidic logic, but a nuisance clinically Clinical example Venturi mask (fixed FiO₂), nebulisers, jet entrainment ports Eccentric MR jet hugging the LA wall, gas maldistribution at carina, fluidic ventilator switching When it matters When you want a calibrated mixture When asymmetric flow distribution affects measurement or delivery
Bottom line

Bernoulli explains why a fast-moving jet has lower lateral pressure; the Venturi effect uses that to entrain gas through a constriction; the Coandă effect uses the same low-pressure region — this time between the jet and a nearby surface — to bend the jet onto that surface. Constriction flow is symmetric and predictable; jet attachment is asymmetric and surface-dependent.

The Coandă effect is a favourite of FRCA Primary SAQs and Final structured orals because it links a single physics principle to several disparate clinical scenarios. Recognising the pattern — a jet, a nearby surface, asymmetric distribution — usually scores the mark.

{/* Vignette 1 */}
Endobronchial intubation suspicion

A patient is ventilated with the ETT tip just above the carina. CXR shows preferential expansion of the right lung with a relatively collapsed left lung, despite the tube being above the carina. Auscultation confirms reduced breath sounds on the left.

Why: The high-velocity inspiratory jet exiting the ETT bevel adheres to the right lateral tracheal wall (the right main bronchus is wider and more axial) and is preferentially deflected into the right main bronchus — Coandă-driven asymmetric ventilation without true endobronchial migration.

Take-home: Asymmetric ventilation with a correctly positioned ETT may be Coandă-mediated. Reposition the bevel, consider a smaller-bore tube or change fresh gas flow to reduce jet velocity.

{/* Vignette 2 */}
Underestimated mitral regurgitation

Pre-operative TTE in a patient for non-cardiac surgery shows a small, eccentric MR jet tracking along the lateral LA wall. The patient is in florid pulmonary oedema with a markedly dilated LA.

Why: Eccentric, wall-hugging regurgitant jets entrain less surrounding blood and appear narrower on colour Doppler than free central jets of the same volume — the classic Coandă-related underestimation of severity.

Take-home: A small wall-impinging jet can mask severe MR. Use PISA, vena contracta and indirect signs (LA size, pulmonary vein flow reversal) rather than jet area alone.

{/* Vignette 3 */}
Variable FiO₂ during high-frequency jet ventilation

During HFJV for rigid bronchoscopy, the measured FiO₂ at the carina swings unpredictably despite a constant driving pressure and entrainment fraction set on the ventilator.

Why: The jet leaving the injector hugs the tracheal wall (Coandă attachment), which alters the geometry available for room-air entrainment. Small changes in catheter position flip the jet from one wall to the other, changing the entrainment ratio and delivered FiO₂.

Take-home: Entrainment in jet ventilation is not as predictable as in a Venturi mask. Always measure delivered FiO₂ and watch SpO₂ closely.

{/* Vignette 4 */}
Bistable fluidic ventilator

An older transport ventilator with no moving parts cycles between inspiration and expiration solely from the gas supply pressure. How does it work?

Why: A jet enters a chamber with two symmetrical curved walls and attaches to one (Coandă). A small control jet at the opposite wall destabilises attachment, flipping the main jet to the other wall — a bistable fluidic switch. The oscillation drives the respiratory cycle.

Take-home: Coandă is the basis of fluidic logic — useful in MRI environments where moving / electrical parts are problematic.

{/* Vignette 5 */}
Asymmetric distribution at a Y-junction

A high-velocity infusion through a triple-lumen catheter, or rapid blood flow at an arterial bifurcation, distributes preferentially down one daughter limb even when the two limbs appear geometrically symmetric.

Why: Tiny asymmetries in the bifurcation cause the jet to attach to one wall; once attached, the low-pressure region locks it there. The branch that the jet receives a disproportionate share of flow.

Take-home: Mixing of drugs and contrast at high flow is not guaranteed to be uniform — relevant for vasoactive infusions co-running with carriers, and for selective angiographic injection.

Exam pearls

    2000 predicts turbulence; in turbulent flow, flow ∝ √(ΔP) and depends on density rather than viscosity. Rotameter is a constant-pressure, variable-orifice flowmeter; calibrated for a specific gas at a specific temperature. At low flows the annulus around the bobbin behaves like a tube (viscosity matters); at high flows like an orifice (density matters). Heliox lowers density to convert turbulent to laminar flow in upper-airway obstruction. Introduction

Accurate temperature measurement is essential in anaesthesia and critical care. Hypothermia and hyperthermia profoundly affect pharmacokinetics, coagulation, and neurological outcome. Understanding the physics behind different thermometry devices is a core Primary FRCA topic and has direct clinical relevance for choosing the right monitoring site and device.

Interactive Diagrams

Thermocouple — The Seebeck Effect

When two dissimilar metals (e.g., copper and constantan) are joined at a junction, a small voltage (EMF) is generated proportional to the temperature difference between the measuring junction (patient end) and the reference junction. This is the Seebeck effect. Type T (copper-constantan) thermocouples produce approximately 40 μV per °C.

Advantages: Fastest response time (milliseconds), very small probe size, self-generating (no battery), wide temperature range (−200 to +400°C). Disadvantages: Very small EMF requires amplification; needs reference junction compensation (cold junction compensation).

Thermocouple voltage represents T1 − T2, not T1 alone. In modern monitors the reference or “cold” junction is inside the monitor; a thermistor measures that internal temperature (T2), and the electronics add the equivalent reference-junction voltage to calculate patient temperature (T1). This electronic correction replaces the historical ice-bath reference Liquid Crystal Thermometers

Disposable forehead strips contain microencapsulated cholesteryl ester liquid crystals. Temperature alters their ordered molecular structure and therefore the wavelength—and colour—of reflected light. They measure skin rather than core temperature, are influenced by ambient conditions and perfusion, and are suitable only for rough trends rather than anaesthetic or critical-care decisions Thermistor — Semiconductor Resistance

A thermistor is a semiconductor (metal oxide bead) with a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) — its resistance falls exponentially as temperature rises. This gives it very high sensitivity (thousands of Ω per °C) but a markedly non-linear response requiring calibration or linearisation circuitry.

Resistance is measured using a Wheatstone bridge circuit. The thermistor is one arm of the bridge; when its resistance changes with temperature, the bridge becomes unbalanced and the resulting voltage is proportional to the temperature change.

Clinical use: The thermistor at the tip of a pulmonary artery (PA) catheter measures blood temperature for thermodilution cardiac output. Also used in skin temperature probes and bladder temperature catheters.

Resistance Thermometer (RTD/Pt100)

A resistance temperature detector uses a metallic conductor (usually platinum) whose resistance increases linearly with temperature — a positive temperature coefficient (PTC). The standard Pt100 has a resistance of 100Ω at 0°C, rising by 0.385Ω per °C.

The relationship is described by: Rₜ = R₀(1 + αΔT) where α = 0.00385 Ω/Ω/°C. The linear response is its main advantage over the thermistor. However, it has lower sensitivity and the slowest response time of all electronic thermometers.

Clinical use: Laboratory reference standard. Rarely used for bedside monitoring due to slow response and large probe size.

Infrared Tympanic Thermometry

All objects at temperatures above absolute zero emit infrared radiation. The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the power radiated is proportional to T⁴ (P = εσAT⁴). An IR tympanic thermometer uses a thermopile (multiple thermocouples in series) to detect the IR radiation emitted by the tympanic membrane.

Although the tympanic membrane is itself supplied predominantly by branches of the external carotid artery, its close anatomical proximity to the internal carotid artery means its emitted infrared radiation acts as a surrogate for the temperature of blood supplying the hypothalamus, making it a reliable reflection of core temperature.

Sources of error: Cerumen (ear wax) absorbs IR radiation → falsely low readings. Otitis media and poor probe positioning (not aimed at TM) also cause inaccuracy. The probe must be placed to form a seal with the ear canal.

Clinical Temperature Monitoring Sites

Core sites: PA catheter (gold standard), distal oesophagus (lower third), nasopharynx, tympanic membrane, bladder. Peripheral sites: Axilla, skin (forehead), rectal (delayed response).

Fever Monitoring in ICU

For a new fever in a critically ill adult, use a central measurement—PA-catheter, bladder-catheter or oesophageal thermistor—when already present or when precision will change diagnosis or treatment. Do not insert an invasive device solely to measure temperature. Without central access, oral or rectal measurement is preferred over less reliable axillary, temporal or non-contact methods. This differs from routine intraoperative practice, where distal oesophageal or nasopharyngeal probes are convenient continuous choices 2 °C suggests significant vasoconstriction; redistribution dominates the first hour of GA. references.excerpt: Induction of anaesthesia should not begin unless the patient's temperature is 36.0°C or above (unless there is a need to expedite surgery because of clinical urgency). The patient's temperature should be measured and documented before induction of anaesthesia and then every 30 minutes until the end of surgery. The temperature setting on forced-air warming devices should be set at maximum and then adjusted to maintain a patient temperature of at least 36.5°C. Hypothermia is defined as a core temperature below 36.0°C.

case_bank.title: Rising CO₂ and rigidity after sevoflurane
case_bank.text:
Case: Rising CO₂ and rigidity after sevoflurane (Analgesia & anaesthetics, Advanced)
Patient: A young adult receives sevoflurane and suxamethonium for emergency surgery. Masseter spasm is noted at induction.
Presentation: End-tidal CO₂ rises to 9 kPa despite increased minute ventilation, with tachycardia, generalised rigidity, temperature climbing 0.5 °C every ten minutes and mixed acidosis.
Stage 1 — Recognise and declare
  Question: What is happening and what are the first actions?
  Model answer: This is malignant hyperthermia: unregulated calcium release through a defective skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor causes sustained contracture, hypermetabolism and heat production.
  Model answer: Declare the emergency, call for help and the MH kit, stop all volatile agent and suxamethonium, and switch to a clean circuit with high-flow oxygen and total intravenous anaesthesia.
  Model answer: Ask the surgeon to stop or expedite closure, and hyperventilate to manage CO₂.
Stage 2 — Give definitive treatment
  Question: What drug and dose?
  Model answer: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenously, repeated as needed up to about 10 mg/kg, with several people reconstituting vials because preparation is the rate-limiting step.
  Model answer: Cool actively, treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis and arrhythmias, and expect myoglobinuria requiring fluid to maintain urine output.
  Model answer: Avoid calcium channel blockers with dantrolene, and continue monitoring in critical care for recrudescence and compartment syndrome.
Stage 3 — Follow up
  Question: What happens after the acute episode?
  Model answer: Continue creatine kinase, potassium, coagulation and renal monitoring in critical care for at least 24 hours.
  Model answer: Refer the patient and family to an MH investigation unit for genetic and in vitro contracture testing, and document the reaction clearly.
  Model answer: Plan future anaesthesia as trigger-free: vapour-free machine, total intravenous anaesthesia, non-depolarising relaxants and dantrolene availability.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Volatile agents and suxamethonium trigger uncontrolled sarcoplasmic calcium release in susceptible individuals, usually through RYR1 variants. Sustained actin–myosin activity and futile ATP consumption produce CO₂ generation, heat, oxygen debt, lactic acidosis, hyperkalaemia and rhabdomyolysis. The earliest and most sensitive sign is an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO₂ despite adequate ventilation; temperature rise is a later feature.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Treatment is simultaneous rather than sequential: remove triggers, give dantrolene early, cool, and correct metabolic derangement while a dedicated person manages drug preparation. Monitor invasive pressure, core temperature, gases, potassium, creatine kinase and urine output. Distinguish MH from thyroid storm, sepsis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, phaeochromocytoma and inadequate anaesthesia — all of which raise CO₂ or temperature but need different treatment.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not wait for pyrexia before treating, and do not forget that masseter spasm after suxamethonium is a warning sign. Quote the dantrolene dose and state that vapour must be removed with a clean circuit, not just switched off.
Take-home: Unexplained rising CO₂ with rigidity is malignant hyperthermia until proven otherwise: remove triggers, give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg early and cool aggressively.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: inhalational agents (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkg002); AAGBI/MHAUS malignant hyperthermia guideline (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.14257)

# Humidity & Gas Analysis Pneumotachographs, mass spectrometry, Raman scattering, humidification physics Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapour per unit volume of gas (mg/L). Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water vapour content to the maximum possible at that temperature (%). At 37°C, the saturated vapour pressure of water is 6.3 kPa, giving an absolute humidity of 44 mg/L at 100% RH Complications of humidification apparatus dead space and resistance; abrupt obstruction by secretions or blood; inadequate humidification with large leaks, high minute ventilation or prolonged use. Heated humidifier: overheating and airway thermal injury; under-heating and rain-out causing resistance, ventilator malfunction or aspiration. Water reservoirs and condensate can become colonised; circuit complexity adds leak and disconnection points. Handle condensate away from the patient and use infection-control procedures. isothermic saturation boundary (ISB) . In a healthy, resting adult this lies in the large bronchi (around the 4th–5th generation; often approximated to the level of the carina for teaching). Endotracheal intubation bypasses the nose, shifting the ISB distally and risking mucociliary damage, secretion thickening, and heat loss heat and moisture exchange filters (HMEFs) passively trap heat and moisture from exhaled gas, typically returning 30–38 mg/L on inspiration depending on the device and ventilation parameters . They add mechanical dead space (30–90 mL). Heated water bath humidifiers hygrometer (mechanical), the wet-and-dry bulb psychrometer (latent heat of evaporation), Regnault's dew-point electrical / capacitance sensor found in every contemporary anaesthetic monitor. Step through each animation to see the underlying physics. Wet-and-dry bulb psychrometer: one thermometer is dry and one is wrapped in a water-soaked wick. Evaporation removes latent heat and cools the wet bulb; a larger temperature difference means drier gas, and a psychrometric chart converts the pair of readings to relative humidity. Regnault dew-point hygrometer: cool a polished silvered surface until condensation first appears. At that dew point the adjacent gas is saturated, allowing absolute humidity to be read from saturated water-vapour data. Hair hygrometer: degreased organic fibres lengthen as humidity rises and mechanically move a pointer; it is simple but slow and requires calibration. type uses parallel capillary tubes to ensure laminar flow; the Q = ΔP/R , with resistance proportional to gas viscosity, tube length and 1/radius⁴. The parallel capillaries of a Fleisch head and mesh of a Lilly head create a known, approximately linear resistance, so a differential transducer converts ΔP into flow. Variable-orifice devices instead use the Bernoulli relationship and are more density dependent integrated electronically to derive volume (tidal volume, minute ventilation). Both types must be heated to body temperature to prevent condensation on the resistance element, which would increase resistance and cause inaccuracy. Changes in gas composition (viscosity, density) also affect readings . At high flow, turbulence breaks the linear ΔP–flow relationship; N₂O, oxygen and air differ in viscosity, so calibration must match gas composition. one of two clinical methods (the other being Raman scattering) capable of identifying all respiratory and anaesthetic gases simultaneously . Gas molecules are ionised by electron bombardment in a high vacuum, then accelerated through a voltage gradient and deflected by a magnetic field. The radius of curvature depends on mass-to-charge ratio: r = mv/qB . Lighter ions curve more tightly N₂O and CO₂ both have m/z = 44 . The mass spectrometer distinguishes them by their different fragmentation patterns (daughter ions). The instrument is expensive, large, and requires a high vacuum pump, but can be multiplexed to serve multiple operating theatres via a rotating valve and long sampling lines Rayleigh scattering — same frequency). A tiny fraction (~1 in 10⁷) scatter inelastically with a frequency shift corresponding to the molecule's vibrational energy — this is Raman scattering Stokes shift (lower frequency) is most commonly measured. Each molecule has a unique Raman shift acting as a fingerprint. Unlike infrared absorption (which requires a changing dipole moment), Raman can detect homonuclear diatomic molecules like N₂ and O₂. It can also distinguish N₂O from CO₂ by their different vibrational modes — something IR absorption finds challenging Clinical Raman analysers (e.g., Rascal™) are fast, measure all gases, and don't require a vacuum. However, the signal is extremely weak, requiring sensitive photodetectors and powerful lasers, making the equipment expensive. They are not widely used in current clinical practice (all electrons paired) and are weakly repelled by a magnetic field. Oxygen is unusual : its molecular orbital structure leaves two unpaired electrons , making it strongly — attracted into a magnetic field. Among medical gases only O₂ and nitric oxide (NO) show this property, so the measurement is essentially specific for O₂ Pauling analyser suspends two nitrogen-filled glass spheres ("dumb-bell") in a non-uniform magnetic field. Sample gas containing O₂ enters the chamber; the O₂ is drawn into the strongest part of the field, displacing the spheres and rotating the dumb-bell. A mirror on the suspension reflects a light beam onto a photocell; a feedback current is applied to hold the dumb-bell stationary, and that current is proportional to the partial pressure of O₂ differential pressure (fast-response) paramagnetic cell : sample gas and a reference gas are alternately pulled into a chamber containing a switched electromagnet. The pressure difference oscillating across a sensitive transducer is proportional to the difference in O₂ concentration — giving a response time fast enough for breath-by-breath inspired/expired O₂ measurement changing dipole moment during vibration absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavelengths. A broad-spectrum IR source illuminates the sample chamber; the gas absorbs specific wavelengths and the residual transmitted intensity is measured by a detector. The fractional absorption follows the Beer-Lambert law (A = εcl), so the signal is proportional to the partial pressure of the target gas Characteristic absorption bands: — 4.26 µm (asymmetric stretch). Used in every capnograph. — 4.5 µm (and a secondary peak near 3.9 µm). Volatile agents (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, halothane, enflurane) — broad absorption in the 8–13 µm "fingerprint" region . Each agent has a slightly different spectrum, so a multi-wavelength analyser (or a tunable filter / Fourier-transform IR) can both the agent and its concentration O₂, N₂, Ar, He — homonuclear or monoatomic → no changing dipole → not detected Pitfalls and corrections: Collision (pressure) broadening: N₂O molecules collide with CO₂ and broaden its 4.26 µm absorption peak, causing the analyser to CO₂. Modern analysers measure N₂O simultaneously and apply software correction Agent cross-sensitivity: volatile spectra overlap. A single-wavelength agent monitor will give a wrong reading if the wrong agent is selected; modern multi-wavelength analysers identify the agent automatically and warn if a mixture is present (e.g. residual desflurane during a sevoflurane case) Water vapour and condensation in the sampling line shift readings — sample lines use Nafion™ tubing that selectively allows water vapour to equilibrate with room air Sidestream sampling delay (≈2–3 s) and aspiration rate (typically 150–200 mL/min) must be matched to tidal volume in neonates to avoid dilution Hardware variants: dispersive IR (rotating filter wheel selects wavelength); non-dispersive IR (NDIR — uses specific optical filters and detectors for each target gas, the original implementation being the dual-chamber Luft cell; NDIR is the dominant design in modern clinical monitors); and photoacoustic spectroscopy (pulsed IR heats the gas → pressure pulse detected by a microphone — used in the Brüel & Kjær multi-gas analyser) where to put the sensor relative to the breathing circuit . Two designs dominate clinical practice Mainstream (in-line) — the IR sensor sits in a cuvette inserted directly between the catheter mount and the breathing circuit; expired gas flows the measuring cell. Sidestream (diverting) — a fine sampling line aspirates ≈ 50–250 mL/min of gas from a T-piece at the airway and delivers it to a remote analyser inside the monitor. Sensor location In the airway, at the catheter mount Inside the monitor; gas aspirated via 2–3 m sample line Response time / delay Real-time (essentially zero transit delay) ~2–4 s transit delay + rise time Waveform fidelity Sharp — best for detecting subtle expired CO₂ changes (e.g. ROSC) Slightly damped; further degraded if sample flow is too low or tubing too long Gases measured Usually CO₂ only (single-wavelength IR) CO₂, N₂O, O₂ and all volatile agents — multi-gas analysis Weight at the airway Heavy cuvette + cable — risk of ETT kinking, accidental extubation Light T-piece adaptor only Dead space added 5–10 mL adult cuvette (significant in neonates) Negligible (< 1 mL adaptor) Water / secretions Cuvette window can fog or soil → drift; heated to 39 °C to prevent condensation Water trap + Nafion™ tubing remove water vapour selectively Gas dilution None — measures actual airway gas Aspiration rate (150–200 mL/min) can dilute small tidal volumes (neonates, HFOV, jet ventilation) → falsely low ETCO₂ Not required (gas returns to circuit) Sampled gas (containing volatile/N₂O) must be returned to the circuit or scavenged; otherwise increases fresh-gas requirement Suitability for non-intubated patients Poor — needs sealed circuit Good — nasal cannula sampling line works during sedation, recovery, procedural sedation Cost / robustness Higher per-use cost (disposable airway sensor or fragile reusable head) Cheap consumable (sample line, water trap) Why modern theatre monitors are sidestream: the multi-gas requirement (O₂ paramagnetic + IR for CO₂/N₂O/agent) is impossible to package into a lightweight in-airway cuvette, so the analyser has to live inside the monitor and the gas must be brought to it. The 2–3 second transit delay is acceptable for steady-state monitoring of a ventilated adult. When mainstream wins: neonatal/paediatric ventilation (no aspiration loss, no dilution), pre-hospital and transport CO₂ monitoring (no pump, lower power), and high-fidelity capnography during CPR where small/early ETCO₂ changes signal ROSC. Common sidestream pitfalls in vivas: kinked or water-blocked sample line → flat trace; disconnection at the T-piece → room-air dilution of the sampled gas → falsely low ETCO₂ with preserved waveform shape; long sample line in low-flow anaesthesia → loss of fresh gas if not returned to the circuit. (O₂) with multi-wavelength infrared (CO₂, N₂O, volatile agent) and an back-up for inspired O₂ alarming. Strength / Limitation O₂ (and NO) Unpaired electrons attracted into magnetic field Fast, accurate, no consumable / sensitive to water vapour Infrared absorption CO₂, N₂O, volatile agents Beer-Lambert at agent-specific wavelengths Cheap, fast / collision broadening, agent cross-sensitivity, blind to O₂/N₂ Galvanic fuel cell O₂ (FiO₂) Spontaneous redox: O₂ + lead → EMF No power needed / consumable lead anode (~6–12 mo) Clark electrode O₂ (PaO₂ in blood) Polarographic — current proportional to PO₂ Gold standard for blood gas / needs polarising voltage, drift Mass spectrometry All respiratory and anaesthetic gases Ionise → deflect by m/z (r = mv/qB) Universal, multiplexable / large, expensive, vacuum required; N₂O ≡ CO₂ at m/z 44 All gases including N₂, O₂ Inelastic photon scatter — vibrational fingerprint Unambiguous, fast / weak signal, expensive laser, niche use Exam tip: if a question gives you a single medical gas to measure, the canonical answer is usually paramagnetic for O₂, infrared for CO₂/N₂O/volatiles, fuel cell for circuit FiO₂ and Clark electrode for arterial blood. Mass spectrometry and Raman appear in "which analyser identifies gases?" stems. Humidity deficit when bypassing the upper airway About 264 mg/min of water (and ~14 W of heat) is lost from the lower airway. Over hours this dries secretions, impairs ciliary function and contributes to hypothermia — mandating an HMEF (≈30–38 mg/L) or active heated humidifier (44 mg/L) in any prolonged anaesthetic. Distinguishing N₂O from CO₂ on a gas analyser Rely on either the fragmentation pattern (m/z 28 vs 30), an IR analyser tuned to CO₂'s 4.26 µm band, or Raman spectroscopy. In modern theatres the dual IR/paramagnetic analyser is the standard solution. Dry gases (medical pipeline 0 % RH) cause mucosal drying, ciliary paralysis, mucus plugging and atelectasis. The upper airway normally conditions gas to 100 % RH at 37 °C (44 mg/L). Intubated patients bypass this — minimum 60 % RH at 30 °C (~17 mg/L) is required; HMEs deliver ~25–30 mg/L; active humidifiers (heated water bath) achieve full 44 mg/L. How does an HME work and what are its limits? Heat and Moisture Exchanger: hygroscopic + hydrophobic layers trap exhaled water vapour and heat, returning them on inspiration. Efficiency 70–90 %. Not adequate for >96 h ventilation — switch to active heated humidification. Compare side-stream and main-stream capnography sampling. Side-stream — sample aspirated at 150–200 mL/min through fine tubing to a remote analyser; small footprint, slight delay (1–4 s) and waveform distortion, suction can dilute paediatric tidal volumes. Deficit per litre of inspired gas ≈ 44 mg. Infrared absorption can resolve them (different absorption bands). Raman scattering is unambiguous: each molecule has a unique vibrational shift, including for homonuclear gases like N₂ that are invisible to IR. # Ultrasound Physics Piezoelectric effect, frequency vs resolution, Doppler effect, artefacts = [ [ "What is the trade-off between ultrasound frequency, resolution and depth?", "Higher frequency (10–15 MHz) — better axial resolution but rapid attenuation, so only superficial structures (vascular access, peripheral nerves). Lower frequency (2–5 MHz) — penetrates deeper (cardiac, abdominal) at the cost of resolution. Resolution improves with shorter wavelength (λ = c/f, c ≈ 1540 m/s in soft tissue)." ], [ "Explain the principle of Doppler in vascular ultrasound.", "Frequency shift (Δf) = 2 × f₀ × v × cosθ / c, where v is blood velocity and θ is the angle between beam and flow. Optimal θ piezoelectric crystals (typically lead zirconate titanate — PZT) that exhibit two complementary effects: the reverse piezoelectric effect (applying alternating voltage causes crystal vibration → ultrasound production) and the direct piezoelectric effect (returning echoes deform the crystal → generate voltage for image formation). backing/damping material (shortens pulse duration → improves axial resolution), the matching layer (λ/4 thickness, reduces impedance mismatch between crystal and skin), and the acoustic lens (focuses the beam laterally). Acoustic impedance (Z = ρc) is density multiplied by propagation speed. The greater the impedance difference across a boundary, the greater the reflected fraction: tissue–air and tissue–bone interfaces produce near-total reflection and acoustic shadowing. Coupling gel removes the air layer between probe and skin. The quarter- wavelength matching layer has impedance intermediate between PZT and tissue, reducing reflection and maximising energy transmission resolution and penetration . Higher frequency produces shorter wavelengths and better resolution, but higher frequency waves are attenuated more rapidly by tissue (~0.5 dB/cm/MHz), limiting penetration depth. Axial resolution (along the beam) = spatial pulse length / 2 = (number of cycles × wavelength) / 2. It is improved by higher frequency and better damping. Lateral resolution (perpendicular to beam) equals beam width and is best at the focal zone. Elevational (slice thickness) resolution depends on the transducer element height. linear 6–15 MHz for superficial structures (nerve blocks, vascular access); curvilinear 2–5 MHz for deep abdominal structures (FAST scan); phased array 1–5 MHz Doppler effect describes the frequency shift when ultrasound reflects off moving red blood cells: Δf = 2f₀v cos θ / c . The angle of insonation (θ) is critical — at 90° (cos 90° = 0) there is no Doppler shift; the angle must be kept for accurate velocity measurement (small angle errors cause large velocity errors at angles approaching 90°). CW Doppler uses separate transmit and receive crystals operating continuously — it can measure very high velocities without aliasing but has no depth discrimination. PW Doppler uses a single crystal alternating between transmit and receive with a sample gate at a specific depth — it is subject to when the Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit (PRF/2). Colour flow Doppler is PW-based and maps velocity as colour: red toward the transducer, blue away (BART convention). It also aliases. Power Doppler displays signal amplitude rather than velocity — more sensitive to slow flow but gives no directional information. Tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) reverses conventional wall filtering to retain low-velocity, high-amplitude myocardial signals while suppressing blood flow. Mitral-annular e′ velocity contributes to assessment of diastolic relaxation and the E/e′ ratio estimates filling pressure, although angle dependence remains. maps deformation or shear-wave propagation to estimate tissue stiffness, supporting characterisation of liver, thyroid, breast and endobronchial lesions ALARA—acoustic output and dwell time as low as reasonably achievable —while obtaining a diagnostic image. thermal index (TI) is the ratio of emitted acoustic power to the power estimated to raise tissue temperature by 1 °C. Use TIS for soft tissue, TIB when bone is near the focus and TIC for cranial scanning. The mechanical index (MI) = peak rarefactional pressure / √frequency estimates non-thermal cavitation risk; lower frequency and higher negative pressure increase it. For routine non-obstetric scanning, keep displayed TI and MI below 1 where practicable, minimise spectral-Doppler dwell time and reduce output before reducing image quality controls Acoustic shadowing occurs behind strong reflectors (bone, gallstones, calcified structures) that absorb or reflect nearly all ultrasound, creating an anechoic region deep to the structure. Conversely, posterior acoustic enhancement occurs behind fluid-filled structures (bladder, cysts) where less attenuation results in brighter echoes beyond. produces equidistant parallel lines (A-lines) when ultrasound bounces repeatedly between two strong parallel reflectors (e.g., pleura-air interface). In lung ultrasound, A-lines indicate normal aerated lung (comet-tail artefact) are vertical hyperechoic lines extending from the pleural line to the screen edge without fading — they indicate interstitial oedema Lung sliding (the shimmering movement of the visceral pleura against the parietal pleura with respiration) rules out pneumothorax at that point. On M-mode, normal lung sliding produces the "seashore sign" ; absent sliding produces the "barcode/stratosphere sign" Probe choice for ultrasound-guided supraclavicular block Use the high-frequency linear probe. The plexus is shallow, so penetration is not limiting and axial resolution at 12 MHz allows fine needle-tip and fascicular discrimination. Reserve curvilinear/phased array probes for deeper structures (FAST, abdominal, cardiac). Aliasing on PW Doppler at the LVOT True velocity is greater than the Nyquist limit. Use CW Doppler aligned through the LVOT to obtain an unaliased peak velocity (often 4–6 m/s in HOCM). Apply the simplified Bernoulli (ΔP = 4v²) to estimate the dynamic LVOT gradient. Ultrasound Physics Piezoelectric effect, frequency–resolution trade-off, Doppler, and artefacts Piezoelectric crystals (PZT) convert electrical to mechanical energy (transmit) and vice versa (receive) — the basis of all ultrasound transducers Higher frequency → better axial resolution but less penetration; axial resolution = SPL/2 Speed of sound in soft tissue is assumed to be 1,540 m/s for depth calculations Doppler equation: Δf = 2f₀v cos θ / c — angle of insonation must be <60° for accurate velocity measurement CW Doppler has no aliasing but no depth discrimination; PW Doppler is depth-specific but aliases above Nyquist limit (PRF/2) A-lines (reverberation) = normal aerated lung; B-lines (comet tail) = interstitial oedema; absent lung sliding → pneumothorax Acoustic shadowing occurs behind bone/calculi; posterior enhancement occurs behind fluid-filled structures Introduction Interactive Diagrams Piezoelectric Effect & Transducer Design Frequency, Resolution & Penetration Doppler Ultrasound Ultrasound Safety & Bioeffects Ultrasound Artefacts What is the trade-off between ultrasound frequency, resolution and depth? Higher frequency (10–15 MHz) — better axial resolution but rapid attenuation, so only superficial structures (vascular access, peripheral nerves). Lower frequency (2–5 MHz) — penetrates deeper (cardiac, abdominal) at the cost of resolution. Resolution improves with shorter wavelength (λ = c/f, c ≈ 1540 m/s in soft tissue). Explain the principle of Doppler in vascular ultrasound. Frequency shift (Δf) = 2 × f₀ × v × cosθ / c, where v is blood velocity and θ is the angle between beam and flow. Optimal θ <60° (cos plateau steepens above this — error increases). Colour Doppler maps direction (toward probe = red, away = blue). Pulsed-wave Doppler gives velocity at a specific depth but is limited by Nyquist; continuous-wave measures any velocity but loses depth resolution. What is the acoustic impedance and how does it cause reflection? Z = ρ × c (density × speed of sound). Reflection occurs at boundaries with different Z. A small mismatch (soft tissue–soft tissue ~1 %) gives weak echoes; a large mismatch (tissue–air or tissue–bone) reflects nearly all the energy, casting a shadow. Coupling gel removes the tissue–air interface at the skin. Explain the piezoelectric effect and the components of a clinical ultrasound transducer Justify probe selection from the frequency–penetration trade-off (linear vs curvilinear vs phased array) Apply the Doppler equation (Δf = 2f₀v cos θ / c) and recognise aliasing on PW Doppler Distinguish CW, PW, colour and power Doppler in terms of velocity range and depth resolution Identify the common B-mode artefacts (shadowing, enhancement, A-lines, B-lines, lung sliding) and their clinical meaning Choosing between a linear high-frequency probe (12 MHz) and a curvilinear probe (3.5 MHz) for a supraclavicular brachial plexus block in an adult. Target depth at the supraclavicular fossa ≈ 1–3 cm. Attenuation ≈ 0.5 dB/cm/MHz × 2 ways → at 12 MHz over 3 cm round trip = 36 dB attenuation (acceptable, image still bright). Axial resolution at 12 MHz ≈ wavelength × ½ × cycles ≈ 0.13 mm × 1 ≈ 0.13 mm — easily resolves individual hypoechoic nerve fascicles. At 3.5 MHz axial resolution ≈ 0.4 mm — fascicles less distinct but probe penetrates 15–20 cm. PW Doppler at the LVOT in a patient with HOCM shows the velocity envelope wrapping around the baseline at a Nyquist limit of 0.8 m/s. Estimate true peak velocity and choose a remedy. Aliasing occurs when Doppler shift > Nyquist limit = PRF/2. Nyquist = 0.8 m/s → true velocity exceeds this and is mis-displayed in the opposite direction. Options: (1) increase PRF (raises Nyquist); (2) shift baseline to use full negative scale; (3) reduce sample depth (deeper sample → lower max PRF); (4) switch to CW Doppler — no aliasing, but loses depth specificity. ], }, ]; const UltrasoundPhysicsTopic = () => { return ( Ultrasound has become indispensable in anaesthesia and critical care — from vascular access and nerve blocks to focused echocardiography and lung assessment. Understanding the underlying physics enables optimal image acquisition, appropriate probe selection, and correct interpretation of artefacts. This topic is heavily examined in both Primary and Final FRCA.

# MRI Physics Nuclear spin, precession, T1/T2 relaxation, MRI safety for anaesthetists hydrogen nuclei (¹H protons) , which are abundant in water and fat. Each proton has quantum spin (½) and acts as a tiny magnet. When placed in a strong external magnetic field (B₀), protons align either (low energy, spin-up) or (high energy, spin-down) to B₀. A slight excess align parallel, creating a small but detectable net magnetisation vector (M₀) along B₀. (wobbles like a gyroscope) around the B₀ axis at a frequency given by the Larmor equation: ω₀ = γ × B₀ . For hydrogen, γ = 42.58 MHz/T, giving a Larmor frequency of 63.87 MHz at 1.5T and 127.74 MHz at 3T. An RF pulse at exactly the Larmor frequency transfers energy to the protons (resonance), tipping M₀ away from B₀ into the transverse plane where it can be detected by receiver coils. T1 (spin-lattice/longitudinal) relaxation describes the recovery of magnetisation along B₀ as protons release energy to the surrounding lattice. T1 is the time for 63% recovery. Fat has a short T1 (efficient energy transfer) while water has a long T1 T2 (spin-spin/transverse) relaxation describes the loss of transverse magnetisation as protons lose phase coherence through interactions with neighbouring spins. T2 is the time to 37% remaining signal. 1/T2* = 1/T2 + γΔB₀ . A 180° pulse in a spin-echo sequence rephases the static field component and therefore measures true T2; gradient-echo sequences omit it and retain T2* susceptibility contrast. This makes GRE fast but sensitive to metal, air-tissue interfaces and blood products; susceptibility-weighted imaging exploits the effect to demonstrate deoxyhaemoglobin and haemosiderin Image weighting is controlled by TR (repetition time) and TE (echo time). T1-weighted images (short TR, short TE) show fat as bright and water as dark — best for anatomical detail. T2-weighted images (long TR, long TE) show water as bright and fat as dark — best for detecting pathology (oedema, inflammation, CSF). Spin echo (SE) A 90° excitation followed by a 180° rephasing pulse corrects static-field dephasing, producing true T2 contrast with fewer susceptibility artefacts, but taking longer. Gradient recalled echo (GRE) Gradient reversal forms the echo without a 180° pulse. It is fast and T2*-weighted, making haemorrhage, haemosiderin, calcification and metal conspicuous. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery is T2-weighted with CSF nulled by an inversion pulse. Periventricular oedema, demyelination and subarachnoid pathology stand out against dark CSF. DWI with ADC Diffusion weighting detects restricted Brownian water motion. case_bank.title: Anaesthesia in the MRI scanner
case_bank.text:
Case: Anaesthesia in the MRI scanner (Imaging & radiation, Intermediate)
Patient: A child needs general anaesthesia for a 3 T MRI brain scan. A non-MR-conditional syringe pump has been brought to the scanner door and the patient has an unlabelled implant.
Presentation: The radiographer asks you to proceed quickly because the list is delayed.
Stage 1 — Name the physical hazards
  Question: Which fields cause which risks?
  Model answer: The always-on static field causes projectile injury, implant torque and displacement, and disables non-MR-safe equipment.
  Model answer: Radiofrequency pulses deposit energy, quantified as specific absorption rate, and can heat tissue, loops of wire and ECG leads, causing burns.
  Model answer: Rapidly switching gradients generate acoustic noise (often over 100 dB) and peripheral nerve stimulation; cryogen loss during a quench causes asphyxiation risk from displaced oxygen.
Stage 2 — Apply the safety system
  Question: How is access controlled and screening performed?
  Model answer: Zones I–IV restrict access, with the scanner room (zone IV) entered only after checklist-based screening by trained staff.
  Model answer: Every implant and device must be documented as MR safe, MR conditional or MR unsafe; unlabelled implants are treated as unsafe until identified.
  Model answer: Only MR-conditional monitoring, pumps and airway equipment enter zone IV, with long extension lines for infusions and remote-controlled ventilation.
Stage 3 — Plan the anaesthetic
  Question: What practical anaesthetic issues follow?
  Model answer: Remote and partly obscured patient access means secured airway, capnography, reliable IV access and a clear evacuation plan to a resuscitation area outside zone IV.
  Model answer: Provide ear protection, temperature care and dose-appropriate depth for immobility, and remove loops from cables and leads.
  Model answer: Rehearse quench and cardiac arrest responses; resuscitation takes place outside the scanner room.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: MRI safety follows directly from physics: a permanent superconducting static field, pulsed radiofrequency excitation and switched gradients each create a distinct hazard. Field strength increases signal but also projectile force and radiofrequency energy deposition, so 3 T scanning demands stricter screening than 1.5 T. Contrast agents raise separate concerns, with gadolinium-based agent choice restricted by renal function.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use a documented screening checklist for patient, staff and equipment; never rely on verbal assurance under time pressure. Anaesthetise where possible outside the magnet or use MR-conditional systems with waveguide-passed lines. Monitor temperature and depth, protect hearing, keep the resuscitation trolley outside zone IV and know who holds the quench button and evacuation responsibility.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not say the magnet is 'switched off between scans' — the static field is permanent. Distinguish MR safe, MR conditional and MR unsafe precisely, and mention SAR heating as a burn mechanism, not just projectile risk.
Take-home: The static field is always on: screen every person, implant and device, use only MR-conditional equipment in zone IV, and resuscitate outside the scanner room.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: MRI physics and safety (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.04.004); Assoc Anaesth 2021: MRI (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.15517)

# X-rays & Radiation Safety
X-ray production, photon–tissue interactions, dose units, ALARA, shielding and dosimetry for anaesthetists

(the target). A high voltage — conventionally
50–150 kVp
— accelerates electrons across the tube; they strike the anode at high velocity.
Two distinct mechanisms then generate X-rays:
Bremsstrahlung ('braking radiation')
— the dominant contributor. As an electron is decelerated and deflected by the field of a tungsten nucleus, the lost kinetic energy is emitted as a photon. This produces a
continuous spectrum
from very low energies up to a maximum equal to the tube voltage in keV.
Characteristic radiation
— when an incident electron ejects an inner-shell (K-shell) tungsten electron, an outer electron drops in to fill the vacancy and releases a photon at a discrete energy (~59 and 67 keV for tungsten). This appears as
line peaks
superimposed on the bremsstrahlung continuum.
controls the maximum photon energy and therefore beam quality (penetration); raising kVp increases mean photon energy and reduces tissue contrast.
(tube current × exposure time) controls beam quantity (photon number) and is the primary determinant of patient dose for a given kVp. Less than 1% of the electron kinetic energy is converted to X-rays — the rest is heat, which is why anodes rotate and are oil-cooled.
Four interactions matter clinically; the first two account for almost all relevant medical physics:
Photoelectric effect
— the photon is fully absorbed by an inner-shell electron, which is ejected. Probability is proportional to
— strongly favoured at low energies and high atomic number. This is what gives the bone–soft-tissue contrast on plain films and why iodinated and barium contrast (high Z) work.
Compton scattering
— the photon is partially absorbed by an outer-shell electron and scattered with reduced energy. Dominates above ~100 keV (CT, fluoroscopy primary beam) and is essentially independent of Z. Compton scattering is the source of the
scatter dose
to staff — the patient becomes the principal scatter source inside the room.
Rayleigh (coherent) scattering
— a minor process where the photon is deflected without losing energy. Contributes a small amount to image noise.
Pair production
— a photon (>1.022 MeV) interacts with a nucleus to create an electron–positron pair. Not relevant in diagnostic imaging but matters in radiotherapy and PET.

half-value layer (HVL)
is the thickness of a given material that halves intensity — for typical 70 kVp scatter, HVL is ~0.2 mm of lead, which is why a 0.5 mm Pb apron attenuates to roughly (½)

Dose modulation
is the headline patient-safety feature: the tube current (mA) is varied in real time with patient diameter (angular and z-axis modulation) and the kVp can be lowered for paediatric and contrast-enhanced studies — together typically halving dose for an equivalent diagnostic image.

Click any descriptor or mode to jump between them.
Anaesthetic relevance:
CT effective doses dwarf plain films — head ~2 mSv, chest ~7 mSv, CTPA 5–10 mSv, abdomen/pelvis ~10 mSv (≈ 100–500 CXRs each). Justification (IR(ME)R 2017) and choice of the lowest-dose adequate protocol are clinical responsibilities, not just radiology decisions. In ICU transfers and intra-operative CT, staff should leave the scanner room or stand behind lead glass during acquisition; only those clinically essential (e.g. managing an unstable airway) remain, wearing a 0.5 mm Pb apron and standing as far from the bore as the case permits.
Distinguish three quantities — the exam favourites:
Activity (becquerel, Bq)
— disintegrations per second of a radionuclide source. Not directly relevant to X-ray equipment.
Absorbed dose (gray, Gy)
— energy deposited per unit mass of tissue (J/kg). A purely physical measurement.
Equivalent dose (sievert, Sv)
— absorbed dose ×
radiation weighting factor (wR)
. wR = 1 for X-rays, γ and β; wR = 20 for α-particles. Sieverts therefore reflect biological effect of the radiation type.
Effective dose (sievert, Sv)
— equivalent dose summed across organs, each weighted by a
tissue weighting factor (wT)
that reflects radiosensitivity (e.g. wT = 0.12 for breast, lung, colon, marrow; 0.04 for thyroid; 0.01 for skin). Effective dose is what is reported in personal dosimetry and for comparing risks across imaging modalities.
(lowest dose for the diagnostic question — the ALARA principle), and
(statutory dose limits). For staff, ALARA reduces to three operational levers:
— minimise screening time, use pulsed rather than continuous fluoroscopy (typical 30–70% dose reduction), avoid 'cine' acquisition unless needed.
— by far the most powerful lever. Dose-rate falls with the inverse square of distance: doubling distance quarters dose; tripling it cuts dose 9-fold. A single step back is usually worth more than any PPE upgrade.
— 0.5 mm Pb-equivalent wrap-around apron (~95% scatter attenuation at 70 kVp), 0.5 mm Pb thyroid shield, leaded glasses (cataract prevention — see deterministic effects), and ceiling-suspended lead screen + table-mounted lead drape. The screen is the single most effective additional measure for the anaesthetist who cannot move the table or beam.
UK Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 (IRR 2017) set the following effective dose limits per calendar year:

Personal dosimetry
uses thermoluminescent (TLD) or optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) badges, read monthly. The standard configuration is a single collar badge worn outside the apron at chest level (estimates effective dose to head/neck/lens) ± a body badge under the apron for true effective dose in high-exposure roles.
Pregnant workers
add a second badge under the apron at waist/abdomen level for foetal dose monitoring.
Stochastic effects
; probability of harm rises with dose, but severity does not. Cancer induction and heritable effects are the principal stochastic risks. Because there is no safe threshold, every avoidable exposure should be avoided.
Deterministic effects
have a
threshold dose
below which the effect does not occur, and severity rises with dose above it. Relevant thresholds for staff:
Lens (cataract)
: 0.5 Gy cumulative (ICRP 2011) — drives mandatory leaded glasses for interventionalists and anaesthetists in IR.
Skin erythema
: ~2 Gy single dose — relevant to long fluoroscopy procedures (TIPS, complex EP ablation, embolisation).
Bone marrow suppression
: ~0.5 Gy single whole-body dose; lethality at ~3–4 Gy without treatment.
Foetal effects
: organogenesis (8–15/56 days post-conception) most sensitive — >100 mGy raises risk of microcephaly and intellectual disability; <50 mGy is generally considered low-risk.
Summary — deterministic vs stochastic, and how risk changes with dose
Deterministic (tissue reactions)
Cell killing — once enough cells in a tissue are lost, function fails
Sub-lethal DNA damage in a surviving cell → mutation → cancer or heritable effect
Yes — clear dose threshold below which the effect does not occur
No threshold (ICRP linear-no-threshold model)
What rises with dose?
of the effect (and probability above threshold approaches 100%)
of the effect — severity is all-or-nothing once it occurs
Days to months (erythema, cataract, marrow suppression)
Years to decades (solid tumours), months to years (leukaemia)
Skin erythema (~2 Gy), cataract (0.5 Gy), marrow suppression (~0.5 Gy), foetal anomalies (~100 mGy)
Solid cancers, leukaemia, heritable mutations
Dominant in clinical practice
High-dose interventional fluoroscopy (TIPS, EP ablation, embolisation, EVAR)
All diagnostic radiology and routine occupational exposure
Mitigated by
Dose limits, procedure planning, leaded glasses, skin-dose monitoring
ALARA — justification, optimisation, time/distance/shielding
Key learning points
Deterministic = dose causes severity
above a threshold;
stochastic = dose changes the probability
of an all-or-nothing harm with no threshold.
Stochastic risk justifies
for routine practice; deterministic thresholds drive specific protections (leaded glasses, skin-dose limits in interventional procedures).
Dose limits (ICRP / IRR17): occupational
20 mSv/yr effective dose
, lens
20 mSv/yr
, skin/extremity
500 mSv/yr
— all set well below deterministic thresholds with a wide stochastic safety margin.
The foetus is a special case — the developing CNS has an effective deterministic threshold (~100 mGy) and is also at higher stochastic risk; declared pregnant workers limit equivalent dose to the abdomen to 1 mSv for the remainder of pregnancy.
Wear a 0.5 mm Pb wrap-around apron, 0.5 mm thyroid shield, and leaded glasses for every fluoroscopic case.
Position behind a ceiling-suspended lead screen during cine runs and DSA acquisitions.
Use long IV/extension lines and remote infusion pumps to allow you to step back during high-dose phases.
Communicate with the radiographer: ask for pulsed fluoroscopy and tight collimation as a routine.
Wear your dosimeter — check it is yours, in date, and read monthly.
Care for the apron: hang it on a stand (not folded); annual integrity testing for cracks.
in resus or ICU transfers, exposure is brief but cumulative for staff who routinely accompany patients. Step out of the room or behind the lead-glass during acquisition; never stay in the bore unless clinically required (e.g. ventilated unstable patient — wear lead and stand at the back).

Doubling the distance cuts dose-rate to ~30 µSv/h (a 4× drop); tripling it to ~13 µSv/h (a 9× drop). Distance is the most powerful single ALARA lever. Combine with a ceiling-suspended lead screen and a 0.5 mm Pb apron and you typically push residual whole-body dose well below 1 µSv/h.
Justifying a CT pulmonary angiogram in a young patient
Justify against the clinical question (a missed PE is high-cost), but in a young woman with a normal CXR and clinically suspected PE, V/Q is often the optimised first-line test. If CTPA is required, use low-dose protocols, dose modulation and lead breast shielding where local protocols allow. Document the discussion in the consent.
Pregnant anaesthetist on the IR list
Continued IR work is usually safe with the additional under-apron dosimeter, full PPE and screen use. Risk-assess monthly; remove from the rota only if doses approach the foetal limit or if procedures place her routinely close to the primary beam (e.g. pain procedures with hand exposure).
X-rays & Radiation Safety
X-ray production, photon–tissue interactions, dose units, and ALARA practice for anaesthetists
Diagnostic X-rays are produced by bombarding a tungsten anode with electrons accelerated across a high-voltage (typically 50–150 kVp) tube — output is a bremsstrahlung continuum plus characteristic K-shell line emissions
kVp controls beam energy (penetration/quality); mAs controls beam quantity (number of photons) — together they determine dose and image contrast
Four photon interactions: photoelectric (∝ Z³/E³, dominant at diagnostic energies, gives bone–soft-tissue contrast), Compton (dominant >100 keV, source of scatter), Rayleigh (minor coherent), pair production (>1.022 MeV only)
Units: activity = becquerel (Bq); absorbed dose = gray (Gy, J/kg); equivalent dose = sievert (Sv) = Gy × wR; effective dose = Sv × tissue weighting factors
ALARA = As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Three pillars: TIME (less exposure), DISTANCE (inverse-square law — doubling distance quarters dose), SHIELDING (0.5 mm Pb apron attenuates ~95% of scatter at 70 kVp)
IRR 2017 occupational limit: 20 mSv/year (avg over 5 years, max 50 mSv/year). Public: 1 mSv/year. Declared-pregnant worker: 1 mSv to the foetus over remainder of pregnancy
Stochastic effects (cancer, hereditary): no threshold, probability rises with dose. Deterministic effects (cataract, skin erythema, marrow suppression): have thresholds — ICRP 2011 lens threshold lowered to 0.5 Gy cumulative
Approximate effective doses: CXR 0.02 mSv · head CT 2 mSv · CTPA 5–10 mSv · abdomen CT 10 mSv · UK background 2.7 mSv/year
Anaesthetist's PPE for fluoroscopy: 0.5 mm Pb wrap-around apron, 0.5 mm thyroid shield, leaded glasses (cataract prevention), and where possible a ceiling-suspended lead screen — plus collar dosimeter outside apron

What are the three principles of radiation protection?
ALARA — As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Achieved by Time (minimise exposure duration), Distance (inverse-square law — doubling distance quarters dose), and Shielding (lead aprons 0.25–0.5 mm Pb equivalent, thyroid collars, lead glasses, mobile screens).

case_bank.title: Radiation exposure in the hybrid theatre
case_bank.text:
Case: Radiation exposure in the hybrid theatre (Imaging & radiation, Foundation)
Patient: A long endovascular aneurysm repair requires prolonged fluoroscopy. You are managing infusions close to the table without a dosimeter or lead apron.
Presentation: A colleague says scatter is negligible at your distance from the image intensifier.
Stage 1 — Quantify the exposure
  Question: What determines your dose?
  Model answer: Scatter dose falls with the inverse square of distance: doubling distance quarters intensity.
  Model answer: Dose also rises with screening time, frame rate, magnification, patient size and steep angulation.
  Model answer: Effective dose in millisieverts weights organ sensitivity; stochastic risk has no threshold, so any exposure carries some risk.
Stage 2 — Apply protection
  Question: What practical measures reduce your dose?
  Model answer: Time, distance and shielding: step back or behind the lead screen during acquisition, wear a correctly fitting lead apron and thyroid shield, and use eye protection for long procedures.
  Model answer: Ask for pulsed fluoroscopy, collimation, last-image hold and reduced magnification.
  Model answer: Wear and read personal dosimetry, and know local dose constraints and pregnancy notification arrangements.
Stage 3 — Know the framework
  Question: What are the regulatory expectations?
  Model answer: Justification, optimisation and dose limitation underpin practice; exposures should be as low as reasonably practicable.
  Model answer: Employers must provide classification, monitoring, local rules and controlled areas; individuals must follow them.
  Model answer: Record patient dose, escalate unusually long screening and report incidents through governance systems.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Occupational exposure in interventional theatres comes almost entirely from scatter, which is greatest on the X-ray tube side of the patient. Because intensity follows the inverse square law, small increases in distance produce large dose reductions, making stepping back the single most effective free intervention. Deterministic effects (skin injury, cataract) have thresholds, whereas stochastic effects are treated as having none.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Combine engineering and behavioural controls: ceiling-mounted and under-table shields, lead aprons and thyroid collars, dosimeters worn at the correct site, pulsed low-dose fluoroscopy and collimation. Plan infusion lines and monitoring so you can work at distance, and use remote lines rather than repeatedly returning to the table. Anyone who is or may be pregnant should follow the local declared-pregnancy pathway.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not answer only 'wear lead'. Cover justification and optimisation, the inverse square law with a worked statement, screening-time factors, dosimetry and the employer/employee duties in the regulations.
Take-home: Scatter dominates staff dose: shorten screening time, step back (dose falls with the square of distance), shield properly and monitor exposure.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: radiation safety (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv055); IR(ME)R 2017 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2017/1322/contents/made)

A single ventilation channel and perilaryngeal seal (classic LMA). Simple rescue oxygenation, but no gastric drainage and less protection from regurgitation.
