# Statistics & Evidence-Based Medicine
Study design, p-values, odds ratios, NNT, sensitivity/specificity, and common statistical tests

Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs)
are the gold standard for evaluating interventions. Randomisation minimises confounding; blinding reduces observer and participant bias.
: neither participant nor investigator knows allocation;
Cohort studies
follow exposed and unexposed groups forward (prospective) or look back (retrospective). They measure
and incidence.
Case-control studies
start with outcome (cases) and compare exposure history with controls — they measure the
odds ratio (OR)
but cannot directly calculate RR.
Cross-sectional studies
measure prevalence at a single time point.
Ecological studies
use population-level data and are prone to the ecological fallacy.
Systematic reviews
sit at the top of the hierarchy of evidence but are only as good as the included studies.
RCT variants
concurrent groups receive different treatments.
each patient receives each treatment, separated by washout; best for stable chronic disease without carry-over.
a 2×2 or larger design tests interventions and interaction efficiently.
tests whether a new treatment is no worse than control by a pre-specified clinically acceptable margin.
Clinical trial phases
first-in-human safety, pharmacokinetics and dose-ranging, usually in few healthy volunteers.
preliminary efficacy, safety and dose selection in affected patients.
large comparative RCTs providing the main efficacy and safety evidence for approval.
post-marketing effectiveness, long-term safety and rare adverse effects.
null hypothesis (H₀)
states there is no difference between groups. The
alternative hypothesis (H₁)
states a difference exists. A
is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as observed, assuming H₀ is true. By convention, p < 0.05 is considered "statistically significant."
Type I error (α)
: rejecting a true null — false positive. The α level is conventionally 0.05.
Type II error (β)
: failing to reject a false null — false negative.
Power (1 − β)
: probability of detecting a true effect; aim for ≥0.8 (80%).
Confidence intervals (CIs)
express the precision of a sample estimate. Strictly: if the study were repeated many times, 95% of the resulting 95% CIs would contain the true population parameter — a single interval either does or does not, so CIs are not a direct probability statement about that interval. A 95% CI that does not cross the null value (0 for differences, 1 for ratios) corresponds to p < 0.05. CIs are more informative than p-values alone — they convey both magnitude and precision.
data type
(nominal, ordinal, interval/ratio) and the
shape of the distribution
. Each measure has a paired measure of spread that should be reported alongside it.
Mean (x̄)
Σx / n
Best for:
symmetric, interval/ratio data (e.g. MAP, weight).
standard deviation (SD), variance, SEM.
middle value when ranked
skewed or ordinal data (e.g. ICU LOS, pain scores, Apgar).
interquartile range (IQR, Q1–Q3), range.
most frequent value
nominal data (e.g. blood group), categorical counts.
frequency table, proportions.
Choosing between them
Symmetric, normally distributed:
mean = median = mode → report mean (SD).
mean is dragged toward the tail → report median (IQR) and consider non-parametric tests.
a single mean can be misleading; report both modes and consider whether two sub-populations are present.
Categorical / nominal:
only the mode is meaningful (e.g. most common ASA grade).
Worked clinical examples
1. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) in a healthy preoperative cohort
mean ± SD →
MAP 92 ± 8 mmHg
the data are continuous, approximately normally distributed and free of meaningful outliers, so the mean is an unbiased central estimate and the SD captures variability efficiently. Use parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA) for between-group comparisons and quote a 95% CI for the mean.
2. ICU length of stay after emergency laparotomy
median (IQR) →
LOS 4 days (IQR 2–8)
LOS is positively skewed and bounded at zero — the mean is dragged up by a handful of long-stay outliers and overstates the "typical" experience. The median resists this; the IQR conveys the spread of the middle 50%. Use non-parametric tests (Mann–Whitney U for two groups, Kruskal–Wallis for three or more), or log-transform before a parametric test.
3. Postoperative pain score (NRS 0–10) at 24 h
11-point scale. In 80 day-case patients the most frequent score is 2 (n = 26), median is 3, IQR 2–5; only a few patients report ≥8.
median (IQR) — and the mode if you want to highlight the typical experience →
NRS 3 (IQR 2–5), mode 2
ordinal categories don't have equal arithmetic spacing, so the mean (e.g. 3.4) implies a precision the scale doesn't support. The median respects rank and the mode identifies the commonest response. Compare groups with non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired, Mann–Whitney U for unpaired); for proportions above a clinical threshold (e.g. NRS ≥4) use χ² or Fisher's exact.
Key learning points
= Σx / n. Uses every value, so it is the most efficient summary for symmetric interval/ratio data — but is dragged toward outliers and the long tail of skewed data. Pair with
(or SEM for an estimate of the mean).
= the middle (50th centile) value when ranked. Robust to outliers and skew because it depends on rank, not magnitude. Pair with
IQR (Q1–Q3)
; it is the preferred summary for skewed or ordinal data.
= the most frequent value (peak of the distribution). The only valid measure for nominal categorical data, and useful for spotting bimodal datasets; unstable in small samples.
In a perfectly symmetric distribution:
mean = median = mode
. As skew increases, the mean moves furthest, the median shifts modestly, and the mode stays at the peak — the gap between them is itself a clue to skew.
Choose the summary that matches the data type and shape, then choose the corresponding test family: parametric (t-test/ANOVA) for mean ± SD on normal data; non-parametric (Mann–Whitney/Wilcoxon) for median (IQR) on skewed data.
spread (dispersion)
quantify this scatter and are essential for choosing reference ranges, statistical tests and clinical thresholds.
Range = max − min
quick descriptive summary; vital signs charts ("HR 60–110 bpm overnight").
Interquartile range (IQR)
IQR = Q3 − Q1 (middle 50% of data)
skewed or ordinal data — pair with median (e.g. ICU LOS, NRS pain).
Variance (s²)
s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1)
intermediate quantity — most often reported as its square root, the SD.
Standard deviation (SD)
SD = √s² (same units as the data)
symmetric interval/ratio data — pair with mean.
Standard error of the mean (SEM)
SEM = SD / √n
sample mean
, not the spread of individuals. Shrinks as the sample grows and forms the basis of the 95% CI (≈ x̄ ± 1.96 × SEM). Reporting "mean ± SEM" makes data look tighter than it is — usually inappropriate as a descriptive statistic.
precision of an estimate; building confidence intervals.
Coefficient of variation (CV)
CV = SD / mean × 100%
comparing variability across units; lab assay quality control.
Quick reference — match the spread to the centre
Data shape
Test family
Symmetric / normal
SD (and 95% CI for the mean)
Parametric (t-test, ANOVA)
Skewed / ordinal
IQR (Q1–Q3); range
Non-parametric (Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis)
Nominal / categorical
Frequency table, proportions
χ², Fisher exact
— calculated from ranked values; robust to skew.
— calculated from deviations around the mean; assume meaningful arithmetic on the values.
describes individuals;
describes the precision of the mean (SEM = SD/√n).
Always report a measure of spread alongside the centre — a mean or median in isolation hides clinically important variability.
normal (Gaussian) distribution
is a symmetrical, bell-shaped probability density curve defined entirely by its mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ). Many biological variables — height, blood pressure, haemoglobin, sample means under the central limit theorem — approximate this shape, which is why it underpins most parametric statistics.
empirical 68–95–99.7 rule
states that ±1σ contains ~68% of values, ±2σ ~95% and ±3σ ~99.7%. The same geometry generates
confidence intervals
: a 95% CI is the mean ± 1.96 × standard error — the central band that would capture the true population mean in 95 of 100 repeated samples. Use the toggle to compare 90%, 95% and 99% intervals; wider intervals trade precision for greater confidence.
Worked example
Calculating a 95% confidence interval
42 s
in 64 patients, with a standard deviation of
8 s
. Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the mean and interpret it.
SE = SD / √n = 8 / √64 = 8 / 8 = 1.0 s
95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SE = 42 ± 1.96 × 1.0
= 42 ± 1.96 s → 40.04 s to 43.96 s
42 s (95% CI 40.0–44.0 s)
include a clinically meaningful comparator (e.g. propofol's typical 30 s), the new agent is unlikely to be non-inferior on speed of onset.
Confidence interval vs standard deviation
describes the
spread of individual values
in the sample. The
95% CI of the mean
precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean
. Crucially, the CI shrinks as the sample grows (because SE = SD/√n), whereas the SD does not — adding patients makes you more certain about the average, not less variable as individuals.
Standard error (SE) — the bridge between SD and CI
standard error of the mean
is the standard deviation of the
sampling distribution of the mean
: if you repeated the study many times, the sample means would themselves scatter around the true population mean, and that scatter has SD equal to the SE.
SE = SD / √n
measures variability between
— a property of the data, roughly stable as n grows.
measures variability of the
— a property of the estimate, shrinks with √n.
95% CI
is built directly from SE:
x̄ ± 1.96 × SE
. So SE is literally the "half-width unit" of the CI.
Quick example.
SD = 8 s, n = 64 → SE = 8/√64 =
1.0 s
; 95% CI ≈ mean ± 1.96 s. Quadruple the sample to n = 256 and SE halves to 0.5 s, halving the CI width — but the SD still describes 8 s of between-patient variability.
95% confidence interval
Question answered
How spread out are the individual values?
How precisely have we estimated the population mean?
√[Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)]
x̄ ± 1.96 × SD/√n
Effect of larger n
Stable — describes the population's natural variability.
Narrows in proportion to 1/√n.
Used for
Reference ranges, describing a sample.
Inference about the underlying population, significance testing.
Same SD, very different CI
120 mmHg
with an
SD of 15 mmHg
. Study A enrols
n = 25
; Study B enrols
n = 400
. Compare the 95% CI of the mean.
Study A (n = 25)
SE = 15 / √25 = 15 / 5 = 3.0 mmHg
95% CI = 120 ± 1.96 × 3.0
= 120 ± 5.88 → 114.1 – 125.9 mmHg
Study B (n = 400)
SE = 15 / √400 = 15 / 20 = 0.75 mmHg
95% CI = 120 ± 1.96 × 0.75
= 120 ± 1.47 → 118.5 – 121.5 mmHg
the SD is identical (15 mmHg) — both studies show the same biological variability between individuals, and the reference range (mean ± 2 SD ≈ 90–150 mmHg) is unchanged. But Study B's CI is roughly four times narrower because n is sixteen times larger (√16 = 4). Study B has therefore
estimated the population mean four times more precisely
, even though the spread of individual readings is the same.
use SD when describing how variable patients are, and CI when describing how confident you are about an average. Quoting "mean ± SD" tells the reader about the population; "mean (95% CI)" tells them about the estimate.
rather than perfectly Gaussian. Skew is named for the direction of the long tail:
positive (right) skew
has a tail extending toward high values (mean > median > mode), while
negative (left) skew
has a tail toward low values (mean < median < mode).
median and IQR
, choose
non-parametric tests
, or apply a transformation (commonly a log-transform for positively skewed variables) before running parametric analyses.
Relative Risk (RR)
= incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed. Calculable only from cohort studies or RCTs.
= (a×d) / (b×c) from a 2×2 table. In case-control studies, OR approximates RR when the outcome is rare (<10%) — the
rare disease assumption
. OR is always further from 1 than the corresponding RR.
Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR)
= control event rate − treatment event rate.
Relative Risk Reduction (RRR)
= ARR / control event rate.
Number Needed to Treat (NNT)
= 1/ARR. Similarly,
= 1/absolute risk increase.
Hazard Ratio (HR)
is used in survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier curves, Cox regression) and accounts for time-to-event data. An HR of 0.7 means a 30% reduction in event rate at any given time point.
Kaplan–Meier analysis
plots time on the x-axis and estimated survival on the y-axis as a stepped curve, falling whenever an event occurs. A censored participant—lost to follow-up or event-free when follow-up ends—contributes information until censoring and is marked with a tick. Median survival is where the curve crosses 50%; the log-rank test compares whole survival curves.
= TP / (TP + FN) — proportion of true positives correctly identified. A highly sensitive test, when negative, helps
rule out
disease (
= TN / (TN + FP) — proportion of true negatives correctly identified. A highly specific test, when positive, helps
rule in
= TP / (TP + FP) — depends heavily on disease prevalence.
= TN / (TN + FN). PPV rises with higher prevalence; NPV falls. This is why screening tests in low-prevalence populations generate many false positives.
Likelihood Ratios (LR)
combine sensitivity and specificity. LR+ = sens / (1 − spec); LR− = (1 − sens) / spec. LRs are prevalence-independent and applied to pre-test probability via Fagan's nomogram or Bayes' theorem.
ROC curves
plot sensitivity (y-axis) against 1 − specificity (x-axis). The AUC (c-statistic) measures overall discriminative ability: 0.5 = no discrimination, 1.0 = perfect; AUC >0.8 is generally considered good.
Parametric Tests (normal distribution assumed)
Student's t-test
— compares means of 2 groups (unpaired) or before/after (paired)
— compares means of ≥3 groups; post-hoc tests (Tukey, Bonferroni) identify which pairs differ
Pearson's r
— linear association between two continuous variables (−1 to +1)
Linear regression
— models a continuous outcome as a function of predictors
Non-Parametric Tests (no distribution assumption)
Mann-Whitney U
— unpaired comparison of 2 groups
Wilcoxon signed-rank
— paired comparison
— compares ≥3 groups
Spearman's ρ
— correlation for non-normal or ordinal data
Categorical Data Tests
Chi-squared (χ²)
— compares proportions between groups (expected frequency ≥5)
Fisher's exact
— used when expected frequencies are small (<5)
McNemar's test
— paired categorical data
Logistic regression
— binary outcome with multiple predictors, yields OR
Selection bias
: systematic differences in who is enrolled (e.g., Berkson's bias).
Information bias
: systematic measurement errors, including recall bias (case-control) and observer bias (unblinded assessors).
occurs when a third variable is associated with both exposure and outcome. Address via randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification, and multivariable regression.
Intention-to-treat (ITT)
preserves randomisation;
only includes compliant patients and is more prone to bias.
Internal validity
: freedom from bias within the study.
External validity (generalisability)
: applicability to other populations. Blinding, allocation concealment, and adequate follow-up are key determinants of internal validity in RCTs.
systematic review
uses a pre-defined protocol (PRISMA) to identify, appraise and synthesise all relevant studies. A
forest plot
: each study as a point estimate with CI, pooled estimate as a diamond.
models assume one true effect;
models allow between-study variation and produce wider CIs.
Publication bias
is assessed using
funnel plots
— asymmetry suggests bias. Egger's test provides a formal statistical assessment.
GRADE methodology
GRADE separates certainty of evidence from strength of recommendation. Certainty is rated
high, moderate, low or very low
. Risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias downgrade certainty; a large effect, dose–response gradient or plausible residual confounding that would reduce an observed effect can upgrade observational evidence. Recommendations then balance certainty with benefits, harms, values and resource use.
Bayes' theorem
: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. The post-test probability depends not only on test performance (sensitivity/specificity) but also on the
pre-test probability (prevalence)
NNT for a perioperative intervention
ARR 2%, RRR 33%, NNT 50 — i.e. 50 patients must receive perioperative beta-blockade to prevent one additional 30-day death.
Post-test probability with likelihood ratios
≈66%. The positive test raises the probability of PE from 30% to 66% — illustrating why pre-test probability matters as much as the test characteristics.
Statistics & Evidence-Based Medicine
Study design, hypothesis testing, p-values, confidence intervals, odds ratios, and common statistical tests
A p-value is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the data, assuming the null hypothesis is true — NOT the probability the null is true
Type I error (α): rejecting a true null (false positive). Type II error (β): failing to reject a false null. Power = 1 − β
OR compares odds of exposure in cases vs controls; RR compares incidence — RR is only valid in cohort/RCT designs
Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 / absolute risk reduction (ARR). Contextualises clinical significance
Parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA) assume normally distributed data; non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis) do not
Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) — rules OUT disease (SnNOut); Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) — rules IN (SpPIn)
Hierarchy of evidence: systematic reviews/meta-analyses > RCTs > cohort > case-control > case series > expert opinion
Introduction
Study Design
Hypothesis Testing & p-Values
Measures of Central Tendency & Spread
Measures of Spread (Dispersion)
Normal Distribution & Confidence Intervals
Skewed Distributions
Measures of Effect
Diagnostic Test Performance
Common Statistical Tests
Bias, Confounding & Validity
Systematic Reviews & Meta-Analysis
Bayesian Concepts
What is the difference between type I and type II error?
Type I (α) — false positive: rejecting a true null hypothesis. Set conventionally at 0.05. Type II (β) — false negative: failing to reject a false null hypothesis. Power = 1 − β, usually set at 0.8. Type I error is reduced by smaller α; Type II error by larger sample size or effect size.
Explain absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction and number needed to treat.
ARR = control event rate − treatment event rate. RRR = ARR / control event rate. NNT = 1 / ARR. Example: mortality 10 % → 8 %. ARR = 2 %, RRR = 20 %, NNT = 50 (treat 50 patients to prevent one death). RRR alone exaggerates clinically small effects; always quote ARR and NNT.
What is the difference between sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratio?
Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives) — ability to detect disease. Specificity = true negatives / (true negatives + false positives) — ability to exclude disease. Likelihood ratio + = sensitivity / (1 − specificity); LR+ >10 strongly increases post-test probability. Unlike PPV/NPV, LRs are independent of disease prevalence.
Distinguish RCT, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional and ecological designs and their measures of effect
Define p-value, type I/II error, power and confidence intervals correctly
Calculate and interpret RR, OR, ARR, RRR and NNT/NNH from a 2×2 table
Choose the correct statistical test based on data type, group number and distribution
Interpret diagnostic test performance (sensitivity, specificity, PPV/NPV, LR, ROC)
An RCT of perioperative beta-blockade reports 30-day mortality of 4% in the intervention group vs 6% in the control group. Calculate the absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction and number needed to treat.
Control event rate (CER) = 6% = 0.06 Experimental event rate (EER) = 4% = 0.04 ARR = CER − EER = 0.06 − 0.04 = 0.02 (2%) RRR = ARR / CER = 0.02 / 0.06 = 0.33 (33%) NNT = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.02 = 50
A patient has a pre-test probability of pulmonary embolism of 30%. A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 80%. What is the post-test probability if the test is positive?
LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) = 0.90 / 0.20 = 4.5 Pre-test odds = 0.30 / 0.70 = 0.43 Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR+ = 0.43 × 4.5 = 1.93 Post-test probability = 1.93 / (1 + 1.93) = 0.66 (66%)

# The Cardiac Cycle Pressure-volume loops, Wiggers diagram, cardiac output aortic ~80 mmHg) → isovolumetric relaxation (aortic closes, dicrotic notch) → rapid filling (mitral opens when LV CPP = aortic DBP − LVEDP 45 mmHg (normal >60). only in diastole O₂ supply ↓ (shorter diastole, low CPP) and demand ↑ (HR, wall tension) → subendocardial ischaemia. Cannon a waves = atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve — occurs when atrial and ventricular systole coincide (AV dissociation). cannon waves = intermittent dissociation → ventricular tachycardia (AV dissociation present in ~50% of beats; ECG shows dissociated p-waves marching through). Regular cannon waves = junctional rhythm or complete heart block (consistent dissociation every beat). ventricular tachycardia (isovolumetric contraction + ejection) and (isovolumetric relaxation + filling). At a heart rate of 70 bpm, the cycle lasts ~860 ms (systole ~300 ms, diastole ~560 ms). As heart rate rises, diastole shortens disproportionately, compromising filling and coronary perfusion. Chamber / Vessel Systolic (mmHg) Diastolic / Mean (mmHg) Right atrium (CVP) mean 2–6 Right ventricle Pulmonary artery 8–15 (mean 10–20) PCWP / LA mean 6–12 Left ventricle 3–12 (LVEDP) 60–90 (mean 70–105) LVEDV ~120 mL · LVESV ~50 mL · SV ~70 mL · EF ~55–70% CO = HR × SV ≈ 5 L/min · CI 2.5–4 L/min/m² SVR 800–1500 · PVR 50–150 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ 1. It is best heard at the apex. results from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole. Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during inspiration: negative intrathoracic pressure increases systemic venous return and RV preload, increasing RV stroke volume and prolonging RV ejection so P2 is delayed. At the same time, transient pooling in the expanded pulmonary vascular bed slightly reduces LV filling and shortens LV ejection, bringing A2 earlier. The A2–P2 interval therefore becomes audible and narrows again on expiration — early diastolic, rapid filling against a stiff or volume-loaded ventricle (HF, MR; normal in young). — late diastolic, atrial contraction into a non-compliant ventricle (LVH, AS, ischaemia); absent in AF. Wide fixed split S2 — ASD. Reversed split — LBBB, severe AS. Opening snap — mitral stenosis. Ejection click — bicuspid AV / AS. Lower pressure system — RV peak ~25 mmHg vs LV ~120 mmHg; thinner, crescentic geometry. Earlier opening, later closure — pulmonary valve opens before aortic and closes after, producing physiological splitting of S2. Continuous ejection profile — low PVR allows ejection throughout most of systole, with shorter isovolumetric phases than the LV. — small rises in PVR (hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, PE) markedly reduce RV stroke volume. Ventricular interdependence — shared septum and pericardium mean RV dilation impairs LV filling (acute PE, RV infarct, tamponade). Wave / descent Pathological correlate Atrial contraction Absent in AF; large in TS, PHT, RVH; cannon in CHB / VT / junctional rhythm TV bulging into RA in early systole Rarely visible clinically Atrial relaxation + downward AV ring movement Prominent in tamponade & constrictive pericarditis Atrial filling against closed TV Giant in TR ("cv" or systolic wave) Rapid atrial emptying when TV opens Steep in constrictive pericarditis ("M/W"); blunted in tamponade Left coronary flow occurs predominantly in diastole because intramyocardial pressure during systole exceeds aortic pressure in the subendocardium. RV perfusion occurs throughout the cycle because RV intramural pressure is low. Coronary Perfusion Pressure (CPP) ≈ Aortic Diastolic Pressure − LVEDP Tachycardia shortens diastole more than systole → reduced subendocardial perfusion (rate control in AS, IHD). Aortic regurgitation and severe hypotension lower diastolic pressure and CPP. LV hypertrophy raises LVEDP and intramural pressure, predisposing to subendocardial ischaemia. , or ejection fraction (load-dependent). dP/dt is the maximal rate of LV or arterial pressure rise and reflects contractile force, although loading and arterial waveform affect non-invasive estimates. Pulse-contour systems such as LiDCO and PiCCO provide continuous CO and derived indices/trends; interpret changes rather than treating any single value as load-independent Heart Rate & Rhythm Reading the pressure–volume loop Bottom right: mitral valve closes at LVEDV; isovolumetric contraction rises vertically at constant volume. Top right: LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens; ejection moves left across the top. Top left: aortic valve closes at LVESV; isovolumetric relaxation falls vertically. Bottom left: LV pressure falls below LA pressure and the mitral valve opens; diastolic filling returns rightwards. Loop width is stroke volume ; enclosed area is stroke work . Increased preload shifts the right boundary right and widens the loop; increased afterload makes it taller and narrower with higher ESV; increased contractility steepens ESPVR, shifts ESV left and widens the loop. Use the sliders below to reproduce each change Pressure–Volume Loop Frank–Starling Curve Grade I (impaired relaxation) — E/A < 0.8, prolonged DT. It comprises systole (isovolumetric contraction + ejection) and diastole (isovolumetric relaxation + filling). At a heart rate of 70 bpm, the cycle lasts ~860 ms (systole ~300 ms, diastole ~560 ms). As heart rate rises, diastole shortens disproportionately, compromising filling and coronary perfusion.

Approximate adult resting values you should be able to quote in the viva.

Chamber / Vessel Systolic (mmHg) Diastolic / Mean (mmHg) Volumes

LVEDV ~120 mL · LVESV ~50 mL · SV ~70 mL · EF ~55–70%

Output

CO = HR × SV ≈ 5 L/min · CI 2.5–4 L/min/m²

Resistance

SVR 800–1500 · PVR 50–150 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵

 1. Atrial Systole

Corresponds to the P wave on ECG. Atrial contraction contributes the final 15–25% of ventricular filling (the ). This becomes increasingly important at higher heart rates when passive filling time is reduced. Loss of atrial systole (e.g., atrial fibrillation) can reduce cardiac output by up to 25%.

2. Isovolumetric Contraction

Begins with mitral valve closure (S1) after the QRS complex triggers ventricular depolarisation. All valves are closed; ventricular pressure rises rapidly with no change in volume. LV pressure must exceed aortic diastolic pressure (~80 mmHg) before the aortic valve opens. This phase lasts ~50 ms.

3. Rapid Ejection

The aortic valve opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure. Approximately two-thirds of the stroke volume is ejected during this phase. Peak LV and aortic pressures occur here (~120 mmHg). Aortic flow velocity is maximal.

4. Reduced Ejection

Ventricular repolarisation occurs (T wave). Ejection rate decreases as the pressure gradient across the aortic valve diminishes. The remaining one-third of stroke volume is ejected. LV pressure begins to fall below aortic pressure, but momentum maintains forward flow briefly.

5. Isovolumetric Relaxation

The aortic valve closes, producing S2 and the dicrotic notch on the aortic pressure trace. All valves are again closed. LV pressure falls rapidly with no change in volume. When LV pressure falls below LA pressure, the mitral valve opens and filling begins.

6. Rapid Filling

The mitral valve opens and blood flows rapidly from LA to LV down the pressure gradient. This passive filling accounts for approximately 70–80% of ventricular filling. A third heart sound (S3) may be heard at the end of this phase in young or pathological hearts.

7. Diastasis (Reduced Filling)

LA and LV pressures equilibrate; filling slows considerably. This phase is shortened at high heart rates and is the first to be compromised with tachycardia, which is why diastolic filling time is rate-dependent and why tachycardia reduces cardiac output in patients with diastolic dysfunction.

The LA pressure trace shows three positive waves and two descents:

    S1 is caused by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the onset of ventricular systole. It is best heard at the apex. S2 results from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole. Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during inspiration: negative intrathoracic pressure increases systemic venous return and RV preload, increasing RV stroke volume and prolonging RV ejection so P2 is delayed. At the same time, transient pooling in the expanded pulmonary vascular bed slightly reduces LV filling and shortens LV ejection, bringing A2 earlier. The A2–P2 interval therefore becomes audible and narrows again on expiration The right ventricle (RV) follows the same sequence of phases but operates at much lower pressures. Key differences relevant to anaesthesia and intensive care:

      The CVP trace reflects right atrial pressure and shares the same a, c, v wave structure as the LA trace but is directly visible at the bedside as the JVP. Recognising abnormal waves is an FFICM exam staple.

      Wave / descent Mechanism Pathological correlate Left coronary flow occurs predominantly in diastole because intramyocardial pressure during systole exceeds aortic pressure in the subendocardium. RV perfusion occurs throughout the cycle because RV intramural pressure is low.

      • Coronary Perfusion Pressure (CPP) ≈ Aortic Diastolic Pressure − LVEDP.
      • Tachycardia shortens diastole more than systole → reduced subendocardial perfusion (rate control in AS, IHD).
      • Aortic regurgitation and severe hypotension lower diastolic pressure and CPP.
      • LV hypertrophy raises LVEDP and intramural pressure, predisposing to subendocardial ischaemia.
      Preload

      LVEDV — determined by venous return, atrial contraction, ventricular compliance, intrathoracic pressure and cycle length. Estimated by CVP, PCWP, IVC distensibility or dynamic indices (PPV, SVV). Static filling pressures describe current loading but poorly predict fluid response. PPV/SVV exploit cyclic heart–lung interactions during positive-pressure ventilation: a preload-responsive ventricle shows larger respiratory changes in stroke volume. They are unreliable with spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia, low tidal volume, open chest, RV failure or poor lung compliance.

      Afterload

      Wall stress during ejection; approximated by SVR and aortic impedance. Influenced by aortic compliance, viscosity and outflow obstruction (AS, HOCM). Laplace: σ = P·r / 2h. SVR = 80 × (MAP − CVP) / CO, normally about 800–1200 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵; it is only an approximation of LV afterload because it omits pulsatile impedance and wall geometry.

      Contractility

      Load-independent inotropy. Best assessed by ESPVR slope, dP/dtmax, or ejection fraction (load-dependent). dP/dtmax is the maximal rate of LV or arterial pressure rise and reflects contractile force, although loading and arterial waveform affect non-invasive estimates. Pulse-contour systems such as LiDCO and PiCCO provide continuous CO and derived indices/trends; interpret changes rather than treating any single value as load-independent Heart Rate & Rhythm

      CO = HR × SV. Optimal HR balances filling time vs output. Loss of AV synchrony (AF, junctional, VVI pacing) loses the atrial kick — significant in stiff ventricles (AS, HCM, diastolic dysfunction).

Loop width is stroke volume; enclosed area is stroke work. Increased preload shifts the right boundary right and widens the loop; increased afterload makes it taller and narrower with higher ESV; increased contractility steepens ESPVR, shifts ESV left and widens the loop. Use the sliders below to reproduce each change Diastole has four sub-phases: isovolumetric relaxation, rapid filling, diastasis and atrial systole. Active relaxation (lusitropy) is ATP-dependent (SERCA reuptake of Ca²⁺) and is impaired by ischaemia. Passive stiffness depends on titin, collagen, fibrosis and hypertrophy.

case_bank.title: Spinal anaesthesia in severe aortic stenosis
case_bank.text:
Case: Spinal anaesthesia in severe aortic stenosis (Cardiovascular, Intermediate)
Patient: An 82-year-old with severe aortic stenosis (peak gradient 70 mmHg, valve area 0.7 cm²) needs hemiarthroplasty after a hip fracture.
Presentation: A single-shot spinal is proposed. Ten minutes after injection the systolic pressure falls from 150 to 80 mmHg and the patient becomes confused.
Stage 1 — Explain the physiology
  Question: Why is this fall in pressure so dangerous?
  Model answer: The concentrically hypertrophied ventricle is stiff: filling depends on atrial contraction and adequate diastolic time, so tachycardia and loss of sinus rhythm are poorly tolerated.
  Model answer: Stroke volume is relatively fixed across the stenotic valve, so cardiac output cannot rise to compensate for vasodilation.
  Model answer: Coronary perfusion of a hypertrophied ventricle occurs almost entirely in diastole and depends on aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure — hypotension rapidly causes subendocardial ischaemia.
Stage 2 — Treat the hypotension
  Question: What is your immediate management?
  Model answer: Restore afterload early with a vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine or metaraminol rather than relying on fluid alone.
  Model answer: Maintain sinus rhythm and a controlled rate (roughly 60–80 beats per minute); treat new atrial fibrillation urgently.
  Model answer: Give measured fluid to preserve preload, keep the patient in a head-down tilt if needed, and give oxygen while reassessing.
Stage 3 — Reconsider the technique
  Question: How would you plan the anaesthetic for the next such patient?
  Model answer: Either a carefully titrated technique with invasive arterial monitoring and vasopressor infusion prepared before block, or a general anaesthetic with slow induction and the same monitoring.
  Model answer: Avoid rapid-onset sympathectomy and large-dose single-shot spinals in fixed-output lesions; consider incremental epidural or low-dose spinal plus nerve block for hip fracture.
  Model answer: Escalate to senior and cardiology review, and do not delay hip fracture surgery unduly for investigations that will not change management.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Severe aortic stenosis converts a normally compliant, output-adaptable circulation into a fixed-output, pressure-dependent one. The ventricular pressure–volume loop is shifted left and steepened, so small volume changes cause large pressure changes; the transvalvular gradient means systolic ventricular pressure greatly exceeds aortic pressure, increasing wall stress and oxygen demand at the same time as diastolic perfusion pressure falls.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Prepare invasive arterial monitoring and a vasopressor infusion before establishing any sympathectomy. Aim for sinus rhythm, adequate preload, normal-to-high systemic vascular resistance and avoidance of tachycardia. Treat hypotension immediately with a vasoconstrictor; if arrest occurs, resuscitation is often ineffective because cardiac massage cannot generate flow across a critically stenotic valve, so prevention is the whole strategy.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not answer 'give fluid' alone, and do not describe ephedrine as first choice where tachycardia will shorten diastole. State the fixed stroke volume, the diastolic coronary perfusion argument and the rhythm target explicitly.
Take-home: In severe aortic stenosis, output is fixed and coronary perfusion is diastolic: protect afterload, preload and sinus rhythm, and monitor invasively before you block.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: the cardiac cycle (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mki024)

It is the product of cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance (MAP = CO × SVR), so any control system must act on heart rate, stroke volume (preload, contractility, afterload), vessel calibre, or circulating volume. The body integrates these effectors through three overlapping time-domains: a fast neural loop, an intermediate neurohormonal loop, and a slow renal–volume loop.

The vasomotor centre in the rostral ventrolateral medulla sets a tonic sympathetic outflow to resistance arterioles and the heart, with continuous parasympathetic counterbalance from the nucleus ambiguus. Sensors feeding this centre are mechanical (high-pressure baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch; low-pressure cardiopulmonary stretch receptors in atria and great veins) and chemical (peripheral and central chemoreceptors). case_bank.title: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting
case_bank.text:
Case: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting (Cardiovascular, Advanced)
Patient: A young adult admitted with prolonged vomiting receives ondansetron and a macrolide. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and magnesium 0.5 mmol/L.
Presentation: The monitor shows a broad, twisting polymorphic tachycardia that self-terminates. QTc before the event was 510 ms.
Stage 1 — Explain the mechanism
  Question: Why has this rhythm occurred?
  Model answer: Phase 3 repolarisation depends mainly on the delayed rectifier potassium currents IKr and IKs; blocking IKr prolongs the action potential and the QT interval.
  Model answer: Prolonged repolarisation permits reactivation of L-type calcium current, producing early afterdepolarisations and triggered beats.
  Model answer: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia reduce repolarisation reserve, so drug effects that are usually tolerated become arrhythmogenic.
Stage 2 — Treat the arrhythmia
  Question: What is your immediate management?
  Model answer: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate even if magnesium is normal, correct potassium towards the upper normal range and stop all QT-prolonging drugs.
  Model answer: Treat sustained or pulseless episodes with defibrillation and follow advanced life support; consider overdrive pacing or isoprenaline for pause-dependent, bradycardia-related torsades.
  Model answer: Avoid class Ia and class III antiarrhythmics, which prolong repolarisation further.
Stage 3 — Prevent recurrence
  Question: What ongoing plan is needed?
  Model answer: Review every drug on the chart against a QT-prolonging list, including antiemetics, antipsychotics, macrolides, antifungals and methadone.
  Model answer: Monitor electrolytes and QTc repeatedly, especially with ongoing vomiting, diuretics or renal replacement.
  Model answer: Refer for cardiology assessment and family screening if congenital long QT syndrome is suspected.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: The cardiac action potential's plateau and repolarisation reflect a balance between inward calcium and outward potassium currents. Repolarisation reserve is the redundancy in this system; congenital channel variants, electrolyte depletion, bradycardia and multiple IKr-blocking drugs erode it additively. Torsades de pointes is the clinical expression of triggered activity on a prolonged, heterogeneous repolarisation substrate.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarisations and is first-line even with normal levels. Keep potassium above 4.5 mmol/L in this setting, remove precipitating drugs, and maintain a heart rate that shortens repolarisation when torsades is pause-dependent. Continuous ECG monitoring with QTc measurement, defibrillator availability and a documented drug-avoidance list should follow the patient.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not give amiodarone reflexively for a broad-complex tachycardia that is torsades. Distinguish polymorphic from monomorphic VT, and name IKr blockade and early afterdepolarisations rather than saying 'the QT was long'.
Take-home: Torsades reflects lost repolarisation reserve: give magnesium, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs and avoid further class III agents.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: cardiac electrophysiology (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkm013); Vaughan Williams classification (https://doi.org/10.1016/0306-039X(75)90019-7)

entries.text:
# Lung Mechanics Compliance, resistance, surfactant, work of breathing = [ [ "What is the difference between static and dynamic compliance?", "Static compliance = ΔV / (plateau pressure − PEEP) — measured at zero flow; reflects elastic properties of lung and chest wall. Normal 60–100 mL/cmH₂O. Dynamic compliance = ΔV / (peak − PEEP) — includes the resistive component, always lower than static. A widening gap between peak and plateau suggests increased airway resistance (bronchospasm, secretions, kinked tube)." ], [ "Define FRC and explain why it falls under anaesthesia.", "Functional Residual Capacity = volume in the lungs at the end of normal tidal expiration ≈ 30 mL/kg (~2.4 L in a 70 kg adult). FRC falls 15–20 % on induction (loss of diaphragmatic tone, supine position, loss of intercostal activity), and another 30–40 % with paralysis. If FRC drops below closing capacity, small airways close in dependent zones → atelectasis and shunt — mitigated by PEEP, recruitment manoeuvres and lower FiO₂." ], [ "State the equation of motion of the respiratory system.", "P = (V / C) + (Flow × R) + PEEP. Pressure applied to the airway = elastic component (volume ÷ compliance) + resistive component (flow × resistance) + baseline PEEP. Used to interpret ventilator waveforms: plateau pressure isolates the elastic load, peak − plateau isolates resistance." ] ]; const objectives = [ "Define static and dynamic compliance and explain why dynamic Driving pressure ΔP = P − PEEP = 28 − 12 = 16 cmH₂O Static C = Vt / ΔP = 420 / 16 ≈ 26 mL/cmH₂O (severely reduced). Amato 2015: ΔP > 15 cmH₂O independently predicts mortality in ARDS. τ = R × C = 25 × 0.05 = 1.25 s 3τ (95% emptying) ≈ 3.75 s Total cycle at 20/min = 3 s; expiratory time = 2 s — well below 3τ → auto-PEEP. VD/VT = (PaCO₂ − PĒCO₂) / PaCO₂ = (5.3 − 2.1) / 5.3 = Physiological VD = 0.60 × 500 = 300 mL (normal ≈ 150 mL). Doubled dead-space fraction with widened EtCO₂–PaCO₂ gap is classic for PE. High VD/VT supports PE — escalate to CTPA, anticoagulate if no contraindication. Lung Volumes & Capacities Compliance Curves Compliance = ΔV / ΔP (ml/cmH₂O). It measures the distensibility of the lung or chest wall. Normal lung compliance ≈ 200 ml/cmH₂O. Chest wall compliance ≈ 200 ml/cmH₂O. Total respiratory system compliance ≈ 100 ml/cmH₂O (reciprocals add: 1/Ctotal = 1/Clung + 1/Cchest wall). Static compliance is measured at zero flow (plateau pressure). Dynamic compliance Conditions Affecting Compliance Decreased lung compliance : pulmonary fibrosis, ARDS, pulmonary oedema, atelectasis, pneumonia. Decreased chest wall compliance : obesity, kyphoscoliosis, circumferential burns, abdominal distension. Increased compliance : emphysema (loss of elastic recoil). Laplace's Law relates the pressure across a curved surface to its wall tension and radius of curvature. For a (two surfaces): P = 2T / r ; for a P = T / r . The clinical significance is the same in both cases — for a given wall tension, pressure rises steeply as radius falls. Pulmonary surfactant resolves the paradox by lowering surface tension preferentially in smaller alveoli, equalising the distending pressures and preventing collapse. , cites: [ ], }, ]; const LungMechanicsTopic = () => { return ( Lung mechanics describes the forces that move air into and out of the lungs. Understanding compliance, resistance, time constants, surfactant, and the work of breathing is fundamental to ventilator management and respiratory physiology.

The four primary lung volumes (IRV, TV, ERV, RV) combine to form four capacities (IC, FRC, VC, TLC). Only RV, FRC, and TLC cannot be measured by spirometry alone.

Explore the pressure-volume relationship of the lung, chest wall, and total respiratory system.

Compliance = ΔV / ΔP (ml/cmH₂O). It measures the distensibility of the lung or chest wall. Normal lung compliance ≈ 200 ml/cmH₂O. Chest wall compliance ≈ 200 ml/cmH₂O. Total respiratory system compliance ≈ 100 ml/cmH₂O (reciprocals add: 1/Ctotal = 1/Clung + 1/Cchest wall).

Static compliance is measured at zero flow (plateau pressure). Dynamic compliance includes airway resistance effects (measured using peak pressure). Dynamic < static because peak pressure > plateau pressure.

Conditions Affecting Compliance

Decreased lung compliance: pulmonary fibrosis, ARDS, pulmonary oedema, atelectasis, pneumonia. Decreased chest wall compliance: obesity, kyphoscoliosis, circumferential burns, abdominal distension. Increased compliance: emphysema (loss of elastic recoil).

relates the pressure across a curved surface to its wall tension and radius of curvature. For a sphere (two surfaces): P = 2T / r; for a cylinder (single surface): P = T / r. The clinical significance is the same in both cases — for a given wall tension, pressure rises steeply as radius falls.

Applied to the lung, Laplace predicts that small alveoli (small r) would generate a higher inward pressure than large ones and empty into them — alveoli would be inherently unstable. Pulmonary surfactant resolves the paradox by lowering surface tension preferentially in smaller alveoli, equalising the distending pressures and preventing collapse. The same equation explains aneurysm rupture risk (rises with diameter), ventricular wall stress (σ = P · r / 2h), and the ease of bag-mask ventilation in larger vs collapsed airways.

Pulmonary surfactant is produced by Type II pneumocytes from 24 weeks gestation. The major component is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC). It reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing collapse according to Laplace > Without surfactant, small alveoli (high P = 2T/r) would empty into large alveoli. Surfactant is more concentrated in smaller alveoli (greater surface tension reduction), equalising pressures and promoting alveolar stability. It also reduces transudation of fluid into alveoli and improves compliance.

Resistance = ΔP / Flow (cmH₂O/L/s). Normal airway resistance ≈ 1–2 cmH₂O/L/s. The major site of resistance is medium-sized bronchi (generations 4–8) — not the smallest airways, which have enormous total cross-sectional area in parallel.

Resistance increases with: bronchospasm, secretions, mucosal oedema, small ETT, high flow rates (turbulence). The time constant (τ = R × C) determines the speed of inflation/deflation. 3τ = 95% equilibration. Lung units with different time constants cause V/Q mismatch.

Flow-volume loops are essential for distinguishing obstructive from restrictive patterns and identifying upper airway obstruction.

    Work = ∫P·dV, measured in joules and represented by area on the pressure–volume loop. Normal WOB is approximately 0.3–0.6 J/L and consumes only 1–3% of whole-body oxygen consumption, but may exceed 30% during respiratory distress, causing muscle fatigue and prompting ventilatory support.

    Patients minimise total work by taking rapid shallow breaths in restrictive disease (less elastic work per breath) and slower deeper breaths in obstructive disease (lower flow-related resistive work).

    Dead space is the portion of tidal volume that does not participate in gas exchange. Physiological dead space = anatomical + alveolar dead space. The Bohr equation quantifies the dead space fraction. V/Q mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxaemia in clinical practice.

    Described by Ward Fowler in 1948, this single-breath nitrogen washout remains the reference technique for anatomical dead space (the volume of conducting airways from the lips to the respiratory bronchioles, where no gas exchange occurs). Anatomical VD ≈ 2 mL/kg (~150 mL in a 70 kg adult).

    Method: the subject takes a single vital-capacity breath of 100% O₂ (washing N₂ out of the conducting airways but not the alveoli, where N₂ is diluted by O₂ from the FRC). They then exhale slowly through a rapid-response nitrogen analyser while exhaled volume is recorded simultaneously by a spirometer. Plotting expired [N₂] against exhaled volume gives the nitrogen expirogram with three characteristic phases:

      Anatomical dead space is found graphically by the equal-area construction: a vertical line is drawn through phase II such that the area between the curve and the plateau on its left (triangle A) equals the area between the plateau and the curve on its right (triangle B). The volume on the x-axis at that vertical is VD(anat).

      Fowler vs Bohr — what does each measure?

      • ↑ Posture (standing > supine), large tidal volume, neck extension, bronchodilators, age.
      • ↓ Tracheostomy / cricothyroidotomy (reduces VD by ~50%).
      • Apparatus dead space (HME, catheter mount, mask) adds to VD.

     The oxygen cascade describes the stepwise fall in PO₂ from atmospheric air to the mitochondrion. Each step represents a physiological loss: humidification dilutes inspired O₂ with water vapour; alveolar gas is further diluted by CO₂ excretion (alveolar gas equation); a small A–a gradient is created by physiological V/Q mismatch and anatomical shunt; tissue offloading drops capillary PO₂; and the mitochondrion sits just above the Pasteur point (~0.5–3 kPa), below which oxidative phosphorylation fails and anaerobic metabolism takes over. Understanding the cascade lets you predict where hypoxaemia arises — high altitude affects the first step, hypoventilation the third, V/Q mismatch the fourth, and circulatory failure the fifth.

    The alveolar gas equation underpins the second-to-third step (humidified inspired → alveolar) and is the basis of the A–a gradient calculation used to assess gas exchange efficiency.

case_bank.title: Hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation
case_bank.text:
Case: Hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation (Respiratory, Advanced)
Patient: A patient in the right lateral position for left thoracotomy desaturates to 86% ten minutes after starting one-lung ventilation of the dependent lung.
Presentation: Airway pressures are acceptable, the double-lumen tube position was confirmed, and the surgeon has begun dissection.
Stage 1 — Describe the shunt
  Question: Why does saturation fall and what limits the fall?
  Model answer: The collapsed non-dependent lung is perfused but not ventilated, creating a true shunt that can approach 40–50% of cardiac output initially.
  Model answer: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts flow away from the hypoxic lung over 20–30 minutes, reducing shunt substantially.
  Model answer: Gravity in the lateral position also favours perfusion of the dependent, ventilated lung, and shunt fraction cannot be corrected by increasing FiO₂ alone.
Stage 2 — Systematically exclude causes
  Question: What do you check before accepting shunt as the cause?
  Model answer: Recheck tube position with fibreoptic bronchoscopy — malposition is the commonest reversible cause.
  Model answer: Exclude secretions, blood, kinking, low cardiac output, dynamic hyperinflation and inadequate FiO₂.
  Model answer: Reassess the dependent lung for atelectasis, which increases shunt further.
Stage 3 — Escalate treatment
  Question: How do you improve oxygenation?
  Model answer: Increase FiO₂, recruit and apply PEEP of about 5 cmH₂O to the dependent lung, and use protective tidal volumes of roughly 4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight.
  Model answer: Apply CPAP or intermittent insufflation to the operative lung, or clamp the appropriate pulmonary artery branch, in discussion with the surgeon.
  Model answer: Avoid high concentrations of volatile agent if the inhibition of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction becomes clinically relevant, and resume two-lung ventilation if hypoxaemia is refractory.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Oxygenation during one-lung ventilation is dominated by shunt fraction; because shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas, its contribution cannot be reversed by raising alveolar oxygen. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is the main protective response, mediated by mitochondrial oxygen sensing and potassium-channel-dependent vasoconstriction in small pulmonary arteries; it is attenuated by vasodilators, high volatile concentrations, hypocapnia, alkalosis and very high or very low pulmonary artery pressures.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Confirm tube position first, then optimise the dependent lung with recruitment, modest PEEP and protective volumes while avoiding both atelectasis and overdistension. Operative-lung CPAP or oxygen insufflation and surgical pulmonary artery clamping are effective adjuncts. Monitor with continuous oximetry, capnography, arterial gases and airway pressures, and communicate a clear plan for resuming two-lung ventilation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not say 'turn the oxygen up' as the whole answer; shunt is relatively refractory to FiO₂. Always place bronchoscopic confirmation of tube position before physiological manoeuvres.
Take-home: One-lung hypoxaemia is mainly shunt: confirm tube position, optimise the dependent lung, support the operative lung and let hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction work.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: ventilation–perfusion relationships (https://doi.org/10.1183/09031936.00037014); PROSEVA 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214103)

case_bank.title: Falling compliance during steep Trendelenburg laparoscopy
case_bank.text:
Case: Falling compliance during steep Trendelenburg laparoscopy (Respiratory, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient with a body mass index of 38 has robotic pelvic surgery in steep head-down tilt with a 15 mmHg pneumoperitoneum.
Presentation: Plateau pressure rises from 18 to 30 cmH₂O, tidal volume is unchanged, and end-tidal CO₂ climbs to 6.8 kPa.
Stage 1 — Interpret the pressures
  Question: Which measurement tells you about the lung itself?
  Model answer: Peak pressure reflects resistive plus elastic loads; plateau pressure reflects the elastic load after an inspiratory pause.
  Model answer: Driving pressure (plateau minus PEEP) reflects tidal strain on the aerated lung and is the pressure that tracks harm.
  Model answer: Here the change is elastic: reduced compliance from cephalad diaphragm displacement, abdominal insufflation and chest wall loading, not increased airway resistance.
Stage 2 — Separate lung from chest wall
  Question: Why does this distinction matter?
  Model answer: Total respiratory system compliance is the series combination of lung and chest wall compliance, so a stiff chest wall raises plateau pressure without proportionate alveolar overdistension.
  Model answer: Transpulmonary pressure, not airway pressure, determines alveolar stress; oesophageal pressure measurement can estimate it when decisions are difficult.
  Model answer: Accepting a somewhat higher plateau pressure may be safe if the rise is chest wall in origin.
Stage 3 — Adjust ventilation
  Question: What do you change?
  Model answer: Use 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, recruit and set PEEP of roughly 5–10 cmH₂O, and increase rate rather than volume to clear CO₂.
  Model answer: Ask for the lowest workable insufflation pressure and the least tilt the surgery allows, and check for endobronchial tube migration in head-down position.
  Model answer: Watch for facial and airway oedema, plan extubation after a cuff-leak and airway assessment, and expect atelectasis to require recruitment at the end of surgery.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Pneumoperitoneum and head-down positioning reduce functional residual capacity and compliance, promote basal atelectasis and increase both shunt and dead space; absorbed carbon dioxide adds to the CO₂ load. Because plateau pressure includes the chest wall contribution, a raised value in this setting does not automatically indicate injurious alveolar distension — driving pressure and, where measured, transpulmonary pressure are more informative.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Protective volumes, individualised PEEP after recruitment, adequate neuromuscular blockade, and rate-based CO₂ control are the mainstays. Monitor plateau and driving pressure with inspiratory pauses, follow end-tidal CO₂ with arterial correlation in longer cases, and recheck tube depth after position change. At the end of surgery, deflate the abdomen, recruit and assess airway oedema before extubation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not treat a rising plateau pressure as automatic evidence of lung injury or bronchospasm; define compliance and driving pressure, and separate lung from chest wall mechanics.
Take-home: Steep tilt and pneumoperitoneum reduce compliance through the chest wall: judge harm by driving pressure, use protective volumes and clear CO₂ with rate.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: respiratory mechanics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr054); Crit Care Med: stress and strain (https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0b013e31827417a6)

case_bank.title: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS
case_bank.text:
Case: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS (Ventilation, Advanced)
Patient: A patient ventilated for pneumonia has a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa on PEEP 12 cmH₂O, bilateral infiltrates and no evidence of cardiac failure.
Presentation: Tidal volume is 9 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau pressure 32 cmH₂O and driving pressure 20 cmH₂O.
Stage 1 — Make the diagnosis
  Question: Does this meet ARDS criteria?
  Model answer: Yes: acute onset within one week, bilateral infiltrates not fully explained by effusion or collapse, no primary cardiogenic cause, and hypoxaemia on at least 5 cmH₂O PEEP.
  Model answer: A PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa (roughly 90 mmHg over FiO₂ 1.0 equivalents) falls in the moderate-to-severe range.
  Model answer: Severity is graded by this ratio and guides therapies such as proning and neuromuscular blockade.
Stage 2 — Correct the ventilation
  Question: What immediate changes are needed?
  Model answer: Reduce tidal volume to 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, keep plateau pressure below 30 cmH₂O and driving pressure below about 15 cmH₂O.
  Model answer: Titrate PEEP to oxygenation and compliance, accept permissive hypercapnia while pH is tolerable, and use conservative fluid management once shock has resolved.
  Model answer: Optimise sedation and consider neuromuscular blockade for severe dyssynchrony.
Stage 3 — Escalate
  Question: What next if hypoxaemia persists?
  Model answer: Prone for at least 16 hours per day when the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio remains below about 20 kPa: PROSEVA showed a substantial mortality reduction in severe ARDS.
  Model answer: Treat the cause with source control and appropriate antimicrobials, and exclude a superimposed pneumothorax or effusion.
  Model answer: Refer early for extracorporeal support if hypoxaemia or hypercapnic acidosis is refractory despite optimal ventilation and proning.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: ARDS is a heterogeneous, inflammatory lung injury in which the aerated compartment is small; delivering normal tidal volumes to a 'baby lung' produces high strain, ventilator-induced injury and biotrauma. Driving pressure captures tidal strain on the aerated lung and correlates with mortality. Proning improves outcome by making transpulmonary pressure and ventilation more homogeneous, recruiting dorsal lung and improving ventilation–perfusion matching.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Deliver the ARDSNet strategy consistently: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau under 30 cmH₂O, individualised PEEP, permissive hypercapnia and conservative fluids. Monitor plateau and driving pressure with inspiratory holds, follow gases and compliance trends, and prone with a trained team and a checklist for line, tube and pressure-area safety. Escalate to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation early rather than after prolonged injurious ventilation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not use actual body weight for tidal volume, and do not chase a normal PaCO₂. State the Berlin criteria and quote PROSEVA's 16-hour minimum.
Take-home: ARDS management is protective ventilation by predicted body weight plus early prolonged proning in severe disease, not higher volumes or normal CO₂.
Cited sources: Berlin definition of ARDS (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.5669); ARDSNet low tidal volume trial (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200005043421801); PROSEVA 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214103)

case_bank.title: Hypotension after intubating life-threatening asthma
case_bank.text:
Case: Hypotension after intubating life-threatening asthma (Ventilation, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with life-threatening asthma is intubated after failing to respond to nebulisers and magnesium.
Presentation: Minutes later the pressure falls to 70/40 mmHg with rising peak pressures, a rate of 22 breaths per minute, tidal volume 8 mL/kg and no audible wheeze.
Stage 1 — Generate a differential
  Question: What are the causes and how do you distinguish them?
  Model answer: Dynamic hyperinflation with intrinsic PEEP is commonest: incomplete exhalation raises intrathoracic pressure and impedes venous return.
  Model answer: Tension pneumothorax must be excluded urgently by examination and ultrasound.
  Model answer: Also consider induction drug vasodilation, hypovolaemia, sedation-related sympatholysis and anaphylaxis as a precipitant.
Stage 2 — Confirm and relieve hyperinflation
  Question: What do you do at the bedside?
  Model answer: Disconnect the circuit briefly and allow prolonged exhalation, watching for haemodynamic improvement — a diagnostic and therapeutic manoeuvre.
  Model answer: Measure intrinsic PEEP with an expiratory hold and inspect the expiratory flow waveform for failure to return to baseline.
  Model answer: Give fluid and vasopressor while reducing the ventilatory load.
Stage 3 — Set the ventilator
  Question: What settings and drugs follow?
  Model answer: Low rate (about 8–12 breaths per minute), tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, high inspiratory flow to maximise expiratory time, and permissive hypercapnia targeting pH rather than PaCO₂.
  Model answer: Continue inhaled beta-2 agonist and ipratropium through the circuit, systemic corticosteroid and magnesium; consider intravenous salbutamol, aminophylline or ketamine as adjuncts.
  Model answer: Use deep sedation with or without neuromuscular blockade to abolish dyssynchrony, and monitor for barotrauma and myopathy.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Severe expiratory flow limitation means each breath begins before the previous one is complete, so alveolar volume and pressure accumulate. The resulting intrinsic PEEP raises right atrial pressure, reduces venous return and can mimic tamponade or tension pneumothorax; it also increases the trigger threshold, producing dyssynchrony. A silent chest indicates minimal airflow, not improvement.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Treat hyperinflation by giving time to exhale: reduce rate and minute ventilation, shorten inspiratory time, and tolerate hypercapnia. Confirm with an expiratory hold and flow-waveform inspection, and exclude pneumothorax with ultrasound or chest radiograph. Continue maximal bronchodilation and steroid, provide adequate sedation, and monitor pH, potassium and lactate — the latter two are commonly deranged by high-dose beta-2 agonists.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not increase the respiratory rate to correct hypercapnia in acute severe asthma, and do not interpret a silent chest as resolution. Name the disconnection test and the expiratory hold measurement.
Take-home: Hypotension after intubating asthma is usually dynamic hyperinflation: disconnect, slow the rate, allow long expiration and accept hypercapnia.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: severe asthma in critical care (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.10.004); BJA Educ: COPD and ventilation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkr054)

case_bank.title: Hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation
case_bank.text:
Case: Hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation (Respiratory, Advanced)
Patient: A patient in the right lateral position for left thoracotomy desaturates to 86% ten minutes after starting one-lung ventilation of the dependent lung.
Presentation: Airway pressures are acceptable, the double-lumen tube position was confirmed, and the surgeon has begun dissection.
Stage 1 — Describe the shunt
  Question: Why does saturation fall and what limits the fall?
  Model answer: The collapsed non-dependent lung is perfused but not ventilated, creating a true shunt that can approach 40–50% of cardiac output initially.
  Model answer: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts flow away from the hypoxic lung over 20–30 minutes, reducing shunt substantially.
  Model answer: Gravity in the lateral position also favours perfusion of the dependent, ventilated lung, and shunt fraction cannot be corrected by increasing FiO₂ alone.
Stage 2 — Systematically exclude causes
  Question: What do you check before accepting shunt as the cause?
  Model answer: Recheck tube position with fibreoptic bronchoscopy — malposition is the commonest reversible cause.
  Model answer: Exclude secretions, blood, kinking, low cardiac output, dynamic hyperinflation and inadequate FiO₂.
  Model answer: Reassess the dependent lung for atelectasis, which increases shunt further.
Stage 3 — Escalate treatment
  Question: How do you improve oxygenation?
  Model answer: Increase FiO₂, recruit and apply PEEP of about 5 cmH₂O to the dependent lung, and use protective tidal volumes of roughly 4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight.
  Model answer: Apply CPAP or intermittent insufflation to the operative lung, or clamp the appropriate pulmonary artery branch, in discussion with the surgeon.
  Model answer: Avoid high concentrations of volatile agent if the inhibition of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction becomes clinically relevant, and resume two-lung ventilation if hypoxaemia is refractory.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Oxygenation during one-lung ventilation is dominated by shunt fraction; because shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas, its contribution cannot be reversed by raising alveolar oxygen. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is the main protective response, mediated by mitochondrial oxygen sensing and potassium-channel-dependent vasoconstriction in small pulmonary arteries; it is attenuated by vasodilators, high volatile concentrations, hypocapnia, alkalosis and very high or very low pulmonary artery pressures.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Confirm tube position first, then optimise the dependent lung with recruitment, modest PEEP and protective volumes while avoiding both atelectasis and overdistension. Operative-lung CPAP or oxygen insufflation and surgical pulmonary artery clamping are effective adjuncts. Monitor with continuous oximetry, capnography, arterial gases and airway pressures, and communicate a clear plan for resuming two-lung ventilation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not say 'turn the oxygen up' as the whole answer; shunt is relatively refractory to FiO₂. Always place bronchoscopic confirmation of tube position before physiological manoeuvres.
Take-home: One-lung hypoxaemia is mainly shunt: confirm tube position, optimise the dependent lung, support the operative lung and let hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction work.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: ventilation–perfusion relationships (https://doi.org/10.1183/09031936.00037014); PROSEVA 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214103)

case_bank.title: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS
case_bank.text:
Case: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS (Ventilation, Advanced)
Patient: A patient ventilated for pneumonia has a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa on PEEP 12 cmH₂O, bilateral infiltrates and no evidence of cardiac failure.
Presentation: Tidal volume is 9 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau pressure 32 cmH₂O and driving pressure 20 cmH₂O.
Stage 1 — Make the diagnosis
  Question: Does this meet ARDS criteria?
  Model answer: Yes: acute onset within one week, bilateral infiltrates not fully explained by effusion or collapse, no primary cardiogenic cause, and hypoxaemia on at least 5 cmH₂O PEEP.
  Model answer: A PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa (roughly 90 mmHg over FiO₂ 1.0 equivalents) falls in the moderate-to-severe range.
  Model answer: Severity is graded by this ratio and guides therapies such as proning and neuromuscular blockade.
Stage 2 — Correct the ventilation
  Question: What immediate changes are needed?
  Model answer: Reduce tidal volume to 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, keep plateau pressure below 30 cmH₂O and driving pressure below about 15 cmH₂O.
  Model answer: Titrate PEEP to oxygenation and compliance, accept permissive hypercapnia while pH is tolerable, and use conservative fluid management once shock has resolved.
  Model answer: Optimise sedation and consider neuromuscular blockade for severe dyssynchrony.
Stage 3 — Escalate
  Question: What next if hypoxaemia persists?
  Model answer: Prone for at least 16 hours per day when the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio remains below about 20 kPa: PROSEVA showed a substantial mortality reduction in severe ARDS.
  Model answer: Treat the cause with source control and appropriate antimicrobials, and exclude a superimposed pneumothorax or effusion.
  Model answer: Refer early for extracorporeal support if hypoxaemia or hypercapnic acidosis is refractory despite optimal ventilation and proning.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: ARDS is a heterogeneous, inflammatory lung injury in which the aerated compartment is small; delivering normal tidal volumes to a 'baby lung' produces high strain, ventilator-induced injury and biotrauma. Driving pressure captures tidal strain on the aerated lung and correlates with mortality. Proning improves outcome by making transpulmonary pressure and ventilation more homogeneous, recruiting dorsal lung and improving ventilation–perfusion matching.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Deliver the ARDSNet strategy consistently: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau under 30 cmH₂O, individualised PEEP, permissive hypercapnia and conservative fluids. Monitor plateau and driving pressure with inspiratory holds, follow gases and compliance trends, and prone with a trained team and a checklist for line, tube and pressure-area safety. Escalate to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation early rather than after prolonged injurious ventilation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not use actual body weight for tidal volume, and do not chase a normal PaCO₂. State the Berlin criteria and quote PROSEVA's 16-hour minimum.
Take-home: ARDS management is protective ventilation by predicted body weight plus early prolonged proning in severe disease, not higher volumes or normal CO₂.
Cited sources: Berlin definition of ARDS (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.5669); ARDSNet low tidal volume trial (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200005043421801); PROSEVA 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214103)

# Oxygen-Haemoglobin Dissociation The ODC, Bohr effect, factors shifting the curve, oxygen delivery CaO₂ = (1.34 × Hb × SaO₂) + (0.0225 × PaO₂) (mL O₂ per dL when Hb in g/dL and PaO₂ in kPa) Bound: 1.34 × 12.0 × 0.98 = 15.76 mL/dL Dissolved: 0.0225 × 13 = 0.29 mL/dL CaO₂ ≈ 16.05 mL/dL ≈ 160.5 mL/L DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ × 10 (×10 to convert dL → L) ~800 mL/min (normal ~1000 mL/min). CO has two effects on the ODC and DO₂: Affinity ~240× greater than O₂ → reduces functional Hb able to carry O₂. Shifts the remaining curve → impaired tissue offloading. ← Left Shift (↑ Affinity) • ↓ Temperature (hypothermia) • ↓ PaCO₂ / Alkalosis (↑ pH) • ↓ 2,3-DPG (stored blood) • Fetal haemoglobin (HbF) • Carbon monoxide (COHb) • Methaemoglobin Right Shift → (↓ Affinity) • ↑ Temperature (fever, exercise) • ↑ PaCO₂ / Acidosis (↓ pH) — Bohr effect • ↑ 2,3-DPG • Sickle haemoglobin (HbS) • Anaemia / chronic hypoxia Bohr effect describes the rightward shift of the ODC caused by increased CO₂ and H⁺ concentration. In metabolically active tissues, CO₂ production lowers pH locally, promoting O₂ release exactly where it is needed. In the lungs, CO₂ excretion raises pH, shifting the curve left and promoting O₂ loading. Haldane effect is the converse: deoxyhaemoglobin carries more CO₂ (as carbamino compound) and buffers more H⁺ than oxyhaemoglobin. As Hb releases O₂ in tissues it picks up CO₂ more efficiently; as Hb binds O₂ in lungs it releases CO₂ — so both gases exchange more efficiently than either would alone. DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ , where SpO₂ cannot distinguish COHb from O₂Hb — in any burn, smoke or suicide-attempt patient, use co-oximetry. : SpO₂ plateaus around 85% regardless of FiO₂ — treat with methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min, repeated after 30–60 min if required (BNF; max 7 mg/kg total). Stored blood is 2,3-DPG depleted → left shift → impaired offloading for ~24 h after transfusion. sits left of adult Hb (P₅₀ ~2.5 kPa) — essential for placental O₂ uptake but means neonates desaturate quickly when offloading is compromised. works by filling the FRC, not by raising SaO₂ further — gains apnoea time on the upper plateau. Calculating arterial oxygen content and DO₂ CO poisoning — why SpO₂ misleads Oxygen-Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve FRCA Primary — Physiology The ODC is sigmoid due to cooperative O₂ binding to haemoglobin's four haem groups (T → R conformational change). P₅₀ is normally 26.7 mmHg (3.5 kPa) — the PaO₂ at which Hb is 50% saturated. Right shift (↓ affinity): ↑ temp, ↑ CO₂, ↓ pH, ↑ 2,3-DPG — aids tissue O₂ delivery. Left shift (↑ affinity): ↓ temp, ↓ CO₂, ↑ pH, HbF, COHb, methaemoglobin — impairs O₂ offloading. Bohr effect: ↑CO₂/H⁺ in tissues → right shift → more O₂ released. Reverses in lungs. DO₂ = CO × [(1.34 × Hb × SaO₂) + (0.0225 × PaO₂)]; normal ~1000 mL/min. SpO₂ is a late indicator of falling PaO₂ — pre-oxygenation provides a reservoir on the flat upper part of the curve. Standard pulse oximetry cannot detect COHb or metHb — use co-oximetry when these are suspected. The Normal Curve Factors Shifting the Curve Bohr & Haldane Effects Oxygen Delivery (DO₂) Clinical Significance What causes a right shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve? Right shift (lower affinity, easier offloading at tissues) is caused by ↑PCO₂, ↑H⁺ (acidaemia), ↑temperature, and ↑2,3-DPG (chronic hypoxia, anaemia). Mnemonic: — CO₂, Acid, DPG, Exercise, Temperature. The Bohr effect refers specifically to the CO₂/H⁺ shift in active tissues. What is the P50 and why does fetal haemoglobin have a lower value? P50 is the PO₂ at which haemoglobin is 50 % saturated — normally 3.5 kPa (26.6 mmHg) for adult HbA. HbF lacks β-chains (has γ-chains instead) which bind 2,3-DPG poorly, giving a left-shifted curve with P50 ~2.5 kPa. This higher O₂ affinity allows the fetus to extract O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta. How does carbon-monoxide poisoning affect the dissociation curve? CO binds Hb with ~240× the affinity of O₂, forming carboxyhaemoglobin which cannot carry O₂. It also left-shifts the residual oxy-Hb curve, impairing O₂ release to tissues. SpO₂ reads falsely normal (~100 %); diagnosis requires co-oximetry. Treat with 100 % O₂ (half-life 60 min on FiO₂ 1.0 vs 4–5 h on air) ± hyperbaric O₂ for severe cases. Describe the structure of haemoglobin and explain why the ODC is sigmoid (cooperativity). Define P₅₀ and identify the factors that shift the ODC left or right. Explain the Bohr and Haldane effects and their physiological significance. Calculate oxygen delivery (DO₂) and arterial oxygen content (CaO₂) and use them clinically. s shape to pre-oxygenation, hypoxaemia and CO/methaemoglobin poisoning. of haemoglobin that includes COHb.

The sigmoid shape reflects cooperativity: binding of the first O₂ molecule facilitates subsequent binding (the T → R conformational change). The P₅₀ — the PaO₂ at which Hb is 50% saturated — is normally 26.7 mmHg (3.5 kPa).

    Key points: at PaO₂ 13.3 kPa (100 mmHg), SaO₂ ≈ 97.5%. At the venous point (PaO₂ ~5.3 kPa / 40 mmHg), SaO₂ ≈ 75%. The steep portion between 20–60 mmHg allows efficient O₂ unloading in the tissues.

    The curve can shift left (increased affinity, harder to offload O₂) or right (decreased affinity, easier to offload O₂).

    ← Left Shift (↑ Affinity)
    • • ↓ Temperature (hypothermia)
    • • ↓ PaCO₂ / Alkalosis (↑ pH)
    • • ↓ 2,3-DPG (stored blood)
    • • Fetal haemoglobin (HbF)
    • • Carbon monoxide (COHb)
    • • Methaemoglobin
  • • ↑ Temperature (fever, exercise)
  • • ↑ PaCO₂ / Acidosis (↓ pH) — Bohr effect
  • • ↑ 2,3-DPG
  • • Sickle haemoglobin (HbS)
  • • Anaemia / chronic hypoxia
The Bohr effect describes the rightward shift of the ODC caused by increased CO₂ and H⁺ concentration. In metabolically active tissues, CO₂ production lowers pH locally, promoting O₂ release exactly where it is needed. In the lungs, CO₂ excretion raises pH, shifting the curve left and promoting O₂ loading.

The Haldane effect is the converse: deoxyhaemoglobin carries more CO₂ (as carbamino compound) and buffers more H⁺ than oxyhaemoglobin. As Hb releases O₂ in tissues it picks up CO₂ more efficiently; as Hb binds O₂ in lungs it releases CO₂ — so both gases exchange more efficiently than either would alone.

The flat upper portion of the curve means that even moderate drops in PaO₂ from normal values cause minimal desaturation — a physiological safety margin. Once PaO₂ falls below ~8 kPa (60 mmHg), the steep portion means saturation drops rapidly, explaining the sudden clinical deterioration of hypoxic patients.
