case_bank.title: Chronic prednisolone before colectomy
case_bank.text:
Case: Chronic prednisolone before colectomy (Steroid cover, Foundation)
Patient: A 64-year-old woman takes prednisolone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica and is listed for open right hemicolectomy.
Presentation: She is stable at pre-assessment. The surgical team has omitted all morning medicines and asks whether dexamethasone for nausea is enough steroid cover.
Stage 1 — Assess suppression and surgical stress
  Question: What determines whether she needs supplementation?
  Model answer: Prednisolone at or above 5 mg daily for more than four weeks makes HPA-axis suppression likely.
  Model answer: Open colectomy is major surgical stress.
  Model answer: Continue her usual glucocorticoid dose; do not create an additional withdrawal stress.
Stage 2 — Write the prescription
  Question: Prescribe a practical major-surgery regimen.
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours, or 50 mg IV six-hourly where an infusion is impractical.
  Model answer: Return towards the usual oral regimen as recovery permits, guided by clinical progress.
Stage 3 — Manage the postoperative risk
  Question: She becomes hypotensive and hypoglycaemic six hours after surgery. What do you do?
  Model answer: Treat adrenal crisis without waiting for confirmatory testing: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately.
  Model answer: Give rapid 0.9% saline, correct hypoglycaemia with IV glucose and check sodium, potassium and acid–base status.
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours and investigate simultaneous causes of shock.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Prednisolone 10 mg daily is above the dose at which clinically important HPA-axis suppression should be assumed after sustained use. Open colectomy produces major stress, while omission of her normal dose adds withdrawal risk. Antiemetic dexamethasone has glucocorticoid activity but does not by itself constitute a documented perioperative replacement plan.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue the usual steroid, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly while major stress persists. Monitor pressure, glucose, sodium and potassium, and restore oral treatment when absorption is reliable. Refractory hypotension, hypoglycaemia or electrolyte disturbance should trigger immediate adrenal-crisis treatment alongside a search for bleeding, sepsis and cardiac causes.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not delay rescue hydrocortisone for cortisol testing, and do not stop supplementation abruptly after major surgery. State the steroid route, timing, postoperative continuation and plan to return to baseline treatment.
Take-home: Major surgery in a patient with likely HPA suppression requires the usual steroid plus hydrocortisone at induction and continued replacement; dexamethasone used for antiemesis is not a substitute for a planned regimen.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: The overlooked inhaled steroid
case_bank.text:
Case: The overlooked inhaled steroid (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: A 49-year-old man with severe asthma uses high-dose inhaled fluticasone and has received three oral prednisolone courses this year. He is listed for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Presentation: He denies taking any ‘regular steroid tablets’ and the initial assessment records no risk of adrenal suppression.
Stage 1 — Identify hidden exposure
  Question: Why should the steroid history be revisited?
  Model answer: High-dose inhaled steroids and repeated systemic courses can suppress the HPA axis.
  Model answer: Ask about dose, duration, recent oral courses, steroid emergency card, Cushingoid features and previous perioperative problems.
  Model answer: If uncertainty cannot be resolved before surgery, a safe supplementation plan is preferable to an unrecognised crisis.
Stage 2 — Plan moderate-stress cover
  Question: How would you manage a patient judged at risk?
  Model answer: Continue usual inhaled therapy and optimise asthma control.
  Model answer: For moderate surgical stress, give hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction followed by 25 mg IV eight-hourly for 24 hours.
  Model answer: Monitor glucose, blood pressure, sodium and potassium; resume the normal regimen promptly.
Stage 3 — Differentiate postoperative hypotension
  Question: What features make adrenal crisis more likely?
  Model answer: Hypotension that responds poorly to fluid and vasopressors, especially with hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia.
  Model answer: Treat immediately with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV and fluids while also excluding bleeding, sepsis, anaphylaxis and cardiac causes.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: HPA suppression depends on cumulative systemic exposure, not whether a patient currently takes tablets. High-dose fluticasone, repeated oral rescue courses, topical preparations and injections all matter. Features such as Cushingoid appearance, a steroid emergency card or recent withdrawal increase concern.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue inhaled therapy and optimise asthma. If moderate-stress surgery proceeds with credible suppression risk, give hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction followed by 25 mg eight-hourly for 24 hours, then resume the established regimen. Observe haemodynamics, glucose and electrolytes and treat unexplained shock promptly.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: A normal-looking medication list can conceal recent systemic exposure. Ask specifically about every route, dose, duration and cessation date rather than accepting ‘no steroid tablets’.
Take-home: A steroid history includes inhaled, topical, injected and recently stopped treatment—not just current tablets.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Primary adrenal insufficiency and emergency laparotomy
case_bank.text:
Case: Primary adrenal insufficiency and emergency laparotomy (Steroid cover, Advanced)
Patient: A 36-year-old woman with Addison’s disease presents with perforated appendicitis, vomiting and fever. BP is 84/48 mmHg, glucose 3.1 mmol/L and sodium 126 mmol/L.
Presentation: She has been unable to take hydrocortisone or fludrocortisone for 24 hours.
Stage 1 — Recognise crisis
  Question: What is the immediate diagnosis and priority?
  Model answer: This is adrenal crisis until proved otherwise, precipitated by infection, vomiting and missed replacement.
  Model answer: Do not delay treatment for cortisol measurement; draw blood first only if it causes no delay.
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, rapid isotonic saline and IV glucose.
Stage 2 — Prepare for theatre
  Question: How should replacement continue?
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion, or 50 mg IV six-hourly.
  Model answer: Correct volume, glucose and electrolyte abnormalities and start source-control antibiotics.
  Model answer: Use invasive monitoring according to haemodynamic response and operative severity.
Stage 3 — Step down safely
  Question: What matters after source control?
  Model answer: Continue stress dosing while severely unwell, then taper according to recovery and endocrine advice.
  Model answer: Restart oral glucocorticoid replacement when absorption is reliable.
  Model answer: Fludrocortisone is generally unnecessary while hydrocortisone exceeds 50 mg daily because mineralocorticoid activity is adequate.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Known primary adrenal insufficiency, missed replacement, vomiting, infection, hypotension, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia make adrenal crisis the working diagnosis. The immediate mortality risk comes from glucocorticoid deficiency and severe volume depletion; treatment precedes biochemical confirmation.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, rapid 0.9% saline and IV glucose, then hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly. Correct electrolytes, give antibiotics and obtain source control. Taper only as illness resolves and oral absorption returns; hydrocortisone above 50 mg daily supplies adequate mineralocorticoid effect, so fludrocortisone is usually temporarily unnecessary.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Blood sampling is optional if it delays treatment. Persistent shock still requires evaluation for sepsis, haemorrhage and cardiogenic causes rather than attributing every abnormality to Addison’s disease.
Take-home: Known adrenal insufficiency plus acute illness, vomiting and shock is a treatment-first emergency: hydrocortisone, saline, glucose and definitive management of the trigger.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Recent joint injections before arthroplasty
case_bank.text:
Case: Recent joint injections before arthroplasty (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: A 72-year-old man is scheduled for revision knee arthroplasty. He stopped prednisolone two months ago and has also had repeated intra-articular steroid injections.
Presentation: He reports fatigue and postural dizziness but has no formal diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency.
Stage 1 — Build the risk picture
  Question: Which details change your plan?
  Model answer: Recent cessation of long-term oral therapy does not guarantee HPA recovery; suppression may persist.
  Model answer: Repeated intra-articular injections add systemic exposure.
  Model answer: Symptoms, treatment records and time available determine whether endocrine testing is useful; urgent surgery should not await testing when risk is credible.
Stage 2 — Cover major surgery
  Question: What is a defensible perioperative plan?
  Model answer: Document likely suppression and give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue 200 mg over 24 hours initially, alongside close haemodynamic and glucose monitoring.
  Model answer: Agree the taper and longer-term assessment with endocrinology or the treating team.
Stage 3 — Avoid the common error
  Question: What should not happen at discharge?
  Model answer: Do not abruptly stop glucocorticoid cover without a recovery plan.
  Model answer: Provide clear written sick-day advice and arrange assessment of ongoing replacement need.
  Model answer: Reconcile every steroid route in the discharge medicines.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: HPA recovery after long-term glucocorticoids is variable and may take months. Repeated intra-articular injections can add meaningful systemic exposure, while fatigue and postural symptoms strengthen concern but are not diagnostic. Testing is useful only when time and clinical stability permit.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: For major revision arthroplasty with credible suppression, continue or replace the baseline requirement, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction and 200 mg over the first 24 hours. Monitor haemodynamics and glucose, then agree a taper and formal endocrine assessment rather than making an unplanned stop.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: ‘Stopped two months ago’ does not prove recovery. Discharge reconciliation should cover oral, inhaled, topical and injected steroids and provide sick-day and emergency advice.
Take-home: Recently stopped oral steroids and repeated injections can remain clinically relevant; route and current prescription alone do not define HPA-axis risk.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Preparing an adrenal phaeochromocytoma
case_bank.text:
Case: Preparing an adrenal phaeochromocytoma (Phaeochromocytoma, Foundation)
Patient: A 43-year-old woman has an adrenal mass, raised plasma metanephrines and episodic headache, sweating and palpitations.
Presentation: She is referred for laparoscopic adrenalectomy with a seated BP of 168/96 mmHg and pulse 104 min⁻¹.
Stage 1 — Sequence preoperative treatment
  Question: How should blockade be introduced?
  Model answer: Start alpha blockade first, commonly phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin, and titrate over about 10–14 days.
  Model answer: Only add beta blockade after adequate alpha blockade if troublesome tachycardia persists.
  Model answer: Never beta block first because unopposed alpha vasoconstriction can provoke a hypertensive crisis.
Stage 2 — Restore circulating volume
  Question: Why are salt and fluid important?
  Model answer: Chronic catecholamine-mediated vasoconstriction leaves the patient intravascularly depleted.
  Model answer: Encourage salt and fluid intake after alpha blockade, while individualising for cardiac or renal disease.
  Model answer: Look for controlled seated BP with tolerable postural reduction rather than simply a normal clinic reading.
Stage 3 — Confirm readiness
  Question: What should the multidisciplinary review cover?
  Model answer: Blood-pressure and rhythm control, postural symptoms, ECG/cardiac effects and glucose.
  Model answer: Availability of experienced endocrine surgery, anaesthesia, critical care and appropriate postoperative monitoring.
  Model answer: A plan for invasive monitoring and rapidly acting vasoactive drugs.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction causes hypertension and contracted circulating volume. Alpha blockade reduces vascular tone; beta blockade is added only after alpha control because isolated beta blockade leaves unopposed alpha vasoconstriction. Preparation is judged by pressure control, tolerable postural change, rhythm and end-organ effects rather than one clinic value.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Titrate phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin for roughly 10–14 days, then add beta blockade only for persistent tachycardia after adequate alpha blockade. Encourage salt and fluid intake where safe. Plan arterial monitoring, large-bore access, short-acting vasodilators, vasopressors, glucose monitoring and postoperative critical-care observation with an experienced multidisciplinary team.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not chase a perfectly normal seated pressure at the cost of disabling orthostasis, and never describe beta blockade before alpha blockade.
Take-home: Successful preparation is alpha blockade followed—if needed—by beta blockade, together with volume expansion and an experienced multidisciplinary plan.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Beta blocker before diagnosis
case_bank.text:
Case: Beta blocker before diagnosis (Phaeochromocytoma, Advanced)
Patient: A 51-year-old man with an undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma receives propranolol in the emergency department for tachycardia.
Presentation: Minutes later he develops severe headache, chest pain and BP 246/132 mmHg with pulmonary oedema.
Stage 1 — Explain the deterioration
  Question: What mechanism has caused this crisis?
  Model answer: Beta blockade removed beta-mediated vasodilation and cardiac compensation while alpha receptors remained intensely stimulated.
  Model answer: Unopposed alpha vasoconstriction caused abrupt hypertension and acute cardiac afterload.
  Model answer: This presentation should trigger urgent specialist help and consideration of catecholamine excess.
Stage 2 — Stabilise the crisis
  Question: What are the immediate principles?
  Model answer: Use titratable vasodilator or alpha-blocking therapy with invasive arterial pressure monitoring in a critical-care setting.
  Model answer: Treat pulmonary oedema and myocardial complications while avoiding further isolated beta blockade.
  Model answer: Once alpha control is established, a short-acting beta blocker may be considered for persistent tachyarrhythmia.
Stage 3 — Plan definitive care
  Question: Should surgery proceed immediately?
  Model answer: If the acute emergency can be stabilised, defer tumour resection until adequate alpha blockade and volume restoration are achieved.
  Model answer: Emergency surgery is reserved for an uncontrollable complication and requires an expert team with vasoactive support ready.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Propranolol removes beta-2 vasodilation and limits cardiac compensation while catecholamine-stimulated alpha receptors continue intense vasoconstriction. The result may be malignant hypertension, myocardial injury and pulmonary oedema. This is a pharmacological crisis, not simple undertreated tachycardia.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Escalate to critical care, establish invasive arterial monitoring and control vascular tone with titratable vasodilation or alpha blockade. Treat pulmonary oedema and myocardial complications and avoid further isolated beta blockade. A short-acting beta blocker is considered only after alpha-mediated hypertension is controlled. Definitive resection is normally deferred until blockade and volume restoration are complete.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Giving more beta blocker for the persistent tachycardia can worsen the crisis. Explain receptor physiology and treatment sequence explicitly.
Take-home: In suspected phaeochromocytoma, beta blockade before alpha blockade can be catastrophic; control vasoconstriction first.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Hypertension during tumour handling
case_bank.text:
Case: Hypertension during tumour handling (Phaeochromocytoma, Advanced)
Patient: During laparoscopic adrenalectomy, BP rises from 124/72 to 228/118 mmHg and HR to 142 min⁻¹ as the surgeon mobilises the tumour.
Presentation: An arterial line is in place. Anaesthetic depth is adequate and ventilation is unchanged.
Stage 1 — Recognise the phase
  Question: What is the likely cause and what should be communicated?
  Model answer: Tumour manipulation has released catecholamines.
  Model answer: Ask the surgeon to stop handling temporarily and announce the haemodynamic crisis clearly.
  Model answer: Exclude contributing hypoxia, hypercarbia, light anaesthesia and drug error without delaying treatment.
Stage 2 — Control the surge
  Question: Which treatment principles apply?
  Model answer: Use rapid, titratable vasodilator or alpha-blocking treatment such as sodium nitroprusside, glyceryl trinitrate or phentolamine according to local practice.
  Model answer: Magnesium can reduce catecholamine release and provide vasodilation; esmolol is reserved for tachycardia after vasoconstriction is controlled.
  Model answer: Avoid long-acting treatment that will worsen the predictable post-ligation hypotension.
Stage 3 — Prepare for vein ligation
  Question: What happens next?
  Model answer: After venous ligation, catecholamine concentration falls abruptly and profound vasodilation/hypotension may follow.
  Model answer: Stop vasodilators, communicate timing, restore preload judiciously and use titrated vasopressor support.
  Model answer: Check glucose because rebound insulin release can cause hypoglycaemia.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Tumour handling can release a sudden catecholamine load, producing severe hypertension and tachyarrhythmia. The anaesthetist must communicate with the surgeon, pause manipulation and exclude amplifiers such as hypercarbia, hypoxia and inadequate anaesthesia while treating immediately.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use short-acting, titratable agents such as nitroprusside, glyceryl trinitrate or phentolamine according to local practice; magnesium offers vasodilation and may reduce catecholamine release. Use esmolol only after vasoconstriction is controlled. Before adrenal-vein ligation, stop vasodilators, prepare vasopressors and assess preload because abrupt catecholamine withdrawal can cause profound hypotension. Check glucose for rebound hypoglycaemia.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Long-acting antihypertensives may turn the predictable post-ligation pressure fall into prolonged shock. Link each drug choice to the rapidly changing surgical phase.
Take-home: Phaeochromocytoma surgery has two opposing haemodynamic phases: a manipulation surge and post-ligation collapse; short-acting, titratable drugs are essential.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Post-adrenalectomy collapse
case_bank.text:
Case: Post-adrenalectomy collapse (Phaeochromocytoma, Intermediate)
Patient: Two hours after phaeochromocytoma resection, a patient is drowsy, clammy and hypotensive despite initial fluid. Capillary glucose is 2.6 mmol/L.
Presentation: The intraoperative record documents difficult tumour mobilisation followed by a marked pressure drop after vein ligation.
Stage 1 — Frame the differential
  Question: Which expected complications coexist here?
  Model answer: Hypotension can reflect residual alpha blockade, vasodilation, catecholamine withdrawal, hypovolaemia or bleeding.
  Model answer: Hypoglycaemia follows loss of catecholamine-mediated insulin suppression and rebound insulin secretion.
  Model answer: Also consider adrenal insufficiency after bilateral surgery and conventional postoperative causes of shock.
Stage 2 — Treat immediately
  Question: What should happen now?
  Model answer: Give IV glucose and recheck frequently.
  Model answer: Assess bleeding and fluid responsiveness, then use titrated vasopressor support where vasodilation persists.
  Model answer: Continue high-acuity monitoring of blood pressure, rhythm, urine output, lactate and glucose.
Stage 3 — Set the recovery plan
  Question: What must handover include?
  Model answer: Explicit risks of recurrent hypotension and hypoglycaemia with scheduled observations.
  Model answer: A steroid replacement plan when bilateral adrenal tissue has been removed or adrenal function is uncertain.
  Model answer: Endocrine follow-up and biochemical surveillance for persistent or recurrent disease.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Post-resection hypotension is often multifactorial: catecholamine withdrawal, residual alpha blockade, vasoplegia and depleted volume coexist, but bleeding must be excluded. Hypoglycaemia occurs because removal of catecholamine-mediated insulin suppression permits rebound insulin release.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give IV glucose, repeat measurements frequently and assess haemorrhage, preload and cardiac function. Use judicious fluid and titrated vasopressor support for persistent vasodilation. Continue high-acuity pressure, rhythm, urine-output, lactate and glucose monitoring. Bilateral adrenalectomy or uncertain residual function requires a clear steroid replacement plan.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not treat drowsiness as residual anaesthesia without checking glucose. Handover must state the specific risks of recurrent hypotension and hypoglycaemia.
Take-home: Post-resection care is active: anticipate hypotension and hypoglycaemia rather than waiting for routine ward observations to detect them.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Minor procedure on replacement hydrocortisone
case_bank.text:
Case: Minor procedure on replacement hydrocortisone (Steroid cover, Foundation)
Patient: An adult with stable primary adrenal insufficiency is listed for a short dental extraction under local anaesthesia.
Presentation: They are well, have taken their usual morning hydrocortisone and ask whether an injection is mandatory.
Stage 1 — Grade the stress
  Question: Does every procedure require parenteral stress dosing?
  Model answer: No: supplementation should reflect procedural stress, illness and ability to absorb usual treatment.
  Model answer: A short uncomplicated procedure under effective local anaesthesia is minor stress.
  Model answer: Confirm emergency steroid and sick-day plans.
Stage 2 — Make a proportionate plan
  Question: What would you do today?
  Model answer: Continue the usual oral replacement.
  Model answer: Use effective local anaesthesia, analgesia and minimise fasting.
  Model answer: Escalate if the procedure becomes prolonged, oral medication is missed or systemic illness develops.
Stage 3 — Recognise deterioration
  Question: What if vomiting and hypotension develop?
  Model answer: Treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM.
  Model answer: Give isotonic fluid and glucose where required and seek urgent care.
  Model answer: Do not wait for cortisol testing.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: A minor procedure under local anaesthesia usually produces little physiological stress. A patient taking a stable physiological replacement dose should continue it; indiscriminate high-dose hydrocortisone adds hyperglycaemia, infection and wound-healing harms without clear benefit.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Confirm adherence, recent illness and ability to take oral medication. Continue the usual morning hydrocortisone, use effective local anaesthesia and analgesia, and give written sick-day advice. Escalate only if the procedure becomes prolonged, the patient cannot absorb oral medication or haemodynamic features suggest crisis.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Steroid cover is proportional to surgical stress and baseline replacement. ‘Any steroid history means 100 mg hydrocortisone’ is not a defensible rule.
Take-home: Match glucocorticoid supplementation to physiological stress; continue baseline replacement and retain a clear rescue plan.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Pituitary insufficiency before major surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Pituitary insufficiency before major surgery (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: An adult with panhypopituitarism takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine and is listed for open abdominal surgery.
Presentation: They have fasted, omitted morning medicines and have glucose 3.5 mmol/L with normal potassium.
Stage 1 — Interpret the pattern
  Question: Does normal potassium exclude adrenal risk?
  Model answer: No. Secondary adrenal insufficiency often preserves aldosterone and potassium.
  Model answer: Missed glucocorticoid, fasting and major stress create crisis risk.
  Model answer: Review diabetes insipidus and other pituitary replacement.
Stage 2 — Provide major-stress cover
  Question: What regimen is appropriate?
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly initially.
  Model answer: Correct hypoglycaemia and monitor sodium, glucose and fluid balance.
Stage 3 — Sequence endocrine treatment
  Question: What endocrine ordering matters?
  Model answer: Ensure glucocorticoid replacement before initiating or escalating thyroid hormone in combined deficiency.
  Model answer: Taper toward baseline when stable and absorbing orally.
  Model answer: Seek endocrine input for complex fluid or sodium disturbance.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Pituitary disease may cause secondary adrenal insufficiency without hyperkalaemia because aldosterone is largely preserved. Fasting, vomiting and omission of hydrocortisone can still precipitate hypotension and hypoglycaemia during major surgery.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue replacement, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction and 200 mg over 24 hours for major stress, then taper toward baseline as recovery permits. Monitor sodium, glucose, pressure and fluid balance; account for coexisting diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Normal potassium does not exclude secondary adrenal crisis. Replace glucocorticoid before starting or increasing thyroxine in untreated combined pituitary deficiency.
Take-home: Secondary adrenal insufficiency can present without hyperkalaemia; major stress still requires timely glucocorticoid replacement.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Catecholamine symptoms in pregnancy
case_bank.text:
Case: Catecholamine symptoms in pregnancy (Phaeochromocytoma, Advanced)
Patient: A pregnant adult at 24 weeks has episodic hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations.
Presentation: Urine protein is absent and symptoms began early in pregnancy; plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated.
Stage 1 — Differentiate the diagnosis
  Question: Why is this not automatically pre-eclampsia?
  Model answer: Paroxysmal symptoms and early onset suggest catecholamine excess.
  Model answer: Confirm biochemistry and localise with pregnancy-appropriate imaging, commonly MRI without gadolinium.
  Model answer: Assess maternal cardiac and fetal effects.
Stage 2 — Prepare safely
  Question: What is the pharmacological sequence?
  Model answer: Establish alpha blockade first and restore circulating volume cautiously.
  Model answer: Add beta blockade only after adequate alpha control for persistent tachycardia.
  Model answer: Coordinate a specialist multidisciplinary plan.
Stage 3 — Plan definitive care
  Question: How is timing decided?
  Model answer: Balance gestation, tumour location, haemodynamic control and maternal-fetal risk.
  Model answer: Use invasive monitoring and short-acting vasoactive drugs for surgery or delivery.
  Model answer: Agree neonatal and postoperative critical-care provision.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Phaeochromocytoma in pregnancy threatens both maternal and fetal circulation. Episodic hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations that predate pre-eclampsia should prompt metanephrine testing and MRI without gadolinium.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Coordinate endocrine, obstetric, anaesthetic, neonatal and surgical care. Establish alpha blockade before any beta blocker, restore volume carefully and use invasive monitoring for surgery or delivery. Timing of adrenalectomy and delivery depends on gestation, tumour anatomy and control.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not treat tachycardia first with isolated beta blockade, and do not assume all hypertension after 20 weeks is pre-eclampsia.
Take-home: Phaeochromocytoma in pregnancy requires early recognition, alpha-before-beta blockade and coordinated maternal-fetal planning.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Adrenal incidentaloma before elective surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Adrenal incidentaloma before elective surgery (Phaeochromocytoma, Intermediate)
Patient: An adult awaiting elective joint replacement has an adrenal incidentaloma and elevated metanephrines.
Presentation: They report few symptoms and the surgical team asks whether the unrelated operation can proceed.
Stage 1 — Assess hidden risk
  Question: Can an asymptomatic patient still develop crisis?
  Model answer: Yes. Anaesthesia, intubation and surgical stress can trigger catecholamine release.
  Model answer: Review biochemical certainty, imaging and end-organ effects.
  Model answer: Do not equate few symptoms with low perioperative risk.
Stage 2 — Prioritise procedures
  Question: What happens to elective surgery?
  Model answer: Postpone non-urgent surgery for endocrine evaluation and preparation.
  Model answer: Institute alpha blockade and volume restoration before definitive management.
  Model answer: Avoid isolated beta blockade.
Stage 3 — Handle an emergency exception
  Question: What if unrelated surgery cannot wait?
  Model answer: Use senior multidisciplinary planning and invasive arterial monitoring.
  Model answer: Prepare titratable vasodilators, vasopressors and postoperative critical care.
  Model answer: Avoid known catecholamine-provoking drugs where alternatives exist.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: An adrenal incidentaloma with biochemical catecholamine excess creates risk even when symptoms are mild. Elective unrelated surgery can trigger crisis through induction, intubation, surgical stress or interacting drugs.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Postpone non-urgent surgery, confirm biochemistry and imaging, assess end-organ effects and establish alpha blockade with volume restoration. If emergency surgery cannot wait, use an arterial line, senior multidisciplinary input and prepared short-acting vasodilator and vasopressor infusions.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not dismiss an asymptomatic tumour or proceed after simply adding a beta blocker. Explain why the unrelated operation should usually be deferred.
Take-home: Biochemically active phaeochromocytoma makes unrelated elective anaesthesia unsafe until appropriately prepared.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

The classical extrinsic/intrinsic pathway model is a useful bedside framework but the cell-based model better reflects in-vivo coagulation." ], [ "What are the indications and ratios for major haemorrhage protocol?", "Activate for ongoing bleeding requiring ≥4 units RBC in 1.5, INR Mast cell tryptase peaks 1–2 h post-event; obtain three samples (immediately after resuscitation, 1–2 h, >24 h baseline). A rise of ≥20% + 2 ng/mL above baseline confirms mast cell activation (NAP6, AAGBI 2018). dilutional coagulopathy — clinically relevant after 1.5–2 blood volumes. PROPPR trial (2015): 1:1:1 reduced 24-h mortality from haemorrhage vs 1:1:2 in trauma; obstetric guidance extrapolates. : hypocalcaemia (citrate chelates Ca²⁺ — give 10 mL 10% calcium chloride after every 4 units), hyperkalaemia (stored RBC), hypothermia (warm all fluids), acidosis, TRALI, TACO. Haemostasis involves primary (platelet plug) and secondary (fibrin clot) phases. The cell-based model describes initiation (TF + VIIa → Xa), amplification (thrombin activates platelets + V, VIII, XI), and propagation (burst of thrombin → fibrin). TF + VII PT / INR Warfarin monitoring; earliest to prolong in liver failure (VII t½ = 6h) XII, XI, IX, VIII Heparin monitoring; haemophilia A (VIII) and B (IX) X, V, II, I (fibrinogen) TT (thrombin time) Final common pathway → fibrin crosslinked by XIII Liver disease reduces procoagulants (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI and sometimes fibrinogen) endogenous anticoagulants (protein C, protein S and antithrombin). Thrombocytopenia reflects portal-hypertensive splenic sequestration and reduced thrombopoietin; platelet dysfunction coexists with increased von Willebrand factor. Fibrinolysis is also unstable because plasminogen falls while tPA clearance falls The new equilibrium is fragile and may tip towards bleeding or thrombosis. PT/INR measures selected procoagulants but not anticoagulant loss, platelets or fibrinolysis, so it does not predict procedural bleeding reliably. TEG/ROTEM provides a global dynamic assessment and can target fibrinogen, platelets or antifibrinolytic treatment rather than empirical FFP. ABO system : Group O = universal donor (no A/B antigens); Group AB = universal recipient. Naturally occurring IgM antibodies → immediate haemolytic reaction if mismatched Rhesus system : D antigen most important. Rh− patients develop anti-D IgG after sensitisation → delayed reaction. Anti-D prophylaxis in Rh− mothers : a two-hit process — recipient neutrophils are primed by sepsis/surgery, then donor anti-HLA/HNA antibodies or biological response modifiers activate them, causing capillary leak and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Plasma-rich FFP and platelets carry greater risk. : rapid transfusion exceeds cardiac reserve, producing hydrostatic oedema; elderly patients and those with cardiac/renal failure are vulnerable. Hypertension, raised JVP and BNP support TACO rather than TRALI. Febrile non-haemolytic reaction : recipient antibodies recognise donor leucocyte antigens, or storage cytokines trigger fever/rigors; universal UK leucodepletion reduces incidence. Massive transfusion : citrate chelates ionised calcium (a common rule is 10 mL 10% calcium chloride or 30 mL 10% calcium gluconate per four units, guided by ionised Ca²⁺). Stored-cell K⁺ leakage makes rapid older-blood transfusion hazardous in neonates and renal failure. Also prevent hypothermia and dilutional coagulopathy. Tranexamic acid is a synthetic lysine analogue that competitively occupies plasminogen lysine-binding sites, reducing binding to fibrin and conversion to plasmin. It is renally excreted, so reduce repeated dosing in renal impairment. High exposure, especially in cardiac surgery or renal failure, increases seizure risk. CRASH-2 showed lower death from bleeding when TXA was given early; give 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h, within 3 h of injury Postpartum haemorrhage: WOMAN reduced death due to bleeding; give 1 g IV promptly, repeating 1 g after 30 min if bleeding continues or within 24 h if it restarts Combat trauma: MATTERs associated TXA with improved survival in severely injured transfused casualties, while recognising its observational design S. pneumoniae E. coli ) are largely countered by the humoral arm; intracellular bacteria (e.g. M. tuberculosis ) require cell-mediated immunity (Th1/macrophage activation). Naïve exposure (first encounter) 0–4 h — Barriers & resident defence: skin/mucosa, lysozyme, antimicrobial peptides (defensins), commensal flora competition. Tissue macrophages recognise bacterial PAMPs (LPS, peptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acid, flagellin) via TLRs (TLR4 = LPS, TLR2 = Gram⁺, TLR5 = flagellin). 4–12 h — Acute inflammation: macrophages release TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, CXCL8 → endothelial activation (selectins, ICAM-1, VCAM-1) → neutrophil rolling, adhesion, diapedesis. Complement activated by alternative (spontaneous on bacterial surfaces) and lectin (MBL → mannose) pathways → C3b opsonisation, C5a chemotaxis, C5b-9 MAC lyses Gram-negatives. 12–96 h — Phagocyte killing: neutrophils ingest opsonised bacteria → respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase → O₂⁻, H₂O₂, HOCl), myeloperoxidase, NETs. Pus = dead neutrophils. Acute-phase response: hepatic CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin (driven by IL-6); fever from hypothalamic PGE₂. 3–7 days — Adaptive priming: dendritic cells migrate to draining lymph node carrying processed antigen on MHC-II. Naïve CD4⁺ T cells differentiate into Th1 (IFN-γ — intracellular pathogens) or Th17 (IL-17 — extracellular bacteria, neutrophil recruitment). B cells encounter antigen, receive T-cell help (CD40L–CD40), undergo germinal centre reaction. 7–14 days — Antibody response: IgM appears first (low affinity, pentameric, complement-fixing) then class-switches to IgG (high affinity, opsonising, crosses placenta) and IgA (mucosal). Plasma cells churn out antibody; memory B and T cells persist for years. 2–4 weeks — Resolution: apoptosis of effector cells, regulatory T cells dampen inflammation, tissue repair, scar/fibrosis if extensive. A small clone of memory lymphocytes is retained. Re-exposure (secondary response) memory B cells produce antibody within 1–3 days (vs 7–14 days). 100–1000× higher antibody titre. predominantly high-affinity, class-switched IgG (somatic hypermutation, affinity maturation has already occurred). Pre-formed circulating IgG opsonises bacteria immediately; complement is fixed via the pathway (Ag–Ab complex → C1q). Memory Th1/Th17 cells recruit and arm macrophages and neutrophils within hours. The pathogen is usually cleared subclinically — this is the basis of vaccination. Anaesthetic relevance: functional/anatomical asplenia (sickle, post-splenectomy) loses the marginal-zone B cells that mount the rapid IgM response to encapsulated organisms ( H. influenzae N. meningitidis ) — vaccinate and consider penicillin prophylaxis. type I interferons NK cells CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes . Antibodies neutralise free virions but cannot reach intracellular virus. 0–24 h — Intracellular sensing: viral nucleic acids detected by endosomal TLRs (TLR3 dsRNA, TLR7/8 ssRNA, TLR9 CpG DNA) and cytoplasmic sensors (RIG-I, MDA5, cGAS-STING) → infected cells secrete type I interferons (IFN-α/β) 1–3 days — Antiviral state: IFN-α/β binds JAK-STAT receptors on neighbouring cells → upregulates PKR, OAS-RNase L (degrade viral RNA), MxA (block replication), ↑ MHC-I (display viral peptides). NK cells kill cells with absent/reduced MHC-I (the "missing-self" recognition) and release IFN-γ. 3–7 days — CTL priming: dendritic cells cross-present viral antigen on MHC-I → activate naïve CD8⁺ T cells in lymph node. CD4⁺ Th1 help via IL-2 and IFN-γ enhances CTL expansion. 7–14 days — Cytotoxic killing: effector CD8⁺ CTLs migrate to infected tissue, recognise viral peptide–MHC-I complex → release perforin + granzymes and engage Fas-FasL → induce apoptosis of infected cells. Concurrent B-cell response generates neutralising IgM → IgG against surface glycoproteins (haemagglutinin, spike, gp120). virus cleared, most effector cells undergo contraction by apoptosis. A long-lived pool of memory CTLs and memory B cells persists. Some viruses (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV, HIV) establish latency. neutralising IgG/IgA at mucosal surfaces blocks viral entry (binds receptor-binding domain → prevents attachment). If virus enters, memory CD8⁺ CTLs mount a response within 24–72 h — orders of magnitude faster than the naïve 7–14 day window — and clear infected cells before significant viraemia. Antigenic drift (point mutations) and antigenic shift (reassortment, e.g. influenza) can escape neutralising antibody, producing recurrent epidemics despite memory. Latent viruses (e.g. VZV → shingles) reactivate when T-cell surveillance wanes (age, immunosuppression, steroids). surgery + GA cause transient cell-mediated immunosuppression (↓ NK activity, ↓ Th1, ↑ Th2 shift, IL-10) — opioids and volatiles contribute. Reactivation of HSV, VZV, CMV is well described post-op, particularly in the immunosuppressed. Adrenaline IV bolus 50 µg titrated to response. Asplenic patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming infection by encapsulated organisms — confirm pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY+B and Hib vaccination plus penicillin prophylaxis. Liver disease coagulopathy is balanced — INR overestimates bleeding risk; use TEG/ROTEM and avoid empiric FFP. : anticipate dilutional thrombocytopenia, hypocalcaemia (citrate), hyperkalaemia and hypothermia — give in 1:1:1 ratio. ABO incompatibility is almost always a clerical error — repeat ID checks at every step. TT = common pathway ABO mismatch causes acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (IgM) — most dangerous transfusion complication Type I hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis): IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation. Asplenic / Hyposplenic Patient — Immunisation Flowchart Outline the coagulation cascade in the cell-based model. Three overlapping phases: 1) Initiation — tissue factor exposed at injury site activates factor VII → small thrombin burst on TF-bearing cells. 2) Amplification — thrombin activates platelets, V, VIII, XI on the platelet surface. 3) Propagation — large-scale thrombin generation on activated platelets converts fibrinogen to fibrin. The classical extrinsic/intrinsic pathway model is a useful bedside framework but the cell-based model better reflects in-vivo coagulation. What are the indications and ratios for major haemorrhage protocol? Activate for ongoing bleeding requiring ≥4 units RBC in <1 h, or anticipated need. Initial pack: 4 units RBC + 4 units FFP + 1 pool platelets (1:1:1 ratio, replicates whole blood). Add cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen <1.5 g/L (or <2.0 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage). Tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 h (CRASH-2, WOMAN, MATTERs). Calcium 1 g for every 4 units (citrate chelation). Aim platelets >50, fibrinogen >1.5, INR <1.5, Ca >1.0, T >36, pH >7.2. What is the difference between innate and adaptive immunity? Innate — non-specific, immediate (mins–hrs), no memory. Components: physical barriers, neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells, complement, cytokines. Recognises pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) via pattern-recognition receptors (e.g. TLRs). Adaptive — specific, delayed (days), generates memory. Components: T cells (cellular) and B cells/antibodies (humoral). Anaesthesia and surgery transiently impair both arms — clinically relevant in immunocompromised and cancer patients. Describe the cell-based model of coagulation (initiation, amplification, propagation) and the laboratory tests of each pathway. Outline the ABO/Rh blood group systems and recognise acute and delayed transfusion reactions. Distinguish innate from adaptive immunity, naming key cellular and humoral effectors. Explain the kinetics of primary vs secondary antibody responses and their relevance to vaccination. Classify hypersensitivity reactions (Types I–IV) with anaesthetic correlates, including anaphylaxis management. Describe the immunological consequences of asplenia and the BSH vaccination/prophylaxis bundle. ], }, ]; const HaematologyImmunityTopic = () => { return ( Haematology and immunity sit at the heart of perioperative medicine — from haemostasis at the surgical wound to the recognition of anaphylaxis on induction and the immune compromise of asplenic, transplant and septic patients. This topic moves from coagulation (the cellular response to vessel injury) through blood-group serology and transfusion, to the architecture of innate and adaptive immunity, finishing with the differential response to bacterial vs viral infection and the rationale for vaccination.

{[ { title: Non-specific, immediate. Physical barriers (skin, mucosa), complement cascade (classical, alternative, lectin pathways), phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), NK cells. Pattern recognition receptors (TLRs) detect PAMPs/DAMPs. Specific, delayed (days). T cells: CD4⁺ helper (Th1 → cell-mediated, Th2 → humoral), CD8⁺ cytotoxic. B cells → plasma cells → antibodies (IgM first, then IgG class switch). Memory cells for secondary response. Type I: immediate IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation. Type II: IgG/IgM targets cell-surface antigen; complement and phagocytes act within minutes–hours (ABO incompatibility, HIT). Type III: circulating immune complexes deposit and activate complement/neutrophils over about 3–8 h (drug vasculitis, post-streptococcal GN). Type IV: sensitised Th1/CTL cells release IFN-γ/TNF-α and recruit macrophages over 48–72 h (chlorhexidine contact dermatitis, non-IgE latex dermatitis, tuberculin test). Systemic inflammation (↑ TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) → vasodilation, capillary leak, coagulopathy. SIRS criteria now replaced by SOFA/qSOFA in Sepsis-3. Toggle between bacterial vs viral pathogens and naïve vs re-exposed states. The pathogen-burden curve, swimlane phases and cellular players all redraw — re-exposure suppresses the burden curve almost entirely, illustrating why vaccination works. >Re-exposure (secondary response)

case_bank.title: Neutropenic sepsis after chemotherapy
case_bank.text:
Case: Neutropenic sepsis after chemotherapy (Infection & immunity, Intermediate)
Patient: Ten days after chemotherapy a patient presents with temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, neutrophils 0.2 × 10⁹/L and lactate 3.4 mmol/L.
Presentation: There is no localising sign, and a tunnelled central line is in situ.
Stage 1 — Define the problem
  Question: How do you classify this presentation?
  Model answer: Sepsis under Sepsis-3: suspected infection with life-threatening organ dysfunction, indicated by hypotension and raised lactate.
  Model answer: Neutropenia means the innate cellular response is absent, so classical inflammatory signs and pus formation may be minimal.
  Model answer: Rapid deterioration is expected, and gram-negative bacteraemia carries particular risk.
Stage 2 — Act within the first hour
  Question: What do you do immediately?
  Model answer: Take blood cultures including from each line lumen, then give empirical broad-spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam without waiting for results.
  Model answer: Give balanced crystalloid for hypoperfusion, measure lactate serially, and start vasopressor if hypotension persists after initial resuscitation.
  Model answer: Escalate to critical care early, and look actively for line, chest, perianal, oral and skin sources.
Stage 3 — Continue and refine
  Question: What happens over the next 48 hours?
  Model answer: Review cultures and de-escalate or broaden accordingly, adding antifungal cover for persistent fever with prolonged neutropenia and considering resistant organisms by local ecology.
  Model answer: Consider line removal for tunnel infection, persistent bacteraemia or specific organisms, and discuss growth factor support with haematology.
  Model answer: Reassess daily for the need for imaging, source control and antimicrobial stewardship.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Neutrophils provide phagocytosis, oxidative killing and pus formation; without them, infection progresses with few local signs and the systemic response may be the only clue. Innate recognition through pattern-recognition receptors still triggers cytokine release, so fever remains a critical warning sign that mandates immediate empirical therapy rather than observation.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Follow the sepsis bundle: cultures, antimicrobials within one hour, lactate measurement, fluid resuscitation for hypoperfusion and vasopressor to a mean arterial pressure of about 65 mmHg. Monitor for progressive organ failure with serial lactate, urine output, gases and coagulation. Coordinate with haematology and microbiology on antimicrobial choice, line management, antifungal and antiviral cover, and consider immunoglobulin or growth factor only on specialist advice.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not wait for cultures or a localising source before giving antibiotics, and do not be reassured by the absence of inflammation. State the one-hour target and the antipseudomonal requirement.
Take-home: In neutropenia, fever is an emergency: culture, give antipseudomonal cover within the hour, resuscitate, and hunt the line and mucosal sources.
Cited sources: Sepsis-3 definitions (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2016.0287); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000005337); BJA Educ: immunology for intensivists (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.02.003)

case_bank.title: Fulminant sepsis in an asplenic patient
case_bank.text:
Case: Fulminant sepsis in an asplenic patient (Infection & immunity, Advanced)
Patient: A patient who had a splenectomy after trauma years ago presents with a few hours of fever, vomiting and a purpuric rash. Blood pressure is 75/40 mmHg with lactate 6 mmol/L.
Presentation: Coagulation is deranged and the platelet count is falling.
Stage 1 — Explain the immunology
  Question: Why is this patient so vulnerable?
  Model answer: The spleen filters encapsulated organisms poorly opsonised elsewhere, and hosts marginal-zone B cells that generate T-independent IgM against polysaccharide capsules.
  Model answer: Loss of splenic macrophages and reduced IgM impair complement-mediated opsonisation, so Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis can multiply unchecked.
  Model answer: The result is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection, which can progress to purpura fulminans and death within hours.
Stage 2 — Resuscitate and treat
  Question: What are your immediate priorities?
  Model answer: Give an immediate third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone after taking cultures, without waiting for investigations.
  Model answer: Resuscitate with balanced crystalloid and vasopressor, correct coagulopathy and involve critical care and microbiology urgently.
  Model answer: Isolate and give meningococcal prophylaxis to close contacts if meningococcal disease is confirmed or strongly suspected.
Stage 3 — Prevent recurrence
  Question: What long-term measures should have been in place?
  Model answer: Vaccination against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcal serogroups and annual influenza, with documented boosters.
  Model answer: Lifelong or at least risk-period antibiotic prophylaxis, usually penicillin, plus a rescue supply and clear written advice.
  Model answer: A patient-held alert card, education about urgent presentation with fever, and travel and animal-bite advice.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Splenic function is central to defence against encapsulated bacteria: capsules resist phagocytosis unless opsonised by antibody and complement, and the spleen provides both the antibody-producing marginal-zone B cells and the filtering macrophage population. The classical and alternative complement pathways then permit opsonophagocytosis and membrane attack complex formation; asplenia removes the essential first step, which is why disease is fulminant rather than gradual.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Time to antibiotic is the dominant determinant of survival. Give ceftriaxone immediately, resuscitate, and support organ failure in critical care with attention to disseminated intravascular coagulation, adrenal haemorrhage and limb ischaemia from purpura fulminans. Long-term prevention combines vaccination, prophylactic antibiotics, an alert card and patient education; check vaccination status whenever an asplenic patient is encountered for any reason.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture or imaging, and do not describe complement in vague terms — name the opsonisation and membrane attack functions and the encapsulated organisms.
Take-home: Asplenia removes antibody- and complement-dependent defence against encapsulated bacteria: give ceftriaxone immediately and ensure lifelong vaccination and prophylaxis.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: immunology for intensivists (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.02.003); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000005337)

case_bank.title: Trauma inside the three-hour window
case_bank.text:
Case: Trauma inside the three-hour window (Antifibrinolytics, Foundation)
Patient: A 29-year-old arrives 70 minutes after a road collision with pelvic disruption, BP 82/46 mmHg and ongoing haemorrhage.
Presentation: The major haemorrhage protocol is active. A colleague asks whether TXA should wait for ROTEM.
Stage 1 — Make the time-critical decision
  Question: Should TXA be delayed?
  Model answer: No. Significant traumatic bleeding within three hours is an indication for early TXA; benefit is greatest when given promptly.
  Model answer: Give 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g over eight hours.
  Model answer: Do not delay haemorrhage control, balanced resuscitation, warming or calcium replacement.
Stage 2 — Use viscoelastic testing
  Question: What role does ROTEM play after initial treatment?
  Model answer: ROTEM/TEG guides fibrinogen, plasma and platelet therapy and can identify ongoing hyperfibrinolysis.
  Model answer: It complements rather than replaces immediate evidence-based TXA in early major trauma.
  Model answer: Trend physiology: temperature, pH, ionised calcium, lactate and surgical control.
Stage 3 — Avoid the timing trap
  Question: What if the patient arrived four hours after injury?
  Model answer: Routine CRASH-2 trauma TXA should not be started beyond three hours because benefit is absent and harm is possible.
  Model answer: Management remains urgent haemorrhage control and goal-directed resuscitation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: TXA inhibits plasminogen activation and limits fibrin breakdown. In significant traumatic haemorrhage, survival benefit is time dependent and greatest with early administration; viscoelastic results are not required before the first dose. Beyond three hours after injury, routine CRASH-2 treatment should not be initiated because benefit is lost and harm is possible.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g over eight hours while continuing definitive haemorrhage control, balanced blood-component resuscitation, warming and calcium replacement. Use ROTEM or TEG to guide subsequent fibrinogen, plasma and platelet therapy and track temperature, pH, ionised calcium and lactate.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: TXA is an adjunct, not a reason to delay theatre, interventional radiology or damage-control resuscitation. Always state the injury-to-dose interval.
Take-home: For bleeding trauma, TXA is a time-dependent adjunct: 1 g then 1 g over eight hours, started as early as possible and within three hours.
Cited sources: CRASH-2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60835-5)

case_bank.title: Postpartum haemorrhage after caesarean birth
case_bank.text:
Case: Postpartum haemorrhage after caesarean birth (Antifibrinolytics, Intermediate)
Patient: A 34-year-old develops uterine atony and 1.4 L blood loss 25 minutes after caesarean delivery.
Presentation: Uterotonics and surgical measures are underway. She remains tachycardic with brisk ongoing bleeding.
Stage 1 — Add antifibrinolytic treatment
  Question: What is the TXA plan?
  Model answer: Give TXA 1 g IV as soon as possible and within three hours of bleeding onset.
  Model answer: If bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours, a second 1 g dose may be given according to the WOMAN regimen and local protocol.
  Model answer: TXA does not replace uterotonics, surgical control or activation of the obstetric major-haemorrhage pathway.
Stage 2 — Resuscitate in parallel
  Question: Which targets deserve repeated attention?
  Model answer: Assess fibrinogen early because it can fall rapidly in obstetric haemorrhage.
  Model answer: Warm patient and products; monitor ionised calcium, acid–base status, platelets and coagulation.
  Model answer: Use blood products and fibrinogen replacement according to clinical bleeding, laboratory or viscoelastic results and local protocol.
Stage 3 — Communicate the endpoint
  Question: What should the team document?
  Model answer: Time of bleeding onset and each TXA dose, cumulative blood loss, interventions and response.
  Model answer: Thrombosis risk assessment later remains important, but appropriate TXA for active PPH is not a reason to withhold indicated prophylaxis indefinitely.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Postpartum haemorrhage activates fibrinolysis early, so TXA should be given promptly once PPH is diagnosed and within three hours of bleeding onset. It reduces death from bleeding but does not correct uterine atony, retained tissue, trauma or coagulopathy by itself.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give TXA 1 g IV as soon as possible; repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours, following local protocol. Continue uterotonics, surgical or radiological control and major-haemorrhage resuscitation. Measure fibrinogen early, warm the patient and products, and monitor platelets, coagulation, pH and ionised calcium.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not postpone TXA until laboratory results return, but also do not let it distract from the four causes of PPH and definitive control. Record bleeding onset and dose times.
Take-home: In postpartum haemorrhage, give TXA early alongside—never instead of—uterotonic, surgical and transfusion management.
Cited sources: WOMAN trial (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(17)30638-4)

case_bank.title: Tranexamic acid in high-risk non-cardiac surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Tranexamic acid in high-risk non-cardiac surgery (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: A 76-year-old with remote provoked DVT is scheduled for major multilevel spine surgery with high anticipated blood loss.
Presentation: The team is weighing reduced bleeding against perioperative vascular risk.
Stage 1 — Balance benefit and uncertainty
  Question: How should the evidence be framed?
  Model answer: TXA reduces major bleeding in non-cardiac surgery.
  Model answer: POISE-3 did not establish non-inferiority for the composite cardiovascular safety outcome, so individual thrombotic and bleeding risks still matter.
  Model answer: A remote provoked DVT is not automatically equivalent to active thrombosis; review timing, recurrence, anticoagulation and local guidance.
Stage 2 — Choose and prescribe deliberately
  Question: What safeguards belong in the plan?
  Model answer: Use the procedure-specific local dose rather than importing a trauma regimen.
  Model answer: Adjust or avoid repeated high dosing in significant renal impairment because TXA is renally cleared.
  Model answer: Avoid accidental neuraxial administration: separate storage, label syringes and use route-specific checks.
Stage 3 — Monitor relevant harms
  Question: What postoperative surveillance is appropriate?
  Model answer: Continue standard VTE prevention once haemostasis permits.
  Model answer: Investigate clinical signs of venous or arterial thrombosis rather than using TXA exposure alone as a diagnosis.
  Model answer: Recognise that seizures are associated particularly with high exposure and renal accumulation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: In major non-cardiac surgery, TXA lowers bleeding, but POISE-3 did not prove non-inferiority for its composite cardiovascular safety outcome. Decision-making therefore combines procedural blood-loss risk with active or previous thrombosis, vascular disease, anticoagulation and renal function. A remote provoked DVT is not the same as active thrombosis.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use the procedure-specific local regimen rather than a trauma dose. Reduce exposure in renal impairment because TXA is predominantly renally cleared, and avoid repeated high doses where accumulation raises seizure risk. Keep ampoules and syringes physically separated from neuraxial drugs and perform explicit route checks. Restart standard VTE prophylaxis when haemostasis permits.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: The catastrophic route error is intrathecal TXA. Mention storage, labelling and checking systems as well as pharmacology and thrombosis assessment.
Take-home: Elective perioperative TXA requires procedure-specific dosing and an individual bleeding–thrombosis assessment; renal function and route safety are practical exam points.
Cited sources: POISE-3 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171)

case_bank.title: Septic DIC with line-site bleeding
case_bank.text:
Case: Septic DIC with line-site bleeding (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: A 67-year-old in septic shock has platelets 42 ×10⁹/L, PT prolonged by 8 seconds, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L and markedly raised D-dimer.
Presentation: There is oozing from cannula sites. A request is made for empirical TXA because ‘the patient is bleeding’.
Stage 1 — Diagnose the coagulopathy
  Question: How should the results be interpreted?
  Model answer: The combination is consistent with overt DIC in the correct clinical context.
  Model answer: Treating the septic source and restoring perfusion are the central interventions.
  Model answer: Replace platelets, fibrinogen and plasma for clinically significant bleeding using laboratory and viscoelastic guidance—not the D-dimer alone.
Stage 2 — Decide on TXA
  Question: Is empirical TXA appropriate?
  Model answer: No. DIC may be thrombosis-predominant, and suppressing fibrinolysis can worsen microvascular thrombosis.
  Model answer: Reserve antifibrinolytic treatment for exceptional severe bleeding where predominant hyperfibrinolysis is demonstrated, ideally with specialist and ROTEM/TEG input.
  Model answer: An elevated D-dimer does not by itself prove that TXA will help.
Stage 3 — Set measurable targets
  Question: What should guide replacement?
  Model answer: Aim for haemostasis appropriate to active bleeding: commonly platelets above 50 ×10⁹/L and fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, individualised to site and procedure.
  Model answer: Trend clotting, fibrinogen, platelets, temperature, pH and ionised calcium while treating infection and organ failure.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Septic DIC simultaneously activates coagulation, consumes platelets and factors and alters fibrinolysis. Raised D-dimer shows fibrin turnover but does not establish dominant hyperfibrinolysis. Empirical antifibrinolysis can worsen microvascular thrombosis when coagulation activation predominates.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Treat infection and restore perfusion first. For clinically important bleeding, replace platelets, fibrinogen and plasma according to serial laboratory and viscoelastic assessment; common pragmatic targets include platelets above 50 ×10⁹/L and fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, individualised to the bleeding site. Consider TXA only for exceptional life-threatening bleeding with demonstrated predominant hyperfibrinolysis and specialist input.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Bleeding plus a high D-dimer is not an automatic TXA indication. State the DIC phenotype, evidence of fibrinolysis and the risk of worsening thrombosis.
Take-home: Bleeding is not synonymous with an indication for TXA. In DIC, correct the cause and replace deficient components; use antifibrinolytics only for demonstrated dominant hyperfibrinolysis.
Cited sources: CRASH-2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60835-5)

case_bank.title: Tranexamic acid in advanced kidney disease
case_bank.text:
Case: Tranexamic acid in advanced kidney disease (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: An adult with stage 4 chronic kidney disease is listed for revision arthroplasty with anticipated major blood loss.
Presentation: A standard repeated-dose TXA regimen has been copied onto the chart.
Stage 1 — Identify accumulation risk
  Question: Why must the prescription be reconsidered?
  Model answer: TXA is predominantly renally eliminated.
  Model answer: Reduced clearance increases exposure from repeated or high dosing.
  Model answer: High exposure is associated with postoperative seizures.
Stage 2 — Prescribe safely
  Question: What practical safeguards are required?
  Model answer: Confirm current renal function and follow the local renal-adjusted protocol.
  Model answer: Document timing and cumulative dose to prevent repetition.
  Model answer: Use blood conservation and haemostatic measures in parallel.
Stage 3 — Respond to neurological signs
  Question: What if postoperative myoclonus occurs?
  Model answer: Consider TXA accumulation among metabolic and neurological causes.
  Model answer: Stop further TXA, correct reversible factors and treat seizures promptly.
  Model answer: Escalate monitoring and specialist review.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: TXA is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney. Advanced renal impairment prolongs exposure, so repeated or high dosing increases accumulation and seizure risk; the indication and local renal-adjustment protocol must be explicit.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Verify current renal function, indication, timing and cumulative dose. Use the lowest evidence-based renal-adjusted regimen in consultation with local guidance, avoid accidental repeat dosing and monitor neurological recovery. New myoclonus or seizures require drug review and supportive seizure management.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not copy a normal-renal-function regimen into advanced kidney disease. Separate efficacy evidence from dosing safety.
Take-home: Renal impairment changes TXA exposure: use an evidence-based adjusted regimen and monitor cumulative dose and neurological toxicity.
Cited sources: POISE-3 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171)

case_bank.title: High-dose TXA during cardiac surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: High-dose TXA during cardiac surgery (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: An older adult with impaired renal function undergoes complex redo valve surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass.
Presentation: Several TXA doses are planned in the loading dose, pump prime and infusion.
Stage 1 — Balance benefit and harm
  Question: Why is careful cumulative dosing important?
  Model answer: Antifibrinolysis can reduce bleeding and transfusion in cardiac surgery.
  Model answer: Bypass, renal dysfunction and high cumulative exposure increase seizure risk.
  Model answer: Benefit does not justify untracked dose escalation.
Stage 2 — Coordinate blood conservation
  Question: What belongs in the complete plan?
  Model answer: Use a weight- and renal-adjusted institutional regimen.
  Model answer: Record every loading, prime and infusion dose.
  Model answer: Combine surgical haemostasis, cell salvage and point-of-care coagulation guidance.
Stage 3 — Plan postoperative surveillance
  Question: What should handover emphasise?
  Model answer: State cumulative TXA exposure and renal function.
  Model answer: Distinguish seizure from delayed emergence, shivering and embolic stroke.
  Model answer: Maintain route separation so TXA cannot enter a neuraxial pathway.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Cardiac surgery activates fibrinolysis and often benefits from antifibrinolysis, but cardiopulmonary bypass, renal dysfunction and high cumulative TXA exposure all increase postoperative seizure risk.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use the unit’s weight- and renal-function-adjusted protocol, document all loading, bypass-prime and infusion doses, and coordinate blood conservation with surgical haemostasis, cell salvage and point-of-care coagulation testing. Protect against medication-route errors.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: More TXA is not automatically better. State the trade-off between reduced transfusion and dose-related neurological toxicity.
Take-home: In cardiac surgery, TXA should be protocolised and dose-accounted; renal function and seizure risk constrain exposure.
Cited sources: POISE-3 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171)

entries.description: Cardiovascular, respiratory, haematological and pharmacological changes in pregnancy
entries.text:
# Maternal Physiology Cardiovascular, respiratory, haematological and pharmacological changes in pregnancy O₂ store ÷ O₂ consumption Non-pregnant: FRC ~2.5 L × FiO₂ 0.9 (after pre-O₂) ≈ 2.25 L O₂; VO₂ ~250 mL/min → ~9 min. Term pregnancy: FRC ~2.0 L (↓ 20%) × 0.9 ≈ 1.8 L; VO₂ ~325 mL/min (↑ 30%) → ~3–4 min at most. Aortocaval compression and supine position drop FRC further (closing capacity may exceed FRC awake). Engorged epidural veins ↓ effective CSF volume in the lumbar sac. Progesterone ↑ neural sensitivity to local anaesthetic. Hyperventilation-induced respiratory alkalosis ↑ non-ionised LA fraction. Aortocaval compression and rapid block onset → profound sympathectomy and hypotension. infusion 25–50 µg/min is preferred over ephedrine; OAA recommends prophylactic infusion from spinal injection). Left uterine displacement (15° tilt or manual displacement) is essential from 20 weeks onwards during supine positioning to prevent aortocaval compression syndrome. ↑ O₂ consumption ↓ FRC means the parturient desaturates rapidly during apnoea — reinforcing the critical importance of pre-oxygenation before RSI. Plasma volume ↑ 45% vs red cell mass ↑ 20% → physiological anaemia of pregnancy Hypercoagulable state : ↑ fibrinogen (4–6 g/L), ↑ factors VII, VIII, X, vWF; ↓ protein S; ↓ fibrinolysis. VTE risk ↑ 5–10× — RCOG-stratified prophylactic LMWH commonly indicated. White cell count ↑ (up to 15 × 10⁹/L in 3rd trimester, up to 25 in labour) — limits WCC as infection marker. Platelet count mildly ↓ (gestational thrombocytopenia ~100–150 × 10⁹/L in ~8% of pregnancies). ↓ Lower oesophageal sphincter tone (progesterone) + ↑ intragastric pressure (gravid uterus) → ↑ aspiration risk. Delayed gastric emptying in labour (opioids compound this further). Airway oedema : capillary engorgement of nasopharyngeal/laryngeal mucosa — use smaller ETT (6.0–6.5), avoid nasal intubation if possible. Mallampati score worsens during pregnancy and especially during labour. Failed intubation rate in obstetrics historically ~1:250 (vs ~1:2000 in general population) — follow OAA/DAS 2015 algorithm. Renal blood flow ↑ 50–80% → GFR ↑ 50% → ↓ creatinine (normal upper limit ~75 µmol/L in pregnancy). common (↓ tubular reabsorption threshold). : ↓ albumin (dilutional), ↓ plasma cholinesterase activity (prolonged suxamethonium action rarely clinically significant). elevated (placental isoenzyme) — not a reliable marker of liver disease in pregnancy. ↑ Volume of distribution : ↑ plasma volume and total body water → larger loading doses may be needed for some drugs. ↓ Protein binding : ↓ albumin → ↑ free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs (thiopentone, diazepam). MAC ↓ 30–40% for volatile agents (progesterone, endorphins). ↑ Sensitivity to local anaesthetics : epidural/spinal doses reduced by ~30% (engorged epidural veins ↓ CSF volume + ↑ neural sensitivity). ↑ Sensitivity to neuromuscular blockers : ↓ plasma cholinesterase (clinically subtle). From 20 weeks : full-stomach precautions and 15° left lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression. Difficult airway : capillary engorgement, weight gain, breast enlargement and full dentition combine — pre-oxygenate well; desaturate fast due to ↓ FRC + ↑ VO₂. Reduced LA dose : epidural/spinal doses ~30% lower than non-pregnant. Total spinal risk if subdural/intrathecal placement missed. Hypotension after spinal : phenylephrine preferred over ephedrine (less foetal acidaemia). Massive obstetric haemorrhage : pregnant patients tolerate large blood loss before becoming overtly shocked — act on heart rate and trend, not single BP. Pre-oxygenation in late pregnancy Spinal anaesthesia dose for caesarean section Maternal Physiology FRCA Primary & Final — Physiology CO ↑ 30–50%, SVR ↓ 20% — left uterine displacement essential from 20 weeks. ↓ FRC + ↑ O₂ consumption ⇒ rapid desaturation during apnoea — pre-oxygenate meticulously. Physiological anaemia: plasma volume ↑ 45% vs RBC mass ↑ 20%; Hb nadir ~110 g/L. Hypercoagulable state: ↑ fibrinogen, ↑ clotting factors, ↓ protein S → VTE risk ↑ 5–10×. MAC ↓ 30–40% and intrathecal/epidural LA dose requirements ↓ ~30%. Aspiration risk ↑: ↓ LOS tone, ↑ intragastric pressure, delayed gastric emptying in labour. Phenylephrine infusion is preferred over ephedrine for spinal hypotension at caesarean section. Overview Physiological Change Timeline Cardiovascular Changes Cardiac Output ↑ 30–50% by 28 weeks (peaks early 3rd trimester); further 50% in labour, peak immediately post-partum. Heart Rate ↑ 15–25 bpm above baseline. Stroke Volume ↑ 25–30% by end of 2nd trimester. ↓ 20% (progesterone-mediated vasodilation, low-resistance placental bed). Blood Pressure ↓ in 2nd trimester (nadir ~20 weeks), returns to baseline at term. Aortocaval Compression Supine position from ~20 weeks → IVC compression → ↓ venous return up to 25%. Respiratory Changes Minute Ventilation ↑ 50% (↑ tidal volume, rate largely unchanged). Tidal Volume ↑ 40% (progesterone-driven). ↓ 20% (diaphragm elevated by gravid uterus). Oxygen Consumption PaCO₂ ↓ to ~4.0 kPa (30 mmHg) — chronic respiratory alkalosis with renal HCO₃⁻ compensation. PaO₂ ↑ slightly due to hyperventilation (13–14 kPa). Haematological Changes Gastrointestinal & Airway Changes Renal & Hepatic Changes Pharmacological Implications Summarise the cardiovascular changes of pregnancy. By term: blood volume ↑40–50 %, plasma > red cell mass (physiological anaemia), cardiac output ↑40–50 % (↑SV early, ↑HR late), SVR ↓20 %, BP unchanged or slightly lower in 2nd trimester. Aortocaval compression from 20 weeks → 15° left lateral tilt mandatory after this. Labour: further ↑CO with each contraction (~30 %), peaks immediately post-delivery (autotransfusion). Returns to baseline by 2 weeks postpartum. Why is the pregnant woman at increased risk of failed intubation and rapid desaturation? Airway: weight gain, mucosal oedema, breast enlargement, full dentition; failed intubation 1:300 (8× the non-pregnant rate). Reduced FRC (15–20 %) and increased oxygen consumption (20 %) cause desaturation within 1 min of apnoea vs ~3 min in non-pregnant. Strategies: ramped position, pre-oxygenation 3 min with end-tidal O₂ >85 %, smaller ETT (6.5–7.0), video laryngoscopy first-line, OAA/DAS failed-intubation algorithm rehearsed. Why does the pregnant patient need a reduced MAC and lower local anaesthetic dose? MAC for volatiles falls ~30 % (progesterone-mediated CNS sensitivity). Spinal/epidural local anaesthetic requirement falls ~30 % because engorged epidural veins reduce the volume of the epidural and subarachnoid space, plus increased neural sensitivity. Use 2.0–2.5 mL of 0.5 % heavy bupivacaine for spinal at C-section rather than 3.0 mL. Describe the major cardiovascular changes of pregnancy and explain aortocaval compression. Outline the respiratory changes and their implications for pre-oxygenation and rapid sequence induction. Summarise the haematological adaptations and the basis of pregnancy-associated hypercoagulability. Recognise the airway and gastrointestinal changes that increase difficult intubation and aspiration risk. Apply pharmacological adaptations (MAC, LA dose, protein binding) to safe perioperative prescribing. ], }, ]; const MaternalPhysiologyTopic = () => { return ( Pregnancy induces profound physiological adaptations across every organ system to meet the metabolic demands of the growing fetus and prepare for delivery. These changes have major implications for anaesthetic management, drug pharmacokinetics, and perioperative risk.
