entries.description: Foetal shunts, HbF, transitional circulation, persistent pulmonary hypertension
entries.text:
# Foetal Circulation Foetal shunts, HbF, transitional circulation, persistent pulmonary hypertension = [ [ "Describe the three fetal shunts and what they become postnatally.", "Ductus venosus — bypasses liver from umbilical vein to IVC; becomes ligamentum venosum. Foramen ovale — bypasses pulmonary circulation, RA → LA; becomes fossa ovalis (patent in 25 % of adults). Ductus arteriosus — bypasses lungs, pulmonary artery → aorta; becomes ligamentum arteriosum. All three shunt blood away from the non-functioning fetal lungs toward systemic circulation." ], [ "What triggers closure of the ductus arteriosus and how is it managed if it fails?", "At birth: ↑PaO₂, ↓pulmonary vascular resistance, ↓circulating prostaglandins (placenta removed). Functional closure within 24 h, anatomical closure by 3 weeks. Persistent PDA in preterm infants is treated with indomethacin or ibuprofen (COX inhibitors reducing PGE₂). In duct-dependent congenital heart disease, prostaglandin E₁ infusion (alprostadil) is used to keep the duct OPEN until surgical repair." ], [ "Why is fetal haemoglobin (HbF) advantageous?", "Two α + two γ chains (vs α₂β₂ in HbA). γ binds 2,3-DPG poorly → left-shifted curve with P50 ~2.5 kPa (vs 3.5 kPa in adult). Higher O₂ affinity allows the fetus to extract O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta (where umbilical venous PO₂ is only 4 kPa). HbF declines from 80 % at birth to rather than series. Oxygenated pulmonary venous blood returns to the LA → LV → pulmonary artery (back to lungs); deoxygenated systemic venous blood returns to RA → RV → aorta (back to body). Survival depends on mixing — through PFO/ASD, VSD or PDA. As the ductus arteriosus closes (10–15 h post-partum, accelerated by ↑ PaO₂), mixing falls and cyanosis worsens. Immediate management: Prostaglandin E₁ (alprostadil) infusion 5–50 ng/kg/min to re-open the duct. Anticipate apnoea, hypotension and pyrexia from PGE₁ — have airway and inotropes ready. Avoid high FiO₂ if not hypoxic — O₂ promotes ductal closure. Refer urgently for balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) and arterial switch. (right subclavian arises from the brachiocephalic trunk proximal to the ductus). Foot sampling is . A gradient >5% suggests right-to-left shunting through a still-patent ductus arteriosus, driven by elevated PVR — i.e. Reverse pulmonary vasoconstriction: Optimise ventilation (avoid acidosis, hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia — the "five H's"). Inhaled nitric oxide 20 ppm (selective pulmonary vasodilator). Surfactant if meconium-related; consider ECMO if refractory (OI >25–40 sustained). Avoid vasodilators that drop SVR — they worsen R→L shunt. Oxygenated blood from the travels via the umbilical vein (SpO₂ ~80%). ~50% passes through the ductus venosus to the IVC; ~50% perfuses the liver. IVC blood (mixed, SpO₂ ~67%) enters the right atrium Oxygenated stream preferentially crosses the foramen ovale to the left atrium → LV → ascending aorta → brain and coronaries (SpO₂ ~65%). Deoxygenated SVC blood enters the RA → RV → pulmonary artery. ~90% of PA blood shunts through the ductus arteriosus → descending aorta → placenta via umbilical arteries. Only ~10% of RV output passes through the lungs (high PVR). First breath : alveolar expansion → dramatic ↓ PVR (8–10×) → ↑ pulmonary blood flow. Cord clamping : removes low-resistance placental circuit → ↑ SVR. LA pressure rises above RA pressure → foramen ovale closes ↑ PaO₂ + ↓ PGE₂ → smooth-muscle constriction → ductus arteriosus closes (10–15 h). closes as umbilical venous flow ceases. Transition from circulation (two ventricles in parallel) to circulation (adult pattern). Persistent high PVR → right-to-left shunting through PDA and/or PFO. Causes: meconium aspiration, sepsis, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, lung hypoplasia. Pre- vs post-ductal SpO₂ difference >5% suggests PDA shunting. Management: optimise oxygenation and ventilation, inhaled nitric oxide (iNO 20 ppm), correct acidosis, consider ECMO. A duct-dependent circulation requires a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) to maintain pulmonary or systemic blood flow until definitive intervention . Suspect it in a collapsing or cyanotic neonate as the duct closes; start alprostadil while obtaining urgent echocardiography. Duct-dependent pulmonary flow The PDA carries blood from systemic circulation/aorta → pulmonary artery → lungs . Examples: pulmonary atresia, critical pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid atresia and severe tetralogy of Fallot. Duct-dependent systemic flow Right-ventricular output passes pulmonary artery → PDA → descending systemic circulation . Examples: hypoplastic left-heart syndrome, critical coarctation, interrupted aortic arch and critical aortic stenosis. Mixing lesions: transposition of the great arteries requires mixing through an ASD/PFO, VSD or PDA; prostaglandin may improve mixing, but urgent balloon atrial septostomy may be required. Duct-dependent lesions : keep PDA open with prostaglandin E₁ until surgical correction. Avoid high FiO₂ which closes the duct. : precipitated by hypoxia, acidosis, hypothermia, sepsis. Treat with oxygen, alkalinisation, inhaled NO ± sildenafil. Maternal hyperoxia in late pregnancy can constrict the foetal ductus — relevant during emergency obstetric anaesthesia. Neonatal R→L shunt through PFO/PDA may reverse with crying, hypoxia or rising PVR — explains transient cyanotic episodes. sits left of adult Hb — facilitates placental O₂ uptake but means neonates desaturate quickly when offloading is impaired. Duct-dependent congenital lesion Pre- vs post-ductal SpO₂ difference Foetal Circulation FRCA Primary & Final — Physiology Three foetal shunts: ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus — all bypass the lungs. HbF has higher O₂ affinity (P₅₀ 2.7 kPa) — left-shifted ODC aids placental O₂ uptake. Double Bohr effect: maternal curve shifts right while foetal curve shifts left simultaneously, enhancing transfer. First breath ↓ PVR dramatically; cord clamping ↑ SVR → parallel becomes series circulation. Ductus arteriosus closes with ↑ PaO₂ and ↓ PGE₂; PGE₁ keeps it open in duct-dependent lesions. Pre- minus post-ductal SpO₂ gradient >5% suggests persistent right-to-left ductal shunting (PPHN). Overview The Three Foetal Shunts Foetal Blood Flow Pathway Foetal Oxygen Delivery Umbilical Vein PaO₂ ~4.0 kPa (30 mmHg) — much lower than adult arterial. Foetal Haemoglobin (HbF) Left-shifted ODC (P₅₀ ~2.7 kPa vs 3.5 kPa adult) → higher O₂ affinity. Foetal Hb Concentration ~180 g/L — compensates for lower PaO₂. Cardiac Output ~450 mL/kg/min (combined ventricular) — much higher than adult per kg. 2,3-DPG Effect HbF binds 2,3-DPG poorly → maintains left-shifted curve. Double Bohr Effect CO₂ transfer to maternal blood shifts maternal ODC right and foetal ODC left simultaneously. Transitional Circulation at Birth Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN) Duct-Dependent Congenital Heart Disease Pharmacological Manipulation of the Ductus Keep PDA Open PGE₁ (alprostadil) infusion — duct-dependent congenital heart disease (e.g. TGA, critical coarctation, pulmonary atresia). Close PDA Indomethacin or ibuprofen (COX inhibitors) — premature infant with symptomatic PDA. Surgical/percutaneous ligation if medical therapy fails. Describe the three fetal shunts and what they become postnatally. Ductus venosus — bypasses liver from umbilical vein to IVC; becomes ligamentum venosum. Foramen ovale — bypasses pulmonary circulation, RA → LA; becomes fossa ovalis (patent in 25 % of adults). Ductus arteriosus — bypasses lungs, pulmonary artery → aorta; becomes ligamentum arteriosum. All three shunt blood away from the non-functioning fetal lungs toward systemic circulation. What triggers closure of the ductus arteriosus and how is it managed if it fails? At birth: ↑PaO₂, ↓pulmonary vascular resistance, ↓circulating prostaglandins (placenta removed). Functional closure within 24 h, anatomical closure by 3 weeks. Persistent PDA in preterm infants is treated with indomethacin or ibuprofen (COX inhibitors reducing PGE₂). In duct-dependent congenital heart disease, prostaglandin E₁ infusion (alprostadil) is used to keep the duct OPEN until surgical repair. Why is fetal haemoglobin (HbF) advantageous? Two α + two γ chains (vs α₂β₂ in HbA). γ binds 2,3-DPG poorly → left-shifted curve with P50 ~2.5 kPa (vs 3.5 kPa in adult). Higher O₂ affinity allows the fetus to extract O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta (where umbilical venous PO₂ is only 4 kPa). HbF declines from 80 % at birth to <2 % by 6 months. Identify the three foetal shunts and the role of each in directing oxygenated blood. Describe foetal oxygen carriage (HbF, double Bohr effect) and explain why a low umbilical PaO₂ is adequate. Outline the transitional circulatory changes at birth and the stimuli that drive them. Recognise persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and outline management. Apply pharmacological manipulation of the ductus arteriosus to duct-dependent congenital heart disease. >Immediate management:

# Pharmacokinetic Principles Compartment models, volume of distribution, clearance, half-life Vd = Dose / C₀ . A large Vd (e.g., amiodarone ~70 L/kg) indicates extensive tissue distribution. A small Vd (e.g., warfarin ~0.1 L/kg) suggests the drug remains largely in plasma. Clinical Application Clearance (Cl) is the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time: Cl = elimination rate / plasma concentration . Total clearance is additive: = Cl + Cl The organ extraction ratio is the fraction removed in one pass: ER = (C − C ) / C , and organ clearance approximates blood flow × ER. High-ER (>0.7) drugs such as propofol, lidocaine and morphine are flow-limited. Low-ER (<0.3) drugs such as warfarin, diazepam and phenytoin are capacity-limited and depend more on unbound fraction and intrinsic enzyme activity Renal clearance combines filtration of unbound drug, active secretion and reabsorption; it falls with renal dysfunction and can exceed GFR when tubular secretion is important. A constant is eliminated per unit time; rate is proportional to concentration and half-life is constant. Most drugs behave this way at therapeutic concentrations. A saturated pathway removes a constant per unit time; no fixed half-life. Small dose increases can cause disproportionate concentration rises and toxicity. Examples: ethanol, phenytoin, and high-dose salicylate; theophylline and warfarin can become capacity-limited near saturation. capillary leak, oedema and fluid resuscitation enlarge hydrophilic-drug Vd; hypoalbuminaemia increases free acidic drug, while raised α₁-acid glycoprotein alters basic-drug binding. shock and hepatic/renal failure reduce clearance, but augmented renal clearance in younger hyperdynamic patients can make standard β-lactam doses subtherapeutic. Organ support: CKRT adds extracorporeal clearance according to membrane, modality, flow and protein binding; ECMO circuitry adds an apparent compartment and may sequester lipophilic, protein-bound drugs. use loading doses based on altered Vd, then individualise maintenance to measured clearance, organ support and therapeutic drug monitoring. t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Cl . It depends on both distribution and elimination. Steady state during continuous infusion is reached after approximately 4-5 half-lives, where the rate of administration equals the rate of elimination. Step-by-step reasoning Use t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Cl. t½ = 0.693 × 70 / 7 = 6.93 h ≈ 7 h Time to steady state ≈ 4–5 × t½ = 28–35 h If urgent therapeutic level needed → give a loading dose = target plasma concentration × Vd. Common traps Using terminal t½ to predict offset after a long infusion — use CSHT instead (e.g. fentanyl). Forgetting that Vd is theoretical (can exceed total body water for highly tissue-bound drugs). Target offset: minutes after infusion stop, regardless of duration. Fentanyl CSHT after 6 h ≈ 250 min (rising to ~280 min by 8 h); remifentanil CSHT ~3–4 min (constant). for predictable rapid offset enabled by ester hydrolysis (independent of organ function). Plan multimodal analgesia (paracetamol, regional, long-acting opioid bridge before stopping) to avoid acute hyperalgesia. Stopping remifentanil without analgesic bridge → severe rebound pain. Assuming fentanyl 'short-acting' from terminal t½ — context-sensitive half-time is what matters. Pharmacokinetic Principles FRCA Primary — Pharmacology Introduction Compartment Models Volume of Distribution (Vd) Clearance First-Order vs Zero-Order Kinetics Pharmacokinetics in Critical Illness Half-Life and Steady State Context-Sensitive Half-Time Half-life and steady state from Vd and Cl t½ ≈ 7 h, steady state in 28–35 h; load with Cp_target × Vd if urgent. Choosing remifentanil vs fentanyl for a long case Remifentanil — flat CSHT ~3–4 min ensures predictable wake-up; bridge with longer-acting analgesia. Pharmacokinetics is ADME: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Elimination. Compartment models describe drug distribution kinetically. The two-compartment model shows bi-exponential decline (α distribution, β elimination). Volume of distribution (Vd) is a theoretical concept; a large Vd indicates extensive tissue distribution. Clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time. High extraction ratio drugs are flow-dependent. Half-life (t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Cl) determines time to steady state (~4-5 half-lives). Context-sensitive half-time is more clinically relevant for infusions than terminal half-life. Remifentanil has a uniquely short and constant CSHT. Define volume of distribution and give a clinical example. Vd = total amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration. It is an apparent volume — it can far exceed total body water if the drug binds extensively to tissues (digoxin Vd ~7 L/kg, amiodarone ~70 L/kg). A large Vd predicts a long elimination half-life (T½ = 0.693 × Vd / Cl) and means dialysis is ineffective for removal. Highly water-soluble, plasma-bound drugs (warfarin, heparin) have small Vd (~0.1 L/kg). What is context-sensitive half-time and why does it matter for TIVA? CSHT = the time for plasma concentration to halve after stopping an infusion that has run for a particular duration (the ). Unlike elimination half-life, CSHT lengthens with infusion duration as peripheral compartments fill. Remifentanil CSHT remains ~3 min regardless of duration (esterase metabolism); fentanyl CSHT rises from 12 min after 1 h to >200 min after 8 h — explains why fentanyl is unsuitable for prolonged TIVA. Explain first-pass metabolism and its anaesthetic relevance. Orally administered drugs absorbed from the gut pass via portal vein to the liver, where they may be largely metabolised before reaching the systemic circulation. Morphine has ~30 % oral bioavailability (heavy first pass), GTN is essentially zero (hence sublingual), midazolam ~40 %. Buccal, sublingual, IV, IM and rectal routes bypass first pass. Hepatic dysfunction increases bioavailability of high-extraction drugs unpredictably. quizQuestions={pharmacokineticsQuiz} objectives={[ Describe one- and two-compartment models and bi-exponential decline. Calculate volume of distribution, clearance, and elimination half-life. Distinguish flow- from capacity-dependent hepatic clearance. Use context-sensitive half-time to predict offset of TIVA infusions. > Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a drug — its absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (ADME). Understanding these principles allows the anaesthetist to predict drug onset, duration, and accumulation with repeated dosing.

Compartment models are mathematical abstractions that describe drug distribution. The body is divided into compartments based on the rate of drug equilibration. The central compartment (V₁) represents the well-perfused tissues (blood, heart, brain, kidneys). Peripheral compartments represent less well-perfused tissues (muscle, fat). The two-compartment model shows a bi-exponential decline: a rapid distribution phase (α) followed by a slower elimination phase (β).

Vd is a theoretical volume that would be required to contain the total amount of drug at the same concentration as in plasma: Vd = Dose / C₀. A large Vd (e.g., amiodarone ~70 L/kg) indicates extensive tissue distribution. A small Vd (e.g., warfarin ~0.1 L/kg) suggests the drug remains largely in plasma.

Clinical Application

Drugs with a large Vd are poorly removed by haemodialysis (e.g., digoxin, Vd = 500 L). Context-sensitive half-time increases with infusion duration for drugs that accumulate in peripheral compartments.

The elimination half-life (t½) is the time for plasma concentration to fall by 50%: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Cl. It depends on both distribution and elimination. Steady state during continuous infusion is reached after approximately 4-5 half-lives, where the rate of administration equals the rate of elimination.

Unlike terminal half-life, the context-sensitive half-time (CSHT) describes the time for plasma concentration to fall by 50% after stopping an infusion of a given duration. Remifentanil has a short, constant CSHT (~3-4 min) regardless of infusion duration, while fentanyl Volume of distribution is a virtual volume — high Vd reflects extensive tissue binding, not actual fluid volume. Clearance, not half-life, drives steady-state concentration on an infusion (Css = rate / clearance). Context-sensitive half-time (not elimination half-life) predicts offset after prolonged infusions — remifentanil stays ~4 min regardless of duration. Five half-lives ≈ 97% steady state or elimination; loading dose = Vd × target concentration. Hepatic extraction ratio: high-ER drugs (propofol, lidocaine, morphine) are flow-limited; low-ER drugs (warfarin, diazepam) are capacity-limited. A drug has Vd = 70 L and clearance Cl = 7 L/h in a 70 kg adult. Calculate t½ and time to steady state on a continuous infusion. >Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Use t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Cl.
  2. t½ = 0.693 × 70 / 7 = 6.93 h ≈ 7 h.
  3. Time to steady state ≈ 4–5 × t½ = 28–35 h.
  4. If urgent therapeutic level needed → give a loading dose = target plasma concentration × Vd.

case_bank.title: Slow wake-up after long TIVA in obesity
case_bank.text:
Case: Slow wake-up after long TIVA in obesity (Kinetics & delivery, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient weighing 145 kg (body mass index 46) has a five-hour propofol and remifentanil anaesthetic. Total body weight was entered into a Marsh model.
Presentation: Forty minutes after stopping the infusion the patient remains unresponsive with normal gases, temperature and glucose.
Stage 1 — Explain the kinetics
  Question: Why is recovery prolonged?
  Model answer: Context-sensitive half-time rises with infusion duration because peripheral compartments are loaded and return drug to plasma after the infusion stops.
  Model answer: Using total body weight in a model derived for lean patients overestimates volumes and delivers a larger absolute dose than intended.
  Model answer: Propofol clearance scales closer to lean or adjusted body weight, so obesity worsens the mismatch between programmed target and actual effect-site concentration.
Stage 2 — Exclude other causes
  Question: What else must you rule out?
  Model answer: Residual neuromuscular block, opioid effect, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, hypercapnia and electrolyte abnormality.
  Model answer: Neurological events, including stroke and seizure, and drug errors such as inadvertent sedative administration.
  Model answer: Confirm the infusion actually stopped and the cannula was patent throughout — a tissued line can cause both awareness and delayed bolus effect.
Stage 3 — Do it better next time
  Question: How would you plan TIVA in this patient?
  Model answer: Use a model validated in obesity (for example Eleveld) or an appropriate weight scalar, and target the effect-site concentration.
  Model answer: Use processed EEG depth monitoring, especially where neuromuscular blockade masks clinical signs, and titrate to the lowest effective target.
  Model answer: Follow national TIVA safety recommendations: a dedicated visible cannula with anti-reflux and anti-siphon protection, and a documented plan for pump failure.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Multi-compartment kinetics mean that plasma concentration after stopping an infusion depends on redistribution from peripheral compartments as well as clearance. Context-sensitive half-time therefore increases with infusion duration and is drug-specific: remifentanil stays short because of organ-independent esterase metabolism, whereas propofol lengthens progressively. Obesity increases total volume of distribution but not proportionately increases clearance, so weight scalar choice dominates dosing accuracy.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Support the airway and ventilation while systematically excluding reversible causes; check a blood glucose, gas and neuromuscular monitoring reading before attributing delay to kinetics. For future cases, use an obesity-appropriate model, effect-site targeting, processed EEG and clear infusion-site checks. Document target concentrations and total dose to allow later interpretation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not say 'propofol has a short half-life so it should wear off'. Define context-sensitive half-time, state which weight scalar each model needs, and mention depth monitoring as a safety measure rather than an optional extra.
Take-home: Long infusions and total-body-weight dosing both prolong recovery: choose an obesity-validated model, target effect site and monitor depth.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: pharmacokinetics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr061); BJA Educ: target-controlled infusion (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkh046); Assoc Anaesth/SIVA TIVA guideline 2019 (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.14428)

case_bank.title: Choosing reversal in a patient with renal failure
case_bank.text:
Case: Choosing reversal in a patient with renal failure (Kinetics & delivery, Intermediate)
Patient: A dialysis-dependent patient needs urgent surgery. Rocuronium was given for a rapid sequence induction 25 minutes ago; the post-tetanic count is 1.
Presentation: Surgery finishes early and rapid, complete reversal is required.
Stage 1 — Explain the elimination
  Question: How do the relevant drugs behave in renal failure?
  Model answer: Rocuronium is mainly hepatobiliary but has a renal component, so duration is prolonged in renal failure.
  Model answer: Neostigmine and sugammadex are both renally cleared; the sugammadex–rocuronium complex depends on renal excretion for elimination.
  Model answer: Atracurium and cisatracurium are independent of organ clearance because of Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis, which is why they are often preferred here.
Stage 2 — Choose reversal now
  Question: What do you give at a post-tetanic count of 1?
  Model answer: Neostigmine cannot reverse this depth of block; it requires at least two twitches on train-of-four and has a ceiling effect from acetylcholinesterase saturation.
  Model answer: Give sugammadex 4 mg/kg for deep block (2 mg/kg once two twitches have returned), and confirm recovery quantitatively to a train-of-four ratio of 0.9 or more.
  Model answer: Although sugammadex is not licensed in severe renal impairment, it is widely used with the caveat of delayed complex clearance; discuss the risk of recurarisation and monitor accordingly.
Stage 3 — Anticipate the pitfalls
  Question: What complications should you plan for?
  Model answer: Recurarisation, especially if surgery is short, dosing marginal or clearance impaired — keep monitoring after reversal.
  Model answer: Sugammadex encapsulates aminosteroids only, so if further blockade is needed within 24 hours use a benzylisoquinolinium drug or a much larger rocuronium dose.
  Model answer: Neostigmine requires an antimuscarinic to limit bradycardia, secretions and bronchospasm; sugammadex can cause bradycardia and rare anaphylaxis.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Reversal choice is a pharmacokinetic decision. Neostigmine increases synaptic acetylcholine but cannot overcome deep receptor occupancy, so its effect plateaus. Sugammadex forms a 1:1 complex with aminosteroid relaxants, creating a concentration gradient away from the junction and reversing any depth of block; because both free and complexed drug rely on glomerular filtration, renal failure prolongs elimination even though clinical reversal is still rapid.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use quantitative monitoring throughout, choose the sugammadex dose by measured depth, and continue observation in recovery for recurarisation. In dialysis-dependent patients, consider planning ahead with cisatracurium for maintenance where a rapid sequence induction is not required, and document the reversal drug and time because it affects subsequent relaxant choice.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not offer neostigmine for deep block, and do not claim sugammadex removes the need for monitoring. Mention the 24-hour aminosteroid re-dosing problem.
Take-home: Match reversal to measured depth and organ function: sugammadex reverses deep aminosteroid block, neostigmine cannot, and Hofmann-eliminated drugs avoid the issue.
Cited sources: Assoc Anaesth 2023: neuromuscular blockade (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.16114); BJA Educ: pharmacokinetics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr061)

case_bank.title: Antibiotic dosing in critical illness and renal replacement
case_bank.text:
Case: Antibiotic dosing in critical illness and renal replacement (Critical care drugs, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient with abdominal sepsis on continuous veno-venous haemofiltration is prescribed meropenem and gentamicin. Serum albumin is 18 g/L and fluid balance is +6 L.
Presentation: The team asks whether doses should be reduced because of renal failure.
Stage 1 — Classify the killing pattern
  Question: Which pharmacodynamic target applies to each drug?
  Model answer: Beta-lactams such as meropenem are time-dependent: efficacy tracks the fraction of the dosing interval that free drug exceeds the minimum inhibitory concentration.
  Model answer: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent: efficacy tracks peak concentration relative to the minimum inhibitory concentration, with post-antibiotic effect permitting extended intervals.
  Model answer: Vancomycin is best described by the ratio of 24-hour area under the curve to minimum inhibitory concentration.
Stage 2 — Adjust for the pathophysiology
  Question: What happens to kinetics in this patient?
  Model answer: Volume of distribution of hydrophilic drugs increases with oedema and fluid loading, so early underdosing is common; loading doses should not be reduced.
  Model answer: Hypoalbuminaemia increases free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs and can increase clearance of unbound drug.
  Model answer: Continuous renal replacement provides substantial clearance of small, water-soluble, poorly protein-bound drugs, so maintenance doses often need to be higher than for anuric patients not receiving filtration.
Stage 3 — Write the plan
  Question: What is your practical prescription strategy?
  Model answer: Give a full loading dose, then adjust maintenance to the measured clearance including filtration effluent rate, prolonging beta-lactam infusions to extend time above the minimum inhibitory concentration.
  Model answer: Use therapeutic drug monitoring for aminoglycosides and vancomycin, and involve microbiology and pharmacy for dose individualisation.
  Model answer: Take cultures, give antimicrobials within one hour of recognised sepsis, achieve source control and review de-escalation daily.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Critical illness alters both volume of distribution and clearance, often in opposite directions and over hours. Capillary leak, aggressive resuscitation and hypoalbuminaemia expand the distribution volume of hydrophilic antimicrobials, while augmented renal clearance in some patients and extracorporeal clearance in others increase elimination. Consequently dose reduction on the basis of a creatinine value alone frequently produces subtherapeutic exposure at the time when killing matters most.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Separate loading from maintenance: loading depends on volume of distribution and should be full; maintenance depends on clearance including renal replacement effluent flow. Extended or continuous beta-lactam infusion improves target attainment, and therapeutic drug monitoring should guide aminoglycoside and vancomycin dosing. Reassess daily against culture results, clinical trajectory and source control, and document stop or review dates.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not reduce the loading dose because of renal failure, and do not describe every antibiotic as if the same target applied. Name the specific pharmacodynamic index for each class.
Take-home: Load fully, then adjust maintenance to real clearance: beta-lactams need time above MIC, aminoglycosides need peaks, and filtration removes drug.
Cited sources: Antimicrobial PK/PD in critical illness (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00134-020-06050-1); BJA Educ: pharmacokinetics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr061)

case_bank.title: Tranexamic acid in high-risk non-cardiac surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Tranexamic acid in high-risk non-cardiac surgery (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: A 76-year-old with remote provoked DVT is scheduled for major multilevel spine surgery with high anticipated blood loss.
Presentation: The team is weighing reduced bleeding against perioperative vascular risk.
Stage 1 — Balance benefit and uncertainty
  Question: How should the evidence be framed?
  Model answer: TXA reduces major bleeding in non-cardiac surgery.
  Model answer: POISE-3 did not establish non-inferiority for the composite cardiovascular safety outcome, so individual thrombotic and bleeding risks still matter.
  Model answer: A remote provoked DVT is not automatically equivalent to active thrombosis; review timing, recurrence, anticoagulation and local guidance.
Stage 2 — Choose and prescribe deliberately
  Question: What safeguards belong in the plan?
  Model answer: Use the procedure-specific local dose rather than importing a trauma regimen.
  Model answer: Adjust or avoid repeated high dosing in significant renal impairment because TXA is renally cleared.
  Model answer: Avoid accidental neuraxial administration: separate storage, label syringes and use route-specific checks.
Stage 3 — Monitor relevant harms
  Question: What postoperative surveillance is appropriate?
  Model answer: Continue standard VTE prevention once haemostasis permits.
  Model answer: Investigate clinical signs of venous or arterial thrombosis rather than using TXA exposure alone as a diagnosis.
  Model answer: Recognise that seizures are associated particularly with high exposure and renal accumulation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: In major non-cardiac surgery, TXA lowers bleeding, but POISE-3 did not prove non-inferiority for its composite cardiovascular safety outcome. Decision-making therefore combines procedural blood-loss risk with active or previous thrombosis, vascular disease, anticoagulation and renal function. A remote provoked DVT is not the same as active thrombosis.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use the procedure-specific local regimen rather than a trauma dose. Reduce exposure in renal impairment because TXA is predominantly renally cleared, and avoid repeated high doses where accumulation raises seizure risk. Keep ampoules and syringes physically separated from neuraxial drugs and perform explicit route checks. Restart standard VTE prophylaxis when haemostasis permits.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: The catastrophic route error is intrathecal TXA. Mention storage, labelling and checking systems as well as pharmacology and thrombosis assessment.
Take-home: Elective perioperative TXA requires procedure-specific dosing and an individual bleeding–thrombosis assessment; renal function and route safety are practical exam points.
Cited sources: POISE-3 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171)

case_bank.title: Tranexamic acid in advanced kidney disease
case_bank.text:
Case: Tranexamic acid in advanced kidney disease (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: An adult with stage 4 chronic kidney disease is listed for revision arthroplasty with anticipated major blood loss.
Presentation: A standard repeated-dose TXA regimen has been copied onto the chart.
Stage 1 — Identify accumulation risk
  Question: Why must the prescription be reconsidered?
  Model answer: TXA is predominantly renally eliminated.
  Model answer: Reduced clearance increases exposure from repeated or high dosing.
  Model answer: High exposure is associated with postoperative seizures.
Stage 2 — Prescribe safely
  Question: What practical safeguards are required?
  Model answer: Confirm current renal function and follow the local renal-adjusted protocol.
  Model answer: Document timing and cumulative dose to prevent repetition.
  Model answer: Use blood conservation and haemostatic measures in parallel.
Stage 3 — Respond to neurological signs
  Question: What if postoperative myoclonus occurs?
  Model answer: Consider TXA accumulation among metabolic and neurological causes.
  Model answer: Stop further TXA, correct reversible factors and treat seizures promptly.
  Model answer: Escalate monitoring and specialist review.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: TXA is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney. Advanced renal impairment prolongs exposure, so repeated or high dosing increases accumulation and seizure risk; the indication and local renal-adjustment protocol must be explicit.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Verify current renal function, indication, timing and cumulative dose. Use the lowest evidence-based renal-adjusted regimen in consultation with local guidance, avoid accidental repeat dosing and monitor neurological recovery. New myoclonus or seizures require drug review and supportive seizure management.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not copy a normal-renal-function regimen into advanced kidney disease. Separate efficacy evidence from dosing safety.
Take-home: Renal impairment changes TXA exposure: use an evidence-based adjusted regimen and monitor cumulative dose and neurological toxicity.
Cited sources: POISE-3 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171)

case_bank.title: High-dose TXA during cardiac surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: High-dose TXA during cardiac surgery (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: An older adult with impaired renal function undergoes complex redo valve surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass.
Presentation: Several TXA doses are planned in the loading dose, pump prime and infusion.
Stage 1 — Balance benefit and harm
  Question: Why is careful cumulative dosing important?
  Model answer: Antifibrinolysis can reduce bleeding and transfusion in cardiac surgery.
  Model answer: Bypass, renal dysfunction and high cumulative exposure increase seizure risk.
  Model answer: Benefit does not justify untracked dose escalation.
Stage 2 — Coordinate blood conservation
  Question: What belongs in the complete plan?
  Model answer: Use a weight- and renal-adjusted institutional regimen.
  Model answer: Record every loading, prime and infusion dose.
  Model answer: Combine surgical haemostasis, cell salvage and point-of-care coagulation guidance.
Stage 3 — Plan postoperative surveillance
  Question: What should handover emphasise?
  Model answer: State cumulative TXA exposure and renal function.
  Model answer: Distinguish seizure from delayed emergence, shivering and embolic stroke.
  Model answer: Maintain route separation so TXA cannot enter a neuraxial pathway.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Cardiac surgery activates fibrinolysis and often benefits from antifibrinolysis, but cardiopulmonary bypass, renal dysfunction and high cumulative TXA exposure all increase postoperative seizure risk.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use the unit’s weight- and renal-function-adjusted protocol, document all loading, bypass-prime and infusion doses, and coordinate blood conservation with surgical haemostasis, cell salvage and point-of-care coagulation testing. Protect against medication-route errors.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: More TXA is not automatically better. State the trade-off between reduced transfusion and dose-related neurological toxicity.
Take-home: In cardiac surgery, TXA should be protocolised and dose-accounted; renal function and seizure risk constrain exposure.
Cited sources: POISE-3 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171)

Efficacy — maximum effect produced once bound (full agonist = 1, partial agonist 0 Step-by-step reasoning Classify each drug. Morphine = full μ-agonist (intrinsic activity ≈ 1). Buprenorphine = high-affinity μ-agonist (intrinsic activity ≈ 0.4) and κ-antagonist. Compare receptor affinity. Buprenorphine Ki ≈ 0.2 nM vs morphine Ki ≈ 1.8 nM → buprenorphine binds ~10× more tightly. Predict the result. When given to a μ-saturated patient, buprenorphine morphine but only delivers a partial signal → net opioid effect falls → precipitated withdrawal. Quantify the timing. Withdrawal onset is rapid (minutes-hours) because buprenorphine reaches peak occupancy within 1–2 h sublingually. Apply the safe induction rule. Wait until COWS ≥ 12 (objective withdrawal) OR use the Bernese 'micro-induction' (0.2 mg buprenorphine repeated while continuing the full agonist). Key pharmacology to recall Buprenorphine has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression but not on analgesia. Reversal needs HIGH-dose naloxone infusion (e.g. 4 mg/h) due to high receptor affinity. Common traps Treating buprenorphine like a weak opioid — its high affinity blocks subsequent full agonists in theatre. Standard naloxone bolus (400 µg) failing to reverse buprenorphine and being misread as 'not opioid'. Stopping the buprenorphine perioperatively without a plan — withdrawal + uncontrolled pain ensues. Step-by-step interpretation Read the axes. X-axis is log[agonist]; Y-axis is response (% Emax). Identify the change. Curve shifted right (↑ EC₅₀) but Emax unchanged → the agonist can still achieve maximum response, just needs more. Match to mechanism. Parallel rightward shift with preserved Emax = competitive (surmountable) antagonism Contrast with non-competitive. Irreversible/allosteric antagonists give a depressed curve (↓ Emax), not a parallel shift. Apply Schild analysis. Dose ratio (DR) = EC₅₀(antagonist)/EC₅₀(control). pA₂ is the −log of antagonist concentration that produces DR = 2 — a measure of antagonist potency. Worked numbers If control EC₅₀ = 10⁻⁸ M and antagonist EC₅₀ = 10⁻⁶ M → DR = 100 → log(DR−1) = ~2 → strong competitive blockade. Examples to memorise Competitive at α₁: Irreversible at α₁: phenoxybenzamine (the phaeochromocytoma curve). Competitive at nAChR: non-depolarising NMBs (atracurium). Channel block: ketamine at NMDA. Confusing 'partial agonist' with 'competitive antagonist' — partial agonists give a curve with REDUCED Emax even alone. Reading 'shift' from a linear (not log) plot — the dose-response only looks parallel on a log scale. Calling a curve flattened by toxicity 'non-competitive antagonism' — confounder, not pharmacology. Dose-response curve : hyperbolic. Log(dose)-response: sigmoid. Emax is the maximal response; EC₅₀ is the concentration producing 50% Emax : position of curve on x-axis (EC₅₀). More potent = lower EC₅₀. Example: fentanyl is more potent than morphine : maximal effect achievable (Emax). Full agonist has high efficacy; partial agonist has lower Emax regardless of dose Therapeutic index : TD₅₀/ED₅₀ (or LD₅₀/ED₅₀). Narrow TI drugs: digoxin, warfarin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline Ligand-gated ion channel Direct ion flow nAChR (Na⁺), GABA_A (Cl⁻), 5-HT₃, NMDA (Ca²⁺) G-protein coupled (GPCR) Gαs/Gαi/Gαq → second messengers β₁ (Gαs→cAMP↑), M₂ (Gαi→cAMP↓), α₁ (Gαq→IP₃/DAG) Tyrosine kinase phosphorylation Insulin receptor, growth factor receptors Gene transcription Steroid receptors, thyroid hormone, vitamin D Spare receptors exist when maximal effect occurs before every receptor is occupied: EC₅₀ is therefore lower than K . Signal amplification increases sensitivity and can accelerate response. A competitive antagonist must occupy more receptors before response falls, while an irreversible antagonist may initially appear surmountable because receptors can be removed without reducing Emax. Cardiac β-adrenoceptors are the classic example: near-maximal inotropy may occur with only a fraction occupied is a lag between plasma concentration (Cp) and clinical effect. Plotting effect against Cp produces a loop because equal plasma concentrations on the rising and falling limbs produce different effects. A counter-clockwise loop means effect peaks after Cp, as with slow fentanyl CNS equilibration, active-metabolite formation, slow receptor kinetics or delayed signal transduction. A clockwise loop (proteresis) suggests acute tolerance, antagonistic metabolites or physiological counter-regulation Effect-site delay: peak effect follows peak plasma concentration. Effect wanes despite concentration: tolerance or counter-regulation. : combined effect > sum of individual effects (e.g., propofol + remifentanil). Shown by isobolograms : rapid tolerance after repeated doses. Mechanisms: receptor desensitisation (phosphorylation), receptor internalisation, depletion of mediator (e.g., ephedrine) Enzyme induction : ↑ CYP450 activity (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) → ↓ drug effect. Takes days-weeks Enzyme inhibition : ↓ CYP450 activity (erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, grapefruit) → ↑ drug effect. Rapid onset Buprenorphine in a patient on chronic morphine Buprenorphine displaced morphine from the μ-receptor; its lower intrinsic activity provided a smaller signal → precipitated withdrawal. Always wait for objective withdrawal (COWS ≥ 12) before initiating buprenorphine in opioid-dependent patients (the 'micro-induction' or Bernese protocol minimises this risk). Reading a parallel right-shift on a dose-response curve A competitive (surmountable) antagonist such as phentolamine. A non-competitive antagonist (e.g. phenoxybenzamine) would lower Emax. Recognising shift vs depression is a high-yield FRCA Primary visual question. Non-competitive: ↓ Emax, insurmountable Partial agonist can antagonise a full agonist when both are present (e.g., buprenorphine vs morphine) 4 receptor types: ion channel (ms), GPCR (seconds), kinase-linked (min-hours), nuclear (hours-days) Gαs → ↑cAMP (β₁), Gαi → ↓cAMP (M₂, μ-opioid), Gαq → IP₃/DAG (α₁, M₁) Tachyphylaxis: receptor desensitisation, internalisation, or mediator depletion (ephedrine) Therapeutic index = TD₅₀/ED₅₀. Narrow TI: digoxin, warfarin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline Dose-Response Relationships Agonists & Antagonists Receptor Types & Signal Transduction Spare Receptors (Receptor Reserve) Hysteresis and Effect-Site Delay Drug Interactions & Tolerance Affinity — strength with which a drug binds its receptor (related to Kd, the concentration giving 50 % occupancy). Efficacy — maximum effect produced once bound (full agonist = 1, partial agonist 0 < ε < 1, antagonist = 0, inverse agonist <0). Potency — dose required to produce a defined effect (EC50). A drug can be highly potent but with low efficacy (e.g. buprenorphine — partial μ-agonist). What is the difference between a competitive and a non-competitive antagonist? Competitive antagonist — binds reversibly at the agonist site; effect overcome by ↑agonist concentration (right-shift of dose-response curve, same maximum). Example: rocuronium reversed by neostigmine raising ACh. Non-competitive — binds at a different site (allosteric) or irreversibly; reduces maximum response and cannot be overcome by increasing agonist. Example: phenoxybenzamine on α-receptors (used in phaeochromocytoma). Explain agonist, partial agonist, antagonist and inverse agonist with opioid examples. Full agonist — produces full receptor response (morphine, fentanyl at μ). Partial agonist — produces submaximal response even at full occupancy; behaves as antagonist in presence of full agonist (buprenorphine — useful for opioid substitution). Antagonist — blocks receptor with no intrinsic activity (naloxone, naltrexone). Inverse agonist — reduces constitutive receptor activity below baseline (no clinically important opioid example; flumazenil at GABA-A is one). case_bank.title: Which vasoactive drug for refractory septic shock?
case_bank.text:
Case: Which vasoactive drug for refractory septic shock? (Critical care drugs, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive at a mean arterial pressure of 55 mmHg on noradrenaline 0.4 micrograms/kg/min despite fluid resuscitation.
Presentation: Cardiac index is 4.2 L/min/m², lactate 4.1 mmol/L, echocardiography shows preserved contractility.
Stage 1 — Interpret the haemodynamics
  Question: Which problem are you treating?
  Model answer: High cardiac index with low pressure indicates a vasodilatory, resistance problem rather than pump failure.
  Model answer: Adding an inotrope would raise output without correcting the vasodilation and may worsen tachyarrhythmia and oxygen demand.
  Model answer: Target mean arterial pressure of about 65 mmHg, individualised upwards in chronic hypertension.
Stage 2 — Choose the next agent
  Question: How do you escalate?
  Model answer: Add vasopressin (typically 0.03 units/min) to spare catecholamine dose, acting through V1 receptors independent of adrenergic pathways.
  Model answer: Consider hydrocortisone for shock requiring ongoing vasopressor support, and reassess for source control, occult bleeding and acidosis limiting catecholamine responsiveness.
  Model answer: Reserve adrenaline or an inotrope for genuine low-output states, guided by echocardiography or cardiac output monitoring.
Stage 3 — Explain the receptors
  Question: Summarise the pharmacodynamics behind the choices.
  Model answer: Noradrenaline acts mainly on alpha-1 receptors with modest beta-1 activity, raising resistance with limited chronotropy.
  Model answer: Adrenaline is dose-dependent: beta effects predominate at low dose, alpha at high dose, with lactate generation through beta-2-mediated glycolysis.
  Model answer: Dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist with beta-2 vasodilation; phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist that may reduce output through reflex bradycardia and increased afterload.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Vasoactive selection follows from the measured physiology: define whether the deficit is resistance, output, preload or rhythm, then choose the receptor profile that corrects it. Catecholamine responsiveness falls with acidosis, hypocalcaemia, hypoxia and receptor downregulation, so escalating dose alone is often ineffective; combining agents with different mechanisms is more effective and less arrhythmogenic than maximising one.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use invasive arterial monitoring, central administration, repeated echocardiography or cardiac output measurement, lactate trend and urine output. Correct calcium, acidosis and hypoxia; ensure source control and antimicrobial adequacy. Add vasopressin early as catecholamine-sparing, consider corticosteroid in vasopressor-dependent shock, and reassess for mechanisms such as tamponade, right ventricular failure or adrenal insufficiency when shock is refractory.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not add an inotrope for a high-output vasodilated state, and do not describe 'renal-dose dopamine'. Give receptor targets and doses, and state the mean arterial pressure goal.
Take-home: Treat the measured defect: vasodilatory shock needs vasopressors and catecholamine-sparing adjuncts, not inotropes for an already high cardiac output.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: vasoactive drugs (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw066); BJA Educ: pharmacodynamics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkm016)

case_bank.title: Antibiotic dosing in critical illness and renal replacement
case_bank.text:
Case: Antibiotic dosing in critical illness and renal replacement (Critical care drugs, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient with abdominal sepsis on continuous veno-venous haemofiltration is prescribed meropenem and gentamicin. Serum albumin is 18 g/L and fluid balance is +6 L.
Presentation: The team asks whether doses should be reduced because of renal failure.
Stage 1 — Classify the killing pattern
  Question: Which pharmacodynamic target applies to each drug?
  Model answer: Beta-lactams such as meropenem are time-dependent: efficacy tracks the fraction of the dosing interval that free drug exceeds the minimum inhibitory concentration.
  Model answer: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent: efficacy tracks peak concentration relative to the minimum inhibitory concentration, with post-antibiotic effect permitting extended intervals.
  Model answer: Vancomycin is best described by the ratio of 24-hour area under the curve to minimum inhibitory concentration.
Stage 2 — Adjust for the pathophysiology
  Question: What happens to kinetics in this patient?
  Model answer: Volume of distribution of hydrophilic drugs increases with oedema and fluid loading, so early underdosing is common; loading doses should not be reduced.
  Model answer: Hypoalbuminaemia increases free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs and can increase clearance of unbound drug.
  Model answer: Continuous renal replacement provides substantial clearance of small, water-soluble, poorly protein-bound drugs, so maintenance doses often need to be higher than for anuric patients not receiving filtration.
Stage 3 — Write the plan
  Question: What is your practical prescription strategy?
  Model answer: Give a full loading dose, then adjust maintenance to the measured clearance including filtration effluent rate, prolonging beta-lactam infusions to extend time above the minimum inhibitory concentration.
  Model answer: Use therapeutic drug monitoring for aminoglycosides and vancomycin, and involve microbiology and pharmacy for dose individualisation.
  Model answer: Take cultures, give antimicrobials within one hour of recognised sepsis, achieve source control and review de-escalation daily.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Critical illness alters both volume of distribution and clearance, often in opposite directions and over hours. Capillary leak, aggressive resuscitation and hypoalbuminaemia expand the distribution volume of hydrophilic antimicrobials, while augmented renal clearance in some patients and extracorporeal clearance in others increase elimination. Consequently dose reduction on the basis of a creatinine value alone frequently produces subtherapeutic exposure at the time when killing matters most.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Separate loading from maintenance: loading depends on volume of distribution and should be full; maintenance depends on clearance including renal replacement effluent flow. Extended or continuous beta-lactam infusion improves target attainment, and therapeutic drug monitoring should guide aminoglycoside and vancomycin dosing. Reassess daily against culture results, clinical trajectory and source control, and document stop or review dates.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not reduce the loading dose because of renal failure, and do not describe every antibiotic as if the same target applied. Name the specific pharmacodynamic index for each class.
Take-home: Load fully, then adjust maintenance to real clearance: beta-lactams need time above MIC, aminoglycosides need peaks, and filtration removes drug.
Cited sources: Antimicrobial PK/PD in critical illness (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00134-020-06050-1); BJA Educ: pharmacokinetics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr061)

case_bank.title: Preparing an adrenal phaeochromocytoma
case_bank.text:
Case: Preparing an adrenal phaeochromocytoma (Phaeochromocytoma, Foundation)
Patient: A 43-year-old woman has an adrenal mass, raised plasma metanephrines and episodic headache, sweating and palpitations.
Presentation: She is referred for laparoscopic adrenalectomy with a seated BP of 168/96 mmHg and pulse 104 min⁻¹.
Stage 1 — Sequence preoperative treatment
  Question: How should blockade be introduced?
  Model answer: Start alpha blockade first, commonly phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin, and titrate over about 10–14 days.
  Model answer: Only add beta blockade after adequate alpha blockade if troublesome tachycardia persists.
  Model answer: Never beta block first because unopposed alpha vasoconstriction can provoke a hypertensive crisis.
Stage 2 — Restore circulating volume
  Question: Why are salt and fluid important?
  Model answer: Chronic catecholamine-mediated vasoconstriction leaves the patient intravascularly depleted.
  Model answer: Encourage salt and fluid intake after alpha blockade, while individualising for cardiac or renal disease.
  Model answer: Look for controlled seated BP with tolerable postural reduction rather than simply a normal clinic reading.
Stage 3 — Confirm readiness
  Question: What should the multidisciplinary review cover?
  Model answer: Blood-pressure and rhythm control, postural symptoms, ECG/cardiac effects and glucose.
  Model answer: Availability of experienced endocrine surgery, anaesthesia, critical care and appropriate postoperative monitoring.
  Model answer: A plan for invasive monitoring and rapidly acting vasoactive drugs.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction causes hypertension and contracted circulating volume. Alpha blockade reduces vascular tone; beta blockade is added only after alpha control because isolated beta blockade leaves unopposed alpha vasoconstriction. Preparation is judged by pressure control, tolerable postural change, rhythm and end-organ effects rather than one clinic value.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Titrate phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin for roughly 10–14 days, then add beta blockade only for persistent tachycardia after adequate alpha blockade. Encourage salt and fluid intake where safe. Plan arterial monitoring, large-bore access, short-acting vasodilators, vasopressors, glucose monitoring and postoperative critical-care observation with an experienced multidisciplinary team.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not chase a perfectly normal seated pressure at the cost of disabling orthostasis, and never describe beta blockade before alpha blockade.
Take-home: Successful preparation is alpha blockade followed—if needed—by beta blockade, together with volume expansion and an experienced multidisciplinary plan.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Beta blocker before diagnosis
case_bank.text:
Case: Beta blocker before diagnosis (Phaeochromocytoma, Advanced)
Patient: A 51-year-old man with an undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma receives propranolol in the emergency department for tachycardia.
Presentation: Minutes later he develops severe headache, chest pain and BP 246/132 mmHg with pulmonary oedema.
Stage 1 — Explain the deterioration
  Question: What mechanism has caused this crisis?
  Model answer: Beta blockade removed beta-mediated vasodilation and cardiac compensation while alpha receptors remained intensely stimulated.
  Model answer: Unopposed alpha vasoconstriction caused abrupt hypertension and acute cardiac afterload.
  Model answer: This presentation should trigger urgent specialist help and consideration of catecholamine excess.
Stage 2 — Stabilise the crisis
  Question: What are the immediate principles?
  Model answer: Use titratable vasodilator or alpha-blocking therapy with invasive arterial pressure monitoring in a critical-care setting.
  Model answer: Treat pulmonary oedema and myocardial complications while avoiding further isolated beta blockade.
  Model answer: Once alpha control is established, a short-acting beta blocker may be considered for persistent tachyarrhythmia.
Stage 3 — Plan definitive care
  Question: Should surgery proceed immediately?
  Model answer: If the acute emergency can be stabilised, defer tumour resection until adequate alpha blockade and volume restoration are achieved.
  Model answer: Emergency surgery is reserved for an uncontrollable complication and requires an expert team with vasoactive support ready.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Propranolol removes beta-2 vasodilation and limits cardiac compensation while catecholamine-stimulated alpha receptors continue intense vasoconstriction. The result may be malignant hypertension, myocardial injury and pulmonary oedema. This is a pharmacological crisis, not simple undertreated tachycardia.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Escalate to critical care, establish invasive arterial monitoring and control vascular tone with titratable vasodilation or alpha blockade. Treat pulmonary oedema and myocardial complications and avoid further isolated beta blockade. A short-acting beta blocker is considered only after alpha-mediated hypertension is controlled. Definitive resection is normally deferred until blockade and volume restoration are complete.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Giving more beta blocker for the persistent tachycardia can worsen the crisis. Explain receptor physiology and treatment sequence explicitly.
Take-home: In suspected phaeochromocytoma, beta blockade before alpha blockade can be catastrophic; control vasoconstriction first.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

entries.description: Propofol, thiopentone, ketamine, etomidate — mechanisms and pharmacology
entries.text:
# Intravenous Anaesthetic Agents Propofol, thiopentone, ketamine, etomidate — mechanisms and pharmacology Step-by-step reasoning Choose TIVA because volatile agents at >0.5 MAC abolish motor evoked potentials. TIVA with propofol + remifentanil preserves SSEP/MEP signals. Use TCI propofol (Schnider or Marsh; effect-site target 3–4 µg/mL) and TCI remifentanil (Minto; effect-site 3–6 ng/mL). Titrate to processed EEG (BIS 40–60). Insert a dedicated, well-secured IV with anti-reflux/anti-siphon valves; pump alarms set; pump line visible throughout. Avoid PRIS: keep propofol infusion <4 mg/kg/h for >48 h, ensure adequate carbohydrate and oxygen delivery, monitor lactate, CK, pH and triglycerides for long cases. Plan emergence: stop remifentanil last to provide a smooth wake-up; pre-emptive long-acting analgesia (morphine, paracetamol, dexamethasone, regional/wound infiltration) given before remifentanil is stopped to prevent acute opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Document: cumulative propofol dose, depth-of-anaesthesia trace, awareness check on emergence (AAGBI Safe TIVA standards). Common traps Running >4 mg/kg/h propofol for prolonged surgery → PRIS. Failing to bolus long-acting opioid before remi is stopped → severe acute pain and hyperalgesia. Omitting depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring with TIVA — explicit recommendation in AAGBI safe-practice guideline. in a lipid emulsion (soybean oil, egg lecithin, glycerol). Induction dose 1.5–2.5 mg/kg . Onset 30–40 s (one arm-brain circulation time). Duration ~5–10 min (redistribution). pKa 11 — almost entirely un-ionised at physiological pH. : enhances GABA_A receptor activity : dose-dependent hypotension (vasodilation + myocardial depression), reduced baroreflex sensitivity. : apnoea, respiratory depression. : anticonvulsant, antiemetic, reduces CMRO₂ and ICP. : pain on injection (attenuated by lidocaine), supports bacterial growth — discard after 6 hours. TIVA & TCI Interactive 3-Compartment TCI Simulator Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS) > 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 h , but it can occur with shorter exposures in susceptible patients Schnider vs Eleveld — General-Purpose TCI Why patients move more often on TIVA than volatile anaesthesia where each class of agent acts to produce immobility how reliably we can measure an adequate dose at the bedside. Site of immobility. Volatile agents produce immobility largely at the spinal cord ; at hypnotic concentrations the spinal motor response to noxious stimulus is comparatively preserved. No agreed "MAC" for propofol. With volatiles, end-tidal monitoring lets you titrate to a known ED₅₀ (and run 1.2–1.3 MAC for surgical stimulation). With TIVA you target a modelled plasma or effect-site concentration — population PK models (Marsh, Schnider, Eleveld) carry a typical bias of 20–30%, so the actual Ce can be well below the value displayed. Pharmacokinetic variability. Volume of distribution, clearance, body composition, cardiac output and drug interactions all shift the true Ce. An obese, high-cardiac-output or enzyme-induced patient may sit substantially below the target Ce — and therefore move — without any change on the pump display. Hysteresis and effect-site lag. After a step-up in target, equilibration between plasma and effect site takes minutes. If surgical stimulus increases before Ce catches up (skin incision, laryngoscopy, peritoneal traction), the patient can move despite an "adequate" target. Loss of opioid synergy. Propofol provides little intrinsic analgesia, so adequate immobility on TIVA is highly dependent on a co-administered opioid (typically remifentanil). Under-dosing or pump occlusion of the opioid line is a classic cause of intra-operative movement on TIVA. Equipment failure modes. Volatile delivery failures are visible on the vaporiser dial and end-tidal trace. TIVA failures (line disconnection, extravasation, three-way tap left off, IV cannula tissued) deliver drug into the dressings instead of the patient — the pump runs normally but Ce falls rapidly. No real-time depth marker. End-tidal volatile concentration is a continuous, validated surrogate for brain partial pressure. There is no equivalent for propofol — processed-EEG monitors (BIS/Entropy) are the recommended substitute, and the Association of Anaesthetists advises their routine use whenever TIVA is combined with neuromuscular blockade Practical implication: when running TIVA, pair propofol with a remifentanil infusion (or adequate intermittent opioid), use processed-EEG monitoring (especially with NMB), inspect the IV site and giving set frequently, and anticipate stimulating moments by raising the effect-site target several minutes in advance. . Highly lipid-soluble, rapid onset. Prepared as 2.5% solution (pH 10.5 — highly alkaline, tissue necrosis if extravasation). Precipitates if mixed with acidic drugs (e.g., suxamethonium, atracurium, opioids). : GABA_A agonist (opens chloride channel directly at high doses, potentiates at low doses). : tachycardia (baroreceptor reflex to vasodilation), myocardial depression. : powerful anticonvulsant, cerebral protectant (reduces CMRO₂). : porphyria is an absolute contraindication. Histamine release. No analgesic properties. NMDA receptor antagonist . Dose: 1–2 mg/kg IV, 5–10 mg/kg IM . The S(+)-enantiomer is 2× more potent. Produces "dissociative anaesthesia" — catalepsy, analgesia, amnesia with eyes open and maintained airway reflexes (relatively). : indirect sympathomimetic (↑HR, ↑BP, ↑SVR) — useful in haemodynamically compromised patients and tamponade. Direct myocardial depressant in catecholamine-depleted states. : bronchodilator, preserves respiratory drive (relatively), increased secretions. : raises ICP and IOP. Emergence phenomena (hallucinations, vivid dreams) — reduced with benzodiazepines. Unique Properties Most haemodynamically stable induction agent — minimal effect on HR, BP, or cardiac output. Ideal for patients with limited cardiovascular reserve. : GABA_A receptor (selective for β₂/β₃ subunit). : adrenocortical suppression (inhibits 11β-hydroxylase — even a single dose suppresses cortisol for up to 24 hours). Pain on injection. Myoclonus (not seizure activity). High incidence of PONV. Not recommended for infusion due to adrenal suppression. open and ionised at pH 3.5 (vial), making it injectable without solvent; at physiological pH the ring closes and the molecule becomes highly lipid-soluble, accounting for its rapid CNS penetration. Doses: sedation 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV, induction 0.2–0.3 mg/kg, premed 0.5 mg/kg PO (paeds). : positive allosteric modulator at the α/γ interface of GABA-A of chloride channel opening (barbiturates increase duration). Selectivity for α₁-containing receptors mediates sedation, anterograde amnesia and anticonvulsant action; α₂/α₃ mediate anxiolysis and muscle relaxation. : mild ↓ SVR, well-preserved cardiac output. : dose-dependent respiratory depression, synergistic with opioids. : t½ 1.5–2.5 h, Vd 1.0–1.5 L/kg, 96% protein-bound. Hepatic CYP3A4 → α-hydroxy-midazolam (10% potency) → UGT-glucuronidation to , which is , water-soluble, and renally excreted . In AKI/CKD the glucuronide accumulates → prolonged sedation for days after stopping an infusion. : flumazenil 200 µg + 100 µg/min titrated; t½ shorter than midazolam → resedation likely. α₂-adrenergic agonist (α₂ : α₁ ≈ 1620 : 1) — the dextro-isomer of medetomidine. Acts at pre-synaptic α₂A autoreceptors in the locus coeruleus , reducing noradrenaline release and disinhibiting the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO). The result is a NREM-stage-2-like sedation — patients are easily roused, follow commands, and have minimal respiratory depression. Dosing (Dexdor) : maintenance infusion 0.2–1.4 µg/kg/h titrated to RASS. Optional loading dose 1 µg/kg over 10 min produces a transient hypertensive peak (peripheral α₂B vasoconstriction) followed by hypotension and bradycardia (central α₂A) — the characteristic biphasic BP response . Slow infusion without a bolus avoids the initial hypertension. Other uses : awake fibre-optic intubation, regional block adjunct, paediatric premedication (intranasal), opioid/alcohol withdrawal. SPICE-III (2019) showed non-inferior 90-day mortality vs standard sedation, with more ventilator-free days and less delirium. Cautions: bradycardia, hypotension, hepatic dysfunction (reduce dose), and rebound hypertension on prolonged-use cessation. . Designed as a "soft drug": a methyl ester side-chain is rapidly hydrolysed by non-specific tissue carboxylesterases (predominantly CES-1A) to an inactive carboxylic-acid metabolite (CNS7054), giving a short, predictable offset that is largely independent of infusion duration and of hepatic/renal function : positive allosteric modulator at the α/γ interface of GABA-A receptors — identical site to midazolam, increasing chloride-channel opening frequency Dosing (procedural sedation) : 5–7 mg IV bolus over 1 min, then 2.5 mg top-ups (≥2 min apart) to effect; onset ~1–3 min, clinical duration ~10 min after a single bolus. : context-sensitive half-time ≈ 7–8 min even after prolonged infusion; Vd ~0.9 L/kg; clearance ~70 L/h, independent of CYP metabolism. : less hypotension than propofol and less respiratory depression than midazolam, but both occur dose-dependently and are synergistic with opioids. : fully antagonised by flumazenil (resedation possible because flumazenil's t½ is shorter than the active drug window when high doses have been used). : examinable as a new UK IV agent with a unique esterase-based metabolic profile — useful where rapid, predictable recovery is needed in frail, renally or hepatically impaired patients Comparative Table Dose (mg/kg) Key Feature Antiemetic, TCI-compatible Anticonvulsant, avoid in porphyria 1–2 IV NMDA antagonist Analgesic, sympathomimetic, IM route GABA_A (β₂/β₃) CV stability, adrenal suppression Induction dose Distinguishing feature Molecular Structures Designing a TIVA technique for a long spine case in a young patient TIVA with TCI propofol (Schnider, 3–4 µg/mL) + TCI remifentanil (Minto, 3–6 ng/mL), titrated to BIS 40–60, with secure dedicated IV access and processed EEG. Keep propofol <4 mg/kg/h, monitor for PRIS biochemistry on long cases, and load long-acting analgesia before stopping remifentanil. This preserves intraoperative MEP/SSEP signals where volatiles would not. Intravenous Anaesthetic Agents FRCA Primary — Pharmacology Propofol: GABA_A agonist. Causes hypotension (vasodilation + myocardial depression). Antiemetic. Pain on injection. Lipid emulsion supports bacterial growth. Thiopentone: alkaline pH 10.5 — tissue necrosis risk. Absolute contraindication in porphyria. Potent anticonvulsant. Ketamine: NMDA antagonist. Only IV agent with significant analgesia. Indirect sympathomimetic. Emergence phenomena. Bronchodilator. Etomidate: most haemodynamically stable agent. Inhibits 11β-hydroxylase (adrenal suppression for ~24h even after single dose). All IV agents (except ketamine) cause dose-dependent respiratory depression and apnoea. TCI models: Marsh (weight-based), Schnider (age, weight, height, LBM), Eleveld (universal — neonates to elderly). PRIS: >4 mg/kg/h for >48h — metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiovascular collapse. Stop infusion, supportive care. IV Induction Agents — Side-by-Side The high-yield comparison across the four FRCA induction agents. Compare propofol, thiopentone, ketamine and etomidate for RSI in shock. Propofol — smooth, antiemetic, but profound cardiovascular depression; reduce dose 50–70 %. Thiopentone — fast onset, but venodilatation and direct myocardial depression; histamine release. Ketamine — preserves SVR/CO via sympathetic activation, ideal for shock (1–2 mg/kg IV); avoid in raised ICP if uncontrolled hypertension. Etomidate — best haemodynamic profile, but adrenal suppression (single dose still measurable for 24 h) — controversial in sepsis. What is propofol infusion syndrome and how is it recognised? Rare but lethal complication of prolonged high-dose propofol (>4 mg/kg/h for >48 h, especially in children/critically ill). Features: metabolic acidosis (lactate), rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, hyperlipidaemia, hepatomegaly, refractory bradycardia, cardiac failure. Mechanism: impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation. Prevention: limit to ≤4 mg/kg/h, monitor lactate/CK/triglycerides; if suspected — stop propofol, switch sedation, supportive care + RRT. What are the advantages of TCI propofol over manual infusion? Target-controlled infusion (TCI) uses pharmacokinetic models (Marsh — weight-based; Schnider — age, weight, height, LBM) to achieve and maintain a target plasma or effect-site concentration. Propofol is ideal for TIVA due to its short context-sensitive half-time at moderate infusion durations.

It uses allometric scaling, a maturation function, and fat-free mass — replacing the need to choose between Schnider, Marsh and paediatric models. Compare the two side by side at population extremes.

Intra-operative movement is consistently reported more frequently with propofol TIVA than with an equivalent MAC-guided volatile technique. The difference is not because propofol is a hypnotic — it is because of where each class of agent acts to produce immobility and how reliably we can measure an adequate dose at the bedside.

An obese, high-cardiac-output or enzyme-induced patient may sit substantially below the target Ce — and therefore move — without any change on the pump display.

  • Loss of opioid synergy. Propofol provides little intrinsic analgesia, so adequate immobility on TIVA is highly dependent on a co-administered opioid (typically remifentanil). Under-dosing or pump occlusion of the opioid line is a classic cause of intra-operative movement on TIVA.
  • Equipment failure modes. Volatile delivery failures are visible on the vaporiser dial and end-tidal trace. TIVA failures (line disconnection, extravasation, three-way tap left off, IV cannula tissued) deliver drug into the dressings instead of the patient — the pump runs normally but Ce falls rapidly.
  • No real-time depth marker. End-tidal volatile concentration is a continuous, validated surrogate for brain partial pressure. There is no equivalent for propofol — processed-EEG monitors (BIS/Entropy) are the recommended substitute, and the Association of Anaesthetists advises their routine use whenever TIVA is combined with neuromuscular blockade Practical implication: when running TIVA, pair propofol with a remifentanil infusion (or adequate intermittent opioid), use processed-EEG monitoring (especially with NMB), inspect the IV site and giving set frequently, and anticipate stimulating moments by raising the effect-site target several minutes in advance.

Thiobarbiturate. Induction dose 3–5 mg/kg Mechanism: GABA_A agonist (opens chloride channel directly at high doses, potentiates at low doses). CVS: tachycardia (baroreceptor reflex to vasodilation), myocardial depression. CNS: powerful anticonvulsant, cerebral protectant (reduces CMRO₂). Other: porphyria is an absolute contraindication. Histamine release. No analgesic properties.

Phencyclidine derivative. NMDA receptor antagonist. Dose: 1–2 mg/kg IV, 5–10 mg/kg IM

CVS: indirect sympathomimetic (↑HR, ↑BP, ↑SVR) — useful in haemodynamically compromised patients and tamponade. Direct myocardial depressant in catecholamine-depleted states. RS: bronchodilator, preserves respiratory drive (relatively), increased secretions. CNS: raises ICP and IOP. Emergence phenomena (hallucinations, vivid dreams) — reduced with benzodiazepines.

Unique Properties

Ketamine is the only IV induction agent that provides significant analgesia. It can be given IM (useful for uncooperative patients/children). It has anti-inflammatory properties and is increasingly used in sub-anaesthetic doses for chronic pain and treatment-resistant depression.

Imidazole derivative. Dose 0.3 mg/kg IV. Most haemodynamically stable induction agent — minimal effect on HR, BP, or cardiac output. Ideal for patients with limited cardiovascular reserve.

Mechanism: GABA_A receptor (selective for β₂/β₃ subunit). Problems: adrenocortical suppression (inhibits 11β-hydroxylase — even a single dose suppresses cortisol for up to 24 hours). Pain on injection. Myoclonus (not seizure activity). High incidence of PONV. Not recommended for infusion due to adrenal suppression.

Water-soluble imidazobenzodiazepine. The diazepine ring is open and ionised at pH 3.5 (vial), making it injectable without solvent; at physiological pH the ring closes and the molecule becomes highly lipid-soluble, accounting for its rapid CNS penetration. Doses: sedation 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV, induction 0.2–0.3 mg/kg, premed 0.5 mg/kg PO (paeds).

Mechanism: positive allosteric modulator at the α/γ interface of GABA-A receptors — increases frequency of chloride channel opening (barbiturates increase duration). Selectivity for α₁-containing receptors mediates sedation, anterograde amnesia and anticonvulsant action; α₂/α₃ mediate anxiolysis and muscle relaxation. CVS: mild ↓ SVR, well-preserved cardiac output. RS: dose-dependent respiratory depression, synergistic with opioids.

PK: t½ 1.5–2.5 h, Vd 1.0–1.5 L/kg, 96% protein-bound. Hepatic CYP3A4 → α-hydroxy-midazolam (10% potency) → UGT-glucuronidation to α-hydroxy-midazolam-glucuronide, which is active, water-soluble, and renally excreted. In AKI/CKD the glucuronide accumulates → prolonged sedation for days after stopping an infusion. Reversal: flumazenil 200 µg + 100 µg/min titrated; t½ shorter than midazolam → resedation likely.

Highly selective α₂-adrenergic agonist (α₂ : α₁ ≈ 1620 : 1) — the dextro-isomer of medetomidine. Acts at pre-synaptic α₂A autoreceptors in the locus coeruleus, reducing noradrenaline release and disinhibiting the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO). The result is a NREM-stage-2-like sedation — patients are easily roused, follow commands, and have minimal respiratory depression.

Switch to TIVA (propofol ± remifentanil). Use a clean (vapour-free) anaesthetic machine if available; otherwise remove the vaporiser, flush with high-flow O₂ ≥10 L/min for ≥20 min, and change the soda lime and circuit. Hyperventilate with 100% O₂ at high fresh-gas flows to wash out CO₂ and minimise rebreathing of any volatile. Give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus, repeated every 5–10 min up to 10 mg/kg until ETCO₂, HR and temperature fall. Active cooling: cold IV saline, surface cooling, stop only when core temp <38.5 °C. Treat hyperkalaemia (calcium chloride, insulin/glucose, salbutamol; avoid suxamethonium); treat acidosis; manage arrhythmias (avoid calcium-channel blockers with dantrolene → risk of hyperkalaemia and cardiovascular collapse). After stabilisation transfer to ICU for ≥24 h: monitor for recrudescence, rhabdomyolysis (CK, urine myoglobin, fluids/forced diuresis to prevent AKI). Refer the patient and first-degree relatives for MH unit testing. Common traps Using verapamil/diltiazem with dantrolene — life-threatening hyperkalaemia. Giving suxamethonium to treat 'masseter spasm' — worsens the crisis. Not reconstituting enough dantrolene early — total dose may exceed 10 mg/kg and each 20 mg vial needs 60 mL of sterile water.
