Apply the 'triple whammy' rule. NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic-or-volume-depletion → AKI. Surgery itself supplies the third hit (fasting, blood loss, third-spacing). Quantify bleeding risk. Apixaban + NSAID roughly doubles GI bleeding and increases surgical-site bleeding. Build the multimodal alternative. Paracetamol 1 g QDS + LIA at the surgical site + adductor-canal block + low-dose oxycodone PRN. Decision points If eGFR were > 60, no ACEi, no anticoagulant and patient < 65 → short-course NSAID acceptable. Always document a stop date (≤ 5 days) when an NSAID is prescribed perioperatively. Common traps Assuming 'topical' or 'PR' diclofenac avoids systemic effects — it doesn't, GFR still falls. Forgetting that COX-2 selective drugs (parecoxib) still cause renal injury — selectivity only spares the GI tract. Restarting the ACEi the morning of surgery 'because the patient takes it at home'. Calculate the dose per kg. 12 g ÷ 50 kg = 240 mg/kg — well above the 150 mg/kg toxic threshold and far above the 75 mg/kg high-risk threshold. Test the nomogram's validity. Rumack-Matthew is only valid for a single ingestion at a known time (4–15 h post-ingestion). A 6-hour staggered ingestion fails this rule. Identify high-risk modifiers. Phenytoin → CYP2E1 induction → ↑ NAPQI. Malnutrition → glutathione depletion. Low body weight → lower absolute reserve. Apply MHRA 2012 guidance. Treat any staggered overdose ≥ 75 mg/kg/24 h with NAC regardless of paracetamol level. Choose the regimen. Standard 21-h IV NAC: 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h. Or SNAP (12 h, lower anaphylactoid rate). Decision points at 24 h Continue NAC if ALT rising, INR > 1.3, paracetamol still detectable, or acidosis. Refer to a transplant centre if King's College Criteria met (pH < 7.3 OR all of: INR > 6.5, creatinine > 300, grade III/IV encephalopathy). Reading a single level off the nomogram for a staggered or unknown-time ingestion. Stopping NAC at 21 h despite ongoing transaminitis or coagulopathy. Confusing the anaphylactoid reaction (flush, bronchospasm in first hour) with true allergy — slow the rate, give antihistamine, do not stop permanently. COX Selectivity Non-selective (irreversible) Irreversibly acetylates COX → permanent platelet inhibition (7-10 days). Low dose: antiplatelet. High dose: analgesic Non-selective (reversible) Shortest half-life, good safety profile. Competitive with aspirin for platelet COX-1 binding Slightly COX-2 preferential Good analgesic. ↑ CV risk (especially MI). Available PO, PR, IM, topical Potent analgesic (IV/IM). Max 2 days use. ↑ GI bleeding risk COX-2 selective ↓ GI side effects but ↑ CV risk. Parecoxib = IV prodrug of valdecoxib : ↓ PGE₂/PGI₂ → ↓ mucosal protection → ulceration, bleeding. Risk factors: age, H. pylori, steroids, anticoagulants. COX-2 selective drugs have lower GI risk : ↓ afferent arteriolar PGE₂ → ↓ GFR. Risk in hypovolaemia, CKD, ACEi/ARB use. Can cause Na⁺/H₂O retention, hyperkalaemia, papillary necrosis : COX-2 inhibition ↓ PGI₂ (vasodilator, antiplatelet) without ↓ TXA₂ → prothrombotic state. All NSAIDs carry some CV risk (except aspirin and naproxen) : aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD) — COX inhibition shunts arachidonic acid to lipoxygenase pathway → ↑ leukotrienes → bronchospasm : ↓ TXA₂ → ↓ aggregation. Aspirin effect lasts platelet lifespan (7-10 days); others reverse when drug clears : not fully understood. Central COX inhibition (COX-3?), serotonergic descending pathways, endocannabinoid system (AM404 metabolite), TRPV1 activation. Weak peripheral anti-inflammatory effect : oral bioavailability ~80%, hepatic metabolism (glucuronidation 60%, sulphation 30%, CYP2E1 5% → NAPQI). IV onset ~5 min, peak effect ~1h. Adult dose 1g QDS (max 4g/day) : NAPQI (toxic metabolite) normally conjugated by glutathione. Overdose → glutathione depletion → NAPQI binds hepatocytes → centrilobular necrosis (Zone 3) : N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — replenishes glutathione. Most effective within 8h. Staggered overdoses are higher risk than single timepoint. Use Rumack-Matthew nomogram (150 mg/kg treatment line) Risk factors for toxicity : enzyme inducers (phenytoin, rifampicin, alcohol), glutathione depletion (malnutrition, HIV, anorexia), low body weight (<50kg — dose reduce) NSAID risk-benefit after a knee replacement Avoid routine NSAIDs in this patient. Use paracetamol, regional analgesia (adductor canal / LIA), and short-course low-dose opioids. Reserve NSAIDs for younger, well-hydrated patients with normal renal function and no anticoagulant — and document a clear stop date. Staggered paracetamol overdose Treat with N-acetylcysteine immediately — do not rely on the nomogram for staggered overdoses or high-risk patients. Use the standard 21-h IV NAC regimen (or the simplified SNAP protocol) and monitor LFTs, INR, creatinine, lactate and pH at 24 h to guide continuation. NSAIDs & Paracetamol COX selectivity, perioperative risks, and paracetamol toxicity COX-1 = constitutive (GI protection, platelets, renal). COX-2 = inducible (inflammation, pain, fever) Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX — platelet effect lasts 7-10 days. All other NSAIDs are reversible NSAID renal toxicity: ↓ afferent arteriolar PGE₂ → ↓ GFR. High risk with hypovolaemia + ACEi/ARB ('triple whammy') Paracetamol toxicity: NAPQI → glutathione depletion → Zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatic necrosis NAC (N-acetylcysteine) replenishes glutathione — most effective within 8h of paracetamol overdose COX-2 selective drugs have ↓ GI risk but ↑ CV risk (prothrombotic: ↓PGI₂ without ↓TXA₂) Rumack-Matthew nomogram is invalid for staggered overdoses — treat empirically based on dose/risk factors NSAIDs — Mechanism of Action NSAID Adverse Effects Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) What is the maximum dose of paracetamol and when must it be reduced? Standard adult: 1 g qds (4 g/day). Reduce to 75 mg/kg/day (max 3 g/day) if weight <50 kg, chronic alcohol use, malnutrition, hepatic impairment, dehydration, glutathione depletion. IV dose: 15 mg/kg up to 1 g per dose, max 4 g/day in adults >50 kg, infused over 15 min. Toxicity above 150 mg/kg single dose (or >75 mg/kg in high-risk groups). What are the contraindications and cautions for NSAID use perioperatively? Avoid in: renal impairment (eGFR <30), active GI bleeding/ulcer, severe heart failure, allergy/asthma exacerbated by NSAIDs (~10 % of asthmatics), 3rd-trimester pregnancy (premature ductus closure), platelet dysfunction or coagulopathy. Outline paracetamol overdose management. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is the antidote — replenishes glutathione and detoxifies NAPQI. Indications: paracetamol level above the 100 mg/L line at 4 h on the UK nomogram (single line since 2012 — treat all above), staggered overdose, unknown timing, late presentation with deranged LFTs. Regime: 150 mg/kg over 1 h, 50 mg/kg over 4 h, 100 mg/kg over 16 h. case_bank.title: Oliguria on the first postoperative night
case_bank.text:
Case: Oliguria on the first postoperative night (Renal, neuromuscular & autonomic, Foundation)
Patient: After open colorectal surgery, an adult passes 15 mL of urine per hour for three hours. Mean arterial pressure is 65 mmHg, and the chart includes an ACE inhibitor and regular ibuprofen.
Presentation: The nurse asks for a fluid bolus. The patient looks comfortable, warm and peripherally well perfused.
Stage 1 — Explain the renal physiology
  Question: How does the kidney normally protect glomerular filtration?
  Model answer: Autoregulation keeps renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate near constant across a mean arterial pressure of roughly 80–180 mmHg through myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms.
  Model answer: Afferent arteriolar dilation depends partly on prostaglandins; efferent tone depends on angiotensin II.
  Model answer: NSAIDs blunt afferent dilation and ACE inhibitors blunt efferent constriction, so both together strip away autoregulatory reserve at low pressure.
Stage 2 — Assess before infusing
  Question: How do you evaluate this oliguria?
  Model answer: Exclude obstruction first: flush or replace a blocked catheter and examine for retention.
  Model answer: Assess perfusion with capillary refill, lactate, pressure trend against the patient's baseline, and dynamic response to a small measured fluid challenge.
  Model answer: Look for bleeding, sepsis, raised intra-abdominal pressure and drug causes; review nephrotoxins and check creatinine trend against KDIGO criteria.
Stage 3 — Treat proportionately
  Question: What do you do?
  Model answer: Stop the NSAID, withhold the ACE inhibitor and restore mean arterial pressure towards the patient's usual value using fluid where hypovolaemic and vasopressor where vasodilated.
  Model answer: Avoid indiscriminate large-volume fluid loading, which causes venous congestion, oedema and worse outcomes without protecting kidneys.
  Model answer: Recheck urine output, creatinine and electrolytes, and escalate for critical care review if oliguria persists or acidosis, hyperkalaemia or fluid overload develop.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Postoperative oliguria is often an appropriate neuroendocrine response to surgery — antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone conserve water and sodium — but it is also the first sign of hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity. Because autoregulation depends on prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent tone, combining an NSAID and a renin–angiotensin blocker at low perfusion pressure predictably reduces glomerular filtration.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Work through obstruction, perfusion and nephrotoxins in order. Use small, repeated fluid challenges with a defined endpoint rather than open-ended boluses, and add vasopressor where vasodilation rather than hypovolaemia dominates. Track hourly urine output, creatinine, potassium, acid–base status and fluid balance; diuretics treat fluid overload but do not treat acute kidney injury or improve outcome.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not give a reflex 500 mL bolus for every low urine output, and do not forget a blocked catheter. Frame the answer around autoregulation, KDIGO staging and drug review.
Take-home: Assess obstruction, perfusion and nephrotoxins before infusing: NSAIDs plus renin–angiotensin blockade at low pressure remove renal autoregulatory reserve.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: renal physiology (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mku047); KDIGO AKI guideline (https://kdigo.org/guidelines/acute-kidney-injury/)

# Vasoactive & Inotropic Agents Catecholamines, vasopressors, inotropes, inodilators, vasodilators, digoxin, calcium, and receptor pharmacology Step-by-step reasoning SSC 2021: noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor — α₁-mediated vasoconstriction with modest β₁ inotropy, lower arrhythmia risk than dopamine (SOAP-II trial) Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min if MAP <65 despite noradrenaline 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min — VASST trial reduces noradrenaline requirements Consider hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if vasopressor-refractory (APROCCHSS, ADRENAL) Reassess fluid responsiveness dynamically (pulse pressure variation, passive leg raise, cardiac output monitor) before further fluid Inotrope (dobutamine) if cardiac output low or echo shows myocardial dysfunction Common traps Dopamine first-line — increases arrhythmias and mortality vs noradrenaline (SOAP-II) Vasopressin alone in pure vasoplegia without noradrenaline cover — risk of mesenteric/digital ischaemia Continuing fluid boluses without responsiveness check — fluid overload increases mortality foundations → mechanisms → individual agents → integrated comparison . Begin with the broad classification and receptor science, then explore each agent grouped by clinical role (vasopressors → inotropes/inodilators → vasodilators → salvage therapy), before consolidating with the haemodynamic effects table. Classification of Vasoactive Agents Primary Action Adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine Adrenoreceptor agonism Synthetic sympathomimetics Phenylephrine, dobutamine, isoprenaline Selective receptor agonism Phosphodiesterase inhibitors Milrinone, enoximone ↑ cAMP → inodilation Vasopressin analogues Vasopressin, terlipressin V1 receptor agonism Calcium sensitisers ↑ Ca²⁺ sensitivity of troponin C GTN, SNP, hydralazine NO donors / direct smooth muscle relaxation Adrenoreceptor Pharmacology Vascular smooth muscle Gq → ↑ IP₃/DAG Presynaptic nerve terminals, CNS Gi → ↓ cAMP ↓ NA release, sedation, analgesia Heart (SA node, myocardium) Gs → ↑ cAMP ↑ HR, ↑ contractility, ↑ conduction Bronchial, uterine, vascular smooth muscle Bronchodilation, vasodilation, tocolysis Adipose tissue, bladder Lipolysis, bladder relaxation Inotrope Classification by Cellular Mechanism ↑ cAMP (receptor-mediated) Adrenaline, dobutamine, dopamine, isoprenaline β₁ agonism → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP → PKA → ↑ Ca²⁺ entry ↑ cAMP (enzyme inhibition) PDE III inhibition → ↓ cAMP breakdown → ↑ cAMP → PKA ↑ cAMP (glucagon receptor) Glucagon receptor → Gs → ↑ cAMP (bypasses β-receptor) Calcium sensitisation Stabilises Ca²⁺–troponin C complex → ↑ contractile force without ↑ [Ca²⁺]ᵢ Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger reversal → ↑ [Ca²⁺]ᵢ Direct Ca²⁺ supplementation Calcium chloride / gluconate ↑ extracellular [Ca²⁺] → ↑ Ca²⁺ available for excitation-contraction coupling Noradrenaline (Norepinephrine) Predominantly α₁ agonist with some β₁ activity but minimal β₂ effect. Dose range: 0.01–1.0 µg/kg/min (typically 0.05–0.3 µg/kg/min) Haemodynamic effect: ↑ SVR, ↑ MAP, ↑ diastolic BP. Reflex bradycardia may occur First-line vasopressor in septic shock (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021) Must be given via central venous access — extravasation causes tissue necrosis pure α₁ agonist . No β-receptor activity. Causes predictable vasoconstriction without direct cardiac stimulation. Reflex bradycardia is common. 50–100 µg IV for acute hypotension (e.g., spinal-induced) 0.25–1.0 µg/kg/min predictable response, no tachycardia, safe in peripheral IV Obstetric use: preferred vasopressor for spinal hypotension in caesarean section (↓ fetal acidosis vs ephedrine) Predominantly indirect sympathomimetic with direct α₁ agonism Bolus: 0.5–1 mg IV. Infusion: 0.5–5 mg/hr Acts as a false transmitter — displaces NA but is a weaker agonist → tachyphylaxis Longer acting than phenylephrine (15–20 min). Causes reflex bradycardia Indirect sympathomimetic — displaces noradrenaline from vesicles + weak direct α and β agonism Mixed α and β effects → ↑ HR, ↑ BP, bronchodilation Bolus: 3–6 mg IV. Duration 10–15 min. Tachyphylaxis with repeated doses Crosses placenta → traditionally used in obstetric hypotension (now largely replaced by phenylephrine) Vasopressin & Terlipressin (ADH) is a nonapeptide hormone acting on V₁ (vascular smooth muscle → vasoconstriction), V₂ (collecting duct → water reabsorption), and V₃/V1b (anterior pituitary → ACTH release) receptors. Dose in septic shock: 0.01–0.04 units/min (added to noradrenaline, not first-line) Catecholamine-sparing effect — particularly useful in catecholamine-refractory shock Causes vasoconstriction via V₁ receptors even in acidotic states (unlike catecholamines) VASST trial: no mortality benefit overall but possible benefit in less severe septic shock is a synthetic vasopressin analogue with greater V₁ selectivity. Used in variceal haemorrhage (splanchnic vasoconstriction) and hepatorenal syndrome (CONFIRM trial 2021). Adrenaline (Epinephrine) dose-dependent selectivity Low dose (0.01–0.05 µg/kg/min): β₂ predominance → vasodilation, bronchodilation, ↑ HR Moderate dose (0.05–0.2 µg/kg/min): β₁ predominance → ↑ inotropy, ↑ chronotropy High dose (>0.2 µg/kg/min): α₁ predominance → vasoconstriction, ↑ SVR, ↑ MAP Key clinical uses: cardiac arrest (1 mg IV every 3–5 min), anaphylaxis (0.5 mg IM), low cardiac output states, added to local anaesthetics (1:200,000 = 5 µg/mL) to prolong block and reduce toxicity. COMT and MAO in the liver, lungs, and kidneys. Very short half-life (~2 min). Metabolised to metanephrine and VMA (urinary markers for phaeochromocytoma). Inotropes & Inodilators β₁ agonist with some β₂ and minimal α₁ activity. An — increases cardiac contractility while reducing afterload. 2.5–20 µg/kg/min Primary indication: low cardiac output states (cardiogenic shock, post-cardiac surgery) ↑ CO, ↓ PCWP, ↓/= SVR. May ↓ MAP due to β₂ vasodilation develops with prolonged use (β-receptor downregulation) Racemic mixture: (+) isomer = β₁ agonist, (−) isomer = α₁ agonist Low dose (1–3 µg/kg/min): D₁ receptors → renal/mesenteric vasodilation (no proven renal protection) Moderate (3–10 µg/kg/min): β₁ → ↑ cardiac output High (>10 µg/kg/min): α₁ → vasoconstriction Isoprenaline (Isoproterenol) Non-selective β agonist (β₁ = β₂) with no α activity. 0.5–10 µg/min IV infusion ↑ HR (potent chronotrope), ↑ contractility, bronchodilation, vasodilation (β₂ → ↓ SVR, ↓ diastolic BP) symptomatic bradycardia (bridge to pacing), torsades de pointes, β-blocker overdose, heart transplant (denervated heart) Increases myocardial O₂ demand while reducing diastolic perfusion pressure → risk of ischaemia No longer first-line for bradycardia (atropine/pacing preferred) Phosphodiesterase III Inhibitors (Milrinone, Enoximone) inhibit PDE III, preventing breakdown of cAMP. This produces : ↑ contractility (cardiac muscle) and vasodilation (vascular smooth muscle). Bypass the β-receptor → effective even in β-blocked or downregulated patients Milrinone dose: loading 50 µg/kg (often omitted), infusion 0.375–0.75 µg/kg/min Reduce PVR — useful in right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension Risk of hypotension (vasodilation) and arrhythmias Renal excretion (milrinone) — reduce dose in renal impairment Calcium sensitiser — binds to troponin C and stabilises the calcium-troponin C complex, enhancing contractile force without increasing intracellular calcium or myocardial oxygen demand. Also opens K channels → vasodilation and cardioprotection Also has PDE III inhibitor activity Active metabolite OR-1896 has 75-hour half-life → effects persist for days after stopping Used in acute decompensated heart failure, post-cardiac surgery low CO LEVO-CTS trial (2017): no benefit over placebo in cardiac surgery Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → reversal of Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ → positive inotropy. Cardiac effects: ↑ contractility (weak inotrope), ↓ AV conduction (vagotonic), ↓ HR Loading dose: 500 µg IV over 2 hours, then 250 µg 6-hourly × 2. Maintenance: 62.5–250 µg/day Primary use: rate control in atrial fibrillation (especially with heart failure). Not for cardioversion Narrow therapeutic index: therapeutic level 1.0–2.0 ng/mL. Toxicity enhanced by hypokalaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypothyroidism, renal impairment Toxicity features: any arrhythmia (classically bidirectional VT, accelerated junctional rhythm), nausea, visual disturbance (xanthopsia — yellow vision) Treatment of toxicity: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab). Correct K⁺/Mg²⁺. Avoid cardioversion (risk of refractory VF) 70% renal excretion. T½ = 36–48 hours. Large Vd (8 L/kg) — not removed by dialysis independently of the β-receptor 50–150 µg/kg IV bolus (typically 5–10 mg), then infusion 1–5 mg/hr β-blocker overdose (bypasses blocked β-receptor to increase cAMP) Also useful in calcium channel blocker toxicity ↑ HR, ↑ contractility, ↑ AV conduction. Also ↑ blood glucose, relaxes smooth muscle Side effects: nausea, vomiting (common), hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia Short duration (15–20 min) — infusion usually required Ca²⁺ content Calcium chloride 10% 6.8 mmol Ca²⁺ per 10 mL 3× more ionised Ca²⁺ than gluconate. Irritant — requires central access ideally. Preferred in cardiac arrest Calcium gluconate 10% 2.2 mmol Ca²⁺ per 10 mL Safer peripherally. Requires hepatic metabolism to release ionised Ca²⁺. Preferred for hyperkalaemia hyperkalaemia (cardiac membrane stabilisation), hypocalcaemia, calcium channel blocker toxicity, massive transfusion (citrate chelation), cardiac arrest (PEA with suspected hypocalcaemia) 10 mL of 10% CaCl₂ IV over 10 min (cardiac arrest: rapid bolus) Antagonises the cardiac effects of hyperkalaemia and hypermagnesaemia Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN) Organic nitrate → releases NO → ↑ cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation Predominantly venodilator at low doses → ↓ preload → ↓ LVEDP Higher doses → arteriolar dilation → ↓ afterload Dose: 0.5–10 µg/kg/min. Tolerance develops within 24–48 hours Uses: myocardial ischaemia, acute heart failure, controlled hypotension Sodium Nitroprusside (SNP) Direct NO donor → balanced arterial and venous dilation Extremely rapid onset and offset (1–2 min). Dose: 0.5–8 µg/kg/min Cyanide toxicity: SNP releases 5 CN⁻ ions per molecule. Metabolised by rhodanase to thiocyanate (needs thiosulphate) Signs of toxicity: tachyphylaxis, lactic acidosis, arrhythmias. Treat with hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulphate Protect from light (photodegradation). Maximum duration 72 hours, max dose 1.5 mg/kg Salvage Therapy for Refractory Vasoplegia Methylene Blue Mechanism of action Inhibits inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) — reducing endothelial NO production driven by sepsis-/CPB-related cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6). Inhibits soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) in vascular smooth muscle — preventing the NO → cGMP → PKG → MLCK-dephosphorylation cascade that causes vasodilation. Net effect: restoration of vascular tone, ↑ SVR and MAP, with little direct effect on cardiac contractility. Also inhibits monoamine oxidase A and is itself a weak serotonin reuptake inhibitor — explains the serotonin-syndrome interaction. Refractory vasoplegic septic shock — unresponsive to noradrenaline + vasopressin (± adrenaline) and adequately fluid-resuscitated. Post-cardiopulmonary bypass vasoplegia — strongest evidence base; reduces noradrenaline requirement, ICU LOS and mortality (Levin 2004 RCT). Anaphylactic shock refractory to adrenaline — case-series evidence. Hepatopulmonary syndrome liver-transplant vasoplegia (different indication, different dose — see below). Vasoplegic shock — bolus 1–2 mg/kg IV over 20–60 min Effect within minutes; duration 1–2 h. Avoid > 2 mg/kg as bolus (pulmonary vasoconstriction, ↑ PVR) Vasoplegic shock — infusion 0.25–2 mg/kg/h Follow-on infusion if response to bolus; titrate to MAP and noradrenaline weaning 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min, repeat in 1 h Reduces Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺ via NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase. Contra-indicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis) Cautions & adverse effects G6PD deficiency — risk of acute haemolytic anaemia; relative contra-indication. Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, MAO-inhibitors) — risk of serotonin syndrome via MAO-A inhibition; avoid where possible. Pulmonary vasoconstriction — ↑ PVR; caution with pre-existing pulmonary hypertension or RV failure. Pulse oximetry artefact — false ↓ SpO₂ for 10–60 min (absorbs at 660 nm). Use ABG SaO₂ for monitoring. Blue–green discolouration of urine and skin ; transient blue tint to the surgical field. High doses may paradoxically methaemoglobinaemia, worsening oxygen delivery. Place in therapy Foundations Vasopressors Inopressor Vasodilators Salvage Therapy Comparison Table Inotropes work by ↑ cAMP (β-agonists, PDE inhibitors, glucagon), Ca²⁺ sensitisation, or Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition (digoxin) Adrenaline has dose-dependent receptor selectivity: low-dose β₂, moderate β₁, high-dose α₁ Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor in septic shock (α₁ predominant with some β₁) Dobutamine is an inodilator (β₁ > β₂ > α₁) — first-line inotrope in cardiogenic shock PDE III inhibitors (milrinone) bypass β-receptors — effective in β-blocked patients and ↓ PVR Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase — toxicity enhanced by ↓K⁺, ↓Mg²⁺, ↑Ca²⁺; treat with DigiFab Glucagon bypasses the β-receptor via glucagon receptor → Gs → ↑ cAMP — key in β-blocker OD CaCl₂ has 3× more ionised Ca²⁺ than Ca gluconate — preferred in cardiac arrest Levosimendan sensitises troponin C to calcium — no increase in myocardial O₂ demand Vasopressin acts via V₁ receptors — works even in acidosis when catecholamines fail GTN is predominantly a venodilator (↓ preload); SNP is a balanced arteriovenous dilator releasing cyanide Methylene blue is a salvage option in refractory vasoplegia — inhibits iNOS and sGC Choosing a vasopressor in septic shock Start noradrenaline (titrate to MAP 65), add vasopressin if refractory, consider hydrocortisone, and reassess fluid responsiveness rather than empirical boluses. Vasoactive & Inotropic Agents FRCA Primary & Final — Pharmacology Molecular Structures of Catecholamines Inotrope Signalling Pathways Interactive Receptor Selectivity Haemodynamic Effects — Side-by-Side Comparison Having reviewed each agent individually, this consolidated table summarises the expected haemodynamic effects of commonly used inotropes and vasopressors at standard clinical doses. Arrows indicate direction and magnitude of change. Compare noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine and vasopressin. What is the difference between metaraminol, phenylephrine and ephedrine for spinal hypotension? Phenylephrine — pure α1 agonist; reduces CO via reflex bradycardia but maintains uteroplacental perfusion best (preferred for obstetric spinal). Metaraminol — predominantly α1 (some indirect β); similar profile to phenylephrine. Ephedrine — direct and indirect α + β; crosses placenta and causes fetal acidosis (linked to neonatal acidaemia in C-section); now second-line in obstetrics. When is milrinone preferred over dobutamine? Milrinone is a PDE-3 inhibitor → ↑cAMP independent of β-receptor activation. Useful when β-receptors are downregulated (chronic heart failure, prolonged catecholamine infusion) or in pulmonary hypertension (selective pulmonary vasodilation). Causes more vasodilation than dobutamine — often needs noradrenaline co-administration. Long half-life (2–3 h) makes it less titratable; significant accumulation in renal failure. Classify vasoactive agents by mechanism (catecholamines, sympathomimetics, PDE inhibitors, vasopressin analogues, Ca²⁺ sensitisers, vasodilators). Describe adrenoreceptor subtypes and their downstream signalling (Gs/Gq/Gi → cAMP / IP₃ / DAG). Choose appropriate first-line agents for septic, cardiogenic and vasoplegic shock with dose ranges. Explain non-catecholamine inotropic strategies (PDE III inhibition, Ca²⁺ sensitisation, glucagon, digoxin, Ca²⁺). Recognise indications, dosing and toxicity of salvage agents (vasopressin, methylene blue, angiotensin II). ] }, ]; const VasoactiveAgentsTopicWorkedExamples: WorkedExample[] = [ { title: A 55-year-old with septic shock remains hypotensive (MAP 55) after 30 mL/kg crystalloid. Which vasopressor first and what is the evidence? >Step-by-step reasoning

  1. SSC 2021: noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor — α₁-mediated vasoconstriction with modest β₁ inotropy, lower arrhythmia risk than dopamine (SOAP-II trial)
  2. Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min if MAP <65 despite noradrenaline 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min — VASST trial reduces noradrenaline requirements
  3. Consider hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if vasopressor-refractory (APROCCHSS, ADRENAL)
  4. Reassess fluid responsiveness dynamically (pulse pressure variation, passive leg raise, cardiac output monitor) before further fluid
  5. Inotrope (dobutamine) if cardiac output low or echo shows myocardial dysfunction

{/* ================= 1. ORIENTATION ================= */}
Vasoactive and inotropic agents are drugs that alter vascular tone and/or cardiac function. They are essential in the management of haemodynamic instability during anaesthesia and critical care. Understanding their receptor pharmacology, mechanisms, and clinical applications is fundamental to FRCA and FFICM examinations.

This topic is structured to build from foundations → mechanisms → individual agents → integrated comparison. Begin with the broad classification and receptor science, then explore each agent grouped by clinical role (vasopressors → inotropes/inodilators → vasodilators → salvage therapy), before consolidating with the haemodynamic effects table.

{/* ================= 2. BIG-PICTURE CLASSIFICATION ================= */}
Vasoactive agents can be grouped by their primary mechanism of action:

Catecholamines Adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine Adrenoreceptor agonism Synthetic sympathomimetics Phenylephrine, dobutamine, isoprenaline Selective receptor agonism Phosphodiesterase inhibitors Milrinone, enoximone ↑ cAMP → inodilation Vasopressin analogues Vasopressin, terlipressin V1 receptor agonism Calcium sensitisers Levosimendan ↑ Ca²⁺ sensitivity of troponin C Vasodilators GTN, SNP, hydralazine NO donors / direct smooth muscle relaxation
{/* ================= 3. RECEPTOR FOUNDATIONS ================= */}
Most vasoactive agents act via adrenoreceptors. Understanding receptor subtypes and their downstream effects is essential:

α₁ Vascular smooth muscle Gq → ↑ IP₃/DAG Vasoconstriction α₂ Presynaptic nerve terminals, CNS Gi → ↓ cAMP ↓ NA release, sedation, analgesia β₁ Heart (SA node, myocardium) Gs → ↑ cAMP ↑ HR, ↑ contractility, ↑ conduction β₂ Bronchial, uterine, vascular smooth muscle Bronchodilation, vasodilation, tocolysis β₃ Adipose tissue, bladder Lipolysis, bladder relaxation
{/* Molecular structures support the receptor section */} Subtle structural differences on the catechol ring and amine side-chain determine receptor selectivity, metabolism by COMT/MAO, and lipid solubility.

{/* ================= 4. INOTROPE MECHANISMS ================= */}
Inotropes increase myocardial contractility through several distinct intracellular pathways. The unifying theme is increased availability of, or sensitivity to, intracellular calcium:

↑ cAMP (receptor-mediated) Adrenaline, dobutamine, dopamine, isoprenaline β₁ agonism → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP → PKA → ↑ Ca²⁺ entry ↑ cAMP (enzyme inhibition) PDE III inhibition → ↓ cAMP breakdown → ↑ cAMP → PKA ↑ cAMP (glucagon receptor) Glucagon Glucagon receptor → Gs → ↑ cAMP (bypasses β-receptor) Calcium sensitisation Stabilises Ca²⁺–troponin C complex → ↑ contractile force without ↑ [Ca²⁺]ᵢ Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition Digoxin ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger reversal → ↑ [Ca²⁺]ᵢ Direct Ca²⁺ supplementation Calcium chloride / gluconate ↑ extracellular [Ca²⁺] → ↑ Ca²⁺ available for excitation-contraction coupling
{/* Signalling diagram supports the mechanism table */} {/* Interactive receptor diagram bridges receptors → individual agents */} Use this tool to visualise how receptor activity changes with dose for each agent — a useful bridge between receptor theory and the agent-by-agent profiles below.

{/* ================= 5. INDIVIDUAL AGENTS — VASOPRESSORS ================= */}
Agents whose primary role is to raise systemic vascular resistance and mean arterial pressure, predominantly via α₁ or V₁ receptors.

Primary neurotransmitter at postganglionic sympathetic nerve terminals. Predominantly α₁ agonist with some β₁ activity but minimal β₂ effect.

    Unlike adrenaline, noradrenaline has minimal β₂ effect → no vasodilation, no bronchodilation, no significant hyperglycaemia or hypokalaemia.

Synthetic pure α₁ agonist. No β-receptor activity. Causes predictable vasoconstriction without direct cardiac stimulation. Reflex bradycardia is common.

  • Predominantly indirect sympathomimetic with direct α₁ agonism
  • Bolus: 0.5–1 mg IV. Infusion: 0.5–5 mg/hr
  • Acts as a false transmitter — displaces NA but is a weaker agonist → tachyphylaxis
  • Longer acting than phenylephrine (15–20 min). Causes reflex bradycardia
Vasopressin (ADH) is a nonapeptide hormone acting on V₁ (vascular smooth muscle → vasoconstriction), V₂ (collecting duct → water reabsorption), and V₃/V1b (anterior pituitary → ACTH release) receptors.

    Terlipressin is a synthetic vasopressin analogue with greater V₁ selectivity. Used in variceal haemorrhage (splanchnic vasoconstriction) and hepatorenal syndrome (CONFIRM trial 2021).

{/* ================= 6. INOPRESSOR (bridge) ================= */}
Adrenaline straddles the vasopressor/inotrope categories

references.excerpt: For adults with septic shock on vasopressors, we recommend an initial target mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 65 mm Hg over higher MAP targets. For adults with septic shock, we recommend norepinephrine as the first-line agent over other vasopressors. For adults with septic shock on norepinephrine with inadequate MAP, we suggest adding vasopressin instead of escalating the dose of norepinephrine. Vasopressin is usually commenced when the dose of norepinephrine is in the range of 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min.

entries.text:
# Antiarrhythmic Drugs Vaughan-Williams classification, Na⁺/K⁺/Ca²⁺ channel blockers, β-blockers, amiodarone, adenosine, and pro-arrhythmic risk Step-by-step reasoning Classify the patient: structural heart disease (ischaemic cardiomyopathy, reduced LVEF) — not a 'normal heart' AF case. Recall the CAST trial: class Ic agents (flecainide, encainide) increase mortality post-MI through pro-arrhythmia. Flecainide is contraindicated here. Filter the safe options: amiodarone (class III with all-class activity, safe in structural heart disease) or digoxin (rate control, useful in HFrEF). Pick the goal: rhythm control with amiodarone IV (300 mg over 1 h, then 900 mg over 23 h via central line); rate control with digoxin if rhythm strategy fails or is inappropriate. Plan monitoring: continuous ECG (QT and rhythm), electrolytes (K⁺ >4.0, Mg²⁺ >1.0), thyroid/LFT baseline before amiodarone, and document long-term thyroid/lung/liver surveillance. Common traps Using flecainide because 'AF without WPW' — forgetting the structural-heart-disease exclusion. Loading amiodarone peripherally beyond brief use — thrombophlebitis. Forgetting that amiodarone potentiates warfarin and digoxin. case_bank.title: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting
case_bank.text:
Case: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting (Cardiovascular, Advanced)
Patient: A young adult admitted with prolonged vomiting receives ondansetron and a macrolide. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and magnesium 0.5 mmol/L.
Presentation: The monitor shows a broad, twisting polymorphic tachycardia that self-terminates. QTc before the event was 510 ms.
Stage 1 — Explain the mechanism
  Question: Why has this rhythm occurred?
  Model answer: Phase 3 repolarisation depends mainly on the delayed rectifier potassium currents IKr and IKs; blocking IKr prolongs the action potential and the QT interval.
  Model answer: Prolonged repolarisation permits reactivation of L-type calcium current, producing early afterdepolarisations and triggered beats.
  Model answer: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia reduce repolarisation reserve, so drug effects that are usually tolerated become arrhythmogenic.
Stage 2 — Treat the arrhythmia
  Question: What is your immediate management?
  Model answer: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate even if magnesium is normal, correct potassium towards the upper normal range and stop all QT-prolonging drugs.
  Model answer: Treat sustained or pulseless episodes with defibrillation and follow advanced life support; consider overdrive pacing or isoprenaline for pause-dependent, bradycardia-related torsades.
  Model answer: Avoid class Ia and class III antiarrhythmics, which prolong repolarisation further.
Stage 3 — Prevent recurrence
  Question: What ongoing plan is needed?
  Model answer: Review every drug on the chart against a QT-prolonging list, including antiemetics, antipsychotics, macrolides, antifungals and methadone.
  Model answer: Monitor electrolytes and QTc repeatedly, especially with ongoing vomiting, diuretics or renal replacement.
  Model answer: Refer for cardiology assessment and family screening if congenital long QT syndrome is suspected.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: The cardiac action potential's plateau and repolarisation reflect a balance between inward calcium and outward potassium currents. Repolarisation reserve is the redundancy in this system; congenital channel variants, electrolyte depletion, bradycardia and multiple IKr-blocking drugs erode it additively. Torsades de pointes is the clinical expression of triggered activity on a prolonged, heterogeneous repolarisation substrate.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarisations and is first-line even with normal levels. Keep potassium above 4.5 mmol/L in this setting, remove precipitating drugs, and maintain a heart rate that shortens repolarisation when torsades is pause-dependent. Continuous ECG monitoring with QTc measurement, defibrillator availability and a documented drug-avoidance list should follow the patient.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not give amiodarone reflexively for a broad-complex tachycardia that is torsades. Distinguish polymorphic from monomorphic VT, and name IKr blockade and early afterdepolarisations rather than saying 'the QT was long'.
Take-home: Torsades reflects lost repolarisation reserve: give magnesium, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs and avoid further class III agents.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: cardiac electrophysiology (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkm013); Vaughan Williams classification (https://doi.org/10.1016/0306-039X(75)90019-7)

# Anticoagulant Pharmacology Heparins (UFH/LMWH), warfarin, DOACs, HIT, reversal agents, and perioperative/neuraxial management Step-by-step reasoning Stratify thrombotic risk: mechanical mitral valve = HIGH risk (annual thromboembolism without anticoagulation ~22%). Bridging is indicated. Stop warfarin 5 days pre-op; check INR daily from day −3. Start therapeutic LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD or 1.5 mg/kg OD) when INR falls below the target range — typically from day −3. Give the last LMWH dose 24 h pre-op (BD regimen: omit evening dose 24 h before; OD regimen: give half-dose 24 h before). On the day of surgery confirm INR <1.5 (or <1.3 for neuraxial). If INR still high, give IV vitamin K 1–2 mg or 4-factor PCC if urgent. Restart LMWH 24 h post-op (48–72 h for high bleeding risk) and warfarin on the evening of surgery; continue LMWH until INR is therapeutic on two consecutive days. Common traps Bridging low-risk AF patients — modern guidance (BRIDGE trial) shows bridging causes more bleeding without thrombotic benefit. Forgetting that mechanical valves cannot use DOACs as a substitute. Resuming full-dose LMWH too early after major abdominal surgery — risk of bleeding. unfractionated heparin (UFH) low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH) direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) , and adjunctive agents. The Coagulation Cascade — Drug Targets Mechanism of Action antithrombin III (AT-III) , accelerating its inhibition of serine proteases (thrombin, Xa, IXa, XIa, XIIa) by ~1,000-fold. UFH requires a minimum chain length of 18 saccharides to form the ternary heparin–AT-III–thrombin complex. LMWH chains are shorter, so they predominantly inhibit Factor Xa with less anti-IIa activity. UFH vs LMWH Comparison Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) Type I (Non-immune) Mild, transient ↓ platelets (days 1–4). Non-immune, direct heparin effect. Benign — no treatment change needed. Type II (Immune-mediated) . ↓ Platelets >50% from baseline. Stop all heparin . Switch to argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux. Protamine Reversal 1 mg per 100 IU UFH . Only ~60% effective for LMWH. Side effects: hypotension, bradycardia, anaphylaxis (fish allergy, prior protamine/insulin exposure), pulmonary hypertension. II, VII, IX, X Non-urgent (INR 5–9, no bleeding): Withhold ± oral vitamin K 1–2 mg Urgent (significant bleeding): IV vitamin K 5 mg + PCC 25–50 IU/kg PCC immediately + IV vitamin K 5 mg. FFP second-line. Warfarin in Pregnancy Other Anticoagulants Synthetic pentasaccharide — binds AT-III, selective Factor Xa only. SC, 100% bioavail, t½ 17–21 h. No HIT risk. Not reversed by protamine. Direct thrombin inhibitor (hirudin analogue). IV only. t½ 25 min. Used for PCI in HIT. No specific reversal. Direct thrombin inhibitor. IV. t½ 45 min. Hepatic metabolism — preferred in renal failure. First-line for HIT in renal impairment. Perioperative & Neuraxial Considerations Stop Before Neuraxial Restart After Based on AAGBI/ESRA/ASRA guidelines. Peri-operative bridging for a patient on warfarin with a mechanical mitral valve This is a high-risk indication that requires bridging. Stop warfarin 5 days pre-op, start therapeutic LMWH when INR drops below the target range, omit LMWH 24 h pre-op, confirm INR <1.5 on the day, and resume LMWH 24 h post-op alongside warfarin until INR is back in range on two consecutive days. Anticoagulant Pharmacology FRCA Primary & Final — Pharmacology UFH potentiates antithrombin III → inhibits thrombin (IIa) + Xa equally. LMWH predominantly inhibits Xa (shorter chains). HIT Type II is immune-mediated (anti-PF4/heparin IgG) → paradoxical thrombosis. Stop ALL heparin. Use argatroban or bivalirudin. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → ↓ factors II, VII, IX, X. Delayed onset (2–7 days). Reversed by vitamin K + PCC. DOACs directly inhibit thrombin (dabigatran) or Xa (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban). Predictable kinetics, no routine monitoring. Idarucizumab specifically reverses dabigatran. Andexanet alfa reverses Xa inhibitors. PCC is used when specific agents are unavailable. Protamine fully reverses UFH (1 mg per 100 IU) but only ~60% reverses LMWH. Side effects: hypotension, anaphylaxis, pulmonary HTN. Warfarin is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy in T1). Heparin does not cross the placenta. Neuraxial timing: LMWH prophylactic 12 h / therapeutic 24 h; DOACs 48–72 h; warfarin INR ≤1.4. Bridging Anticoagulation — Decision Pathway What are the perioperative timing recommendations for stopping common anticoagulants? Warfarin — stop 5 days before; bridge with LMWH if high thrombotic risk (mechanical valve, recent VTE). DOACs — stop 24–48 h if normal renal function (longer for dabigatran in CKD: 2–4 days). LMWH — prophylactic 12 h, treatment 24 h before neuraxial. Aspirin — usually continued for high cardiovascular risk except neurosurgery/posterior chamber eye. Clopidogrel — 7 days; ticagrelor — 5 days. AAGBI/RCoA regional anaesthesia and antithrombotic guidelines should be followed. How are warfarin, heparin, dabigatran and rivaroxaban reversed? Warfarin — vitamin K 5–10 mg IV (24 h to act) + 4-factor PCC (Beriplex) 25–50 IU/kg for life-threatening bleeding (immediate). Unfractionated heparin — protamine 1 mg per 100 IU (max 50 mg). LMWH — protamine reverses ~60 % of anti-Xa. Dabigatran — idarucizumab 5 g IV (specific antibody). Rivaroxaban/apixaban — andexanet alfa where available; otherwise 4-factor PCC 25–50 IU/kg. Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia: immune-mediated platelet activation by anti-PF4-heparin antibodies, causing thrombocytopenia (>50 % drop) AND paradoxical thrombosis 5–10 days after exposure. 4T score for probability. Stop ALL heparin (including flushes/HIT-coated catheters). Anticoagulate with a non-heparin agent (argatroban, danaparoid, or bivalirudin) — do NOT use platelet transfusion or warfarin acutely (paradoxical worsening). Lifelong avoidance of heparin. Only DOAC with specific reversal agent. Requires acid pH for absorption (avoid PPIs). Dialysable. Once daily dosing. Take with food for optimal absorption. CYP3A4 & P-gp substrate. Twice daily. Safest DOAC in renal impairment. Lowest bleeding risk in ARISTOTLE trial. Once daily. Dose reduce if CrCl 15–50 mL/min or body weight ≤60 kg. A 62-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve (target INR 3.0) requires elective laparotomy for colorectal resection. He is on warfarin only. How do you plan peri-operative anticoagulation? >Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Stratify thrombotic risk: mechanical mitral valve = HIGH risk (annual thromboembolism without anticoagulation ~22%). Bridging is indicated.
  2. Stop warfarin 5 days pre-op; check INR daily from day −3.
  3. Start therapeutic LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD or 1.5 mg/kg OD) when INR falls below the target range — typically from day −3.
  4. Give the last LMWH dose 24 h pre-op (BD regimen: omit evening dose 24 h before; OD regimen: give half-dose 24 h before).
  5. On the day of surgery confirm INR <1.5 (or <1.3 for neuraxial). If INR still high, give IV vitamin K 1–2 mg or 4-factor PCC if urgent.
  6. Restart LMWH 24 h post-op (48–72 h for high bleeding risk) and warfarin on the evening of surgery; continue LMWH until INR is therapeutic on two consecutive days.

Understanding their mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, monitoring, and reversal is essential for safe perioperative and critical care management. This topic covers unfractionated heparin (UFH), low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH), warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), and adjunctive agents.

Anticoagulants act at different points in the coagulation cascade. The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge at Factor Xa, which activates thrombin (Factor IIa) to convert fibrinogen to fibrin.

Heparins bind antithrombin III (AT-III), accelerating its inhibition of serine proteases (thrombin, Xa, IXa, XIa, XIIa) by ~1,000-fold. UFH requires a minimum chain length of 18 saccharides to form the ternary heparin–AT-III–thrombin complex. LMWH chains are shorter, so they predominantly inhibit Factor Xa with less anti-IIa activity.

{heparinComparison.map((row) => ( Type I (Non-immune)

Mild, transient ↓ platelets (days 1–4). Non-immune, direct heparin effect. Benign — no treatment change needed.

Type II (Immune-mediated)

IgG antibodies against heparin–PF4 complexes. Onset days 5–14. Paradoxical thrombosis. ↓ Platelets >50% from baseline. Stop all heparin. Switch to argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux.

Protamine is a polycationic protein (salmon sperm) that binds acidic heparin via ionic bonds. Dose: 1 mg per 100 IU UFH. Only ~60% effective for LMWH. Side effects: hypotension, bradycardia, anaphylaxis (fish allergy, prior protamine/insulin exposure), pulmonary hypertension.

Mechanism

Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), preventing γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S. Onset delayed (2–7 days). Factor VII has shortest t½ (~6 h), so INR rises first.

Pharmacokinetics

Oral bioavailability ~100%. ~99% protein-bound. CYP2C9 (S-warfarin) and CYP3A4 (R-warfarin). t½ 36–42 h. Monitored by INR. Therapeutic range 2.0–3.0 (mechanical valves: 2.5–3.5).

Reversal
Warfarin in Pregnancy

Crosses placenta. Teratogenic in first trimester (warfarin embryopathy: nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses). Use LMWH in T1 and peripartum.

DOACs directly inhibit a single coagulation factor without requiring antithrombin. Predictable PK, fixed dosing, no routine monitoring.

monitor troughs (15–20 mg/L); red man syndrome is histamine-mediated, not allergy Amphotericin B binds ergosterol (fungicidal, broadest spectrum); liposomal form reduces nephrotoxicity Echinocandins inhibit β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase — first-line for invasive candidiasis; IV only Aciclovir is selectively activated by viral thymidine kinase — excellent safety profile due to selective toxicity Rifampicin is a potent CYP inducer — reduces levels of warfarin, OCP, midazolam, ciclosporin MRSA resistance: PBP2a (mecA gene); VRE resistance: D-Ala-D-Lac modification of vancomycin target Dosing meropenem in septic AKI on CVVHDF 1 g loading then 1 g 8-hourly by extended infusion on CVVHDF, with TDM if available. Do not reduce dose for AKI on full-dose CVVHDF. Antimicrobials FRCA Primary / Final / FFICM — Pharmacology Bactericidal vs Bacteriostatic Bactericidal: kills bacteria (β-lactams, aminoglycosides). Bacteriostatic: inhibits growth (macrolides, tetracyclines). Distinction matters in immunosuppression. Time-Dependent Killing Efficacy depends on time above MIC (T>MIC). β-lactams, vancomycin. Optimised by frequent dosing or continuous infusion. Concentration-Dependent Killing Efficacy depends on peak concentration/MIC ratio (Cmax/MIC). Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones. Optimised by high-dose, extended-interval dosing. Post-Antibiotic Effect (PAE) Persistent suppression of bacterial growth after drug levels fall below MIC. Prolonged for aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones. MIC & MBC MIC: minimum inhibitory concentration. MBC: minimum bactericidal concentration. MBC/MIC ratio >4 suggests tolerance. Surgical Prophylaxis Ideally within 60 min of incision (120 min for vancomycin). Repeat if surgery >2 half-lives. Usually single dose. Antibacterials Antifungals Antivirals Enzymatic hydrolysis of the β-lactam ring. Extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) hydrolyse 3rd-gen cephalosporins. Carbapenemases (e.g., NDM-1, KPC) hydrolyse carbapenems. Countered by inhibitors: clavulanate, tazobactam, avibactam. Mutation of the drug target reduces binding. PBP2a in MRSA (mecA gene), altered ribosomal binding sites (macrolide resistance), modified DNA gyrase (quinolone resistance). Active transport of antibiotic out of the cell. Common in Gram-negatives. Contributes to multidrug resistance in Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter. Loss or modification of outer membrane porins (OmpF, OmpC) in Gram-negatives, reducing drug entry. Important for carbapenems and aminoglycosides. VanA/VanB gene clusters modify D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac, reducing vancomycin binding 1000-fold. Responsible for VRE. Augmented Renal Clearance Young, septic patients may have CrCl >130 ml/min, leading to sub-therapeutic levels of renally-cleared drugs. Consider TDM and extended/continuous infusions. Continuous β-Lactam Infusion Maximises T>MIC. Evidence supports continuous or extended infusions of piperacillin/tazobactam and meropenem in critically ill patients. Aminoglycoside Dosing Once-daily (Hartford nomogram) vs multiple daily dosing. ODD maximises Cmax/MIC and reduces nephrotoxicity. Monitor troughs (<1 mg/L for gentamicin). Antifungal Empirical Therapy Echinocandins first-line for invasive candidiasis. Voriconazole first-line for invasive aspergillosis. Consider in patients failing to respond to broad-spectrum antibacterials. Antimicrobials — Class, Mechanism, ICU Pearl The headline drug classes you need to recognise on a viva. When should surgical antibiotic prophylaxis be given? Within 60 min before knife-to-skin (within 120 min for vancomycin or fluoroquinolones — slow infusions). Re-dose intra-operatively if procedure exceeds 2 × antibiotic half-life or blood loss >1500 mL. Single dose usually sufficient; continuing beyond 24 h does not reduce SSI but selects for resistance. Allergy: cefuroxime is safe in penicillin allergy unless anaphylaxis (cross-reactivity <1 %); use clindamycin or teicoplanin if severe. What are the indications for vancomycin therapeutic drug monitoring? Narrow therapeutic index; nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Target AUC₂₄ 400–600 mg·h/L (preferred) or trough 15–20 mg/L for serious infections. Monitor pre-4th dose, daily in unstable renal function, every 3–4 days when stable. Loading dose 25–30 mg/kg (actual body weight, max 3 g) gives faster therapeutic levels. Slow infusion ≥1 g/h reduces red-man syndrome (histamine release). What is the difference between concentration-dependent and time-dependent killing? Concentration-dependent (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole) — efficacy correlates with Cmax/MIC ratio; give large doses at extended intervals (once-daily gentamicin). Time-dependent (β-lactams, vancomycin) — efficacy correlates with time above MIC; give frequent doses or extended/continuous infusion (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam continuous infusion in severe sepsis). Bactericidal, time-dependent killing. Benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, flucloxacillin, piperacillin/tazobactam, co-amoxiclav Narrow (benzylpenicillin) to broad (piperacillin/tazobactam). Flucloxacillin: anti-staphylococcal. Hypersensitivity (0.7–10%), anaphylaxis (0.01–0.05%), seizures at high doses, C. difficile, interstitial nephritis Same mechanism as penicillins (β-lactam ring binds PBPs). Classified by generation (1st–5th) with progressively broader Gram-negative cover. Cefalexin (1st), cefuroxime (2nd), ceftriaxone (3rd), ceftazidime (3rd, anti-pseudomonal), ceftaroline (5th, anti-MRSA) 1st: Gram-positive. 3rd: Gram-negative including CNS penetration. 5th: MRSA. Cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy (~1–2%), biliary sludging (ceftriaxone), C. difficile Broadest-spectrum β-lactams. Resistant to most β-lactamases. Bind PBPs with high affinity. Reserved for resistant organisms. Meropenem, imipenem/cilastatin, ertapenem, doripenem Very broad: Gram-positive, Gram-negative, anaerobes. NOT MRSA. Ertapenem: no Pseudomonas. Erythromycin: potent CYP3A4 inhibitor and prokinetic agent. Bind 30S ribosomal subunit reversibly, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA binding. Bacteriostatic. Broad-spectrum. Photosensitivity, dental staining in children, oesophageal ulceration, teratogenic Bind 50S ribosomal subunit (same site as macrolides). Bacteriostatic. Excellent bone penetration. Gram-positive cocci, anaerobes. Good for bone/joint and dental infections. Strong association with C. difficile colitis. Used in penicillin allergy. Bind 50S subunit at an early stage, preventing formation of the 70S initiation complex. Bacteriostatic. 100% oral bioavailability. Gram-positive only: MRSA, VRE, multi-resistant pneumococci. Thrombocytopenia (monitor FBC weekly), serotonin syndrome (MAO inhibitor), peripheral neuropathy, lactic acidosis (mitochondrial toxicity) Inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling and replication. Bactericidal, concentration-dependent. Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin Cipro: Gram-negatives, Pseudomonas. Levo/Moxi: respiratory pathogens including atypicals. Tendon rupture (especially with steroids), QT prolongation, CNS effects, aortic aneurysm risk, C. difficile Reduced intracellularly to reactive intermediates that damage DNA. Only active in anaerobic/microaerophilic organisms (require low redox potential for activation). Bactericidal. Anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridium), protozoa (Giardia, Entamoeba, Trichomonas). Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, metallic taste, peripheral neuropathy (prolonged use) Inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking transcription. Bactericidal. Potent CYP450 inducer. Mycobacteria (TB), staphylococci (used in combination for prosthetic infections), Legionella. Orange discolouration of body fluids, hepatotoxicity, potent CYP inducer (reduces efficacy of warfarin, OCP, steroids, antiretrovirals) Sequential blockade of folate synthesis: sulfonamides inhibit dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. Bacteriostatic individually, bactericidal in combination. Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole), trimethoprim alone UTIs, PCP (Pneumocystis jirovecii), Nocardia, Stenotrophomonas. Hyperkalaemia (trimethoprim blocks ENaC), bone marrow suppression, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (sulfonamides), renal impairment Bind lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the Gram-negative outer membrane, disrupting membrane integrity. Bactericidal. Last-resort agents for MDR Gram-negatives. MDR Gram-negatives: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Klebsiella (including carbapenem-resistant). Nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting), neurotoxicity, bronchospasm (nebulised) Lipopeptide that inserts into the Gram-positive cell membrane, forming ion channels causing depolarisation. Rapidly bactericidal, concentration-dependent. Gram-positive: MRSA, VRE. NOT for pneumonia (inactivated by surfactant). Myopathy (monitor CK weekly), eosinophilic pneumonia Bind ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, creating pores that cause leakage of intracellular contents. Fungicidal. Amphotericin B (deoxycholate and liposomal), nystatin Broadest spectrum: Candida, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus, Mucor. Nystatin: topical only. Nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting — distal RTA, Mg²⁺/K⁺ wasting), rigors, hypotension. Liposomal formulation reduces toxicity. Pre-treat with paracetamol/hydrocortisone. IV only (not absorbed orally). Lipid formulations improve therapeutic index. Inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis. Fungistatic (fluconazole) or fungicidal (voriconazole vs Aspergillus). Fluconazole, voriconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole Fluconazole: Candida (not C. krusei or C. glabrata), Cryptococcus. Voriconazole: Aspergillus (first-line). Posaconazole: Mucor. Hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, visual disturbances (voriconazole), potent CYP inhibitors (drug interactions with midazolam, ciclosporin, warfarin). Good oral bioavailability. Voriconazole: non-linear PK, TDM recommended (trough 1–5.5 mg/L). Inhibit β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase, disrupting cell wall synthesis. Fungicidal against Candida, fungistatic against Aspergillus. Candida (including azole-resistant species), Aspergillus. NOT Cryptococcus or Mucor. Well tolerated. Histamine-like reactions, hepatotoxicity (rare). No renal dose adjustment. IV only. Not absorbed orally. Highly protein-bound. Hepatic metabolism. Prodrug converted to 5-fluorouracil inside fungal cells, inhibiting DNA and RNA synthesis. Always used in combination (prevents resistance). Cryptococcal meningitis (with amphotericin B), some Candida. Bone marrow suppression (monitor FBC), hepatotoxicity. TDM: peak 25–50 mg/L. Excellent oral bioavailability. Good CSF penetration. Inhibits squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis at an earlier step than azoles. Fungicidal. Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum). First-line for onychomycosis. GI upset, taste disturbance, hepatotoxicity (rare), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (rare). Oral, accumulates in skin/nails. Long half-life in tissues. Phosphorylated intracellularly to active triphosphate form. Incorporated into viral DNA/RNA, causing chain termination. Require viral or cellular kinases for activation. Aciclovir (HSV, VZV), ganciclovir (CMV), tenofovir (HIV, HBV), entecavir (HBV), sofosbuvir (HCV), remdesivir (SARS-CoV-2) Aciclovir: HSV, VZV (activated by viral thymidine kinase — selective toxicity). Ganciclovir: CMV. Aciclovir: crystalluria (hydrate well), renal impairment. Ganciclovir: myelosuppression (neutropenia). Tenofovir: renal tubular toxicity, osteoporosis. Block neuraminidase on the influenza viral surface, preventing release of new virions from infected cells. Must be given early (within 48h of symptoms). GI upset (oseltamivir), bronchospasm (zanamivir — avoid in asthma). Inhibit viral proteases required for cleavage of polyprotein precursors into functional viral proteins. Used in HIV, HCV, and COVID-19. HIV: ritonavir, darunavir, atazanavir. HCV: simeprevir. COVID-19: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) HIV (combined in ART regimens), HCV (direct-acting antivirals), SARS-CoV-2. Ritonavir: potent CYP3A4 inhibitor (used as PK booster), lipodystrophy, dyslipidaemia, hepatotoxicity. Bind directly to HIV reverse transcriptase at an allosteric site, causing conformational change. Do not require phosphorylation. Efavirenz: CNS effects (vivid dreams, dizziness), rash. Nevirapine: hepatotoxicity, Stevens-Johnson. CYP inducers. Block HIV integrase, preventing insertion of viral DNA into the host genome. Now first-line in most HIV ART regimens. Generally well tolerated. Dolutegravir: insomnia, weight gain, neural tube defects (early pregnancy — now considered low risk). Target specific HCV proteins: NS3/4A protease, NS5A, NS5B polymerase. Introduction

A thorough understanding of antimicrobial pharmacology is essential for anaesthetists and intensivists. Surgical prophylaxis, treatment of sepsis, and management of hospital-acquired infections all require knowledge of mechanisms of action, spectrum, pharmacokinetics, and adverse effects. This topic covers the major classes of antibacterials, antifungals, and antivirals relevant to the FRCA and FFICM examinations.

Standard combination: dexamethasone (induction) + ondansetron (end of surgery) + cyclizine on the ward; TIVA + regional analgesia further halves rebound risk. Rescue with a drug from a class not already used. Drug interactions and the QTc Build prophylaxis around dexamethasone + cyclizine ± aprepitant. Avoid droperidol; use ondansetron only at the lowest dose with ECG monitoring. Always check the cumulative QTc-prolonging burden in patients on methadone, antipsychotics or amiodarone. Four risk factors: female sex, non-smoker, history of PONV/motion sickness, postoperative opioid use. Each scores 1; predicted risk 10/20/40/60/80 %. Score 0–1: no prophylaxis or 1 agent. Score 2: 2 agents. Score 3–4: 3 agents + consider TIVA + avoid N₂O. Use drugs from different classes (5-HT3 antagonist + steroid + droperidol or cyclizine). Compare the mechanisms of common antiemetics. Ondansetron — 5-HT3 antagonist at vagal afferents and chemoreceptor trigger zone; QT prolongation. Dexamethasone — anti-inflammatory and central effects; given at induction (delayed onset 1–2 h, duration 24 h). Cyclizine — H1 antihistamine + anticholinergic; useful for opioid- and motion-related PONV; tachycardia limits use in cardiac disease. Droperidol — D2 antagonist; effective but QT prolongation black-box. Aprepitant — NK1 antagonist; long-acting (24 h). Propofol TIVA reduces PONV incidence by ~25 % compared with volatile anaesthesia (number needed to treat ~6 for high-risk patients). Mechanism is multifactorial — antiemetic action of propofol at low concentrations and avoidance of emetogenic volatiles. case_bank.title: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting
case_bank.text:
Case: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting (Cardiovascular, Advanced)
Patient: A young adult admitted with prolonged vomiting receives ondansetron and a macrolide. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and magnesium 0.5 mmol/L.
Presentation: The monitor shows a broad, twisting polymorphic tachycardia that self-terminates. QTc before the event was 510 ms.
Stage 1 — Explain the mechanism
  Question: Why has this rhythm occurred?
  Model answer: Phase 3 repolarisation depends mainly on the delayed rectifier potassium currents IKr and IKs; blocking IKr prolongs the action potential and the QT interval.
  Model answer: Prolonged repolarisation permits reactivation of L-type calcium current, producing early afterdepolarisations and triggered beats.
  Model answer: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia reduce repolarisation reserve, so drug effects that are usually tolerated become arrhythmogenic.
Stage 2 — Treat the arrhythmia
  Question: What is your immediate management?
  Model answer: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate even if magnesium is normal, correct potassium towards the upper normal range and stop all QT-prolonging drugs.
  Model answer: Treat sustained or pulseless episodes with defibrillation and follow advanced life support; consider overdrive pacing or isoprenaline for pause-dependent, bradycardia-related torsades.
  Model answer: Avoid class Ia and class III antiarrhythmics, which prolong repolarisation further.
Stage 3 — Prevent recurrence
  Question: What ongoing plan is needed?
  Model answer: Review every drug on the chart against a QT-prolonging list, including antiemetics, antipsychotics, macrolides, antifungals and methadone.
  Model answer: Monitor electrolytes and QTc repeatedly, especially with ongoing vomiting, diuretics or renal replacement.
  Model answer: Refer for cardiology assessment and family screening if congenital long QT syndrome is suspected.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: The cardiac action potential's plateau and repolarisation reflect a balance between inward calcium and outward potassium currents. Repolarisation reserve is the redundancy in this system; congenital channel variants, electrolyte depletion, bradycardia and multiple IKr-blocking drugs erode it additively. Torsades de pointes is the clinical expression of triggered activity on a prolonged, heterogeneous repolarisation substrate.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarisations and is first-line even with normal levels. Keep potassium above 4.5 mmol/L in this setting, remove precipitating drugs, and maintain a heart rate that shortens repolarisation when torsades is pause-dependent. Continuous ECG monitoring with QTc measurement, defibrillator availability and a documented drug-avoidance list should follow the patient.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not give amiodarone reflexively for a broad-complex tachycardia that is torsades. Distinguish polymorphic from monomorphic VT, and name IKr blockade and early afterdepolarisations rather than saying 'the QT was long'.
Take-home: Torsades reflects lost repolarisation reserve: give magnesium, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs and avoid further class III agents.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: cardiac electrophysiology (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkm013); Vaughan Williams classification (https://doi.org/10.1016/0306-039X(75)90019-7)

# Corticosteroids & Endocrine Pharmacology Steroid potency, HPA suppression, perioperative steroid cover, mineralocorticoid effects Step-by-step reasoning Decide if HPA suppression is likely. Prednisolone ≥ 5 mg/day for > 4 weeks → assume axis is suppressed. Convert to hydrocortisone equivalent. 10 mg prednisolone × 4 (potency) = 40 mg hydrocortisone equivalent (her endogenous output is essentially abolished). Stratify the surgical stress. Hemicolectomy = MAJOR surgery (per AAGBI/AOMRC 2020). Continue usual prednisolone 10 mg PO morning of surgery + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction , then 200 mg/24 h infusion (or 50 mg IV 6-hourly) for 24 h. Wean to oral usual dose over 48–72 h. BP, glucose 4-hourly, U&E daily. Watch for refractory hypotension → suspect adrenal crisis. Quick reference (AOMRC 2020) Minor (e.g. cataract): usual dose only. Moderate (e.g. lap chole): 50 mg IV at induction → 25 mg 8-hourly × 24 h. Major (e.g. laparotomy): 100 mg IV at induction → 200 mg/24 h × 24–48 h. Common traps Stopping the patient's usual steroid 'because we'll cover with hydrocortisone' — adds a withdrawal hit on top of the surgical hit. Forgetting that inhaled (high-dose fluticasone), topical, and intra-articular steroids can also suppress the HPA axis. Using dexamethasone for cover — gives no mineralocorticoid effect, doesn't replace cortisol's full action. Assess length of starvation. One missed meal only → no need for VRIII (per CPOC 2021 guidance). Continue basal insulin. Lantus (glargine) at 80% of usual dose the night before. Type 1 patients must never stop basal insulin (DKA within hours). Omit short-acting boluses. Hold Novorapid the morning of surgery while NBM. Check CBG hourly. Target 6–10 mmol/L (acceptable 4–12). Have rescue plan. If CBG > 12 → correction Novorapid (typical correction = 1 unit per 3 mmol above target). If CBG < 4 → 100 mL of 20% dextrose IV. Restart usual regimen with the first meal post-op; check ketones if CBG > 12 mmol/L. When to use VRIII instead Missing > 1 meal, poor diabetes control (HbA1c > 69 mmol/mol), emergency surgery, or established DKA risk. VRIII = Actrapid 50 units in 50 mL 0.9% NaCl, run via dedicated line + glucose-containing maintenance fluid (e.g. 5% dextrose + KCl 20 mmol/L). Stopping Lantus in a type 1 patient → DKA on the table. Running VRIII without a substrate (dextrose-containing fluid) → hypoglycaemia. Forgetting to scan for ketones if hyperglycaemic — euglycaemic DKA is now common with SGLT2 inhibitors (stop 3 days pre-op). (↓ NF-κB, ↓ cytokines, ↓ COX-2, ↓ phospholipase A₂ via lipocortin-1); many side effects come from (gluconeogenesis, Na⁺ retention). A small subset of effects is and acts within minutes. Inhibits thyroid peroxidase (iodination/coupling). Takes 4–6 weeks for full effect. Risk: agranulocytosis Propylthiouracil (PTU) : also inhibits peripheral T₄ → T₃ conversion. Used in thyroid storm and first-trimester pregnancy Lugol's iodine : reduces thyroid vascularity pre-surgery (Wolff-Chaikoff effect). Given 10–14 days preoperatively : T₄ replacement in hypothyroidism. Long half-life (~7 days) — can omit on day of surgery Steroid cover for major surgery in a chronic prednisolone user Continue her usual prednisolone, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction and 200 mg/24 h for 24 h, then wean back to her baseline dose over 48–72 h. Monitor BP and glucose closely; treat any refractory hypotension as an Addisonian crisis with a 100 mg bolus. Managing a patient with type 1 diabetes for elective surgery Reduce Lantus to 80% the night before, omit morning Novorapid, place him first on the list, and check CBG hourly with a target 6–10 mmol/L. No VRIII needed for one missed meal. Treat hypoglycaemia with 20% dextrose; restart usual insulin with the first post-op meal. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg Type 1 diabetes: NEVER stop basal insulin (DKA risk). Continue Lantus at 80% the night before surgery Carbimazole inhibits thyroid peroxidase; takes 4–6 weeks. PTU also blocks peripheral T₄→T₃. Risk: agranulocytosis SGLT2 inhibitors → euglycaemic DKA. Stop 3 days before elective surgery (CPOC 2021) Corticosteroid Pharmacodynamics Steroid potency & duration Perioperative Steroid Cover (AAGBI/AOMRC 2020) Insulin Preparations Thyroid Pharmacology What is the equivalent dose conversion between common steroids? Hydrocortisone 20 mg = prednisolone 5 mg = methylprednisolone 4 mg = dexamethasone 0.75 mg. Mineralocorticoid activity: hydrocortisone ++, prednisolone +, methylprednisolone trace, dexamethasone none. For pure glucocorticoid replacement use dexamethasone; for shock/Addisonian crisis use hydrocortisone (mineralocorticoid effect retains Na⁺/water). When is perioperative steroid cover required and what regimen is used? Required for patients on >5 mg prednisolone/day for >3 weeks (HPA suppression). Minor surgery (e.g. hernia): usual oral dose + 25 mg hydrocortisone IV at induction. Moderate surgery (e.g. colectomy): 25 mg at induction + 100 mg/day for 24 h. Major surgery/critically ill: 100 mg at induction + 200 mg/day for 48–72 h then taper. Continue maintenance dose throughout.
