TIVA (total intravenous anaesthesia) is the technique of using intravenous agents exclusively to induce and maintain anaesthesia, avoiding volatile agents. TCI (target-controlled infusion) is a delivery method used during TIVA — a microprocessor-controlled pump uses pharmacokinetic models to calculate infusion rates that achieve and maintain a user-defined target drug concentration. TIVA can be performed without TCI (manual infusion regimens), but TCI provides more precise and titratable drug delivery.
When should I use plasma (Cp) vs effect-site (Ce) targeting?
Plasma targeting achieves the target Cp rapidly, but the effect-site concentration (Ce) lags behind — there is a delay before clinical effect. This mode requires a higher initial Cp target and waiting for equilibration. Effect-site targeting transiently overshoots Cp above the target to drive drug into the effect site faster, resulting in faster onset of clinical effect. Modern practice prefers Ce targeting because it is more intuitive — you target the concentration that produces the clinical effect. However, Ce targeting produces a larger initial Cp overshoot with models that have a low ke0 (e.g., Marsh ke0 0.26 min⁻¹), which can cause more haemodynamic instability. Schnider (ke0 0.456 min⁻¹) has faster equilibration and a smaller overshoot, making it the preferred model for Ce targeting.
Why is Schnider preferred over Marsh in elderly patients?
Marsh is a weight-only model — all compartment volumes and clearances scale linearly with total body weight. In a 78-year-old, 60 kg woman, Marsh would give the same induction bolus as a young 60 kg adult, ignoring age-related reductions in clearance and cardiac output. Schnider incorporates age, weight, height, sex, and lean body mass (LBM). Its central volume (V1) is fixed at 4.27 L regardless of weight, producing a smaller initial bolus and less haemodynamic instability. Schnider also reduces clearance for age, which more accurately reflects elderly pharmacokinetics. For these reasons, the AAGBI/RCoA recommend Schnider as the preferred propofol model for effect-site TCI in UK practice.
What is context-sensitive half-time (CSHT) and why does it matter?
CSHT is the time required for the effect-site concentration to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of a given duration. It matters because it predicts how quickly a patient will recover after a TIVA. For propofol, CSHT increases with infusion duration because the slowly equilibrating peripheral compartment (V3, primarily fat) becomes saturated during long infusions. After stopping the infusion, drug redistributes from V3 back into V1, prolonging elimination: ~10 min after 1 hour, ~25–30 min after 4 hours, and ~40 min after 8 hours. For remifentanil, CSHT remains constant at ~3–4 minutes regardless of duration because it is metabolised by plasma and tissue esterases — this predictable, rapid offset is one of its greatest advantages.
What are typical TCI target concentrations for propofol and remifentanil?
For propofol using Schnider effect-site targeting: induction Ce 4–6 µg/mL; maintenance Ce 3–5 µg/mL for surgical anaesthesia; titrate to BIS 40–60. In elderly patients, start at Ce 2.5–3 µg/mL. For remifentanil using Minto effect-site targeting: analgesia Ce 2–4 ng/mL; surgical anaesthesia (with propofol) Ce 4–8 ng/mL; blunting intubation response Ce 6–10 ng/mL. Co-administration of an opioid reduces propofol requirements by approximately 30% — Eleveld is the only model that explicitly accounts for this interaction.
What is propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) and how is it prevented?
PRIS is a rare but potentially fatal complication of prolonged, high-dose propofol infusion. It is characterised by metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, cardiac failure, renal failure, lipaemia, and hepatomegaly. The mechanism involves mitochondrial respiratory chain inhibition leading to impaired fatty acid oxidation and lactic acidosis. Risk factors include: propofol >4 mg/kg/hr for >48 hours, catecholamine or steroid co-administration, critical illness (particularly neurosurgical or septic patients), and paediatric patients. Prevention: limit propofol to <4 mg/kg/hr in ICU, monitor lactate, CK, and triglycerides daily, and time-limit propofol sedation. Treatment: stop propofol immediately, provide supportive care, and consider renal replacement therapy for refractory metabolic derangement. Switch to alternative sedation (midazolam, dexmedetomidine, or ketamine).
How should TIVA be set up safely to prevent awareness?
Safety measures for TIVA include: (1) Dedicated, reliable IV access with an anti-reflux valve — consider a proximal (antecubital) cannula to minimise dead space. (2) The IV line and pump must be visible and monitored at all times; disconnection = awareness. (3) Processed EEG monitoring (BIS or Entropy) is mandatory when TIVA is combined with neuromuscular blockade — NAP5 identified TIVA + NMB as the highest-risk combination for awareness. (4) Use anti-syphon and anti-reflux valves to prevent gravity free-flow or backflow. (5) Check cannula site frequently — a tissued line is the classic cause of awareness under TIVA. (6) Pair propofol with remifentanil for fast, titratable anaesthesia and give transitional analgesia before stopping remifentanil to prevent hyperalgesic emergence.
What are the Eleveld model advantages over Marsh and Schnider?
Eleveld (published 2018) is a universal pharmacokinetic model that covers the entire age spectrum from neonates to elderly adults, including obese patients. It uses allometric scaling (weight^0.75 for clearances, weight for volumes) which is more physiologically appropriate than the linear scaling used by Marsh. Key advantages: (1) it accounts for age-related maturation of clearance in neonates and infants; (2) it includes an opioid interaction term — when remifentanil is co-administered, the model automatically reduces propofol Ce50 by ~30%; (3) it is validated across a wider population (30 studies, ~1,300 patients) than any previous model. The main limitation is that it is not yet available on all TCI pump platforms — check your pump
How does obesity affect TCI propofol dosing?
Obesity poses challenges for all TCI models. Marsh scales all volumes and clearances linearly with total body weight (TBW) — in obesity, this overestimates V1 and gives excessive induction boluses. Schnider uses lean body mass (LBM) calculated from the James formula, but this formula becomes unreliable at extreme BMI (>35–42) and can even produce negative values. Options for obese patients: (1) use adjusted body weight with Marsh (ABW = IBW + 0.4 × [TBW − IBW]); (2) use Schnider with height-limited LBM input; (3) use Eleveld, which employs allometric scaling and has been validated in obese patients. Regardless of model, all pharmacokinetic predictions are less reliable in extreme obesity, and clinical titration to processed EEG and haemodynamic response is essential.
What is the role of processed EEG monitoring during TIVA?
Processed EEG monitoring (BIS, Entropy, or spectrogram) is essential during TIVA because there is no end-tidal volatile agent concentration to confirm drug delivery. NAP5 (the 5th National Audit Project of the Royal College of Anaesthetists) found that awareness with recall was approximately 5 times more common with TIVA than with volatile-based anaesthesia (1:8,000 vs 1:135,000). The highest-risk group was TIVA combined with neuromuscular blockade. Target BIS 40–60 or Entropy 40–60 for surgical anaesthesia. BIS values <20 indicate burst suppression and excessive depth; values >60 indicate inadequate hypnosis and increased awareness risk. In elderly patients, BIS monitoring is even more critical because pharmacokinetic models may over-predict drug concentrations, leading to excessive depth.

# Pain Medicine
Acute and chronic pain, neuropathic pain, multimodal analgesia, interventions

Pain Medicine: Multimodal, Neuropathic & Cancer | FRCA
Ascending Pathways
Aδ fibres (fast, sharp, myelinated) and C fibres (slow, burning, unmyelinated) → dorsal horn (Rexed laminae I, II, V) → spinothalamic tract → thalamus → somatosensory cortex.
Descending Modulation
Periaqueductal grey (PAG) → rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) → dorsal horn. Serotonergic and noradrenergic inhibition. Gate control theory (Melzack & Wall).
Key Points
Central COX inhibition, serotonergic pathways
1g QDS (max 4g/day). Hepatotoxic in overdose. IV onset 5 min.
COX-1 & COX-2 inhibition
Renal, GI, platelet effects. Avoid post-CABG. Ibuprofen, diclofenac, ketorolac.
α₂δ calcium channel subunit binding
Pregabalin, gabapentin. Neuropathic pain. NICE recommends for post-op. Sedation, dizziness.
NMDA receptor antagonist
Prevents central sensitisation, opioid-sparing. 0.1–0.5 mg/kg/hr infusion. Psychomimetic effects.
Analgesic, opioid-sparing, anxiolytic. Dexmedetomidine: cooperative sedation without respiratory depression.
IV Magnesium
NMDA receptor antagonist, Ca²⁺ channel blocker
30–50 mg/kg bolus then 6–15 mg/kg/hr. Opioid-sparing (20–25%). Monitor for hypotension, muscle weakness.
IV Lidocaine
Na⁺ channel blockade, anti-inflammatory cytokine modulation
1–1.5 mg/kg bolus then 1–2 mg/kg/hr. Abdominal surgery evidence strongest. Monitor for LAST.
Mechanism of Action
Voltage-dependent block of NMDA receptor ion channel (Mg²⁺ plug) — prevents glutamate-mediated central sensitisation and wind-up
L-type and N-type calcium channel antagonism → reduces neurotransmitter release at dorsal horn
Potentiates opioid receptor binding and reduces tolerance development
Anti-inflammatory effects: reduces IL-6, TNF-α, and CRP
Dosing & Monitoring
30–50 mg/kg IV over 15–30 min at induction
6–15 mg/kg/hr intraoperatively
Target serum Mg²⁺:
2–4 mmol/L (therapeutic range)
Deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate. Risk of hypotension, muscle weakness, prolonged NMBA effect
Evidence Summary
Albrecht et al. (2013) — Cochrane Review:
25 RCTs (1461 patients). IV MgSO₄ reduced morphine consumption by ~25% at 24h, reduced pain scores at rest and movement, and decreased PONV. No increase in haemodynamic instability.
De Oliveira et al. (2013) — Meta-analysis:
Perioperative Mg reduced opioid use (mean 10.5 mg morphine equivalents), reduced pain scores at 4–6h and 24h, and decreased shivering.
Murphy et al. (2013):
Demonstrated that Mg potentiates morphine analgesia via attenuation of NMDA-mediated central sensitisation.
Most consistent benefit in orthopaedic, abdominal, and cardiac surgery. Limited evidence for ambulatory surgery.
Mechanisms of Action
Na⁺ channel blockade:
Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels on peripheral and central neurons, reducing ectopic firing and nociceptive transmission
Inhibits neutrophil priming, reduces IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and complement activation. Attenuates the surgical inflammatory response
NMDA antagonism:
Weak antagonism at NMDA receptors — contributes to anti-hyperalgesic effect
Potentiates inhibitory glycine receptors in the dorsal horn
Accelerates return of GI function (anti-ileus effect) — likely via anti-inflammatory mechanism and sympatholysis
Dosing & Safety
1–1.5 mg/kg IV over 10 min at induction
1–2 mg/kg/hr intraoperatively (some protocols continue 24–48h post-op at 0.5–1 mg/kg/hr)
Therapeutic level:
2–5 µg/mL (toxic >5 µg/mL)
LAST risk:
Perioral tingling → tinnitus → seizures → arrhythmia → cardiac arrest. Treat with Intralipid® 20%
Heart block, severe hepatic impairment, concurrent amiodarone, allergy to amide LAs
Weibel et al. (2018) — Cochrane Review:
68 RCTs (4525 patients). IV lidocaine reduced pain scores at 1–4h (low-certainty evidence), reduced opioid consumption, reduced ileus duration, and shortened hospital stay — primarily in open abdominal surgery.
LOLIPOP trial (2024):
Large multicentre RCT (n=562) found no significant benefit of IV lidocaine over placebo for quality of recovery after laparoscopic surgery. Questioned the role in minimally invasive surgery.
Vigneault et al. (2011) — Meta-analysis:
Demonstrated significant reductions in pain, opioid consumption, PONV, ileus, and length of stay in abdominal surgery.
Strongest evidence in open abdominal surgery. Less convincing for laparoscopic, orthopaedic, or breast surgery. ERAS protocols include IV lidocaine as an option when epidural not feasible.
disease in its own right
when it cannot be better explained by another condition (chronic primary pain) — encompassing fibromyalgia, chronic primary low back pain, primary headaches and CRPS. The dominant biological substrate is
central sensitisation / nociplastic pain
: amplified central nervous system processing without ongoing tissue or nerve damage. Genetic predisposition, adverse childhood experiences, sleep disruption, mood disorder and autonomic dysregulation all contribute.
NICE NG193, 2021
) marks a deliberate shift away from pharmacological and procedural management of chronic primary pain toward
supported self-management, exercise, psychological therapy and acupuncture
. Notably, paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, gabapentinoids and benzodiazepines are
recommended for chronic primary pain (excluding established neuropathic pain, which still follows NICE CG173). Antidepressants (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline)
be considered.
Biopsychosocial model — the modern formulation
British Pain Society / FPM Core Standards (2021)
and the
NHS Long Term Plan
. Specialised pain MDTs offer the best functional outcomes for complex, refractory or high-impact chronic pain.
1 — Self-management
Community / online
Patient education, exercise apps, peer-support, NHS "Live Well with Pain" resources.
2 — Primary care
GP, practice physio, social prescriber
Initial assessment, NICE NG193 / CG173 first-line management, screening for red/yellow flags.
3 — Community pain MDT
Pain physician/GPwER, physio, psychologist
Pain Management Programmes (PMPs), assessment for tier-4 referral.
4 — Specialist hospital MDT
Tertiary pain centre
Complex/refractory pain, interventional procedures (radiofrequency, neuromodulation, intrathecal pumps), opioid stewardship clinics.
5 — Highly specialised
Supraregional commissioned centre (NHS England SCS service)
Spinal cord stimulation, intrathecal drug delivery, paediatric chronic pain, complex CRPS, post-amputation pain.
Core MDT membership
Pain physician(s)
(consultant anaesthetist with FPM accreditation, ± neurologist, ± rheumatologist)
Clinical psychologist
trained in CBT / ACT for pain
Specialist physiotherapist
(graded activity, pacing, desensitisation)
Occupational therapist
(functional adaptation, vocational rehab)
Specialist pain nurse
(medication review, opioid taper, self-management coaching)
(deprescribing, complex polypharmacy)
Liaison psychiatry, social worker, peer-support worker as required
Pain Management Programmes (PMPs)
Strongest evidence base of any chronic-pain intervention
— Cochrane 2012 (Williams) and subsequent reviews show medium-effect-size improvements in disability, mood and self-efficacy that
persist at 12 months
, even where pain intensity itself changes little. The aim is restored function, not abolition of pain.
Opioid stewardship
FPM "Opioids Aware"
resource and the
Royal College "Painkillers Don't Exist"
campaign emphasise that long-term opioids are rarely effective for chronic non-cancer pain and carry harms (hyperalgesia, hormonal suppression, falls, dependence). Specialist MDTs increasingly run dedicated opioid-tapering clinics; doses >120 mg oral morphine equivalents per day rarely confer additional benefit and should prompt review.
2016 revised ACR criteria
: Widespread Pain Index (WPI) ≥7 + Symptom Severity Score (SSS) ≥5 (or WPI 4–6 + SSS ≥9) for ≥3 months, with no condition that better explains the pain. The original 1990 tender-point criteria are obsolete.
Mechanism — current evidence
Nociplastic pain
— augmented central pain processing (functional MRI shows enhanced activation of insula, S1/S2, ACC; reduced descending inhibition from PAG/RVM).
substance P
in CSF; reduced serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine signalling.
Evidence of
small-fibre neuropathy
on skin biopsy in ~40% (Üçeyler 2013) — challenges the purely "central" view.
Strong genetic component (heritability ~50%); polymorphisms in catecholamine and serotonin transporter genes.
Frequent comorbidities: IBS, migraine, restless legs, depression, anxiety, sleep disorder.
Best-evidenced management (EULAR 2016)
Aerobic + strengthening exercise
— strongest single evidence (Cochrane Bidonde 2017). Graded, low-impact (swimming, cycling, tai chi).
CBT / ACT
— improves function and mood; effect persists at 12 months.
Multicomponent rehabilitation
(PMP) — recommended for refractory cases.
Pharmacological (selected patients):
amitriptyline 10–50 mg ON, duloxetine 60 mg OD, pregabalin 150–450 mg/day, low-dose naltrexone (emerging — Younger 2013).
NSAIDs (ineffective), opioids (worsen central sensitisation, FDA black-box for tramadol misuse), corticosteroids.
NICE NG206, 2021
; IOM 2015 criteria) by ≥3 months of
debilitating fatigue + post-exertional malaise (PEM) + unrefreshing sleep + cognitive dysfunction or orthostatic intolerance
, after exclusion of alternative diagnoses. Often follows a viral illness; long-COVID overlaps clinically and may share mechanisms.
Mitochondrial / bioenergetic dysfunction
— impaired oxidative phosphorylation, abnormal lactate kinetics on repeat CPET (Snell 2013, Davenport 2019).
— PET imaging shows microglial activation in cingulate, thalamus and midbrain (Nakatomi 2014).
Autonomic dysregulation
— high prevalence of POTS / orthostatic intolerance.
Immune dysregulation
— altered NK-cell function, persistent cytokine signatures (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α).
HPA-axis hypofunction
— mild hypocortisolism in many patients.
Long-COVID has revitalised mechanistic research; significant overlap suggests shared post-viral pathophysiology.
Management (NICE NG206)
Energy management ("pacing")
within an individual energy envelope is the cornerstone —
graded exercise therapy (GET), which NG206 explicitly removed after the PACE trial controversies and patient harm reports.
CBT may be offered to
support coping
, but is no longer presented as curative.
Symptom-targeted treatment: sleep hygiene, low-dose amitriptyline for pain/sleep, postural management for POTS (compression, salt, fludrocortisone).
Avoid: prescribed exercise programmes, "psychogenic" framing, dismissing PEM.
Anaesthetic implications:
heightened sensitivity to opioids and sedatives; risk of post-operative crash; plan day-case carefully; consider regional anaesthesia; warn re: prolonged recovery.
= no identifiable nerve lesion (~90%);
= following identifiable peripheral nerve injury. Female:male ~3–4:1, peak 40–60 yr. Diagnosed clinically using the
Budapest criteria (Harden 2010, IASP-endorsed)
Budapest criteria — all four must be met
Continuing pain disproportionate to any inciting event.
reported in ≥3 of 4 categories: sensory (hyperalgesia, allodynia); vasomotor (temperature/skin colour asymmetry); sudomotor/oedema (sweating, swelling); motor/trophic (weakness, tremor, dystonia, hair/nail/skin changes).
at examination in ≥2 of the same 4 categories.
No alternative diagnosis better explains the signs and symptoms.
Mechanisms — current understanding
neurogenic inflammation (substance P, CGRP, bradykinin), small-fibre denervation, microvascular dysfunction.
early sympathetic dysregulation → vasomotor/sudomotor changes; later sympatho-adrenergic receptor up-regulation.
cortical reorganisation (shrinkage of S1 representation of affected limb — Maihöfner 2003), central sensitisation, altered body schema.
auto-antibodies against β2-adrenergic and M2 muscarinic receptors (Goebel 2011) — basis for IVIG trials.
HLA associations; family clustering reported.
Best-evidenced management (RCP / BPS 2018; Goebel 2018)
Early MDT referral & rehabilitation is the single most important intervention
— outcomes are time-critical (better if treated <6 months).
graded motor imagery (laterality recognition → imagined movement → mirror therapy — Moseley 2004), desensitisation, functional restoration.
CBT, ACT, addressing fear-avoidance and kinesiophobia.
neuropathic agents (amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentinoids); short course of oral steroids in early/inflammatory phase (Christensen 1982); bisphosphonates (zoledronate / pamidronate — Varenna 2013) have RCT support in early CRPS with bone marrow oedema.
Interventional (selected, refractory):
sympathetic blocks (limited evidence — Cochrane O'Connell 2016 found no significant effect);
spinal cord stimulation
NICE TA159 — best-evidenced interventional therapy, sustained benefit at 5 yr (Kemler 2008); ketamine infusion; intrathecal baclofen for CRPS dystonia.
Vitamin C 500 mg/day for 50 days post wrist fracture reduces CRPS incidence (Zollinger 2007; meta-analysis Aïm 2017) — recommended by RCP guideline.
immobilisation, repeat surgery on the affected limb, opioid escalation.
under-treated in around one-third
of patients (the "pain treatment gap"). Modern cancer pain care is mechanism-based, multimodal, integrated with oncology and palliative care, and increasingly involves interventional techniques alongside opioids.
WHO Analgesic Ladder — Revisited (2018 update)
WHO 2018 cancer-pain guideline
moved away from the rigid stepwise progression in favour of
tailoring opioid choice and route to pain severity and mechanism from the outset
. Key updates:
Original 3-step ladder (1986)
Step 1:
Non-opioid (paracetamol, NSAID) ± adjuvant
Step 2:
Weak opioid (codeine, tramadol) ± non-opioid ± adjuvant
Step 3:
Strong opioid (morphine) ± non-opioid ± adjuvant
By the clock, by the mouth, by the ladder, for the individual, attention to detail
Modern modifications
Step 2 increasingly skipped — start
low-dose strong opioid
(morphine 5 mg q4h) for moderate–severe pain (better titration, fewer ceiling effects).
4th step
proposed: interventional techniques (neuraxial, neurolytic blocks, intrathecal delivery, neuromodulation) for refractory pain.
Adjuvants are
not optional add-ons
— they're the cornerstone for neuropathic and bone pain.
Mechanism-based selection: bone (NSAID + bisphosphonate ± radiotherapy), neuropathic (gabapentinoid/TCA/SNRI), visceral (opioid + antispasmodic), inflammatory (steroid).
Breakthrough cancer pain (BTcP)
rescue dose = 1/6 to 1/10 of the 24-h oral morphine equivalent
(immediate-release oral morphine, oxycodone IR or, for incident/predictable pain with rapid onset,
transmucosal/intranasal fentanyl
). If >3–4 rescue doses/day are needed, increase the background dose by ~30–50%.
Opioid Rotation (Switching)
incomplete cross-tolerance
between opioids — different μ-receptor binding, intracellular signalling and active metabolites mean a different opioid often achieves analgesia at a lower equianalgesic dose with a better side-effect profile.
Equianalgesic ratio (oral morphine = 1)
Oral morphine
1 (reference)
Active metabolites M3G (neurotoxic) and M6G (analgesic) accumulate in renal failure.
Oral oxycodone
~1.5–2× more potent
30 mg morphine ≈ 15–20 mg oxycodone. Less histamine release; partial CYP2D6 metabolism.
Oral hydromorphone
~5–7× more potent
Useful in renal impairment; smaller volumes for SC infusion.
Transdermal fentanyl
25 µg/h ≈ 60–90 mg oral morphine/day
Useful for stable pain, dysphagia, bowel obstruction, renal failure. NOT for opioid-naïve or unstable pain.
Transdermal buprenorphine
5 µg/h ≈ ~10–15 mg oral morphine/day
Partial agonist with high receptor affinity; safe in renal impairment; ceiling for respiratory depression.
SC morphine
2× oral morphine
Common in palliative syringe drivers (with anti-emetic ± hyoscine).
Variable (5–15× depending on dose)
NMDA antagonism, no active metabolites — useful in refractory neuropathic pain. Long, unpredictable half-life —
specialist initiation only
Safe rotation principles
Calculate the 24-h oral morphine equivalent dose (OMEDD).
Convert to the equianalgesic dose of the new opioid using a published table.
Reduce by 25–50%
for incomplete cross-tolerance (50% reduction if elderly, frail, renal/hepatic impairment, very high doses).
Provide rescue at 1/6 of the new 24-h dose; titrate up over 2–3 days.
Methadone rotation requires a
different ratio at higher OMEDDs
and is typically done under specialist palliative care supervision, often with admission.
, then rotate to a target opioid with the standard 25–50% incomplete cross-tolerance reduction applied automatically. Use the high-risk toggle for elderly/frail patients, renal/hepatic impairment, very high doses, or patch rotations.
Interventional Techniques — When Opioids Fail
10–20% of cancer-pain patients
have pain refractory to systemic analgesia or develop intolerable side effects. Interventional ("4th-step") techniques can achieve dramatic improvements and reduce systemic opioid burden.
Coeliac plexus block / neurolysis
upper-abdominal visceral pain — particularly
pancreatic cancer
, also gastric, hepatic and biliary malignancy. The coeliac plexus (T5–T12 sympathetic afferents) lies anterolateral to the aorta at L1.
percutaneous posterior (CT- or fluoroscopy-guided, retrocrural or anterocrural), anterior trans-aortic, or
endoscopic ultrasound-guided
(transgastric — increasingly the technique of choice when EUS expertise is available).
Diagnostic block
with local anaesthetic first;
with 50–100% absolute alcohol (or 6% phenol) if effective.
Wong RCT (2004, JAMA) and Cochrane (Arcidiacono 2011) — significant pain reduction and ~40–50% lower opioid requirement vs systemic analgesia alone in pancreatic cancer; possibly improved quality of life. Effect lasts weeks–months.
orthostatic hypotension (sympathetic blockade), diarrhoea (unopposed parasympathetic), back pain, retroperitoneal haemorrhage; rare but devastating
from inadvertent injection into the artery of Adamkiewicz.
Best performed
in pancreatic cancer pain rather than as a last resort — outcomes correlate inversely with disease burden.
Other neurolytic / interventional options by site
Hypogastric plexus block
Pelvic visceral pain (cervical, prostate, rectal cancer).
Ganglion impar block
Perineal / coccygeal pain (rectal, anal, vulval cancer).
Stellate ganglion block
Head/neck/upper-limb sympathetic pain; post-radiation neuropathy.
Intercostal / paravertebral neurolysis
Chest-wall metastases, post-thoracotomy pain in cancer.
Vertebral augmentation (kyphoplasty / vertebroplasty)
Painful vertebral metastases / pathological compression fractures.
Cordotomy (percutaneous cervical)
Unilateral cancer pain below C5 with limited prognosis (e.g. mesothelioma); largely confined to specialist UK centres.
Intrathecal Drug Delivery (IDD) Pumps
~1/300 of the equivalent oral morphine dose
, dramatically reducing systemic side effects.
Indications & evidence
Refractory cancer pain (life expectancy ≥3 months, failed systemic opioids).
Refractory non-cancer pain (chronic spinal pain, FBSS) — more controversial; PACC (Polyanalgesic Consensus Conference) 2017 guidelines.
Smith RCT (2002, J Clin Oncol):
IDD vs comprehensive medical management in cancer pain — better pain control, fewer toxicities, and a 6-month survival benefit (likely from reduced opioid morbidity).
Always preceded by a
(intrathecal bolus, continuous external infusion, or epidural) before permanent implant.
Drugs (PACC 2017 recommendations)
intrathecal morphine, ziconomide, or hydromorphone.
bupivacaine (for incident/somatic pain), clonidine, baclofen (for spasticity-related pain).
oral morphine : IV morphine : epidural morphine : intrathecal morphine ≈
infection / meningitis, catheter migration or kinking, granuloma at catheter tip (especially with high-dose morphine), pump malfunction,
opioid withdrawal or overdose if pump fails
— patients carry a wallet card and need 24/7 access to a specialist centre.
Palliative Care Multidisciplinary Team
"total pain"
(physical, psychological, social, spiritual) demands an MDT response. Early integration of palliative care (Temel NEJM 2010 — early palliative care in metastatic NSCLC improved quality of life
survival) is now a cornerstone of oncology practice.
Palliative care consultant
(medicine of palliative care)
Pain physician
(FPM-accredited anaesthetist) for interventional input
& clinical nurse specialist (CNS)
Specialist palliative care nurse
(community / hospice / hospital)
— complex polypharmacy, syringe-driver compatibility, controlled drug supply
Psychologist / psychiatrist
, social worker, occupational therapist, physiotherapist
Chaplain / spiritual care
, bereavement support
Family / informal carers as central members of the team
Service structure (UK)
Hospital specialist palliative care team
— inpatient referrals, complex symptom control, end-of-life care planning.
Community palliative care
— Macmillan / Marie Curie nurses, GPs, district nurses; supports preferred place of care/death.
— inpatient (symptom control, end-of-life), day units, hospice-at-home.
Anaesthetic / pain interventional clinics
— coeliac plexus, IDD, neuromodulation.
Advance care planning
: ReSPECT process, DNACPR discussions, lasting power of attorney, preferred place of care.
End-of-life care guided by individualised care plans (replaced the discredited Liverpool Care Pathway after Neuberger 2013).
failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS)
with predominant radicular leg pain (PROCESS trial, Kumar 2007),
complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
, refractory angina, and painful diabetic neuropathy (SENZA-PDN, Petersen 2021). Newer waveforms — 10 kHz high-frequency (SENZA-RCT, Kapural 2015), burst (DeRidder), and closed-loop ECAP-controlled (Mekhail 2020) — provide sub-perception analgesia without paraesthesia.
System components
Epidural lead
— 8 or 16 cylindrical contacts (percutaneous) or paddle (surgical laminotomy, lower migration risk)
sutured to supraspinous fascia at the entry level
Tunnelled extension
wires running subcutaneously to the IPG pocket
Implantable pulse generator (IPG)
— primary-cell or rechargeable Li-ion, sited in upper buttock, flank, or lower abdomen
Patient and clinician programmers
via wireless telemetry
Indications & level of evidence
FBSS with neuropathic leg pain (Level I)
CRPS type I/II (Level I — Kemler NEJM 2000)
Painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy (Level I — SENZA-PDN)
Refractory angina pectoris (Level II)
Critical limb ischaemia (selected, Level II)
Post-amputation / post-herpetic neuralgia (Level III)
Mandatory trial:
5–10 day percutaneous trial — >50 % pain reduction
functional improvement before permanent implant
Lead targets
Low back / lower limb:
tip at T8–T10 (T9 sweet spot for FBSS)
Upper limb:
T1–T2 left-sided
Pelvic / perineal pain:
conus or DRG (T12–S1)
Tuohy puncture two levels below the target; loss-of-resistance to
(air risks pneumocephalus and patchy stimulation)
Contraindications & risks
active sepsis, untreated coagulopathy, inability to consent or operate device, untreated psychological comorbidity (mandatory pre-implant psychology assessment)
immunosuppression, anticipated whole-body MRI need (most modern systems are MR-conditional), demand pacemaker / ICD (programmer interaction)
lead migration (most common, 13–22 %), infection (3–6 %), epidural haematoma, dural puncture & CSF leak, lead fracture, IPG pocket pain, loss of efficacy, hardware failure
Anaesthesia for SCS Implantation
local anaesthesia with conscious sedation
, because intra-operative paraesthesia mapping requires a co-operative, communicating patient (paraesthesia–pain overlap is the historical predictor of long-term success, although high-frequency systems may be placed asleep with anatomical landmarks alone). The IPG pocket and tunnelling are usually performed under deeper sedation or short GA after lead position is confirmed.

# Obstetric Anaesthesia
Caesarean section, epidural labour analgesia, high-risk obstetrics, PPH

= [ [ "What is obstetric anaesthesia?", "Obstetric anaesthesia is the subspecialty providing pain relief and anaesthesia for labour, caesarean section, instrumental delivery and pregnancy-related surgery. It encompasses labour epidurals, spinal and combined spinal–epidural (CSE) anaesthesia for caesarean section, general anaesthesia for category 1 emergencies, management of pregnancy-related physiological change, and care of high-risk obstetric patients (pre-eclampsia, placenta accreta, haemorrhage, cardiac disease).", ], [ "How does a labour epidural work?", "A 16–18 G Tuohy needle is sited at L3/4 or L4/5 using loss-of-resistance to saline. A multi-orifice catheter is threaded 4–5 cm into the epidural space. A test dose (3 ml 2% lidocaine + adrenaline) is given to exclude intravascular or intrathecal placement, followed by a low-dose bolus (e.g. 15 ml 0.1% levobupivacaine + 2 µg/ml fentanyl). Maintenance is via patient-controlled epidural analgesia (PCEA) or programmed intermittent epidural bolus (PIEB), which gives better analgesia and lower motor block than continuous infusion.", ], [ "What is the difference between an epidural and a spinal for childbirth?", "A labour epidural uses a catheter to titrate dilute local anaesthetic for hours of analgesia, preserving motor power so the mother can push. A spinal is a single intrathecal injection of concentrated heavy bupivacaine 0.5% (2.2–2.5 ml + fentanyl 15 µg + diamorphine 300 µg) used for caesarean section — it produces a dense, rapid block to T4 lasting 2–3 hours but is not used for labour analgesia. A combined spinal–epidural (CSE) gives the rapid onset of a spinal with the titratability of an epidural catheter.", ], [ "Are labour epidurals safe and what are the risks?", "Epidurals are very safe in modern UK obstetric practice. Common side effects: hypotension (~10%), shivering, pruritus (opioid-related), incomplete block (~10%), need for top-up. Serious complications from NAP3 (RCoA, 2009): permanent neurological injury 1:80,000–1:320,000, epidural haematoma 1:168,000, epidural abscess 1:145,000, accidental dural puncture 1% with PDPH in ~70% of those. Maternal mortality directly attributable to neuraxial anaesthesia is
Step-by-step reasoning
Pre-induction in <10 min: 30° left tilt or manual displacement, pre-oxygenate to FeO₂ >0.9 (3 min or 8 vital capacity breaths), aspiration prophylaxis (Na citrate 0.3 M 30 mL ± ranitidine/metoclopramide if time)
RSI with thiopentone 5–7 mg/kg or propofol 2 mg/kg + suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg (TBW); cricoid pressure (per local policy)
Use videolaryngoscopy first if available (OAA/DAS); have plan B (2nd-generation SAD) and plan C (FONA) ready
Maintain with sevoflurane 1 MAC + 50% N₂O until delivery, then deepen and add opioid; uterotonics: oxytocin 5 IU slow bolus then 30 IU/500 mL infusion (RCOG/MBRRACE)
Awareness mitigation: avoid muscle relaxant overdose without depth monitoring; document ABCDE and post-op visit; NAP5 highlights obstetric GA awareness risk
Common traps
Hypotension from aortocaval compression — left tilt mandatory
High-pressure oxytocin bolus causing hypotension/ischaemia — give slowly
Failing to plan extubation: awake, head-up, suction, anti-emetics
and the
obstetric general anaesthesia guideline; airway / failed-intubation incidence and maternal mortality data from
Anaesthetic Implication
CO ↑40% (↑SV & HR), SVR ↓, aortocaval compression from ~20 wk
Left lateral tilt 15°; rapid hypotension with neuraxial; supine hypotensive syndrome
FRC ↓20% (diaphragmatic splinting), O₂ consumption ↑20%, MV ↑50% (driven by ↑V
, RR ~unchanged)
Rapid desaturation on apnoea;
compensated respiratory alkalosis
— PaCO₂ ~4.0 kPa, HCO₃⁻ ~20 mmol/L, pH ~7.44 (target normocapnia for pregnant baseline, not 5.3 kPa)
Mucosal oedema, capillary engorgement, full dentition, breast enlargement
Higher Mallampati grade, smaller ETT (6.0–7.0), short-handle laryngoscope; failed intubation ~1:300
Reduced LOS tone (progesterone), gastric emptying preserved in pregnancy but
delayed in labour/with opioids
, ↑gastric acid
Treat any pregnant woman ≥16–18 wk as
at risk of aspiration
: aspiration prophylaxis (sodium citrate 0.3 M 30 mL ± H₂-blocker / metoclopramide) and RSI for GA caesarean
Plasma vol ↑45% > RBC ↑20% → dilutional anaemia. Hypercoagulable: ↑fibrinogen, ↑factors VII/VIII/X, ↓protein S, ↓fibrinolysis. Physiological leucocytosis.
VTE prophylaxis throughout pregnancy and 6 wk post-partum; raised WCC alone does not imply infection
Renal / Hepatic
GFR ↑50% (↓urea, ↓creatinine — "normal" Cr in pregnancy <75 µmol/L). ↓Albumin → ↑free fraction of bound drugs. ALP ↑ (placental).
Renally cleared drugs (e.g. magnesium, low-MW heparins) cleared faster; "normal" adult Cr may signal AKI in pregnancy
Plasma cholinesterase activity ↓25–30%
but Vd ↑ → suxamethonium duration
clinically unchanged
. ↓MAC ~30%. ↑Sensitivity to LA (~30%).
Standard sux dose (1.5 mg/kg) remains effective; reduce LA neuraxial doses; risk of awareness if MAC mis-targeted
Engorged epidural veins (↓epidural space volume), ↓CSF volume, ↑progesterone & β-endorphins
Lower spinal/epidural doses (~30–40% reduction), higher intravascular catheter / bloody tap risk
Spinal (Gold Standard)
Heavy bupivacaine 0.5% 2.2–2.6 ml + fentanyl 15 µg + diamorphine 0.3 mg. Target block T4. Left lateral tilt 15°. Phenylephrine infusion to prevent hypotension.
General Anaesthesia
Reserved for failed/contraindicated neuraxial, time-critical Cat 1, or maternal refusal. RSI with cricoid pressure. Significant airway and aspiration risk — failed intubation ~1:300, awareness 1:670 (NAP5).
), with most units aiming for <15 min. GA is chosen when there is no functioning epidural and there is insufficient time for spinal, when neuraxial is contraindicated (coagulopathy, sepsis at site, severe maternal cardiac disease, refusal), or when neuraxial has failed. The
failed-intubation algorithm and
reports emphasise team-based preparation and meticulous airway management.
1 · Preparation (in parallel with transfer)
Call for senior help; declare Cat 1; brief team (WHO, allergies, weight, airway).
Two large-bore IVs, group & save / crossmatch, FBC, coag, point-of-care Hb/lactate.
Aspiration prophylaxis:
30 ml 0.3M sodium citrate PO
, ranitidine 50 mg IV (or omeprazole 40 mg IV), metoclopramide 10 mg IV if time allows.
Difficult-airway trolley, videolaryngoscope, second-generation SAD, bougie, smaller ETTs (6.0–6.5).
Pre-drawn drug tray: induction agent, sux, phenylephrine 100 µg/ml, oxytocin 5 IU, ephedrine, atropine, magnesium, antibiotic.
Position: 15° left lateral tilt or manual uterine displacement, ramped (HELP) position for obese patients.
2 · Pre-oxygenation
Tight-fitting mask, 100% O₂ for 3 min OR 8 vital-capacity breaths if extreme urgency. Target end-tidal O₂ >90%.
as adjunct (does not replace standard pre-ox in obstetrics; evidence still emerging — OptimISE trial).
Surgeon scrubbed, prepped and draped
induction — knife on skin only after intubation confirmed.
3 · Induction (RSI)
Induction agent:
thiopentone 5–7 mg/kg
propofol 2–2.5 mg/kg
(see evidence section below).
Neuromuscular blocker:
suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg
(use actual body weight);
rocuronium 1.0–1.2 mg/kg
with sugammadex 16 mg/kg available is an accepted alternative (faster intubating conditions, longer duration; useful if sux contraindicated).
Cricoid pressure: 10 N awake → 30 N at loss of consciousness; release if view is poor or if vomiting occurs.
Cuffed ETT 6.5–7.0 (mucosal oedema), confirm with ETCO₂ and bilateral auscultation.
Follow DAS obstetric failed-intubation algorithm; declare early, prioritise oxygenation, decide whether to wake or proceed based on maternal/fetal status.
4 · Maintenance & intra-operative targets
O₂/air (FiO₂ 0.5) + volatile, OR TIVA (see below).
Target MAC:
remember pregnancy ↓ MAC by ~30%.
Maintain normocapnia (ETCO₂ ~4.0 kPa — pregnant baseline), normothermia, normotension.

(NAP5: obstetric GA is highest awareness-risk population).
Phenylephrine infusion 25–50 µg/min titrated to baseline SBP; avoid prolonged hypotension.
5 · After delivery
Slow IV oxytocin 5 IU (or 3 IU per MBRRACE/cardiac patients), then infusion 10 IU/h.

Onset / intubating conditions
~30 s, predictable
~30 s, equivalent
Awareness risk
Higher with under-dosing (NAP5 — most reported obstetric awareness cases used thiopentone, often <5 mg/kg)
Lower at equipotent dose; titration easier

More hypotension & cardiac depression — caution in shock/severe PET
Neonatal Apgar / cord gases
No clinically significant difference (Cochrane 2020)
Equivalent neonatal outcomes
Reconstitution required, syringe swap risk (Wrong drug — NAP5)
Ready-mixed, familiar from non-obstetric practice; allows seamless TIVA
~1:60,000; fewer cross-reactions
Bottom line:
No outcome difference for mother or baby in head-to-head RCTs (Lucas 2013; Houthoff Khemlani 2018; Cochrane 2020). Choose the drug you can dose confidently. If using propofol, use ≥2 mg/kg (lean body weight, not actual) — under-dosing is the dominant awareness mechanism.

Reduced PONV; reliable after-delivery analgesia with remifentanil.
Avoids OT pollution; usable in MRI/remote sites.
Disadvantages / cautions
(NAP5 highlighted TIVA + NMB in obstetrics) — processed EEG mandatory.
Pharmacokinetic models (Marsh, Schnider)
not validated in pregnancy
— Vd and clearance altered.

Suggested regimen
propofol 2–2.5 mg/kg + sux 1.5 mg/kg (RSI). Some use remifentanil bolus 0.5–1 µg/kg pre-induction — see opioid section.

After delivery:
add long-acting opioid (morphine/fentanyl), reduce remifentanil, give oxytocin.
Always run
BIS or Entropy

Kinsella (2010)
and now incorporated into OAA guidance, RSS is a streamlined spinal technique for Cat 1 LSCS where neuraxial is feasible but every minute matters. The aim is to avoid GA without significantly extending DDI.
Key elements
No-touch technique,
single attempt

Limit/omit aseptic drape time; consider chlorhexidine spray + sterile gloves only.
Pre-prepared spinal pack and drug syringe.

(with consent / clear pre-brief).
Omit intrathecal opioid if it will delay; can give IV/epidural opioid later.
Vasopressor running before injection.
Kinsella's case series (n=25) and subsequent UK audits show RSS achieves anaesthesia in 5–7 min with high success and no documented intra-operative pain when applied to selected patients.

Pre-eclampsia / HELLP
Labetalol/nifedipine/hydralazine; MgSO₄ 4 g load + 1 g/h for severe PET or eclampsia; aim BP <140/90; deliver by 37 wk (earlier if severe).
Early epidural (improves placental flow, avoids GA airway); platelets ≥75 ×10⁹/L & normal coag for neuraxial; obtund pressor response at GA induction (remi/alfentanil); MgSO₄ potentiates NMBs; avoid ergometrine (severe HTN).
Gestational / pre-existing diabetes
Insulin infusion in labour to maintain CBG 4–7 mmol/L; planned delivery 37–38⁺⁶ wk if on therapy.
Avoid glucose-containing co-load; continue VRIII intra-op; macrosomia → shoulder dystocia / instrumental risk; neonatal hypoglycaemia.
Cardiac disease (mWHO II–IV)
MDT planning, joint cardiac-obstetric clinic, controlled vaginal delivery usually preferred over CS; assisted second stage to avoid Valsalva.
Slow-titrated epidural (avoid spinal hypotension); invasive monitoring for severe lesions; avoid ergometrine (pulmonary HTN, HOCM); careful fluid balance — cardiac output peaks immediately post-partum from auto-transfusion.
VTE / thromboprophylaxis
RCOG GTG-37a risk-score; LMWH antenatal & for 6 wk post-partum if intermediate/high risk.
Neuraxial timing: 12 h after prophylactic, 24 h after therapeutic LMWH; remove catheter ≥12 h after last dose, next dose ≥4 h post-removal.
Obstetric sepsis
Sepsis-6 within 1 h; broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam ± gentamicin); deliver if intrauterine source.
Coagulopathy & bacteraemia may preclude neuraxial; consider GA or remifentanil PCA; vasopressor + invasive monitoring; leading direct cause of maternal death (MBRRACE).
Obstetric cholestasis / AFLP
UDCA; deliver 37–38 wk for ICP; immediate delivery for AFLP.
Coagulopathy in AFLP — check INR/fibrinogen before neuraxial; hypoglycaemia.
Placenta praevia / accreta spectrum
Elective CS 36–37 wk; MDT with interventional radiology; cell salvage available.
Large-bore access × 2, group-and-save / cross-match 4 units, activate MHP pathway; regional feasible but convert to GA early if massive haemorrhage.
Mental health / substance misuse
Perinatal mental health team; opioid substitution continued through labour.
cause of maternal death (MBRRACE); higher analgesic requirements; naloxone caution in opioid-dependent women.
Conduct & stages of labour
First stage (latent → active)
Latent: irregular contractions, cervix <4 cm. Active: regular contractions, ≥4 cm dilatation, expected ~0.5 cm/h (nullip) / 1 cm/h (multip). Intermittent auscultation for low-risk; continuous CTG for high-risk. Anaesthetic: site epidural early once active labour established and woman requests; review any high-risk plan.
Second stage
Full dilatation → delivery. Passive (descent) then active (pushing). Prolonged: >2 h nullip / >1 h multip with epidural add 1 h. Anaesthetic: top-up for instrumental delivery (lidocaine 2% + adrenaline ± bicarbonate, or low-dose CSE); avoid dense motor block early.
Third stage & active management
Delivery of placenta.
Active management
(oxytocin 10 IU IM / 5 IU slow IV at delivery, controlled cord traction, uterine massage) reduces PPH by ~60%. Ergometrine 500 µg IM
in HTN/PET/cardiac disease. Carboprost (250 µg IM, max 8) avoid in asthma; misoprostol 800 µg PR adjunct.
Induction & augmentation
Indications: post-dates ≥41 wk, PROM, diabetes, IUGR, IUD. Methods: membrane sweep → vaginal prostaglandin (dinoprostone) or oral misoprostol → ARM → oxytocin infusion (start 1–4 mU/min, titrate). Anaesthetic: oxytocin causes vasodilatation and tachycardia;
bolus >5 IU
can precipitate severe hypotension — give 3 IU slow IV at CS (NICE).
Fetal monitoring
CTG (DR-C-BRA-VADO): Baseline 110–160, variability 5–25, accelerations reassuring, decelerations classified (early/variable/late). Pathological CTG → fetal blood sampling (pH ≥7.25 normal; ≤7.20 deliver). Anaesthetic should anticipate Cat-1 CS when CTG deteriorates.
Categories of caesarean (RCOG)
Cat 1
: immediate threat to life — DDI <30 min (audit standard); GA or rapid spinal/epidural top-up.
Cat 2
: maternal/fetal compromise not immediately life-threatening — DDI <75 min.
Cat 3
: needs early delivery, no compromise.
Cat 4
: elective.
Instrumental delivery
Ventouse / forceps in theatre if mid-cavity or rotational ("trial"). Anaesthetic provides regional top-up to T10 (perineal block) — failed instrumental converts to CS, so plan for higher block.
Post-partum haemorrhage (PPH)
≥500 ml vaginal / ≥1000 ml CS; major ≥1000 ml or ongoing.
4 Ts
: Tone (80%), Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin. Bundle: uterotonics ladder (oxytocin → ergometrine → carboprost → misoprostol), TXA 1 g within 3 h (WOMAN trial), bimanual compression, balloon tamponade, B-Lynch, IR embolisation, hysterectomy. Activate MHP; aim fibrinogen >2 g/L (ROTEM-guided).
Immediate post-natal period
Auto-transfusion ↑CO ~60–80% in first 10 min — risk of pulmonary oedema in cardiac/PET. Continue MgSO₄ 24 h post-delivery in severe PET. Restart LMWH 6–12 h post-delivery (later after PPH or epidural removal). Early mobilisation; analgesia ladder paracetamol + NSAID (avoid in severe PET / renal impairment) + opioid PRN.
Low-dose bupivacaine 0.1% + fentanyl 2 µg/ml. PIEB (programmed intermittent epidural bolus) superior to continuous infusion — better spread, less motor block, higher satisfaction.
Remifentanil PCA
Bolus 30–40 µg, lockout 2 min, no background infusion. Requires 1:1 midwifery, continuous SpO₂ + capnography (or apnoea alarm), supplemental O₂ available, and naloxone at the bedside.
RCT (Wilson 2018) have defined contemporary practice.

and desaturation — most serious risk; case reports of cardiac arrest

Cannot be converted — requires separate spinal/GA

references.label: OAA/DAS 2015
references.citation: Mushambi MC, Kinsella SM, Popat M et al. OAA/DAS guidelines for the management of difficult and failed tracheal intubation in obstetrics. Anaesthesia. 2015;70:1286-1306.
references.excerpt: These guidelines, developed by the Obstetric Anaesthetists' Association and the Difficult Airway Society, describe a structured approach to airway management for general anaesthesia in obstetric patients, with Master, Obstetric and Rescue algorithms and emphasis on early decision-making about waking, surgery via supraglottic airway, or front-of-neck access. Reported failed-intubation rates in obstetrics are approximately 1 in 300 general anaesthetics.

references.label: MBRRACE-UK
references.citation: Knight M et al. Saving Lives, Improving Mothers' Care (MBRRACE-UK). National Perinatal Epidemiology Unit, Oxford. 2022.

references.label: RCoA GPAS Ch 9 2024
references.citation: Royal College of Anaesthetists. Guidelines for the Provision of Anaesthesia Services for an Obstetric Population (GPAS Chapter 9). RCoA; 2024.
references.excerpt: Chapter 9 sets UK service standards for obstetric anaesthesia, including consultant-led 24/7 cover for high-risk delivery units, mandatory monitoring (AAGBI standards) for all neuraxial blocks and general anaesthetics, decision-to-delivery interval targets (<30 minutes for Category 1 caesarean section, <75 minutes for Category 2), availability of difficult-airway equipment and major-haemorrhage protocols, and team-based simulation training for failed intubation and maternal collapse.

references.label: OAA PDPH 2023
references.citation: Russell R, Laxton C, Lucas DN, Niewiarowski J, Scrutton M, Stocks G. Treatment of obstetric post-dural puncture headache. Part 1: conservative and pharmacological management. Anaesthesia. 2019;74:61-77 (updated OAA guidance 2023).
references.excerpt: Accidental dural puncture during epidural insertion occurs in approximately 1% of obstetric epidurals, and 70–80% of affected women develop post-dural puncture headache. Epidural blood patch remains the most effective treatment, with around 70% achieving complete relief after a single patch.

references.label: OAA Nerve Injury 2023
references.citation: Obstetric Anaesthetists' Association / RCoA. Management of postpartum nerve injuries following childbirth. OAA; 2023.
references.excerpt: Postpartum neurological symptoms occur in approximately 1% of vaginal deliveries; the majority are intrinsic obstetric palsies (lateral femoral cutaneous, lumbosacral trunk, femoral, common fibular) rather than neuraxial complications. Red flags requiring urgent imaging include bilateral weakness, bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, and symptoms persisting beyond the expected dermatomal regression of the block.

references.label: NAP5
references.citation: Pandit JJ, Andrade J, Bogod DG et al. 5th National Audit Project (NAP5) on accidental awareness during general anaesthesia: summary of main findings and risk factors. Br J Anaesth. 2014;113(4):549-559.
references.excerpt: Obstetric general anaesthesia carries the highest reported incidence of accidental awareness during general anaesthesia (~1:670). Contributory factors included thiopentone under-dosing, rapid sequence induction with delayed volatile, and use of neuromuscular blockade before adequate hypnotic effect.

case_bank.title: Postpartum haemorrhage after caesarean birth
case_bank.text:
Case: Postpartum haemorrhage after caesarean birth (Antifibrinolytics, Intermediate)
Patient: A 34-year-old develops uterine atony and 1.4 L blood loss 25 minutes after caesarean delivery.
Presentation: Uterotonics and surgical measures are underway. She remains tachycardic with brisk ongoing bleeding.
Stage 1 — Add antifibrinolytic treatment
  Question: What is the TXA plan?
  Model answer: Give TXA 1 g IV as soon as possible and within three hours of bleeding onset.
  Model answer: If bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours, a second 1 g dose may be given according to the WOMAN regimen and local protocol.
  Model answer: TXA does not replace uterotonics, surgical control or activation of the obstetric major-haemorrhage pathway.
Stage 2 — Resuscitate in parallel
  Question: Which targets deserve repeated attention?
  Model answer: Assess fibrinogen early because it can fall rapidly in obstetric haemorrhage.
  Model answer: Warm patient and products; monitor ionised calcium, acid–base status, platelets and coagulation.
  Model answer: Use blood products and fibrinogen replacement according to clinical bleeding, laboratory or viscoelastic results and local protocol.
Stage 3 — Communicate the endpoint
  Question: What should the team document?
  Model answer: Time of bleeding onset and each TXA dose, cumulative blood loss, interventions and response.
  Model answer: Thrombosis risk assessment later remains important, but appropriate TXA for active PPH is not a reason to withhold indicated prophylaxis indefinitely.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Postpartum haemorrhage activates fibrinolysis early, so TXA should be given promptly once PPH is diagnosed and within three hours of bleeding onset. It reduces death from bleeding but does not correct uterine atony, retained tissue, trauma or coagulopathy by itself.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give TXA 1 g IV as soon as possible; repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours, following local protocol. Continue uterotonics, surgical or radiological control and major-haemorrhage resuscitation. Measure fibrinogen early, warm the patient and products, and monitor platelets, coagulation, pH and ionised calcium.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not postpone TXA until laboratory results return, but also do not let it distract from the four causes of PPH and definitive control. Record bleeding onset and dose times.
Take-home: In postpartum haemorrhage, give TXA early alongside—never instead of—uterotonic, surgical and transfusion management.
Cited sources: WOMAN trial (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(17)30638-4)

case_bank.title: Catecholamine symptoms in pregnancy
case_bank.text:
Case: Catecholamine symptoms in pregnancy (Phaeochromocytoma, Advanced)
Patient: A pregnant adult at 24 weeks has episodic hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations.
Presentation: Urine protein is absent and symptoms began early in pregnancy; plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated.
Stage 1 — Differentiate the diagnosis
  Question: Why is this not automatically pre-eclampsia?
  Model answer: Paroxysmal symptoms and early onset suggest catecholamine excess.
  Model answer: Confirm biochemistry and localise with pregnancy-appropriate imaging, commonly MRI without gadolinium.
  Model answer: Assess maternal cardiac and fetal effects.
Stage 2 — Prepare safely
  Question: What is the pharmacological sequence?
  Model answer: Establish alpha blockade first and restore circulating volume cautiously.
  Model answer: Add beta blockade only after adequate alpha control for persistent tachycardia.
  Model answer: Coordinate a specialist multidisciplinary plan.
Stage 3 — Plan definitive care
  Question: How is timing decided?
  Model answer: Balance gestation, tumour location, haemodynamic control and maternal-fetal risk.
  Model answer: Use invasive monitoring and short-acting vasoactive drugs for surgery or delivery.
  Model answer: Agree neonatal and postoperative critical-care provision.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Phaeochromocytoma in pregnancy threatens both maternal and fetal circulation. Episodic hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations that predate pre-eclampsia should prompt metanephrine testing and MRI without gadolinium.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Coordinate endocrine, obstetric, anaesthetic, neonatal and surgical care. Establish alpha blockade before any beta blocker, restore volume carefully and use invasive monitoring for surgery or delivery. Timing of adrenalectomy and delivery depends on gestation, tumour anatomy and control.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not treat tachycardia first with isolated beta blockade, and do not assume all hypertension after 20 weeks is pre-eclampsia.
Take-home: Phaeochromocytoma in pregnancy requires early recognition, alpha-before-beta blockade and coordinated maternal-fetal planning.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

# Paediatric Anaesthesia
Neonatal physiology, paediatric pharmacology, common procedures

= [ [ "How is paediatric airway anatomy different from adults?", "Children have several anatomical differences that make airway management more challenging: a relatively large head and tongue; a high anterior larynx at C3–C4 (adult: C4–C5); a long, floppy epiglottis; a narrowest airway at the subglottic cricoid ring (cylindrical) rather than the glottis; and a short trachea (4–5 cm in neonates). These features explain why straight blades (Miller) are preferred in infants, why uncuffed endotracheal tubes were traditionally used under age 8 (though modern cuffed tubes are now accepted from ~3 kg), and why neonates desaturate rapidly after apnoea due to high oxygen consumption (6–8 mL/kg/min) and low functional reserve capacity.", ], [ "What is the correct ETT size for a child?", "For children over 1 year, use the age-based formulas: uncuffed ETT size (mm) = age/4 + 4; cuffed ETT size = age/4 + 3.5. Oral insertion depth (cm at lips) = age/2 + 12. For a 4-year-old: uncuffed 5.0 mm, cuffed 4.5 mm, depth 14 cm. Neonates and infants: 3.0–3.5 mm (uncuffed) or 3.0 mm (cuffed) for term neonates, at 9–10 cm depth. Always have one size smaller and one size larger immediately available. Cuffed tubes are now accepted in most paediatric centres because they reduce re-intubation rates and improve ventilation dynamics, provided the cuff pressure is monitored and kept
48 hours, particularly in critically ill, septic, or steroid/catecholamine-treated children. Prevention: keep propofol
Clinical Relevance

Straight blade (Miller), uncuffed ETT <8y (traditional), cuffed now accepted >3kg
High O₂ consumption (6-8 ml/kg/min), low FRC, high closing capacity
Rapid desaturation, prone to atelectasis

Common Paediatric Scenarios
Key Paediatric Surgical Procedures
Paediatric TIVA — Including "Remi-Prop" / "Remifol"
— is the workhorse paediatric TIVA technique because both agents are titratable, rapidly cleared (remifentanil by non-specific tissue/plasma esterases, independent of age beyond the neonatal period) and produce minimal accumulation.
Propofol — paediatric TCI
models (children 1–16 yr, >5 kg). Higher Vd and clearance per kg than adults — paediatric models target larger doses to achieve equivalent plasma levels. Typical maintenance Cp 3–6 µg/ml. Manual: induction 4 mg/kg, then 15-13-11-10-9 mg/kg/hr stepped down (Roberts/McFarlan-style regimen).
Single-syringe propofol + remifentanil ("Remi-mix")
= 5 µg remifentanil per ml of 10 mg/ml propofol. Practical preparation: reconstitute a 1 mg remifentanil vial in 10 ml water (→ 100 µg/ml), draw up
2.5 ml (250 µg)
and add to a 50 ml syringe of 1% propofol → 250 µg remi in 50 ml = 5 µg/ml remi alongside 10 mg/ml propofol. (For Remi 10 add 5 ml = 500 µg; for Remi 2 add 1 ml = 100 µg.) Stable physico-chemically for at least 6 hr at room temperature.
Remi (µg/ml)
Propofol (mg/ml)
Typical use
Effective ratio
Remi 2
Sedation / non-stimulating MRI, sedated cardiac cath, infants where a lower opioid load is wanted
1 µg remi : 5 mg propofol
Remi 5
Default workhorse mix
— dental, strabismus, MRI under GA, tonsillectomy, day-case general surgery
1 µg remi : 2 mg propofol
Remi 10
Stimulating shared-airway work — microlaryngoscopy, rigid bronchoscopy, adenotonsillectomy with OSA
1 µg remi : 1 mg propofol
Remi 20
Brief, very stimulating procedures (laser airway, rigid oesophagoscopy) where opioid demand exceeds propofol demand
2 µg remi : 1 mg propofol
10 ml/hr per 10 kg
of Remi 5 delivers ~10 mg/kg/hr propofol + ~0.08 µg/kg/min remifentanil — a sensible starting point, then titrated to clinical effect (movement, HR, RR, BIS if used).
Advantages of the single-syringe technique
One pump, one line
— simpler in MRI bores, on transfers and on small children with limited venous access
No risk of differential disconnection
— propofol and remifentanil cannot become uncoupled mid-case, so the child cannot inadvertently receive opioid without hypnotic (or vice versa)
No dead-space or back-flow problems from a Y-connector — both drugs travel together in the same lumen at the same rate
Faster set-up and lower kit cost — useful on remote-site and emergency lists
Reduced drug-error opportunity at programming (a single rate, single drug-name field)
Drawbacks & cautions
Loss of independent titration
— cannot increase opioid for a stimulating moment without also increasing hypnotic (and vice versa). Choose the mix to match the expected stimulus profile
Unlicensed / off-label
mixing — must be prepared by the anaesthetist with a clear local SOP, two-person check and bold syringe labelling stating both drugs and their concentrations
TCI models cannot be used — the pump only "knows" propofol, so manual rate-based dosing is mandatory; depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring (BIS/Entropy) is therefore strongly recommended
Bolus doses give a paired remifentanil bolus — risk of
bradycardia, chest-wall rigidity and hypotension
, especially in neonates and small infants. Avoid rescue boluses from the running syringe; give separate small propofol boluses instead
Wastage if the case is shorter than expected; the mixed syringe cannot be re-used for another patient
Not suitable for prolonged ICU sedation or for cases where opioid requirement is likely to fall sharply (e.g. once a regional block is sited)

infusions >4 mg/kg/hr for >48 hr

Avoid prolonged propofol sedation in PICU; use dexmedetomidine or midazolam-based regimens. Monitor lactate, CK, triglycerides if propofol must continue beyond 24 hr.
Paediatric PCA & NCA
PCA (patient-controlled analgesia)
is suitable from approximately
5–6 years
, when the child can reliably understand cause-and-effect ("press the button → less pain"). Below this age, or when developmental delay/severe pain prevents the child operating the handset,
NCA (nurse-controlled analgesia)
is used — the same pump and safety architecture but the bolus is delivered by a trained nurse using protocolised pain assessment (FLACC, Wong-Baker faces).

Safety essentials
One-way anti-syphon and anti-reflux valves on a dedicated IV line. Continuous SpO₂ ± capnography for NCA or PCA with background. Hourly nursing observations including sedation score (UMSS) and respiratory rate. Naloxone (10 µg/kg) and oxygen at the bedside.
Special situations
Avoid morphine in renal impairment (M6G accumulation) — use fentanyl. Codeine is contraindicated <12 yr (MHRA, 2013) due to unpredictable CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolism. Tramadol contraindicated <12 yr post-tonsillectomy for OSA. Always combine with multimodal analgesia (paracetamol, ibuprofen, regional).

Not yet. Correct the alkalosis and electrolyte deficit (Cl ≥100, HCO₃ ≤26, K ≥3.5) over 24–48 h before theatre, then proceed with modified RSI.

Children have several anatomical differences that make airway management more challenging: a relatively large head and tongue; a high anterior larynx at C3–C4 (adult: C4–C5); a long, floppy epiglottis; a narrowest airway at the subglottic cricoid ring (cylindrical) rather than the glottis; and a short trachea (4–5 cm in neonates). These features explain why straight blades (Miller) are preferred in infants, why uncuffed endotracheal tubes were traditionally used under age 8 (though modern cuffed tubes are now accepted from ~3 kg), and why neonates desaturate rapidly after apnoea due to high oxygen consumption (6–8 mL/kg/min) and low functional reserve capacity.
What is the correct ETT size for a child?
For children over 1 year, use the age-based formulas: uncuffed ETT size (mm) = age/4 + 4; cuffed ETT size = age/4 + 3.5. Oral insertion depth (cm at lips) = age/2 + 12. For a 4-year-old: uncuffed 5.0 mm, cuffed 4.5 mm, depth 14 cm. Neonates and infants: 3.0–3.5 mm (uncuffed) or 3.0 mm (cuffed) for term neonates, at 9–10 cm depth. Always have one size smaller and one size larger immediately available. Cuffed tubes are now accepted in most paediatric centres because they reduce re-intubation rates and improve ventilation dynamics, provided the cuff pressure is monitored and kept <20–25 cmH₂O.
What is the WETFLAG emergency drug dose framework?
WETFLAG is a paediatric emergency checklist used to rapidly estimate weight and calculate critical drug doses and equipment sizes: W (Weight = (age + 4) × 2 kg), E (Energy for defibrillation = 4 J/kg), T (Tube size = age/4 + 4 mm uncuffed), F (Fluids = 10–20 mL/kg bolus), L (Length of ETT at lips = age/2 + 12 cm), A (Adrenaline = 10 µg/kg IV/IO for cardiac arrest; 0.1 µg/kg/min for infusion), G (Glucose = 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose for hypoglycaemia). This ensures standardised, rapid preparation during paediatric emergencies and arrests.
How do you manage laryngospasm in a child?
Laryngospasm is the most common paediatric airway emergency. Management follows a graded approach: (1) apply 100% oxygen with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) via a tight-fitting face mask; (2) perform jaw thrust and head tilt; (3) apply firm bilateral pressure at Larson
What is remi-prop (remifol) and how is it used in paediatric TIVA?
Remi-prop (or remifol) is the colloquial name for a single-syringe mixture of propofol and remifentanil used for total intravenous anaesthesia in children. The mixture is named by its remifentanil concentration in micrograms per millilitre of 1% propofol: Remi 5 = 5 µg remifentanil per ml of 10 mg/ml propofol (the default workhorse mix for dental, MRI, day-case surgery). Preparation: reconstitute 1 mg remifentanil in 10 ml water (100 µg/ml), draw up 2.5 ml (250 µg) and add to 50 ml of 1% propofol → 5 µg/ml remifentanil. A maintenance rate of 10 ml/hr per 10 kg delivers ~10 mg/kg/hr propofol + ~0.08 µg/kg/min remifentanil. Advantages: one pump, one line, no differential disconnection risk, simpler in MRI bores. Cautions: loss of independent titration, unlicensed mixing requiring local SOP, boluses from the running syringe risk bradycardia and chest-wall rigidity.
What is propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) and how do you prevent it?
Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) is a rare but potentially fatal metabolic complication of prolonged propofol infusion, characterised by metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, lipaemia, cardiac arrhythmias and heart failure. Risk rises sharply with infusions >4 mg/kg/hr for >48 hours, particularly in critically ill, septic, or steroid/catecholamine-treated children. Prevention: keep propofol <4 mg/kg/hr, limit duration, avoid in septic or mitochondrial disorder patients, and monitor lactate, creatine kinase and triglycerides if infusion exceeds 24 hours. In PICU, use dexmedetomidine or midazolam-based sedation instead of prolonged propofol.
How do you anaesthetise a child with pyloric stenosis?
Pyloric stenosis presents with projectile vomiting leading to a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. It is a MEDICAL emergency, not a surgical one — the alkalosis must be corrected before theatre because post-operative apnoea is common if HCO₃ >26 mmol/L. Resuscitate with 0.9% saline 10–20 ml/kg boluses to restore intravascular volume, then 0.45% saline + 5% dextrose with 20 mmol/L KCl at 1.5 × maintenance. Targets before surgery: Na ≥135, K ≥3.5, Cl ≥100, HCO₃ ≤26, and adequate urine output. In theatre, use a modified RSI (full stomach) with ketamine or propofol and rocuronium, maintain normothermia, and monitor glucose closely.
What is a caudal block and when is it used in children?
A caudal block is a single-shot epidural injection via the sacral hiatus that provides analgesia for sub-umbilical surgery. It is the commonest paediatric regional technique because the sacral cornua are easily palpable in young children and the sacrococcygeal membrane gives a definite
. Use the Armitage volume regimen with 0.25% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine: 0.5 ml/kg for sacral spread (circumcision), 1.0 ml/kg for high lumbar/low thoracic (orchidopexy, hernia), and 1.25 ml/kg for mid-thoracic (maximum — motor block and local anaesthetic toxicity risk). Always use a test dose with adrenaline 0.5 µg/kg to detect intravascular placement. Adjuncts like clonidine 1–2 µg/kg extend duration by 50–100%. Contraindications: local infection, coagulopathy, raised ICP, spina bifida at the hiatus, sacral abnormalities.
What fluids should be used for paediatric maintenance and resuscitation?
For maintenance, use the Holliday-Segar 4-2-1 rule: 4 ml/kg/hr for the first 10 kg, 2 ml/kg/hr for the next 10 kg, and 1 ml/kg/hr for each kg thereafter. Use isotonic balanced crystalloids (Plasmalyte, Hartmann
What is the difference between PCA and NCA in children?
PCA (patient-controlled analgesia) is suitable from approximately 5–6 years of age, when the child can understand the cause-and-effect relationship of pressing the button for pain relief. NCA (nurse-controlled analgesia) uses the same pump and safety architecture but the bolus is delivered by a trained nurse based on protocolised pain assessment (FLACC score, Wong-Baker faces), and is used in children under 5 or those with developmental delay who cannot operate the handset. Both typically use morphine 1 mg/kg in 50 ml (20 µg/kg/ml): bolus 20 µg/kg, lockout 5 min (PCA) or 20–30 min (NCA), with an optional background infusion. Safety essentials include one-way anti-syphon valves, continuous SpO₂ monitoring, hourly nursing observations, and naloxone at the bedside.

Weight (APLS): (age + 4) × 2 = 16 kg. Uncuffed ETT: age/4 + 4 = 5.0 mm; cuffed: age/4 + 3.5 = 4.5 mm. ETT length (oral): age/2 + 12 = 14 cm at the lips. case_bank.title: Anaesthesia in the MRI scanner
case_bank.text:
Case: Anaesthesia in the MRI scanner (Imaging & radiation, Intermediate)
Patient: A child needs general anaesthesia for a 3 T MRI brain scan. A non-MR-conditional syringe pump has been brought to the scanner door and the patient has an unlabelled implant.
Presentation: The radiographer asks you to proceed quickly because the list is delayed.
Stage 1 — Name the physical hazards
  Question: Which fields cause which risks?
  Model answer: The always-on static field causes projectile injury, implant torque and displacement, and disables non-MR-safe equipment.
  Model answer: Radiofrequency pulses deposit energy, quantified as specific absorption rate, and can heat tissue, loops of wire and ECG leads, causing burns.
  Model answer: Rapidly switching gradients generate acoustic noise (often over 100 dB) and peripheral nerve stimulation; cryogen loss during a quench causes asphyxiation risk from displaced oxygen.
Stage 2 — Apply the safety system
  Question: How is access controlled and screening performed?
  Model answer: Zones I–IV restrict access, with the scanner room (zone IV) entered only after checklist-based screening by trained staff.
  Model answer: Every implant and device must be documented as MR safe, MR conditional or MR unsafe; unlabelled implants are treated as unsafe until identified.
  Model answer: Only MR-conditional monitoring, pumps and airway equipment enter zone IV, with long extension lines for infusions and remote-controlled ventilation.
Stage 3 — Plan the anaesthetic
  Question: What practical anaesthetic issues follow?
  Model answer: Remote and partly obscured patient access means secured airway, capnography, reliable IV access and a clear evacuation plan to a resuscitation area outside zone IV.
  Model answer: Provide ear protection, temperature care and dose-appropriate depth for immobility, and remove loops from cables and leads.
  Model answer: Rehearse quench and cardiac arrest responses; resuscitation takes place outside the scanner room.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: MRI safety follows directly from physics: a permanent superconducting static field, pulsed radiofrequency excitation and switched gradients each create a distinct hazard. Field strength increases signal but also projectile force and radiofrequency energy deposition, so 3 T scanning demands stricter screening than 1.5 T. Contrast agents raise separate concerns, with gadolinium-based agent choice restricted by renal function.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use a documented screening checklist for patient, staff and equipment; never rely on verbal assurance under time pressure. Anaesthetise where possible outside the magnet or use MR-conditional systems with waveguide-passed lines. Monitor temperature and depth, protect hearing, keep the resuscitation trolley outside zone IV and know who holds the quench button and evacuation responsibility.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not say the magnet is 'switched off between scans' — the static field is permanent. Distinguish MR safe, MR conditional and MR unsafe precisely, and mention SAR heating as a burn mechanism, not just projectile risk.
Take-home: The static field is always on: screen every person, implant and device, use only MR-conditional equipment in zone IV, and resuscitate outside the scanner room.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: MRI physics and safety (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.04.004); Assoc Anaesth 2021: MRI (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.15517)
