# Transfer of the Critically Ill Patient Pre-departure stabilisation, packaging, ventilation/sedation in transit, neuroprotection, in-transit emergencies, ECMO retrieval, aeromedical physiology Step-by-step calculation O₂ delivered to patient. FiO₂ 0.5 × MV 8 L/min = 4 L/min Add ventilator driving gas. 5 L/min total consumption. Convert duration to volume. 5 L/min × 90 min = 450 L baseline Apply 2× safety factor. 900 L minimum to carry (covers traffic, FiO₂ escalation, transfer delay). Choose cylinders. E-cylinder = 680 L; CD-cylinder = 460 L. Carry 2 × E (1,360 L) or 1 × E + 1 × CD (1,140 L). Decision points Check gauges fully open before departure — gauge reads pressure, not volume. Confirm receiving unit O₂ is connected on arrival before disconnecting cylinders. If FiO₂ rises to 1.0, recalculate (consumption doubles → reserve halves). Common traps Forgetting the driving gas — turbine ventilators use little, but pneumatic ventilators can use 1–2 L/min on top of patient flow. Calculating without a safety factor and arriving with an empty cylinder in a lift. Using cylinder content tables instead of measuring the actual gauge — partially used cylinders are a major cause of in-transit hypoxia. Step-by-step reasoning Estimate cabin pressure. 8,000 ft cabin altitude ≈ 75 kPa (sea level 101 kPa). Apply Boyle's law. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → V₂/V₁ = 101/75 ≈ — gas-filled cavities expand by ~35% (commonly quoted as 25–35%). List affected spaces. Pneumothorax, ETT cuff, bowel, middle ear, sinuses, pneumocephalus, eye gas after vitrectomy. Mitigate each. Drain on continuous underwater seal or Heimlich valve (NEVER clamp). Replace ETT cuff air with saline OR monitor cuff manometer (target ≤ 30 cmH₂O). Compensate for ↓ PaO₂. Increase FiO₂; aim SpO₂ ≥ 94% in flight (≥ 96% if TBI). If pneumothorax untreated → insert chest drain BEFORE flight, not at altitude. Acute desaturation in flight = exclude tension pneumothorax (re-examine, consider needle decompression). Clamping a chest drain 'just for the transfer' — converts simple pneumothorax to tension. Ignoring middle-ear/sinus expansion in conscious patients (severe pain on descent). Forgetting that recent diving (within 24 h) is a relative contraindication to flight (residual nitrogen). : specialist care unavailable (neurosurgery, cardiothoracic, ECMO, burns), investigations (MRI, angiography), repatriation : senior-to-senior communication. Referring and receiving teams agree on timing and clinical plan : minimum doctor + assistant (nurse/ODP). Doctor experienced in transfer medicine. Both trained in equipment : ECG, SpO₂, ETCO₂, invasive BP, temperature — minimum standard. Battery backup essential O₂ calculation : E-cylinder (680L) at 10L/min = 68 min. D-cylinder (340L). Always carry spare : emergency drugs drawn up and labelled. Adrenaline, atropine, midazolam, propofol, suxamethonium, rocuronium, vasopressors : transfer form with observations every 15 min, interventions, clinical events. Handover at receiving unit using SBAR/ISBAR : affects BP measurement (transducer position relative to heart changes), ↑ ICP risk, equipment movement Altitude (air transfer) : ↓ barometric pressure → gas expansion (Boyle's law). ETT cuff, pneumothorax, bowel gas all expand. ↓ PaO₂ (cabin altitude ~6,000-8,000 ft) : artefact on monitoring, patient discomfort, equipment damage : makes auscultation impossible — rely on capnography and SpO₂. Communication difficult By geography : intra-hospital (e.g. ICU → CT/MRI/IR), inter-hospital (district general → tertiary), international/repatriation By urgency : time-critical (rupturing AAA, extradural haematoma, STEMI for PCI) vs clinically urgent vs elective/repatriation By mode : road ambulance (default in UK; cheap, flexible), rotary-wing (helicopter; faster >50 miles, weather-limited), fixed-wing (long distance >150 miles, cabin altitude effects) By team : parent team, regional retrieval service (e.g. neonatal/paediatric — STRS, NTS; adult ECMO retrieval), critical care transfer service (e.g. ACCTS in England) : ETT position confirmed (CXR + cm at teeth), tube tied not taped, bite block, suction immediately available, spare ETT and difficult airway kit : ventilator settings replicated and observed for ≥15 min before departure; ETCO₂ trace visible; chest auscultated; CXR reviewed; chest drain on Heimlich/underwater seal kept upright and below patient : 2 × secured large-bore IV access plus a dedicated central or large peripheral line for vasopressors; arterial line zeroed at tragus (TBI) or phlebostatic axis; cross-matched blood if bleeding Drugs & pumps : all infusions on battery-powered pumps with adequate charge and labelled; spare syringes drawn up (sedation, paralysis, vasopressor); push-dose pressors ready : secured to trolley with straps; eyes taped; pressure points padded; NG tube on free drainage (gas expansion at altitude); urinary catheter; temperature probe; warming blanket Notes & imaging : copy of notes, drug chart, imaging on disc/PACS link, blood results, consent/best-interests documentation, next-of-kin contact Transport ventilator : must replicate the patient's ICU settings (PEEP, FiO₂, mode). Confirm it triggers, alarms (disconnect, high pressure, low gas) and has a self-inflating bag as backup Lung-protective ventilation : TV 6 mL/kg IBW, plateau ≤30 cmH₂O, PEEP titrated to oxygenation. Recruit before disconnecting from ICU ventilator to avoid de-recruitment Oxygenation target : SpO₂ 94–98% (≥96% if TBI). Pre-oxygenate with FiO₂ 1.0 for moves between ventilators Capnography is mandatory : sudden ↓ETCO₂ = disconnection, cardiac arrest or massive PE; sudden ↑ETCO₂ = hypoventilation or rising metabolic rate : continue propofol + opioid (or midazolam if cardiovascularly unstable). Light sedation in a noisy, vibrating ambulance risks awareness, cough, ↑ICP and accidental extubation Neuromuscular blockade : routinely consider for ventilated patients during transfer to prevent dys-synchrony, coughing and line/tube displacement : intubate before transfer if GCS ≤8, falling GCS, loss of airway reflexes, seizures, or for any agitated TBI patient requiring CT : SpO₂ ≥96%, PaO₂ >13 kPa, PaCO₂ 4.5–5.0 kPa, MAP ≥80 mmHg (CPP >60 mmHg), temperature 36–37°C, glucose 6–10 mmol/L, Na 140–145 mmol/L : head-up 30°, neutral neck, tube ties not too tight (avoid jugular venous obstruction) Osmotherapy ready : mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline (e.g. 3% 250 mL) for acute deterioration (blown pupil, Cushing response) : prophylactic hyperventilation (vasoconstriction → ischaemia), hypotonic fluids, dextrose-containing solutions General principle : continue the patient's existing ICU regimen if effective; do not start a new agent immediately before departure. Aim RASS −4 to −5 for ventilated TBI/ARDS transfers, RASS −2 to −3 for stable ventilated patients Hypnotic — propofol : 1–4 mg/kg/h infusion; predictable, short context-sensitive half-time, antiepileptic, ↓CMRO₂ and ICP. Watch for hypotension on acceleration/deceleration; reduce dose or add noradrenaline rather than under-sedate Hypnotic — midazolam : 0.03–0.2 mg/kg/h preferred when haemodynamically unstable or for prolonged transfers; accumulates, slower wake-up at destination — flag in handover Hypnotic — ketamine : 1–3 mg/kg/h; sympathomimetic, bronchodilator, analgesic — useful in shocked/asthmatic patients. Modern evidence does not support an absolute contraindication in TBI when CO₂ is controlled Analgesia — opioid : fentanyl 1–5 µg/kg/h or alfentanil 30–100 µg/kg/h (rapid offset, useful when neuro reassessment planned at destination); morphine acceptable but slower-offset Analgesia — adjuncts : paracetamol 1 g IV for pyrexia/analgesia (also helps neuroprotective normothermia); regional blocks placed before transfer (e.g. fascia iliaca for # NOF) reduce opioid requirement : routinely consider rocuronium 0.3–0.6 mg/kg/h (or boluses) for ventilated transfers — abolishes coughing, dys-synchrony, ↑ICP and prevents tube/line displacement. Always combine with adequate hypnosis to avoid awareness; ensure sugammadex available Bolus / push-dose drugs ready : pre-drawn fentanyl 50 µg, propofol 20 mg, rocuronium 50 mg, plus push-dose vasopressor (e.g. metaraminol 0.5 mg/mL or adrenaline 10 µg/mL) for surges in stimulation (suctioning, road handover, lift transfers) Awareness risk : paralysed + under-sedated in a noisy moving vehicle is a high-risk scenario. If unsure, deepen sedation; document depth at every set of obs Pre-departure neuro exam : document GCS, pupils (size, symmetry, reactivity), focal signs, sedation hold result if safe — this is the baseline the receiving team will use Pupillary assessment : the single most useful in-transit neuro sign. Check every 15 min and on any deterioration. New unilateral dilated unreactive pupil = uncal herniation until proven otherwise → osmotherapy, hyperventilate transiently to PaCO₂ 4.0–4.5 kPa, alert neurosurgeons. Quantitative pupillometry (NPi) increasingly used where available Invasive ICP / EVD : if monitor in situ, transduce continuously, zero at the tragus, target ICP <22 mmHg and CPP 60–70 mmHg. EVD: clamp before any change in patient height (lift, ramp) to avoid over-drainage; document open/closed status, drainage volume and CSF appearance Arterial line : mandatory for any neuro transfer — beat-to-beat MAP for CPP calculation, repeated ABGs for PaCO₂/PaO₂. Re-zero at the tragus after every position change Continuous capnography : surrogate for PaCO₂; remember the ETCO₂–PaCO₂ gradient widens with shock, PE, and altitude. Cross-check with ABG at 30 min intervals or after any major event Brain tissue oxygen / NIRS / jugular bulb : not routine in transit, but if already in place continue and document trends. Falling PbtO₂ or SjvO₂ <55% suggests inadequate cerebral oxygen delivery Processed EEG / BIS : useful when paralysed to titrate sedation depth and detect non-convulsive seizures; vibration and electrical noise produce frequent artefact — interpret with caution Glucose, sodium, temperature : hourly point-of-care glucose, Na (i-STAT or equivalent), continuous core temperature — all act as 'metabolic neuromonitors' avoid hypoxia, hypotension, hypercarbia, hyperthermia, hyperglycaemia and hyponatraemia . Every parameter that drifts in transit costs neurones. ECMO retrieval : undertaken by regional centres (e.g. UK adult severe respiratory failure service). Cannulation at the referring hospital, then transfer on VV/VA-ECMO. Risks: cannula displacement, circuit air, anticoagulation bleeding IABP / mechanical circulatory support : continue counterpulsation; secure femoral cannula; trigger from ECG/arterial waveform robust to vibration; check battery life and helium reserve : warmed environment, accurate fluid resuscitation (Parkland), consider escharotomy before flight if circumferential : left lateral tilt, anticipate delivery en route (pack delivery kit), liaise with receiving obstetric and neonatal teams : regional retrieval team (e.g. STRS, NWTS, KIDS); weight-based equipment; thermoregulation paramount Team safety : high-visibility clothing, seat belts, safe driving (no 'blue lights' for stable patients — most ambulance crashes occur on emergency response) Fatigue & communication : long transfers degrade vigilance; brief receiving unit before departure and en route; use closed-loop communication Cognitive aids : pre-departure checklist (ICS proforma), drug calculation cards, escalation phone numbers Documentation & audit : every transfer audited for adverse events (hypoxia, hypotension, equipment failure, time delays); feedback to referring and retrieval teams Consent & indemnity : best-interests documentation when patient lacks capacity; medical indemnity for transfers including air/international Oxygen requirement for a 90-minute road transfer Take a minimum of two full E-cylinders (1,360 L). Always pre-calculate using flow × time × 2 safety factor (ICS 2019), check cylinder gauges before departure, and confirm receiving unit O₂ is available on arrival. A single cylinder would risk run-out before reaching destination. Air transfer of a patient with a chest drain Maintain the chest drain on continuous underwater seal (kept upright, below the patient) or a Heimlich valve — never clamp. Fill the ETT cuff with saline or monitor the cuff manometer at altitude. Counsel the team that any new desaturation in flight should prompt assessment for a tension pneumothorax. Transfer of the Critically Ill Patient Pre-departure stabilisation, packaging, in-transit care and the physiology of transport Standard of care during transfer must be at least as good as at the referring hospital (ICS Transfer 2019) Secure airway BEFORE transfer if any concern. Chest drains must NEVER be clamped — use Heimlich valve O₂ calculation: E-cylinder = 680L. Calculate flow × time × 2 safety factor. Always carry spare (ICS 2019) Altitude: gas expands (Boyle's law) — ETT cuff, pneumothorax, bowel gas. ↓ PaO₂ at cabin altitude Minimum monitoring: ECG, SpO₂, ETCO₂, invasive BP, temperature. Battery backup essential Senior-to-senior decision; transfer team minimum doctor (ST4+ or equivalent) + assistant, both familiar with equipment (ICS 2019) End-to-End Transfer Checklist Principles of Safe Transfer Preparation — ABCDE Stabilisation Secure airway before transfer if any concern. ETT preferred (secured, documented at teeth). Carry difficult airway equipment. Portable ventilator with disconnect alarm. Sufficient O₂ (calculate: flow rate × duration × 2 for safety). Chest drain clamping is NEVER safe — use underwater seal or Heimlich valve. Two large-bore IV cannulae (secured). Adequate fluids/blood. Vasopressors prepared in syringes. Invasive arterial monitoring recommended. Sedation/analgesia infusions prepared. ICP management if relevant. Seizure prophylaxis/treatment available. Temperature management: active warming, space blanket. Prevent hypothermia during prolonged transfers. Equipment & Documentation Physics of Transport Classification of Transfers Packaging the Critically Ill Patient Ventilation & Sedation in Transit Neuroprotective Transfer (TBI / Raised ICP) Sedation & Analgesia in Transit Neuromonitoring Considerations Neuroprotection Strategies in Transit In-Transit Emergencies Specialist Transfers Human Factors, Safety & Governance What are the AAGBI categories of inter-hospital transfer? Category 1 — life- or limb-threatening (requires consultant anaesthetist and ICU nurse). Category 2 — urgent (specialty input needed but not immediate). Category 3 — non-urgent (repatriation). Category 4 — return to local hospital. Staffing, monitoring and vehicle choice escalate with category. What is the minimum monitoring required for a critical-care transfer? ECG, SpO₂, NIBP (every 5 min) or invasive arterial pressure, EtCO₂ if intubated, temperature, and infusion pump status. A means of measuring CVP if cardiovascularly unstable. All monitors must be battery-powered with ≥2× expected transfer duration and a printed transfer chart kept. How do you calculate oxygen requirements for a ventilated transfer? Oxygen needed (L) = minute ventilation (L/min) × FiO₂ × transfer time (min) × 2 (safety margin) + ventilator driving gas. A full E-cylinder contains ~680 L. Always carry at least double the calculated requirement and a self-inflating bag with reservoir as backup. Apply current UK standards — primarily the Intensive Care Society (ICS) Guidance on the Transfer of the Critically Ill Adult (2019), supplemented by FICM/RCoA recommendations — to plan a safe inter-hospital transfer of the critically ill patient (decision, personnel, equipment) Stabilise a critically ill patient using an ABCDE-led pre-departure checklist and a Calculate oxygen reserve required for transfer and identify when supplies are inadequate Set up a portable ventilator and infusion pumps for safe transfer, anticipating ventilation, sedation and haemodynamic challenges in transit Apply neuroprotective transfer principles to the patient with traumatic brain injury or raised ICP Predict the physiological effects of acceleration, altitude and vibration on the transferred patient Recognise and manage in-transit emergencies (hypoxia, hypotension, accidental extubation, equipment failure) Hand over effectively at the receiving unit (SBAR/ISBAR) with complete documentation, and audit/learn from each transfer A ventilated TBI patient needs transfer to a neurosurgical centre 90 min away. Minute ventilation 8 L/min, FiO₂ 0.5 on a transport ventilator that uses ~1 L/min driving gas. How much O₂ do you carry? >Step-by-step calculation

    Decision points

    • Check gauges fully open before departure — gauge reads pressure, not volume.
    • Confirm receiving unit O₂ is connected on arrival before disconnecting cylinders.
    • If FiO₂ rises to 1.0, recalculate (consumption doubles → reserve halves).
    Step-by-step reasoning

    1. If pneumothorax untreated → insert chest drain BEFORE flight, not at altitude.
    2. Acute desaturation in flight = exclude tension pneumothorax (re-examine, consider needle decompression).
    3. Ignoring middle-ear/sinus expansion in conscious patients (severe pain on descent).
    4. Forgetting that recent diving (within 24 h) is a relative contraindication to flight (residual nitrogen).

entries.text:
# Patient Positioning in Anaesthesia Supine, lithotomy, lateral, prone (Wilson/Jackson/Relton-Hall), park-bench and sitting positions — pressure points, nerve injury, physiological effects, neuro-anaesthesia positioning Step-by-step reasoning Brachial plexus: arms tucked, shoulders padded, no shoulder braces (compress plexus against clavicle); arm boards <90° abduction, forearm supinated Eye injury: tape eyelids, protect from pressure; risk of ischaemic optic neuropathy in prolonged head-down — monitor and document Airway oedema: face/tongue swelling — assess cuff leak before extubation Pressure injury: gel pads at heels, sacrum, knees; reposition every 2 h if surgery allows Compartment syndrome (lithotomy): calf compartment pressure rises with steep Trendelenburg + lithotomy >4 h — calf relaxation periods and post-op monitoring Common traps Shoulder braces causing brachial plexus stretch palsy Hyperabduction (>90°) of arm boards Sliding cephalad in steep Trendelenburg — secure with bean-bag or shoulder support across the manubrium (not lateral) ("standard"); return ( Maintain physiological neutrality — joints in mid-range, spine aligned, no extreme flexion/extension/rotation, no traction on nerves. Distribute pressure — gel pads, foam, fluidised positioners; no skin-on-metal, no IV lines or ECG electrodes under the patient, heels floated. Protect the eyes and airway — lubricate and tape eyes (or use ProneView for prone), confirm ETT position and bilateral air entry after every move, plan for facial / airway oedema in prolonged head-down or prone cases. Anticipate and monitor the haemodynamic shift — preload swings on tilt, V/Q mismatch on lateral, cerebral hypoperfusion sitting/beach-chair, IVC compression prone. Anaesthesia and patient positioning for adults , published Anaesthesia 2020;75:1212-1223), the Association of Anaesthetists 2021 Management of Peri-operative Peripheral Nerve Injuries guideline ( ) and the on perioperative peripheral neuropathies are the standard references. Anti-slip strategy. The 2020 Association of Anaesthetists guideline ( ) and the 2021 guideline both recommend AGAINST shoulder braces / supports in steep Trendelenburg because of the risk of brachial plexus traction or compression regardless of where the brace is applied. Use a non-slip gel / vacuum mattress, a bean-bag or a memory-foam pad with the arms tucked at the sides instead. to the axilla (not the axilla). The “kidney rest” + table break opens the costo-iliac space for renal surgery. Anaesthetised + paralysed + open chest creates significant V/Q mismatch (ventilation to non-dependent compliant lung; perfusion to dependent lung). Turning to prone is a high-risk moment: a minimum of five trained staff, anaesthetist at the head controlling the airway, all monitoring disconnected from the patient side and reconnected once prone, eye care reapplied, ETT taped securely (consider switching to an armoured tube before turning), and bilateral air entry / EtCO₂ / SpO₂ confirmed before the surgeon scrubs. Prone positioning checklist — key visual cues Neutral head & neck — ear, shoulder and greater trochanter in one straight line; no rotation, flexion or extension; chin 2 finger-breadths off the chest. Face cut-out fit — forehead, malar eminences and chin take the load; eyes and nose suspended in the cut-out with zero contact ; ETT and circuit exit cleanly through the slot, retape and re-confirm depth after turning. Foam support contact points — chest rolls / bolsters from clavicle to iliac crest leaving the abdomen hanging free (check by passing a hand under it); ASIS padded, breasts and genitalia free of compression. — < 90° abduction at shoulder, elbows flexed, palms down, axillae free; or tucked at sides with neutral wrists. — pillow under shins so toes hang free, knees slightly flexed and padded, heels offloaded. tumours are usually done supine with a head turn; posterior fossa, cerebellopontine angle, vestibular schwannoma, microvascular decompression and foramen magnum work uses park-bench, sitting or prone. Cervical-spine surgery uses supine (anterior cervical discectomy) or prone (posterior approach). All of these typically use 3-pin Mayfield head fixation — anticipate the hypertensive response (treat with remifentanil bolus, lidocaine or LA infiltration). Park-bench position axillary compression. The head is pinned and rotated towards the floor for posterior-fossa / CPA access. Less VAE risk than full sitting and easier to set up; more limited surgical exposure than sitting. Sitting position Pre-op screen for PFO with bubble echo — a positive PFO is a relative contraindication because of paradoxical air embolism. Mandatory monitoring: precordial Doppler ± TOE, EtCO₂, EtN₂, invasive arterial line zeroed at the external auditory meatus, multi-orifice CVC at the SVC-RA junction. Avoid N₂O (expands intracranial air; converts micro-emboli into clinically significant VAE). VAE management: alert surgeon to flood field with saline + apply bone wax, jugular venous compression, aspirate from CVC, FiO₂ 1.0, position patient left lateral / head-down if able, supportive haemodynamics. Beach-chair position (shoulder surgery) Worst-offender position Ulnar neuropathy Supine (arms tucked, pronated) Supinate forearm, pad medial epicondyle Brachial plexopathy Steep Trendelenburg; lateral; arms abducted >90° Abduct < 90°, axillary roll caudal to axilla; AVOID shoulder braces (AoA 2020); use non-slip / vacuum mattress to prevent sliding Common peroneal (foot drop) Lithotomy, lateral Pad fibular head, boot-style stirrups POVL (ION / CRAO) Prone spine (> 6 h), steep Trendelenburg robotic Head neutral / above heart, no globe pressure, MAP > 70, document eye check 15-min Cerebral hypoperfusion / stroke Sitting, beach-chair Zero arterial line at tragus, treat hypotension Venous air embolism Sitting (25–45 %), park-bench, posterior craniotomy Doppler / TOE, EtN₂, CVC at SVC-RA, avoid N₂O ↓ FRC, atelectasis, ↑ shunt Trendelenburg, prone, lateral (anaesthetised) PEEP, recruitment, lung-protective ventilation ETT migration / endobronchial Prone, sitting, beach chair Re-check after every move, armoured tube, tape securely Macroglossia / supraglottic oedema Prolonged sitting, steep Trendelenburg Limit duration, cuff-leak test, plan delayed extubation Well-leg compartment syndrome Lithotomy / Lloyd-Davies > 4 h Lower legs every 2 h, avoid hypotension Pressure ulcer Any prolonged position Pressure-redistributing surface, float heels, reposition padding Minimal Standard Rich Diagram realism Preventing brachial plexus injury in steep Trendelenburg Tuck arms with padding, avoid shoulder braces and >90° abduction, protect eyes, periodic leg release for lithotomy, post-op assessment for compartment syndrome and airway oedema. Patient Positioning in Anaesthesia Surgical positions, dedicated operating tables, neurosurgical positioning and prevention of position-related complications Anaesthetist owns positioning shared with the surgical team — document position, padding, eye care and pulses checked AFTER every move. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is the commonest peripheral nerve injury after general anaesthesia (~28% of all anaesthesia-related nerve claims). Supinate the forearm and pad the medial epicondyle. Brachial plexus injury — abduct arms <90°, externally rotate; the Association of Anaesthetists 2020 positioning guideline recommends AGAINST shoulder braces in steep Trendelenburg (risk of brachial plexus traction / compression regardless of placement). Use non-slip / vacuum mattresses or bean-bags to prevent sliding instead. Common peroneal nerve at the fibular head is the commonest stirrup-related injury (lithotomy / lateral) → foot drop. Well-leg compartment syndrome risk rises sharply after 4 h in stirrups — consider lowering legs every 2 h on long Lloyd-Davies cases. Prone position must keep the abdomen FREE — abdominal compression ↑ IAP → ↓ venous return, ↑ epidural venous engorgement and ↑ surgical bleeding. Post-operative visual loss (POVL) is associated with prone spine surgery (>6 h, large blood loss) and steep Trendelenburg robotic surgery — keep head neutral or above heart, avoid direct globe pressure, maintain MAP. Sitting and beach-chair positions: ZERO the arterial transducer at the EXTERNAL AUDITORY MEATUS (Circle of Willis) — MAP measured at the heart overestimates cerebral pressure by 12–20 mmHg. Sitting position has a 25–45% incidence of venous air embolism — screen for PFO pre-op, use precordial Doppler/TOE, EtCO₂/EtN₂, multi-orifice CVC at SVC-RA junction. ETT migrates ~2 cm caudally on prone repositioning — re-confirm position and bilateral air entry after every turn; use a reinforced (armoured) tube. Principles of Safe Positioning Supine Position Trendelenburg & Reverse Trendelenburg Lithotomy & Lloyd-Davies Lateral Decubitus Prone Position & Operating Tables / Frames Positioning for Neuroanaesthesia Position-Related Complications — Summary Common Procedures by Position What are the physiological consequences of steep Trendelenburg? Increased ICP and IOP, cephalad shift of diaphragm with reduced FRC and atelectasis, increased airway pressures, facial and laryngeal oedema, conjunctival oedema, and increased risk of regurgitation. Cardiovascular: increased preload but reduced cardiac output if prolonged. Mitigate with limited tilt time, PEEP, and lung-protective ventilation. Which nerves are most commonly injured by intraoperative positioning? Ulnar nerve at the elbow (commonest — supine, arms tucked or abducted >90°), brachial plexus (shoulder abduction >90° or shoulder braces in Trendelenburg), common peroneal at the fibular head (lithotomy/lateral), and sciatic (sitting position). ASA Closed Claims show ulnar and brachial plexus injuries account for ~70 % of positioning claims. How is perioperative visual loss prevented in prone surgery? Avoid direct pressure on the globe (use Mayfield pins or a free-floating headrest with mirror check every 20 min), maintain head above heart, keep haematocrit >25 %, avoid prolonged hypotension, limit crystalloid, and consider staging cases predicted to exceed 6 h. ASA Practice Advisory on POVL (2019) recommends informed consent for high-risk prone spinal surgery. Describe the principal surgical positions (supine, Trendelenburg, lithotomy, lateral, prone, park bench, sitting, beach chair) and their physiological consequences List the operating tables and frames available for prone surgery (Wilson, Jackson, Montreal/Relton-Hall, standard table with bolsters) and choose the appropriate frame for the procedure Outline neurosurgical positioning (park bench and sitting) including head fixation, monitoring requirements and the management of venous air embolism Identify the pressure points and peripheral-nerve injuries associated with each position and the strategies used to prevent them Match common surgical procedures to the appropriate operating position Manage cardiovascular, respiratory, ophthalmic and airway complications related to patient positioning Flat silhouettes, no surface shading — fast, schematic. Balanced gown + drapes + lighting (default). }, ]; const RealismToggle = ({ level, onChange, }: { level: RealismLevel; onChange: (l: RealismLevel) => void }) => (

  1. Brachial plexus: arms tucked, shoulders padded, no shoulder braces (compress plexus against clavicle); arm boards <90° abduction, forearm supinated
  2. Eye injury: tape eyelids, protect from pressure; risk of ischaemic optic neuropathy in prolonged head-down — monitor and document
  3. Airway oedema: face/tongue swelling — assess cuff leak before extubation
  4. Pressure injury: gel pads at heels, sacrum, knees; reposition every 2 h if surgery allows
  5. Compartment syndrome (lithotomy): calf compartment pressure rises with steep Trendelenburg + lithotomy >4 h — calf relaxation periods and post-op monitoring

references.excerpt: Patient positioning is a shared responsibility between the surgical and anaesthetic teams. The anaesthetist retains particular responsibility for protection of pressure points, the eyes, peripheral nerves, the airway and haemodynamics during and after every position change. Joints should be kept in mid-range; eyes lubricated and taped; padded supports used at vulnerable nerves (ulnar, common fibular, brachial plexus); arms abducted no more than 90°; and steep head-down positions limited where possible because of the risks of raised intra-ocular and intracranial pressure, facial and airway oedema, and the patient slipping.

case_bank.title: Falling compliance during steep Trendelenburg laparoscopy
case_bank.text:
Case: Falling compliance during steep Trendelenburg laparoscopy (Respiratory, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient with a body mass index of 38 has robotic pelvic surgery in steep head-down tilt with a 15 mmHg pneumoperitoneum.
Presentation: Plateau pressure rises from 18 to 30 cmH₂O, tidal volume is unchanged, and end-tidal CO₂ climbs to 6.8 kPa.
Stage 1 — Interpret the pressures
  Question: Which measurement tells you about the lung itself?
  Model answer: Peak pressure reflects resistive plus elastic loads; plateau pressure reflects the elastic load after an inspiratory pause.
  Model answer: Driving pressure (plateau minus PEEP) reflects tidal strain on the aerated lung and is the pressure that tracks harm.
  Model answer: Here the change is elastic: reduced compliance from cephalad diaphragm displacement, abdominal insufflation and chest wall loading, not increased airway resistance.
Stage 2 — Separate lung from chest wall
  Question: Why does this distinction matter?
  Model answer: Total respiratory system compliance is the series combination of lung and chest wall compliance, so a stiff chest wall raises plateau pressure without proportionate alveolar overdistension.
  Model answer: Transpulmonary pressure, not airway pressure, determines alveolar stress; oesophageal pressure measurement can estimate it when decisions are difficult.
  Model answer: Accepting a somewhat higher plateau pressure may be safe if the rise is chest wall in origin.
Stage 3 — Adjust ventilation
  Question: What do you change?
  Model answer: Use 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, recruit and set PEEP of roughly 5–10 cmH₂O, and increase rate rather than volume to clear CO₂.
  Model answer: Ask for the lowest workable insufflation pressure and the least tilt the surgery allows, and check for endobronchial tube migration in head-down position.
  Model answer: Watch for facial and airway oedema, plan extubation after a cuff-leak and airway assessment, and expect atelectasis to require recruitment at the end of surgery.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Pneumoperitoneum and head-down positioning reduce functional residual capacity and compliance, promote basal atelectasis and increase both shunt and dead space; absorbed carbon dioxide adds to the CO₂ load. Because plateau pressure includes the chest wall contribution, a raised value in this setting does not automatically indicate injurious alveolar distension — driving pressure and, where measured, transpulmonary pressure are more informative.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Protective volumes, individualised PEEP after recruitment, adequate neuromuscular blockade, and rate-based CO₂ control are the mainstays. Monitor plateau and driving pressure with inspiratory pauses, follow end-tidal CO₂ with arterial correlation in longer cases, and recheck tube depth after position change. At the end of surgery, deflate the abdomen, recruit and assess airway oedema before extubation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not treat a rising plateau pressure as automatic evidence of lung injury or bronchospasm; define compliance and driving pressure, and separate lung from chest wall mechanics.
Take-home: Steep tilt and pneumoperitoneum reduce compliance through the chest wall: judge harm by driving pressure, use protective volumes and clear CO₂ with rate.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: respiratory mechanics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr054); Crit Care Med: stress and strain (https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0b013e31827417a6)

NAP4 found aspiration was the single commonest cause of anaesthesia-related death , but in most cases either RSI was omitted when indicated or basics (pre-oxygenation, suction, head-up tilt) were poorly applied — not failure of cricoid pressure itself. Evidence for individual RSI components Current practice 3 min tidal-volume or 8 vital-capacity breaths achieves ETO₂ >90%; head-up 20–25° + HFNO/THRIVE prolongs apnoea time, especially in obese/obstetric patients (Patel & Nouraei, Mandatory; aim ETO₂ ≥85–90%; routine apnoeic oxygenation in high-risk patients. Suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg Faster onset and superior intubating conditions vs rocuronium 0.6 mg/kg, but rocuronium 1.0–1.2 mg/kg is non-inferior (Cochrane 2015 — Tran et al.) and reversible by sugammadex 16 mg/kg. Either acceptable; rocuronium-sugammadex preferred when sux contraindicated (hyperkalaemia, burns >24 h, denervation, MH risk). "No ventilation" rule Gentle facemask ventilation at peak pressure <15–20 cmH₂O does not distend the stomach and reduces desaturation, particularly in critically ill ICU patients ( , Casey Permitted in obese, ICU, paediatric and obstetric RSI (controlled gentle ventilation). Opioid co-induction Sole-agent induction worsens haemodynamics; alfentanil/fentanyl/remifentanil obtund the pressor response and improve intubating conditions without measurable aspiration risk. Routine inclusion of a short-acting opioid (alfentanil 10–20 µg/kg or fentanyl 1–3 µg/kg). Choice of induction agent Etomidate causes adrenal suppression and increases mortality in septic shock (KETASED, Jabre , Matchett Intensive Care Med 2022 — higher 7-day mortality vs ketamine in critically ill). Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg first-line in shock; reduced-dose propofol/thiopentone if cardiovascularly stable. trial (Prekker 2023, n=1417 critically ill): VL improved first-pass success 85% vs 71% DL with no increase in adverse events. VL recommended as first-choice device for emergency intubation (DAS 2018; UK ICS). Cricoid pressure — the evidence IRIS trial JAMA Surgery 2019, n≈3,500) — multicentre RCT of cricoid vs sham during RSI. Aspiration 0.6% vs 0.5% (non-inferiority not formally met but no significant difference); cricoid prolonged intubation time and worsened laryngoscopic view in ~10%. The largest RCT to date — does not support routine use MRI/imaging studies (Smith 2003; Zeidan 2014) show the oesophagus lies lateral to the cricoid in >50% of adults, so compression often distorts rather than occludes it. Cricoid pressure can worsen the laryngoscopic view, displace the larynx, impede face-mask ventilation, and obstruct insertion of supraglottic airways — a particular concern in CICO. Force is poorly calibrated in practice — most assistants apply <20 N or >40 N unless specifically trained on a weighing scale. Current UK/European guidance DAS 2015 (unanticipated difficult intubation) & DAS 2018 (critically ill adult): cricoid pressure remains recommended for RSI but should be reduced or removed if it impairs laryngoscopy, mask ventilation, or SGA placement. OAA/DAS obstetric guideline 2015 : cricoid pressure retained given high aspiration risk and short pre-oxygenation reserve. Scandinavian SSAI 2010 and several French/German societies have downgraded or abandoned routine cricoid following IRIS. NAP4 explicitly stated cricoid pressure should not be considered a substitute for good RSI technique. Practical synthesis for the FRCA/FFICM viva Perform a modified RSI : ramped/head-up position, pre-oxygenation to ETO₂ >85% ± apnoeic O₂, opioid co-induction, ketamine if shocked, rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg or sux 1.5 mg/kg, videolaryngoscope first-line. Apply cricoid 10 N awake → 30 N asleep, but be prepared to release immediately if view is poor, mask ventilation difficult, or an SGA is required as rescue. Use gentle (peak <15 cmH₂O) facemask ventilation between induction and intubation in patients at high risk of desaturation (obese, septic, ICU, paediatric). Document the rationale for any deviation from classical RSI — defensible because it reflects current best evidence (NAP4, DAS, IRIS, DEVICE, EvK).     Introduction

    Emergency surgery accounts for a significant proportion of anaesthetic workload and carries substantially higher morbidity and mortality than elective procedures. The NCEPOD classification (immediate, urgent, expedited, elective) guides timing. Key challenges include incomplete assessment, full stomach, physiological derangement, and limited time for optimisation.

    NCEPOD Classification

    Preoperative Considerations

      RSI & Cricoid Pressure — The Evidence

      Classical RSI (pre-oxygenation, predetermined dose of induction agent + suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg, no bag-mask ventilation, cricoid pressure 10 N awake → 30 N asleep) was described by Sellick in 1961 from cadaveric and small case-series data. More than six decades later almost every component has been challenged by higher-quality evidence, and contemporary RSI is now standard UK/European practice.

      Aspiration — the risk being mitigated

      • Aspiration incidence under GA is ~1:2,000–10,000 elective and ~1:600–800 emergency anaesthesia (NAP4, 2011); mortality from clinically significant aspiration is ~5%.
      • NAP4 found aspiration was the single commonest cause of anaesthesia-related death, but in most cases either RSI was omitted when indicated or basics (pre-oxygenation, suction, head-up tilt) were poorly applied — not failure of cricoid pressure itself.

      • Risk assessment documented (P-POSSUM or NELA risk calculator)
      • CT performed and reported within 90 minutes of request if required (NELA 2021 standard)
      • Antibiotics within 1 h for known or suspected sepsis (local / national guidelines)
      • Consultant surgeon and anaesthetist present for high-risk cases (predicted mortality >5%)
      • Arrival in theatre within timescale appropriate to urgency
      • Goal-directed fluid therapy (cardiac output monitoring if high risk)
      • Postoperative critical care admission for high-risk patients
    • RSI — ketamine preferred if haemodynamically unstable; propofol with caution if stable
    • Arterial line and large-bore IV access pre-induction; consider CVC
    • Vasopressors drawn up and ready (metaraminol, phenylephrine, or noradrenaline infusion)
    • Anticipate large fluid shifts and blood loss — have blood products available
    • Epidural for postoperative analgesia (if coagulation normal and patient stable); alternatively rectus sheath block or TAP blocks
    • Temperature management — active warming throughout

    Emergency Appendicectomy

    Appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency. Typically affects young, otherwise healthy patients, but elderly patients may present late with perforation and sepsis.

      Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy

      A life-threatening obstetric emergency. Patients may present with catastrophic haemoperitoneum and haemodynamic collapse. The priority is rapid surgical haemorrhage control.

    • Do NOT delay surgery for investigations or optimisation — haemorrhage control is the resuscitation
    • Prepare for cardiovascular collapse at induction (loss of sympathetic drive)
    • Surgeon scrubbed and ready before induction — knife-to-skin within seconds
    • Cell salvage may be available but should not delay surgery
    • Anti-D immunoglobulin if Rh-negative
    • Emotional support — this is a pregnancy loss; debrief team and patient

    Intestinal Obstruction

    Patients with bowel obstruction present unique anaesthetic challenges including massive fluid shifts, electrolyte derangement, high aspiration risk, and abdominal compartment syndrome.

case_bank.title: Chronic prednisolone before colectomy
case_bank.text:
Case: Chronic prednisolone before colectomy (Steroid cover, Foundation)
Patient: A 64-year-old woman takes prednisolone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica and is listed for open right hemicolectomy.
Presentation: She is stable at pre-assessment. The surgical team has omitted all morning medicines and asks whether dexamethasone for nausea is enough steroid cover.
Stage 1 — Assess suppression and surgical stress
  Question: What determines whether she needs supplementation?
  Model answer: Prednisolone at or above 5 mg daily for more than four weeks makes HPA-axis suppression likely.
  Model answer: Open colectomy is major surgical stress.
  Model answer: Continue her usual glucocorticoid dose; do not create an additional withdrawal stress.
Stage 2 — Write the prescription
  Question: Prescribe a practical major-surgery regimen.
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours, or 50 mg IV six-hourly where an infusion is impractical.
  Model answer: Return towards the usual oral regimen as recovery permits, guided by clinical progress.
Stage 3 — Manage the postoperative risk
  Question: She becomes hypotensive and hypoglycaemic six hours after surgery. What do you do?
  Model answer: Treat adrenal crisis without waiting for confirmatory testing: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately.
  Model answer: Give rapid 0.9% saline, correct hypoglycaemia with IV glucose and check sodium, potassium and acid–base status.
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours and investigate simultaneous causes of shock.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Prednisolone 10 mg daily is above the dose at which clinically important HPA-axis suppression should be assumed after sustained use. Open colectomy produces major stress, while omission of her normal dose adds withdrawal risk. Antiemetic dexamethasone has glucocorticoid activity but does not by itself constitute a documented perioperative replacement plan.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue the usual steroid, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly while major stress persists. Monitor pressure, glucose, sodium and potassium, and restore oral treatment when absorption is reliable. Refractory hypotension, hypoglycaemia or electrolyte disturbance should trigger immediate adrenal-crisis treatment alongside a search for bleeding, sepsis and cardiac causes.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not delay rescue hydrocortisone for cortisol testing, and do not stop supplementation abruptly after major surgery. State the steroid route, timing, postoperative continuation and plan to return to baseline treatment.
Take-home: Major surgery in a patient with likely HPA suppression requires the usual steroid plus hydrocortisone at induction and continued replacement; dexamethasone used for antiemesis is not a substitute for a planned regimen.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Primary adrenal insufficiency and emergency laparotomy
case_bank.text:
Case: Primary adrenal insufficiency and emergency laparotomy (Steroid cover, Advanced)
Patient: A 36-year-old woman with Addison’s disease presents with perforated appendicitis, vomiting and fever. BP is 84/48 mmHg, glucose 3.1 mmol/L and sodium 126 mmol/L.
Presentation: She has been unable to take hydrocortisone or fludrocortisone for 24 hours.
Stage 1 — Recognise crisis
  Question: What is the immediate diagnosis and priority?
  Model answer: This is adrenal crisis until proved otherwise, precipitated by infection, vomiting and missed replacement.
  Model answer: Do not delay treatment for cortisol measurement; draw blood first only if it causes no delay.
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, rapid isotonic saline and IV glucose.
Stage 2 — Prepare for theatre
  Question: How should replacement continue?
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion, or 50 mg IV six-hourly.
  Model answer: Correct volume, glucose and electrolyte abnormalities and start source-control antibiotics.
  Model answer: Use invasive monitoring according to haemodynamic response and operative severity.
Stage 3 — Step down safely
  Question: What matters after source control?
  Model answer: Continue stress dosing while severely unwell, then taper according to recovery and endocrine advice.
  Model answer: Restart oral glucocorticoid replacement when absorption is reliable.
  Model answer: Fludrocortisone is generally unnecessary while hydrocortisone exceeds 50 mg daily because mineralocorticoid activity is adequate.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Known primary adrenal insufficiency, missed replacement, vomiting, infection, hypotension, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia make adrenal crisis the working diagnosis. The immediate mortality risk comes from glucocorticoid deficiency and severe volume depletion; treatment precedes biochemical confirmation.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, rapid 0.9% saline and IV glucose, then hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly. Correct electrolytes, give antibiotics and obtain source control. Taper only as illness resolves and oral absorption returns; hydrocortisone above 50 mg daily supplies adequate mineralocorticoid effect, so fludrocortisone is usually temporarily unnecessary.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Blood sampling is optional if it delays treatment. Persistent shock still requires evaluation for sepsis, haemorrhage and cardiogenic causes rather than attributing every abnormality to Addison’s disease.
Take-home: Known adrenal insufficiency plus acute illness, vomiting and shock is a treatment-first emergency: hydrocortisone, saline, glucose and definitive management of the trigger.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

The protocol delivers pre-thawed blood products in fixed 1:1:1 ratios (PRBC:FFP:platelets) via a rapid infuser, with point-of-care viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) to guide individual component therapy once available.", ], [ "What are the complications of massive transfusion?", "The major complications are: (1) hypothermia — warmed fluids and forced-air warming are mandatory; (2) citrate toxicity — citrate in stored blood chelates ionised calcium, causing myocardial depression and coagulopathy; treat with 10 mL 10% calcium chloride IV when iCa²⁺ 110 mmHg or MAP ≥80 mmHg at all times; (3) prevent hypercapnia and hypocapnia — target PaCO₂ 4.5–5.0 kPa (mild hypocapnia 4.0–4.5 kPa only if herniation suspected); (4) head-up 15–30° to reduce ICP; (5) osmotherapy with mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 3% 250 mL for signs of raised ICP; (6) urgent CT imaging and neurosurgical consultation; (7) avoid hyperglycaemia and hyponatraemia; (8) seizure prophylaxis if indicated. Hypothermia (core temp Step-by-step RSI plan Resuscitate before you intubate. Activate MHP, give 1 g TXA IV (CRASH-2 window: within 3 h), start 1:1:1 product through a rapid infuser. Damage control resuscitation (DCR) is a strategy for severe trauma that targets the of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy. Its four pillars are: (1) permissive hypotension — allowing SBP 80–90 mmHg in bleeding trauma without TBI until surgical haemorrhage control, to reduce clot disruption; (2) haemostatic resuscitation — using 1:1:1 ratios of PRBC:FFP:platelets rather than crystalloid; (3) tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2); and (4) limiting crystalloid to prevent dilutional coagulopathy. Active warming and early surgical control of bleeding are simultaneous priorities. When should a massive transfusion protocol (MTP) be activated? Activate the MTP when any of the following are met: anticipated need for ≥10 units PRBC in 24 hours, >4 units PRBC in 1 hour, haemodynamic instability despite initial fluid resuscitation, ongoing uncontrolled surgical bleeding, or a base deficit >6 mmol/L with tachycardia suggesting significant occult haemorrhage. The protocol delivers pre-thawed blood products in fixed 1:1:1 ratios (PRBC:FFP:platelets) via a rapid infuser, with point-of-care viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) to guide individual component therapy once available. What are the complications of massive transfusion? The major complications are: (1) hypothermia — warmed fluids and forced-air warming are mandatory; (2) citrate toxicity — citrate in stored blood chelates ionised calcium, causing myocardial depression and coagulopathy; treat with 10 mL 10% calcium chloride IV when iCa²⁺ <0.9 mmol/L; (3) hyperkalaemia — from extracellular potassium in stored PRBC; treat with insulin/dextrose, salbutamol, and calcium; (4) dilutional coagulopathy and thrombocytopaenia; (5) TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury); (6) TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload); and (7) hypomagnesaemia. Monitor ABG including iCa²⁺, K⁺ and temperature every 30 minutes during active MTP. What is permissive hypotension and when is it contraindicated? Permissive hypotension is the deliberate restriction of fluid resuscitation to maintain SBP 80–90 mmHg (or mean arterial pressure ~50–60 mmHg) in a bleeding trauma patient before definitive surgical haemorrhage control. The rationale is that restoring normal blood pressure in uncontrolled bleeding disrupts fragile clots and worsens haemorrhage. It is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in traumatic brain injury (TBI), where the injured brain has lost autoregulation and relies on adequate perfusion pressure — target SBP >110 mmHg or MAP ≥80 mmHg in TBI to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure and prevent secondary brain injury. When should tranexamic acid (TXA) be given in trauma? Give TXA 1 g IV over 10 minutes as early as possible, followed by 1 g IV infusion over 8 hours. The CRASH-2 trial showed a mortality benefit when given within 3 hours of injury. There is no benefit — and possible harm — if given >3 hours after injury, so timing is critical. TXA inhibits fibrinolysis by blocking plasminogen activation and should be administered in all trauma patients with significant bleeding or at risk of significant haemorrhage unless there is a clear contraindication such as subarachnoid haemorrhage where antifibrinolytics may increase thrombotic complications. How do you manage a traumatic brain injury (TBI) patient? : (1) prevent hypoxia — target SpO₂ >94% with early definitive airway if GCS ≤8 or risk of aspiration; (2) prevent hypotension — maintain SBP >110 mmHg or MAP ≥80 mmHg at all times; (3) prevent hypercapnia and hypocapnia — target PaCO₂ 4.5–5.0 kPa (mild hypocapnia 4.0–4.5 kPa only if herniation suspected); (4) head-up 15–30° to reduce ICP; (5) osmotherapy with mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 3% 250 mL for signs of raised ICP; (6) urgent CT imaging and neurosurgical consultation; (7) avoid hyperglycaemia and hyponatraemia; (8) seizure prophylaxis if indicated. Permissive hypotension is contraindicated in TBI. The lethal triad is the mutually reinforcing cycle of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy that develops during severe trauma and massive haemorrhage. Hypothermia (core temp <35°C) slows enzyme kinetics and platelet function; acidosis (pH <7.2) impairs clotting factor activity and fibrinogen function; coagulopathy leads to ongoing bleeding which causes more hypothermia and acidosis. Breaking the triad requires active warming, blood product resuscitation (not crystalloid), calcium replacement, fibrinogen supplementation, and rapid surgical control of bleeding. How do you choose an induction agent for a haemodynamically unstable trauma patient? Ketamine is the agent of choice in haemodynamically unstable trauma patients. At doses of 0.5–2 mg/kg IV, it preserves sympathetic tone, maintains cardiac output and blood pressure, provides analgesia, and is a bronchodilator — all valuable in the shocked polytrauma patient. Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg is an acceptable alternative and is often preferred in TBI because it reduces cerebral metabolic rate and ICP, though it can cause adrenal suppression. Propofol and thiopentone should be AVOIDED in hypovolaemic trauma patients because they cause profound vasodilation and myocardial depression, potentially causing cardiovascular collapse on induction. What is the role of TEG/ROTEM in massive transfusion? Thromboelastography (TEG) and rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) are point-of-care viscoelastic coagulation tests that assess clot formation, stability and lysis in real time. In massive transfusion they enable goal-directed therapy: a flat r-time / CT suggests give FFP; low alpha-angle / low fibrinogen amplitude suggests give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate; low maximum amplitude suggests give platelets; rapid lysis suggests give TXA. Using TEG/ROTEM reduces unnecessary blood product administration, identifies fibrinolysis, and allows individualised component therapy rather than blind fixed-ratio resuscitation alone. case_bank.title: Trauma inside the three-hour window
case_bank.text:
Case: Trauma inside the three-hour window (Antifibrinolytics, Foundation)
Patient: A 29-year-old arrives 70 minutes after a road collision with pelvic disruption, BP 82/46 mmHg and ongoing haemorrhage.
Presentation: The major haemorrhage protocol is active. A colleague asks whether TXA should wait for ROTEM.
Stage 1 — Make the time-critical decision
  Question: Should TXA be delayed?
  Model answer: No. Significant traumatic bleeding within three hours is an indication for early TXA; benefit is greatest when given promptly.
  Model answer: Give 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g over eight hours.
  Model answer: Do not delay haemorrhage control, balanced resuscitation, warming or calcium replacement.
Stage 2 — Use viscoelastic testing
  Question: What role does ROTEM play after initial treatment?
  Model answer: ROTEM/TEG guides fibrinogen, plasma and platelet therapy and can identify ongoing hyperfibrinolysis.
  Model answer: It complements rather than replaces immediate evidence-based TXA in early major trauma.
  Model answer: Trend physiology: temperature, pH, ionised calcium, lactate and surgical control.
Stage 3 — Avoid the timing trap
  Question: What if the patient arrived four hours after injury?
  Model answer: Routine CRASH-2 trauma TXA should not be started beyond three hours because benefit is absent and harm is possible.
  Model answer: Management remains urgent haemorrhage control and goal-directed resuscitation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: TXA inhibits plasminogen activation and limits fibrin breakdown. In significant traumatic haemorrhage, survival benefit is time dependent and greatest with early administration; viscoelastic results are not required before the first dose. Beyond three hours after injury, routine CRASH-2 treatment should not be initiated because benefit is lost and harm is possible.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g over eight hours while continuing definitive haemorrhage control, balanced blood-component resuscitation, warming and calcium replacement. Use ROTEM or TEG to guide subsequent fibrinogen, plasma and platelet therapy and track temperature, pH, ionised calcium and lactate.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: TXA is an adjunct, not a reason to delay theatre, interventional radiology or damage-control resuscitation. Always state the injury-to-dose interval.
Take-home: For bleeding trauma, TXA is a time-dependent adjunct: 1 g then 1 g over eight hours, started as early as possible and within three hours.
Cited sources: CRASH-2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60835-5)

# Critical Incidents Anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia, LA toxicity, awareness, can't intubate Step-by-step management NMBA + bronchospasm + shock + flush = grade 3 anaphylaxis. Stop trigger, call for help, note the time. Discontinue all suspect agents (NMBA, antibiotic, chlorhexidine). IM 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1,000) into anterolateral thigh, OR IV 50 µg boluses (5 mL of 1:100,000) titrated. Repeat every 1–2 min. Airway and oxygen. 100% O₂; deepen anaesthesia; treat bronchospasm with salbutamol/MgSO₄ if refractory. Fluid bolus. 20 mL/kg crystalloid (1–2 L); start vasopressor infusion if persistent hypotension. Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV (no proven mortality benefit but reduces biphasic reactions). Tryptase samples. ASAP after resuscitation, at 1–2 h , and a baseline at ≥ 24 h . Yellow-top serum, label with exact times. Specialist allergy clinic within 6 weeks (NAP6); document on anaesthetic chart and warning bracelet. Common traps Reaching for chlorphenamine/hydrocortisone before adrenaline — adrenaline saves lives, the others don't. Using IV adrenaline 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) — dilute to 1:100,000 first. Forgetting the baseline tryptase at 24 h — without it the acute level is uninterpretable. Missing chlorhexidine as a culprit (catheter coatings, skin prep). Step-by-step approach Recognise the pattern. Unexplained rising EtCO₂ + tachycardia + masseter spasm post-sux on a volatile = MH until proven otherwise. Hyperthermia is a LATE sign. Call for help and the MH trolley. Declare 'malignant hyperthermia' to the team. Stop triggers. Discontinue volatile, change circuit to vapour-free anaesthetic machine (or activated-charcoal filters), ventilate with 100% O₂ at high flows. Convert to TIVA. 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus . For a 70 kg patient = 175 mg = ~9 vials of 20 mg dantrolene. Repeat every 5–10 min up to 10 mg/kg until EtCO₂ and HR settle. Active cooling. Cold IV fluids, surface ice packs to groin/axillae, gastric/bladder lavage if temp > 39 °C. Stop cooling at 38.5 °C. Treat hyperkalaemia. Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL, insulin/dextrose, salbutamol; haemofilter if refractory. ABG, K⁺, CK (peak at 12–24 h), urine for myoglobin, coagulation (DIC). ICU minimum 24 h; refer to MH Unit (Leeds in UK) for IVCT muscle biopsy; counsel family (autosomal dominant). Quick dantrolene maths Each vial = 20 mg in 60 mL water. For 70 kg × 2.5 mg/kg = 175 mg → reconstitute 9 vials. Maximum 10 mg/kg = 700 mg = 35 vials. Stock check matters. Waiting for hyperthermia before treating — it's the last sign. Continuing volatile during preparation — change circuits IMMEDIATELY. Underdosing dantrolene because reconstitution is slow — assign one person to mix while another resuscitates. Missing rebound 6–12 h later — MH can recrudesce; ICU monitoring is mandatory. are the commonest cause (~60%), followed by antibiotics (especially teicoplanin), chlorhexidine, and patent blue dye. AAGBI/RCoA Management Algorithm Remove trigger, call for help, note the time Adrenaline IM 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) — repeat every 1–2 min. IV: 50 µg boluses if trained High-flow O₂, secure airway, IV access Fluid bolus: 20 mL/kg crystalloid Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV Take mast cell tryptase at presentation, 1–2 h, and a baseline at ≥ 24 h Refer to allergy clinic; document on records and warning bracelet . Incidence ~1:5,000–15,000. Mortality now < 5% with dantrolene. Early Signs ↑ EtCO₂ (earliest), tachycardia, masseter spasm, metabolic acidosis Late Signs Hyperthermia (> 2 °C/h rise), rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, DIC Treatment: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV Repeat every 5–10 min up to 10 mg/kg. Discontinue triggers, hyperventilate with 100% O₂, active cooling, treat hyperkalaemia. AAGBI LAST Protocol Stop injection, call for help ABCDE, secure airway, 100% O₂ Seizures → benzodiazepine (avoid propofol in cardiac arrest) If cardiac arrest → CPR, AVOID lidocaine/amiodarone/vasopressin Intralipid 20% : 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 15 mL/kg/h infusion (max 12 mL/kg total) communication / governance , and aftercare of staff and family 1. Immediate clinical management Call for help early — declare "cardiac arrest" out loud; activate theatre arrest call; second anaesthetist + ODP/anaesthetic assistant to the head; runner for drugs/blood. ALS algorithm adapted to theatre : turn off volatile/TIVA, FiO₂ 1.0, confirm ETT position with ETCO₂ (a sudden ETCO₂ drop is often the first sign), high-quality CPR — surgeons stop and step back from the field; consider open chest cardiac massage in cardiothoracic / abdominal surgery already opened. Reversible causes (4 Hs & 4 Ts) with anaesthesia-specific add-ons : anaphylaxis (give IM/IV adrenaline early), LAST (Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus + 0.25 mL/kg/min), MH (stop trigger, dantrolene), high spinal, gas embolism, haemorrhage, vagal reflex (e.g. peritoneal traction), tension pneumothorax (especially after CVC, brachial plexus, intercostal block), tamponade. Surgical control of haemorrhage takes priority alongside resuscitation — activate major haemorrhage protocol, give TXA, use cell salvage, accept permissive hypotension until source controlled. Decision to stop : by consensus of the senior anaesthetist and senior surgeon, after exclusion of reversible causes and an adequate ALS effort. Document time of death, rhythm, and last interventions. 2. Immediately after death is declared Preserve the scene : leave all lines, tubes, drains, drug ampoules and infusion syringes in situ — do not discard. Photograph the drug tray. The Coroner / Medical Examiner may require this. Document contemporaneously : anaesthetic chart, drugs given (with batch numbers), times, vital signs trend, interventions, who attended and when, decision-making. Bloods at the time of arrest if anaphylaxis is possible — mast-cell tryptase at 0, 1–2 h and 24 h. Stop the next case on that list. The remaining theatre list should usually be cancelled or transferred to another team. 3. Communication : a senior surgeon and senior anaesthetist together, in a private quiet room, as soon as possible. Use the patient's name; be honest about what happened and what is not yet known. Offer to view the body. Provide written follow-up contact. Apply the statutory Duty of Candour (CQC Regulation 20). Theatre team : brief "hot debrief" once safe — what happened, immediate welfare, who is following up. Avoid blame. Identify staff who should not drive home alone or continue clinical work that day. Hospital chain : inform clinical director, on-call manager, bed manager, mortuary, bereavement office, GP, and (if relevant) transplant coordinator. 4. Statutory & governance reporting Coroner / Procurator Fiscal : any death within 24 h of an anaesthetic, any unexpected death, death from a procedure, or death where the cause is uncertain — referral is mandatory. The body becomes the property of the Coroner and a post-mortem is likely. Datix / local incident reporting within 24 h. Serious Incident (SI) declaration via the trust governance team; trigger a Patient Safety Incident Investigation (PSII) under the NHS PSIRF. Medical Examiner scrutiny of the death certificate. External reporting where applicable : MHRA Yellow Card (suspected drug reaction), NRLS / LFPSE, MHRA medical device incident, NAP7 contribution, Specialist society registries (e.g. UK MH Investigation Unit, NIAA Anaphylaxis pathway). Mortality & Morbidity meeting in the department; anonymised case discussion within 4–6 weeks. 5. Staff welfare & second-victim support Recognise the "second victim" phenomenon — anaesthetists, ODPs, scrub teams and surgeons commonly suffer acute stress, sleep disturbance, intrusive recollection and loss of confidence. structured peer support (e.g. AAGBI/Royal College mentor, TRiM, occupational health). Avoid mandatory single-session psychological debriefing — evidence suggests it does not reduce PTSD. Consider time off from clinical duties; do not allow the involved anaesthetist to be the sole clinician for the next case. Provide ongoing follow-up — anniversary of the event, inquest preparation, Coroner's hearing support, GMC/legal advice via the medical defence organisation. Key references Suspected anaphylaxis at induction IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (or IV 50 µg titrated) is the immediate priority, followed by oxygen, fluids, and second-line agents. Send tryptase at presentation, 1–2 h, and ≥ 24 h, refer to allergy clinic, and document the suspected trigger on the patient's records. Rising EtCO₂ in a young patient on volatile Treat as MH: stop volatile, hyperventilate with 100% O₂, give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV repeated to effect (max 10 mg/kg), cool actively, and treat hyperkalaemia. ICU admission for ≥ 24 h with referral for IVCT and family counselling. Anaphylaxis Malignant Hyperthermia Accidental Awareness Death on the Table Critical Incidents Anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia, LAST, and accidental awareness Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (or IV 50 µg titrated) is FIRST-line — antihistamine and steroid are adjuncts only Tryptase: take at presentation, 1–2 h, and a baseline at ≥ 24 h — labelled with exact times MH: rising EtCO₂ + tachycardia is the earliest sign. Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeat to 10 mg/kg LAST: Intralipid 20% bolus 1.5 mL/kg, infusion 15 mL/kg/h. AVOID propofol, lidocaine, and amiodarone in arrest Awareness: NAP5 incidence ~1:19,000. BIS 40-60 reduces risk in TIVA; document, acknowledge, and refer for psychological follow-up NMBAs cause ~60% of perioperative anaphylaxis (NAP6). Chlorhexidine and antibiotics are next commonest Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) Local Anaesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) Accidental Awareness Under Anaesthesia What is the immediate management of a never event in theatre? Stop the procedure, ensure patient safety, escalate to consultant and theatre lead, preserve evidence (devices, packaging, monitor traces), follow local critical-incident pathway, complete a Duty of Candour conversation with the patient/family, and submit a Datix/StEIS report. A structured debrief and root-cause analysis follow within 72 hours. How is a hot debrief structured after a critical incident? Use the STOP5 model: Summarise the case, Things that went well, Opportunities to improve, Points to action, then Set a date for follow-up. Run within 30 minutes of the event, include the whole theatre team, focus on systems not individuals, and document outcomes in a learning log. When a notifiable safety incident causes moderate harm, severe harm, prolonged psychological harm, or death. The clinician must inform the patient (or NOK) as soon as reasonably practicable, provide a verbal and written apology, explain what happened, what will be done, and offer support. Failure is a regulatory breach (CQC Regulation 20). case_bank.title: Weak in recovery after rocuronium
case_bank.text:
Case: Weak in recovery after rocuronium (Renal, neuromuscular & autonomic, Intermediate)
Patient: An adult is extubated after laparoscopic surgery following neostigmine reversal judged on clinical signs alone. In recovery there is diplopia, weak grip, difficulty swallowing and oxygen saturation of 90%.
Presentation: Train-of-four monitoring is now applied and the ratio is 0.6 at the adductor pollicis.
Stage 1 — Explain the physiology
  Question: Why can a patient breathe yet still be significantly paralysed?
  Model answer: There is a large safety margin: about 70–80% of postsynaptic nicotinic receptors can be occupied before twitch height falls, so tidal breathing returns long before full recovery.
  Model answer: Fade during repetitive stimulation reflects presynaptic effects on acetylcholine mobilisation and is the sensitive indicator of residual block.
  Model answer: Upper airway and pharyngeal muscles are more sensitive than the diaphragm, so aspiration risk and airway obstruction persist at a train-of-four ratio below 0.9.
Stage 2 — Manage the patient now
  Question: What do you do immediately?
  Model answer: Give oxygen, support the airway, sit the patient up and stay with them; do not sedate the agitation.
  Model answer: Reverse residual block: sugammadex is effective for rocuronium and vecuronium even at deep levels, and can rescue inadequate neostigmine reversal.
  Model answer: Continue quantitative monitoring until the train-of-four ratio is 0.9 or greater, and reassess swallowing before any oral intake.
Stage 3 — Prevent the recurrence
  Question: What should have happened?
  Model answer: Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring whenever a neuromuscular blocking drug is given, from before induction until recovery.
  Model answer: Recognise that neostigmine cannot reverse deep block and has a ceiling effect; give it only when at least two or more twitches are present, and prefer sugammadex for deep block or when rapid, complete reversal is needed.
  Model answer: Consider potentiating factors: hypothermia, respiratory acidosis, hypokalaemia, hypermagnesaemia, aminoglycosides, renal or hepatic impairment and myasthenia.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Non-depolarising drugs are competitive antagonists at postsynaptic nicotinic receptors, but the junction's safety margin means clinical signs are insensitive. Fade reflects reduced acetylcholine mobilisation with repetitive stimulation and is why the train-of-four ratio, not twitch presence, defines adequate recovery. Residual block below a ratio of 0.9 is associated with impaired airway protection, hypoxaemia and postoperative pulmonary complications.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis is the standard; site the stimulator away from surgical fields and calibrate before relaxant administration. Sugammadex encapsulates aminosteroid relaxants in a 1:1 complex and works at any depth; neostigmine requires spontaneous recovery and is limited by acetylcholinesterase saturation. Document the recovery ratio before extubation and manage recovery-area weakness as an airway emergency.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not accept head lift, tidal volume or a subjective train-of-four count as evidence of full reversal, and do not give neostigmine for deep block. Quote the 0.9 threshold and the receptor safety margin.
Take-home: Clinical signs miss residual block: monitor quantitatively, reverse appropriately and only extubate at a train-of-four ratio of 0.9 or above.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: neuromuscular junction (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.02.003); Assoc Anaesth 2023: neuromuscular blockade (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.16114)

case_bank.title: Rising CO₂ and rigidity after sevoflurane
case_bank.text:
Case: Rising CO₂ and rigidity after sevoflurane (Analgesia & anaesthetics, Advanced)
Patient: A young adult receives sevoflurane and suxamethonium for emergency surgery. Masseter spasm is noted at induction.
Presentation: End-tidal CO₂ rises to 9 kPa despite increased minute ventilation, with tachycardia, generalised rigidity, temperature climbing 0.5 °C every ten minutes and mixed acidosis.
Stage 1 — Recognise and declare
  Question: What is happening and what are the first actions?
  Model answer: This is malignant hyperthermia: unregulated calcium release through a defective skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor causes sustained contracture, hypermetabolism and heat production.
  Model answer: Declare the emergency, call for help and the MH kit, stop all volatile agent and suxamethonium, and switch to a clean circuit with high-flow oxygen and total intravenous anaesthesia.
  Model answer: Ask the surgeon to stop or expedite closure, and hyperventilate to manage CO₂.
Stage 2 — Give definitive treatment
  Question: What drug and dose?
  Model answer: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenously, repeated as needed up to about 10 mg/kg, with several people reconstituting vials because preparation is the rate-limiting step.
  Model answer: Cool actively, treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis and arrhythmias, and expect myoglobinuria requiring fluid to maintain urine output.
  Model answer: Avoid calcium channel blockers with dantrolene, and continue monitoring in critical care for recrudescence and compartment syndrome.
Stage 3 — Follow up
  Question: What happens after the acute episode?
  Model answer: Continue creatine kinase, potassium, coagulation and renal monitoring in critical care for at least 24 hours.
  Model answer: Refer the patient and family to an MH investigation unit for genetic and in vitro contracture testing, and document the reaction clearly.
  Model answer: Plan future anaesthesia as trigger-free: vapour-free machine, total intravenous anaesthesia, non-depolarising relaxants and dantrolene availability.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Volatile agents and suxamethonium trigger uncontrolled sarcoplasmic calcium release in susceptible individuals, usually through RYR1 variants. Sustained actin–myosin activity and futile ATP consumption produce CO₂ generation, heat, oxygen debt, lactic acidosis, hyperkalaemia and rhabdomyolysis. The earliest and most sensitive sign is an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO₂ despite adequate ventilation; temperature rise is a later feature.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Treatment is simultaneous rather than sequential: remove triggers, give dantrolene early, cool, and correct metabolic derangement while a dedicated person manages drug preparation. Monitor invasive pressure, core temperature, gases, potassium, creatine kinase and urine output. Distinguish MH from thyroid storm, sepsis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, phaeochromocytoma and inadequate anaesthesia — all of which raise CO₂ or temperature but need different treatment.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not wait for pyrexia before treating, and do not forget that masseter spasm after suxamethonium is a warning sign. Quote the dantrolene dose and state that vapour must be removed with a clean circuit, not just switched off.
Take-home: Unexplained rising CO₂ with rigidity is malignant hyperthermia until proven otherwise: remove triggers, give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg early and cool aggressively.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: inhalational agents (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkg002); AAGBI/MHAUS malignant hyperthermia guideline (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.14257)
