# Anaesthesia in Resource-Poor Settings WHO–WFSA standards, draw-over vaporisers, ketamine, spinal-first practice, Lifebox, SAFE courses, global surgery Step-by-step approach Default to spinal anaesthesia. Hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% 2–2.2 mL gives a reliable T4 block, avoids airway management, preserves uterine tone and removes dependence on continuous oxygen and a ventilator. Pre-load and co-load. 10 mL/kg crystalloid; left lateral tilt or manual uterine displacement; vasopressor drawn up — phenylephrine 100 µg or ephedrine 6 mg boluses titrated to maternal SBP ≥ 100 mmHg. Plan for failure of spinal. If failed/inadequate or contraindicated: ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV induction with cricoid pressure, suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg, intubate, maintain on draw-over halothane/isoflurane in air with O₂ enrichment from the concentrator (target SpO₂ ≥ 94%, accept lower briefly if concentrator fails). Lifebox oximeter. Battery-powered, mandatory under WHO–WFSA standards — apply before induction. Oxytocin 5 IU slow IV after delivery; misoprostol 800 µg sublingual if oxytocin cold-chain has failed. Intrathecal morphine 100 µg (if available and trained monitoring exists) OR wound infiltration + paracetamol + diclofenac + pethidine PRN. Decision points Spinal first — ketamine GA only if spinal fails or refused; awake fibreoptic and TIVA pumps are not realistic. Confirm the concentrator works on the generator before induction; have a self-inflating bag (Ambu/Laerdal) at the head of the bed. Common traps Using high-dose volatile in air without O₂ enrichment — SpO₂ falls quickly, especially in anaemic obstetric patients. Forgetting that ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia — common in late presenters. Allowing the only working pulse oximeter to be moved to recovery before the patient is reversed. Choose regional first. Spinal anaesthesia with hyperbaric bupivacaine 2.5–3 mL gives 2–3 h surgical time and avoids airway management entirely. If spinal contraindicated (sepsis at puncture site, refusal, severe hypovolaemia): landmark sciatic + femoral block using lidocaine 2% with adrenaline (1:200 000), max 7 mg/kg — accept slower onset without nerve stimulator. Backup GA plan. Ketamine 1.5 mg/kg + midazolam 0.05 mg/kg, spontaneous ventilation via face mask with draw-over halothane 0.5–1% in O₂-enriched air. Avoid suxamethonium unless intubation truly required (limited monitoring of K⁺). Power and oxygen contingency. Concentrator fails when generator is off — keep self-inflating bag and a full E-cylinder in theatre. Do the case during generator hours where possible. Tetanus and antibiotics. Tetanus toxoid + immunoglobulin if status unknown; benzylpenicillin + metronidazole + gentamicin (Gustilo III). Wash-out is the analgesic intervention with the largest survival impact. Single-injection spinal is the highest-yield, lowest-risk choice when surgical time fits. Prefer halothane or isoflurane via draw-over over TIVA — pumps drain batteries and ampoules of propofol are scarce. Using ketamine alone without a benzodiazepine — high incidence of emergence phenomena in awake adults. Forgetting that draw-over vaporisers deliver lower concentrations at high minute volumes — consider supplementary IV agent if patient is light. Running concentrator and ventilator from the same socket on a generator switchover — both fail simultaneously. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED . The HIGHLY RECOMMENDED level is the irreducible minimum below which anaesthesia should not proceed. : trained anaesthesia provider physically present from induction to recovery handover : continuous pulse oximetry, intermittent NIBP, continuous clinical observation; capnography wherever a tracheal tube or supraglottic device is used : a reliable supply — cylinder, concentrator or piped — with a backup; means to deliver positive-pressure ventilation (self-inflating bag) Drugs & equipment : emergency drugs (adrenaline, atropine, suxamethonium, induction agent), suction, laryngoscope, range of tubes, IV access, fluids : dedicated area with oxygen, suction and oximetry until patient is awake and stable Oxygen concentrators : deliver 90–96% O₂ at up to 5–10 L/min, require electricity. Useful for enrichment of draw-over circuits and recovery. Vulnerable to dust, humidity and intermittent power. Cylinder oxygen : scarce and expensive. Reserve for transport, induction, intubation and emergencies. Maintain a full E-cylinder backup in theatre at all times. Self-inflating bag (Ambu/Laerdal): mandatory — provides positive-pressure ventilation independent of any gas supply. Reservoir bag attached to O₂ source delivers ≥ 85% FiO₂. : most LMIC hospitals run intermittent grid + diesel generator + UPS only for theatres. Plan elective lists around generator hours; identify which sockets are on UPS before induction. Lifebox pulse oximeter : WHO-WFSA endorsed, battery-powered, designed to survive humidity, dust and rough handling. Distributed with structured training in oximetry interpretation. Non-physician anaesthesia providers deliver the majority of anaesthesia in many LMICs (clinical officers, nurse anaesthetists, anaesthetic medical officers). Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (2015) target: ≥ 20 surgical/anaesthetic/obstetric specialists per 100 000 population. WHO Surgical Safety Checklist : simple, no-cost intervention reducing mortality and complications by ~30–40% across all settings. SAFE courses (Safer Anaesthesia From Education — Obstetric, Paediatric, OR) deliver context-appropriate refresher training; run jointly by AAGBI/WFSA with national societies. Mentorship and equipment : donations should match local capacity to repair/maintain — 'graveyards' of unused equipment are a common harm. Standardise to a small number of robust, repairable devices (e.g., Glostavent® anaesthetic machine). : visiting teams should support local services, not substitute for them; long-term partnerships and capacity building outperform short missions. Concentrator/power failure mid-case : switch to cylinder O₂, hand-ventilate with self-inflating bag, complete or pause surgery as clinical priority dictates. No blood available : tranexamic acid 1 g (CRASH-2 evidence within 3 h of trauma); permissive hypotension until surgical control; cell salvage where ethically/practically possible. LA toxicity without lipid emulsion : airway, ventilation, anticonvulsant (benzodiazepine), prolonged CPR — most centres now stock 20% Intralipid as part of the LAST kit; advocate for this provision. Difficult airway, no fibreoptic : prioritise awake intubation under ketamine sedation + topical lidocaine; surgical airway via cricothyroidotomy must be a trained, drilled skill. Emergency caesarean section with no reliable cylinder oxygen Single-shot spinal with hyperbaric bupivacaine, phenylephrine/ephedrine support and Lifebox oximetry is the safest default. Reserve ketamine RSI with draw-over volatile in O₂-enriched air for failed/contraindicated spinal. Plan uterotonics around the available cold chain. Open tibial fracture in a rural hospital with intermittent power Spinal anaesthesia is the default. Backup is landmark femoral + sciatic block; if both unsuitable, ketamine sedation with draw-over halothane in O₂-enriched air. Plan around the generator, keep a self-inflating bag and cylinder oxygen ready, and give tetanus prophylaxis and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Anaesthesia in Resource-Poor Settings Safe practice when oxygen, electricity, drugs and trained assistance cannot be assumed WHO–WFSA International Standards (2018) define HIGHLY RECOMMENDED minimums: trained anaesthesia provider, pulse oximeter, oxygen, suction, self-inflating bag, emergency drugs Pulse oximetry is the single highest-impact monitor — Lifebox provides robust, battery-powered oximeters specifically for low-resource theatres Default to regional/spinal anaesthesia when surgical access allows — independence from oxygen, electricity and ventilators Ketamine is the workhorse induction/maintenance agent: preserves airway reflexes, supports BP, runs without infusion pumps; combine with benzodiazepine to attenuate emergence phenomena Draw-over vaporisers (EMO, Diamedica DPA) deliver volatile in air ± O₂ enrichment from a concentrator — independent of compressed gas Always have a self-inflating bag (Ambu/Laerdal), Magill forceps and a working laryngoscope — these are non-negotiable even in austere settings WHO Surgical Safety Checklist reduces mortality by ~40% — adopt regardless of resource level; SAFE Obstetrics & Paediatrics courses build local capacity WHO–WFSA International Standards Anaesthetic Techniques of Choice Workhorse for caesarean section, lower limb, perineal and lower abdominal surgery. Independent of oxygen and ventilators. Hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% is the standard agent. Always have phenylephrine/ephedrine and IV fluid running. 1–2 mg/kg IV (or 5–10 mg/kg IM) for induction; 0.5 mg/kg IV top-ups for maintenance. Preserves airway and ventilation, supports BP. Combine with midazolam 0.03–0.05 mg/kg to reduce emergence phenomena. EMO (ether/halothane), Diamedica DPA, Oxford Miniature Vaporiser. Patient inspiration draws room air through the vaporiser; O₂ is enriched from a concentrator. Works with no compressed gas, no electricity for the vaporiser itself. Femoral, sciatic, brachial plexus (axillary/supraclavicular) using anatomical landmarks. Lidocaine with adrenaline extends duration and raises maximum dose to ~7 mg/kg. Ultrasound and nerve stimulators improve safety where available. Wound infiltration, TAP, ilio-inguinal blocks for hernia. Reduces opioid requirement when none is available. Ketamine is the workhorse: preserves airway reflexes and cardiovascular stability, provides analgesia and amnesia, can be given IM (5–10 mg/kg) or IV (1–2 mg/kg), needs no oxygen or ventilator, and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List. Combine with a benzodiazepine to reduce emergence phenomena. Mains electricity is intermittent, the single oxygen concentrator is shared with paediatrics, no piped gas, no opioids except pethidine, and one ampoule of phenylephrine in the cupboard. # Mass Casualty, CRM & Military Anaesthesia Major-incident planning (METHANE), triage (Sieve/Sort/MPTT-24), crisis resource management, damage-control resuscitation & surgery, deployed military Roles 1–4, CBRN and blast injury = [ [ "What is the difference between primary, secondary and tertiary triage?", "Primary triage (Triage Sieve) at scene uses walking/breathing/pulse-or-capillary-refill to assign P1/P2/P3/Dead in Step-by-step approach (METHANE → CRM) METHANE report from scene confirmed: Major incident declared, Exact location, Type (vehicle-as-weapon), Hazards (secondary device possible), Access, Number of casualties, Emergency services on scene. Activate hospital plan : cascade call, cancel all non-urgent activity, free theatres & ICU beds, surge anaesthetic and surgical rota, call blood bank for major haemorrhage stand-by. Establish command : Gold (strategic — exec on call), Silver (tactical — site MEDCO), Bronze (operational — ED/theatre/ICU leads). Wear tabards. Use action cards from the plan, do not rely on memory. Triage at the door : senior clinician using Triage Sieve → Sort. P1 (immediate) to resus, P2 (urgent) to majors, P3 (delayed) to minors area, P4/expectant to a designated area with palliation. Re-triage every 15 min. CRM principles : stay hands-off as MEDCO — your value is overview. Allocate teams (anaesthetist + surgeon + nurse + ODP) to each P1 bay; demand SBAR updates every 10 min; appoint a runner; use a whiteboard tracker for casualties and theatres. Damage-control resuscitation for haemorrhagic shock: permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90 mmHg, >110 if TBI), 1:1:1 RBC:FFP:platelets, TXA <3 h, calcium, warming, early surgical control. Avoid clear fluids. Theatre prioritisation : damage-control surgery first (haemorrhage control, bowel stapling, packs and abbreviated closure), definitive surgery later. Theatre coordinator allocates lists. Communication out : regular sit-reps to Gold; liaise with mortuary, police, families' liaison; debrief team in waves; preserve documentation for inquiry. Common traps MEDCO becoming a hands-on clinician — loses overview, decisions stall. Failing to re-triage — physiology changes faster than labels. Using crystalloid resuscitation in penetrating trauma — worsens dilution and coagulopathy. Forgetting CBRN — undress, decontaminate and don PPE before bringing casualties inside. Step-by-step (<C>ABC + DCR + DCS) Catastrophic haemorrhage first : apply / tighten CAT tourniquet to stump, direct pressure or haemostatic gauze to torso wounds. Then ABC. Airway & breathing : RSI with ketamine 1–2 mg/kg + rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (preserves BP), in-line stabilisation, eFAST and bilateral chest decompression (finger/needle) if any chest signs. : activate massive transfusion. Whole blood (low-titre group O if available) is the military standard; otherwise 1:1:1. TXA 1 g IV bolus + 1 g infusion. Calcium chloride 1 g per 4 units. Warm everything (Belmont / fluid warmer / blankets). Permissive hypotension SBP 80–90 mmHg until haemorrhage controlled. Damage-control surgery : laparotomy / thoracotomy as needed for haemorrhage and contamination control; pack, staple bowel, temporary abdominal closure (Bogota bag / negative-pressure dressing); revise amputation. <90 min in theatre. Critical care & tactical evacuation : continue sedation (ketamine + fentanyl), paralysis, lung-protective ventilation, ongoing blood products via en-route CCAST team. Forward to Role 3 for definitive surgery and ICU. : blast lung (delayed ARDS), tympanic rupture (always check), traumatic brain injury (tight CO₂/MAP), rhabdomyolysis, fat embolism, infection (early antibiotics including anti-Pseudomonal cover for war wounds). Using crystalloid in haemorrhagic shock — worsens the lethal triad (acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy). Definitive surgery at Role 2 — risks instability and second-hit inflammation; aim to abbreviate and evacuate. Forgetting to release tourniquets when haemorrhage is controlled — limb-threatening if >2 h without reassessment. Inadequate analgesia — ketamine 0.1–0.3 mg/kg boluses or low-dose infusion is the deployed analgesic of choice. : Major incident standby/declared · Exact location · Type · Hazards · Access · Number of casualties · Emergency services present : simple vs compound (infrastructure damaged), compensated vs uncompensated, natural vs human-caused, CBRN Hospital response phases : Activation → Reception & triage → Definitive care → Recovery & debrief Command structure : Gold (strategic) – Silver (tactical) – Bronze (operational); pre-printed action cards and tabards Know the environment — equipment, drugs, who is in the room and their capability Anticipate and plan ; verbalise the plan; "share the mental model" Call for help early — the senior, the porter, the runner, blood bank, theatres Leadership & followership : clear leader (hands-off when possible), explicit role allocation by name Communicate effectively : closed-loop ("give 1 g TXA" → "1 g TXA given"), SBAR, no ambiguity Distribute workload ; allocate the cognitive task to the leader, technical tasks to the team Use all available information (monitors, labs, history) and cross-check Mobilise resources : cognitive aids (checklists, action cards), pre-prepared kit, mass-haemorrhage proformas repeatedly; avoid fixation error; "Is the patient getting better?" Hot & cold debrief : psychological safety, learning not blaming, document for governance Permissive hypotension : SBP 80–90 mmHg until haemorrhage controlled (>110 if TBI). Avoids "pop-the-clot" rebleeding and dilution Haemostatic resuscitation : 1:1:1 ratio of RBC:FFP:platelets (PROPPR trial), or whole blood (military standard, growing civilian uptake) Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h (CRASH-2; CRASH-3 for TBI); maintenance 1 g over 8 h. Activate the plan, command and control with action cards, triage and re-triage, push damage-control resuscitation and damage-control surgery for P1s, and communicate ruthlessly. Hot debrief and welfare for the team afterwards. Forward military critical care: blast injury at a Role 2 facility Stop the bleeding, support physiology with damage-control resuscitation (whole blood, TXA, calcium, warming, permissive hypotension), perform damage-control surgery in < 90 min, and evacuate to definitive care under critical-care escort. The lethal triad — hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy — is the enemy at every step. Mass Casualty, CRM & Military Anaesthesia Major-incident planning, triage, crisis resource management, damage-control resuscitation and deployed military critical care Major incident = casualty load exceeds normal resources. Declared by first emergency service on scene; cascade activates hospital plan. METHANE message structures the alert: Major incident, Exact location, Type, Hazards, Access, Number, Emergency services. Triage Sieve (walking? breathing? RR? CRT or radial pulse?) → categorises P1/P2/P3/P4 within 30 s per casualty. RR <10 or >30 = P1 (current NARU 2021 threshold; legacy MIMMS uses >29). Circulation step uses CRT >2 s OR absent radial pulse (not a heart-rate cut-off). Triage Sort uses TRTS for in-hospital re-triage. Crisis Resource Management: leadership, role clarity, closed-loop communication, situational awareness, workload distribution, calling for help early. Damage-control resuscitation: permissive hypotension, 1:1:1 ratio (or whole blood), TXA <3 h, calcium, warmth, early surgical haemostasis. Damage-control surgery: abbreviated procedure to control haemorrhage and contamination, with planned return for definitive surgery once physiology corrected. Military Role 1 (point of wounding) → Role 2 (forward surgical) → Role 3 (deployed hospital) → Role 4 (home) — same paradigm informs civilian disaster pathways. CBRN casualties: decontaminate before treatment; PPE for staff; antidotes rehearsed (atropine/pralidoxime, hydroxocobalamin, dicobalt edetate). Defining and Declaring a Major Incident Triage Tools Pre-hospital, <30 s. Walking → P3 (delayed). Not breathing despite airway opening → Dead. Then RR <10 or >29 → P1; CRT >2 s or absent radial pulse → P1; otherwise P2 (NARU 2021 — no heart-rate threshold). In hospital. Scores RR, SBP, GCS to give Triage Revised Trauma Score 0–12. ≤10 = P1, 11 = P2, 12 = P3. Modified Physiological Triage Tool — RR <10 or >22, HR >100, GCS motor <6 = P1. Better discrimination for needs-immediate-intervention than civilian sieve. When demand vastly exceeds capacity (austere or wartime), the most resource-intensive may be designated expectant (P4) to maximise survivors. Ethically reviewed by senior team and documented. Length-based vital sign thresholds (e.g. JumpSTART) — children's normal ranges differ; do not apply adult sieve directly. Crisis Resource Management (CRM) Damage-Control Resuscitation & Surgery Military Anaesthesia & Critical Care Point of wounding / unit aid post. CABC, tourniquets, haemostatic dressings, decompression, IV/IO access, TXA, ketamine analgesia, basic airway. Combat Application Tourniquet, chest seals. Forward surgical capability. Damage-control resuscitation and damage-control surgery; small ICU footprint; blood-on-the-shelf (whole blood / 1:1:1). Aim: stabilise <90 min, evacuate. Deployed hospital with full surgical specialties, CT, ICU, blood bank. Definitive haemorrhage control, complex orthopaedics/neurosurgery, burns stabilisation. Equivalent to a UK MTC deployed forward. Home-base definitive and rehabilitative care (e.g. Royal Centre for Defence Medicine, Birmingham). Prosthetics, plastics, neuro-rehabilitation, mental-health support. Critical Care Air Support Team — RAF anaesthetists/intensivists with ventilator, monitoring, blood and pumps, transferring ventilated patients between Roles by C-17 / A400M. Special Casualty Categories Team Welfare, Debriefing & Governance What is the difference between primary, secondary and tertiary triage? Primary triage (Triage Sieve) at scene uses walking/breathing/pulse-or-capillary-refill to assign P1/P2/P3/Dead in <30 s. Secondary triage (Triage Sort) at casualty clearing applies the Triage Revised Trauma Score (GCS, RR, SBP). Tertiary triage occurs in hospital after initial resuscitation and continuously thereafter. What are the principles of damage-control resuscitation? Permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90 mmHg until haemorrhage controlled, except TBI), haemostatic resuscitation with 1:1:1 plasma:platelets:red cells, early tranexamic acid (1 g within 3 h — CRASH-2/MATTERs), avoidance of crystalloid, active rewarming, and rapid surgical haemorrhage control. How are nerve-agent (organophosphate) casualties managed? Don PPE and decontaminate before any clinical contact. Treat with atropine 2 mg IV repeated every 5 min until secretions dry, pralidoxime 30 mg/kg IV (reactivates acetylcholinesterase if given before ageing), and diazepam for seizures. Support airway, ventilation, and circulation. Avoid suxamethonium — prolonged paralysis. case_bank.title: Trauma inside the three-hour window
case_bank.text:
Case: Trauma inside the three-hour window (Antifibrinolytics, Foundation)
Patient: A 29-year-old arrives 70 minutes after a road collision with pelvic disruption, BP 82/46 mmHg and ongoing haemorrhage.
Presentation: The major haemorrhage protocol is active. A colleague asks whether TXA should wait for ROTEM.
Stage 1 — Make the time-critical decision
  Question: Should TXA be delayed?
  Model answer: No. Significant traumatic bleeding within three hours is an indication for early TXA; benefit is greatest when given promptly.
  Model answer: Give 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g over eight hours.
  Model answer: Do not delay haemorrhage control, balanced resuscitation, warming or calcium replacement.
Stage 2 — Use viscoelastic testing
  Question: What role does ROTEM play after initial treatment?
  Model answer: ROTEM/TEG guides fibrinogen, plasma and platelet therapy and can identify ongoing hyperfibrinolysis.
  Model answer: It complements rather than replaces immediate evidence-based TXA in early major trauma.
  Model answer: Trend physiology: temperature, pH, ionised calcium, lactate and surgical control.
Stage 3 — Avoid the timing trap
  Question: What if the patient arrived four hours after injury?
  Model answer: Routine CRASH-2 trauma TXA should not be started beyond three hours because benefit is absent and harm is possible.
  Model answer: Management remains urgent haemorrhage control and goal-directed resuscitation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: TXA inhibits plasminogen activation and limits fibrin breakdown. In significant traumatic haemorrhage, survival benefit is time dependent and greatest with early administration; viscoelastic results are not required before the first dose. Beyond three hours after injury, routine CRASH-2 treatment should not be initiated because benefit is lost and harm is possible.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g over eight hours while continuing definitive haemorrhage control, balanced blood-component resuscitation, warming and calcium replacement. Use ROTEM or TEG to guide subsequent fibrinogen, plasma and platelet therapy and track temperature, pH, ionised calcium and lactate.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: TXA is an adjunct, not a reason to delay theatre, interventional radiology or damage-control resuscitation. Always state the injury-to-dose interval.
Take-home: For bleeding trauma, TXA is a time-dependent adjunct: 1 g then 1 g over eight hours, started as early as possible and within three hours.
Cited sources: CRASH-2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60835-5)

Trial / Regimen
Cheng et al. meta-analysis (2006)
Multiple doses of steroids before extubation reduced post-extubation stridor (RR 0.26) and re-intubation rates. Single dose was ineffective.
François et al. (2007)
Methylprednisolone 20 mg IV every 4 hours for 12 hours before planned extubation. Reduced post-extubation laryngeal oedema (3% vs 22%) and re-intubation (4% vs 8%) in patients with a failed cuff leak test.
Recommended regimen
Methylprednisolone 20–40 mg IV every 4–6 hours, starting 12–24 hours before planned extubation (≥4 doses). Alternatively, dexamethasone 5 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 doses. Start once extubation decision is made — single doses at time of extubation are insufficient.
Who to treat
High-risk patients: failed cuff leak test, intubated >48–72 hours, traumatic/repeated intubation, female, history of post-extubation stridor. Not recommended routinely for all patients.
Post-Extubation Stridor Management
Assess severity:
Inspiratory stridor at rest = significant obstruction. Assess work of breathing, SpO₂, voice quality, and ability to clear secretions.
Nebulised adrenaline:
1 mg (1 mL of 1:1000) in 4 mL saline, nebulised. Causes mucosal vasoconstriction and reduces oedema. Onset 1–5 minutes, duration 1–2 hours. Can repeat. Monitor for rebound oedema.
IV dexamethasone:
8 mg stat if not already given prophylactically. Takes 4–6 hours for maximal effect.
Helium–oxygen mixture (70:30 or 80:20). Lower density reduces turbulent flow through narrowed airway, decreasing work of breathing. Bridge therapy only — does not treat the underlying oedema. Limited by maximum FiO₂ of 0.2–0.3.
CPAP or HFNO may splint the upper airway and reduce work of breathing while steroids take effect. Use cautiously — may delay re-intubation if deteriorating.

Post-Extubation Respiratory Support
High-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO):
Reduces re-intubation in low-risk surgical patients (OPERA trial) and non-inferior to NIV in high-risk patients (FLORALI-2). Provides PEEP effect (2–5 cmH₂O), humidification, and dead space washout.
Prophylactic NIV after extubation reduces re-intubation in high-risk patients (obesity, COPD, heart failure, hypercapnia). Should be applied immediately post-extubation, not as rescue after failure.
Do not delay re-intubation:
If NIV/HFNO used as rescue for post-extubation respiratory failure, re-intubation should not be delayed. The Esteban trial (2004) showed increased mortality with NIV for post-extubation respiratory failure compared with standard therapy — likely due to delayed re-intubation.
Physiological Mechanisms
Clinical Evidence
Practical Settings
Flow rate
Type 1 respiratory failure
40–60 L/min
Titrate to SpO₂ 92–96%
Start at 40 L/min and increase for comfort. Higher flows = more dead space washout and PEEP.
40–50 L/min
Start immediately post-extubation. Continue for ≥24 hours. Wean flow before FiO₂.
Pre-oxygenation / apnoeic oxygenation
60–70 L/min
Apply during pre-oxygenation, leave running during apnoea for RSI. Extends safe apnoea time.
Procedural sedation / bronchoscopy
50–70 L/min
Maintains oxygenation during conscious sedation. Use jaw thrust nasal prong positioning.
Palliative / comfort care
20–30 L/min
As needed
Lower flows for comfort. Reduces dyspnoea even without improving SpO₂.
Monitoring & Escalation Triggers
ROX index:
(SpO₂/FiO₂) ÷ respiratory rate. At 2, 6, and 12 hours: ROX ≥4.88 predicts HFNO success; ROX <3.85 predicts failure and need for intubation. Validated in pneumonia-related hypoxaemia.
Respiratory rate >30:
Persistent tachypnoea despite HFNO suggests high respiratory drive and risk of P-SILI from large tidal volumes.
Thoracoabdominal asynchrony:
Paradoxical breathing pattern indicates diaphragmatic fatigue and impending failure.
Accessory muscle use:
Worsening suprasternal or intercostal recession despite escalating flow/FiO₂.
FiO₂ ≥0.7 with no improvement:
Consider intubation rather than prolonged high FiO₂ HFNO. Oxygen toxicity and delayed intubation both worsen outcomes.
Contraindications & Limitations
Type 2 respiratory failure:
HFNO provides modest CO₂ clearance via dead space washout but is not a substitute for NIV in acute hypercapnic failure (COPD exacerbation). NIV remains first-line for pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6 kPa.
Base of skull fracture:
Relative contraindication — risk of pneumocephalus with high nasal flow (theoretical, case reports only).
Nasal obstruction:
Severe nasal polyps, septal deviation, or recent nasal surgery may prevent cannula placement.
Aerosol generation:
HFNO is an aerosol-generating procedure (AGP). Requires appropriate PPE and isolation in infectious cases (e.g., COVID-19, influenza, TB).
CPAP vs BiPAP
BiPAP (NIV-PS)
Single constant positive pressure throughout the respiratory cycle
Two pressure levels: IPAP (inspiratory) and EPAP (expiratory). Pressure support = IPAP − EPAP.
Ventilatory support
Does NOT augment tidal volume — not true ventilation. Splints airways and recruits alveoli only.
Augments tidal volume during inspiration. Provides true ventilatory support — offloads respiratory muscles and assists CO₂ clearance.
Effect on CO₂
Minimal direct effect on PaCO₂ (may improve indirectly by reducing WOB)
Directly reduces PaCO₂ by augmenting alveolar ventilation
Typical settings
5–15 cmH₂O
IPAP 12–20, EPAP 4–8 cmH₂O (PS 8–12 cmH₂O)
Primary indication
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, obstructive sleep apnoea
Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease)
Simple — can be delivered by any flow generator or ventilator
Requires dedicated NIV ventilator with trigger/cycle sensing
Key Clinical Evidence
Full face mask most common in acute setting (reduces mouth leak). Alternatives: nasal mask, total face mask, helmet CPAP. Ensure correct fit — air leaks reduce efficacy and cause eye irritation.
Starting settings (BiPAP):
IPAP 12–15, EPAP 4–5 cmH₂O. Titrate IPAP up by 2–5 cmH₂O every 10–15 minutes to target Vt 6–8 ml/kg, RR <25, improving pH/PaCO₂. Maximum IPAP usually 25–30 cmH₂O.
Starting settings (CPAP):
5 cmH₂O, increase by 2–3 cmH₂O to maximum 10–15 cmH₂O. Titrate to SpO₂ and work of breathing.
ABG at 1–2 hours to assess response. If pH not improving or worsening, escalate to intubation. Continuous SpO₂, RR, and clinical assessment.
Escalation criteria:
Worsening pH despite escalating IPAP, persistent RR >35, reduced consciousness, inability to clear secretions, haemodynamic deterioration, patient distress or non-compliance.
Weaning NIV:
As underlying condition improves, reduce hours of NIV use (e.g., 2h on / 2h off), then nocturnal only. Wean IPAP before discontinuing. Ensure adequate oxygenation off NIV before stopping.
NIV Failure — Predictors
pH <7.25 at presentation (success rate ~50% on ward; needs ICU-level care)
pH not improving after 1–2 hours of NIV
APACHE II score >29
GCS <11 at initiation
Pneumonia as cause of COPD exacerbation (higher failure rate than infective exacerbation alone)
Excessive secretions or poor cough
Poor mask tolerance or frequent removal

Disuse atrophy:
Complete diaphragmatic unloading during controlled ventilation activates proteolytic pathways (ubiquitin-proteasome, calpain, caspase-3), causing rapid type I and II fibre atrophy — up to 50% cross-sectional area loss within 5 days.
Oxidative stress:
Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production increases within hours of CMV, driving protein oxidation and lipid peroxidation in diaphragm myofibres.
Structural remodelling:
Sarcomere disruption, myofilament protein degradation (myosin heavy chain loss), and impaired excitation-contraction coupling reduce force-generating capacity.
Mitochondrial dysfunction:
Decreased mitochondrial biogenesis and increased autophagy lead to reduced ATP production and further contractile impairment.
Concurrent ICU insults:
Sepsis, corticosteroids, NMBAs, systemic inflammation, and malnutrition compound diaphragmatic injury beyond mechanical ventilation alone (ICU-acquired diaphragm weakness).
Risk Factors
Ultrasound Assessment of the Diaphragm
Diaphragm Thickness (Tdi) — Zone of Apposition
High-frequency linear (10–15 MHz) at the zone of apposition (8th–10th intercostal space, anterior axillary line)
Normal Tdi:
1.5–5.0 mm at end-expiration (FRC)
Tdi <2.0 mm at end-expiration suggests significant atrophy and predicts weaning failure
Rate of atrophy:
>10% decrease in Tdi over 72 hours is associated with prolonged ventilation (Zambon et al., 2017)
Diaphragm Thickening Fraction (TFdi)
TFdi = (Tdi
− Tdi
) / Tdi
TFdi >30–36% during spontaneous breathing
Weaning predictor:
TFdi >30% predicts successful extubation (DiNino et al., 2014). TFdi <20% associated with weaning failure.
Optimal effort:
TFdi 15–30% during assisted ventilation suggests appropriate level of diaphragmatic loading — both under- and over-assistance are harmful (Goligher et al., 2018)
Diaphragm Excursion
Low-frequency curvilinear (3–5 MHz) subcostal, using M-mode to measure dome excursion
Normal excursion:
≥10 mm during tidal breathing, ≥40 mm during deep breathing
Excursion <10 mm or paradoxical movement (cephalad during inspiration) indicates paralysis or severe weakness
Prevention & Management Strategies
Monitoring Diaphragmatic Effort
Airway occlusion pressure at 100 ms — reflects respiratory drive. Target 1–4 cmH₂O. <1 = low effort (over-assisted); >4 = excessive effort (under-assisted or high load).
Electrical activity of the diaphragm (Edi):
Measured via specialised nasogastric catheter (NAVA). Reflects neural respiratory drive. Edi <5 µV suggests excessive unloading; Edi >15 µV suggests excessive loading.
Transdiaphragmatic pressure (Pdi):
Gold standard for diaphragm strength — requires oesophageal and gastric balloon catheters. Pdi
<11 cmH₂O after magnetic phrenic nerve stimulation confirms severe weakness.
Serial ultrasound:
Repeat Tdi and TFdi measurements every 48–72 hours to track trajectory. A decreasing Tdi trend should prompt reduction in ventilatory support if clinically safe.

ICUAW is independently associated with prolonged ventilation, weaning failure, increased ICU/hospital mortality, and long-term functional disability.
Critical Illness Polyneuropathy (CIP)
Primary axonal degeneration of motor and sensory peripheral nerves. Microvascular injury from sepsis-driven cytokine-mediated endoneural oedema and ischaemia.
Symmetrical, flaccid limb weakness (distal > proximal). Reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes. Sensory loss may be present but difficult to assess in sedated patients.
Reduced compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes with preserved conduction velocities (axonal pattern). Sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) also reduced. Fibrillation potentials on needle EMG.
Slow and often incomplete — axonal regeneration occurs at ~1 mm/day. Severe cases may have persistent weakness at 1–2 years.
Critical Illness Myopathy (CIM)
Selective loss of thick myosin filaments, type II fibre atrophy, and muscle membrane inexcitability (channelopathy). Corticosteroids and NMBAs are major contributors.
Symmetrical proximal > distal weakness. Facial muscles often spared. Reflexes may be preserved (unlike CIP). Diaphragm involvement contributes to weaning failure.

references.excerpt: We recommend using low tidal volume (4–8 mL/kg of predicted body weight) ventilation over higher tidal volumes in adult patients with ARDS. case_bank.title: Confusing gas in acute-on-chronic respiratory failure
case_bank.text:
Case: Confusing gas in acute-on-chronic respiratory failure (Acid–base, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with severe COPD on long-term oxygen presents drowsy after three days of increasing breathlessness. Gas on 60% oxygen: pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 9.8 kPa, PaO₂ 9.0 kPa, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L, lactate 1.2 mmol/L.
Presentation: The referring team says the gas is 'normal for him'.
Stage 1 — Interpret the gas
  Question: Is this chronic or acute?
  Model answer: Bicarbonate of 32 mmol/L indicates established renal compensation for chronic hypercapnia, which takes days.
  Model answer: The pH of 7.22 is far too low for fully compensated chronic retention, so there is an acute rise in PaCO₂ on top of a chronic state.
  Model answer: Uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen has probably worsened hypercapnia by increasing dead space through reversal of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, the Haldane effect and reduced ventilatory drive.
Stage 2 — Treat immediately
  Question: What do you do first?
  Model answer: Titrate oxygen to a target saturation of 88–92% using a controlled delivery device, and repeat the gas within 30–60 minutes.
  Model answer: Give bronchodilators, corticosteroid, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and treat any coexisting heart failure.
  Model answer: Start non-invasive ventilation for persistent respiratory acidosis, with a documented escalation plan.
Stage 3 — Plan escalation
  Question: When would you intubate, and what ventilator settings?
  Model answer: Intubate for failure of non-invasive ventilation, exhaustion, reduced consciousness, inability to protect the airway or haemodynamic instability, taking prior function and patient wishes into account.
  Model answer: Set a long expiratory time with low rate, tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, and permissive hypercapnia targeting pH rather than normal PaCO₂.
  Model answer: Monitor intrinsic PEEP with an expiratory hold and watch for barotrauma and haemodynamic compromise from hyperinflation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Chronic hypercapnia with renal bicarbonate retention shifts the baseline, so pH — not PaCO₂ — indicates acuity. A patient in whom pH is markedly reduced with a raised bicarbonate has an acute-on-chronic picture demanding intervention. Excess oxygen contributes through several mechanisms, of which increased physiological dead space is the dominant one, so controlled oxygen therapy is treatment, not restraint.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Controlled oxygen, bronchodilation, steroid, treatment of infection and early non-invasive ventilation form the bundle. Reassess gases serially, monitor conscious level and work of breathing, and agree ceilings of treatment early with the patient and family. If invasive ventilation is needed, prioritise expiratory time, accept hypercapnia, avoid dynamic hyperinflation and check intrinsic PEEP.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not accept 'this is his normal gas' when pH is low, and do not remove oxygen entirely. Quote the 88–92% target and the pH-based interpretation of chronicity.
Take-home: Judge acuity by pH, not PaCO₂: acute-on-chronic hypercapnia needs controlled oxygen at 88–92% and early non-invasive ventilation.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: COPD and ventilation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkr054); BJA Educ: acid–base interpretation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx008)

case_bank.title: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS
case_bank.text:
Case: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS (Ventilation, Advanced)
Patient: A patient ventilated for pneumonia has a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa on PEEP 12 cmH₂O, bilateral infiltrates and no evidence of cardiac failure.
Presentation: Tidal volume is 9 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau pressure 32 cmH₂O and driving pressure 20 cmH₂O.
Stage 1 — Make the diagnosis
  Question: Does this meet ARDS criteria?
  Model answer: Yes: acute onset within one week, bilateral infiltrates not fully explained by effusion or collapse, no primary cardiogenic cause, and hypoxaemia on at least 5 cmH₂O PEEP.
  Model answer: A PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa (roughly 90 mmHg over FiO₂ 1.0 equivalents) falls in the moderate-to-severe range.
  Model answer: Severity is graded by this ratio and guides therapies such as proning and neuromuscular blockade.
Stage 2 — Correct the ventilation
  Question: What immediate changes are needed?
  Model answer: Reduce tidal volume to 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, keep plateau pressure below 30 cmH₂O and driving pressure below about 15 cmH₂O.
  Model answer: Titrate PEEP to oxygenation and compliance, accept permissive hypercapnia while pH is tolerable, and use conservative fluid management once shock has resolved.
  Model answer: Optimise sedation and consider neuromuscular blockade for severe dyssynchrony.
Stage 3 — Escalate
  Question: What next if hypoxaemia persists?
  Model answer: Prone for at least 16 hours per day when the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio remains below about 20 kPa: PROSEVA showed a substantial mortality reduction in severe ARDS.
  Model answer: Treat the cause with source control and appropriate antimicrobials, and exclude a superimposed pneumothorax or effusion.
  Model answer: Refer early for extracorporeal support if hypoxaemia or hypercapnic acidosis is refractory despite optimal ventilation and proning.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: ARDS is a heterogeneous, inflammatory lung injury in which the aerated compartment is small; delivering normal tidal volumes to a 'baby lung' produces high strain, ventilator-induced injury and biotrauma. Driving pressure captures tidal strain on the aerated lung and correlates with mortality. Proning improves outcome by making transpulmonary pressure and ventilation more homogeneous, recruiting dorsal lung and improving ventilation–perfusion matching.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Deliver the ARDSNet strategy consistently: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau under 30 cmH₂O, individualised PEEP, permissive hypercapnia and conservative fluids. Monitor plateau and driving pressure with inspiratory holds, follow gases and compliance trends, and prone with a trained team and a checklist for line, tube and pressure-area safety. Escalate to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation early rather than after prolonged injurious ventilation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not use actual body weight for tidal volume, and do not chase a normal PaCO₂. State the Berlin criteria and quote PROSEVA's 16-hour minimum.
Take-home: ARDS management is protective ventilation by predicted body weight plus early prolonged proning in severe disease, not higher volumes or normal CO₂.
Cited sources: Berlin definition of ARDS (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.5669); ARDSNet low tidal volume trial (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200005043421801); PROSEVA 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214103)

case_bank.title: Hypotension after intubating life-threatening asthma
case_bank.text:
Case: Hypotension after intubating life-threatening asthma (Ventilation, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with life-threatening asthma is intubated after failing to respond to nebulisers and magnesium.
Presentation: Minutes later the pressure falls to 70/40 mmHg with rising peak pressures, a rate of 22 breaths per minute, tidal volume 8 mL/kg and no audible wheeze.
Stage 1 — Generate a differential
  Question: What are the causes and how do you distinguish them?
  Model answer: Dynamic hyperinflation with intrinsic PEEP is commonest: incomplete exhalation raises intrathoracic pressure and impedes venous return.
  Model answer: Tension pneumothorax must be excluded urgently by examination and ultrasound.
  Model answer: Also consider induction drug vasodilation, hypovolaemia, sedation-related sympatholysis and anaphylaxis as a precipitant.
Stage 2 — Confirm and relieve hyperinflation
  Question: What do you do at the bedside?
  Model answer: Disconnect the circuit briefly and allow prolonged exhalation, watching for haemodynamic improvement — a diagnostic and therapeutic manoeuvre.
  Model answer: Measure intrinsic PEEP with an expiratory hold and inspect the expiratory flow waveform for failure to return to baseline.
  Model answer: Give fluid and vasopressor while reducing the ventilatory load.
Stage 3 — Set the ventilator
  Question: What settings and drugs follow?
  Model answer: Low rate (about 8–12 breaths per minute), tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, high inspiratory flow to maximise expiratory time, and permissive hypercapnia targeting pH rather than PaCO₂.
  Model answer: Continue inhaled beta-2 agonist and ipratropium through the circuit, systemic corticosteroid and magnesium; consider intravenous salbutamol, aminophylline or ketamine as adjuncts.
  Model answer: Use deep sedation with or without neuromuscular blockade to abolish dyssynchrony, and monitor for barotrauma and myopathy.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Severe expiratory flow limitation means each breath begins before the previous one is complete, so alveolar volume and pressure accumulate. The resulting intrinsic PEEP raises right atrial pressure, reduces venous return and can mimic tamponade or tension pneumothorax; it also increases the trigger threshold, producing dyssynchrony. A silent chest indicates minimal airflow, not improvement.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Treat hyperinflation by giving time to exhale: reduce rate and minute ventilation, shorten inspiratory time, and tolerate hypercapnia. Confirm with an expiratory hold and flow-waveform inspection, and exclude pneumothorax with ultrasound or chest radiograph. Continue maximal bronchodilation and steroid, provide adequate sedation, and monitor pH, potassium and lactate — the latter two are commonly deranged by high-dose beta-2 agonists.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not increase the respiratory rate to correct hypercapnia in acute severe asthma, and do not interpret a silent chest as resolution. Name the disconnection test and the expiratory hold measurement.
Take-home: Hypotension after intubating asthma is usually dynamic hyperinflation: disconnect, slow the rate, allow long expiration and accept hypercapnia.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: severe asthma in critical care (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.10.004); BJA Educ: COPD and ventilation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkr054)

diffuse alveolar damage (DAD)
— a stereotyped inflammatory injury to the alveolar–capillary unit triggered by a wide variety of pulmonary (direct) or extra-pulmonary (indirect) insults. The pathological course is conventionally divided into three overlapping phases: an early
phase (0–7 days) of barrier breakdown and protein-rich oedema, a
phase (7–21 days) of epithelial repair, and, in a minority, a late
phase (>3 weeks) of collagen deposition and persistent functional impairment.
“baby lung”
: a small aerated compartment surrounded by flooded and atelectatic units.
true intrapulmonary shunt
(perfused but unventilated alveoli) producing refractory hypoxaemia, and
increased dead space
from microthrombosis and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, raising pulmonary vascular resistance and risking acute cor pulmonale. Because oxygenation depends on opening these collapsed units, hypoxaemia responds far better to PEEP and prone positioning than to raising FiO₂ alone.

This pathophysiology underpins the lung-protective strategy proven to reduce mortality: low tidal volume (6 mL/kg IBW), plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O, driving pressure ≤15 cmH₂O, individualised PEEP, and early prone positioning in moderate–severe disease.

patient selection, timing of initiation, daily duration, and the number of sessions delivered
Patient selection — who benefits
Moderate–severe ARDS
: PaO₂/FiO₂ <150 mmHg on FiO₂ ≥0.6 and PEEP ≥5 cmH₂O (PROSEVA entry criteria).
Earlier trials (Gattinoni 2001, Guérin 2004, Taccone 2009 "Prone-Supine II", Mancebo 2006) enrolled milder disease or used shorter sessions and showed
mortality benefit — meta-analyses (Sud 2014, Beitler 2014, Munshi 2017) confirm benefit is restricted to P/F <150 and ≥12–16 h/session.
Timing of initiation — "early and after stabilisation"
(Guérin, NEJM 2013): proned
within 12–24 h
of meeting moderate–severe criteria, after a
12–24 h stabilisation period
on lung-protective ventilation (Vt 6 mL/kg, plateau ≤30, FiO₂ ≥0.6, PEEP ≥5). 28-day mortality 16.0% vs 32.8% (HR 0.39); 90-day mortality 23.6% vs 41.0%.
The stabilisation window matters: ~15% of patients improve sufficiently with lung-protective ventilation alone and no longer meet criteria — these patients do not benefit from proning and incur its risk profile.
ESICM 2023 and ATS/ESICM/SCCM 2024 guidelines: initiate proning
within the first 36 hours
of meeting criteria; do not delay for trials of recruitment or NMB alone.
Late proning (after >48–72 h of mechanical ventilation) is associated with attenuated benefit — fibroproliferative changes reduce recruitability ("baby lung" becomes fixed).
Duration per session — the 16-hour rule
≥16 h/day
is the evidence-based dose (PROSEVA mean 17 h/session). Shorter sessions (8 h in Gattinoni 2001, ~8 h in Taccone 2009) did not improve survival.
Mechanistic rationale: oxygenation improves within 1–2 h, but alveolar recruitment and resolution of dorsal atelectasis continue over 12–16 h. Premature supination causes derecruitment and a "yo-yo" effect.
Practical UK delivery: turn in the morning (e.g. 09:00) and return supine the next morning, giving ~16–18 h prone with a 6–8 h supine window for line/skin care, bronchoscopy, and re-assessment.
Number of sessions — when to stop
PROSEVA delivered a
median of 4 sessions
(IQR 2–8) per patient; benefit was seen across this range.
Continue proning
while the patient remains in moderate–severe ARDS (P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6, PEEP ≥10) — each session offers incremental benefit.
Stop criteria
(PROSEVA, widely adopted): in the supine position for ≥4 h after a prone session, PaO₂/FiO₂ ≥150 with PEEP ≤10 and FiO₂ ≤0.6. Other reasons to stop: life-threatening complication (unplanned extubation, displaced lines, haemodynamic collapse, severe pressure injury), or transition to palliation/ECMO.
There is
no fixed maximum
: case series and COVID-19 cohorts report 5–10+ sessions in responders; durability of oxygenation response (rather than first-session response alone) predicts survival.
"Non-responders" (no improvement in P/F or compliance after 2–3 sessions) should prompt re-evaluation: consider ECMO referral (EOLIA criteria), reassess for unaddressed causes (fluid overload, ventilator dyssynchrony, undrained pleural collection, secondary infection).
Awake proning (non-intubated, predominantly COVID-era evidence)
Meta-trial (Ehrmann, Lancet Respir Med 2021): in COVID-19 hypoxaemic respiratory failure on HFNO, awake proning reduced intubation (HR 0.75) but not mortality. Effect size proportional to time prone — target ≥8 h/day (often split into 2–4 h blocks).
Outside COVID-19 the evidence is weaker; awake proning is reasonable in cooperative patients on HFNO/NIV but should not delay intubation in clinical deterioration.
⚠ Contraindications & key complications
unstable spinal/pelvic fracture, open abdomen, raised ICP unmonitored, severe haemodynamic instability, recent sternotomy/anterior tracheostomy (relative — needs head-out frame).
facial & chest-wall pressure injury (highest with multiple sessions — daily skin review), endotracheal tube displacement/obstruction, line/drain dislodgement, brachial-plexus injury, vomiting/aspiration, transient haemodynamic dip on turning, ischaemic optic neuropathy. A trained turning team (≥5 staff) and a written checklist (eyes taped, NG decompressed, lines cleared, FiO₂ 1.0 for the turn) materially reduce adverse events.

High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation (HFOV)
(Ferguson, NEJM 2013): stopped early for
— in-hospital mortality 47% vs 35% (RR 1.33), with more vasopressor and sedation use.
(Young, NEJM 2013): no mortality difference (41.7% vs 41.1%); no benefit.
Subsequent meta-analyses (Sud 2016) confirm no overall benefit and possible harm in moderate–severe ARDS.
Current role:
not recommended as a routine strategy (ATS/ESICM/SCCM 2023). Occasionally considered as rescue in highly selected centres, but ECMO referral is generally preferred.
Inhaled Nitric Oxide (iNO) and inhaled prostacyclin (epoprostenol / iloprost)
Cochrane (Gebistorf 2016, 14 RCTs, n=1303):
no mortality benefit; transient oxygenation improvement only;
increased risk of AKI
(RR 1.59).
Oxygenation response is not durable beyond 24–48 h (tachyphylaxis); rebound pulmonary hypertension on abrupt withdrawal.
Cost: £2,000–£5,000 per patient per day.

Recruitment manoeuvres & high-PEEP "open-lung" strategy
Earlier trials (ALVEOLI, LOVS, EXPRESS) showed at best a trend toward benefit in severe disease only.
ART trial
(Cavalcanti, JAMA 2017): aggressive stepwise recruitment + decremental PEEP titration
28-day mortality (55.3% vs 49.3%) and barotrauma vs conventional PEEP.
Current guidance (ATS/ESICM/SCCM 2023): avoid prolonged/high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres. Use higher (vs lower) PEEP only in moderate–severe ARDS, titrated to compliance / oesophageal pressure rather than fixed tables.
Continuous neuromuscular blockade (cisatracurium infusion)
(Papazian, NEJM 2010): 48 h cisatracurium in P/F <150 reduced adjusted 90-day mortality (HR 0.68) without increased ICU-acquired weakness.
(NHLBI PETAL, NEJM 2019): in patients managed with higher PEEP and lighter sedation, 48 h cisatracurium showed
no mortality benefit
(42.5% vs 42.8%) and more cardiovascular adverse events.
reserve for patients with refractory ventilator dyssynchrony, very high driving pressure, or severe hypoxaemia despite deep sedation — not as routine for all moderate–severe ARDS.
Other strategies with negative or no evidence
Exogenous surfactant
— adult RCTs (Spragg 2004, 2011) negative; no role outside neonatal/paediatric practice.
Activated protein C (drotrecogin alfa)
— withdrawn 2011 after PROWESS-SHOCK showed no benefit and bleeding harm.
— HARP-2 and SAILS trials negative; not indicated for ARDS itself.
β₂-agonists (salbutamol)
— BALTI-2 (Lancet 2012)
stopped early for harm
(more tachyarrhythmia, trend to mortality); ALTA also negative. Do not use to "dry the lung".
Routine high-dose corticosteroids in
— heterogeneous evidence; DEXA-ARDS (Villar 2020) showed benefit but is balanced against negative older trials. Current practice is targeted (COVID-19, severe CAP, vasculitis), not blanket.
Conservative vs liberal fluid strategy
— FACTT (NHLBI 2006) improved ventilator-free days but
mortality; conservative balance after resuscitation remains reasonable but is not a survival intervention.
Permissive hypercapnia as a target
— tolerated as a consequence of low-Vt ventilation, but not pursued for its own sake; very high PaCO₂ worsens RV function and ICP.
Prophylactic antibiotics, immunonutrition, omega-3 / antioxidants (OMEGA, EDEN)
— neutral or harmful; not recommended.
VV-ECMO — Refractory Hypoxaemia
EOLIA criteria:
PaO₂/FiO₂ <80 mmHg for >6 hours, OR PaO₂/FiO₂ <50 for >3 hours, OR pH <7.25 + PaCO₂ ≥60 mmHg for >6 hours — despite optimal conventional management (prone, PEEP, NMB). Refer early to ECMO centre. UK: 5 designated centres (Glenfield, Royal Papworth, St Thomas', Aberdeen, GICU).
VA-ECMO — Cardiogenic Shock
⚠ Contraindications to ECMO
Irreversible condition with no plan (bridge to nowhere), advanced directives refusing.
Prolonged MV >10 days, severe immunosuppression, uncontrolled bleeding, severe aortic regurgitation (VA-ECMO), aortic dissection.
Optimal timing of SARF / ECMO centre discussion
Severe Acute Respiratory Failure (SARF) service
at five adult centres (Glenfield/Leicester, Royal Papworth, Guy's & St Thomas', Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, Wythenshawe), accessed via a single 24/7 referral pathway. The principle is
"refer early, transfer if needed"
— discussion is not a commitment to cannulation.
Discuss with SARF as soon as the patient is failing optimal conventional therapy
, not when they are
in extremis
. Trigger thresholds for a phone call:
PaO₂/FiO₂ <150 mmHg with FiO₂ ≥0.6 and PEEP ≥10 despite lung-protective ventilation, OR
Murray score ≥2.5, OR
Uncompensated hypercapnia (pH <7.25) with Pplat >30 cmH₂O, OR
Anticipated escalation: failing on HFNO/NIV with rising oxygen requirement, or pre-intubation in fulminant viral pneumonitis / status asthmaticus.
Do not wait for EOLIA criteria
(P/F <80 for 6 h, P/F <50 for 3 h, or pH <7.25 + PaCO₂ ≥60 for 6 h) before
— these are cannulation criteria. By the time they are met, retrieval logistics (4–8 h door-to-door in the UK) may make transfer hazardous.
Refer within the first 7 days of mechanical ventilation.
Mechanical ventilation >7 days is a relative contraindication (ELSO/EOLIA); >10 days approaches absolute. Outcomes deteriorate sharply once fibroproliferative change is established.
Initiate proning and NMB before or in parallel with the referral call
— do not delay either. SARF teams expect the referring unit to have optimised PEEP, attempted ≥1 prone session where feasible, and corrected fluid balance/sepsis source before retrieval.
What to have ready for the call
(UK SARF proforma): demographics & weight, premorbid functional status & comorbidities, aetiology & day of illness, current ventilator settings + last ABG (with FiO₂/PEEP), Murray score components (P/F, PEEP, compliance, CXR quadrants), vasopressor dose, recent imaging, COVID/PCR status, and bleeding/anticoagulation status.
Special groups warranting earlier discussion
: pregnant or peripartum patients, young patients (<65) with single-organ respiratory failure, suspected reversible aetiology (viral pneumonitis, asthma, eosinophilic pneumonia, AAV/anti-GBM, smoke inhalation), and any patient where awake/pre-intubation VV-ECMO is being considered.
Mobile ECMO retrieval
: if the patient is too unstable to transfer conventionally, SARF centres can deploy a mobile cannulation team — this option only exists if you have referred early enough for the team to mobilise.
Clinical Effect
Typical Range
Blood flow rate (RPM)
Oxygenation (primary)
↑ flow = ↑ O₂ delivery. In VA-ECMO also ↑ cardiac output support
3–6 L/min (60–80 ml/kg/min)
Sweep gas flow
CO₂ removal (primary)
↑ sweep = ↑ CO₂ clearance. Independent of blood flow. Very efficient — even low flows clear CO₂
1–10 L/min (start 1:1 with blood flow)
FdO₂ (sweep gas FiO₂)
Fraction of O₂ in sweep gas. Usually kept at 1.0 initially, can wean as lung recovers
Temperature (heater)
Patient temperature
Heat exchanger integrated into circuit. Can actively warm or cool (TTM post-arrest)
Ventilator settings
Lung rest
"Rest settings" to minimise VILI: FiO₂ 0.3, PEEP 10, RR 10, Pplat <25. Lungs kept open but not stressed
Ultra-protective: TV 3–4 ml/kg
Oxygenation Troubleshooting
CO₂ Troubleshooting
Rapid CO₂ correction can cause cerebral vasoconstriction → seizures. Reduce PaCO₂ slowly (<10 mmHg/hr).
Unfractionated Heparin (UFH)
AT-III dependent thrombin/Xa inhibition
APTT, anti-Xa, ACT
APTT 50–70s or anti-Xa 0.3–0.5 IU/mL (ACT 180–220s)
Direct thrombin inhibitor (AT-III independent)
APTT, ECT, ACT
APTT 50–80s. No antidote (short t½ ~25 min). Dose: 0.05–0.2 mg/kg/hr
Direct thrombin inhibitor
APTT 1.5–3× baseline. Used in HIT. Hepatic metabolism — caution in liver failure
No anticoagulation
Close circuit inspection
Considered in active bleeding, recent surgery, DIC. Higher blood flows (>3.5 L/min) + heparin-bonded circuits reduce clotting risk
Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) on ECMO
. Do NOT use LMWH (cross-reactivity).
Acquired Von Willebrand Syndrome (AVWS)
Practical Anticoagulation Strategy
UFH bolus 50–100 IU/kg at cannulation → infusion 10–20 IU/kg/hr.
APTT 4–6 hourly initially. Anti-Xa more reliable in critical illness (less affected by factor depletion).
If APTT unresponsive to heparin escalation → check AT-III levels → supplement if <60% (AT-III concentrate).
Most centres accept lower targets (APTT 40–50s) or withhold anticoagulation with high blood flows.
VV-ECMO Weaning
Sweep-off trial:
Reduce sweep gas to 0 (blood still flowing) → assess native gas exchange on "rest" ventilator settings. If PaO₂ >60 mmHg and PaCO₂ <50 mmHg on FiO₂ ≤0.5 and PEEP ≤10 for 4–6 hours → decannulate. Do NOT reduce blood flow (clotting risk).
VA-ECMO Weaning
Turndown trial:
Gradually reduce flow (by 0.5 L/min every few hours) to minimum (1–1.5 L/min) while monitoring haemodynamics. Assess: MAP, CVP, lactate, echo (LV function, filling). If stable at minimum flow → decannulate. Ensure adequate anticoagulation during low flows.
Key Finding
CESAR (2009)
Severe ARDS (Murray ≥3)
Transfer to ECMO centre improved survival (63% vs 47%), but not all received ECMO — benefit may be centre expertise
EOLIA (2018)
Very severe ARDS (P/F <80)
60-day mortality 35% vs 46% (p=0.09). Not significant but 28% crossover. Bayesian post-hoc: ~88% probability of benefit. Changed practice despite failing primary endpoint.
ELSO Registry
Global ECMO data
Adult respiratory ECMO survival ~60%. Cardiac ~40%. eCPR ~30%. COVID-era survival lower (~48% respiratory).
Phenotypes of COVID-19 Respiratory Failure
Type L (early / "silent hypoxia"):
Low elastance (high compliance), low V/Q ratio, low lung weight, low recruitability. Patients may tolerate hypoxia well initially. Responds to supplemental O₂, CPAP/HFNO, prone positioning (awake).
Type H (later / classic ARDS):
High elastance (low compliance), high right-to-left shunt, high lung weight, high recruitability. Requires intubation, lung-protective ventilation, higher PEEP. Some patients transition from L → H phenotype.
Pharmacological Management — Current Evidence
RECOVERY trial: 6 mg/day × 10 days reduced 28-day mortality in ventilated patients (29.3% → 23.3%, NNT 8) and those on O₂ (26.2% → 23.3%). No benefit if no O₂ requirement.
Standard of care for all hospitalised patients requiring O₂
Tocilizumab (IL-6 inhibitor)
REMAP-CAP & RECOVERY: Reduced mortality and organ support duration when given within 24h of ICU admission alongside corticosteroids. CRP >75 mg/L used as eligibility marker.
Recommended within 24h of organ support + CRP >75
Baricitinib (JAK inhibitor)
COV-BARRIER & RECOVERY: Reduced 28-day mortality (HR 0.87). Alternative to tocilizumab if IL-6 inhibitors unavailable. Can be combined with corticosteroids.
Alternative to tocilizumab, especially if IL-6 inhibitor unavailable
REMAP-CAP/ATTACC/ACTIV-4a: Therapeutic-dose LMWH improved organ support-free days in moderate illness (ward patients).
No benefit in critically ill / ICU patients
— standard prophylactic dose recommended in ICU.
Therapeutic in moderate (non-ICU); prophylactic in ICU
Antivirals (Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir, Remdesivir)
Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid): reduces hospitalisation in high-risk outpatients (EPIC-HR). Remdesivir: modest benefit if given early (<7 days symptoms), ACTT-1 showed faster recovery. No mortality benefit in ventilated patients.
Early treatment in high-risk patients; limited role once ventilated
Convalescent plasma / HCQ / Lopinavir-ritonavir
RECOVERY, REMAP-CAP, SOLIDARITY: No benefit demonstrated. Hydroxychloroquine showed possible harm.
Not recommended — no benefit
Respiratory Support Escalation
COVID-Specific ICU Considerations
RECOVERY (2020–)
6 mg/d × 10d: ↓ mortality in ventilated (NNT 8) and O₂-dependent. Largest COVID RCT (12,000+ patients).
REMAP-CAP (2021)
Tocilizumab / Sarilumab
IL-6 inhibitors within 24h of organ support: ↓ mortality + ↓ organ support duration. aOR for hospital survival 1.64.
COV-BARRIER (2021)
JAK inhibitor: ↓ 28-day mortality (HR 0.57 in ventilated subgroup). WHO strong recommendation.
RECOVERY-RS (2022)
CPAP vs HFNO vs O₂
CPAP ↓ intubation + death vs standard O₂. HFNO non-inferior to CPAP.
REMAP-CAP / ATTACC / ACTIV-4a
Therapeutic anticoagulation
Benefit in moderate (non-critically ill). No benefit (possible harm) in critically ill.
SOLIDARITY (WHO)
Remdesivir, HCQ, Lopinavir, IFN
None showed mortality benefit. Remdesivir: modest ↓ recovery time (ACTT-1) but no benefit once ventilated.
Berlin 2012
ESICM 2023
ATS/ESICM/SCCM 2024 (Global Definition)
6h, OR pH
Where they all agree
Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg PBW), plateau ≤30, driving pressure ≤15
Prone positioning ≥12–16h for moderate–severe ARDS (PROSEVA)
VV-ECMO referral for severe refractory ARDS (EOLIA)
Avoid sustained recruitment manoeuvres (ART trial harm)
Conservative fluid balance once shock resolved (FACTT)
Where they differ
Diagnostic scope
: Global 2024 includes HFNO/NIV patients and SpO₂/FiO₂; Berlin requires invasive ventilation + ABG
: ESICM/Global narrow indication after ROSE; older practice was routine for moderate–severe
PEEP titration
: Global emphasises personalisation (transpulmonary pressure, EIT) vs older PEEP/FiO₂ table
: stronger endorsement in Global (post-COVID evidence) than earlier guidance
standard care in severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP) and COVID-19 pneumonia requiring oxygen
. The picture for influenza and non-severe CAP remains more nuanced.
COVID-19 pneumonia — the paradigm shifter
RECOVERY (Horby, NEJM 2021)
6,425 hospitalised COVID-19
Dexamethasone 6 mg OD × 10 d vs usual care
28-day mortality ↓ overall (22.9% vs 25.7%, RR 0.83). Benefit confined to those on O₂ (RR 0.82) or IMV (RR 0.64);
harm signal in patients NOT requiring oxygen
REMAP-CAP steroid domain (Angus, JAMA 2020)
384 ICU COVID-19
Hydrocortisone 50 mg QDS × 7 d vs no steroid
Bayesian probability of superiority ≥93% for organ-support-free days. Stopped early after RECOVERY.
COVID STEROID 2 (Munch, JAMA 2021)
1,000 patients on ≥10 L/min O₂
Dexamethasone 12 mg vs 6 mg × 10 d
No significant difference in days alive without life support at 28 days.
6 mg remains standard.
RECOVERY high-dose (2023, Lancet)
Hypoxic, escalating O₂ need
Dex 20 mg × 5 d then 10 mg × 5 d vs 6 mg × 10 d
No mortality benefit;
more hyperglycaemia & infection
. High dose not recommended outside trials.
Practice point:
dexamethasone 6 mg OD (PO/IV) for up to 10 days, in any hospitalised COVID-19 patient requiring supplemental oxygen or organ support. Equivalent doses: hydrocortisone 50 mg QDS, methylprednisolone 32 mg OD, prednisolone 40 mg OD. Combine with tocilizumab (single 8 mg/kg) if CRP ≥75 mg/L or escalating O₂ requirement (REMAP-CAP / RECOVERY).
Severe community-acquired pneumonia (non-COVID)
CAPE COD (Dequin, NEJM 2023)
800 ICU sCAP (PSI >130, mech vent, HFNO with PaO₂/FiO₂ <300, or NIV)
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day × 4–7 d then taper vs placebo.
Excluded influenza & septic shock.
28-day mortality 6.2% vs 11.9% (ARR 5.6%, NNT 18).
Less intubation (18% vs 29.5%), less vasopressor use. No ↑ in nosocomial infection or GI bleed; mild ↑ in insulin requirement.
ESCAPe (Meduri, ICM 2022)
584 US veterans, severe CAP within 96 h of ICU admission
Methylprednisolone 40 mg/day taper × 20 d
No 60-day mortality benefit (16% vs 18%). Late enrolment (median 60 h) and predominantly male/older cohort. Less compelling than CAPE COD.
Torres (JAMA 2015)
120 sCAP with ↑CRP (>150 mg/L)
Methylpred 0.5 mg/kg BD × 5 d
Treatment failure 13% vs 31%; no mortality difference. Hyperinflammatory signal.
Stern Cochrane (2017, updated 2023)
17 RCTs, ~3,000 hospitalised CAP
Steroids vs placebo
All-cause mortality reduced in
severe CAP only
(RR 0.58); no benefit in non-severe. Reduced LOS, time to clinical stability across all severities. Trade-off: hyperglycaemia (NNH ~10).
Current consensus (ATS/IDSA 2024 update, ESICM/SCCM 2024):
hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (continuous infusion or 50 mg QDS) for 4–7 days then taper, in adults admitted to ICU with severe CAP
caused by influenza, ideally started within 24 h of ICU admission. CAPE COD-style dosing is now recommended over older methylprednisolone regimens.
CAPE COD
influenza, septic shock requiring high-dose vasopressors, and immunocompromised hosts. Benefit may not extend to these groups. Always send respiratory viral PCR + atypical screen before committing to steroids — particularly to exclude influenza.
Influenza pneumonia — caution
increased mo

case_bank.title: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS
case_bank.text:
Case: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS (Ventilation, Advanced)
Patient: A patient ventilated for pneumonia has a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa on PEEP 12 cmH₂O, bilateral infiltrates and no evidence of cardiac failure.
Presentation: Tidal volume is 9 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau pressure 32 cmH₂O and driving pressure 20 cmH₂O.
Stage 1 — Make the diagnosis
  Question: Does this meet ARDS criteria?
  Model answer: Yes: acute onset within one week, bilateral infiltrates not fully explained by effusion or collapse, no primary cardiogenic cause, and hypoxaemia on at least 5 cmH₂O PEEP.
  Model answer: A PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa (roughly 90 mmHg over FiO₂ 1.0 equivalents) falls in the moderate-to-severe range.
  Model answer: Severity is graded by this ratio and guides therapies such as proning and neuromuscular blockade.
Stage 2 — Correct the ventilation
  Question: What immediate changes are needed?
  Model answer: Reduce tidal volume to 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, keep plateau pressure below 30 cmH₂O and driving pressure below about 15 cmH₂O.
  Model answer: Titrate PEEP to oxygenation and compliance, accept permissive hypercapnia while pH is tolerable, and use conservative fluid management once shock has resolved.
  Model answer: Optimise sedation and consider neuromuscular blockade for severe dyssynchrony.
Stage 3 — Escalate
  Question: What next if hypoxaemia persists?
  Model answer: Prone for at least 16 hours per day when the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio remains below about 20 kPa: PROSEVA showed a substantial mortality reduction in severe ARDS.
  Model answer: Treat the cause with source control and appropriate antimicrobials, and exclude a superimposed pneumothorax or effusion.
  Model answer: Refer early for extracorporeal support if hypoxaemia or hypercapnic acidosis is refractory despite optimal ventilation and proning.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: ARDS is a heterogeneous, inflammatory lung injury in which the aerated compartment is small; delivering normal tidal volumes to a 'baby lung' produces high strain, ventilator-induced injury and biotrauma. Driving pressure captures tidal strain on the aerated lung and correlates with mortality. Proning improves outcome by making transpulmonary pressure and ventilation more homogeneous, recruiting dorsal lung and improving ventilation–perfusion matching.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Deliver the ARDSNet strategy consistently: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau under 30 cmH₂O, individualised PEEP, permissive hypercapnia and conservative fluids. Monitor plateau and driving pressure with inspiratory holds, follow gases and compliance trends, and prone with a trained team and a checklist for line, tube and pressure-area safety. Escalate to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation early rather than after prolonged injurious ventilation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not use actual body weight for tidal volume, and do not chase a normal PaCO₂. State the Berlin criteria and quote PROSEVA's 16-hour minimum.
Take-home: ARDS management is protective ventilation by predicted body weight plus early prolonged proning in severe disease, not higher volumes or normal CO₂.
Cited sources: Berlin definition of ARDS (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.5669); ARDSNet low tidal volume trial (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200005043421801); PROSEVA 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214103)
