entries.text:
# Cardiac Output Monitoring PA catheter, PiCCO, oesophageal Doppler, echocardiography 1. Introduction & Curriculum Scope Curriculum mapping FRCA Final (RCoA): principles of CO measurement; Fick principle; indicator dilution and thermodilution; pulse contour analysis; oesophageal Doppler; echocardiography for haemodynamic assessment; advantages and limitations of available monitors. FFICM (FICM): haemodynamic monitoring in shock; fluid responsiveness assessment; SvO₂/ScvO₂ interpretation; appropriate selection and interpretation of CO monitoring; evidence base (PAC-Man, FACTT, OPTIMISE) and limitations of each modality. Common SBA / structured oral themes: Stewart-Hamilton equation, dynamic vs static preload markers, sources of error, choosing a monitor for a clinical scenario. 2. Why Measure Cardiac Output? Define the type of shock using a haemodynamic profile (CO, SVR, preload, oxygenation indices). Predict fluid responsiveness before committing to volume that may worsen lung water. Titrate vasoactive drugs (inotropes vs vasopressors) to a physiological endpoint. Calculate oxygen delivery (DO₂ = CO × CaO₂) — the link between haemodynamics and tissue oxygenation. Detect and trend deterioration earlier than BP, lactate, or urine output. 3. Physiological Foundations Fick principle (the reference standard) Indicator dilution & the Stewart-Hamilton equation CO = (V × (T − T ) × K) / ∫ ΔT · dt = volume injected, T = blood/injectate temperature, K = computation constant, and ∫ΔT·dt = area under the temperature-time curve at the thermistor. A small AUC reflects rapid wash-out and high CO; a large AUC reflects slow wash-out and low CO. Doppler principle v cos θ) / c. Multiplying the velocity-time integral (VTI, "stroke distance") by the cross-sectional area of the vessel gives stroke volume. Underpins both the oesophageal Doppler (descending aorta) and echocardiographic SV (LVOT VTI × LVOT area). Pulse contour analysis Bioimpedance & bioreactance 4. Reference Standard & Validation Hierarchy Gold standard (research) Direct Fick Validation only — too cumbersome clinically Clinical reference PAC bolus thermodilution (mean of 3) Reference for new device studies Calibrated continuous PiCCO / LiDCO / continuous-CO PAC Bedside, beat-to-beat, periodic recalibration Uncalibrated continuous FloTrac, oesophageal Doppler Trending, intra-operative GDT NICOM, ClearSight (volume-clamp), TTE Screening, ambulatory, perioperative 5. Thermodilution Methods Right-heart thermodilution (PAC) 10 mL iced saline injected via the RA port; thermistor at the PA tip detects the temperature change. Short transit time. Provides intermittent (or continuous via a heated filament) CO, plus PAOP, CVP, PAP, SvO₂, and derived PVR/SVR. Transpulmonary thermodilution (TPTD, PiCCO/EV1000) 15–20 mL iced saline via CVC; thermistor at the femoral artery. The longer transit through both ventricles and the pulmonary circulation allows mathematical derivation of GEDV (preload) and EVLW (lung water) from the mean transit time and exponential down-slope of the curve. Sources of error: respiratory variation (inject at end-expiration), tricuspid regurgitation (recirculation distorts the curve), intracardiac shunts (loss of indicator), warm/incorrect injectate volume, thermistor drift, and rapid changes in patient temperature (CRRT, ECMO). 6. Pulse Contour & Uncalibrated Devices 6a. The Edwards Acumen IQ Sensor & Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI) Acumen IQ is a next-generation arterial-line pressure transducer from Edwards Lifesciences that plugs into the platform. It uses the fourth-generation FloTrac pulse-contour algorithm, so it is minimally invasive and uncalibrated — a peripheral (typically radial) arterial cannula is the only vascular access required. What sets it apart from a standard FloTrac is that it also outputs advanced haemodynamic variables and the machine-learned Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI) , a scalar (0–100) that forecasts an impending hypotensive episode (MAP < 65 mmHg for ≥ 1 min) approximately 15 minutes in advance. How it works Signal acquisition A high-fidelity pressure transducer samples the arterial waveform at 100 Hz. No thermodilution or lithium calibration is required; patient demographics (age, sex, height, weight) initialise the vascular-compliance estimate. FloTrac 4th-gen — CO/SV SV = , where σ is the standard deviation of the arterial pressure over a 20 s window and χ is a compliance/impedance factor updated every 20 s from waveform morphology (skewness, kurtosis, heart rate). CO = SV × HR. Advanced parameters (preload responsiveness); (maximal upstroke slope — a surrogate of LV contractility); (dynamic arterial elastance = PPV/SVV — predicts MAP response to fluid). HPI — the ML layer A logistic-regression model trained on more than 20 features extracted from each pressure beat (upstroke slope, dicrotic notch position and height, systolic area, complexity, beat-to-beat variability). Output is a 0–100 probability score updated every 20 s; an alarm at HPI ≥ 85 flags likely hypotension within ~15 min, prompting a "hypotension bundle" (fluid, vasopressor, or inotrope guided by SVV, SVR and dP/dt). Evidence base Hatib et al., Anesthesiology 2018 Algorithm derivation & validation on 1334 arterial waveforms HPI predicted hypotension 15 min ahead: sensitivity 88%, specificity 87%, AUROC 0.95. 10 min: 89/90%. 5 min: 92/92%. Wijnberge et al., , JAMA 2020 Single-centre RCT, 68 adults, elective non-cardiac surgery HPI-guided care reduced median time-weighted average of hypotension from 0.44 to 0.10 mmHg (a 74% reduction). No change in AKI or 30-day outcomes in this small trial. Maheshwari et al., Intensive Care Med 2020 Multicentre RCT, 214 ICU patients No significant reduction in time-weighted MAP < 65 mmHg vs standard care — a reminder that pre-warning alone is not enough; the accompanying treatment protocol matters. Schneck et al., BJA 2020; Davies et al., A&A 2020 External validations Reproduced 15-min prediction performance, but noted that HPI is strongly correlated with the current MAP itself — some of the "prediction" reflects a MAP already trending down. Interpret HPI in the context of the arterial trace, not in isolation. EU-HYPROTECT registry, 2023 Prospective observational, 749 major non-cardiac surgical patients HPI-guided haemodynamic management associated with a low burden of intra-operative hypotension, supporting real-world feasibility. Limitations & controversy: HPI shares all the pulse-contour caveats (aortic regurgitation, IABP, severe arrhythmia, rapid SVR change, damped or under-damped arterial trace). Independent analyses (Enevoldsen & Vistisen, 2022) have argued that a simple "MAP < 72 mmHg now" rule performs almost as well, so HPI's incremental value over vigilant MAP monitoring plus a good treatment protocol remains debated. Currently endorsed as a decision-support tool rather than a standalone target. 7. Echocardiography for Haemodynamic Assessment of haemodynamic derangement, not just the haemodynamic profile. SV is calculated as LVOT VTI × LVOT cross-sectional area (π × (LVOT diameter / 2)²); CO = SV × HR. TTE — focused protocols FATE, FUSIC HD, FOCUS, RUSH. Rapid binary assessment of LV function, RV strain, pericardial fluid, IVC collapsibility, and gross valve disease. Accreditation routes via BSE Level 1 / FUSIC. TOE — when to use Better windows in the ventilated, obese, or post-cardiac-surgery patient; intra-operative cardiac surgery; suspected endocarditis or aortic dissection; persistent unexplained shock when TTE windows are inadequate. Risks: oesophageal injury (~0.02%), bleeding, displacement of ETT. 8. Assessing Fluid Responsiveness Requirements / pitfalls SVV / PPV Sinus rhythm, mandatory ventilation, V ≥ 8 mL/kg, closed chest, no significant RV failure or raised intra-abdominal pressure Passive leg raise (PLR) ↑ SV ≥10% Reversible "auto-bolus" of ~300 mL — works in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmia. Needs continuous SV monitoring (Doppler, PiCCO, echo VTI) End-expiratory occlusion ↑ CO ≥5% 15 s expiratory hold ↑ preload; useful when SVV/PPV unreliable IVC distensibility (TTE) ΔIVC >18% (vent) / >50% collapse (SB) Subcostal view; affected by raised intra-abdominal pressure and RV failure Mini-fluid challenge ↑ SV ≥6% after 100 mL over 1 min Avoids overload if non-responsive FTc (oesophageal Doppler) <330 ms Static surrogate of preload — historically used to drive intra-op GDT 9. Oxygen Delivery, SvO₂ & ScvO₂ DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ = CO × (1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂) ≈ 1000 mL/min in a 70 kg adult. Tissue extraction (VO₂ ≈ 250 mL/min) gives a normal mixed venous saturation of 65–75%. SvO₂ (PA sample) True mixed venous, sampled from the PA via a PAC. Normal 65–75%. Falls when DO₂ falls (low CO, anaemia, hypoxaemia) or VO₂ rises (fever, shivering, agitation). Continuous fibre-optic measurement is possible. ScvO₂ (CVC sample) Sampled from a CVC tip in the SVC — surrogate for SvO₂, usually ~5% higher. Easier to obtain. Used in early goal-directed sepsis bundles (target >70%); subsequent trials (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe) showed no mortality benefit from protocolised ScvO₂-guided care, but it remains a useful marker of global DO₂/VO₂ balance. Veno-arterial CO₂ gap (Pv-aCO₂): a normal gap is <6 mmHg. A widened gap with normal ScvO₂ suggests inadequate CO despite preserved oxygen extraction — useful when ScvO₂ is misleadingly high (sepsis, cyanide, AV shunting). 10. Choosing a Monitor — Clinical Scenarios Preferred monitor Major non-cardiac surgery (GDT) Oesophageal Doppler / FloTrac Quick, intra-operative, evidence-based for SV optimisation (OPTIMISE, NICE MTG3) Severe ARDS with shock PiCCO (TPTD) EVLWI quantifies pulmonary oedema; PVPI distinguishes hydrostatic vs permeability oedema; supports conservative fluid strategy (FACTT) Severe pulmonary hypertension / RV failure Direct PAP, PVR, response to pulmonary vasodilators; SvO₂ trending Cardiogenic shock / mechanical complications post-MI PAC + echo Identify VSD, papillary muscle rupture; titrate inotropes, IABP, MCS Undifferentiated shock Focused TTE/TOE first Identifies cause (tamponade, RV strain, severe LV failure, hypovolaemia) before committing to invasive monitoring Day-case / ambulatory perioperative ClearSight / NICOM Non-invasive, continuous, no arterial line 11. Pitfalls & Sources of Error 12. Evidence Base — Key Trials PAC-Man (2005) Routine PAC in ICU No mortality benefit; 10% complication rate — PAC use should be selective, not routine ESCAPE (2005) PAC in severe heart failure No improvement in days alive out of hospital FACTT (2006) PAC vs CVC in ARDS; conservative vs liberal fluids PAC no benefit over CVC; conservative fluids ↑ ventilator-free days OPTIMISE (2014) Intra-operative GDT (Doppler/LiDCO) in major GI surgery Reduced complications (30-day composite); mortality not significant alone — meta-analysis supports benefit ProCESS / ARISE / ProMISe (2014–15) Protocolised EGDT (incl. ScvO₂) in septic shock No mortality benefit over usual care — early antibiotics & fluids are the key drivers NICE MTG3 (2011, updated) Oesophageal Doppler intra-operatively Recommended for major or high-risk surgery — reduces complications and length of stay Stroke volume from LVOT VTI (echo) SV ≈ 57 mL, CO ≈ 5.1 L/min, CI ≈ 2.8 L/min/m² — within normal limits. A small error in LVOT diameter is squared, so this is the dominant source of error in echo-derived CO. Stewart-Hamilton & oxygen delivery from a PAC DO₂ is preserved by a high CO, but the low SvO₂ and widened extraction ratio show that VO₂ has outstripped delivery — typical 'high-output but inadequate' septic profile. Treat the cause; do not be reassured by a normal CO. Fluid responsiveness — when SVV is invalid Do not act on the low SVV. Perform PLR (or mini-fluid challenge) and, given the ARDS context, also check EVLWI on PiCCO before further volume — high EVLWI argues for vasopressor and inotrope rather than fluid. Choosing a monitor — RV failure on the unit Insert a PAC. Trend PAP, PVR and SvO₂ as therapy is escalated. Avoid fluid loading guided by CVP alone — RV is preload-sensitive both ways. CO = SV × HR; CI 2.5–4.0 L/min/m². BP can be preserved despite a falling CO via compensatory vasoconstriction — measure flow, don't assume it. Direct Fick is the research gold standard; bolus PAC thermodilution is the clinical reference against which other devices are validated (Bland-Altman, percentage error ≤30% = interchangeable). Stewart-Hamilton: CO is inversely proportional to the area under the indicator concentration-time curve. TPTD (PiCCO) uniquely yields GEDI (volumetric preload), EVLWI (lung water) and PVPI (permeability vs hydrostatic oedema) because of the longer pulmonary transit time. Pulse contour devices need calibration (PiCCO, LiDCO) or a demographic compliance estimate (FloTrac); all degrade in aortic regurgitation, IABP, severe arrhythmia and rapid SVR change. Oesophageal Doppler is the workhorse of intra-operative GDT (NICE MTG3, OPTIMISE) — FTc < 330 ms suggests hypovolaemia. SVV / PPV > 10–13% predicts fluid responsiveness only with sinus rhythm, mandatory ventilation, V_T ≥ 8 mL/kg and a closed chest. Passive leg raise works when these conditions fail. ScvO₂ is a useful surrogate for SvO₂ but protocolised EGDT targeting ScvO₂ > 70% does not improve mortality (ProCESS / ARISE / ProMISe). PAC-Man and FACTT showed routine PAC use does not improve mortality — reserve for selective indications (RV failure, pulmonary hypertension, complex cardiogenic shock). Echo is unique: it identifies the cause of shock, not just the haemodynamic profile. Use focused TTE/TOE first in undifferentiated shock. Cardiac Output Monitoring FRCA Final / FFICM — Intensive Care What is the principle behind transpulmonary thermodilution (PiCCO)? Cold saline is injected centrally and the temperature change detected at a femoral arterial thermistor; the Stewart–Hamilton equation gives CO, and the curve also yields global end-diastolic volume and extravascular lung water. Why does the LVOT diameter dominate echo-derived CO error? Stroke volume = π(D/2)² × VTI, so a 10% error in LVOT diameter produces a 20% error in SV; meticulous measurement in mid-systole at the annulus is essential. What does a widened veno-arterial CO₂ gap (>6 mmHg) indicate? Inadequate cardiac output relative to metabolic demand — even with a normal ScvO₂; it suggests fluid responsiveness or need for inotropy in shock. Describe the Fick principle, Stewart-Hamilton equation, Doppler equation and pulse contour analysis as the four physiological bases of bedside CO measurement. Compare PAC, transpulmonary thermodilution (PiCCO), pulse contour (LiDCO/FloTrac), oesophageal Doppler and echocardiography in terms of invasiveness, derived variables and limitations. Calculate cardiac output, stroke volume and oxygen delivery from PAC and echo (LVOT VTI) data. Apply dynamic markers of fluid responsiveness (SVV, PPV, PLR, end-expiratory occlusion) and recognise the conditions under which each is valid. Interpret SvO₂ / ScvO₂ and the veno-arterial CO₂ gap as markers of global DO₂/VO₂ balance. Select the most appropriate CO monitor for a given clinical scenario (intra-op GDT, ARDS, RV failure, undifferentiated shock). Summarise the evidence base (PAC-Man, FACTT, OPTIMISE, ProCESS/ARISE/ProMISe) shaping current CO monitoring practice. 70 kg patient on focused echo: LVOT diameter 2.0 cm, LVOT VTI 18 cm, HR 90/min. Calculate SV, CO and CI (BSA 1.8 m²). LVOT area = π × (2.0/2)² = 3.14 cm². SV = VTI × area = 18 × 3.14 = 56.5 mL. CO = SV × HR = 56.5 × 90 = 5085 mL/min ≈ 5.1 L/min. CI = 5.1 / 1.8 = 2.8 L/min/m². Septic patient with a PAC: thermodilution CO 8.5 L/min, Hb 90 g/L, SaO₂ 96%, PaO₂ 11 kPa, SvO₂ 58%. Comment on DO₂ and oxygen extraction. CaO₂ = 1.34 × 9.0 × 0.96 + 0.003 × 11 × 7.5 ≈ 11.6 + 0.25 ≈ 11.8 mL/dL = 118 mL/L. DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ = 8.5 × 118 ≈ 1000 mL/min (normal). Extraction ratio ≈ (SaO₂ − SvO₂) / SaO₂ = (96 − 58)/96 ≈ 40% (normal ~25%). DO₂ is preserved by a high CO, but the low SvO₂ and widened extraction ratio show that VO₂ has outstripped delivery — typical septic profile. Treat the cause; do not be reassured by a normal CO. 65-year-old in AF, ventilated with Vt 5 mL/kg for ARDS. PiCCO shows SVV 8%. Lactate rising, MAP 60 on noradrenaline 0.4 µg/kg/min. Is the patient fluid responsive? SVV is invalidated by AF (loss of sinus rhythm) and by Vt < 8 mL/kg. SVV here is uninterpretable. Use a method that is rhythm- and Vt-independent: passive leg raise with continuous SV monitoring (PiCCO pulse contour or LVOT VTI on echo). PLR ↑ SV ≥ 10% = responsive; otherwise an end-expiratory occlusion test (CO ↑ ≥ 5%) or 100 mL mini-fluid challenge (SV ↑ ≥ 6%). Patient with severe pulmonary hypertension is admitted with worsening hypoxaemia, low MAP, raised CVP and reduced urine output. Echo: dilated RV with reduced TAPSE, septal flattening. Which CO monitor adds most? Pulse contour devices and oesophageal Doppler do not measure PAP or PVR and may be inaccurate with severe TR. Echo confirms RV failure but cannot give continuous PAP. A PAC directly measures PAP, PVR and SvO₂, allowing titration of pulmonary vasodilators (inhaled NO, prostacyclin) and inotrope (dobutamine, milrinone) to fall in PVR and rise in SvO₂. ], }, ]; const keyPoints = [ { text: >1. Introduction & Curriculum Scope

Cardiac output (CO) monitoring quantifies the volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle per minute (CO = SV × HR, normal 4–8 L/min; CI 2.5–4.0 L/min/m²). It underpins assessment of shock, fluid responsiveness, and the response to vasoactive therapy. No single device is — each technology trades invasiveness, accuracy, continuity, and the range of derived variables.

Common SBA / structured oral themes: Stewart-Hamilton equation, dynamic vs static preload markers, sources of error, choosing a monitor for a clinical scenario.
{/* 2. Why measure CO */}

2. Why Measure Cardiac Output?

Blood pressure alone is a poor surrogate for tissue perfusion: MAP can be preserved despite a falling CO through compensatory vasoconstriction. Direct or derived CO measurement allows the clinician to:

    Detect and trend deterioration earlier than BP, lactate, or urine output.
{/* 3. Physiological foundations */}

3. Physiological Foundations

CO = VO₂ / (CaO₂ − CvO₂). The volume of oxygen consumed per minute equals the difference in O₂ content between arterial and mixed venous blood multiplied by the flow. Requires steady-state VO₂ (metabolic cart), arterial blood gas, and a true mixed venous sample from the PA. Accurate but cumbersome — used to validate other methods rather than at the bedside.

A known dose of indicator (cold saline, lithium, dye) is injected upstream and its concentration sampled downstream. CO is inversely proportional to the area under the resulting concentration-time curve:

CO = (Vi × (Tb − Ti) × K) / ∫ ΔT · dt

Where Vi = volume injected, Tb/Ti = blood/injectate temperature, K = computation constant, and ∫ΔT·dt = area under the temperature-time curve at the thermistor. A small AUC reflects rapid wash-out and high CO; a large AUC reflects slow wash-out and low CO.

Frequency shift of reflected ultrasound is proportional to red cell velocity: Δf = (2 f0 v cos θ) / c. Multiplying the velocity-time integral (VTI, ) by the cross-sectional area of the vessel gives stroke volume. Underpins both the oesophageal Doppler (descending aorta) and echocardiographic SV (LVOT VTI × LVOT area).

Stroke volume is estimated beat-to-beat from the area under the systolic portion of the arterial pressure waveform, scaled by an estimate of aortic compliance. Requires either a calibration step (PiCCO via TPTD, LiDCO via lithium) or a demographic/waveform-derived compliance estimate (FloTrac — uncalibrated). Accuracy degrades when compliance changes rapidly (vasoplegia, vasopressor titration, aortic regurgitation, IABP, arrhythmia).

Thoracic bioimpedance measures changes in resistance to a small applied current as blood volume in the aorta varies. Bioreactance (NICOM) measures the phase shift of the signal — less susceptible to motion and electrical noise. Completely non-invasive but limited absolute accuracy, particularly in low-flow states, oedema, and with diathermy.

{/* 4. Reference standard & validation hierarchy */}

4. Reference Standard & Validation Hierarchy

Devices are validated by Bland-Altman analysis (bias, precision, limits of agreement) and percentage error vs a reference. A percentage error ≤30% (Critchley & Critchley, 1999) is regarded as clinically interchangeable.

5. Thermodilution Methods

Both PAC and PiCCO use cold saline as the indicator and the Stewart-Hamilton equation, but the geometry of the dilution path differs.

Right-heart thermodilution (PAC)

10 mL iced saline injected via the RA port; thermistor at the PA tip detects the temperature change. Short transit time. Provides intermittent (or continuous via a heated filament) CO, plus PAOP, CVP, PAP, SvO₂, and derived PVR/SVR.

Transpulmonary thermodilution (TPTD, PiCCO/EV1000)

15–20 mL iced saline via CVC; thermistor at the femoral artery. The longer transit through both ventricles and the pulmonary circulation allows mathematical derivation of GEDV (preload) and EVLW (lung water) from the mean transit time and exponential down-slope of the curve.

Sources of error: respiratory variation (inject at end-expiration), tricuspid regurgitation (recirculation distorts the curve), intracardiac shunts (loss of indicator), warm/incorrect injectate volume, thermistor drift, and rapid changes in patient temperature (CRRT, ECMO).

case_bank.title: The arterial line that under-reads
case_bank.text:
Case: The arterial line that under-reads (Monitoring artefact, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient in theatre has a radial arterial line. The trace looks rounded, the systolic reading is 30 mmHg lower than a cuff measurement, and vasopressor is being escalated.
Presentation: The flush test shows a slow return to baseline without oscillation. There is a long compliant extension and an air bubble near the transducer.
Stage 1 — Interpret the flush test
  Question: What does the square-wave test tell you?
  Model answer: Optimal damping gives one or two brisk oscillations before the trace settles.
  Model answer: Overdamping — a sluggish return with no oscillation — under-reads systolic and over-reads diastolic pressure while mean pressure stays comparatively reliable.
  Model answer: Underdamping (resonance) produces prolonged ringing and falsely high systolic values.
Stage 2 — Find the physical cause
  Question: Which components produce this pattern?
  Model answer: Air bubbles, clot, kinks, compliant tubing, excessive tubing length, a partially open tap or arterial spasm all add damping.
  Model answer: Zeroing at the wrong height changes mean pressure by roughly 7.5 mmHg for every 10 cm of height error.
  Model answer: Transducer natural frequency must be well above the pressure waveform harmonics for faithful reproduction.
Stage 3 — Correct before you treat
  Question: What action do you take?
  Model answer: Aspirate and flush, remove bubbles, shorten and stiffen the tubing, and re-zero at the phlebostatic axis.
  Model answer: Base decisions on mean arterial pressure and perfusion while the trace is unreliable, cross-checked with a cuff.
  Model answer: Do not escalate vasopressor for an artefact; document the corrected values.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: The catheter–tubing–transducer assembly is a second-order system whose behaviour depends on natural frequency and damping coefficient. Because the arterial waveform contains harmonics up to about 20 Hz, a low natural frequency or excessive damping distorts systolic and diastolic peaks. Mean pressure is the most robust derived value, which is why it guides therapy when the trace quality is uncertain.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Perform and document a square-wave test at set-up and whenever readings look implausible. Keep tubing short, stiff and bubble-free, avoid multiple taps and extensions, re-zero after any patient or transducer movement, and reconcile with non-invasive measurement. Persistent damping despite optimisation suggests thrombus or spasm and may need a new line.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not say 'the arterial line is wrong' without a systematic answer: state zeroing and levelling, the flush test result, the direction of error for over- and underdamping, and which derived value remains usable.
Take-home: Test damping before treating a number: overdamped traces under-read systolic pressure, and mean pressure is the value to trust while you fix the system.
Cited sources: BJA: arterial pressure measurement (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.06.047); Assoc Anaesth monitoring standards (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.13316)

case_bank.title: Which vasoactive drug for refractory septic shock?
case_bank.text:
Case: Which vasoactive drug for refractory septic shock? (Critical care drugs, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive at a mean arterial pressure of 55 mmHg on noradrenaline 0.4 micrograms/kg/min despite fluid resuscitation.
Presentation: Cardiac index is 4.2 L/min/m², lactate 4.1 mmol/L, echocardiography shows preserved contractility.
Stage 1 — Interpret the haemodynamics
  Question: Which problem are you treating?
  Model answer: High cardiac index with low pressure indicates a vasodilatory, resistance problem rather than pump failure.
  Model answer: Adding an inotrope would raise output without correcting the vasodilation and may worsen tachyarrhythmia and oxygen demand.
  Model answer: Target mean arterial pressure of about 65 mmHg, individualised upwards in chronic hypertension.
Stage 2 — Choose the next agent
  Question: How do you escalate?
  Model answer: Add vasopressin (typically 0.03 units/min) to spare catecholamine dose, acting through V1 receptors independent of adrenergic pathways.
  Model answer: Consider hydrocortisone for shock requiring ongoing vasopressor support, and reassess for source control, occult bleeding and acidosis limiting catecholamine responsiveness.
  Model answer: Reserve adrenaline or an inotrope for genuine low-output states, guided by echocardiography or cardiac output monitoring.
Stage 3 — Explain the receptors
  Question: Summarise the pharmacodynamics behind the choices.
  Model answer: Noradrenaline acts mainly on alpha-1 receptors with modest beta-1 activity, raising resistance with limited chronotropy.
  Model answer: Adrenaline is dose-dependent: beta effects predominate at low dose, alpha at high dose, with lactate generation through beta-2-mediated glycolysis.
  Model answer: Dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist with beta-2 vasodilation; phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist that may reduce output through reflex bradycardia and increased afterload.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Vasoactive selection follows from the measured physiology: define whether the deficit is resistance, output, preload or rhythm, then choose the receptor profile that corrects it. Catecholamine responsiveness falls with acidosis, hypocalcaemia, hypoxia and receptor downregulation, so escalating dose alone is often ineffective; combining agents with different mechanisms is more effective and less arrhythmogenic than maximising one.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use invasive arterial monitoring, central administration, repeated echocardiography or cardiac output measurement, lactate trend and urine output. Correct calcium, acidosis and hypoxia; ensure source control and antimicrobial adequacy. Add vasopressin early as catecholamine-sparing, consider corticosteroid in vasopressor-dependent shock, and reassess for mechanisms such as tamponade, right ventricular failure or adrenal insufficiency when shock is refractory.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not add an inotrope for a high-output vasodilated state, and do not describe 'renal-dose dopamine'. Give receptor targets and doses, and state the mean arterial pressure goal.
Take-home: Treat the measured defect: vasodilatory shock needs vasopressors and catecholamine-sparing adjuncts, not inotropes for an already high cardiac output.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: vasoactive drugs (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw066); BJA Educ: pharmacodynamics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkm016)

entries.description: WHO classification, RV-protective strategy, targeted vasodilators, perioperative care and crisis management
entries.text:
# Pulmonary Hypertension Management WHO classification, RV-protective strategy, targeted vasodilators, perioperative care and crisis management reduce PVR support the failing RV inhaled NO 20 ppm (or nebulised iloprost 5–10 µg). Push vasopressin 0.01–0.04 U/min dobutamine 5 µg/kg/min or milrinone (offset hypotension with noradrenaline). Treat the trigger: drain pneumothorax, suction, antibiotics, lyse PE. Refractory: VA-ECMO bridge to recovery or transplantation. Definition & Classification Haemodynamic Definition (2022 ESC/ERS) Pulmonary hypertension: resting mPAP ≥20 mmHg measured by right heart catheterisation (lowered from the previous ≥25 mmHg threshold) Pre-capillary PH: mPAP ≥20, PAWP ≤15 mmHg, PVR >2 Wood units (e.g. PAH, chronic thromboembolic, lung disease) Isolated post-capillary PH: mPAP ≥20, PAWP >15 mmHg, PVR ≤2 (left heart disease) Combined pre- and post-capillary PH: mPAP ≥20, PAWP >15, PVR >2 (advanced left heart disease with reactive pulmonary remodelling) Exercise PH: mPAP/CO slope >3 mmHg/L/min between rest and exercise — recognised in 2022 update WHO Clinical Groups Group 1 — PAH: idiopathic, heritable (BMPR2), drug-induced (anorexigens, methamphetamine), connective tissue disease (scleroderma), HIV, portopulmonary, congenital L→R shunts Group 2 — Left heart disease: HFrEF, HFpEF, valvular disease (commonest cause of PH overall) Group 3 — Lung disease/hypoxia: COPD, ILD, OSA, high altitude Group 4 — Chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH): potentially curable by pulmonary endarterectomy Group 5 — Multifactorial/unclear: sarcoidosis, haematological disorders (sickle cell), metabolic disorders Severity Markers WHO functional class III/IV, syncope, signs of right heart failure (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral oedema) 6-minute walk test <165 m, NT-proBNP >1100 ng/L, RA area >26 cm², pericardial effusion Cardiac index <2.0 L/min/m², RA pressure >14 mmHg, mixed venous saturation <60% These translate to a 1-year mortality >20% in the ESC/ERS risk stratification table Pathophysiology — From Endothelial Injury to RV Failure The thin-walled RV is designed for a low-impedance circulation; it tolerates volume but not pressure overload Acute rises in PVR cause RV dilatation → tricuspid regurgitation → further RV dilatation (a vicious cycle) RV dilatation shifts the interventricular septum leftwards (reverse Bernheim effect) → reduced LV preload, reduced cardiac output, systemic hypotension Unlike the LV, the RV is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle; once RV pressure approaches aortic pressure, RV perfusion becomes systolic-only and ischaemia develops The result is a "spiral of death": ↑PVR → RV failure → ↓LV filling → ↓MAP → ↓RV coronary perfusion → worsening RV failure Targeted Pulmonary Vasodilator Therapy Three Pathways of PAH Therapy Nitric oxide / cGMP pathway: phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil); soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator (riociguat — used in CTEPH) Endothelin pathway: endothelin receptor antagonists — bosentan (dual ETA/ETB), ambrisentan and macitentan (selective ETA). Hepatotoxicity with bosentan; teratogenic Prostacyclin pathway: inhaled iloprost, IV epoprostenol (very short half-life, 3–5 min — abrupt cessation is fatal), subcutaneous/IV treprostinil, oral selexipag (IP receptor agonist) Group 1 PAH is treated with combination therapy from diagnosis (AMBITION trial — ambrisentan + tadalafil) These agents are indicated for groups 2 or 3 — they may worsen pulmonary oedema by increasing pulmonary blood flow Inhaled Selective Pulmonary Vasodilators Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO): 10–40 ppm — selective for ventilated alveoli, no systemic vasodilatation (rapidly inactivated by haemoglobin). Rebound PH on cessation; wean over hours. Methaemoglobinaemia risk >40 ppm Nebulised iloprost or epoprostenol: alternatives where iNO unavailable; cheaper, similar efficacy in many series Inhaled agents preserve V/Q matching, unlike IV vasodilators which dilate poorly ventilated regions and worsen shunt Comparative Table — Targeted Pulmonary Vasodilators Doses are typical adult starting/maintenance values; check local protocols. Pathway colour: Class / Mechanism Route & Dose Key Side Effects / Cautions PDE-5 inhibitor → ↑cGMP → pulmonary vasodilation PO 20 mg TDS (up to 80 mg TDS); IV 10 mg TDS ~4 h Headache, flushing, dyspepsia, visual disturbance (NAION); contraindicated with nitrates and riociguat Soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator (NO-independent ↑cGMP) PO 1 mg TDS, titrated to 2.5 mg TDS 5–10 h Hypotension, syncope, haemoptysis; teratogenic (REMS programme); only oral agent licensed for CTEPH; never combine with PDE-5i or nitrates Dual ET endothelin receptor antagonist PO 62.5 mg BD × 4 wk → 125 mg BD ~5 h (active metabolite ~9 h) Hepatotoxicity (monthly LFTs mandatory), anaemia, peripheral oedema; teratogenic; CYP3A4/2C9 inducer — reduces warfarin and OCP levels antagonist (high tissue affinity) PO 10 mg OD ~16 h (parent), ~48 h (active metabolite) Anaemia (monitor Hb), nasopharyngitis, headache; less hepatotoxicity than bosentan but still teratogenic; SERAPHIN trial — first to show morbidity/mortality benefit Synthetic prostacyclin (PGI₂) analogue → IP receptor → ↑cAMP Inhaled (nebulised) 2.5–5 µg, 6–9 times/day; IV in crisis 20–30 min Cough, jaw pain, flushing, hypotension; bronchospasm; frequent dosing burdens patients Native prostacyclin (PGI₂) — most potent pulmonary vasodilator Continuous IV via tunnelled central line; start 2 ng/kg/min, titrate 3–5 min Abrupt cessation is fatal — rebound PH crisis. Line sepsis, jaw pain, diarrhoea, thrombocytopenia. Only agent with mortality benefit in WHO IV PAH Stable prostacyclin analogue (longer half-life) SC infusion (1.25 ng/kg/min, titrated), IV, inhaled QDS, or PO SC infusion site pain (limits use); same prostacyclin class effects; longer t½ allows safer transient interruption than epoprostenol Selective oral IP-receptor agonist (non-prostanoid) PO 200 µg BD, titrated weekly to max 1600 µg BD ~1 h (active metabolite ~10 h) Headache, diarrhoea, jaw pain, nausea; GRIPHON trial showed reduced morbidity events; oral alternative to parenteral prostacyclins indicated in Group 2 (left heart) or uncomplicated Group 3 PH — they may worsen pulmonary oedema or V/Q mismatch. Never abruptly stop any of these drugs perioperatively. Perioperative & ICU Management Goals (the "RV-protective" strategy) Maintain MAP > PAP — coronary perfusion of the failing RV depends on systemic pressure Keep PVR low: avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain, light anaesthesia, high airway pressures Optimise preload — neither under- nor over-filled. CVP target typically 8–12 mmHg; bedside echo to assess RV filling Maintain sinus rhythm — atrial kick contributes ≥30% of RV output in PH; cardiovert AF promptly Continue background pulmonary vasodilator therapy without interruption — convert oral agents to IV/inhaled if NBM Vasopressors & Inotropes first-line vasopressor — increases SVR > PVR, restores RV coronary perfusion Vasopressin (0.01–0.04 U/min): increases SVR with little effect on PVR; useful adjunct, particularly in vasoplegia Dobutamine (2–10 µg/kg/min): RV inodilator of choice; mild pulmonary vasodilatation; watch for tachyarrhythmias at higher doses PDE-3 inhibitor — inotrope and pulmonary vasodilator; often combined with noradrenaline to offset systemic vasodilatation. Inhaled milrinone selective for pulmonary circulation phenylephrine (raises PVR more than SVR), high-dose adrenaline (tachyarrhythmia, ↑PVR) Anaesthetic Conduct Pre-induction arterial line; large-bore IV access; Perioperative and ICU mortality is high; the central principle is to protect the right ventricle by maintaining systemic perfusion pressure above pulmonary pressure while avoiding any insult that acutely raises PVR.

Haemodynamic Definition (2022 ESC/ERS)
    WHO Clinical Groups
      Severity Markers
      • WHO functional class III/IV, syncope, signs of right heart failure (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral oedema)
      • 6-minute walk test <165 m, NT-proBNP >1100 ng/L, RA area >26 cm², pericardial effusion
      • Cardiac index <2.0 L/min/m², RA pressure >14 mmHg, mixed venous saturation <60%
      • These translate to a 1-year mortality >20% in the ESC/ERS risk stratification table
    • The thin-walled RV is designed for a low-impedance circulation; it tolerates volume but not pressure overload
    • Acute rises in PVR cause RV dilatation → tricuspid regurgitation → further RV dilatation (a vicious cycle)
    • RV dilatation shifts the interventricular septum leftwards (reverse Bernheim effect) → reduced LV preload, reduced cardiac output, systemic hypotension
    • Unlike the LV, the RV is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle; once RV pressure approaches aortic pressure, RV perfusion becomes systolic-only and ischaemia develops
    • The result is a : ↑PVR → RV failure → ↓LV filling → ↓MAP → ↓RV coronary perfusion → worsening RV failure
    Three Pathways of PAH Therapy
      Inhaled Selective Pulmonary Vasodilators
        Comparative Table — Targeted Pulmonary Vasodilators

        Doses are typical adult starting/maintenance values; check local protocols. Pathway colour: Prostacyclin.

        PDE-5 inhibitor → ↑cGMP → pulmonary vasodilation PO 20 mg TDS (up to 80 mg TDS); IV 10 mg TDS ~4 h Headache, flushing, dyspepsia, visual disturbance (NAION); contraindicated with nitrates and riociguat Soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator (NO-independent ↑cGMP) PO 1 mg TDS, titrated to 2.5 mg TDS 5–10 h Hypotension, syncope, haemoptysis; teratogenic (REMS programme); only oral agent licensed for CTEPH; never combine with PDE-5i or nitrates Dual ETA/ETB endothelin receptor antagonist PO 62.5 mg BD × 4 wk → 125 mg BD ~5 h (active metabolite ~9 h) Hepatotoxicity (monthly LFTs mandatory), anaemia, peripheral oedema; teratogenic; CYP3A4/2C9 inducer — reduces warfarin and OCP levels Dual ETA/ETB antagonist (high tissue affinity) PO 10 mg OD ~16 h (parent), ~48 h (active metabolite) Anaemia (monitor Hb), nasopharyngitis, headache; less hepatotoxicity than bosentan but still teratogenic; SERAPHIN trial — first to show morbidity/mortality benefit Synthetic prostacyclin (PGI₂) analogue → IP receptor → ↑cAMP Inhaled (nebulised) 2.5–5 µg, 6–9 times/day; IV in crisis 20–30 min Cough, jaw pain, flushing, hypotension; bronchospasm; frequent dosing burdens patients Native prostacyclin (PGI₂) — most potent pulmonary vasodilator Continuous IV via tunnelled central line; start 2 ng/kg/min, titrate Stable prostacyclin analogue (longer half-life) SC infusion (1.25 ng/kg/min, titrated), IV, inhaled QDS, or PO SC infusion site pain (limits use); same prostacyclin class effects; longer t½ allows safer transient interruption than epoprostenol Selective oral IP-receptor agonist (non-prostanoid) PO 200 µg BD, titrated weekly to max 1600 µg BD ~1 h (active metabolite ~10 h) Headache, diarrhoea, jaw pain, nausea; GRIPHON trial showed reduced morbidity events; oral alternative to parenteral prostacyclins

        Group 1 PAH is treated with upfront combination therapy (e.g. ambrisentan + tadalafil, AMBITION trial). These agents are not indicated in Group 2 (left heart) or uncomplicated Group 3 PH — they may worsen pulmonary oedema or V/Q mismatch. Never abruptly stop any of these drugs perioperatively.

        • Maintain MAP > PAP — coronary perfusion of the failing RV depends on systemic pressure
        • Keep PVR low: avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain, light anaesthesia, high airway pressures
        • Optimise preload — neither under- nor over-filled. CVP target typically 8–12 mmHg; bedside echo to assess RV filling
        • Maintain sinus rhythm — atrial kick contributes ≥30% of RV output in PH; cardiovert AF promptly
        • Continue background pulmonary vasodilator therapy without interruption — convert oral agents to IV/inhaled if NBM
        Vasopressors & Inotropes
          Anaesthetic Conduct
          • Pre-induction arterial line; large-bore IV access; vasopressor running before induction
          • Induction: etomidate or careful ketamine + opioid; avoid bolus propofol which causes precipitous SVR drop
          • Maintenance: opioid-based, low-dose volatile or TIVA; avoid N₂O (raises PVR and expands air emboli)
          • Ventilation: tidal volume 6 mL/kg, lowest plateau pressure achievable, PEEP titrated (excess PEEP raises PVR and reduces RV preload)
          • Regional/neuraxial anaesthesia is attractive (avoids IPPV) but profound sympathectomy can be catastrophic — incremental epidural preferred over single-shot spinal
          • Postoperative HDU/ICU; high risk of decompensation in first 48 h, particularly after fluid shifts and re-mobilisation
         Recognition
        • Acute rise in PAP toward or above systemic pressure with falling cardiac output
        • Sudden hypotension, desaturation, rising CVP, falling EtCO₂, distended neck veins, RV dilatation on echo
        • Triggers: hypoxia, hypercarbia, pain, suctioning, high PEEP, sepsis, missed pulmonary vasodilator dose, pulmonary embolism
      • FiO₂ 1.0; mild hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 4.0–4.5 kPa, target pH 7.45–7.50
      • Deepen anaesthesia/sedation; opioid bolus to suppress sympathetic drive
      • Start inhaled NO 20 ppm (or nebulised iloprost 5–10 µg) — selective pulmonary vasodilatation
      • Noradrenaline ± vasopressin to push MAP > PAP and restore RV coronary perfusion
      • Add dobutamine or milrinone for RV inotropic support
      • Treat the trigger: drain pneumothorax, evacuate gastric distension, suction airway, give antibiotics, lyse/embolectomy for PE
      • Consider VA-ECMO as a bridge to recovery, transplantation, or pulmonary endarterectomy in refractory cases
      Eisenmenger Syndrome
      • Long-standing L→R shunt that has reversed to R→L due to suprasystemic pulmonary pressures — pulmonary vasculature is fixed
      • Perioperative mortality 7–30%; falls in SVR worsen the R→L shunt and cause profound desaturation
      • Strict de-airing of all IV lines (paradoxical air embolism); maintain SVR aggressively; avoid pulmonary vasodilators (no benefit, may worsen shunt)
      Pregnancy
      • Maternal mortality with PAH 16–30%; pregnancy is contraindicated and termination should be discussed
      • Highest risk in the third trimester and early postpartum (up to 4 weeks) due to autotransfusion and fluid shifts
      • Multidisciplinary care in a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre; planned early delivery, incremental epidural, avoidance of ergometrine
      Acute (Massive) Pulmonary Embolism
      • Acute RV failure on a normal RV — clot burden + hypoxic vasoconstriction + neurohumoral release
      • Systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h) for haemodynamic instability; surgical/catheter embolectomy or VA-ECMO if thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated
      • Cautious fluid (≤500 mL); avoid over-filling the dilated RV. Noradrenaline + dobutamine; iNO if

New LBBB + chest pain or ROSC — treat as STEMI equivalent; consider PPCI. QTc > 500 ms — stop QT-prolonging drugs, replete K⁺ > 4.5 and Mg²⁺ > 1.0 mmol/L. Peaked T waves + wide QRS — hyperkalaemia, give 10 mL 10 % calcium gluconate U waves + flat T + long QU — hypokalaemia → torsades risk. Reciprocal change is your friend Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) often shows ST depression in I/aVL. Posterior STEMI shows tall R + ST depression in V1–V3 — confirm with V7–V9. Right-sided leads Inferior STEMI: always do V4R. ST elevation = RV infarct → preload-dependent → cautious nitrates, fluid load, avoid β-blockers. at the time of the ECG, the ST segment is isoelectric , and the troponin is often normal — yet without angiography they are at very high risk of an extensive anterior MI within days. Definitive: transvenous pacing wire ± permanent device. Minimise hands-off time. • Adrenaline 1 mg IV after the 3rd shock, then every 3–5 min. Amiodarone 300 mg after the 3rd shock; further 150 mg after the 5th. • Search for the 4 Hs and 4 Ts : Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hyper/hypokalaemia & metabolic, Hypothermia · Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis. eFAST + arterial line + ETCO₂ during CPR: ETCO₂ < 10 mmHg suggests poor compressions or futility; sudden ↑ ETCO₂ heralds ROSC. Immediate post-ROSC 12-lead within 10 min. STEMI / new LBBB → urgent PPCI. Aim SpO₂ 94–98 %, normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa), MAP ≥ 65 mmHg. Targeted temperature management TTM2 trial: target 33–36 °C vs strict normothermia < 37.7 °C; avoid fever for 72 h. Recurrent arrhythmia prevention Replace K⁺ to 4.5 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ > 1.0 mmol/L. Continue / start β-blocker. Amiodarone infusion for refractory VT/VF. ICD considerations Survivors of VF/VT arrest without reversible cause meet secondary-prevention ICD criteria. Liaise with cardiology before discharge from ICU. Wide-complex tachycardia in a septic ventilated patient Synchronised DCCV is the immediate priority because adverse features are present. Electrolyte correction and reversible-cause search run alongside but do not delay shock. Hyperkalaemia with peaked T waves Calcium first (cardio-protection within 1–3 min), then insulin–dextrose ± salbutamol to shift K⁺, then RRT for definitive removal. Re-check K⁺ at 30 min and 1 h. Arrhythmias & ECG Interpretation FFICM / Final FRCA — Cardiovascular Critical Care Apply the same 8-step ECG analysis (rate · rhythm · P · PR · QRS · ST/T · QT · compare) to every strip — speed comes from consistency, not shortcuts Wide-complex tachycardia in an ICU patient = VT until proven otherwise New-onset AF in ventilated sepsis is usually a marker of evolving shock, fluid overload, or electrolyte derangement — treat the trigger, not just the rhythm Site of AV block predicts the device: nodal (1°/Mobitz I) tolerate observation; infranodal (Mobitz II/complete) need urgent pacing Adverse features (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure) drive the algorithm: synchronised DCCV for unstable tachy, atropine → pacing for unstable brady Always replace magnesium when replacing potassium — refractory hypoK⁺ is often hypoMg²⁺ Hyperkalaemia: treat the rhythm with calcium first, the number afterwards Post-ROSC: 12-lead within 10 min, MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, SpO₂ 94–98 %, normocapnia, fever avoidance for 72 h A Systematic ECG Approach in the ICU 300 / number of large squares between R waves (regular). Or count complexes in a 6 s strip × 10 (irregular). Brady < 60, tachy > 100. Regular vs irregular vs irregularly irregular. Identify the underlying pacemaker (sinus, atrial, junctional, ventricular). Present? Uniform? One per QRS? Inverted (junctional / retrograde)? Sawtooth (flutter)? Absent / fibrillatory (AF)? Normal 120–200 ms. Long → 1°/2° AV block. Short + delta wave → WPW. Width (narrow ≤ 120 ms vs wide > 120 ms), morphology (RBBB/LBBB), axis. Wide QRS = ventricular origin OR aberrant supraventricular conduction. Elevation (STEMI, pericarditis, BER, LBBB), depression (ischaemia, posterior MI, digoxin), T inversion. Compare to old ECGs. Corrected QT (Bazett: QT/√RR). Prolonged > 500 ms = torsades risk. What is the initial management of polymorphic VT (torsades)? IV magnesium 2 g, correct K⁺ and Ca²⁺, stop QT-prolonging drugs, overdrive pacing or isoprenaline if bradycardia-dependent; DC shock if unstable. How are wide-complex tachycardias approached when the diagnosis is uncertain? Assume VT until proven otherwise — particularly with structural heart disease; treat with synchronised DC if unstable, amiodarone 300 mg IV if stable, avoid verapamil which can collapse VT into VF. BP 78/42, MAP 54, lactate rising. K⁺ 3.2, Mg²⁺ 0.6. Recent amiodarone load. Adverse features present (shock, ischaemia risk). Step 2 — intracellular shift: 10 units actrapid in 50 mL 50% dextrose IV over 15 min; salbutamol 10–20 mg neb. Step 3 — removal: urgent RRT given anuria. case_bank.title: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting
case_bank.text:
Case: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting (Cardiovascular, Advanced)
Patient: A young adult admitted with prolonged vomiting receives ondansetron and a macrolide. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and magnesium 0.5 mmol/L.
Presentation: The monitor shows a broad, twisting polymorphic tachycardia that self-terminates. QTc before the event was 510 ms.
Stage 1 — Explain the mechanism
  Question: Why has this rhythm occurred?
  Model answer: Phase 3 repolarisation depends mainly on the delayed rectifier potassium currents IKr and IKs; blocking IKr prolongs the action potential and the QT interval.
  Model answer: Prolonged repolarisation permits reactivation of L-type calcium current, producing early afterdepolarisations and triggered beats.
  Model answer: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia reduce repolarisation reserve, so drug effects that are usually tolerated become arrhythmogenic.
Stage 2 — Treat the arrhythmia
  Question: What is your immediate management?
  Model answer: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate even if magnesium is normal, correct potassium towards the upper normal range and stop all QT-prolonging drugs.
  Model answer: Treat sustained or pulseless episodes with defibrillation and follow advanced life support; consider overdrive pacing or isoprenaline for pause-dependent, bradycardia-related torsades.
  Model answer: Avoid class Ia and class III antiarrhythmics, which prolong repolarisation further.
Stage 3 — Prevent recurrence
  Question: What ongoing plan is needed?
  Model answer: Review every drug on the chart against a QT-prolonging list, including antiemetics, antipsychotics, macrolides, antifungals and methadone.
  Model answer: Monitor electrolytes and QTc repeatedly, especially with ongoing vomiting, diuretics or renal replacement.
  Model answer: Refer for cardiology assessment and family screening if congenital long QT syndrome is suspected.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: The cardiac action potential's plateau and repolarisation reflect a balance between inward calcium and outward potassium currents. Repolarisation reserve is the redundancy in this system; congenital channel variants, electrolyte depletion, bradycardia and multiple IKr-blocking drugs erode it additively. Torsades de pointes is the clinical expression of triggered activity on a prolonged, heterogeneous repolarisation substrate.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarisations and is first-line even with normal levels. Keep potassium above 4.5 mmol/L in this setting, remove precipitating drugs, and maintain a heart rate that shortens repolarisation when torsades is pause-dependent. Continuous ECG monitoring with QTc measurement, defibrillator availability and a documented drug-avoidance list should follow the patient.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not give amiodarone reflexively for a broad-complex tachycardia that is torsades. Distinguish polymorphic from monomorphic VT, and name IKr blockade and early afterdepolarisations rather than saying 'the QT was long'.
Take-home: Torsades reflects lost repolarisation reserve: give magnesium, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs and avoid further class III agents.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: cardiac electrophysiology (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkm013); Vaughan Williams classification (https://doi.org/10.1016/0306-039X(75)90019-7)

Setting post-ROSC ventilation & oxygen targets
Wean FiO₂ for SpO₂ 94–98 %, reduce RR for PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa, TV ~ 480 mL (6.8 mL/kg PBW), increase noradrenaline to MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, then start active normothermia ≤ 37.7 °C and book early coronary angiography.
Multimodal neuroprognostication at 72 h
Four concordant poor-outcome markers across clinical, biochemical, electrophysiological and SSEP modalities — poor neurological outcome can be predicted with high specificity. Discuss WLST with family, refer to SNOD before withdrawal for potential DCD donation.
eCPR candidate selection
Suitable eCPR candidate. Activate ECMO team, continue mechanical CPR, transport directly to ECMO bay/cath lab, target femoral VA cannulation within 60 min of arrest, then immediate coronary angiography after stable flow. Insert distal limb perfusion catheter at the time of cannulation.
Harlequin (north–south) syndrome on VA-ECMO
Optimise native lung function first (recruit, increase PEEP/FiO₂, diuresis). If persistent, convert to VAV-ECMO by adding an internal jugular return cannula to oxygenate the upper body, or move to central VA-ECMO. Monitor right radial saturation continuously as the early warning.
Post-cardiac-arrest syndrome = brain injury + myocardial dysfunction + ischaemia–reperfusion + precipitating pathology — treat all four.
Avoid hyperoxia and hypocapnia: target SpO₂ 94–98 %, PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa, MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, glucose 7.8–10 mmol/L.
TTM2 (2021): normothermia ≤ 37.7 °C is the contemporary default; whichever target chosen, deliver strict fever control to ≥ 72 h with closed-loop feedback cooling.
Rewarm slowly (0.25–0.5 °C/h) — watch for hyperkalaemic rebound and prolonged drug clearance during cooling.
Neuroprognostication is multimodal, performed ≥ 72 h after ROSC, after confounders are excluded, and requires ≥ 2 concordant poor-outcome markers.
Specific markers: bilaterally absent pupil + corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20 SSEPs, NSE > 60 (48 h) / > 75 (72 h) µg/L or rising, highly malignant unreactive EEG, loss of grey-white differentiation on CT or restricted diffusion on MRI.
eCPR: ARREST and Prague OHCA show benefit only in highly selected witnessed shockable arrests with rapid cannulation (< 60 min); INCEPTION emphasises system speed.
VA-ECMO: anticipate limb ischaemia (distal perfusion cannula), Harlequin syndrome (right radial sat monitoring → consider VAV), LV distension (vent with IABP/Impella).
Avoid the self-fulfilling prophecy — do not withdraw before multimodal assessment is complete.
Refer DCD candidates to SNOD before WLST is raised with the family — preserves donation potential without altering care.

Haemodynamic & Ventilatory Targets
Multimodal Neuroprognostication
Clinical examination (≥ 72 h)
Bilateral absent pupillary light reflex AND absent corneal reflex at ≥ 72 h is the single most specific bedside sign of poor outcome (FPR ~ 1 %). Quantitative pupillometry (NPi < 2) is more reproducible than manual examination. GCS Motor 1–2 at 72 h is the trigger for formal multimodal assessment, but is NOT sufficient on its own. Status myoclonus within 72 h is concerning but does not equal status epilepticus.
Neuron-specific enolase (NSE)
Serum NSE at 48–72 h. NSE > 60 µg/L at 48 h or > 75 µg/L at 72 h, OR a rising trend, predicts poor outcome (FPR < 5 %). Confounders: haemolysis (RBC contain NSE — recheck if rising in isolation), neuroendocrine tumours. Trend matters more than a single value. Take samples in non-haemolysed serum; many labs report NSE alongside S100B.
Electroencephalography (EEG)
Continuous EEG within 24 h if available; targeted EEG ≥ 72 h. Highly malignant patterns (suppression < 10 µV background, burst-suppression with or without superimposed discharges) at ≥ 72 h predict poor outcome. Reactivity testing is essential — a reactive background is reassuring even in the comatose patient. Confounders: sedation, hypothermia, metabolic derangement.
Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs)
Bilaterally absent N20 cortical responses to median nerve stimulation at ≥ 72 h is one of the most specific markers of poor outcome (FPR ~ 0–1 %). Less affected by sedation and hypothermia than EEG. Operator-dependent; requires technical expertise. Best performed off muscle relaxant. A present N20 does not predict good outcome — it just removes one piece of bad evidence.
Brain imaging (CT and MRI)
CT within 24 h: loss of grey-white differentiation, decreased grey-white ratio (GWR < 1.10–1.20) and effacement of sulci predict poor outcome. MRI at 2–7 days is more sensitive — restricted diffusion (low ADC) in cortex, basal ganglia, hippocampus and thalamus on DWI is a strong negative prognostic marker. Quantitative ADC mapping is increasingly used in research protocols.
S100B and emerging biomarkers
S100B has lower specificity than NSE. Neurofilament light chain (NfL) shows promising performance — high serum NfL at 24–72 h post-arrest correlates strongly with poor outcome and may discriminate earlier than NSE. Not yet routinely available in UK labs.

faq-${i}
Cardiac Arrest & Post-Resuscitation Care
FRCA Final / FFICM / EDIC — TTM, multimodal neuroprognostication & eCPR
What does the 2021 Resuscitation Council UK / ERC ALS algorithm say for an adult in cardiac arrest?
Confirm arrest, call for help and start chest compressions at 100–120 min⁻¹, depth 5–6 cm, with full recoil and minimal interruptions. Attach defibrillator pads as soon as available and assess rhythm every 2 minutes. For VF/pVT: deliver a shock (biphasic 120–200 J per manufacturer, then equal or escalating), resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes, give adrenaline 1 mg IV after the third shock and every 3–5 minutes thereafter, and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock with a further 150 mg after the fifth. For non-shockable rhythms (asystole / PEA): give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as access is obtained and every 3–5 minutes, continue CPR, and actively look for reversible causes. Secure the airway (supraglottic device or tracheal tube) and switch to continuous compressions with asynchronous ventilations once an advanced airway is in place. Use waveform capnography throughout.
What are the 4 Hs and 4 Ts and how do I treat each at the bedside?
The reversible causes are Hypoxia (high-flow O₂, secure airway, check ETT position and ventilation), Hypovolaemia (rapid IV/IO crystalloid, control haemorrhage, consider blood/MTP), Hyper/hypokalaemia and other metabolic disorders (10 mL 10% calcium chloride, 10 U insulin + 50 mL 50% dextrose, salbutamol, sodium bicarbonate; correct hypoglycaemia and acidosis), and Hypothermia (active rewarming, extended resuscitation and consider eCPR —
); Tension pneumothorax (needle decompression / finger thoracostomy then chest drain), Tamponade (pericardiocentesis or resuscitative thoracotomy in trauma), Toxins (antidotes — naloxone, flumazenil, digibind, intralipid 20% for local-anaesthetic toxicity, sodium bicarbonate for TCAs), and Thrombosis (thrombolysis with alteplase 50 mg for suspected pulmonary embolism, then continue CPR for 60–90 minutes; primary PCI for coronary cause).
When should defibrillation energy be escalated and what
Use the manufacturer-recommended first biphasic energy (typically 120–200 J). If the manufacturer dose is unknown, default to the maximum available. Subsequent shocks should be of equal or higher energy. The DOSE-VF trial (Cheskes, NEJM 2022) randomised refractory VF after 3 standard shocks to (a) continued standard defibrillation, (b) vector-change (pad reposition anterior-posterior), or (c) double sequential external defibrillation (DSED, two defibrillators delivered ~1 second apart): DSED improved survival to hospital discharge (30.4% vs 13.3%) and survival with good neurological outcome. Vector-change was also superior to standard. UK and ERC guidance now permit vector change or DSED for refractory VF after the third shock where local protocols allow.
Does adrenaline actually improve outcome — what did PARAMEDIC2 show?
PARAMEDIC2 (Perkins, NEJM 2018, n = 8 014 OHCA) compared 1 mg IV adrenaline every 3–5 minutes with placebo. Adrenaline increased survival to 30 days (3.2% vs 2.4%, OR 1.39) but the absolute increase in survivors with favourable neurological outcome (modified Rankin 0–3) was small (2.2% vs 1.9%) and no different statistically, with a higher proportion of survivors having severe neurological impairment (31% vs 18%). Interpretation: adrenaline improves ROSC and short-term survival but the marginal neurological benefit is debated. UK/ERC guidance retains 1 mg IV after the third shock in shockable rhythms and as soon as access is obtained in non-shockable rhythms, recognising the trade-off and the absence of a superior alternative.
Should I cool post-arrest patients to 33 °C or aim for active normothermia? What changed after TTM2?
HACA (NEJM 2002) and Bernard (NEJM 2002) first showed benefit of 32–34 °C for 12–24 h after witnessed VF OHCA. TTM (Nielsen, NEJM 2013, n = 950) demonstrated equivalence of 33 °C and 36 °C — both were
and both prevented fever. TTM2 (Dankiewicz, NEJM 2021, n = 1 850) compared 33 °C with active normothermia (≤ 37.5 °C, fever treated aggressively) and found no difference in 6-month mortality (50% vs 48%) or neurological outcome. Contemporary ERC/ESICM 2021 guidance therefore recommends a constant temperature 32–36 °C, with active normothermia ≤ 37.7 °C now the most common pragmatic default; fever (> 37.7 °C) must be prevented for at least 72 hours regardless of strategy. Rewarming should be slow (0.25–0.5 °C / h) when starting from 33 °C.
Who is an appropriate candidate for eCPR and what does ARREST, Prague OHCA and INCEPTION tell us?
ARREST (Yannopoulos, Lancet 2020, n = 30, single-centre Minnesota) randomised refractory shockable OHCA and was stopped early for benefit — 43% vs 7% survival to discharge with eCPR. Prague OHCA (Belohlavek, JAMA 2022, n = 256) compared invasive (eCPR + cath lab) with standard advanced ALS and showed a non-significant trend to better 180-day favourable neurological outcome (31.5% vs 22.0%); subgroup analysis favoured the invasive strategy with longer arrest durations. INCEPTION (Suverein, NEJM 2023, n = 134) was a multicentre Dutch trial and was neutral — reflecting the impact of system speed and operator volume. Suitable candidates have: witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, initial shockable rhythm, age < 65–75, no major comorbidity, ETCO₂ > 10 mmHg sustained, and a realistic prospect of cannulation within 60 minutes of collapse. Outside high-volume eCPR centres with rapid pathways, benefit is unlikely.
What is multimodal neuroprognostication and when do I perform it?
Neuroprognostication is performed in the comatose post-cardiac-arrest patient at ≥ 72 hours after ROSC, only once confounders (sedation, NMBA, hypothermia, severe metabolic derangement, hypoglycaemia, hypotension, ongoing seizure activity) are excluded. The entry criterion is GCS motor ≤ 2. ERC/ESICM 2021 require at least two concordant poor-outcome markers from independent modalities before predicting poor outcome: (1) bilaterally absent pupillary AND corneal reflexes (or NPi < 2 on automated pupillometry); (2) bilaterally absent N20 cortical SSEPs; (3) NSE > 60 µg/L at 48 h or > 75 µg/L at 72 h, or a rising trend; (4) highly malignant EEG (suppression < 10 µV, or unreactive burst-suppression); (5) diffuse anoxic injury on CT (loss of grey-white differentiation, GWR < 1.10) or MRI (widespread restricted diffusion). Status myoclonus alone is not sufficient. Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy in the first 72 hours risks self-fulfilling prophecy.
How should I manage the airway and ventilator in the first 6 hours post-ROSC?
Intubate if not already (or replace a supraglottic with a tracheal tube once stable). Set tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, PEEP 5–10 cmH₂O, FiO₂ titrated to SpO₂ 94–98% (avoid hyperoxia — observational data link PaO₂ > 40 kPa to higher mortality; the EXACT pilot RCT supports normoxic targeting). Set minute ventilation to PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa (avoid hypocapnia which causes cerebral vasoconstriction and is independently associated with worse neurological outcome — TAME trial 2023 found no benefit from mild hypercapnia 6.7–7.3 kPa over normocapnia). Use continuous waveform capnography. Sedate with short-acting agents (propofol + remifentanil or fentanyl ± dexmedetomidine) to facilitate later neuroprognostication. Avoid prolonged NMBA except briefly for shivering not controlled by sedation and counter-warming.
Deliver the ERC/ESICM 2021 post-ROSC bundle including airway, ventilation, haemodynamic and metabolic targets within the first 6 hours.
Choose between TTM 33 °C, 36 °C and normothermia ≤ 37.7 °C citing TTM2 (2021) and apply strict fever control to 72 hours.
Set evidence-based MAP, SpO₂, PaCO₂, glucose and Hb targets and justify each in terms of secondary brain injury.
Perform multimodal neuroprognostication ≥ 72 h post-ROSC using clinical exam, NSE, EEG, SSEPs and imaging while excluding confounders.
Identify suitable candidates for ECMO-CPR (eCPR) and outline the cannulation pathway, complications and Harlequin physiology.
Manage VA-ECMO complications — limb ischaemia, LV distension, recirculation and differential hypoxia — at the bedside.
Communicate honestly with families, time WLST appropriately and refer DCD candidates to SNOD before withdrawal.
55-year-old, witnessed VF OHCA, ROSC at 18 min after 3 shocks. Now intubated, sedated, FiO₂ 1.0, SpO₂ 100 %, PaO₂ 38 kPa, PaCO₂ 3.4 kPa on TV 550 mL (PBW 70 kg). MAP 60 on noradrenaline 0.15 µg/kg/min. Lactate 6.2.
Hyperoxia (PaO₂ 38 kPa) is associated with worse outcome — wean FiO₂ to target SpO₂ 94–98 %. Hypocapnia (PaCO₂ 3.4 kPa) causes cerebral vasoconstriction — reduce minute ventilation to target 4.5–6.0 kPa. Tidal volume 550 mL = 7.9 mL/kg PBW — acceptable but trim to 6–8 mL/kg. MAP 60 is below the ≥ 65 mmHg target — uptitrate noradrenaline.
Day 4 post-OHCA, fully rewarmed, off sedation for 36 h. GCS E1 VT M2. Pupils fixed bilaterally, corneals absent, NPi 0. NSE 88 µg/L at 72 h (rising from 62 at 48 h). Continuous EEG: burst-suppression unreactive. SSEPs: bilaterally absent N20.
Confounders excluded (rewarmed, sedation washed out, no metabolic derangement, no status epilepticus). Apply ERC/ESICM 2021 algorithm — entry criterion (GCS M ≤ 2) met. Look for ≥ 2 concordant poor-outcome markers from independent modalities: (1) bilaterally absent pupillary + corneal reflexes, (2) NSE > 75 at 72 h with rising trend, (3) highly malignant unreactive burst-suppression EEG, (4) bilaterally absent N20 SSEPs.
42-year-old collapses in front of bystander, immediate CPR. EMS arrive at 6 min — VF, 3 shocks, mechanical CPR (LUCAS) commenced. ETCO₂ 22 mmHg. No ROSC at 25 min. Initial rhythm shockable, no significant comorbidities, transport time to ECMO centre 15 min.
ARREST/Prague OHCA criteria favouring eCPR: witnessed arrest, bystander CP

Why prognostication matters

Hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury (HIBI) is the leading cause of death after cardiac arrest admission. Two-thirds of in-hospital deaths in comatose post-arrest patients are preceded by withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (WLST) for predicted poor neurological outcome. Premature or wrong prognostication therefore causes bad outcomes — making a structured, multimodal, evidence-based approach an ethical imperative, not a procedural one.

Poor neurological outcome — CPC 3–5 or modified Rankin 4–6 (severe disability, vegetative state, or death) at 3–6 months. Good outcome — CPC 1–2 (no/moderate disability, independent living).

{/* Entry criteria & timing */}

ERC/ESICM 2021 — entry criteria & timing

Formal prognostication begins only when all of the following are true. Premature assessment is the single commonest source of false-positive predictions.

  • ≥ 72 h have elapsed since ROSC (not since rewarming).
  • Patient remains comatose with motor score M ≤ 3.
  • Sedation and analgesia have been stopped long enough for clearance (≥ 5 half-lives — longer in obesity, hepatic / renal failure, prolonged infusions).
  • Neuromuscular blockade has been excluded (train-of-four).
  • Normothermia (≥ 36 °C) for at least 24 h.
  • No major metabolic or electrolyte derangement, severe shock, or hepatic/renal failure causing drug accumulation.

If any criterion is unmet, defer prognostication. Continue active care and re-evaluate every 24–72 h. Late awakening (≥ 7 days post-ROSC) is not rare, particularly after TTM.

{/* Modality 1: Clinical */}

1. Clinical examination

{[ { sign: >2. Electroencephalography

Use standardised ACNS terminology. The robust prognostic patterns are the highly malignant categories — older terms such as have been superseded.

Highly malignant (poor outcome): suppressed background (< 10 µV) with or without periodic discharges; burst-suppression with identical bursts. Specificity approaches 100 % at > 24 h post-ROSC.

Malignant (intermediate): burst-suppression with non-identical bursts; abundant rhythmic/periodic discharges; electrographic status epilepticus. Not by itself sufficient — combine with another modality.

Benign: continuous background with reactivity. Strong predictor of good outcome when seen early.

{/* Modality 3: Evoked potentials */}

3. Short-latency somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs)

Bilateral absence of the N20 cortical response ≥ 24 h after ROSC (and after rewarming) predicts poor outcome with a false-positive rate close to 0 % when recorded and interpreted by an experienced neurophysiologist. Among the most robust single criteria — but still must be paired with a second concordant modality.

Pitfalls: technical noise (peripheral nerve injury, electrical interference), prior cervical spine pathology, profound hypothermia, and severe sedation can all abolish N20 without irreversible brain injury.

{/* Modality 4: Biomarkers */}

4. Biomarkers — Neuron-Specific Enolase

  • NSE released from injured neurons; concentrations peak 48–72 h after ROSC.
  • Threshold for poor outcome: NSE > 60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h; a rising trend strengthens the prediction.
  • Reject haemolysed samples — NSE is abundant in erythrocytes and even mild haemolysis falsely elevates results.
  • Other sources of false elevation: neuroendocrine tumours, small-cell lung cancer, ECMO-related haemolysis.
  • S100B and neurofilament light chain (NfL) are promising but not yet in the ERC algorithm.
{/* Modality 5: Neuroimaging */}

5. Neuroimaging

CT brain (early, < 24 h)

Generalised oedema with effacement of sulci and loss of grey–white matter differentiation (GWR < 1.10–1.15 at basal ganglia level) predicts poor outcome. Useful when MRI not feasible.

MRI brain (2–7 days)

Diffuse restricted diffusion on DWI involving cortex and deep grey nuclei. ADC values < 650 × 10⁻⁶ mm²/s in > 10 % of brain tissue predict poor outcome. Best obtained 2–5 days post-ROSC.

{/* The multimodal algorithm */}

Putting it together — multimodal algorithm

  1. At ≥ 72 h, confirm entry criteria (comatose, M ≤ 3, confounders excluded).
  2. Examine pupillary and corneal reflexes — if both absent, this is criterion 1.
  3. Document any status myoclonus within the first 72 h — criterion 2 if present.
  4. Send NSE at 48 h and 72 h (non-haemolysed) — criterion 3 if > 60 µg/L and/or rising.
  5. Record SSEPs after rewarming — bilateral absent N20 = criterion 4.
  6. EEG (continuous or routine ≥ 24 h post-ROSC) — highly malignant pattern = criterion 5.
  7. Imaging — diffuse anoxic injury on CT or MRI = criterion 6.
  8. Poor outcome is when ≥ 2 criteria are concordant. If only one is positive, the result is indeterminate — continue care and re-evaluate.

The ERC/ESICM algorithm explicitly avoids predicting good outcome — clinicians must remain open to late recovery and avoid premature WLST in indeterminate cases.

{/* Confounders */}

Confounders that invalidate the assessment

    Communication, ethics & WLST
    • Document the modalities used, the time after ROSC, and the named clinicians performing the assessment.
    • Discuss findings with a second senior intensivist before any family conversation about WLST.
    • Frame the conversation as likely poor outcome — not certainty. Acknowledge the indeterminate band and the self-fulfilling prophecy risk.

    • Accepting a haemolysed NSE result.
    • Mistaking Lance–Adams syndrome for status myoclonus.
    • Forgetting that the M ≤ 3 entry criterion is not itself a prognostic finding.

Two configurations
— gas exchange only. Blood drained from and returned to the venous system. Use for refractory respiratory failure with preserved cardiac output.
— cardiac and respiratory support. Venous drainage, arterial return. Use for refractory cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest (ECPR).
Typical cannulae
Femoral V → Femoral V (VV)
Drainage 23–25 Fr femoral V (tip at hepatic IVC), return 19–21 Fr contralateral femoral V (tip at RA)
Fastest peripheral access; suitable for percutaneous insertion in ED/ICU
Highest recirculation (10–30%); patient bed-bound; femoral access compromises mobilisation
Femoral V → Internal Jugular V (VV)
Drainage 25 Fr femoral V, return 21 Fr right IJ (tip at SVC/RA junction)
Lower recirculation; permits limb mobilisation
Two access sites; IJ cannulation in coagulopathy
Dual-lumen single-cannula (Avalon, Crescent)
27–31 Fr right IJ dual-lumen — drainage ports in SVC and IVC, return port directed at tricuspid valve
Single access; awake ECMO and ambulation; bridge to lung transplantation
Requires fluoroscopy or TOE for accurate positioning; malposition causes recirculation or RV/PA injury
Peripheral femoro-femoral VA
Drainage 23–25 Fr femoral V (tip at RA), return 15–19 Fr femoral A + 6–8 Fr distal perfusion cannula
Rapid bedside or cath-lab insertion; standard for cardiogenic shock and ECPR
Harlequin syndrome; LV distension; limb ischaemia without distal perfusion cannula
Central VA (post-cardiotomy)
RA drainage, ascending aorta return via open chest
Antegrade aortic flow eliminates Harlequin; high flow achievable
Sternotomy with open or covered chest; bleeding and mediastinitis risk
VAV (peripheral VA + IJ return)
Femoral V drainage, femoral A return, plus an IJ return cannula
Treats Harlequin by delivering oxygenated blood to the upper body
More complex circuit; balance of flow split between A and V return
Sizing rule of thumb:
target circuit blood flow of 60–80 mL/kg/min (full VV support) or 50–70 mL/kg/min (VA support). For a 70 kg adult, this is 4–5 L/min — achievable with a 23–25 Fr drainage and a 19–21 Fr return cannula. The most common cause of inadequate flow is undersized drainage.
