is highly efficient and depends almost entirely on
sweep gas flow
. A small change in sweep (1–2 L/min) can produce large PaCO₂ swings — change slowly to avoid cerebral vasoconstriction.
Recirculation fraction
in VV-ECMO: a portion of returned oxygenated blood is re-aspirated by the drainage cannula. Suspect when SvO₂ pre-membrane is unexpectedly high but PaO₂ remains low.
Differential hypoxia
(Harlequin) in peripheral VA-ECMO — see complications below.
VV-ECMO: indications & EOLIA / CESAR evidence
PaO₂/FiO₂ < 50 mmHg for > 3 h,
pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h, with Vt reduced to 4 mL/kg and RR up to 35.
CESAR (2009)
randomised severe respiratory failure to referral to a single UK ECMO centre vs conventional management; referral improved 6-month disability-free survival.
EOLIA (2018)
stopped early for futility (60 % vs 46 % 60-day mortality, p = 0.09) but a pre-specified Bayesian re-analysis estimated a 96 % probability of mortality benefit at the trial's chosen prior. Practice has converged on referral for EOLIA-eligible patients.
Refractory cardiogenic shock (post-cardiotomy, fulminant myocarditis, decompensated cardiomyopathy, massive PE, drug toxicity).
Bridge to recovery, transplantation, or durable LVAD.
Refractory cardiac arrest (ECPR) in selected patients.
Right ventricular failure with preserved gas exchange (consider RV-protective configurations or VV with added cannula for selected cases).
Monitoring & target
Unfractionated heparin
APTT 1.5–2× normal, ACT 180–220 s, anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 IU/mL
Anti-Xa is most reliable in critical illness (raised acute-phase reactants distort APTT)
Confirmed HIT or heparin failure
APTT 1.5–2× normal; dilute pharmacokinetics in renal failure
No reversal agent; useful in HIT; growing use as a primary alternative to heparin
HIT, hepatically cleared
APTT 1.5–2× normal
Avoid in hepatic failure
No anticoagulation (heparin-bonded circuit)
Major active bleeding
Hourly visual circuit inspection, trans-membrane pressure, oxygenator gas exchange
Time-limited; accept higher circuit-change frequency
Daily haematology bundle:
platelets (target > 50 × 10⁹/L, > 80 if bleeding), fibrinogen (> 1.5 g/L), Hb (target 70–90 g/L unless ischaemic), D-dimer trend (rising suggests circuit thrombosis), anti-Xa, ACT 4–6 hourly, free Hb (haemolysis), LDH. Acquired von Willebrand syndrome from high shear is a major contributor to bleeding — consider tranexamic acid for mucocutaneous bleeding and DDAVP cautiously.
: ultra-protective settings on VV-ECMO — Vt 3–4 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤ 25 cmH₂O, PEEP 10–15, RR 10, FiO₂ 0.3 to allow lung rest. Avoid spontaneous over-breathing causing patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI).
: deep sedation initially (RASS −4 to −5) ± neuromuscular blockade during cannulation; then light sedation (RASS −1 to 0) and consider awake-ECMO programmes for bridge-to-transplant.
: physiotherapy and ambulation are achievable with single-cannula dual-lumen VV configurations and dedicated ECMO–rehab pathways (notably for lung-transplant bridging).
: restrictive Hb threshold 70–90 g/L unless ischaemic; platelets > 50 × 10⁹/L (> 80 if bleeding); fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L; FFP only for active bleeding or invasive procedures.
: AKI is common (60–80%); CRRT is usually integrated into the ECMO circuit via a haemofilter or a separate access. Drug clearance is altered by adsorption to the oxygenator (lipophilic drugs, sedatives) and the larger circuit volume.
: surveillance cultures; no routine prophylactic antibiotics; CRBSI rate 10–20 per 1000 ECMO days.
: enteral feeding within 24–48 h is safe even on full ECMO support; energy targets per critical-care guidance.
ECPR — extracorporeal CPR for refractory arrest
Witnessed arrest with bystander CPR within 5 min.
Shockable initial rhythm (VF / pulseless VT).
No-flow time < 5 min, low-flow time < 60 min.
Age < 70 (centre-dependent), no major comorbidity.
End-tidal CO₂ > 1.3 kPa (10 mmHg) during CPR — surrogate for adequate compressions and tissue perfusion.
Reversible cause suspected (commonly ACS for downstream PCI).
ARREST (2020)
Prague-OHCA (2022)
INCEPTION (2023)
VV-ECMO — sweep-down trial
VA-ECMO — flow-down trial
Trial (year)
Intervention vs comparator
Severe adult respiratory failure (Murray ≥ 3 or uncompensated hypercapnia)
Referral to a single UK ECMO centre vs conventional management
↑ 6-month disability-free survival (63% vs 47%, RR 0.69, p = 0.03) — referral effect; not all referred patients received ECMO
Severe ARDS meeting EOLIA criteria
Early VV-ECMO vs continued conventional management with crossover
Stopped early for futility — 60-day mortality 35% vs 46% (RR 0.76, p = 0.09); 28% crossover. Bayesian re-analysis: ≥96% probability of mortality benefit
EOLIA Bayesian re-analysis (2018)
Same cohort
Bayesian framework with multiple priors
Robust ≥ 88% probability of mortality reduction across priors; underpins current ELSO referral criteria
Refractory OHCA with shockable rhythm, Minneapolis (single-centre)
ECPR vs standard ACLS
Stopped early for benefit — survival to hospital discharge 43% vs 7%; selected, system-supported cohort
Refractory OHCA, Prague (single-centre)
Invasive strategy (ECPR + immediate angiography) vs standard ACLS
No difference in primary 180-day neurologic outcome; signal for benefit in pre-specified subgroups
Refractory OHCA, 10 Dutch centres
Neutral — 30-day survival with good neurologic outcome 20% vs 16% (OR 1.4, p = 0.52); highlights system-performance dependence
SUPERNOVA (2019) / REST (2022)
Moderate ARDS
Low-flow ECCO₂R to enable ultra-protective ventilation
SUPERNOVA: feasibility, no mortality signal. REST stopped early — increased serious adverse events, no mortality benefit
RESP — VV-ECMO for respiratory failure
SAVE — VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock
bridge to nowhere
. Agreeing the exit strategy at cannulation and reviewing it daily prevents protracted, non-beneficial support.
Pre-cannulation conversation:
document the bridge (e.g. "bridge to recovery within 14 days"), the criteria for withdrawal, and what will not be offered (e.g. transplant in a contraindicated patient).
Daily review:
trajectory, organ recovery, neurology, eligibility for transplant or VAD. If none of the exits remains achievable, escalate to MDT discussion.
Family communication:
ECMO support is highly visible and patients may look "well". Explicit communication about prognosis and the meaning of the device prevents false hope.
Withdrawal of ECMO:
usually achieved by reducing sweep gas (VV) or flow (VA) to zero, with continued sedation and symptom management. Decannulation post-mortem may be required for organ donation pathways.
Donation after circulatory death on ECMO:
emerging pathway — engage the donation team early.
Confusing VV (gas exchange only) with VA (cardiac + respiratory) — the indication, cannulation and complications differ entirely.
Monitoring a left-sided SpO₂ on peripheral VA-ECMO and missing Harlequin syndrome.
Adjusting FdO₂ to clear CO₂ — sweep gas, not FdO₂, controls CO₂ clearance.
Forgetting the distal perfusion cannula and causing limb ischaemia.
Clamping the circuit during a weaning trial — guaranteed circuit thrombosis.
Quoting CESAR as proof that "ECMO saves lives" — CESAR proved
to an ECMO centre improved outcomes; the intervention bundle matters.
Conflating ARREST (positive, single-centre) with INCEPTION (neutral, multicentre) — both are true; system performance reconciles them.
Treating SAVE/RESP scores as absolute cut-offs; they are decision-support, not gates.
Severe ARDS — is this patient a VV-ECMO candidate?
Right radial SpO₂ 82 % on peripheral VA-ECMO
Refractory VF arrest — is ECPR indicated?
VV-ECMO provides respiratory support only (gas exchange); VA-ECMO provides combined respiratory and haemodynamic support but generates LV afterload and risks Harlequin syndrome in peripheral configurations.
EOLIA criteria for VV-ECMO referral in severe ARDS: PaO₂/FiO₂ < 50 mmHg for > 3 h, or < 80 mmHg for > 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h, despite optimal lung-protective ventilation and proning.
CESAR (2009) showed referral to an ECMO centre improved 6-month disability-free survival in severe respiratory failure; EOLIA (2018) was stopped early for futility but a Bayesian re-analysis suggested a mortality benefit. Modern ELSO criteria reflect both.
Harlequin (North–South) syndrome in peripheral VA-ECMO: monitor the right radial pulse oximeter — it reflects upper-body / coronary / cerebral oxygenation. Manage by optimising native lung function, increasing ECMO flow, or converting to VAV.
LV distension on VA-ECMO is driven by increased afterload from retrograde aortic flow plus persistent venous return. Recognised by rising PAOP, pulmonary oedema, absent aortic valve opening. Manage by inotropy, IABP, atrial septostomy or trans-aortic vent (Impella).
Recirculation in VV-ECMO: oxygenated blood from the return cannula is re-aspirated by the drainage cannula, falsely raising pre-membrane SvO₂ and limiting effective oxygen delivery. Reduce flow, reposition cannulae, or change configuration.
Anticoagulation: unfractionated heparin to APTT 1.5–2× normal or ACT 180–220 s. Bivalirudin is the agent of choice if HIT is confirmed. Balance bleeding (commonest complication) against circuit thrombosis.
Sweep gas (gas flow through the oxygenator) controls CO₂ clearance; FdO₂ and blood flow control oxygenation. Increasing sweep without changing FdO₂ removes more CO₂ but does not improve PaO₂.
ECPR (ELSO criteria): witnessed arrest with bystander CPR < 5 min, shockable initial rhythm, low-flow < 60 min, age < 70, no major comorbidity, end-tidal CO₂ > 1.3 kPa during CPR. ARREST and Prague-OHCA support; INCEPTION negative — outcomes depend on system performance.
Weaning: VV-ECMO is weaned by reducing sweep gas to zero while maintaining blood flow (the sweep-down trial) and assessing native gas exchange. VA-ECMO is weaned by stepwise flow reduction with echo assessment of LV / RV function — never clamp the circuit while flow continues.
Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO)
FFICM / EDIC — Intensive Care (ELSO / EOLIA / CESAR-based practice)
Large-bore (21–29 Fr), multi-fenestrated. Femoral vein → IVC/RA most common. Pre-pump pressure should be negative but > –100 mmHg to avoid haemolysis and cavitation.
Magnetically levitated impeller (e.g. CentriMag, Rotaflow). Preload- and afterload-sensitive — flow drops if venous return is poor or systemic resistance rises. Watch for line chatter (hypovolaemia).
Polymethylpentene hollow-fibre. Blood flows on one side, sweep gas the other. FdO₂ controls oxygenation; sweep flow controls CO₂ removal. Integrated heat exchanger.
VV: internal jugular → SVC/RA, or contralateral femoral vein. VA: femoral artery (peripheral) or aorta (central). Distal perfusion cannula essential for femoral arterial return.
Bleeding
Commonest complication. Cannulation sites, ICH, GI, surgical sites. Driven by heparin, acquired vWF deficiency (high shear), thrombocytopaenia. Target the lowest acceptable APTT/ACT and platelets > 50–80 × 10⁹/L.
Thrombosis / oxygenator failure
Visible fibrin in the oxygenator, rising trans-membrane pressure, falling post-oxygenator PaO₂, falling platelets and fibrinogen, rising D-dimer. Plan elective circuit change before catastrophic failure.
Harlequin / North–South syndrome
Peripheral VA-ECMO: poorly oxygenated native blood ejected by recovering heart perfuses upper body. Monitor right radial SpO₂. Manage with native lung optimisation, ↑ flow, or VAV conversion.
LV distension
Increased afterload from retrograde aortic flow + persistent venous return. Watch PAOP, pulmonary oedema, absent aortic valve opening on echo. Decompress with inotropy, IABP, atrial septostomy, or Impella vent.
Limb ischaemia
Femoral arterial cannula obstructs distal flow. Distal perfusion cannula (small antegrade catheter into superficial femoral artery) is now standard. Assess pulses, NIRS or Doppler hourly.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopaenia: 4Ts score, anti-PF4 antibody, confirmatory functional assay. Switch to bivalirudin or argatroban; do not give platelets unless bleeding.
Haemolysis
Pre-pump pressure < –100 mmHg, kinks, or oxygenator thrombus. Rising free Hb, LDH, pink plasma. Optimise drainage geometry, transfuse, plan circuit change.
Infection
Cannula-related bloodstream infection rates 10–20 %. Daily review, low threshold for cultures, no prophylactic antibiotics — surveillance and source control.
What is the difference between VV and VA ECMO?
VV-ECMO drains and returns blood to the venous system — it provides gas exchange only and is used for refractory respiratory failure with preserved cardiac output. VA-ECMO drains venous blood and returns oxygenated blood to a major artery, providing both gas exchange and circulatory support; it is used for refractory cardiogenic shock and refractory cardiac arrest (ECPR). VA-ECMO increases LV afterload and carries the risk of differential hypoxia (Harlequin syndrome) when cannulated peripherally.
What is Harlequin (North–South) syndrome?
In peripheral femoro-femoral VA-ECMO, oxygenated blood is returned retrograde up the descending aorta while a recovering heart ejects native, poorly oxygenated blood antegrade. The watershed between the two flows determines which territory perfuses the coronaries, brain and right arm. Monitor SpO₂ on the right upper limb. Manage by optimising native lung function (increase PEEP and FiO₂, recruit), increasing ECMO flow, adding an internal jugular return cannula (VAV configuration) or converting to central cannulation.
What are the EOLIA criteria for VV-ECMO referral in ARDS?
EOLIA criteria for severe ARDS refractory to optimal ventilation and proning: PaO₂/FiO₂ < 50 mmHg for > 3 h, or PaO₂/FiO₂ < 80 mmHg for > 6 h, or arterial pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h with respiratory rate increased to 35 and tidal volume reduced to 4 mL/kg PBW. EOLIA stopped early for futility (p = 0.09) but a pre-specified Bayesian re-analysis estimated a 96% probability of mortality benefit, and contemporary ELSO criteria mirror EOLIA.
When is ECPR indicated for refractory cardiac arrest?
ELSO criteria for ECPR: witnessed arrest with bystander CPR started within 5 min, initial shockable rhythm (VF/pVT), no-flow time < 5 min and low-flow time < 60 min, age < 70 with no major comorbidity, end-tidal CO₂ > 1.3 kPa during CPR (a surrogate for adequate chest compressions), and a suspected reversible cause (most commonly acute coronary syndrome). ARREST (Minneapolis) and Prague-OHCA showed mortality benefit in selected single-centre cohorts; INCEPTION (multicentre Dutch RCT) was neutral — the size and reliability of any ECPR benefit depend on low low-flow time and a straight-to-cath-lab pathway.
First-line is unfractionated heparin bolus 50–100 units/kg at cannulation, followed by continuous infusion titrated to APTT 1.5–2× normal or ACT 180–220 s. Anti-Xa (target 0.3–0.7 IU/mL) is more reliable than APTT in critically ill patients with raised acute-phase reactants. Bivalirudin is the agent of choice when heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is confirmed (4Ts score and anti-PF4 antibody, then functional assay). Bleeding is the commonest complication of ECMO — accept lower anticoagulation targets when active bleeding outweighs thrombotic risk.
What is the SAVE score and what is the RESP score?
The SAVE (Survival After Veno-Arterial ECMO) score predicts in-hospital survival for adults receiving VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock. The RESP (Respiratory ECMO Survival Prediction) score predicts in-hospital survival for adults receiving VV-ECMO for severe acute respiratory failure. Both scores assign points for age, organ failure, pre-ECMO ventilation duration, diagnosis and acute clinical variables, then stratify patients into risk classes from I (lowest mortality) to V (highest). They are decision-support tools — not absolute contraindications — and are most useful when patient selection is borderline.
Use a sweep-down trial. Maintain blood flow on the circuit (this prevents thrombosis) and reduce sweep gas stepwise to zero over 30–60 min, ventilating the patient on lung-protective settings (Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 10, FiO₂ 0.5). Re-check ABG and lung mechanics. If PaO₂/FiO₂ > 150, pH and PaCO₂ stable, and respiratory mechanics acceptable, plan decannulation. Restart sweep promptly if the patient deteriorates.
Distinguish veno-venous (VV) and veno-arterial (VA) ECMO by indication, cannulation, physiology and target outputs.
Apply ELSO / EOLIA / CESAR criteria to select adults with severe respiratory or cardiac failure for ECMO referral.
Describe the components of an ECMO circuit (drainage / centrifugal pump / membrane oxygenator / heat exchanger / return) and the meaning of blood flow, sweep gas, FdO₂.
Recognise and manage major ECMO complications: recirculation, Harlequin / North–South syndrome, LV distension, limb ischaemia, bleeding, HIT, oxygenator failure.
Plan anticoagulation, transfusion thresholds and daily monitoring during ECMO support.
Outline a structured weaning trial for VV (sweep-down) and VA (flow-down) ECMO, and the role of ECPR in refractory cardiac arrest.

Source Control
Human Albumin Solution — the evidence
Population & intervention
Key result
SAFE (NEJM 2004, n≈7000)
General ICU; 4% albumin vs 0.9% saline for resuscitation.
No overall mortality difference (RR 0.99). Pre-specified sepsis subgroup: trend to
mortality with albumin (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.74–1.02).
Albumin is
in sepsis; signal of possible benefit (hypothesis-generating).
SAFE TBI subgroup (NEJM 2007)
Traumatic brain injury subgroup of SAFE.
Increased 24-month mortality with albumin (RR 1.63).
Avoid albumin in TBI
— even when sepsis coexists.
ALBIOS (NEJM 2014, n=1818)
Severe sepsis / septic shock; 20% albumin to keep serum albumin ≥30 g/L + crystalloid vs crystalloid alone, for 28 days.
No 28- or 90-day mortality difference. Better haemodynamics (higher MAP, lower fluid balance, faster vasopressor weaning). Post-hoc: ↓ mortality in the septic-shock subgroup (RR 0.87).
improves haemodynamics
but no proven survival benefit overall; possible benefit in established septic shock.
CRISTAL (JAMA 2013)
Hypovolaemic shock (incl. sepsis); colloids (mostly albumin/HES) vs crystalloids.
No 28-day mortality difference; lower 90-day mortality with colloids (secondary outcome).
Hypothesis-generating only — heterogeneous colloid mix limits conclusions for albumin specifically.
Meta-analyses (Patel 2014, Xu 2014, Cochrane 2018)
Pooled RCTs of albumin vs other fluids in sepsis.
No clear all-cause mortality benefit; signal toward reduced mortality when compared specifically to
rather than balanced crystalloids.
Effect size — if real — is small and may largely reflect avoidance of saline-related hyperchloraemia.
CHEST (2012) & 6S (2012)
Comparator trials of HES vs crystalloid in ICU/sepsis.
HES caused increased AKI / RRT and (6S) increased mortality.
Established that
synthetic colloids are harmful
, leaving albumin as the only colloid still considered in sepsis.
Guideline positions
Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021
weak recommendation
for albumin in patients who have received
large volumes of crystalloid
(e.g. >60–80 mL/kg) for sepsis or septic shock; balanced crystalloid remains first-line. Not recommended as the initial resuscitation fluid.
NICE NG51
— crystalloid first;
do not use
tetrastarch; albumin not routinely recommended but may be considered in ongoing large-volume resuscitation.
IDSA 2024
— emphasises individualised, dynamic fluid assessment over fixed volumes; reserves albumin for the same large-volume scenario, noting absence of robust mortality benefit.
albumin in
traumatic brain injury
(SAFE TBI signal of harm) and use cautiously in decompensated heart failure (volume load).
Mechanistic rationale & caveats
Oncotic pressure:
albumin contributes ~75–80% of plasma colloid osmotic pressure; iso-oncotic 4–5% expands plasma volume by ~80% of the volume infused vs ~20–25% for crystalloid.
Glycocalyx in sepsis
is shed → increased capillary leak. The classical "colloid stays intravascular" advantage is
, which may explain why trials show smaller volume-sparing effects than predicted.
Non-oncotic effects:
antioxidant (binds free radicals, NO carrier), drug/bilirubin transport, possible glycocalyx-stabilising actions — biologically plausible but not proven to translate to survival.
Hyperchloraemia avoidance:
apparent "albumin benefit" vs saline is attenuated when balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) is the comparator (SMART, BaSICS).
Cost & supply:
albumin is ~30–50× the cost of crystalloid — a key reason routine first-line use is not endorsed despite a favourable safety profile.
Practical dosing — when and how to give albumin in sepsis
When to consider it
persistent hypotension or ongoing vasopressor requirement
~30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid (SSC 2021 initial bolus), and especially once cumulative crystalloid approaches
60–80 mL/kg
in the first 24 h.
reduce further crystalloid load (limit interstitial oedema, hyperchloraemia and abdominal pressure) while maintaining MAP ≥65 mmHg and adequate end-organ perfusion.
in traumatic brain injury (SAFE TBI). Use cautiously in decompensated heart failure and oliguric AKI with established fluid overload.
4–5% (iso-oncotic) — for ongoing volume replacement
Use when
the primary aim is plasma-volume expansion in a fluid-responsive patient who has already had substantial crystalloid.
250–500 mL boluses (≈ 5 mL/kg) over 15–30 min, reassessing fluid responsiveness (passive leg raise, stroke-volume variation, lactate trend) between boluses. Typical 24-h ceiling 1–2 L.
~80% of the infused volume retained intravascularly (vs ~20–25% for crystalloid).
20% (hyper-oncotic) — for hypoalbuminaemia / oedematous patient
serum albumin is low (typically <25–30 g/L), the patient is already fluid-overloaded/oedematous, or further large crystalloid boluses are undesirable. This is the ALBIOS strategy — top up to keep serum albumin ≥30 g/L.
100 mL of 20% (= 20 g albumin) over 30–60 min, repeated 1–2× daily as needed. Some units give up to 200 mL/day in divided doses while titrating to serum albumin ≥30 g/L.
pulls fluid into the intravascular space — risk of acute pulmonary oedema if the patient is not fluid-deplete; pair with diuresis if total body fluid overload exists.
Monitoring & stop rules
Reassess MAP, lactate, urine output and dynamic indices after each bolus; stop if no haemodynamic response (non-responder) or if signs of pulmonary oedema appear.
Do not chase serum albumin above 30–35 g/L — there is no evidence of benefit and cost/supply is significant.
Document clearly that synthetic colloids (HES, gelatins) are
to be used.
Practical viva-ready summary
Sepsis Biomarkers
Source & Kinetics
Clinical Utility
Hepatic acute-phase protein. Rises 6–8 h, peaks 36–50 h. Half-life ~19 h. Triggered by IL-6.
Widely available, inexpensive. Tracks trends and treatment response. Values >100 mg/L suggest significant bacterial infection but not diagnostic.
Non-specific — elevated post-surgery, trauma, autoimmune disease, malignancy. Slow kinetics. Poor bacterial vs viral discrimination. Low in hepatic failure.
Procalcitonin (PCT)
Calcitonin precursor. Extra-thyroidal production induced by endotoxin and TNF-α/IL-6. Rises 2–4 h, peaks 12–24 h, half-life 24–30 h.
Best evidence for guiding antibiotic duration
(PRORATA, SAPS trials). SSC 2021 recommends PCT-guided de-escalation. <0.1 ng/mL: bacterial infection unlikely. >0.5 ng/mL: systemic bacterial infection likely. 80% decline from peak supports stopping antibiotics.
Elevated post-surgery, burns, cardiogenic shock, renal failure. Not reliably raised in localised infections. Cost higher than CRP. Viral infections generally suppress PCT (helps differentiate).
Anaerobic glycolysis end-product. Normal <2 mmol/L. In sepsis: tissue hypoperfusion AND β₂-adrenergic aerobic glycolysis. Rapid point-of-care assay.
Prognostic marker and resuscitation target
. Lactate >2 mmol/L defines septic shock (+ vasopressors). Clearance >20% in 2 h → improved outcomes. Part of Hour-1 bundle. Serial measurements guide resuscitation.
Non-specific: seizures, mesenteric ischaemia, liver failure, β₂-agonists, metformin, thiamine deficiency. Type A (hypoperfusion) vs Type B (non-hypoperfusion) distinction important. Hepatic impairment reduces clearance.
Presepsin (sCD14-ST)
Soluble fragment of CD14 (monocyte LPS receptor). Rises within 2 h (faster than PCT), peaks 3 h. Half-life 1–3 h — very rapid kinetics.
Emerging biomarker with fastest kinetics. >600 pg/mL suggests sepsis. May have superior diagnostic accuracy to PCT for early bacterial sepsis in some studies. Rising levels predict worse prognosis.
Not widely available — requires specific immunoassay. Elevated in renal failure. Limited evidence vs PCT/CRP — few large RCTs. Not yet in SSC guidelines. Assay standardisation evolving.
Endotoxin Activity Assay (EAA)
Measures LPS-induced neutrophil oxidative burst. Reflects circulating endotoxin. Results <30 min. Scale 0–1: low (<0.4), intermediate (0.4–0.59), high (≥0.6).
Specific for Gram-negative sepsis. High EAA (≥0.6) → worse outcomes. Guided polymyxin B haemoperfusion in EUPHRATES trial (post-hoc benefit in EAA 0.6–0.89 subgroup). May differentiate Gram-negative vs Gram-positive source.
Gram-negative only — normal in Gram-positive/fungal sepsis. EUPHRATES failed primary endpoint. Limited availability. Does not distinguish viable bacteria from LPS fragments. Antibiotic-induced endotoxin release may confound.

Diagnosis
No biomarker replaces clinical assessment. PCT >0.5 ng/mL with compatible clinical picture supports bacterial sepsis. Presepsin may add value in early detection but availability is limited.
Antibiotic Stewardship
PCT-guided algorithms reduce antibiotic duration by 2–3 days without increasing mortality (multiple RCTs). SSC 2021 recommends daily PCT for de-escalation. PCT that fails to decline suggests inadequate source control, resistant organism, or non-infectious cause.
Prognostication
Lactate >4 mmol/L: mortality ~30–40%. Persistently elevated lactate despite resuscitation is the strongest predictor of poor outcome. Rising PCT/CRP despite treatment suggests treatment failure.
Serial Monitoring
Trends are more informative than single values. Lactate 2–4 hourly during resuscitation, CRP daily, PCT 24–48 hourly. Declining trajectory supports current management; plateau or rise mandates reassessment.
Sepsis — Hour-1 Bundle Synthesis
The Surviving Sepsis 2021 bundle distilled to the actions that change outcome.

Sepsis (Singer, JAMA 2016) is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalised as a rise of ≥ 2 points in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score from baseline in the presence of suspected or proven infection. Septic shock is the subset requiring vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure ≥ 65 mmHg AND a serum lactate > 2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitation, identifying a group with hospital mortality > 40%. qSOFA (RR ≥ 22, altered mentation, SBP ≤ 100) is a bedside prompt to consider sepsis — it is a screening tool, not a diagnostic criterion.
What is the Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 bundle?
The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 bundle is a recognition-to-action package that should be initiated within 1 hour of sepsis recognition: (1) measure lactate and re-measure if > 2 mmol/L; (2) obtain blood cultures before antibiotics; (3) administer broad-spectrum antibiotics; (4) begin rapid 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L; (5) start vasopressors during or after fluid if MAP < 65 mmHg. For sepsis without shock where infection is possible but not proven, SSC 2021 permits up to 3 hours for antibiotics while diagnostic work-up continues.
Why does every hour of delayed antibiotics matter in septic shock?
Observational data (Kumar 2006; Ferrer 2014; Seymour NEJM 2017 — New York State sepsis mandate cohort) show that each hour of delay in effective antibiotic administration in septic shock is associated with a ~4–8% absolute increase in in-hospital mortality. The 2017 New York data demonstrated an OR of 1.04 per hour for the 3-hour bundle. Empirical cover should target the suspected source and local resistance patterns, be broad enough to cover MRSA and Pseudomonas where clinical features suggest it, and be de-escalated once cultures and clinical course allow.
Is 30 mL/kg of crystalloid still the recommended initial fluid bolus?
Yes — SSC 2021 retains a 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid bolus over the first 3 hours in sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock as a weak recommendation. case_bank.title: Which vasoactive drug for refractory septic shock?
case_bank.text:
Case: Which vasoactive drug for refractory septic shock? (Critical care drugs, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive at a mean arterial pressure of 55 mmHg on noradrenaline 0.4 micrograms/kg/min despite fluid resuscitation.
Presentation: Cardiac index is 4.2 L/min/m², lactate 4.1 mmol/L, echocardiography shows preserved contractility.
Stage 1 — Interpret the haemodynamics
  Question: Which problem are you treating?
  Model answer: High cardiac index with low pressure indicates a vasodilatory, resistance problem rather than pump failure.
  Model answer: Adding an inotrope would raise output without correcting the vasodilation and may worsen tachyarrhythmia and oxygen demand.
  Model answer: Target mean arterial pressure of about 65 mmHg, individualised upwards in chronic hypertension.
Stage 2 — Choose the next agent
  Question: How do you escalate?
  Model answer: Add vasopressin (typically 0.03 units/min) to spare catecholamine dose, acting through V1 receptors independent of adrenergic pathways.
  Model answer: Consider hydrocortisone for shock requiring ongoing vasopressor support, and reassess for source control, occult bleeding and acidosis limiting catecholamine responsiveness.
  Model answer: Reserve adrenaline or an inotrope for genuine low-output states, guided by echocardiography or cardiac output monitoring.
Stage 3 — Explain the receptors
  Question: Summarise the pharmacodynamics behind the choices.
  Model answer: Noradrenaline acts mainly on alpha-1 receptors with modest beta-1 activity, raising resistance with limited chronotropy.
  Model answer: Adrenaline is dose-dependent: beta effects predominate at low dose, alpha at high dose, with lactate generation through beta-2-mediated glycolysis.
  Model answer: Dobutamine is a beta-1 agonist with beta-2 vasodilation; phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist that may reduce output through reflex bradycardia and increased afterload.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Vasoactive selection follows from the measured physiology: define whether the deficit is resistance, output, preload or rhythm, then choose the receptor profile that corrects it. Catecholamine responsiveness falls with acidosis, hypocalcaemia, hypoxia and receptor downregulation, so escalating dose alone is often ineffective; combining agents with different mechanisms is more effective and less arrhythmogenic than maximising one.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use invasive arterial monitoring, central administration, repeated echocardiography or cardiac output measurement, lactate trend and urine output. Correct calcium, acidosis and hypoxia; ensure source control and antimicrobial adequacy. Add vasopressin early as catecholamine-sparing, consider corticosteroid in vasopressor-dependent shock, and reassess for mechanisms such as tamponade, right ventricular failure or adrenal insufficiency when shock is refractory.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not add an inotrope for a high-output vasodilated state, and do not describe 'renal-dose dopamine'. Give receptor targets and doses, and state the mean arterial pressure goal.
Take-home: Treat the measured defect: vasodilatory shock needs vasopressors and catecholamine-sparing adjuncts, not inotropes for an already high cardiac output.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: vasoactive drugs (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw066); BJA Educ: pharmacodynamics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkm016)

case_bank.title: Antibiotic dosing in critical illness and renal replacement
case_bank.text:
Case: Antibiotic dosing in critical illness and renal replacement (Critical care drugs, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient with abdominal sepsis on continuous veno-venous haemofiltration is prescribed meropenem and gentamicin. Serum albumin is 18 g/L and fluid balance is +6 L.
Presentation: The team asks whether doses should be reduced because of renal failure.
Stage 1 — Classify the killing pattern
  Question: Which pharmacodynamic target applies to each drug?
  Model answer: Beta-lactams such as meropenem are time-dependent: efficacy tracks the fraction of the dosing interval that free drug exceeds the minimum inhibitory concentration.
  Model answer: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent: efficacy tracks peak concentration relative to the minimum inhibitory concentration, with post-antibiotic effect permitting extended intervals.
  Model answer: Vancomycin is best described by the ratio of 24-hour area under the curve to minimum inhibitory concentration.
Stage 2 — Adjust for the pathophysiology
  Question: What happens to kinetics in this patient?
  Model answer: Volume of distribution of hydrophilic drugs increases with oedema and fluid loading, so early underdosing is common; loading doses should not be reduced.
  Model answer: Hypoalbuminaemia increases free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs and can increase clearance of unbound drug.
  Model answer: Continuous renal replacement provides substantial clearance of small, water-soluble, poorly protein-bound drugs, so maintenance doses often need to be higher than for anuric patients not receiving filtration.
Stage 3 — Write the plan
  Question: What is your practical prescription strategy?
  Model answer: Give a full loading dose, then adjust maintenance to the measured clearance including filtration effluent rate, prolonging beta-lactam infusions to extend time above the minimum inhibitory concentration.
  Model answer: Use therapeutic drug monitoring for aminoglycosides and vancomycin, and involve microbiology and pharmacy for dose individualisation.
  Model answer: Take cultures, give antimicrobials within one hour of recognised sepsis, achieve source control and review de-escalation daily.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Critical illness alters both volume of distribution and clearance, often in opposite directions and over hours. Capillary leak, aggressive resuscitation and hypoalbuminaemia expand the distribution volume of hydrophilic antimicrobials, while augmented renal clearance in some patients and extracorporeal clearance in others increase elimination. Consequently dose reduction on the basis of a creatinine value alone frequently produces subtherapeutic exposure at the time when killing matters most.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Separate loading from maintenance: loading depends on volume of distribution and should be full; maintenance depends on clearance including renal replacement effluent flow. Extended or continuous beta-lactam infusion improves target attainment, and therapeutic drug monitoring should guide aminoglycoside and vancomycin dosing. Reassess daily against culture results, clinical trajectory and source control, and document stop or review dates.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not reduce the loading dose because of renal failure, and do not describe every antibiotic as if the same target applied. Name the specific pharmacodynamic index for each class.
Take-home: Load fully, then adjust maintenance to real clearance: beta-lactams need time above MIC, aminoglycosides need peaks, and filtration removes drug.
Cited sources: Antimicrobial PK/PD in critical illness (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00134-020-06050-1); BJA Educ: pharmacokinetics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr061)

case_bank.title: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS
case_bank.text:
Case: Refractory hypoxaemia in ARDS (Ventilation, Advanced)
Patient: A patient ventilated for pneumonia has a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa on PEEP 12 cmH₂O, bilateral infiltrates and no evidence of cardiac failure.
Presentation: Tidal volume is 9 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau pressure 32 cmH₂O and driving pressure 20 cmH₂O.
Stage 1 — Make the diagnosis
  Question: Does this meet ARDS criteria?
  Model answer: Yes: acute onset within one week, bilateral infiltrates not fully explained by effusion or collapse, no primary cardiogenic cause, and hypoxaemia on at least 5 cmH₂O PEEP.
  Model answer: A PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 12 kPa (roughly 90 mmHg over FiO₂ 1.0 equivalents) falls in the moderate-to-severe range.
  Model answer: Severity is graded by this ratio and guides therapies such as proning and neuromuscular blockade.
Stage 2 — Correct the ventilation
  Question: What immediate changes are needed?
  Model answer: Reduce tidal volume to 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, keep plateau pressure below 30 cmH₂O and driving pressure below about 15 cmH₂O.
  Model answer: Titrate PEEP to oxygenation and compliance, accept permissive hypercapnia while pH is tolerable, and use conservative fluid management once shock has resolved.
  Model answer: Optimise sedation and consider neuromuscular blockade for severe dyssynchrony.
Stage 3 — Escalate
  Question: What next if hypoxaemia persists?
  Model answer: Prone for at least 16 hours per day when the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio remains below about 20 kPa: PROSEVA showed a substantial mortality reduction in severe ARDS.
  Model answer: Treat the cause with source control and appropriate antimicrobials, and exclude a superimposed pneumothorax or effusion.
  Model answer: Refer early for extracorporeal support if hypoxaemia or hypercapnic acidosis is refractory despite optimal ventilation and proning.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: ARDS is a heterogeneous, inflammatory lung injury in which the aerated compartment is small; delivering normal tidal volumes to a 'baby lung' produces high strain, ventilator-induced injury and biotrauma. Driving pressure captures tidal strain on the aerated lung and correlates with mortality. Proning improves outcome by making transpulmonary pressure and ventilation more homogeneous, recruiting dorsal lung and improving ventilation–perfusion matching.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Deliver the ARDSNet strategy consistently: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau under 30 cmH₂O, individualised PEEP, permissive hypercapnia and conservative fluids. Monitor plateau and driving pressure with inspiratory holds, follow gases and compliance trends, and prone with a trained team and a checklist for line, tube and pressure-area safety. Escalate to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation early rather than after prolonged injurious ventilation.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not use actual body weight for tidal volume, and do not chase a normal PaCO₂. State the Berlin criteria and quote PROSEVA's 16-hour minimum.
Take-home: ARDS management is protective ventilation by predicted body weight plus early prolonged proning in severe disease, not higher volumes or normal CO₂.
Cited sources: Berlin definition of ARDS (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.5669); ARDSNet low tidal volume trial (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200005043421801); PROSEVA 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214103)

case_bank.title: Neutropenic sepsis after chemotherapy
case_bank.text:
Case: Neutropenic sepsis after chemotherapy (Infection & immunity, Intermediate)
Patient: Ten days after chemotherapy a patient presents with temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, neutrophils 0.2 × 10⁹/L and lactate 3.4 mmol/L.
Presentation: There is no localising sign, and a tunnelled central line is in situ.
Stage 1 — Define the problem
  Question: How do you classify this presentation?
  Model answer: Sepsis under Sepsis-3: suspected infection with life-threatening organ dysfunction, indicated by hypotension and raised lactate.
  Model answer: Neutropenia means the innate cellular response is absent, so classical inflammatory signs and pus formation may be minimal.
  Model answer: Rapid deterioration is expected, and gram-negative bacteraemia carries particular risk.
Stage 2 — Act within the first hour
  Question: What do you do immediately?
  Model answer: Take blood cultures including from each line lumen, then give empirical broad-spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam without waiting for results.
  Model answer: Give balanced crystalloid for hypoperfusion, measure lactate serially, and start vasopressor if hypotension persists after initial resuscitation.
  Model answer: Escalate to critical care early, and look actively for line, chest, perianal, oral and skin sources.
Stage 3 — Continue and refine
  Question: What happens over the next 48 hours?
  Model answer: Review cultures and de-escalate or broaden accordingly, adding antifungal cover for persistent fever with prolonged neutropenia and considering resistant organisms by local ecology.
  Model answer: Consider line removal for tunnel infection, persistent bacteraemia or specific organisms, and discuss growth factor support with haematology.
  Model answer: Reassess daily for the need for imaging, source control and antimicrobial stewardship.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Neutrophils provide phagocytosis, oxidative killing and pus formation; without them, infection progresses with few local signs and the systemic response may be the only clue. Innate recognition through pattern-recognition receptors still triggers cytokine release, so fever remains a critical warning sign that mandates immediate empirical therapy rather than observation.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Follow the sepsis bundle: cultures, antimicrobials within one hour, lactate measurement, fluid resuscitation for hypoperfusion and vasopressor to a mean arterial pressure of about 65 mmHg. Monitor for progressive organ failure with serial lactate, urine output, gases and coagulation. Coordinate with haematology and microbiology on antimicrobial choice, line management, antifungal and antiviral cover, and consider immunoglobulin or growth factor only on specialist advice.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not wait for cultures or a localising source before giving antibiotics, and do not be reassured by the absence of inflammation. State the one-hour target and the antipseudomonal requirement.
Take-home: In neutropenia, fever is an emergency: culture, give antipseudomonal cover within the hour, resuscitate, and hunt the line and mucosal sources.
Cited sources: Sepsis-3 definitions (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2016.0287); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000005337); BJA Educ: immunology for intensivists (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.02.003)

case_bank.title: Fulminant sepsis in an asplenic patient
case_bank.text:
Case: Fulminant sepsis in an asplenic patient (Infection & immunity, Advanced)
Patient: A patient who had a splenectomy after trauma years ago presents with a few hours of fever, vomiting and a purpuric rash. Blood pressure is 75/40 mmHg with lactate 6 mmol/L.
Presentation: Coagulation is deranged and the platelet count is falling.
Stage 1 — Explain the immunology
  Question: Why is this patient so vulnerable?
  Model answer: The spleen filters encapsulated organisms poorly opsonised elsewhere, and hosts marginal-zone B cells that generate T-independent IgM against polysaccharide capsules.
  Model answer: Loss of splenic macrophages and reduced IgM impair complement-mediated opsonisation, so Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis can multiply unchecked.
  Model answer: The result is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection, which can progress to purpura fulminans and death within hours.
Stage 2 — Resuscitate and treat
  Question: What are your immediate priorities?
  Model answer: Give an immediate third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone after taking cultures, without waiting for investigations.
  Model answer: Resuscitate with balanced crystalloid and vasopressor, correct coagulopathy and involve critical care and microbiology urgently.
  Model answer: Isolate and give meningococcal prophylaxis to close contacts if meningococcal disease is confirmed or strongly suspected.
Stage 3 — Prevent recurrence
  Question: What long-term measures should have been in place?
  Model answer: Vaccination against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcal serogroups and annual influenza, with documented boosters.
  Model answer: Lifelong or at least risk-period antibiotic prophylaxis, usually penicillin, plus a rescue supply and clear written advice.
  Model answer: A patient-held alert card, education about urgent presentation with fever, and travel and animal-bite advice.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Splenic function is central to defence against encapsulated bacteria: capsules resist phagocytosis unless opsonised by antibody and complement, and the spleen provides both the antibody-producing marginal-zone B cells and the filtering macrophage population. The classical and alternative complement pathways then permit opsonophagocytosis and membrane attack complex formation; asplenia removes the essential first step, which is why disease is fulminant rather than gradual.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Time to antibiotic is the dominant determinant of survival. Give ceftriaxone immediately, resuscitate, and support organ failure in critical care with attention to disseminated intravascular coagulation, adrenal haemorrhage and limb ischaemia from purpura fulminans. Long-term prevention combines vaccination, prophylactic antibiotics, an alert card and patient education; check vaccination status whenever an asplenic patient is encountered for any reason.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture or imaging, and do not describe complement in vague terms — name the opsonisation and membrane attack functions and the encapsulated organisms.
Take-home: Asplenia removes antibody- and complement-dependent defence against encapsulated bacteria: give ceftriaxone immediately and ensure lifelong vaccination and prophylaxis.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: immunology for intensivists (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.02.003); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000005337)

case_bank.title: Septic DIC with line-site bleeding
case_bank.text:
Case: Septic DIC with line-site bleeding (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: A 67-year-old in septic shock has platelets 42 ×10⁹/L, PT prolonged by 8 seconds, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L and markedly raised D-dimer.
Presentation: There is oozing from cannula sites. A request is made for empirical TXA because ‘the patient is bleeding’.
Stage 1 — Diagnose the coagulopathy
  Question: How should the results be interpreted?
  Model answer: The combination is consistent with overt DIC in the correct clinical context.
  Model answer: Treating the septic source and restoring perfusion are the central interventions.
  Model answer: Replace platelets, fibrinogen and plasma for clinically significant bleeding using laboratory and viscoelastic guidance—not the D-dimer alone.
Stage 2 — Decide on TXA
  Question: Is empirical TXA appropriate?
  Model answer: No. DIC may be thrombosis-predominant, and suppressing fibrinolysis can worsen microvascular thrombosis.
  Model answer: Reserve antifibrinolytic treatment for exceptional severe bleeding where predominant hyperfibrinolysis is demonstrated, ideally with specialist and ROTEM/TEG input.
  Model answer: An elevated D-dimer does not by itself prove that TXA will help.
Stage 3 — Set measurable targets
  Question: What should guide replacement?
  Model answer: Aim for haemostasis appropriate to active bleeding: commonly platelets above 50 ×10⁹/L and fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, individualised to site and procedure.
  Model answer: Trend clotting, fibrinogen, platelets, temperature, pH and ionised calcium while treating infection and organ failure.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Septic DIC simultaneously activates coagulation, consumes platelets and factors and alters fibrinolysis. Raised D-dimer shows fibrin turnover but does not establish dominant hyperfibrinolysis. Empirical antifibrinolysis can worsen microvascular thrombosis when coagulation activation predominates.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Treat infection and restore perfusion first. For clinically important bleeding, replace platelets, fibrinogen and plasma according to serial laboratory and viscoelastic assessment; common pragmatic targets include platelets above 50 ×10⁹/L and fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, individualised to the bleeding site. Consider TXA only for exceptional life-threatening bleeding with demonstrated predominant hyperfibrinolysis and specialist input.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Bleeding plus a high D-dimer is not an automatic TXA indication. State the DIC phenotype, evidence of fibrinolysis and the risk of worsening thrombosis.
Take-home: Bleeding is not synonymous with an indication for TXA. In DIC, correct the cause and replace deficient components; use antifibrinolytics only for demonstrated dominant hyperfibrinolysis.
Cited sources: CRASH-2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60835-5)

# Infectious Disease in ICU
Organisms causing critical illness, pneumonia, urosepsis, CNS infections, necrotising fasciitis, fungal infections

Common Organisms
Key Points
CAP (severe)
S. pneumoniae
S. aureus
, influenza, SARS-CoV-2
CURB-65 / PSI for severity. Empiric: co-amoxiclav + macrolide or β-lactam + respiratory fluoroquinolone.
HAP / VAP
VAP: >48 h after intubation. Quantitative BAL. Anti-pseudomonal β-lactam ± aminoglycoside.
, Gram-negatives
Chemical pneumonitis → secondary infection. Co-amoxiclav or pip-tazo.
Pneumocystis jirovecii
, CMV,
PJP: bilateral ground-glass, high-dose co-trimoxazole ± steroids. Aspergillus: voriconazole first-line.
Legionella pneumophila
(serogroup 1) causes ~5% of severe CAP. Intracellular Gram-negative rod from contaminated water systems — no person-to-person transmission.
Clinical Features
High fever, dry cough, confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia (SIADH), raised CK, lymphopenia, deranged LFTs.
Urinary antigen (rapid, ~80% sens for serogroup 1). PCR on respiratory samples. Notifiable disease.
Macrolide (azithromycin) or fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin). 7–14 days (21 if immunocompromised). β-lactams ineffective.
ICU Relevance
Rapidly progressive respiratory failure, MOF, rhabdomyolysis, AKI. Mortality 10–30% in ICU.
Staphylococcus aureus
Cell wall
Thick peptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acid; no outer membrane.
Outer membrane with LPS (endotoxin); thin peptidoglycan.
PAMP / receptor
LTA, peptidoglycan, superantigens (TSST-1, PVL); TLR-2.
LPS lipid A; TLR-4 via MD-2/CD14. Nanogram quantities trigger systemic inflammation.
, GAS,
, CoNS
E. coli
Common sources
Skin/soft tissue, intravascular devices, endocarditis, bone/joint, surgical wounds
UTI (most common), intra-abdominal, HAP/VAP, meningitis
DIC association
Less common but occurs (purpura fulminans-like with GAS)
Strongly associated — LPS activates tissue factor. Meningococcal sepsis is the archetype.
Empiric antibiotics
Flucloxacillin (MSSA), vancomycin (MRSA risk), clindamycin for toxin suppression
Pip-tazo, ceftriaxone, or meropenem (ESBL/CRE risk). Anti-pseudomonal cover for HAP/VAP.
Toxic Shock Syndromes
Staphylococcal TSS
TSST-1 superantigen. Fever, diffuse erythroderma, desquamation, hypotension, ≥3 organ systems. Treatment: source control + flucloxacillin + clindamycin + IVIG.
Streptococcal TSS
Group A Strep pyrogenic exotoxins. Mortality 30–70%. Often with necrotising fasciitis. Pain out of proportion. Surgical debridement + benzylpenicillin + clindamycin + IVIG.
Source Control
Urgent imaging. Nephrostomy/stent for obstructed pyelonephritis. Remove/replace catheters.
Empiric Therapy
Pip-tazo or gentamicin + amoxicillin. Meropenem if previous ESBL.
Overview by syndrome
Bacterial meningitis
N. meningitidis
H. influenzae
, GBS (neonates)
Ceftriaxone 2 g BD + dexamethasone 10 mg QDS. Add amoxicillin 2 g 4-hrly if >50 y or immunocompromised (Listeria). Vancomycin if pneumococcal resistance suspected.
Viral encephalitis
HSV-1, VZV, enterovirus, arboviruses, JCV (PML)
IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg TDS empirically until HSV PCR negative. MRI: medial temporal/limbic in HSV. CSF PCR.
Brain abscess
Mixed anaerobes, viridans Streptococci,
, Gram-negatives (post-op/trauma)
Ceftriaxone + metronidazole (add vancomycin if MRSA/post-op). Stereotactic aspiration if >2.5 cm or diagnostic uncertainty. 6–8 wk IV.
Subdural empyema / epidural abscess
Streptococci, anaerobes,
Surgical drainage is definitive — neurosurgical emergency. Same antibiotics as brain abscess. Watch for cord compression in spinal epidural abscess.
Fungal meningitis
Cryptococcus neoformans
Liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine ×2 wk → fluconazole. Serial LPs / EVD for ↑ICP. Treat HIV.
TB meningitis
M. tuberculosis
RIPE × 2 mo → RI × 10 mo. Adjuvant dexamethasone (Thwaites regimen) reduces mortality. Hydrocephalus common — EVD.
Healthcare-associated (post-neurosurgical, EVD, shunt)
Coag-neg staph,
, Gram-negatives,
Cutibacterium acnes
Vancomycin + meropenem or ceftazidime. Remove/exchange device. Intraventricular vancomycin/gentamicin for resistant cases.
Classic triad (fever, neck stiffness, altered mental state) present in only ~45%; ≥2 of triad + headache in >95%. Photophobia, Kernig/Brudzinski signs. Non-blanching petechial rash → meningococcaemia. Septic shock and DIC may dominate. In elderly/immunocompromised: confusion or fever alone.
Altered consciousness >24 h, personality/behavioural change, focal neurology, seizures (often temporal lobe in HSV), fever. Meningoencephalitis if both meningism and parenchymal signs.
Brain abscess / empyema
Subacute headache, focal deficit, seizures; fever in only ~50%. Source: contiguous (sinus, ear, dental), haematogenous (endocarditis, lung), or post-traumatic/operative.
Raised ICP features
Reducing GCS, pupillary asymmetry, Cushing reflex (hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respiration), papilloedema, posturing. Demands urgent imaging and ICP-directed care.
Indications for critical care admission
GCS ≤ 12, rapidly falling GCS, or inability to protect the airway
Status epilepticus or recurrent seizures
Septic shock / haemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors
Respiratory failure (aspiration, ARDS, neuromuscular weakness)
Clinical or radiological raised ICP / impending herniation requiring osmotherapy, EVD or decompression
Need for invasive monitoring (ICP, EEG, intra-arterial BP) or neurosurgical intervention
DIC, purpura fulminans, multi-organ failure (often meningococcal)
Post-neurosurgical / shunt infection requiring device removal

ICU management bundles
Airway & ventilation
Intubate for GCS ≤8, status epilepticus, refractory shock or airway soiling. Neuro-protective induction: optimise haemodynamics, blunt laryngoscopy response. Avoid hypercapnia (worsens ICP); target PaCO₂ 4.5–5.0 kPa, PaO₂ >13 kPa. Head-up 30°.
Balanced crystalloid + early noradrenaline to MAP target preserving CPP >60 mmHg. Avoid hypotension absolutely. Steroids do NOT preclude vasopressor use. Treat DIC with platelets/FFP/cryoprecipitate as needed.
Raised ICP / seizures
Sedation, analgesia, normocapnia, normothermia, normonatraemia (avoid hyponatraemia — Na⁺ 140–145). Osmotherapy: mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline 2.7–3% bolus. EVD for hydrocephalus. Levetiracetam first-line for seizures; cEEG if persistent altered consciousness.
Source control & adjuncts
Neurosurgery for abscess >2.5 cm, empyema, infected shunt/EVD removal. Dexamethasone for first 4 days in suspected pneumococcal meningitis (stop if not pneumococcal). Public health notification + chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin) for meningococcal contacts. VTE prophylaxis after 24 h if no haemorrhage.
Why give dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis?
host inflammatory response
in the subarachnoid space. Bactericidal antibiotics rapidly lyse bacteria, releasing
cell-wall components
(pneumococcal lipoteichoic acid, peptidoglycan; meningococcal LPS) that activate Toll-like receptors on leukocytes, microglia and CSF macrophages.
TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6
) and matrix metalloproteinase release produces the four mechanisms of secondary brain injury that determine outcome:
Blood–brain-barrier breakdown
→ vasogenic cerebral oedema and raised ICP.
Cerebral vasculitis & vasospasm
→ arterial / venous infarction (especially of cortical perforators and cranial nerves).
Impaired CSF reabsorption
at the arachnoid villi and basal exudate → communicating hydrocephalus.
Cochlear inflammation
via the cochlear aqueduct → sensorineural deafness (the commonest neurological sequela of pneumococcal meningitis).
(potent, long-acting glucocorticoid with negligible mineralocorticoid effect and good CSF penetration) blunts NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription, stabilises the BBB and reduces neutrophil chemotaxis. To work, it must be present
antibiotic-induced bacteriolysis releases its inflammatory cargo — hence the rule to give it
with or before the first antibiotic dose
de Gans & van de Beek, N Engl J Med. 2002;347(20):1549–56
) showed adjuvant dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h for 4 days reduced unfavourable outcome (RR 0.59) and mortality (RR 0.48) in adult bacterial meningitis, with the largest benefit in
(mortality 14% vs 34%). The Cochrane review (
Brouwer MC et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;(9):CD004405
) confirms reduced hearing loss and short-term neurological sequelae in high-income settings, with no overall mortality benefit in low-income / HIV-prevalent populations — but pneumococcal subgroup benefit persists. ESCMID 2016, IDSA 2004 and NICE NG240 (2024) all endorse use, with the proviso to
stop early if a non-pneumococcal organism is identified
Duration of adjunctive dexamethasone
Dose & timing:
dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 h, started
with or before
the first dose of antibiotic (within 4 h at the latest — no benefit if given after antibiotics in adults).
continue for
4 days total
if CSF/blood culture confirms

Do not start

TB meningitis:
separate, longer regimen — dexamethasone 0.3–0.4 mg/kg/day IV tapered over
6–8 weeks
(Thwaites NEJM 2004).
add PPI for GI prophylaxis; monitor glucose; steroids may reduce CSF vancomycin penetration — use higher doses + TDM if pneumococcal resistance suspected.
Cerebral oedema, herniation, infarction (vasculitis), venous sinus thrombosis, sensorineural deafness (esp. pneumococcal — early audiology), cranial nerve palsies, cognitive impairment, abscess formation.
(Seizures & hydrocephalus — see below.)
Septic shock, myocardial dysfunction, purpura fulminans / limb ischaemia (meningococcal), Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal haemorrhage).
(DIC — see below.)
Aspiration pneumonia, ARDS, neurogenic pulmonary oedema.
Endocrine / metabolic
Cerebral salt wasting, diabetes insipidus, hyperglycaemia (steroids).
(SIADH — see below.)
Epilepsy, focal deficits, cognitive/behavioural sequelae, deafness, hydrocephalus requiring shunt; psychiatric morbidity in survivors and families.
Targeted monitoring & immediate treatment for key complications
Seizures / status epilepticus
hourly GCS, pupils and limb tone; capillary glucose; Na⁺ 6-hrly; continuous EEG if persistently obtunded, paralysed, or refractory status (non-convulsive status occurs in ~25% of comatose meningitis patients); urgent CT to exclude haemorrhage/herniation.
Immediate Tx:
ABC + O₂, correct glucose/Na⁺.
lorazepam 4 mg IV (or midazolam 10 mg IM/buccal) — repeat once at 5 min.
levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g)
phenytoin 20 mg/kg
sodium valproate 40 mg/kg over 10 min (ESETT).
RSI with thiopentone/propofol, intubate, midazolam or propofol infusion to burst suppression on cEEG; involve neurology. Continue levetiracetam prophylaxis ≥7 days after a single seizure.
Hydrocephalus / raised ICP
hourly GCS & pupils; watch for Cushing reflex (hypertension + bradycardia); fundoscopy / optic nerve sheath US (>5 mm suggestive); urgent CT for ventricular dilatation; ICP monitor or EVD for objective measurement; CPP target >60 mmHg.
head-up 30°, neutral neck, loosen ETT ties; sedate & analgese; PaCO₂ 4.5–5.0 kPa, PaO₂ >13 kPa, Na⁺ 140–145, temp ≤37 °C. Osmotherapy:
hypertonic saline 2.7–3% 250 mL
mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg
over 15 min (check serum osmolality <320). Urgent neurosurgical referral for
EVD insertion
in obstructive/communicating hydrocephalus; decompressive craniectomy for refractory ICP. Brief hyperventilation (PaCO₂ ≈4.0 kPa) only as a bridge to definitive treatment.
DIC / purpura fulminans
6-hrly FBC, PT/APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer; ISTH DIC score; serial lactate; hourly limb perfusion checks (capillary refill, pulses, mottling) — photograph & mark advancing purpura; arterial line; urine output.
aggressive source control (antibiotics within 1 h) and shock resuscitation — DIC will not resolve until sepsis is controlled. Transfuse
only if bleeding or pre-procedure
: platelets to >50 (×10⁹/L), FFP 15 mL/kg if PT/APTT ratio >1.5, cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <1.5 g/L. Vitamin K 10 mg IV. Consider
protein C concentrate
in meningococcal purpura fulminans. Avoid heparin in active bleeding/purpura. Discuss limb ischaemia with vascular/plastics early; do not amputate prematurely (demarcation takes weeks). Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if vasopressor-dependent (consider Waterhouse–Friderichsen).
SIADH (vs cerebral salt wasting / DI)
Na⁺ 6-hrly initially; paired serum & urine osmolality and urinary Na⁺; hourly fluid balance & urine output; daily weights; fluid status (CVP, passive leg raise). SIADH = euvolaemic hyponatraemia with urine osm >100 mosm/kg, urine Na⁺ >30 mmol/L, low serum urate.
if symptomatic (seizures, GCS drop) give
hypertonic saline 2.7% 150 mL over 10 min
, repeat × up to 3 until Na⁺ rises 4–6 mmol/L; then stop. Asymptomatic:
fluid restrict to 800–1000 mL/24 h
; correct Na⁺ no faster than
8–10 mmol/L per 24 h
(risk of osmotic demyelination). Treat the cause. Tolvaptan only with endocrine input.
Distinguish from CSW
(hypovolaemic, high urine output, high urine Na⁺) — give isotonic saline, never restrict.
Distinguish from DI
(polyuria >3 mL/kg/h, dilute urine, rising Na⁺) — give desmopressin 1–2 µg IV.
Pneumococcal meningitis:
mortality 20–30% (up to 50% with septic shock); ~30% of survivors have neurological sequelae (deafness, cognitive deficit).
Meningococcal disease:
overall mortality 5–10%; up to 40% with fulminant septicaemia / purpura fulminans. Survivors may have limb loss, scarring, hearing loss.
Listeria meningoencephalitis:
mortality 20–30%, higher in elderly/immunocompromised.
HSV encephalitis:
untreated mortality >70%; with timely aciclovir mortality ~20%, but ~50% of survivors have long-term cognitive/behavioural sequelae.
mortality 20–50%; worse with HIV co-infection or stage III disease (coma, focal deficit).
Brain abscess:
mortality now <15% with imaging + neurosurgery; epilepsy in ~30% of survivors.
Cryptococcal meningitis (HIV):
10-week mortality 20–40% even with optimal therapy; raised ICP is the strongest modifiable predictor.
Key prognostic factors: time to first antibiotic dose, GCS at presentation, age, septic shock, seizures, CSF lactate, and need for mechanical ventilation.
Perforated viscus, anastomotic leak, cholangitis, diverticular abscess, infected pancreatic necrosis.

Type I (Polymicrobial)
Mixed aerobes + anaerobes. Post-op or perineal (Fournier's). Risk: diabetes, immunosuppression, PVD.
Type II (Monomicrobial)
Group A Strep, S. aureus, Clostridium. Healthy patients. STSS in ~50%.
CoNS, S. aureus, Candida, Enterococcus, Gram-negatives. S. aureus bacteraemia: always echo + prolonged therapy.
Prevention Bundle
Hand hygiene, full barrier, chlorhexidine prep, avoid femoral, daily review, aseptic technique.
Remove/exchange line. Paired cultures (differential time to positivity). Empiric vancomycin + Gram-negative cover.
Diagnosis & Treatment
Candidaemia, intra-abdominal, candiduria. C. auris emerging MDR.
Cultures (~50% sens), 1,3-β-D-glucan. Empiric echinocandin (IDSA). Remove lines.
IPA: halo/air-crescent. CAPA in COVID.

HIV with CD4 <200
(subacute, lower mortality but higher organism burden) and
non-HIV immunosuppressed
— solid-organ/HSCT recipients, high-dose steroids (≥20 mg prednisolone >4 wk), biologics (rituximab, anti-TNF), haematological malignancy, congenital immunodeficiency. Non-HIV PCP is more fulminant, with higher ICU mortality (30–60%).
Subacute (days–weeks in HIV; days in non-HIV) progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, low-grade fever. Profound exertional desaturation; clear chest on auscultation despite marked hypoxaemia. Type 1 respiratory failure → ARDS. Pneumothorax in ~10% (cyst rupture).
HRCT: bilateral perihilar ground-glass opacification ± upper-zone cysts; sparing of subpleural regions. CXR may be normal early. Confirm on

Screen for co-pathogens (CMV, bacterial, TB, fungal). Document immunosuppression history.
Severity grading
PaO₂ >9.3 kPa (>70 mmHg)
A–a <4.7 kPa (<35 mmHg) on room air.
Moderate–severe (steroid threshold):
PaO₂ <9.3 kPa (≤70 mmHg)
A–a ≥4.7 kPa (≥35 mmHg) — adjuvant corticosteroids indicated.
UK ICU practice often uses the rounded cut-off PaO₂ <8 kPa to flag patients needing escalation.
1st line:
co-trimoxazole (TMP–SMX)
15–20 mg/kg/day of TMP component IV in 3–4 divided doses
, switch to oral when stable. Total course
21 days
(HIV) or 14–21 days (non-HIV).
Adjuvant steroids
(mortality benefit if PaO₂ <9.3 kPa / 70 mmHg or A–a >4.7 kPa / 35 mmHg on room air, especially HIV):
prednisolone 40 mg PO BD × 5 d → 40 mg OD × 5 d → 20 mg OD × 11 d
(or equivalent IV methylprednisolone at 75% dose). Start with or before the first dose of co-trimoxazole, ideally within 72 h.
Mortality reduction (RR 0.59, NNT ≈ 9) confirmed by Cochrane meta-analysis.
Benefit in non-HIV PCP less clear (refs 23, 24) but commonly used.
2nd line / intolerance / sulfa allergy:
IV pentamidine 4 mg/kg/day (nephrotoxic, hypoglycaemia, QT, pancreatitis); clindamycin + primaquine (check G6PD); atovaquone (mild–moderate only); dapsone + trimethoprim.
Supportive ICU care:

Immune reconstitution:
in HIV, start ART within 2 weeks of PCP treatment (ACTG A5164). In non-HIV, taper immunosuppression where possible in discussion with the parent team.

Non-HIV PCP:

Mandatory review at 48–72 h: stop, switch (IV→PO), de-escalate (narrower spectrum), continue, or refer. Document the decision and review date. Shorter is safer: CAP 5 days (NICE), HAP/VAP 7 days (PneumA), uncomplicated Gram-neg bacteraemia 7 days (Yahav 2019), intra-abdominal 4 days post-source control (STOP-IT). Procalcitonin-guided de-escalation reduces exposure further. ESBL: meropenem (MERINO). MRSA: vancomycin/linezolid/daptomycin. VRE: linezolid/daptomycin. CPE: ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, cefiderocol. C. difficile: oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin (NOT metronidazole first-line). Always consult microbiology. Switch to oral when tolerating diet, afebrile 24 h, falling inflammatory markers, no high-risk infection (endocarditis, CNS, prosthetic). TDM mandatory: vancomycin, gentamicin, voriconazole; consider for β-lactams in ARC or CRRT. Why does volume of distribution change for hydrophilic antibiotics in sepsis? Capillary leak and aggressive fluid resuscitation expand Vd for β-lactams, aminoglycosides and glycopeptides, often requiring loading doses (e.g. meropenem 2 g, vancomycin 25–30 mg/kg) to reach therapeutic levels. entries.description: Stewart approach, strong ion difference, anion gap, base excess
entries.text:
# Acid-Base Disorders Stewart approach, strong ion difference, anion gap, base excess Assess oxygenation: P/F ratio, A-a gradient Identify the primary disorder (pH + PaCO₂ + HCO₃⁻) Calculate compensation (Winter's formula for metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × [HCO₃⁻] + 8 ± 2) Calculate anion gap: Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Normal 8-12 mEq/L If HAGMA: calculate delta ratio (ΔAG/ΔHCO₃⁻) to detect hidden disorders given today's CO₂ tension and bicarbonate concentration, what is the pH? It is the framework taught at medical school, used in every ABG machine's report, and remains the fastest bedside tool for classifying a disturbance as respiratory or metabolic and judging compensation. 1. Start with the dissociation of carbonic acid CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ Carbonic anhydrase makes this equilibrium effectively instantaneous in red cells. CO₂ behaves as a volatile acid (excreted by the lung); HCO₃⁻ is the conjugate base, regulated by the kidney. 2. Apply the law of mass action [H⁺] = K × [CO₂] / [HCO₃⁻] Take the negative log of both sides — the pK of this system at 37 °C is 6.1 and [CO₂] = 0.03 × PaCO₂ (kPa: × 0.23). This gives the clinical equation. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation pH = 6.1 + log ([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PaCO₂)) It is the , not the absolute concentrations, that fixes pH. A patient with HCO₃⁻ 36 and PaCO₂ 8 kPa has the same pH as one with HCO₃⁻ 18 and PaCO₂ 4 kPa — both ratios = 75. Compensation is the body restoring the 20:1 ratio of HCO₃⁻ to dissolved CO₂. The lung adjusts CO₂ in minutes; the kidney adjusts HCO₃⁻ over 2–5 days. The lung and kidney act as the two arms of one feedback loop. A primary fall in one variable provokes a predictable secondary change in the other — quantified by Winter's formula and the acute/chronic respiratory compensation rules below. Primary disorder Expected compensation Time course Metabolic acidosis PaCO₂ = 1.5 × [HCO₃⁻] + 8 ± 2 (mmHg) (Winter) Metabolic alkalosis ΔPaCO₂ ≈ 0.7 × Δ[HCO₃⁻] (mmHg) Minutes–hours (limited — hypoxia) Acute respiratory acidosis Δ[HCO₃⁻] = 1 per 10 mmHg Δ PaCO₂ Minutes (cell buffering) Chronic respiratory acidosis Δ[HCO₃⁻] = 4 per 10 mmHg Δ PaCO₂ 2–5 days (renal) Acute respiratory alkalosis Δ[HCO₃⁻] = −2 per 10 mmHg Δ PaCO₂ Chronic respiratory alkalosis Δ[HCO₃⁻] = −5 per 10 mmHg Δ PaCO₂ Extending the framework — anion gap & delta ratio a metabolic acidosis exists, but not . The anion gap (AG = Na⁺ − [Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻], normal 8–12) detects unmeasured anions (lactate, ketones, toxins, urate, sulphate). Hypoalbuminaemia masks a raised AG — correct by adding 2.5 × (40 − measured albumin g/L). The delta ratio (Δ AG / Δ HCO₃⁻) detects mixed disorders: <0.4 = pure NAGMA, 0.4–1 = mixed HAGMA + NAGMA, 1–2 = pure HAGMA, >2 = HAGMA with concurrent metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis. ⚠ Where the descriptive approach breaks down HCO₃⁻ is treated as causal. But [HCO₃⁻] cannot be regulated in isolation from water dissociation, strong ions or weak acids — it is a variable. This causes circular reasoning ("acidosis happened because HCO₃⁻ fell; HCO₃⁻ fell because of the acidosis"). Hyperchloraemic acidosis after large-volume 0.9% NaCl looks "unexplained" on a Henderson–Hasselbalch analysis — there is no extra acid generated and no buffer consumption. The Stewart approach (below) explains it directly through a fall in SID. Hypoalbuminaemia hides acidosis. Each 10 g/L fall in albumin generates a metabolic alkalosis of ~2.5 mEq/L base excess, which can mask a coexisting lactic or ketoacidosis on a casual ABG read. Compensation rules are empirical regressions , not derivations from the equation — they fit the average patient and become unreliable in extreme or rapidly changing physiology. Definition & underlying physiology elevated anion gap : AG = [Na⁺] − ([Cl⁻] + [HCO₃⁻]); normal 8–12 mEq/L (some labs 3–11 if K⁺ excluded). The gap reflects unmeasured anions — predominantly albumin (negatively charged at physiological pH), phosphate and sulphate, plus pathological additions of lactate, ketoacids, or exogenous toxin anions. When a strong acid HA is added, H⁺ is buffered by HCO₃⁻ (consumed) while A⁻ accumulates: HCO₃⁻ falls, Cl⁻ does rise, so the gap widens. This distinguishes HAGMA from (hyperchloraemic acidosis), where HCO₃⁻ loss is matched 1:1 by Cl⁻ gain (GI/renal HCO₃⁻ loss, RTA, large-volume 0.9% saline). Albumin correction is non-negotiable in ICU Corrected AG = measured AG + 2.5 × (40 − albumin g/L) . An ICU patient with albumin 20 g/L and "normal" AG of 12 actually has a corrected AG of 17 — a HAGMA hiding in plain sight. Causes — GOLD MARK (modern, preferred to MUDPILES) (Mehta, Lancet 2008) captures the realistic differential: Narrowing the differential — the osmolar gap osmolar gap : measured osmolality − calculated (2×Na⁺ + urea + glucose, all mmol/L); normal < 10 mOsm/kg. A raised osmolar gap + raised AG strongly suggests methanol or ethylene glycol (their parent alcohols are osmotically active before metabolism). Early on the AG may be near-normal (alcohol unmetabolised → high osmolar gap, low AG); late, after ADH metabolism, the osmolar gap closes and AG climbs as formate/glycolate accumulate. Urinary oxalate crystals (ethylene glycol) and Wood's-lamp fluorescence (fluorescein in antifreeze) support the diagnosis. Lactic acidosis — type A vs type B Type A (hypoxic): shock of any aetiology, severe hypoxaemia, regional ischaemia (mesenteric, limb), seizures, severe exercise. Lactate generation exceeds hepatic/renal clearance. Type B (non-hypoxic): — underlying disease (liver failure → ↓clearance; malignancy, sepsis-associated metabolic reprogramming, thiamine deficiency, DKA); — drugs/toxins (metformin, linezolid, NRTIs, propofol infusion syndrome, β₂-agonists, cyanide, paracetamol); — inborn errors of metabolism. D-lactic acidosis: short bowel/blind loop → carbohydrate fermentation by Gram-positives → D-lactate; presents with encephalopathy and HAGMA but L-lactate (standard assay is L-specific). Lactate > 4 mmol/L in sepsis triggers Sepsis-6/SSC bundles; trend with serial measurement is more useful than a single value. Delta ratio (ΔAG / ΔHCO₃⁻) — detecting mixed disorders < 0.4: pure NAGMA (the AG hasn't really risen). mixed HAGMA + NAGMA (e.g. DKA + saline resuscitation, or diarrhoea + lactic acidosis). pure HAGMA (1:1 stoichiometric exchange of HCO₃⁻ for unmeasured anion). > 2.0: HAGMA with concurrent metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis (HCO₃⁻ has been preserved or augmented — e.g. DKA in a vomiting patient, or COPD with superimposed sepsis). Pure lactic acidosis classically gives a ratio ≈ 1.6 (lactate clears partly via tissues other than HCO₃⁻ regeneration); pure DKA ≈ 1.0. A ratio outside expectation always prompts a hunt for a second disorder. Stewart re-framing driven by accumulation of unmeasured strong anions (lactate⁻, ketoanions, formate, glycolate, oxalate, sulphate). The strong ion gap (SIG = SID − SID quantifies these directly and, unlike the AG, is automatically corrected for albumin and phosphate — particularly useful in critical illness with hypoalbuminaemia and mixed disorders. Management principles Treat the cause — fluids/insulin/K⁺ for DKA, antidote (fomepizole ± dialysis) for toxic alcohols, urinary alkalinisation ± dialysis for salicylates, source control + perfusion for septic lactic acidosis, withdraw offending drug for type B. routinely indicated. BICAR-ICU (Lancet 2018) showed no 28-day mortality benefit for sodium bicarbonate in severe metabolic acidaemia overall, but a signal for renal-replacement-free days and reduced mortality in the AKI (KDIGO 2–3) subgroup when pH < 7.20. Reasonable to consider in life-threatening acidaemia (pH < 7.1) with AKI, or to facilitate vasopressor responsiveness. Renal replacement therapy for toxic alcohols (high clearance, removes parent + toxic metabolites), severe salicylate toxicity (level > 700 mg/L, CNS features, refractory acidosis), metformin-associated lactic acidosis with AKI, refractory uraemic acidosis. Avoid harm: aggressive 0.9% saline resuscitation adds a hyperchloraemic NAGMA on top of HAGMA — prefer balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) unless contraindicated. serum osmolality (by freezing-point depression osmometer) and the osmolarity from the major osmotically active solutes: − Osm = 2 × [Na⁺] + [urea] + [glucose]  (all in mmol/L) Normal < 10 mOsm/kg. A widened gap means unmeasured, osmotically active particles are present in plasma. Why osmolality vs osmolarity matters (mOsm/kg water) is measured directly — temperature-independent, unaffected by lipids/proteins displacing plasma water. (mOsm/L solution) is calculated — falsely low in pseudohyponatraemia (hyperlipidaemia, hyperproteinaemia) because the measured Na⁺ is diluted by the non-aqueous fraction. Always pair the gap with the AG and clinical picture — a raised osmolar gap in isolation is non-specific. Causes of a raised osmolar gap Combining the osmolar gap with the anion gap — toxic alcohol time course Early (0–6 h): ↑↑ osmolar gap, AG normal — parent alcohol present, metabolism not yet started. osmolar gap falling, AG rising — alcohol being converted to toxic anions.
