    The Henderson–Hasselbalch approach treats the body as a single dominant buffer pair — bicarbonate and dissolved CO₂ — and asks: given today s report, and remains the fastest bedside tool for classifying a disturbance as respiratory or metabolic and judging compensation.

    1. Start with the dissociation of carbonic acid

    CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

    Carbonic anhydrase makes this equilibrium effectively instantaneous in red cells. CO₂ behaves as a volatile acid (excreted by the lung); HCO₃⁻ is the conjugate base, regulated by the kidney.

    2. Apply the law of mass action

    [H⁺] = K × [CO₂] / [HCO₃⁻]

    Take the negative log of both sides — the pKa of this system at 37 °C is 6.1 and [CO₂] = 0.03 × PaCO₂ (kPa: × 0.23). This gives the clinical equation.

    pH = 6.1 + log10 ([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PaCO₂))

    Three logical consequences fall out immediately:

      Metabolic acidosis PaCO₂ = 1.5 × [HCO₃⁻] + 8 ± 2 (mmHg) (Winter) Minutes–hours Metabolic alkalosis ΔPaCO₂ ≈ 0.7 × Δ[HCO₃⁻] (mmHg) Minutes–hours (limited — hypoxia) Acute respiratory acidosis Δ[HCO₃⁻] = 1 per 10 mmHg Δ PaCO₂ Minutes (cell buffering) Chronic respiratory acidosis Δ[HCO₃⁻] = 4 per 10 mmHg Δ PaCO₂ 2–5 days (renal) Acute respiratory alkalosis Δ[HCO₃⁻] = −2 per 10 mmHg Δ PaCO₂ Minutes Chronic respiratory alkalosis Δ[HCO₃⁻] = −5 per 10 mmHg Δ PaCO₂ 2–5 days (renal)
    Henderson–Hasselbalch tells you that a metabolic acidosis exists, but not why. The anion gap (AG = Na⁺ − [Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻], normal 8–12) detects unmeasured anions (lactate, ketones, toxins, urate, sulphate). Hypoalbuminaemia masks a raised AG — correct by adding 2.5 × (40 − measured albumin g/L). The delta ratio (Δ AG / Δ HCO₃⁻) detects mixed disorders: <0.4 = pure NAGMA, 0.4–1 = mixed HAGMA + NAGMA, 1–2 = pure HAGMA, >2 = HAGMA with concurrent metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis.

    Definition & underlying physiology

    HAGMA is a metabolic acidosis (low HCO₃⁻, low pH) accompanied by an elevated anion gap: AG = [Na⁺] − ([Cl⁻] + [HCO₃⁻]); normal 8–12 mEq/L (some labs 3–11 if K⁺ excluded). The gap reflects unmeasured anions — predominantly albumin (negatively charged at physiological pH), phosphate and sulphate, plus pathological additions of lactate, ketoacids, or exogenous toxin anions. When a strong acid HA is added, H⁺ is buffered by HCO₃⁻ (consumed) while A⁻ accumulates: HCO₃⁻ falls, Cl⁻ does not rise, so the gap widens. This distinguishes HAGMA from NAGMA (hyperchloraemic acidosis), where HCO₃⁻ loss is matched 1:1 by Cl⁻ gain (GI/renal HCO₃⁻ loss, RTA, large-volume 0.9% saline).

    Albumin correction is non-negotiable in ICU

    Each 10 g/L fall in albumin lowers the apparent AG by ~2.5 mEq/L. Corrected AG = measured AG + 2.5 × (40 − albumin g/L). An ICU patient with albumin 20 g/L and AG of 12 actually has a corrected AG of 17 — a HAGMA hiding in plain sight.

    Causes — GOLD MARK (modern, preferred to MUDPILES)

    MUDPILES is the traditional mnemonic but includes obsolete agents (paraldehyde) and omits common ICU causes (pyroglutamic acid, D-lactate). GOLD MARK (Mehta, Lancet 2008) captures the realistic differential:

Early on the AG may be near-normal (alcohol unmetabolised → high osmolar gap, low AG); late, after ADH metabolism, the osmolar gap closes and AG climbs as formate/glycolate accumulate. case_bank.title: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting
case_bank.text:
Case: Torsades after ondansetron and vomiting (Cardiovascular, Advanced)
Patient: A young adult admitted with prolonged vomiting receives ondansetron and a macrolide. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and magnesium 0.5 mmol/L.
Presentation: The monitor shows a broad, twisting polymorphic tachycardia that self-terminates. QTc before the event was 510 ms.
Stage 1 — Explain the mechanism
  Question: Why has this rhythm occurred?
  Model answer: Phase 3 repolarisation depends mainly on the delayed rectifier potassium currents IKr and IKs; blocking IKr prolongs the action potential and the QT interval.
  Model answer: Prolonged repolarisation permits reactivation of L-type calcium current, producing early afterdepolarisations and triggered beats.
  Model answer: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia reduce repolarisation reserve, so drug effects that are usually tolerated become arrhythmogenic.
Stage 2 — Treat the arrhythmia
  Question: What is your immediate management?
  Model answer: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate even if magnesium is normal, correct potassium towards the upper normal range and stop all QT-prolonging drugs.
  Model answer: Treat sustained or pulseless episodes with defibrillation and follow advanced life support; consider overdrive pacing or isoprenaline for pause-dependent, bradycardia-related torsades.
  Model answer: Avoid class Ia and class III antiarrhythmics, which prolong repolarisation further.
Stage 3 — Prevent recurrence
  Question: What ongoing plan is needed?
  Model answer: Review every drug on the chart against a QT-prolonging list, including antiemetics, antipsychotics, macrolides, antifungals and methadone.
  Model answer: Monitor electrolytes and QTc repeatedly, especially with ongoing vomiting, diuretics or renal replacement.
  Model answer: Refer for cardiology assessment and family screening if congenital long QT syndrome is suspected.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: The cardiac action potential's plateau and repolarisation reflect a balance between inward calcium and outward potassium currents. Repolarisation reserve is the redundancy in this system; congenital channel variants, electrolyte depletion, bradycardia and multiple IKr-blocking drugs erode it additively. Torsades de pointes is the clinical expression of triggered activity on a prolonged, heterogeneous repolarisation substrate.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Magnesium suppresses early afterdepolarisations and is first-line even with normal levels. Keep potassium above 4.5 mmol/L in this setting, remove precipitating drugs, and maintain a heart rate that shortens repolarisation when torsades is pause-dependent. Continuous ECG monitoring with QTc measurement, defibrillator availability and a documented drug-avoidance list should follow the patient.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not give amiodarone reflexively for a broad-complex tachycardia that is torsades. Distinguish polymorphic from monomorphic VT, and name IKr blockade and early afterdepolarisations rather than saying 'the QT was long'.
Take-home: Torsades reflects lost repolarisation reserve: give magnesium, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs and avoid further class III agents.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: cardiac electrophysiology (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkm013); Vaughan Williams classification (https://doi.org/10.1016/0306-039X(75)90019-7)

case_bank.title: High anion gap acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis
case_bank.text:
Case: High anion gap acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis (Acid–base, Intermediate)
Patient: A young adult presents with pH 7.08, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 2.4 kPa, glucose 28 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L.
Presentation: After 4 L of 0.9% sodium chloride and an insulin infusion, ketones fall to 1.0 mmol/L but pH is still 7.20 with bicarbonate 14 mmol/L and chloride 116 mmol/L.
Stage 1 — Interpret the first gas
  Question: Describe the disorder quantitatively.
  Model answer: Severe metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation: expected PaCO₂ is close to the measured value, so there is no additional respiratory disorder.
  Model answer: Anion gap is raised at about 31 mmol/L, consistent with ketoacidosis; the modest lactate rise reflects hypovolaemia and catecholamine-driven glycolysis.
  Model answer: Delta ratio confirms a pure high anion gap picture rather than a mixed acidosis at presentation.
Stage 2 — Explain the second gas
  Question: Why is the patient still acidotic after ketones have cleared?
  Model answer: The anion gap has normalised while a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis has appeared from large-volume 0.9% sodium chloride.
  Model answer: In Stewart terms, the infused fluid has a strong ion difference of zero, so it reduces plasma strong ion difference and lowers pH independently of ketones.
  Model answer: Bicarbonate regeneration also lags behind ketone clearance because ketoanions were excreted rather than metabolised.
Stage 3 — Manage from here
  Question: What do you change?
  Model answer: Switch to a balanced crystalloid, continue fixed-rate insulin with glucose-containing fluid once glucose falls below about 14 mmol/L, and replace potassium aggressively.
  Model answer: Do not give bicarbonate for a resolving ketoacidosis; treat the cause and monitor ketone clearance rather than pH alone.
  Model answer: Look for the precipitant — infection, non-adherence, myocardial infarction, pregnancy — and monitor for cerebral oedema in younger patients.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Two acidoses appear in sequence here: an organic high anion gap acidosis from ketoacid production, then an iatrogenic hyperchloraemic acidosis from resuscitation with saline. Only anion gap and chloride tracking reveals the switch; following pH or bicarbonate alone suggests treatment failure and risks unnecessary bicarbonate or insulin escalation. Ketone measurement, not glucose, defines resolution.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use fixed-rate weight-based insulin, balanced crystalloid, early and generous potassium replacement, hourly ketone and glucose measurement, and regular electrolyte and gas review. Add glucose-containing fluid to permit continued insulin. Watch for hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypophosphataemia, fluid overload and, especially in adolescents, cerebral oedema. Address the precipitant and involve the diabetes team before discharge.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not attribute persistent acidosis to ongoing ketosis without recalculating the anion gap, and do not reach for bicarbonate. Show the compensation calculation and name hyperchloraemia explicitly.
Take-home: Recalculate the anion gap: persistent acidosis after ketone clearance is usually saline-induced hyperchloraemia, treated by changing fluid, not giving bicarbonate.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: acid–base interpretation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx008); Stewart approach to acid–base (https://doi.org/10.1186/cc3927)

case_bank.title: Confusing gas in acute-on-chronic respiratory failure
case_bank.text:
Case: Confusing gas in acute-on-chronic respiratory failure (Acid–base, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with severe COPD on long-term oxygen presents drowsy after three days of increasing breathlessness. Gas on 60% oxygen: pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 9.8 kPa, PaO₂ 9.0 kPa, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L, lactate 1.2 mmol/L.
Presentation: The referring team says the gas is 'normal for him'.
Stage 1 — Interpret the gas
  Question: Is this chronic or acute?
  Model answer: Bicarbonate of 32 mmol/L indicates established renal compensation for chronic hypercapnia, which takes days.
  Model answer: The pH of 7.22 is far too low for fully compensated chronic retention, so there is an acute rise in PaCO₂ on top of a chronic state.
  Model answer: Uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen has probably worsened hypercapnia by increasing dead space through reversal of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, the Haldane effect and reduced ventilatory drive.
Stage 2 — Treat immediately
  Question: What do you do first?
  Model answer: Titrate oxygen to a target saturation of 88–92% using a controlled delivery device, and repeat the gas within 30–60 minutes.
  Model answer: Give bronchodilators, corticosteroid, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and treat any coexisting heart failure.
  Model answer: Start non-invasive ventilation for persistent respiratory acidosis, with a documented escalation plan.
Stage 3 — Plan escalation
  Question: When would you intubate, and what ventilator settings?
  Model answer: Intubate for failure of non-invasive ventilation, exhaustion, reduced consciousness, inability to protect the airway or haemodynamic instability, taking prior function and patient wishes into account.
  Model answer: Set a long expiratory time with low rate, tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, and permissive hypercapnia targeting pH rather than normal PaCO₂.
  Model answer: Monitor intrinsic PEEP with an expiratory hold and watch for barotrauma and haemodynamic compromise from hyperinflation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Chronic hypercapnia with renal bicarbonate retention shifts the baseline, so pH — not PaCO₂ — indicates acuity. A patient in whom pH is markedly reduced with a raised bicarbonate has an acute-on-chronic picture demanding intervention. Excess oxygen contributes through several mechanisms, of which increased physiological dead space is the dominant one, so controlled oxygen therapy is treatment, not restraint.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Controlled oxygen, bronchodilation, steroid, treatment of infection and early non-invasive ventilation form the bundle. Reassess gases serially, monitor conscious level and work of breathing, and agree ceilings of treatment early with the patient and family. If invasive ventilation is needed, prioritise expiratory time, accept hypercapnia, avoid dynamic hyperinflation and check intrinsic PEEP.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not accept 'this is his normal gas' when pH is low, and do not remove oxygen entirely. Quote the 88–92% target and the pH-based interpretation of chronicity.
Take-home: Judge acuity by pH, not PaCO₂: acute-on-chronic hypercapnia needs controlled oxygen at 88–92% and early non-invasive ventilation.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: COPD and ventilation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkr054); BJA Educ: acid–base interpretation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx008)

Risk factors
are conventionally divided into
(CKD — especially eGFR <30, diabetic nephropathy, age >75, anaemia, heart failure, hypovolaemia, hypotension, IABP, nephrotoxic drugs) and

KDIGO 2012 Recommendations for Prevention
Risk-stratify all patients
before elective contrast-enhanced procedures using eGFR (CKD-EPI) and clinical risk score (e.g. Mehran). Avoid contrast where a non-contrast alternative (ultrasound, non-contrast MRI, V/Q scan) gives comparable diagnostic information.
Iso-osmolar (290 mOsm/kg, e.g. iodixanol)
low-osmolar non-ionic
avoid high-osmolar
contrast and
minimise total volume
IV volume expansion with isotonic crystalloid
(KDIGO grade 1A) is the cornerstone of prevention. Standard regimen: 0.9% saline 1 ml/kg/hr for 6–12 h pre-procedure and 6–12 h post (total ~1–1.5 L). Sodium bicarbonate (1.26%/1.4%) is no longer recommended over saline (PRESERVE 2018: no difference). Oral hydration alone is insufficient in high-risk patients.
Withhold nephrotoxins
: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, amphotericin, calcineurin inhibitors. Hold ACEi/ARB and diuretics on the day if euvolaemic and at risk. Stop metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors 48 h pre-procedure if eGFR <30 (lactic acidosis / euglycaemic DKA risk if AKI develops).
Minimise contrast dose
: aim for contrast volume (mL) < 3 × eGFR. Avoid repeat exposure within 48–72 h if possible (cumulative risk).
N-acetylcysteine and prophylactic RRT are NOT recommended
. PRESERVE (2018, n = 5177) showed no benefit of NAC over placebo. Prophylactic haemofiltration/dialysis does not improve outcomes and exposes patients to procedural risks.

Anaesthetic/perioperative pearls
Maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg throughout — hypotension is the most modifiable peri-procedural risk factor.
Avoid hyperchloraemic fluids (large-volume 0.9% saline can cause hyperchloraemic acidosis); balanced crystalloid is reasonable but saline retains the strongest evidence base for CI-AKI prophylaxis.

Document risk-benefit discussion when contrast is given in eGFR <30 or established AKI.

Frequently asked questions
faq-${i}
AKI & RRT — At a Glance
Bringing together staging, prevention, and decision points for renal replacement.
How is AKI defined and staged using KDIGO 2012?
KDIGO defines AKI as ANY of: a rise in serum creatinine of ≥ 26.5 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) within 48 hours; or a rise to ≥ 1.5 × baseline known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Staging: Stage 1 = creatinine 1.5–1.9 × baseline (or ↑ ≥ 26.5 µmol/L) OR UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h; Stage 2 = 2.0–2.9 × baseline OR UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥ 12 h; Stage 3 = ≥ 3.0 × baseline OR creatinine ≥ 354 µmol/L OR initiation of RRT OR (< 18 y) eGFR < 35 mL/min/1.73 m² OR UO < 0.3 mL/kg/h ≥ 24 h OR anuria ≥ 12 h. Stage by whichever criterion (creatinine or urine output) is worst.
What are the AEIOU indications for renal replacement therapy?
A — refractory Acidosis (pH < 7.15 despite optimal therapy); E — refractory Electrolyte disturbance, classically hyperkalaemia K⁺ > 6.5 mmol/L or rising despite medical management; I — Intoxication with a dialysable toxin (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, lithium, valproate, metformin-associated lactic acidosis); O — fluid Overload refractory to diuretics, especially with hypoxaemia; U — Uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, neuropathy, bleeding diathesis, severe symptomatic uraemia, typically urea > 30 mmol/L). These are the conventional/emergency triggers retained after STARRT-AKI and AKIKI showed no benefit from pre-emptive initiation.
What did STARRT-AKI, AKIKI and IDEAL-ICU tell us about timing of RRT initiation?
AKIKI (Gaudry, NEJM 2016, n = 620) randomised KDIGO stage 3 AKI without emergent indications to early (within 6 h) vs delayed RRT (only on conventional indication) — no 60-day mortality difference (48.5% vs 49.7%); 49% of the delayed arm avoided RRT entirely. IDEAL-ICU (Barbar, NEJM 2018, n = 488) in septic shock with RIFLE-F: early (12 h) vs delayed (48 h) — no 90-day mortality difference; stopped early for futility. STARRT-AKI (Bagshaw, NEJM 2020, n = 3 019, the definitive trial) compared accelerated (within 12 h) vs standard initiation — no 90-day mortality difference (43.9% vs 43.7%) and the accelerated arm had MORE dialysis dependence at 90 days (10.4% vs 6.0%) and more adverse events. Conclusion: wait for conventional AEIOU triggers; do not initiate pre-emptively.
When should I choose CRRT, IHD, SLED or peritoneal dialysis?
CRRT (CVVHDF most commonly in UK): first-line in the haemodynamically unstable patient, raised ICP (slow solute shift avoids cerebral oedema), and where continuous fluid removal is needed. Effluent dose 20–25 mL/kg/h (RENAL and ATN trials showed no benefit from higher doses — 35–40 mL/kg/h). IHD (intermittent haemodialysis, 3–4 h sessions): preferred in stable patients, urgent K⁺ or toxin removal where rapid clearance is wanted, mobilisation/rehabilitation, and to ease nurse workload. SLED / PIRRT (sustained low-efficiency dialysis, 6–12 h sessions): a hybrid useful when CRRT capacity is limited and patient is borderline-stable. PD: rarely used in adult ICU in the UK; standard in paediatric AKI and resource-limited settings. CONVINT and HEMODIAFE trials show no clear mortality difference between modalities in stable patients — choice is haemodynamics-led.
How do I prescribe regional citrate anticoagulation safely and what are the pitfalls?
Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) is first-line in most UK ICUs (KDIGO 2012). Trisodium citrate is infused into the pre-filter line; it chelates ionised calcium in the circuit (target circuit iCa²⁺ < 0.35 mmol/L), then calcium is replaced into the patient post-filter (target systemic iCa²⁺ 1.0–1.2 mmol/L). Citrate is metabolised in the liver to bicarbonate (3 mol HCO₃⁻ per mol citrate). Monitor: systemic iCa²⁺ 4–6-hourly, total Ca²⁺ : ionised Ca²⁺ ratio (> 2.5 = citrate accumulation), acid-base, sodium (some citrate preparations are hypertonic). Pitfalls: citrate accumulation in liver failure or shock (rising tCa : iCa ratio, metabolic acidosis with anion gap, hypocalcaemia despite ongoing replacement) — switch to systemic anticoagulation or no anticoagulation; alkalosis from over-feeding citrate; hypernatraemia. RICH (Zarbock, JAMA 2020) showed RCA gave longer circuit life (47 h vs 26 h) and fewer bleeding events than systemic heparin, with similar mortality.
How do I prevent contrast-induced AKI and is N-acetylcysteine still recommended?
Risk-stratify with the Mehran score (hypotension, IABP, CCF, age > 75, anaemia, diabetes, eGFR < 60, contrast volume). High risk = eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m², diabetes, hypovolaemia, CCF, age > 75. Prevention: pre/post-procedure IV isotonic crystalloid 1 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h before and after; use iso-osmolar (iodixanol) or low-osmolar contrast; minimise contrast volume; withhold ACE-i / ARB / NSAID / metformin on the day of the procedure. PRESERVE (Weisbord, NEJM 2018, n = 5 177) showed N-acetylcysteine offered NO benefit over placebo, and saline was non-inferior to sodium bicarbonate. Statins given peri-procedure may attenuate risk in statin-naive patients (modest evidence). The major risk factor for AKI in modern practice is procedural haemodynamic instability rather than contrast itself.
Which drugs require renal dose adjustment in AKI / CRRT and which are nephrotoxic?
Avoid where possible: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin — therapeutic-drug monitoring mandatory if used), IV contrast in high-risk

case_bank.title: Oliguria on the first postoperative night
case_bank.text:
Case: Oliguria on the first postoperative night (Renal, neuromuscular & autonomic, Foundation)
Patient: After open colorectal surgery, an adult passes 15 mL of urine per hour for three hours. Mean arterial pressure is 65 mmHg, and the chart includes an ACE inhibitor and regular ibuprofen.
Presentation: The nurse asks for a fluid bolus. The patient looks comfortable, warm and peripherally well perfused.
Stage 1 — Explain the renal physiology
  Question: How does the kidney normally protect glomerular filtration?
  Model answer: Autoregulation keeps renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate near constant across a mean arterial pressure of roughly 80–180 mmHg through myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms.
  Model answer: Afferent arteriolar dilation depends partly on prostaglandins; efferent tone depends on angiotensin II.
  Model answer: NSAIDs blunt afferent dilation and ACE inhibitors blunt efferent constriction, so both together strip away autoregulatory reserve at low pressure.
Stage 2 — Assess before infusing
  Question: How do you evaluate this oliguria?
  Model answer: Exclude obstruction first: flush or replace a blocked catheter and examine for retention.
  Model answer: Assess perfusion with capillary refill, lactate, pressure trend against the patient's baseline, and dynamic response to a small measured fluid challenge.
  Model answer: Look for bleeding, sepsis, raised intra-abdominal pressure and drug causes; review nephrotoxins and check creatinine trend against KDIGO criteria.
Stage 3 — Treat proportionately
  Question: What do you do?
  Model answer: Stop the NSAID, withhold the ACE inhibitor and restore mean arterial pressure towards the patient's usual value using fluid where hypovolaemic and vasopressor where vasodilated.
  Model answer: Avoid indiscriminate large-volume fluid loading, which causes venous congestion, oedema and worse outcomes without protecting kidneys.
  Model answer: Recheck urine output, creatinine and electrolytes, and escalate for critical care review if oliguria persists or acidosis, hyperkalaemia or fluid overload develop.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Postoperative oliguria is often an appropriate neuroendocrine response to surgery — antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone conserve water and sodium — but it is also the first sign of hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity. Because autoregulation depends on prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent tone, combining an NSAID and a renin–angiotensin blocker at low perfusion pressure predictably reduces glomerular filtration.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Work through obstruction, perfusion and nephrotoxins in order. Use small, repeated fluid challenges with a defined endpoint rather than open-ended boluses, and add vasopressor where vasodilation rather than hypovolaemia dominates. Track hourly urine output, creatinine, potassium, acid–base status and fluid balance; diuretics treat fluid overload but do not treat acute kidney injury or improve outcome.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not give a reflex 500 mL bolus for every low urine output, and do not forget a blocked catheter. Frame the answer around autoregulation, KDIGO staging and drug review.
Take-home: Assess obstruction, perfusion and nephrotoxins before infusing: NSAIDs plus renin–angiotensin blockade at low pressure remove renal autoregulatory reserve.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: renal physiology (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mku047); KDIGO AKI guideline (https://kdigo.org/guidelines/acute-kidney-injury/)

case_bank.title: Choosing reversal in a patient with renal failure
case_bank.text:
Case: Choosing reversal in a patient with renal failure (Kinetics & delivery, Intermediate)
Patient: A dialysis-dependent patient needs urgent surgery. Rocuronium was given for a rapid sequence induction 25 minutes ago; the post-tetanic count is 1.
Presentation: Surgery finishes early and rapid, complete reversal is required.
Stage 1 — Explain the elimination
  Question: How do the relevant drugs behave in renal failure?
  Model answer: Rocuronium is mainly hepatobiliary but has a renal component, so duration is prolonged in renal failure.
  Model answer: Neostigmine and sugammadex are both renally cleared; the sugammadex–rocuronium complex depends on renal excretion for elimination.
  Model answer: Atracurium and cisatracurium are independent of organ clearance because of Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis, which is why they are often preferred here.
Stage 2 — Choose reversal now
  Question: What do you give at a post-tetanic count of 1?
  Model answer: Neostigmine cannot reverse this depth of block; it requires at least two twitches on train-of-four and has a ceiling effect from acetylcholinesterase saturation.
  Model answer: Give sugammadex 4 mg/kg for deep block (2 mg/kg once two twitches have returned), and confirm recovery quantitatively to a train-of-four ratio of 0.9 or more.
  Model answer: Although sugammadex is not licensed in severe renal impairment, it is widely used with the caveat of delayed complex clearance; discuss the risk of recurarisation and monitor accordingly.
Stage 3 — Anticipate the pitfalls
  Question: What complications should you plan for?
  Model answer: Recurarisation, especially if surgery is short, dosing marginal or clearance impaired — keep monitoring after reversal.
  Model answer: Sugammadex encapsulates aminosteroids only, so if further blockade is needed within 24 hours use a benzylisoquinolinium drug or a much larger rocuronium dose.
  Model answer: Neostigmine requires an antimuscarinic to limit bradycardia, secretions and bronchospasm; sugammadex can cause bradycardia and rare anaphylaxis.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Reversal choice is a pharmacokinetic decision. Neostigmine increases synaptic acetylcholine but cannot overcome deep receptor occupancy, so its effect plateaus. Sugammadex forms a 1:1 complex with aminosteroid relaxants, creating a concentration gradient away from the junction and reversing any depth of block; because both free and complexed drug rely on glomerular filtration, renal failure prolongs elimination even though clinical reversal is still rapid.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use quantitative monitoring throughout, choose the sugammadex dose by measured depth, and continue observation in recovery for recurarisation. In dialysis-dependent patients, consider planning ahead with cisatracurium for maintenance where a rapid sequence induction is not required, and document the reversal drug and time because it affects subsequent relaxant choice.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not offer neostigmine for deep block, and do not claim sugammadex removes the need for monitoring. Mention the 24-hour aminosteroid re-dosing problem.
Take-home: Match reversal to measured depth and organ function: sugammadex reverses deep aminosteroid block, neostigmine cannot, and Hofmann-eliminated drugs avoid the issue.
Cited sources: Assoc Anaesth 2023: neuromuscular blockade (https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anae.16114); BJA Educ: pharmacokinetics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr061)

case_bank.title: Antibiotic dosing in critical illness and renal replacement
case_bank.text:
Case: Antibiotic dosing in critical illness and renal replacement (Critical care drugs, Intermediate)
Patient: A patient with abdominal sepsis on continuous veno-venous haemofiltration is prescribed meropenem and gentamicin. Serum albumin is 18 g/L and fluid balance is +6 L.
Presentation: The team asks whether doses should be reduced because of renal failure.
Stage 1 — Classify the killing pattern
  Question: Which pharmacodynamic target applies to each drug?
  Model answer: Beta-lactams such as meropenem are time-dependent: efficacy tracks the fraction of the dosing interval that free drug exceeds the minimum inhibitory concentration.
  Model answer: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent: efficacy tracks peak concentration relative to the minimum inhibitory concentration, with post-antibiotic effect permitting extended intervals.
  Model answer: Vancomycin is best described by the ratio of 24-hour area under the curve to minimum inhibitory concentration.
Stage 2 — Adjust for the pathophysiology
  Question: What happens to kinetics in this patient?
  Model answer: Volume of distribution of hydrophilic drugs increases with oedema and fluid loading, so early underdosing is common; loading doses should not be reduced.
  Model answer: Hypoalbuminaemia increases free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs and can increase clearance of unbound drug.
  Model answer: Continuous renal replacement provides substantial clearance of small, water-soluble, poorly protein-bound drugs, so maintenance doses often need to be higher than for anuric patients not receiving filtration.
Stage 3 — Write the plan
  Question: What is your practical prescription strategy?
  Model answer: Give a full loading dose, then adjust maintenance to the measured clearance including filtration effluent rate, prolonging beta-lactam infusions to extend time above the minimum inhibitory concentration.
  Model answer: Use therapeutic drug monitoring for aminoglycosides and vancomycin, and involve microbiology and pharmacy for dose individualisation.
  Model answer: Take cultures, give antimicrobials within one hour of recognised sepsis, achieve source control and review de-escalation daily.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Critical illness alters both volume of distribution and clearance, often in opposite directions and over hours. Capillary leak, aggressive resuscitation and hypoalbuminaemia expand the distribution volume of hydrophilic antimicrobials, while augmented renal clearance in some patients and extracorporeal clearance in others increase elimination. Consequently dose reduction on the basis of a creatinine value alone frequently produces subtherapeutic exposure at the time when killing matters most.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Separate loading from maintenance: loading depends on volume of distribution and should be full; maintenance depends on clearance including renal replacement effluent flow. Extended or continuous beta-lactam infusion improves target attainment, and therapeutic drug monitoring should guide aminoglycoside and vancomycin dosing. Reassess daily against culture results, clinical trajectory and source control, and document stop or review dates.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not reduce the loading dose because of renal failure, and do not describe every antibiotic as if the same target applied. Name the specific pharmacodynamic index for each class.
Take-home: Load fully, then adjust maintenance to real clearance: beta-lactams need time above MIC, aminoglycosides need peaks, and filtration removes drug.
Cited sources: Antimicrobial PK/PD in critical illness (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00134-020-06050-1); BJA Educ: pharmacokinetics (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkr061)

case_bank.title: High anion gap acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis
case_bank.text:
Case: High anion gap acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis (Acid–base, Intermediate)
Patient: A young adult presents with pH 7.08, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 2.4 kPa, glucose 28 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L.
Presentation: After 4 L of 0.9% sodium chloride and an insulin infusion, ketones fall to 1.0 mmol/L but pH is still 7.20 with bicarbonate 14 mmol/L and chloride 116 mmol/L.
Stage 1 — Interpret the first gas
  Question: Describe the disorder quantitatively.
  Model answer: Severe metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation: expected PaCO₂ is close to the measured value, so there is no additional respiratory disorder.
  Model answer: Anion gap is raised at about 31 mmol/L, consistent with ketoacidosis; the modest lactate rise reflects hypovolaemia and catecholamine-driven glycolysis.
  Model answer: Delta ratio confirms a pure high anion gap picture rather than a mixed acidosis at presentation.
Stage 2 — Explain the second gas
  Question: Why is the patient still acidotic after ketones have cleared?
  Model answer: The anion gap has normalised while a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis has appeared from large-volume 0.9% sodium chloride.
  Model answer: In Stewart terms, the infused fluid has a strong ion difference of zero, so it reduces plasma strong ion difference and lowers pH independently of ketones.
  Model answer: Bicarbonate regeneration also lags behind ketone clearance because ketoanions were excreted rather than metabolised.
Stage 3 — Manage from here
  Question: What do you change?
  Model answer: Switch to a balanced crystalloid, continue fixed-rate insulin with glucose-containing fluid once glucose falls below about 14 mmol/L, and replace potassium aggressively.
  Model answer: Do not give bicarbonate for a resolving ketoacidosis; treat the cause and monitor ketone clearance rather than pH alone.
  Model answer: Look for the precipitant — infection, non-adherence, myocardial infarction, pregnancy — and monitor for cerebral oedema in younger patients.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Two acidoses appear in sequence here: an organic high anion gap acidosis from ketoacid production, then an iatrogenic hyperchloraemic acidosis from resuscitation with saline. Only anion gap and chloride tracking reveals the switch; following pH or bicarbonate alone suggests treatment failure and risks unnecessary bicarbonate or insulin escalation. Ketone measurement, not glucose, defines resolution.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use fixed-rate weight-based insulin, balanced crystalloid, early and generous potassium replacement, hourly ketone and glucose measurement, and regular electrolyte and gas review. Add glucose-containing fluid to permit continued insulin. Watch for hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypophosphataemia, fluid overload and, especially in adolescents, cerebral oedema. Address the precipitant and involve the diabetes team before discharge.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not attribute persistent acidosis to ongoing ketosis without recalculating the anion gap, and do not reach for bicarbonate. Show the compensation calculation and name hyperchloraemia explicitly.
Take-home: Recalculate the anion gap: persistent acidosis after ketone clearance is usually saline-induced hyperchloraemia, treated by changing fluid, not giving bicarbonate.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: acid–base interpretation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx008); Stewart approach to acid–base (https://doi.org/10.1186/cc3927)

case_bank.title: Tranexamic acid in advanced kidney disease
case_bank.text:
Case: Tranexamic acid in advanced kidney disease (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: An adult with stage 4 chronic kidney disease is listed for revision arthroplasty with anticipated major blood loss.
Presentation: A standard repeated-dose TXA regimen has been copied onto the chart.
Stage 1 — Identify accumulation risk
  Question: Why must the prescription be reconsidered?
  Model answer: TXA is predominantly renally eliminated.
  Model answer: Reduced clearance increases exposure from repeated or high dosing.
  Model answer: High exposure is associated with postoperative seizures.
Stage 2 — Prescribe safely
  Question: What practical safeguards are required?
  Model answer: Confirm current renal function and follow the local renal-adjusted protocol.
  Model answer: Document timing and cumulative dose to prevent repetition.
  Model answer: Use blood conservation and haemostatic measures in parallel.
Stage 3 — Respond to neurological signs
  Question: What if postoperative myoclonus occurs?
  Model answer: Consider TXA accumulation among metabolic and neurological causes.
  Model answer: Stop further TXA, correct reversible factors and treat seizures promptly.
  Model answer: Escalate monitoring and specialist review.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: TXA is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney. Advanced renal impairment prolongs exposure, so repeated or high dosing increases accumulation and seizure risk; the indication and local renal-adjustment protocol must be explicit.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Verify current renal function, indication, timing and cumulative dose. Use the lowest evidence-based renal-adjusted regimen in consultation with local guidance, avoid accidental repeat dosing and monitor neurological recovery. New myoclonus or seizures require drug review and supportive seizure management.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not copy a normal-renal-function regimen into advanced kidney disease. Separate efficacy evidence from dosing safety.
Take-home: Renal impairment changes TXA exposure: use an evidence-based adjusted regimen and monitor cumulative dose and neurological toxicity.
Cited sources: POISE-3 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171)

# Endocrine Emergencies in ICU DKA, HHS, thyroid storm, adrenal (Addisonian) crisis, myxoedema coma, phaeochromocytoma crisis, pituitary apoplexy = [ ["How is diabetic ketoacidosis managed in the first hour?", "0.9% saline 500–1000 mL bolus, fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h, replace K⁺ once Glucose 32 mmol/L · ketones 5.8 · pH 7.08 · HCO₃⁻ 6 · K⁺ 5.6 · Na⁺ 132 . Weight 70 kg. Diagnostic triad met: glucose > 11, ketones ≥ 3, pH < 7.30 → severe DKA (pH < 7.10 or HCO₃⁻ < 5 or K⁺ < 3.5 → HDU/ICU). Hour 1: 0.9% NaCl 1 L over 1 h . Start fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h = 7 U/h as soon as fluid running. Continue patient's long-acting insulin. K⁺ 5.6 → no KCl in first bag. Once K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → add 40 mmol KCl/L. K⁺ < 3.5 → halt insulin until replaced. Switch to 10% dextrose at 125 ml/h when glucose < 14 (run alongside saline) — keeps insulin running until ketones clear. Aim ketones falling ≥ 0.5/h (or HCO₃⁻ rising ≥ 3/h, or glucose falling ≥ 3/h). If not met: increase fixed-rate by 1 U/h. Resolution: ketones < 0.6 + venous pH > 7.30 + HCO₃⁻ > 18. BWPS components: T 40.2 = 25 · agitation = 20 · diarrhoea/jaundice = 20 · AF = 10 · HR 158 = 25 · precipitating event = 10 → ~ 110 → highly suggestive of storm Step 1 — β-blockade : propranolol 1 mg IV titrated, or esmolol infusion (also blocks T₄→T₃). Step 2 — block synthesis : PTU 500–1000 mg PO/NG load then 250 mg q4h (PTU preferred — also blocks peripheral conversion). Step 3 — block release : Lugol's iodine 5 drops PO q6h ≥ 1 h after PTU (otherwise iodine fuels storm). Step 4 — steroid : hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h (blocks conversion + treats relative adrenal insufficiency). case_bank.title: Chronic prednisolone before colectomy
case_bank.text:
Case: Chronic prednisolone before colectomy (Steroid cover, Foundation)
Patient: A 64-year-old woman takes prednisolone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica and is listed for open right hemicolectomy.
Presentation: She is stable at pre-assessment. The surgical team has omitted all morning medicines and asks whether dexamethasone for nausea is enough steroid cover.
Stage 1 — Assess suppression and surgical stress
  Question: What determines whether she needs supplementation?
  Model answer: Prednisolone at or above 5 mg daily for more than four weeks makes HPA-axis suppression likely.
  Model answer: Open colectomy is major surgical stress.
  Model answer: Continue her usual glucocorticoid dose; do not create an additional withdrawal stress.
Stage 2 — Write the prescription
  Question: Prescribe a practical major-surgery regimen.
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours, or 50 mg IV six-hourly where an infusion is impractical.
  Model answer: Return towards the usual oral regimen as recovery permits, guided by clinical progress.
Stage 3 — Manage the postoperative risk
  Question: She becomes hypotensive and hypoglycaemic six hours after surgery. What do you do?
  Model answer: Treat adrenal crisis without waiting for confirmatory testing: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately.
  Model answer: Give rapid 0.9% saline, correct hypoglycaemia with IV glucose and check sodium, potassium and acid–base status.
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours and investigate simultaneous causes of shock.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Prednisolone 10 mg daily is above the dose at which clinically important HPA-axis suppression should be assumed after sustained use. Open colectomy produces major stress, while omission of her normal dose adds withdrawal risk. Antiemetic dexamethasone has glucocorticoid activity but does not by itself constitute a documented perioperative replacement plan.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue the usual steroid, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly while major stress persists. Monitor pressure, glucose, sodium and potassium, and restore oral treatment when absorption is reliable. Refractory hypotension, hypoglycaemia or electrolyte disturbance should trigger immediate adrenal-crisis treatment alongside a search for bleeding, sepsis and cardiac causes.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not delay rescue hydrocortisone for cortisol testing, and do not stop supplementation abruptly after major surgery. State the steroid route, timing, postoperative continuation and plan to return to baseline treatment.
Take-home: Major surgery in a patient with likely HPA suppression requires the usual steroid plus hydrocortisone at induction and continued replacement; dexamethasone used for antiemesis is not a substitute for a planned regimen.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: The overlooked inhaled steroid
case_bank.text:
Case: The overlooked inhaled steroid (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: A 49-year-old man with severe asthma uses high-dose inhaled fluticasone and has received three oral prednisolone courses this year. He is listed for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Presentation: He denies taking any ‘regular steroid tablets’ and the initial assessment records no risk of adrenal suppression.
Stage 1 — Identify hidden exposure
  Question: Why should the steroid history be revisited?
  Model answer: High-dose inhaled steroids and repeated systemic courses can suppress the HPA axis.
  Model answer: Ask about dose, duration, recent oral courses, steroid emergency card, Cushingoid features and previous perioperative problems.
  Model answer: If uncertainty cannot be resolved before surgery, a safe supplementation plan is preferable to an unrecognised crisis.
Stage 2 — Plan moderate-stress cover
  Question: How would you manage a patient judged at risk?
  Model answer: Continue usual inhaled therapy and optimise asthma control.
  Model answer: For moderate surgical stress, give hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction followed by 25 mg IV eight-hourly for 24 hours.
  Model answer: Monitor glucose, blood pressure, sodium and potassium; resume the normal regimen promptly.
Stage 3 — Differentiate postoperative hypotension
  Question: What features make adrenal crisis more likely?
  Model answer: Hypotension that responds poorly to fluid and vasopressors, especially with hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia.
  Model answer: Treat immediately with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV and fluids while also excluding bleeding, sepsis, anaphylaxis and cardiac causes.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: HPA suppression depends on cumulative systemic exposure, not whether a patient currently takes tablets. High-dose fluticasone, repeated oral rescue courses, topical preparations and injections all matter. Features such as Cushingoid appearance, a steroid emergency card or recent withdrawal increase concern.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue inhaled therapy and optimise asthma. If moderate-stress surgery proceeds with credible suppression risk, give hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction followed by 25 mg eight-hourly for 24 hours, then resume the established regimen. Observe haemodynamics, glucose and electrolytes and treat unexplained shock promptly.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: A normal-looking medication list can conceal recent systemic exposure. Ask specifically about every route, dose, duration and cessation date rather than accepting ‘no steroid tablets’.
Take-home: A steroid history includes inhaled, topical, injected and recently stopped treatment—not just current tablets.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Primary adrenal insufficiency and emergency laparotomy
case_bank.text:
Case: Primary adrenal insufficiency and emergency laparotomy (Steroid cover, Advanced)
Patient: A 36-year-old woman with Addison’s disease presents with perforated appendicitis, vomiting and fever. BP is 84/48 mmHg, glucose 3.1 mmol/L and sodium 126 mmol/L.
Presentation: She has been unable to take hydrocortisone or fludrocortisone for 24 hours.
Stage 1 — Recognise crisis
  Question: What is the immediate diagnosis and priority?
  Model answer: This is adrenal crisis until proved otherwise, precipitated by infection, vomiting and missed replacement.
  Model answer: Do not delay treatment for cortisol measurement; draw blood first only if it causes no delay.
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, rapid isotonic saline and IV glucose.
Stage 2 — Prepare for theatre
  Question: How should replacement continue?
  Model answer: Continue hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion, or 50 mg IV six-hourly.
  Model answer: Correct volume, glucose and electrolyte abnormalities and start source-control antibiotics.
  Model answer: Use invasive monitoring according to haemodynamic response and operative severity.
Stage 3 — Step down safely
  Question: What matters after source control?
  Model answer: Continue stress dosing while severely unwell, then taper according to recovery and endocrine advice.
  Model answer: Restart oral glucocorticoid replacement when absorption is reliable.
  Model answer: Fludrocortisone is generally unnecessary while hydrocortisone exceeds 50 mg daily because mineralocorticoid activity is adequate.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Known primary adrenal insufficiency, missed replacement, vomiting, infection, hypotension, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia make adrenal crisis the working diagnosis. The immediate mortality risk comes from glucocorticoid deficiency and severe volume depletion; treatment precedes biochemical confirmation.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, rapid 0.9% saline and IV glucose, then hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly. Correct electrolytes, give antibiotics and obtain source control. Taper only as illness resolves and oral absorption returns; hydrocortisone above 50 mg daily supplies adequate mineralocorticoid effect, so fludrocortisone is usually temporarily unnecessary.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Blood sampling is optional if it delays treatment. Persistent shock still requires evaluation for sepsis, haemorrhage and cardiogenic causes rather than attributing every abnormality to Addison’s disease.
Take-home: Known adrenal insufficiency plus acute illness, vomiting and shock is a treatment-first emergency: hydrocortisone, saline, glucose and definitive management of the trigger.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Recent joint injections before arthroplasty
case_bank.text:
Case: Recent joint injections before arthroplasty (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: A 72-year-old man is scheduled for revision knee arthroplasty. He stopped prednisolone two months ago and has also had repeated intra-articular steroid injections.
Presentation: He reports fatigue and postural dizziness but has no formal diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency.
Stage 1 — Build the risk picture
  Question: Which details change your plan?
  Model answer: Recent cessation of long-term oral therapy does not guarantee HPA recovery; suppression may persist.
  Model answer: Repeated intra-articular injections add systemic exposure.
  Model answer: Symptoms, treatment records and time available determine whether endocrine testing is useful; urgent surgery should not await testing when risk is credible.
Stage 2 — Cover major surgery
  Question: What is a defensible perioperative plan?
  Model answer: Document likely suppression and give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue 200 mg over 24 hours initially, alongside close haemodynamic and glucose monitoring.
  Model answer: Agree the taper and longer-term assessment with endocrinology or the treating team.
Stage 3 — Avoid the common error
  Question: What should not happen at discharge?
  Model answer: Do not abruptly stop glucocorticoid cover without a recovery plan.
  Model answer: Provide clear written sick-day advice and arrange assessment of ongoing replacement need.
  Model answer: Reconcile every steroid route in the discharge medicines.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: HPA recovery after long-term glucocorticoids is variable and may take months. Repeated intra-articular injections can add meaningful systemic exposure, while fatigue and postural symptoms strengthen concern but are not diagnostic. Testing is useful only when time and clinical stability permit.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: For major revision arthroplasty with credible suppression, continue or replace the baseline requirement, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction and 200 mg over the first 24 hours. Monitor haemodynamics and glucose, then agree a taper and formal endocrine assessment rather than making an unplanned stop.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: ‘Stopped two months ago’ does not prove recovery. Discharge reconciliation should cover oral, inhaled, topical and injected steroids and provide sick-day and emergency advice.
Take-home: Recently stopped oral steroids and repeated injections can remain clinically relevant; route and current prescription alone do not define HPA-axis risk.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Preparing an adrenal phaeochromocytoma
case_bank.text:
Case: Preparing an adrenal phaeochromocytoma (Phaeochromocytoma, Foundation)
Patient: A 43-year-old woman has an adrenal mass, raised plasma metanephrines and episodic headache, sweating and palpitations.
Presentation: She is referred for laparoscopic adrenalectomy with a seated BP of 168/96 mmHg and pulse 104 min⁻¹.
Stage 1 — Sequence preoperative treatment
  Question: How should blockade be introduced?
  Model answer: Start alpha blockade first, commonly phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin, and titrate over about 10–14 days.
  Model answer: Only add beta blockade after adequate alpha blockade if troublesome tachycardia persists.
  Model answer: Never beta block first because unopposed alpha vasoconstriction can provoke a hypertensive crisis.
Stage 2 — Restore circulating volume
  Question: Why are salt and fluid important?
  Model answer: Chronic catecholamine-mediated vasoconstriction leaves the patient intravascularly depleted.
  Model answer: Encourage salt and fluid intake after alpha blockade, while individualising for cardiac or renal disease.
  Model answer: Look for controlled seated BP with tolerable postural reduction rather than simply a normal clinic reading.
Stage 3 — Confirm readiness
  Question: What should the multidisciplinary review cover?
  Model answer: Blood-pressure and rhythm control, postural symptoms, ECG/cardiac effects and glucose.
  Model answer: Availability of experienced endocrine surgery, anaesthesia, critical care and appropriate postoperative monitoring.
  Model answer: A plan for invasive monitoring and rapidly acting vasoactive drugs.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction causes hypertension and contracted circulating volume. Alpha blockade reduces vascular tone; beta blockade is added only after alpha control because isolated beta blockade leaves unopposed alpha vasoconstriction. Preparation is judged by pressure control, tolerable postural change, rhythm and end-organ effects rather than one clinic value.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Titrate phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin for roughly 10–14 days, then add beta blockade only for persistent tachycardia after adequate alpha blockade. Encourage salt and fluid intake where safe. Plan arterial monitoring, large-bore access, short-acting vasodilators, vasopressors, glucose monitoring and postoperative critical-care observation with an experienced multidisciplinary team.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not chase a perfectly normal seated pressure at the cost of disabling orthostasis, and never describe beta blockade before alpha blockade.
Take-home: Successful preparation is alpha blockade followed—if needed—by beta blockade, together with volume expansion and an experienced multidisciplinary plan.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Beta blocker before diagnosis
case_bank.text:
Case: Beta blocker before diagnosis (Phaeochromocytoma, Advanced)
Patient: A 51-year-old man with an undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma receives propranolol in the emergency department for tachycardia.
Presentation: Minutes later he develops severe headache, chest pain and BP 246/132 mmHg with pulmonary oedema.
Stage 1 — Explain the deterioration
  Question: What mechanism has caused this crisis?
  Model answer: Beta blockade removed beta-mediated vasodilation and cardiac compensation while alpha receptors remained intensely stimulated.
  Model answer: Unopposed alpha vasoconstriction caused abrupt hypertension and acute cardiac afterload.
  Model answer: This presentation should trigger urgent specialist help and consideration of catecholamine excess.
Stage 2 — Stabilise the crisis
  Question: What are the immediate principles?
  Model answer: Use titratable vasodilator or alpha-blocking therapy with invasive arterial pressure monitoring in a critical-care setting.
  Model answer: Treat pulmonary oedema and myocardial complications while avoiding further isolated beta blockade.
  Model answer: Once alpha control is established, a short-acting beta blocker may be considered for persistent tachyarrhythmia.
Stage 3 — Plan definitive care
  Question: Should surgery proceed immediately?
  Model answer: If the acute emergency can be stabilised, defer tumour resection until adequate alpha blockade and volume restoration are achieved.
  Model answer: Emergency surgery is reserved for an uncontrollable complication and requires an expert team with vasoactive support ready.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Propranolol removes beta-2 vasodilation and limits cardiac compensation while catecholamine-stimulated alpha receptors continue intense vasoconstriction. The result may be malignant hypertension, myocardial injury and pulmonary oedema. This is a pharmacological crisis, not simple undertreated tachycardia.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Escalate to critical care, establish invasive arterial monitoring and control vascular tone with titratable vasodilation or alpha blockade. Treat pulmonary oedema and myocardial complications and avoid further isolated beta blockade. A short-acting beta blocker is considered only after alpha-mediated hypertension is controlled. Definitive resection is normally deferred until blockade and volume restoration are complete.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Giving more beta blocker for the persistent tachycardia can worsen the crisis. Explain receptor physiology and treatment sequence explicitly.
Take-home: In suspected phaeochromocytoma, beta blockade before alpha blockade can be catastrophic; control vasoconstriction first.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Hypertension during tumour handling
case_bank.text:
Case: Hypertension during tumour handling (Phaeochromocytoma, Advanced)
Patient: During laparoscopic adrenalectomy, BP rises from 124/72 to 228/118 mmHg and HR to 142 min⁻¹ as the surgeon mobilises the tumour.
Presentation: An arterial line is in place. Anaesthetic depth is adequate and ventilation is unchanged.
Stage 1 — Recognise the phase
  Question: What is the likely cause and what should be communicated?
  Model answer: Tumour manipulation has released catecholamines.
  Model answer: Ask the surgeon to stop handling temporarily and announce the haemodynamic crisis clearly.
  Model answer: Exclude contributing hypoxia, hypercarbia, light anaesthesia and drug error without delaying treatment.
Stage 2 — Control the surge
  Question: Which treatment principles apply?
  Model answer: Use rapid, titratable vasodilator or alpha-blocking treatment such as sodium nitroprusside, glyceryl trinitrate or phentolamine according to local practice.
  Model answer: Magnesium can reduce catecholamine release and provide vasodilation; esmolol is reserved for tachycardia after vasoconstriction is controlled.
  Model answer: Avoid long-acting treatment that will worsen the predictable post-ligation hypotension.
Stage 3 — Prepare for vein ligation
  Question: What happens next?
  Model answer: After venous ligation, catecholamine concentration falls abruptly and profound vasodilation/hypotension may follow.
  Model answer: Stop vasodilators, communicate timing, restore preload judiciously and use titrated vasopressor support.
  Model answer: Check glucose because rebound insulin release can cause hypoglycaemia.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Tumour handling can release a sudden catecholamine load, producing severe hypertension and tachyarrhythmia. The anaesthetist must communicate with the surgeon, pause manipulation and exclude amplifiers such as hypercarbia, hypoxia and inadequate anaesthesia while treating immediately.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use short-acting, titratable agents such as nitroprusside, glyceryl trinitrate or phentolamine according to local practice; magnesium offers vasodilation and may reduce catecholamine release. Use esmolol only after vasoconstriction is controlled. Before adrenal-vein ligation, stop vasodilators, prepare vasopressors and assess preload because abrupt catecholamine withdrawal can cause profound hypotension. Check glucose for rebound hypoglycaemia.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Long-acting antihypertensives may turn the predictable post-ligation pressure fall into prolonged shock. Link each drug choice to the rapidly changing surgical phase.
Take-home: Phaeochromocytoma surgery has two opposing haemodynamic phases: a manipulation surge and post-ligation collapse; short-acting, titratable drugs are essential.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Post-adrenalectomy collapse
case_bank.text:
Case: Post-adrenalectomy collapse (Phaeochromocytoma, Intermediate)
Patient: Two hours after phaeochromocytoma resection, a patient is drowsy, clammy and hypotensive despite initial fluid. Capillary glucose is 2.6 mmol/L.
Presentation: The intraoperative record documents difficult tumour mobilisation followed by a marked pressure drop after vein ligation.
Stage 1 — Frame the differential
  Question: Which expected complications coexist here?
  Model answer: Hypotension can reflect residual alpha blockade, vasodilation, catecholamine withdrawal, hypovolaemia or bleeding.
  Model answer: Hypoglycaemia follows loss of catecholamine-mediated insulin suppression and rebound insulin secretion.
  Model answer: Also consider adrenal insufficiency after bilateral surgery and conventional postoperative causes of shock.
Stage 2 — Treat immediately
  Question: What should happen now?
  Model answer: Give IV glucose and recheck frequently.
  Model answer: Assess bleeding and fluid responsiveness, then use titrated vasopressor support where vasodilation persists.
  Model answer: Continue high-acuity monitoring of blood pressure, rhythm, urine output, lactate and glucose.
Stage 3 — Set the recovery plan
  Question: What must handover include?
  Model answer: Explicit risks of recurrent hypotension and hypoglycaemia with scheduled observations.
  Model answer: A steroid replacement plan when bilateral adrenal tissue has been removed or adrenal function is uncertain.
  Model answer: Endocrine follow-up and biochemical surveillance for persistent or recurrent disease.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Post-resection hypotension is often multifactorial: catecholamine withdrawal, residual alpha blockade, vasoplegia and depleted volume coexist, but bleeding must be excluded. Hypoglycaemia occurs because removal of catecholamine-mediated insulin suppression permits rebound insulin release.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Give IV glucose, repeat measurements frequently and assess haemorrhage, preload and cardiac function. Use judicious fluid and titrated vasopressor support for persistent vasodilation. Continue high-acuity pressure, rhythm, urine-output, lactate and glucose monitoring. Bilateral adrenalectomy or uncertain residual function requires a clear steroid replacement plan.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not treat drowsiness as residual anaesthesia without checking glucose. Handover must state the specific risks of recurrent hypotension and hypoglycaemia.
Take-home: Post-resection care is active: anticipate hypotension and hypoglycaemia rather than waiting for routine ward observations to detect them.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Minor procedure on replacement hydrocortisone
case_bank.text:
Case: Minor procedure on replacement hydrocortisone (Steroid cover, Foundation)
Patient: An adult with stable primary adrenal insufficiency is listed for a short dental extraction under local anaesthesia.
Presentation: They are well, have taken their usual morning hydrocortisone and ask whether an injection is mandatory.
Stage 1 — Grade the stress
  Question: Does every procedure require parenteral stress dosing?
  Model answer: No: supplementation should reflect procedural stress, illness and ability to absorb usual treatment.
  Model answer: A short uncomplicated procedure under effective local anaesthesia is minor stress.
  Model answer: Confirm emergency steroid and sick-day plans.
Stage 2 — Make a proportionate plan
  Question: What would you do today?
  Model answer: Continue the usual oral replacement.
  Model answer: Use effective local anaesthesia, analgesia and minimise fasting.
  Model answer: Escalate if the procedure becomes prolonged, oral medication is missed or systemic illness develops.
Stage 3 — Recognise deterioration
  Question: What if vomiting and hypotension develop?
  Model answer: Treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM.
  Model answer: Give isotonic fluid and glucose where required and seek urgent care.
  Model answer: Do not wait for cortisol testing.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: A minor procedure under local anaesthesia usually produces little physiological stress. A patient taking a stable physiological replacement dose should continue it; indiscriminate high-dose hydrocortisone adds hyperglycaemia, infection and wound-healing harms without clear benefit.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Confirm adherence, recent illness and ability to take oral medication. Continue the usual morning hydrocortisone, use effective local anaesthesia and analgesia, and give written sick-day advice. Escalate only if the procedure becomes prolonged, the patient cannot absorb oral medication or haemodynamic features suggest crisis.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Steroid cover is proportional to surgical stress and baseline replacement. ‘Any steroid history means 100 mg hydrocortisone’ is not a defensible rule.
Take-home: Match glucocorticoid supplementation to physiological stress; continue baseline replacement and retain a clear rescue plan.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Pituitary insufficiency before major surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Pituitary insufficiency before major surgery (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: An adult with panhypopituitarism takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine and is listed for open abdominal surgery.
Presentation: They have fasted, omitted morning medicines and have glucose 3.5 mmol/L with normal potassium.
Stage 1 — Interpret the pattern
  Question: Does normal potassium exclude adrenal risk?
  Model answer: No. Secondary adrenal insufficiency often preserves aldosterone and potassium.
  Model answer: Missed glucocorticoid, fasting and major stress create crisis risk.
  Model answer: Review diabetes insipidus and other pituitary replacement.
Stage 2 — Provide major-stress cover
  Question: What regimen is appropriate?
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly initially.
  Model answer: Correct hypoglycaemia and monitor sodium, glucose and fluid balance.
Stage 3 — Sequence endocrine treatment
  Question: What endocrine ordering matters?
  Model answer: Ensure glucocorticoid replacement before initiating or escalating thyroid hormone in combined deficiency.
  Model answer: Taper toward baseline when stable and absorbing orally.
  Model answer: Seek endocrine input for complex fluid or sodium disturbance.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Pituitary disease may cause secondary adrenal insufficiency without hyperkalaemia because aldosterone is largely preserved. Fasting, vomiting and omission of hydrocortisone can still precipitate hypotension and hypoglycaemia during major surgery.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue replacement, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction and 200 mg over 24 hours for major stress, then taper toward baseline as recovery permits. Monitor sodium, glucose, pressure and fluid balance; account for coexisting diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Normal potassium does not exclude secondary adrenal crisis. Replace glucocorticoid before starting or increasing thyroxine in untreated combined pituitary deficiency.
Take-home: Secondary adrenal insufficiency can present without hyperkalaemia; major stress still requires timely glucocorticoid replacement.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Catecholamine symptoms in pregnancy
case_bank.text:
Case: Catecholamine symptoms in pregnancy (Phaeochromocytoma, Advanced)
Patient: A pregnant adult at 24 weeks has episodic hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations.
Presentation: Urine protein is absent and symptoms began early in pregnancy; plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated.
Stage 1 — Differentiate the diagnosis
  Question: Why is this not automatically pre-eclampsia?
  Model answer: Paroxysmal symptoms and early onset suggest catecholamine excess.
  Model answer: Confirm biochemistry and localise with pregnancy-appropriate imaging, commonly MRI without gadolinium.
  Model answer: Assess maternal cardiac and fetal effects.
Stage 2 — Prepare safely
  Question: What is the pharmacological sequence?
  Model answer: Establish alpha blockade first and restore circulating volume cautiously.
  Model answer: Add beta blockade only after adequate alpha control for persistent tachycardia.
  Model answer: Coordinate a specialist multidisciplinary plan.
Stage 3 — Plan definitive care
  Question: How is timing decided?
  Model answer: Balance gestation, tumour location, haemodynamic control and maternal-fetal risk.
  Model answer: Use invasive monitoring and short-acting vasoactive drugs for surgery or delivery.
  Model answer: Agree neonatal and postoperative critical-care provision.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Phaeochromocytoma in pregnancy threatens both maternal and fetal circulation. Episodic hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations that predate pre-eclampsia should prompt metanephrine testing and MRI without gadolinium.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Coordinate endocrine, obstetric, anaesthetic, neonatal and surgical care. Establish alpha blockade before any beta blocker, restore volume carefully and use invasive monitoring for surgery or delivery. Timing of adrenalectomy and delivery depends on gestation, tumour anatomy and control.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not treat tachycardia first with isolated beta blockade, and do not assume all hypertension after 20 weeks is pre-eclampsia.
Take-home: Phaeochromocytoma in pregnancy requires early recognition, alpha-before-beta blockade and coordinated maternal-fetal planning.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Adrenal incidentaloma before elective surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Adrenal incidentaloma before elective surgery (Phaeochromocytoma, Intermediate)
Patient: An adult awaiting elective joint replacement has an adrenal incidentaloma and elevated metanephrines.
Presentation: They report few symptoms and the surgical team asks whether the unrelated operation can proceed.
Stage 1 — Assess hidden risk
  Question: Can an asymptomatic patient still develop crisis?
  Model answer: Yes. Anaesthesia, intubation and surgical stress can trigger catecholamine release.
  Model answer: Review biochemical certainty, imaging and end-organ effects.
  Model answer: Do not equate few symptoms with low perioperative risk.
Stage 2 — Prioritise procedures
  Question: What happens to elective surgery?
  Model answer: Postpone non-urgent surgery for endocrine evaluation and preparation.
  Model answer: Institute alpha blockade and volume restoration before definitive management.
  Model answer: Avoid isolated beta blockade.
Stage 3 — Handle an emergency exception
  Question: What if unrelated surgery cannot wait?
  Model answer: Use senior multidisciplinary planning and invasive arterial monitoring.
  Model answer: Prepare titratable vasodilators, vasopressors and postoperative critical care.
  Model answer: Avoid known catecholamine-provoking drugs where alternatives exist.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: An adrenal incidentaloma with biochemical catecholamine excess creates risk even when symptoms are mild. Elective unrelated surgery can trigger crisis through induction, intubation, surgical stress or interacting drugs.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Postpone non-urgent surgery, confirm biochemistry and imaging, assess end-organ effects and establish alpha blockade with volume restoration. If emergency surgery cannot wait, use an arterial line, senior multidisciplinary input and prepared short-acting vasodilator and vasopressor infusions.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not dismiss an asymptomatic tumour or proceed after simply adding a beta blocker. Explain why the unrelated operation should usually be deferred.
Take-home: Biochemically active phaeochromocytoma makes unrelated elective anaesthesia unsafe until appropriately prepared.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

Exam pearl:
Volume status is the key discriminator between SIADH and CSW — both have hyponatraemia with high urine Na⁺ and high urine osmolality. SIADH is euvolaemic, CSW is hypovolaemic. Getting it wrong is dangerous: fluid restriction in CSW worsens cerebral perfusion and precipitates vasospasm-related infarction in SAH.
Diagnostic flowchart
Sequential bedside approach: serum Na⁺ → plasma/urine osmolality → urine Na⁺ → urine output → volume status.

Step 4 — Urine output & volume status (the decider)
Euvolaemic + normal/low UO
Normal CVP, no postural drop, neutral/positive balance, low urate, normal Hct/urea.
→ SIADH

→ Cerebral salt wasting
Rx: 0.9% or hypertonic saline + fludrocortisone 0.1–0.4 mg/day. Never fluid restrict.
