Diagnosis is clinical and repeated — misdiagnosis rates approach 40% when based on a single bedside exam; validated tools (Coma Recovery Scale–Revised, CRS-R) improve accuracy.
Vegetative State (VS) / Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (UWS)
Brainstem and autonomic function preserved (breathing, BP, cardiac).
Reflexive responses only (grimace, withdrawal, roving eye movements).
Term "persistent" (>1 month); "permanent" (>3 months non-traumatic; >12 months traumatic) — RCP 2020 deprecates "permanent" in favour of prognostic statements.
Minimally Conscious State (MCS)
minimal but definite
behavioural evidence of self- or environmental awareness, reproducible on examination.
: low-level responses (visual pursuit, localisation to noxious stimuli, contingent emotional response).
: command following, intelligible verbalisation, or intentional communication (yes/no, gesture) — not necessarily accurate.
Emergence from MCS: reliable functional communication
functional object use.
VS / UWS
Eye opening
Sleep–wake cycles
Awareness of self/environment
Partial, inconsistent
Purposeful motor response
None (reflex only)
Vertical eye/eyelid only
Language comprehension
Respiratory drive
Why the distinction matters
MCS carries better prognosis for further functional recovery than VS.
MCS patients may experience pain — analgesia and sedation planning differ.
Decisions on CANH withdrawal: in UK no longer require Court of Protection if consensus + best-interest process is followed.
Functional MRI / EEG paradigms (covert command following) identify "cognitive-motor dissociation" in ~15% of behaviourally VS patients.
Mimics to exclude
Locked-in syndrome
(ventral pontine lesion): fully aware, quadriplegic, only vertical eye movements/blinking preserved.
Akinetic mutism
(frontal/mesencephalic): wakeful, immobile, mute but tracks.
Sedation, non-convulsive status epilepticus, severe aphasia, profound neuromuscular weakness.
References (click for source)
Diagnoses should be made by a clinician experienced in prolonged disorders of consciousness (PDoC) using serial Coma Recovery Scale–Revised (CRS-R) assessments, not a single bedside exam.
dominates: TBI recovers better than anoxic/hypoxic-ischaemic injury.
: meaningful recovery becomes progressively unlikely beyond 6 months (non-traumatic) and 12 months (traumatic) for VS; longer windows for MCS.
MCS > VS
for further functional recovery; MCS+ (language) better than MCS−.
: SSEP (bilateral absent N20 = poor in anoxic injury), NSE, MRI, fMRI/EEG paradigms for covert awareness.
Avoid early (<72 h) prognostic statements after cardiac arrest — follow ERC/ESICM multimodal algorithm.
Pain, sedation & symptom control
MCS patients can plausibly experience pain — assume nociception, use validated tools (NCS-R).
Document analgesia/sedation rationale; balance against suppression of behavioural responses needed for diagnosis.
Treat reversible contributors (spasticity, constipation, urinary retention, infection) before attributing behavioural change to underlying state.
Medico-legal framework (UK)
Mental Capacity Act 2005
: patients lack capacity — decisions made in
best interests
(s.4), consulting family/those interested in welfare, and any ADRT or LPA (health & welfare).
CANH withdrawal
: following
An NHS Trust v Y
, court application is no longer mandatory where there is clinical and family consensus and the RCP/BMA/GMC best-interest process has been followed. Refer to the Court of Protection where dispute, uncertainty, or finely-balanced decisions arise.
second opinion
from a clinician external to the treating team is required before CANH withdrawal in PDoC.
appointment if no appropriate family/friend to consult on serious medical treatment.
Brain death (DNC) is a separate legal/clinical entity — VS and MCS patients are
; organ donation pathways differ (DCD only, if treatment withdrawn).
Clear, contemporaneous documentation of diagnosis, prognosis, decision-making and family meetings is essential.
Key learning points
Diagnosis of PDoC is clinical, serial, and uses CRS-R — single assessments misdiagnose ~40%.
VS = wakefulness without awareness; MCS = minimal but reproducible awareness; both have preserved brainstem function and are
brain death.
Aetiology and time since injury are the strongest prognostic factors; MCS prognosis exceeds VS.
Treat MCS patients as capable of pain perception until proven otherwise.
CANH withdrawal in PDoC is lawful via the MCA best-interest process with second opinion; court only where dispute or uncertainty exists.
Always exclude mimics: locked-in syndrome, NCSE, severe sedation, neuromuscular weakness.
Cited guidance (click to open)
Respiratory Support
Respiratory Muscles Lost
Diaphragm, intercostals, abdominals — all lost
Apnoea — immediate ventilatory support. Long-term phrenic nerve pacing may be possible.
Partial/complete diaphragm loss (C3,4,5 keeps the diaphragm alive). Intercostals and abdominals lost.
Severely reduced VC (20–30% predicted). High risk of ventilatory failure, especially with ascending oedema in first 48–72h. Early intubation threshold.
Intercostals and abdominals lost. Diaphragm intact.
VC 30–50% predicted. Paradoxical breathing. Impaired cough → secretion retention → atelectasis/pneumonia.
Variable intercostal and abdominal loss
VC 50–80% predicted. Lower thoracic injuries: may manage without ventilatory support but cough remains impaired.
Ventilation Strategy
Secretion Management & Cough Augmentation
Cardiovascular & Blood Pressure Management
Spinal Shock vs Neurogenic Shock
Spinal Shock
Neurogenic Shock
Temporary loss of all spinal cord function (motor, sensory, reflex) below injury level
Haemodynamic instability from loss of sympathetic tone
Neurological — areflexia, flaccid paralysis
Cardiovascular — vasodilation, bradycardia
Days to weeks (ends when bulbocavernosus reflex returns)
Hours to weeks
Cannot assess final neurological deficit until resolved
Requires vasopressor support and monitoring
Bowel & Bladder Care
Neurogenic Bladder
Acute (spinal shock):
Areflexic/atonic bladder → urinary retention. Insert indwelling catheter.
After spinal shock resolves:
Upper motor neurone (suprasacral) → spastic/reflex bladder (overactive detrusor, DSD). Lower motor neurone (conus/cauda equina) → flaccid/atonic bladder (overflow incontinence).
Neurogenic Bowel
Upper motor neurone (above conus):
Spastic bowel — intact reflex arc. Manage with timed digital rectal stimulation, suppositories (bisacodyl/glycerine), high-fibre diet, adequate hydration, stool softeners. Aim regular scheduled bowel programme every 1–2 days.
Lower motor neurone (conus/cauda):
Flaccid bowel — no reflex. Requires manual evacuation, bulking agents, Valsalva/abdominal straining.
Faecal impaction is the most common trigger for autonomic dysreflexia — prevention is critical.
Other ICU Considerations
Temperature Regulation
Pressure Area Care & Nutrition
Suxamethonium Contraindication
CONTRAINDICATED from 48 hours to ~6–12 months post-SCI
due to upregulation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors → life-threatening hyperkalaemia on depolarisation. Safe in the first 24–48 hours. Use rocuronium for RSI after this window.
Psychological Support
⚠ Exam Alert — Methylprednisolone in SCI
NASCIS II/III trials
suggested benefit of high-dose methylprednisolone within 8 hours. However, these trials had significant methodological flaws. Current guidelines (NICE, AANS/CNS)
do NOT recommend
routine methylprednisolone for acute SCI due to lack of evidence for benefit and increased complications (infections, GI bleeding, hyperglycaemia). This is frequently examined.
ICP rises or PbtO₂ falls. Used predominantly in poor-grade SAH and severe TBI in selected neuro-ICU centres (Cambridge, Lund, Edinburgh, Addenbrooke's-style protocols).
Catheter & Principle
How it Works
0.3 µL/min
. Small molecules diffuse across the membrane down their concentration gradient between brain ECF and perfusate. Effluent (microdialysate) is collected in microvials, changed hourly, and analysed at the bedside (ISCUS analyser — enzymatic / colorimetric) for glucose, lactate, pyruvate, glutamate and glycerol.
Catheter Placement
Target Location
Diffuse TBI
Right frontal (non-dominant), normal-appearing white matter
Detect global secondary insults; standard "Lund/Cambridge" position
Focal TBI / contusion
Pericontusional "penumbra" (~1 cm from visible lesion)
Tissue at risk — most likely to benefit from intervention
Poor-grade SAH
Vascular territory at highest risk of DCI (often A2/MCA territory ipsilateral to ruptured aneurysm)
Early detection of delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm
Measured Markers & Normal Ranges
Normal (mmol/L*)
1.7–2.5 (alarm <0.8)
Substrate delivery; tracks systemic glucose with delay
Anaerobic metabolism, mitochondrial dysfunction or hyperglycolysis
70–150 µmol/L
Substrate flux through glycolysis
Lactate / Pyruvate Ratio (LPR)
<25 (alarm >25; severe >40)
The single most useful marker — cellular redox state (NADH:NAD⁺); ↑ in ischaemia AND mitochondrial dysfunction
<10 µmol/L
Excitotoxicity — released from injured neurons; also reflects ischaemia
<100 µmol/L
Membrane phospholipid breakdown — structural cell damage
— true ECF values are higher because recovery across the membrane is incomplete (typically 60–70% at 0.3 µL/min). Trends over time matter more than single absolute values.
Interpreting the Patterns
Clinical Use
Severe TBI
respond to further haemodynamic escalation). Endorsed by the 2014 international consensus statement on multimodal monitoring (Le Roux et al, Neurocrit Care/ICM).
Other Uses
💡 Exam Pearl
Lactate:Pyruvate Ratio (LPR)
is the single highest-yield CMD value. Threshold >25 = metabolic crisis; >40 = severe. Distinguish ischaemia (LPR ↑
↓ pyruvate) from mitochondrial dysfunction (LPR ↑
normal/↑ pyruvate) — they look similar but have completely different management implications. CMD also drove the move
from tight glycaemic control in TBI after evidence of brain neuroglycopenia at systemic glucose 4.5–6 mmol/L (Vespa, Oddo).
tier 3 / last-line
intervention for ICP refractory to medical therapy. Three landmark RCTs define current practice.
DECRA (NEJM 2011, Cooper et al.)
Bifrontotemporoparietal DC for
refractory ICP in diffuse TBI.
155 adults <60 y, diffuse TBI, ICP >20 mmHg for >15 min within any 1 h despite tier-1/2 therapy.
DC lowered ICP and ICU/ventilator days but produced
worse 6-month neurological outcome
(extended GOS) than medical management. No mortality difference.
Criticised for an early ICP trigger (>20 mmHg for just 15 min) and post-randomisation pupil-reactivity imbalance.
Bottom line:
DC should
be used for early/modestly refractory ICP — escalate medical therapy first.
RESCUEicp (NEJM 2016, Hutchinson et al.)
DC as a
intervention for sustained refractory ICP.
408 patients 10–65 y; ICP >25 mmHg for 1–12 h despite tier-1 and tier-2 therapy (sedation, osmotherapy, hyperventilation, CSF drainage). Barbiturates allowed in the medical arm.
At 6 months: mortality 26.9% (DC) vs 48.9% (medical),
(NNT ≈ 5). However, survivors had higher rates of vegetative state and severe disability; rates of upper-severe disability and good recovery were similar.
12- and 24-month follow-up: survival benefit persists, with a small increase in favourable outcomes over time as some patients improve.
DC saves lives in truly refractory ICP, but at the cost of survival with severe disability — frame the trade-off explicitly with family before consent.
Hemicraniectomy for malignant MCA infarction
DESTINY, DECIMAL, HAMLET (pooled analysis, Lancet Neurol 2007) and DESTINY II (NEJM 2014).
Pooled analysis (age ≤60, DC within 48 h): mortality 22% vs 71%; mRS ≤3 at 12 months 43% vs 21%. NNT ≈ 2 for survival, ≈ 4 for mRS ≤4.
DESTINY II (age >60): survival improved (57% vs 24%), but most survivors had mRS 4–5; no patient achieved mRS ≤2.
hemicraniectomy <48 h is standard of care in malignant MCA infarction <60 y; in >60 y, individualised discussion about acceptable disability.
Guideline position
BTF 4th edition (2017):
bifrontal DC
recommended to improve outcomes in diffuse TBI with early refractory ICP (DECRA), but recommended to reduce ICP and ICU days. Large fronto-temporo-parietal DC recommended over small DC for better outcomes.
Seattle International Consensus (SIBICC, 2019/2020):
DC sits at
tier 3
, alongside barbiturate coma and hypothermia, reserved for ICP refractory to optimised tier 1 and 2 management.
NICE NG232 (TBI, 2023):
consider DC after multidisciplinary discussion when medical management has failed, with explicit counselling on survival-with-disability trade-off.
Complications & later issues
Early: haemorrhage at craniectomy edge, expansion of contralateral haematoma (loss of tamponade), CSF leak, infection, seizures, herniation through the defect.
syndrome of the trephined
(orthostatic neurological deterioration), hydrocephalus, subdural hygroma, bone flap resorption after cranioplasty.
Cranioplasty timing: typically 6–12 weeks once swelling resolves; earlier replacement may improve neurological recovery but increases infection risk.
💡 Exam framing
"Would you offer this patient a decompressive craniectomy?"
Structure your answer around (1) is ICP truly refractory to optimised tier-1/2 therapy? (2) RESCUEicp shows mortality benefit but increased severe disability — survivors trade death for dependency; (3) DECRA warns against premature DC; (4) decision is MDT with neurosurgery and family, framed around acceptable outcome states, not just survival.
Classification & Antibody Types
ICU Management
IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day × 3–5 days
IV immunoglobulin (IVIg) 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days
Plasma exchange (PLEX) — 5–7 sessions
Often combine steroids + IVIg or steroids + PLEX
Start empirically — do not wait for antibody results
Second-line (if no response by 2–4 weeks)
Rituximab 375 mg/m² weekly × 4 doses
Cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m² monthly
Second-line agents improve outcomes in anti-NMDAR if started early
Tocilizumab and bortezomib used in refractory cases
Tumour Removal
💡 Exam Tip
Indications for ICU Admission
System-Based ICU Management
IVIg (first-line in most centres)
0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days (total 2 g/kg)
Start within 2 weeks of symptom onset
Equal efficacy to PLEX
Easier to administer, fewer haemodynamic effects
Monitor for renal impairment, thrombosis, aseptic meningitis
Plasma Exchange (PLEX)
5 exchanges over 1–2 weeks
Effective if started within 4 weeks
Requires large-bore vascular access
Haemodynamic instability may limit use in autonomic GBS
Do NOT combine IVIg + PLEX (PLEX removes IVIg)
⚠️ Corticosteroids Are NOT Effective in GBS
Prognostic Factors
60, rapid onset (
cholinergic crisis
(anticholinesterase overdose) — clinically similar (weakness + respiratory failure) but treatment is opposite.
Common Triggers
Recognition & Indications for ICU
Myasthenic vs Cholinergic Crisis
Myasthenic Crisis
Insufficient ACh effect at NMJ (antibodies + trigger)
Excess ACh — anticholinesterase overdose
Normal or mydriatic
Normal / dry from atropine therapy
: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI cramps, Emesis
Pure weakness
Weakness +
Normal / tachycardia
Edrophonium (Tensilon) test
within 30–60 s
(have atropine + airway ready)
Continue/optimise pyridostigmine + immunotherapy
anticholinesterases; atropine 0.5–1 mg IV; supportive ventilation
IVIg (often first-line)
Onset 1–2 weeks; peak benefit at 3–6 weeks
Equal efficacy to PLEX (Cochrane / RCTs)
Easier logistics, no large-bore access needed
Watch for renal impairment, thrombosis, aseptic meningitis, anaphylaxis (IgA deficiency)
5 exchanges over 7–14 days
Faster onset (days) — preferred if very severe / rapid deterioration
Removes anti-AChR / anti-MuSK antibodies directly
Requires large-bore vascular access; haemodynamic effects
Do NOT combine with IVIg (PLEX removes IVIg)
⚠️ Steroid-Induced Worsening
Always start steroids AFTER IVIg or PLEX
in established crisis, or up-titrate gradually (5–10 mg q3–5d) in the outpatient setting. Cover with continued anticholinesterase + monitor FVC.
Ventilator & ICU Care Specifics
any neurological condition assessed at presentation as an immediate threat to life or incompatible with good functional recovery, and where early limitation or withdrawal of therapy is being considered within 72 hours of admission to ICU
. Common causes: severe TBI, large intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage, malignant MCA infarction, hypoxic-ischaemic injury post-cardiac arrest, devastating CNS infection.
Why it matters
Early withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (WLST) within hours of presentation has historically been common, but
early prognostication is unreliable
— confounders (sedation, hypothermia, metabolic derangement, evolving oedema) mean patients can be wrongly judged to have an unsurvivable injury.
Patients deemed "futile" early have sometimes survived with meaningful recovery when given more time and full supportive therapy.
Premature WLST also denies potential opportunities for organ donation (DBD or DCD).

Preferred sedative in the delirious or agitated patient. SPICE III: no mortality difference vs usual care but shorter time to extubation; useful for agitation impeding weaning. MIND-USA and AID-ICU: no benefit for treatment or prevention of ICU delirium. Reserve for distressing hyperactive symptoms not controlled by non-pharmacological measures; balance against QT prolongation and EPSE. Triad: metabolic acidosis + rhabdomyolysis/hyperkalaemia + cardiac dysfunction (Brugada-like ECG, RBBB). Risk: >4 mg/kg/h for >48 h, young / lean / catecholamine-loaded patients. Treat: stop propofol, switch agent, supportive care, CRRT for refractory acidosis/hyperkalaemia. Assess/treat pain, Both spontaneous awakening and breathing trials, Choice of sedation, Delirium monitoring, Early mobility, Family engagement; bundle adherence reduces ICU mortality and delirium (Pun et al., Crit Care Med 2019). Which sedation agent is preferred for delirium prevention? Dexmedetomidine reduces delirium duration vs benzodiazepines (MENDS, SEDCOM trials) and may reduce mortality in septic patients (DESIST); propofol is acceptable but avoid benzodiazepines except for alcohol withdrawal or seizures. CAM-ICU or ICDSC at least once per shift; CAM-ICU requires RASS ≥−3 and assesses acute change, inattention (letters A test), altered consciousness and disorganised thinking. Score sedation depth using RASS and target light sedation (0 to −2) unless a specific indication for deep sedation exists. Compare propofol, midazolam, dexmedetomidine and remifentanil for ICU sedation, including PRIS risk and pharmacokinetics in organ failure. Screen for delirium with CAM-ICU and apply the ABCDEF bundle to reduce ventilator days, delirium and mortality. Manage hyperactive and hypoactive delirium with non-pharmacological measures first; recognise that haloperidol does not improve outcomes (MIND-USA, AID-ICU). Recognise, prevent and treat propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS). Sedation Assessment (RASS)

Target light sedation (RASS 0 to −2) unless specific indication for deep sedation (refractory ICP, severe ARDS with paralysis, status epilepticus). Daily sedation holds (SAT) paired with spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) — the ABC trial — reduce ventilator days and mortality.

Sedative Agents

{/* Delirium */}

ICU Delirium

Affects up to 80 % of ventilated patients. Independently associated with increased mortality, prolonged ventilation and long-term cognitive impairment. Three subtypes: hyperactive (5 %, easily recognised), hypoactive (most common, frequently missed) and mixed. Screen with CAM-ICU each shift.

CAM-ICU

4 features: (1) acute onset / fluctuating course + (2) inattention + (3) altered consciousness OR (4) disorganised thinking. Positive = 1 + 2 + (3 or 4). Feature 4: 4 yes/no questions + 2-step command; ≥1 error = positive .

ABCDEF bundle

Assess pain · Both SAT & SBT · Choice of sedation · Delirium monitoring · Early mobility · Family engagement. Reduces delirium, ventilator days and mortality.

{/* Prevention & treatment */}

Delirium Prevention & Treatment

{[ { approach: >Daily SAT & SBT
Spontaneous Awakening Trial (SAT)

Stop sedation each morning unless contraindicated (paralysis, ICP, status, severe ARDS with intolerance, escalating vasopressors). Failure: agitation, RR > 35 for > 5 min, SpO₂ < 88 %, acute arrhythmia. Restart at half the prior rate.

Spontaneous Breathing Trial (SBT)

If SAT passes — 30–120 min on PSV ≤ 8 cmH₂O / PEEP ≤ 5 or T-piece. Pass if RSBI (RR/VT) < 105, stable haemodynamics, SpO₂ ≥ 90 %, no distress. Coupled SAT + SBT (ABC trial) ↓ ventilator days & mortality.

references.excerpt: We suggest the use of light rather than deep sedation in adult mechanically ventilated ARDS patients (target RASS 0 to −2), except when deep sedation is required for specific clinical reasons (e.g., neuromuscular blockade, refractory intracranial hypertension, severe hypoxaemia with high ventilatory asynchrony). Analgesia should be assessed and treated before initiating sedation (analgesia-first approach).

This patient meets the pH criterion AND the triple criteria. Refer immediately to transplant centre. Without transplant, mortality approaches 90%. Continue NAC, manage cerebral oedema (head-up 30°, target Na 145–155, consider ICP monitoring, hypertonic saline for surges), CRRT for renal failure (also controls ammonia and avoids ICP swings of IHD). (ICA 2015). Common precipitant: SBP. terlipressin 2 mg IV q4–6h (or 2–4 mg/24 h infusion — fewer ischaemic side effects, CONFIRM trial) + albumin 20–40 g/day. Target Cr <133 µmol/L. If contraindicated (IHD, PVD): noradrenaline to ↑ MAP by 10 mmHg + albumin. Non-responder by day 4 → CRRT bridge to transplant assessment. . DF ≥32 = severe → steroids indicated provided no contraindication (sepsis, GI bleed, active TB, AKI). Lille at day 7: >0.45 = non-responder stop prednisolone (continued steroids in non-responders worsen infection without survival benefit). Refer for early liver transplant assessment per ACCELERATE-AH criteria; palliative care input if not a candidate (6-month untreated mortality ~75%). SBP, pneumonia, UTI, cellulitis. Impaired immune function (cirrhosis-associated immune dysfunction — CAID). Active drinking or alcoholic hepatitis. Superimposed on alcoholic cirrhosis. High short-term mortality if severe (Maddrey DF ≥32). Variceal haemorrhage. May precipitate renal failure, infection, and encephalopathy. In ~40% of ACLF cases no identifiable precipitant is found — emphasises the systemic inflammatory nature of the syndrome. Overall ICU mortality for decompensated ALD: 30–50%. ACLF grade 3: ICU mortality approaches 70–80%. Patients whose CLIF-C ACLF score improves by day 3–7 have significantly better survival. Worsening or static grade 3 ACLF at day 3–7 has >90% mortality. Historically required 6 months abstinence. Increasingly, early transplant considered for selected patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis not responding to medical therapy (post ACCELERATE-AH trial data). Aim for serum sodium 145–155 mmol/L with hypertonic saline, head-up 30°, mannitol or hypertonic saline boluses for surges, mild hypothermia (35–36 °C) if refractory, and avoid hypotonic fluids and hypercapnia. Definition & Aetiology

Acute liver failure (ALF): severe liver injury with coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing liver disease. Classified by jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval: hyperacute ({ }7 days), acute (7–28 days), subacute (28 days–6 months).

Hyperdynamic circulation (high CO, low SVR) — similar to sepsis. Noradrenaline first-line. Relative adrenal insufficiency — consider hydrocortisone. Balanced coagulopathy (↓ pro- and anti-coagulant factors). High infection risk (impaired innate immunity). Low threshold for cultures and empiric antibiotics. Fungal infection common — consider antifungals. s College Criteria for Transplantation

Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure (ACLF)

ACLF is a distinct syndrome: acute deterioration in a patient with pre-existing chronic liver disease, characterised by organ failure(s) and high short-term mortality. It differs from a simple acute decompensation (AD) event (ascites, variceal bleed, encephalopathy, infection) by the presence of extra-hepatic organ failures.

EASL–CLIF Definition & Grading

The CLIF-SOFA / CLIF-C OF score defines organ failures. ACLF is graded by number of organ failures, which directly predicts 28-day mortality:

Consider antifungals if deteriorating on antibiotics. High protein requirement (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day) — do NOT restrict protein. Calorie target 25–30 kcal/kg/day. Correct micronutrient deficiencies (thiamine, zinc, fat-soluble vitamins). Nasogastric feeding if unable to eat. >Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)

Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure in advanced liver disease caused by splanchnic arterial vasodilation → reduced effective circulating volume → renal vasoconstriction. Kidneys are structurally normal (may function post-transplant). Revised ICA 2015 criteria classify HRS into two types:

  • Now termed HRS-CKD (chronic) or HRS-AKD (acute kidney disease, 3–90 days)

Contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, PVD, mesenteric ischaemia. Monitor for cardiovascular ischaemia, arrhythmias, peripheral/splanchnic ischaemia, hyponatraemia, and fluid overload. The CONFIRM trial (2021) showed terlipressin improved HRS reversal but increased serious adverse events (respiratory failure) — careful patient selection essential.

Functional hepatic mass falls below the threshold needed for urea synthesis, gluconeogenesis and detoxification. Onset of encephalopathy within 8 weeks of jaundice (in a previously healthy liver) defines ALF. Ornithine cycle ↓ Ammonia accumulates The hepatic urea cycle (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-1 → ornithine transcarbamylase → arginase) normally clears ammonia from portal blood. With hepatocyte loss, NH₃ bypasses conversion and arterial ammonia rises. Levels > 150 µmol/L predict cerebral oedema; > 200 µmol/L predict herniation. Crosses BBB freely Ammonia enters the brain Unionised NH₃ diffuses across the blood–brain barrier down its concentration gradient. The brain has no urea cycle; the only detoxification route is amidation of glutamate to glutamine by glutamine synthetase, which is concentrated in astrocytes. Osmotic load ↑ Osmotic swelling Glutamine accumulates inside astrocytes — an osmotically active solute that draws water in (the 'Trojan-horse' hypothesis). Plateau waves (Lundberg A) signal exhausted compliance. Clinical features: hypertension, bradycardia, abnormal pupils, posturing. # Acute Severe Pancreatitis Atlanta classification, Glasgow score, fluid resuscitation, step-up necrosectomy, tertiary referral = [ ["How is severity stratified in acute pancreatitis?", "Use the revised Atlanta classification: mild (no organ failure or complications), moderate (transient organ failure Definition & Severity Revised Atlanta Classification (2012) stratifies severity: hands-off in the first 4 weeks until a wall has formed. Step through the timeline to see how interstitial oedema evolves to necrosis, then to walled-off necrosis amenable to step-up drainage. Causes — "I GET SMASHED" 2 of 3 of the following (Atlanta criteria): Characteristic abdominal pain (epigastric, radiating to back) Serum amylase or lipase ≥3× ULN (lipase more specific, stays elevated longer) Characteristic findings on contrast-enhanced CT, MRI or transabdominal ultrasound Initial investigations Glasgow (Imrie) score — score ≥3 within 48h = severe PaO₂ <8 kPa · Age >55 · Neutrophils (WBC) >15 · Calcium <2.0 mmol/L · Renal urea >16 mmol/L · Enzymes (LDH >600 / AST >200) · Albumin <32 g/L · Sugar (glucose) >10 mmol/L Initial Management (first 24–72h) Ongoing Management (beyond 72h) Daily reassessment : SOFA score, fluid balance, abdominal girth (intra-abdominal hypertension is common — measure bladder pressure if oliguric/distended; IAH >12 mmHg, ACS >20 mmHg with new organ failure). Repeat CECT at 7–10 days (or sooner if deterioration) to assess for necrosis, walled-off necrosis (WON), pseudocyst, vascular complications. Step-up approach to necrosis (PANTER trial 2010, MISER trial): drainage first (percutaneous or endoscopic transgastric) → minimally invasive video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement (VARD) → open necrosectomy only as last resort. Delay any intervention beyond 4 weeks if possible to allow demarcation. Infected necrosis : suspect if clinical deterioration after 7–10 days, gas on CT, positive FNA. Carbapenem cover (meropenem, imipenem). Source control via step-up approach. Renal replacement therapy for AKI per KDIGO indications. CRRT preferred in haemodynamically unstable or raised intra-abdominal pressure. : continue enteral. If gastric outlet obstruction from inflammatory mass, advance to NJ. Address vitamin (esp. B1 in alcohol) and trace-element deficiencies. : high VTE risk (immobility, inflammation, splanchnic vein thrombosis). LMWH unless active bleeding. : early mobilisation, ICU-acquired weakness prophylaxis, dietetic and physiotherapy input. Acute peripancreatic fluid collection (<4 weeks, no wall) — most resolve Pseudocyst (>4 weeks, fibrous wall, no necrosis) — drain if symptomatic / infected Acute necrotic collection (<4 weeks, contains necrosis) Walled-off necrosis (WON, >4 weeks) — endoscopic transgastric drainage ± necrosectomy Infected necrosis — leading cause of late mortality Splanchnic vein thrombosis (splenic, portal, SMV) — anticoagulate if no bleeding Pseudoaneurysm (splenic, GDA) — IR embolisation; can cause catastrophic haemorrhage Gastrointestinal: gastric outlet obstruction, colonic ischaemia, fistulae Abdominal compartment syndrome — decompressive laparotomy if refractory Systemic / Late SIRS → MODS (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal failure) ARDS — lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning Acute kidney injury — pre-renal then ATN; CRRT if needed Pleural effusion (left-sided, exudative, high amylase) DIC and coagulopathy Hyperglycaemia, hypocalcaemia (saponification), hypomagnesaemia ICU-acquired weakness, delirium, PICS Long-term: exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhoea, weight loss — pancreatic enzyme replacement), endocrine (diabetes mellitus type 3c), chronic pancreatitis, recurrent attacks Indications for Tertiary Centre Referral Predicted or established severe pancreatitis (Glasgow ≥3, APACHE-II ≥8, CRP >150 at 48h, persistent SIRS >48h) Persistent organ failure >48h despite optimal initial resuscitation Pancreatic necrosis on CT (>30% of gland, or any necrosis with deterioration) Suspected or proven infected necrosis requiring step-up drainage / necrosectomy Symptomatic walled-off necrosis or pseudocyst requiring intervention Vascular complications : pseudoaneurysm, splanchnic vein thrombosis with bleeding, haemosuccus pancreaticus Abdominal compartment syndrome requiring decompression Refractory ACS, ARDS or AKI requiring advanced organ support (ECMO, CRRT in unstable patient) Cholangitis with biliary obstruction needing urgent ERCP not available locally Recurrent / idiopathic pancreatitis for EUS / specialist work-up Major Guideline Comparison IAP/APA 2013 AGA 2018 / 2024 update BSG 2024 (UK) WSES 2019 (revised 2023) Where they all agree Balanced crystalloid (Ringer's lactate) over 0.9% saline NO prophylactic antibiotics — even in necrotising AP Urgent ERCP only for concurrent cholangitis (not for severe AP per se) Step-up approach to necrosis; delay intervention >4 weeks if possible Early enteral nutrition over TPN; same-admission cholecystectomy for mild gallstone AP Where they differ Fluid rate : older IAP/APA 2013 (5–10 mL/kg/h) vs post-WATERFALL moderate (1.5 mL/kg/h) — newer guidelines have converged on moderate Endoscopic vs percutaneous drainage : AGA & BSG favour endoscopic-first for retrogastric WON; WSES treats them as equivalent Oral refeeding timing : AGA most permissive (start as tolerated, do not wait for enzymes) Antibiotic choice for infected necrosis : carbapenem universal first line; WSES allows quinolone + metronidazole Glasgow (Imrie) severity at 48 h WATERFALL fluid prescription Suspected infected necrosis at day 12 Diagnose with 2 of 3: typical pain + amylase/lipase ≥3× ULN + characteristic imaging (Atlanta 2012) Severity stratification: Glasgow (Imrie), APACHE-II ≥8, BISAP, CRP >150 at 48h, persistent organ failure >48h I GET SMASHED — gallstones (50%) and ethanol (25%) account for most UK cases Fluids (WATERFALL/AGA 2024): balanced crystalloid (Ringer's lactate) — 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h, reassess at 12/24/48/72h. Aggressive resuscitation causes fluid overload (20.5% vs 6.3%) with no clinical benefit Early enteral nutrition (NG/NJ) within 24–72h reduces infectious complications and mortality vs TPN Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT indicated — only for proven infection or infected necrosis (carbapenem) ERCP within 24–72h only for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; cholecystectomy same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis Step-up approach to necrosis (PANTER trial): drainage → minimally invasive → open necrosectomy as last resort, delay >4 weeks Refer early to tertiary HPB/ICU centre for severe disease, necrosis, organ failure, or need for IR/advanced endoscopy Acute Severe Pancreatitis FRCA Final / FFICM — Intensive Care Axial CT Features of Severe Acute Pancreatitis Evolution of Necrosis & Fluid Collections Over Time 10–20% — diagnosis of exclusion. Microlithiasis often missed; consider EUS. ~50% in UK. ERCP within 72h if cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. Cholecystectomy on same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis. ~25%. Often relapsing. Address dependence. Blunt abdominal injury, post-ERCP (5–10% risk; reduced by rectal NSAIDs + pancreatic stenting). Drug-induced (azathioprine, valproate, thiazides, GLP-1 agonists, asparaginase). Mumps, CMV, Coxsackie, HIV, hepatitis. IgG4-related (type 1) — responds to steroids. Diffuse 'sausage' pancreas on CT. TG >11.3 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL). Hyperparathyroidism, malignancy. Plasma exchange or insulin infusion for severe HTG. Post-procedure pancreatitis. Rectal indomethacin/diclofenac is standard prophylaxis. See above. Always review medication list. FBC, U&E, LFT (ALT >150 IU/L = 95% PPV for gallstone aetiology), Ca²⁺, glucose, lipids, CRP, lactate, ABG, coagulation, group & save. Glasgow (Imrie ≥3), Ranson, APACHE-II ≥8, BISAP ≥3, CTSI/Balthazar. CRP >150 mg/L at 48h predicts severe disease. Transabdominal US within 24h to identify gallstones / dilated CBD. Erect CXR (exclude perforation, ARDS). Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen at 72–96h (not earlier — necrosis takes time to declare). Use modified CT severity index. MRCP if persistent jaundice or stone suspected. Supplemental O₂. Up to 60% develop hypoxaemia (atelectasis, pleural effusion, ARDS). Monitor for early ARDS — admit to HDU/ICU early if SpO₂ requirement, RR >20, or working hard. Intubate for airway protection if encephalopathic or for ARDS lung-protective ventilation. Use balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's / Ringer's lactate) — avoid 0.9% saline (hyperchloraemic acidosis, worsens SIRS). Assess volume status first: if hypovolaemic give a 10 mL/kg bolus of Ringer's lactate; if normovolaemic, no bolus is needed. Then run maintenance at 1.5 mL/kg/h LR. Reassess clinically and biochemically at 12, 24, 48 and 72h and titrate to MAP ≥65 mmHg, urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h, lactate clearance, falling BUN and HCT. The WATERFALL trial (NEJM 2022) was stopped early because aggressive resuscitation (20 mL/kg bolus + 3 mL/kg/h) caused significantly more fluid overload (20.5% vs 6.3%) and longer hospital stay without reducing progression to moderate/severe disease — moderate, goal-directed resuscitation is now standard (endorsed by AGA 2024 and BSG 2024). Vasopressors (noradrenaline) if MAP target unmet despite adequate volume — do NOT chase MAP with more fluid once euvolaemic. Multimodal. Paracetamol + opioid (morphine or fentanyl PCA). Opioid concerns about Sphincter of Oddi spasm are largely theoretical — do not withhold. Consider thoracic epidural in severe cases (improves splanchnic perfusion, may reduce mortality — small trials). Early enteral feeding within 24–72h (NG or NJ tube — both equivalent per multiple RCTs). Reduces infectious complications, MODS and mortality vs TPN. NBM only if ileus/obstruction. TPN reserved for those who fail enteral after 5–7 days. NOT routinely indicated. Prophylactic antibiotics do not reduce mortality or infected necrosis. Use only for proven extra-pancreatic infection (cholangitis, pneumonia, line sepsis) or proven infected necrosis (positive culture from FNA or gas on CT). Carbapenem (meropenem) if needed — best pancreatic penetration. Target glucose 6–10 mmol/L. Correct hypocalcaemia (sign of severity, fat saponification). Replace Mg²⁺, K⁺, PO₄³⁻. Insulin infusion if HTG-induced (drops triglycerides rapidly). ERCP within 24–72h if acute cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction (NOT routinely for all gallstone pancreatitis). Cholecystectomy on same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis (reduces recurrence). For HTG-induced: insulin infusion ± plasmapheresis if persistent TG >11 mmol/L with organ failure. How is severity stratified in acute pancreatitis? Use the revised Atlanta classification: mild (no organ failure or complications), moderate (transient organ failure <48 h or local complications), severe (persistent organ failure >48 h); supplement with APACHE II and CRP >150 at 48 h. What is the role of early enteral nutrition? Start enteral feeding within 24–72 h via nasogastric or nasojejunal route — it maintains gut barrier, reduces infected necrosis and lowers mortality compared with TPN (PYTHON trial, IAP/APA guidelines). When should antibiotics be given in severe pancreatitis? Only for proven or strongly suspected infected necrosis (gas on CT, positive FNA culture) or extra-pancreatic infection — routine prophylactic antibiotics do not improve outcome and promote fungal superinfection. Diagnose acute pancreatitis using the Atlanta 2012 criteria and stratify severity with Glasgow (Imrie), APACHE-II and CRP at 48 h. Apply the WATERFALL moderate fluid strategy with balanced crystalloid and avoid the harms of aggressive resuscitation. Justify the use of early enteral nutrition (NG/NJ within 24–72 h) over TPN. # Abdominal Compartment Syndrome WSACS definitions and grading, intravesical IAP measurement, APP target, primary vs secondary ACS, medical bundle, decompressive laparotomy and open abdomen decompressive laparotomy and leave open abdomen with a negative-pressure temporary closure (e.g. ABThera). Definitions & Grading (WSACS 2013) World Society of the Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (WSACS) consensus defines: Intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) — steady-state pressure in the abdominal cavity. Normal in the critically ill ≈ 5–7 mmHg. Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) — sustained or repeated pathological elevation of IAP ≥ 12 mmHg. Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) — sustained IAP > 20 mmHg (with or without APP < 60 mmHg) new organ dysfunction or failure. Abdominal perfusion pressure (APP) = MAP − IAP; target ≥ 60 mmHg. Causes & Classification WSACS risk factors — screen IAP 4–6 hourly if any are present Pathophysiology — a multi-organ disease Clinical Presentation Tense, distended abdomen (insensitive sign). New or worsening oliguria refractory to fluid or vasopressor escalation. Rising plateau and peak airway pressures; falling lung and chest-wall compliance. Hypotension with rising vasopressor requirement and rising CVP / PAOP (paradoxical). Rising lactate, metabolic acidosis, falling MvO₂ — gut hypoperfusion. Rising ICP in TBI patients with abdominal pathology. Diagnosis & Measurement of IAP intravesical (Foley) technique is the gold standard. It is cheap, reproducible and the reference method in all WSACS literature. Patient fully supine (head-up < 20°) and at end-expiration. No abdominal muscle contraction — deepen sedation ± neuromuscular blockade if needed. Empty the bladder, then instil 25 mL of warmed sterile saline via the Foley. Zero the transducer at the mid-axillary line at the iliac crest Read after 30–60 s equilibration. Express in Trend every 4–6 h in at-risk patients; isolated values are misleading. Pitfalls falsely raising IAP Alternative routes Management — WSACS Medical Bundle all five domains in parallel as IAH worsens; reassess IAP every 1–2 h. Escalate to surgical decompression if IAP remains ≥ 20 mmHg with organ failure. Surgical decompression ACS refractory to medical management , or as a primary strategy in damage-control laparotomy where the abdomen is anticipated not to close (massive transfusion, bowel oedema, prolonged operating time). Midline laparotomy under general anaesthesia — anticipate profound reperfusion hypotension on opening (ischaemia-reperfusion mediators, abrupt drop in SVR). Pre-load with fluid and have vasopressor running. Leave abdomen open with a temporary abdominal closure (TAC) : negative-pressure systems (ABThera, vacuum-pack) are preferred over Bogotá bag for fluid handling, reducing visceral oedema, and improving rates of primary fascial closure. Plan for early delayed primary fascial closure within 7–10 days. Beyond this, consider mesh-mediated traction or component separation; otherwise expect a planned ventral hernia. Continue IAP monitoring even with an open abdomen — recurrent ACS can occur through the dressing. IAH is independently associated with increased mortality even in the absence of ACS. Established ACS carries hospital mortality of , highest in secondary ACS from burns and septic shock. Early recognition with structured IAP monitoring and the WSACS bundle significantly reduces mortality and progression to surgical decompression. Survivors face prolonged ventilation, AKI requiring RRT in up to 50 %, gut dysfunction with enterocutaneous fistula in 5–15 % of open abdomens, and high rates of planned ventral hernia requiring later reconstruction. Long-term: increased risk of PICS (post-intensive-care syndrome), reduced HRQoL at 6–12 months, and significant rehabilitation needs. Post-laparotomy oliguria with rising airway pressures Severe burns and secondary ACS Measuring IAP correctly Normal IAP in the critically ill ≈ 5–7 mmHg. IAH = sustained IAP ≥ 12 mmHg. ACS = sustained IAP ≥ 20 mmHg WITH new organ dysfunction (WSACS 2013). Grades: I 12–15, II 16–20, III 21–25, IV > 25 mmHg. Risk of organ failure rises steeply above grade III. Measure via Foley: supine, end-expiration, 25 mL saline, transducer zeroed at mid-axillary line at iliac crest, no abdominal contraction. Primary ACS = intra-abdominal/pelvic pathology (trauma, ruptured AAA, pancreatitis, peritonitis). Secondary ACS = extra-abdominal cause, typically massive resuscitation (burns, sepsis). Recurrent ACS = re-develops after decompression. Pathophysiology is global: ↓ venous return, ↓ CO, ↑ SVR; ↑ ITP → ↓ FRC, ↑ plateau pressures, V/Q mismatch; renal vein compression + ↓ RBF → AKI; ↑ ICP via ↑ CVP; gut ischaemia and bacterial translocation; hepatic congestion. Abdominal perfusion pressure (APP = MAP − IAP) ≥ 60 mmHg correlates with survival better than IAP alone — the resuscitation target in IAH. WSACS medical bundle (5 domains): (1) evacuate intraluminal contents (NG, rectal tube, prokinetics); (2) evacuate intra-abdominal collections (percutaneous drain); (3) improve abdominal-wall compliance (sedation, NMB, escharotomy, head-up < 20°); (4) optimise fluid balance (avoid positive balance, HAS + diuretic, RRT); (5) optimise systemic perfusion (APP-guided). Surgical decompression: indicated for ACS unresponsive to medical management. Midline laparotomy left open with temporary abdominal closure (Bogotá bag, Wittmann patch, ABThera negative-pressure dressing). Aim for delayed primary fascial closure within 7–10 days. Risk factors to screen 4–6-hourly: massive resuscitation (> 3.5 L/24 h crystalloid), damage-control laparotomy, severe pancreatitis, major burns > 30 % TBSA, ileus, prone position, high PEEP, capillary leak, intra-abdominal infection. Prognosis: established ACS carries mortality 40–70 %; early recognition and decompression reduce mortality; survivors have prolonged ventilation, AKI requiring RRT in up to 50 %, and high rates of ventral hernia and enteric fistula. Abdominal Compartment Syndrome FRCA Final / FFICM — Intensive Care Intra-abdominal or pelvic pathology — abdominal trauma (haematoma, packing), ruptured AAA, severe pancreatitis, perforated viscus / peritonitis, mesenteric ischaemia, ileus, post-laparotomy haemorrhage, retroperitoneal bleed. No intra-abdominal injury — typically massive resuscitation: major burns > 30 % TBSA, septic shock, prolonged CPR, polytrauma without abdominal injury, capillary-leak states (Parkland > 250 mL/kg/24 h is the recognised threshold). Recurrence after surgical or medical resolution of a previous episode — usually in patients with an open abdomen who fail to achieve early fascial closure or develop ongoing capillary leak. ↓ IVC return → ↓ preload, ↓ CO; ↑ intrathoracic pressure → falsely elevated CVP/PAOP; ↑ SVR and PVR. Cardiac output falls long before BP, masked by vasopressors. Diaphragmatic splinting → ↓ FRC and chest-wall compliance → ↑ plateau and peak pressures, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, V/Q mismatch. Mimics ARDS. Renal vein compression + ↓ cardiac output + ↑ renal parenchymal pressure → oliguria → AKI. Oliguria is often the earliest sign; unresponsive to fluid challenge. ↑ intrathoracic pressure obstructs cerebral venous drainage → ↑ ICP, ↓ CPP. Particularly dangerous in TBI. ↓ mesenteric perfusion → mucosal ischaemia, bacterial translocation, lactic acidosis, anastomotic breakdown. Hepatic congestion → impaired lactate clearance and drug metabolism. Ischaemia of rectus sheath → necrosis, dehiscence, surgical-site infection, late ventral hernia. Hourly IAP, hourly UO, APP (MAP − IAP), ventilator plateau pressure trend, ABG (lactate, base deficit), abdominal US (free fluid, AAA, bladder volume). FBC, U&E, LFT, CK, coagulation, lactate, CRP, group & save; troponin if myocardial demand-ischaemia suspected. CT abdomen-pelvis with contrast if cause unclear or to plan surgery — narrow IVC, round-belly sign, bowel-wall thickening, free fluid, retroperitoneal haematoma, ileus. Amylase/lipase (pancreatitis), CT angiogram (AAA, mesenteric ischaemia), bedside echocardiography (LV/RV function, IVC), surgical review for damage-control or perforation. Large-bore NG tube on free drainage, rectal tube, prokinetics (metoclopramide, erythromycin), stop enteral feed, neostigmine for pseudo-obstruction, endoscopic decompression if needed. Percutaneous catheter drainage of large-volume ascites, haematoma or abscess under US/CT guidance — can avoid laparotomy in selected cases. Deepen sedation, trial of neuromuscular blockade (often dramatic effect within minutes), nurse supine / head-up < 20°, decompressive escharotomy for circumferential torso burns, treat pain and ventilator dyssynchrony. Avoid further positive balance — switch from crystalloid to colloid (20 % HAS) for ongoing losses, diuretics (furosemide) once euvolaemic, early CRRT for negative balance and uraemia. Target neutral-to-negative balance after the first 24 h. Resuscitate to APP ≥ 60 mmHg (MAP target rises as IAP rises), noradrenaline first-line, avoid excessive PEEP that does not recruit, treat the underlying cause (source control, definitive haemostasis). How is intra-abdominal pressure measured and what defines ACS? Bladder pressure with 25 mL saline at end-expiration, supine, transduced at the mid-axillary line; intra-abdominal hypertension ≥12 mmHg, ACS = sustained IAP >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction (WSACS 2013). What are the physiological consequences of raised intra-abdominal pressure? Reduced venous return and CO, raised airway pressure with reduced FRC, oliguria from renal venous congestion, raised ICP from impaired cerebral venous drainage, and gut ischaemia from reduced splanchnic perfusion. What are the non-surgical options before decompressive laparotomy? Nasogastric and rectal decompression, neuromuscular blockade, prokinetics, percutaneous drainage of ascites, deep sedation, and conservative fluid strategy; surgery is reserved for refractory ACS with organ failure. Define intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) and abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) using WSACS 2013 criteria. Measure intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) correctly via the intravesical (Foley) technique and interpret the IAH grading. Recognise primary, secondary and recurrent ACS and the at-risk populations (trauma, burns, pancreatitis, massive resuscitation, post-laparotomy). Apply the WSACS medical management algorithm to lower IAP (sedation, NMB, decompression of hollow viscera, fluid balance, escharotomy). Identify the indications and techniques for surgical decompression and the management of the resulting open abdomen. Counsel on prognosis: ACS independently increases mortality, AKI, prolonged ventilation and ICU length of stay. ], }, ]; const keyPoints = [ { text: ] }, ]; const AbdominalCompartmentSyndromeTopic = () => { return ( {/* Definitions */}

    Causes & Classification
    {[ { type: > Diminished abdominal-wall compliance (mechanical ventilation, high PEEP, prone position, abdominal-wall burns) · Increased intraluminal contents (gastroparesis, ileus, pseudo-obstruction) · Increased intra-abdominal contents (haemoperitoneum, ascites, intra-abdominal infection, tumour) · Capillary leak / massive resuscitation (sepsis, burns, pancreatitis, damage-control surgery, polytrauma, > 3.5 L crystalloid/24 h)

    {/* Pathophysiology */}

    Pathophysiology — a multi-organ disease

    Raised IAP transmits to every adjacent compartment and impairs venous return globally. Even moderate IAH (12–15 mmHg) reduces splanchnic perfusion before any clinical sign is apparent.

    {[ { sys: >Clinical Presentation

    Examination is insensitive — palpation correctly identifies IAH in fewer than 50 % of cases. Have a high index of suspicion in any at-risk patient and measure IAP.

    • Tense, distended abdomen (insensitive sign).
    • New or worsening oliguria refractory to fluid or vasopressor escalation.
    • Rising plateau and peak airway pressures; falling lung and chest-wall compliance.
    • Hypotension with rising vasopressor requirement and rising CVP / PAOP (paradoxical).
    • Rising lactate, metabolic acidosis, falling MvO₂ — gut hypoperfusion.
    • Rising ICP in TBI patients with abdominal pathology.
    {/* Diagnosis */}

    Diagnosis & Measurement of IAP

    The intravesical (Foley) technique is the gold standard. It is cheap, reproducible and the reference method in all WSACS literature.

    1. Patient fully supine (head-up < 20°) and at end-expiration.
    2. No abdominal muscle contraction — deepen sedation ± neuromuscular blockade if needed.
    3. Empty the bladder, then instil 25 mL of warmed sterile saline via the Foley.
    4. Zero the transducer at the mid-axillary line at the iliac crest.
    5. Read after 30–60 s equilibration. Express in mmHg.
    6. Trend every 4–6 h in at-risk patients; isolated values are misleading.
    Pitfalls falsely raising IAP

    Head-up position, coughing, asynchrony, high PEEP, full rectum, large instillation volume (> 25 mL), transducer zeroed at the symphysis pubis, neurogenic bladder spasm.

    Alternative routes

    Intragastric (nasogastric transducer), intracolonic and direct intraperitoneal (via catheter) — used if Foley not possible (e.g. cystectomy, ruptured bladder). All correlate reasonably with intravesical measurement.

# Toxicology & Poisoning Paracetamol, opioid, TCA overdose, LAST, antidotes, toxidromes, lipid emulsion above the treatment line . Treatment is indicated regardless of symptoms, INR or LFTs. IV N-acetylcysteine (SNAP 12-h regimen: 100 mg/kg over 2 h, then 200 mg/kg over 10 h). Send baseline INR, ALT, U&E, paracetamol, salicylate, VBG. Repeat ALT and INR at end of NAC; continue NAC if ALT >2× ULN, INR >1.3, or paracetamol still detectable. fast Na⁺ channel blockade — risk of VT/VF. Sodium bicarbonate overcomes this by sodium loading and alkalinisation (target pH 7.45–7.55). NaHCO₃ 8.4% 1–2 mmol/kg IV bolus intermittent haemodialysis ; expect rebound from intracellular redistribution → either prolong session (≥6 h) or follow with CVVHDF and recheck level 6 h after stopping. Stop lithium and the ACE inhibitor. Aggressive IV crystalloid to restore renal perfusion. lipid sink sequestering lipophilic LA + provides metabolic substrate. 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 min (≈ 100 mL in a 70 kg adult), then 15 mL/kg/h infusion ABCDE approach : stabilise first, identify toxin second. Contact National Poisons Information Service (NPIS/TOXBASE) : activated charcoal (1 g/kg) within 1 h of ingestion (most effective <30 min). Not for hydrocarbons, metals, alcohols, acids/alkalis Enhanced elimination : urinary alkalinisation (salicylates, methotrexate), haemodialysis (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, lithium), haemoperfusion (rarely used) : see the comparator below — pattern recognition narrows the differential before a tox screen returns Key Points N-acetylcysteine (NAC) Replenishes glutathione. Most effective <8 h. Use UK 100 mg/L nomogram. Anaphylactoid reaction common Competitive μ-antagonist. Short t½ (~30–70 min) — may need repeat/infusion. Rarely used in ED Glucagon (+ high-dose insulin) Glucagon: ↑ cAMP via non-adrenergic pathway. High-dose insulin-euglycaemia therapy (1–2 U/kg/h) Atropine + pralidoxime Atropine (large doses, titrate to secretions). Pralidoxime reactivates AChE if given early (<24 h) Methanol / ethylene glycol Fomepizole (or ethanol) Inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase. Prevent toxic metabolite formation. Dialysis for severe cases Digoxin-specific Fab fragments Binds free digoxin. Indicated for life-threatening arrhythmias or K⁺ >5 mmol/L Local anaesthetic toxicity Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus then 15 mL/kg/h infusion. Acts as 'lipid sink' + metabolic support Mechanism of toxicity : Na⁺ channel blockade (→ wide QRS, arrhythmias), anticholinergic effects, α₁ blockade (→ hypotension), serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake inhibition ECG features : sinus tachycardia, QRS >100 ms (risk of seizures), QRS >160 ms (risk of VT/VF). Right axis deviation of terminal 40 ms (R in aVR >3 mm) : IV sodium bicarbonate 8.4% (50–100 mL) for QRS >120 ms or arrhythmias. Target pH 7.45–7.55. Overcomes Na⁺ channel block. Avoid class Ia antiarrhythmics Early: respiratory alkalosis (central stimulation) → mixed metabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis → late: metabolic acidosis predominates Other features: tinnitus, hypoglycaemia (children), hyperthermia, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, coagulopathy : activated charcoal (if <1 h), urinary alkalinisation (NaHCO₃ to pH 7.5–8.5), haemodialysis (level >700 mg/L, renal failure, pulmonary oedema, seizures) (Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning) workgroup provides evidence-based recommendations. Larger molecules up to ~20 kDa Lower clearance per unit time vs intermittent HD. Prolonged treatment needed Adsorption onto activated charcoal or resin cartridge Protein-bound or lipophilic toxins (theophylline, carbamazepine). Now rarely used Cartridge saturation, thrombocytopenia, hypocalcaemia. Largely replaced by high-flux HD Ricinus communis (castor bean). The B-chain binds galactose residues on cell surfaces; the A-chain is internalised and depurinates 28S rRNA, irreversibly halting protein synthesis and causing apoptosis. It is a Schedule 1 chemical weapon and a CDC Category B bioterror agent (1978 Markov "umbrella" assassination, 2013 US ricin letters). Routes & clinical syndromes (lethal dose ~1–10 µg/kg): 4–8 h latency → fever, cough, dyspnoea, ARDS, refractory hypoxaemia, shock; death within 36–72 h. (lethal dose ~1–20 mg/kg, requires chewing seeds): haemorrhagic gastroenteritis, hepatic and renal failure, multi-organ failure over days. Injection / dart (Markov, 0.5 mg pellet): local pain and induration → fever, hypotension, vascular collapse, MOF in 24–72 h. Clinical (cluster of casualties + epidemiology). ⚠️ The Lethal Triad
Principles — what the machine actually does
— surgical blood is aspirated through a dual-lumen suction tip with anticoagulant (heparinised saline or ACD-A citrate) dripping at the tip. Vacuum is kept low (≤−150 mmHg, ideally −100 mmHg) to minimise mechanical haemolysis. The collected blood enters a filtered reservoir.
— once ~500–1000 mL is in the reservoir, blood is pumped into a spinning centrifuge bowl (Latham bowl 125–225 mL, or continuous-flow disc). Red cells, being densest, layer outwards; plasma, platelets, anticoagulant, free Hb, activated complement and inflammatory cytokines layer centrally.
— 1–1.5 L of 0.9% saline is passed through the spinning bowl to elute the unwanted layer to a waste bag. Wash quality is the single most important determinant of returned product safety.
Re-suspension & return
— washed RBCs are pumped into a re-infusion bag at Hct ~50–70% suspended in saline. They are returned through a standard blood-giving set with a 40 µm screen filter; in obstetrics or malignancy a leucodepletion (LDF, ~40 nm) filter is added in series.
What is ACD (ACD-A)?
Acid–Citrate–Dextrose, formula A
— a sterile anticoagulant solution containing
citric acid
(anhydrous 0.73 g/100 mL),
sodium citrate
(2.20 g/100 mL) and
(2.45 g/100 mL), pH ~5. The citrate
chelates ionised calcium
, blocking the coagulation cascade at multiple Ca²⁺-dependent steps; the dextrose preserves red-cell metabolism (ATP and 2,3-DPG). In cell salvage, ACD-A is dripped into the suction tubing at the operative tip at roughly
15 mL per 100 mL of shed blood
(≈1 drop per second) and is washed out during the centrifuge wash cycle, so systemic citrate toxicity is rare. ACD-A is preferred over heparinised saline whenever
systemic heparin must be avoided
(e.g. HIT, recent neurosurgery, active intracranial bleeding) and is the standard anticoagulant for apheresis circuits.
Hypocalcaemia risk & monitoring
ionised hypocalcaemia
arises when the wash cycle is shortened or bypassed (emergency unwashed return), when very large volumes are reinfused rapidly, or when concurrent allogeneic FFP/platelets (also citrated) are given to a patient with impaired hepatic citrate clearance (liver failure, neonates, hypothermia, transplant anhepatic phase).
Watch for
Perioral & digital paraesthesiae (awake patient)
Prolonged QT, T-wave flattening, ↓ contractility
Hypotension unresponsive to fluid
Metabolic alkalosis (citrate → HCO₃⁻ in liver)
Chvostek / Trousseau signs (rare, late)
iCa²⁺ on ABG
— every 30 min during high-volume salvage; target > 1.0 mmol/L
Continuous ECG (QTc trend)
Invasive BP if > 1500 mL salvaged or rapid return
Lactate, pH, base excess (alkalosis trend)
Total transfused citrate load (salvage + FFP + platelets)
Calcium chloride 10% — 5–10 mL IV
via a central line (provides ~3× the elemental Ca²⁺ of equivalent gluconate)
calcium gluconate 10% — 10–20 mL IV
peripherally. Repeat to iCa²⁺ > 1.0 mmol/L. Slow the rate of unwashed return where possible; never co-administer with bicarbonate (precipitates CaCO₃).
High-risk scenarios:
liver transplant (anhepatic phase), massive obstetric haemorrhage, paediatric salvage with low circulating volume, ECMO/CRRT regional citrate anticoagulation running concurrently, hypothermic cardiac surgery.
ACD-A vs heparinised saline — anticoagulant choice for cell salvage
ACD-A (citrate)
Heparinised saline
Chelates ionised Ca²⁺ — blocks Ca²⁺-dependent steps of cascade
Potentiates antithrombin → inhibits thrombin (IIa) and Xa
Typical preparation
ACD-A solution, ready-made (citric acid + Na citrate + dextrose, pH ~5)
30,000 IU UFH in 1 L 0.9% NaCl (30 IU/mL)
Dose to suction tip
~15 mL per 100 mL shed blood (≈1 drop/sec)
~60 mL per 100 mL anticipated blood (prime + drip)
Systemic effect after wash
Negligible — citrate washed out; dextrose preserves 2,3-DPG/ATP
Negligible — heparin washed out; trace residual possible if wash inadequate
Preferred when
Systemic heparin contraindicated: HIT, recent neurosurgery, active intracranial bleed; standard for apheresis
Default choice in most UK theatres — cheap, familiar, widely stocked
Risks / caveats
Citrate toxicity (hypocalcaemia, metabolic alkalosis) only if wash bypassed or massive unwashed return
Heparin rebound if washing inadequate; contraindicated in HIT
IV calcium (chloride or gluconate) if symptomatic
Protamine 1 mg per 100 IU residual heparin
What you get back
Washed packed red cells, Hct 50–70%, ~225 mL per processed bowl. Functionally equivalent to (or better than) stored allogeneic RBCs — fresh, normal 2,3-DPG, normal K⁺.
What you do NOT get back
No platelets, no fibrinogen, no clotting factors, no plasma proteins. After 1500–2000 mL of returned salvaged blood expect dilutional coagulopathy — replace FFP/cryo/platelets guided by ROTEM.
Setting it up — practical checklist
Trained operator present and a recent competency check (AAGBI 2018: ICS should not be run by an untrained user).
Patient consent — discuss with Jehovah's Witness patients pre-operatively and document which components of the circuit are acceptable (continuous-circuit ICS is usually accepted).
Disposables: collection reservoir, processing set (bowl size matched to anticipated loss), wash saline (1–3 L 0.9% NaCl), heparinised saline (30,000 IU UFH in 1 L 0.9% NaCl) or ACD-A, dual-lumen suction tubing, re-infusion bag, 40 µm filter ± leucodepletion filter.
Prime the reservoir with ~200 mL anticoagulant and run anticoagulant at ~60 mL per 100 mL anticipated blood loss (≈1 drop per second initially).
Use two suckers:
sucker (low vacuum, kept beneath blood level, no skimming of air) and a separate
high-vacuum sucker for irrigation, contaminated fluid, or anything below.
Label the re-infusion bag with patient identifiers, time of processing, and a 4-hour expiry.
Document salvaged volume returned in the anaesthetic record; many trusts require a SHOT-style traceability entry equivalent to allogeneic transfusion.
Contraindications & cautions
Topical agents not licensed for IV use
Betadine, chlorhexidine, hydrogen peroxide, topical thrombin, gelatin/collagen haemostats, bone cement, distilled water
Switch to standard sucker until field is irrigated and dry; avoid salvaging blood in contact with these agents
Bowel contents / pus
Faecal contamination, frank infection
Standard sucker only; resume ICS after washout if surgical field clean
Tumour-bearing surgical field
Acceptable with leucodepletion filter (NICE IPG 144); also consider irradiation of salvaged blood
Caesarean delivery, PPH
Acceptable with separate suction of amniotic fluid before salvage and a leucodepletion filter (OAA-AAGBI 2018)
Sickle cell disease
Avoid — washing/centrifugation may precipitate sickling. HbAS / trait is acceptable
Catecholamine-secreting tumours (phaeochromocytoma — wash adequately), thalassaemia (use shorter-stored cells)
Case-by-case discussion with haematology
⚠️ Salvaged blood syndrome
ROTEM Parameters
EXTEM CT: extrinsic pathway (FFP). FIBTEM A5/MCF: fibrinogen (cryo if <12 mm). EXTEM MCF: platelet contribution. HEPTEM: heparin effect.
Goal-Directed Algorithm
FIBTEM low → cryo. EXTEM CT prolonged → FFP. EXTEM MCF low (FIBTEM normal) → platelets. HEPTEM shorter than INTEM → protamine.
ISTH DIC Score (≥5 = overt)
Platelets ×10⁹/L
Moderate ↑
Strong ↑

<3 s

<1.0 g/L
Management Principles
⚠️ DIC vs TTP/HUS
Massive haemorrhage in blunt trauma
Activate MHP, TXA within 3 h, 1:1:1 ratio, calcium replacement, active warming, permissive hypotension, urgent damage-control surgery/IR. Transition to ROTEM-guided once available.
Setting up cell salvage for a redo aortic case
Document continuous-circuit consent. Prime reservoir with heparinised saline, use dual-suction technique at low vacuum, process when ≥500 mL collected, return washed RBCs through a 40 µm (± leucodepletion) filter, and supplement with FFP/cryo/platelets once >1500 mL has been re-infused or ROTEM signals coagulopathy. Avoid topical haemostats, betadine and unlicensed irrigants in the salvage field.
ISTH DIC scoring in septic shock
Overt DIC (score 8). Treat the cause (source control + appropriate antimicrobials). Replace to clinical targets: platelets >50, fibrinogen >1.5 g/L (cryo or fibrinogen concentrate), FFP if PT ratio >1.5 + bleeding. Avoid TXA unless ROTEM confirms hyperfibrinolysis (ML >15%).
Transfusion & Coagulation
FRCA / FFICM — Intensive Care
Restrictive transfusion (Hb 70 g/L trigger) is safe in most ICU patients — TRICC, TRISS
Red cells: 35-day shelf life at 2–6°C; storage lesion (↓2,3-DPG, ↑K⁺, ↓pH) reverses over 24 h in the recipient
Platelets: only 5–7 days at 20–24°C with agitation — bacterial contamination is the leading infectious risk
FFP/cryo: 2 years at −30°C; once thawed, use within 24 h (FFP) or 4 h (cryo, room temperature)
TRALI: leading cause of transfusion-related death; strongly associated with FFP and apheresis platelets from multiparous donors (anti-HLA/HNA antibodies). UK male-donor FFP policy has reduced incidence ~10-fold
TRALI vs TACO: both cause pulmonary oedema within 6 h — TRALI has normal CVP/JVP and worsens with diuretics; TACO improves with diuresis
Cell salvage washes shed blood, suspends RBCs in saline (Hct ~50–70%), and removes plasma, platelets, heparin, free Hb and most cytokines — returned blood has NO clotting factors or platelets
ICS contraindications are largely relative — sickle cell disease, contamination with iodine/topical haemostats, and pharmacological agents not licensed for IV use; obstetric and oncological use is now supported with a leucodepletion filter (NICE TA/OAA-AAGBI)
ROTEM/TEG enables goal-directed transfusion — FIBTEM guides fibrinogen, EXTEM guides FFP/platelets
TXA within 3 hours of trauma reduces mortality (CRASH-2)
Massive transfusion: hypocalcaemia is the most dangerous metabolic complication — give CaCl₂ early
Lethal triad: hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy — damage control resuscitation breaks the cycle
DIC: ISTH score ≥5 = overt DIC. Treat the underlying cause — the most important intervention
DIC vs TTP: coagulation screen normal in TTP, abnormal in DIC. Never give platelets in TTP
TXA contraindicated in DIC with predominant thrombosis — only if hyperfibrinolysis dominant
Coagulation Cascade — Foundations
Blood Products
Component Lifespans & In-vivo Survival
Cryoprecipitate vs Fibrinogen Concentrate
Early cryoprecipitate (within 90 min) vs standard care in major trauma haemorrhage. No mortality benefit despite higher fibrinogen levels.
Empiric fibrinogen concentrate 2 g vs placebo in PPH — no reduction in RBC transfusion. Empiric replacement without confirmed hypofibrinogenaemia not beneficial.
Cardiac surgery, fibrinogen concentrate vs cryo for fibrinogen <2 g/L. Non-inferior, faster to administer.
Transfusion Reactions
Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP)
Intra-operative Cell Salvage (ICS)
Hypocalcaemia risk and monitoring during ACD-A cell salvage
Viscoelastic Testing (ROTEM/TEG)
Key Transfusion Trials
Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation
The single most important step — DIC will not resolve without it (antibiotics, delivery, ATRA in APML).
Transfuse to clinical targets, not lab values. Platelets >50 if bleeding; FFP if PT ratio >1.5 + bleeding; fibrinogen >1.5 g/L.
Only if hyperfibrinolysis dominant (ROTEM ML >15%). Contraindicated if thrombosis predominates.
Low-dose heparin only if thrombosis dominant (purpura fulminans) and bleeding controlled. Full anticoagulation rarely appropriate.
What ratios are used in major haemorrhage protocols?
Empirical 1:1:1 (RBC:FFP:platelets) until ROTEM/TEG-guided, based on PROPPR trial; activate at predicted 4+ units in 1 h, give TXA 1 g within 3 h (CRASH-2) and target ionised Ca²⁺ >1.0 mmol/L.
When is prothrombin complex concentrate preferred over FFP?
For warfarin reversal in major bleeding (25–50 U/kg with vitamin K, BSH 2018), or factor replacement in liver disease where volume load from FFP is harmful; PCC restores INR within minutes versus hours for FFP.
How is ROTEM/TEG used to guide blood product use?
FIBTEM A5 <12 mm → fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate; EXTEM CT >80 s → FFP or PCC; EXTEM A5 <40 mm with normal FIBTEM → platelets; ML >15% → tranexamic acid (ITACTIC trial).
Describe the composition, shelf-life, donor-to-recipient survival and storage requirements of each blood component
Recognise and manage the major transfusion reactions (acute haemolytic, FNHTR, TRALI, TACO, anaphylaxis, TA-GvHD, TTI)
Map product-specific risks (e.g. TRALI with FFP/platelets, TACO with red cells in elderly) to their mechanisms and prevention
Apply the Massive Haemorrhage Protocol — triggers, ratios, targets and complications (lethal triad, hypocalcaemia)
Explain the principles of intra-operative cell salvage (ICS), the wash cycle, and the practical steps to set it up and run it safely
List the absolute and relative contraindications to cell salvage and the situations where leucodepletion filters extend its use (obstetrics, malignancy)
Interpret viscoelastic (ROTEM/TEG) tracings to direct goal-directed product replacement
Diagnose DIC using the ISTH score and distinguish it from TTP/HUS and hepatic coagulopathy
Quote the major trial evidence shaping practice (TRICC, TRISS, PROPPR, CRASH-2, CRYOSTAT-2, FIBRES)
32-year-old, RTC, pelvic and femur fractures, BP 78/40, HR 138, FAST positive, Hb 68 on point-of-care. ABG: pH 7.18, lactate 6.8, iCa²⁺ 0.86, temperature 34.4°C.
Activate MHP: 1:1:1 (PRBC:FFP:platelets) packs. Give TXA 1 g IV bolus + 1 g over 8 h (CRASH-2: within 3 h reduces mortality). Address lethal triad: warm fluids/forced-air warming → temperature; correct acidosis by source control + perfusion; coagulopathy by 1:1:1 + cryo or fibrinogen concentrate to keep fibrinogen >1.5–2 g/L. Citrate-induced hypocalcaemia: 10 mL CaCl₂ 10% per 4 units PRBC and whenever iCa²⁺ <1.0. Damage control resuscitation — permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90) until surgical/IR control. s Witness is listed for redo open AAA repair. She declines allogeneic blood but accepts intra-operative cell salvage if the circuit remains in continuity with her body. How do you set up and run cell salvage for this case?
Confirm consent and document the agreed components (red cells via continuous circuit). Two suction lines: a low-vacuum (≤−150 mmHg) salvage suction kept on the surgical field below blood level, and a separate standard high-vacuum sucker for irrigation/contaminants. Anticoagulate the collection reservoir — heparinised saline (30,000 IU in 1 L 0.9% NaCl) primed at 60 mL per 100 mL anticipated blood, dripping into the suction tubing tip; citrate (ACD-A) is the alternative when systemic heparin is contraindicated. When the reservoir holds ~500–1000 mL, the wash cycle starts: blood is centrifuged in a spinning bell, plasma + heparin + free Hb + cytokines are decanted to waste, and packed RBCs are washed with 1–1.5 L saline before being suspended in 0.9% saline at Hct ~50–70%. The processed unit is returned through a standard blood-giving set with a 40 µm filter; in obstetrics or malignancy add a leucodepletion filter to remove amniotic/tumour debris. Returned blood has no platelets, fibrinogen or clotting factors — anticipate dilutional coagulopathy after 1500–2000 mL salvaged volume and replace with FFP/cryo/platelets guided by ROTEM.
Septic shock from urosepsis, day 2 ICU. Platelets 42 ×10⁹/L, PT prolonged 8 s above control, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, D-dimer strongly raised, oozing from cannulae.

Differentiate from TTP (normal coag screen + ADAMTS13 <10%) and from hepatic coagulopathy (FVIII low in liver disease, preserved in DIC).
