entries.text:
# Non-Technical Skills & Human Factors ANTS framework, situation awareness, decision-making, teamwork, leadership, crisis resource management, debriefing, just culture Step-by-step reasoning Situation awareness: declare 'CICO' aloud, recognise SpO₂ trend, time-stamp events Decision-making: commit to DAS Plan D (FONA) rather than persistent intubation attempts — avoid task fixation Team-working: assign explicit roles (airway lead, surgical airway, drugs, runner, scribe), use closed-loop communication, call for senior help early Task management: prepare FONA kit, ensure adequate paralysis, monitor SpO₂/ETCO₂, plan post-event debrief Cognitive aids: use the DAS CICO cognitive aid on the wall; rehearse with simulation Common traps Hierarchy preventing junior team members from speaking up — graded assertiveness (CUS, PACE) Plan continuation bias — repeated DL attempts after failure Failing to debrief after the event — second-victim impact and learning loss framework, the model of human factors, and Crisis Resource Management (CRM) principles are core to FFICM, EDIC and CCT-level practice. This topic frames the four ANTS categories, the cognitive traps that lead to error, and the team and organisational tools used to mitigate them. ANTS — Anaesthetists' Non-Technical Skills ICU example Situation awareness Gathering information · recognising & understanding · anticipating Spotting a rising lactate trend before haemodynamic collapse; mental model of where the patient is on their illness trajectory. Decision making Identifying options · balancing risks & selecting · re-evaluating Choosing between further volume, vasopressor escalation, or RRT; setting time-limited trial endpoints. Task management Planning & preparing · prioritising · resource ID & utilisation · standards WHO checklist before bedside tracheostomy; pre-briefing for prone positioning; cognitive aids for crisis algorithms. Team working Coordinating · exchanging information · using authority & assertiveness · supporting others Closed-loop communication during peri-arrest; nominating roles in MET call; calling for help early. Cognitive Errors & Bias Fixation error / plan continuation bias — sticking with an action plan when the situation has changed (the laryngoscopy example). Confirmation bias — interpreting new data as confirming the working diagnosis. — over-weighting the first piece of information (the handover diagnosis). Premature closure — accepting a diagnosis before fully verifying it. Availability heuristic — recent or memorable cases bias the differential. Authority gradient — junior team members fail to challenge the senior. Cognitive overload — task saturation in a crisis impairs decision-making (Yerkes-Dodson curve). Crisis Resource Management — Key Principles Team behaviours Call for help early Establish clear leadership; leader hands-off when possible Nominate role allocation aloud (airway / circulation / drugs / scribe / runner) Closed-loop communication ("adrenaline 1 mg IV given — confirmed") Use names not pronouns; use SBAR for handover Graded assertiveness: PACE (Probe → Alert → Challenge → Emergency) Cognitive behaviours Use cognitive aids (don't rely on memory under stress) Anticipate and plan ahead ("if this fails we will…") Distribute workload — leader not task-saturated Re-evaluate frequently ("10-second-for-10-minutes") Mobilise all available resources (people, equipment, expertise) Know your environment — equipment locations, switchboard codes Human Factors — SHEEP Model ystems — protocols, equipment design, IT, staffing levels uman interaction — communication, hierarchy, team dynamics nvironment — noise, lighting, interruptions, ergonomics quipment — usability, alarm fatigue, default settings ersonal — fatigue, stress, hunger, illness, cognitive bias (the "IM SAFE" check: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Eating) Swiss Cheese Model : incidents occur when latent system holes line up with active human error. Effective interventions usually target the system layers, not the individual. Briefing, Debriefing & Handover Pre-procedure brief WHO checklist (ICU adaptation), patient ID, planned procedure, anticipated difficulties, role allocation, equipment check, escalation plan. Hot debrief (within 24 h) — STOP-5 Brief (3–5 min), at the bedside or in the coffee room, led by any team member. The STOP-5 structure (Walker et al., BJA Educ 2020): ummary of the case — one-sentence factual recap. hings that went well — reinforce positive behaviours. pportunities to improve — non-judgmental. oints to action — concrete, assigned to a named individual with a deadline. esponsibilities — close the loop on who owns each action. Reduces moral distress and supports learning. Cold debrief / case review (1–2 weeks) — PEARLS Multidisciplinary, psychologically safe, action-oriented. The PEARLS framework (Eppich & Cheng 2015) blends learner self-assessment, focused facilitation and directive feedback across four phases: — invite initial thoughts and emotions to defuse affect. — establish a shared understanding of what actually happened. — explore why things happened (advocacy–inquiry, focused facilitation, directive teaching as needed). Summary / Application — agree take-home messages and a plan to change practice. Diamond and Plus-Delta are alternative structured models with the same intent. Handover tools SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation); ISBAR (adds Identification); ICU board rounds with daily goals (FAST-HUG-BID, ABCDEF bundle). Patient Safety & Incident Response Just culture (Reason; Marx 2001) — distinguish three categories of behaviour and respond proportionately. Neither blame-free nor punitive: Human error — an unintentional slip or lapse. the individual and fix the system that allowed the error. At-risk behaviour — a choice where the risk is not recognised or is mistakenly believed justified (e.g. a workaround). the individual; remove incentives for the workaround. Reckless behaviour — conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk. (NHS England Patient Safety Incident Response Framework, 2022) — replaces SI framework; emphasises learning, proportionate response, family/staff involvement. Duty of candour — statutory (England, since 2014); be open and honest when something goes wrong. Datix / equivalent — incident reporting; NRLS, learn from incidents. Speaking up — Freedom to Speak Up Guardians; PACE/CUSS scripts. Second victim — clinicians involved in adverse events need active support; structured peer support programmes (e.g. RISE). During a difficult intubation, the consultant continues with direct laryngoscopy despite three failed attempts and falling saturations. The trainee believes a videolaryngoscope or front-of-neck access is now indicated but says nothing. Which non-technical skill failure is most prominently demonstrated? Which of the following best describes a 'just culture' as applied to a serious incident in ICU? Applying ANTS in a 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' scenario Use ANTS categories (situation awareness, decision-making, teamwork, task management) alongside DAS algorithms and cognitive aids to maintain coordinated CICO management and debrief afterwards. Non-Technical Skills & Human Factors FFICM / EDIC — Intensive Care ANTS taxonomy: Situation awareness · Decision making · Task management · Team working — memorise for SOEs. Up to 70% of critical care adverse events are non-technical; competence is examinable and assessable. Fixation error and plan continuation bias are the most cited cognitive failures in airway disasters (Bromiley case). PACE / CUSS provides graded assertiveness language to flatten authority gradients. Closed-loop communication and named role allocation are CRM cornerstones in any crisis. Cognitive aids reduce error in low-frequency / high-stakes events — use them, don't rely on memory. A just culture distinguishes error and at-risk behaviour (system response) from reckless behaviour (accountability). Hot debriefs within 24 h support team wellbeing and learning; cold debriefs drive system change. The Swiss Cheese Model frames adverse events as system holes aligning — fix the system, not just the person. Statutory duty of candour applies in England since 2014 — be open promptly when harm occurs. What are the four domains of ANTS (Anaesthetists Task management, team working, situation awareness and decision making — each with behavioural markers used for structured debrief and assessment (Fletcher et al., BJA 2003). Situation awareness is individual perception of cues, comprehension and projection (Endsley); shared mental model is the team-wide common understanding of the problem and plan — built by closed-loop communication and structured handover (e.g. SBAR). How does cognitive aid use improve crisis management? Cognitive aids (e.g. AAGBI Quick Reference Handbook, ASA Critical Events) reduce omission errors in low-frequency emergencies — RCTs show measurable improvement when a dedicated reader is appointed within the team. Define the four ANTS categories (situation awareness, decision making, task management, team working) and their elements. Recognise common cognitive biases and fixation errors that contribute to ICU adverse events. Apply Crisis Resource Management principles in simulated and real ICU emergencies. Use structured tools (SBAR, SPIKES, STOP-5, PACE/CUSS, WHO checklist) to support safe communication and handover. C-spine pathology, ankylosing spondylitis, RA. Weight, head/neck movement, jaw movement, receding mandible, buck teeth. Previous difficult intubation is the strongest predictor. case_bank.title: Recent joint injections before arthroplasty
case_bank.text:
Case: Recent joint injections before arthroplasty (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: A 72-year-old man is scheduled for revision knee arthroplasty. He stopped prednisolone two months ago and has also had repeated intra-articular steroid injections.
Presentation: He reports fatigue and postural dizziness but has no formal diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency.
Stage 1 — Build the risk picture
  Question: Which details change your plan?
  Model answer: Recent cessation of long-term oral therapy does not guarantee HPA recovery; suppression may persist.
  Model answer: Repeated intra-articular injections add systemic exposure.
  Model answer: Symptoms, treatment records and time available determine whether endocrine testing is useful; urgent surgery should not await testing when risk is credible.
Stage 2 — Cover major surgery
  Question: What is a defensible perioperative plan?
  Model answer: Document likely suppression and give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue 200 mg over 24 hours initially, alongside close haemodynamic and glucose monitoring.
  Model answer: Agree the taper and longer-term assessment with endocrinology or the treating team.
Stage 3 — Avoid the common error
  Question: What should not happen at discharge?
  Model answer: Do not abruptly stop glucocorticoid cover without a recovery plan.
  Model answer: Provide clear written sick-day advice and arrange assessment of ongoing replacement need.
  Model answer: Reconcile every steroid route in the discharge medicines.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: HPA recovery after long-term glucocorticoids is variable and may take months. Repeated intra-articular injections can add meaningful systemic exposure, while fatigue and postural symptoms strengthen concern but are not diagnostic. Testing is useful only when time and clinical stability permit.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: For major revision arthroplasty with credible suppression, continue or replace the baseline requirement, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction and 200 mg over the first 24 hours. Monitor haemodynamics and glucose, then agree a taper and formal endocrine assessment rather than making an unplanned stop.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: ‘Stopped two months ago’ does not prove recovery. Discharge reconciliation should cover oral, inhaled, topical and injected steroids and provide sick-day and emergency advice.
Take-home: Recently stopped oral steroids and repeated injections can remain clinically relevant; route and current prescription alone do not define HPA-axis risk.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Preparing an adrenal phaeochromocytoma
case_bank.text:
Case: Preparing an adrenal phaeochromocytoma (Phaeochromocytoma, Foundation)
Patient: A 43-year-old woman has an adrenal mass, raised plasma metanephrines and episodic headache, sweating and palpitations.
Presentation: She is referred for laparoscopic adrenalectomy with a seated BP of 168/96 mmHg and pulse 104 min⁻¹.
Stage 1 — Sequence preoperative treatment
  Question: How should blockade be introduced?
  Model answer: Start alpha blockade first, commonly phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin, and titrate over about 10–14 days.
  Model answer: Only add beta blockade after adequate alpha blockade if troublesome tachycardia persists.
  Model answer: Never beta block first because unopposed alpha vasoconstriction can provoke a hypertensive crisis.
Stage 2 — Restore circulating volume
  Question: Why are salt and fluid important?
  Model answer: Chronic catecholamine-mediated vasoconstriction leaves the patient intravascularly depleted.
  Model answer: Encourage salt and fluid intake after alpha blockade, while individualising for cardiac or renal disease.
  Model answer: Look for controlled seated BP with tolerable postural reduction rather than simply a normal clinic reading.
Stage 3 — Confirm readiness
  Question: What should the multidisciplinary review cover?
  Model answer: Blood-pressure and rhythm control, postural symptoms, ECG/cardiac effects and glucose.
  Model answer: Availability of experienced endocrine surgery, anaesthesia, critical care and appropriate postoperative monitoring.
  Model answer: A plan for invasive monitoring and rapidly acting vasoactive drugs.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction causes hypertension and contracted circulating volume. Alpha blockade reduces vascular tone; beta blockade is added only after alpha control because isolated beta blockade leaves unopposed alpha vasoconstriction. Preparation is judged by pressure control, tolerable postural change, rhythm and end-organ effects rather than one clinic value.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Titrate phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin for roughly 10–14 days, then add beta blockade only for persistent tachycardia after adequate alpha blockade. Encourage salt and fluid intake where safe. Plan arterial monitoring, large-bore access, short-acting vasodilators, vasopressors, glucose monitoring and postoperative critical-care observation with an experienced multidisciplinary team.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not chase a perfectly normal seated pressure at the cost of disabling orthostasis, and never describe beta blockade before alpha blockade.
Take-home: Successful preparation is alpha blockade followed—if needed—by beta blockade, together with volume expansion and an experienced multidisciplinary plan.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

case_bank.title: Tranexamic acid in high-risk non-cardiac surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Tranexamic acid in high-risk non-cardiac surgery (Antifibrinolytics, Advanced)
Patient: A 76-year-old with remote provoked DVT is scheduled for major multilevel spine surgery with high anticipated blood loss.
Presentation: The team is weighing reduced bleeding against perioperative vascular risk.
Stage 1 — Balance benefit and uncertainty
  Question: How should the evidence be framed?
  Model answer: TXA reduces major bleeding in non-cardiac surgery.
  Model answer: POISE-3 did not establish non-inferiority for the composite cardiovascular safety outcome, so individual thrombotic and bleeding risks still matter.
  Model answer: A remote provoked DVT is not automatically equivalent to active thrombosis; review timing, recurrence, anticoagulation and local guidance.
Stage 2 — Choose and prescribe deliberately
  Question: What safeguards belong in the plan?
  Model answer: Use the procedure-specific local dose rather than importing a trauma regimen.
  Model answer: Adjust or avoid repeated high dosing in significant renal impairment because TXA is renally cleared.
  Model answer: Avoid accidental neuraxial administration: separate storage, label syringes and use route-specific checks.
Stage 3 — Monitor relevant harms
  Question: What postoperative surveillance is appropriate?
  Model answer: Continue standard VTE prevention once haemostasis permits.
  Model answer: Investigate clinical signs of venous or arterial thrombosis rather than using TXA exposure alone as a diagnosis.
  Model answer: Recognise that seizures are associated particularly with high exposure and renal accumulation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: In major non-cardiac surgery, TXA lowers bleeding, but POISE-3 did not prove non-inferiority for its composite cardiovascular safety outcome. Decision-making therefore combines procedural blood-loss risk with active or previous thrombosis, vascular disease, anticoagulation and renal function. A remote provoked DVT is not the same as active thrombosis.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use the procedure-specific local regimen rather than a trauma dose. Reduce exposure in renal impairment because TXA is predominantly renally cleared, and avoid repeated high doses where accumulation raises seizure risk. Keep ampoules and syringes physically separated from neuraxial drugs and perform explicit route checks. Restart standard VTE prophylaxis when haemostasis permits.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: The catastrophic route error is intrathecal TXA. Mention storage, labelling and checking systems as well as pharmacology and thrombosis assessment.
Take-home: Elective perioperative TXA requires procedure-specific dosing and an individual bleeding–thrombosis assessment; renal function and route safety are practical exam points.
Cited sources: POISE-3 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2201171)

case_bank.title: Pituitary insufficiency before major surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Pituitary insufficiency before major surgery (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: An adult with panhypopituitarism takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine and is listed for open abdominal surgery.
Presentation: They have fasted, omitted morning medicines and have glucose 3.5 mmol/L with normal potassium.
Stage 1 — Interpret the pattern
  Question: Does normal potassium exclude adrenal risk?
  Model answer: No. Secondary adrenal insufficiency often preserves aldosterone and potassium.
  Model answer: Missed glucocorticoid, fasting and major stress create crisis risk.
  Model answer: Review diabetes insipidus and other pituitary replacement.
Stage 2 — Provide major-stress cover
  Question: What regimen is appropriate?
  Model answer: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction.
  Model answer: Continue 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg six-hourly initially.
  Model answer: Correct hypoglycaemia and monitor sodium, glucose and fluid balance.
Stage 3 — Sequence endocrine treatment
  Question: What endocrine ordering matters?
  Model answer: Ensure glucocorticoid replacement before initiating or escalating thyroid hormone in combined deficiency.
  Model answer: Taper toward baseline when stable and absorbing orally.
  Model answer: Seek endocrine input for complex fluid or sodium disturbance.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Pituitary disease may cause secondary adrenal insufficiency without hyperkalaemia because aldosterone is largely preserved. Fasting, vomiting and omission of hydrocortisone can still precipitate hypotension and hypoglycaemia during major surgery.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue replacement, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction and 200 mg over 24 hours for major stress, then taper toward baseline as recovery permits. Monitor sodium, glucose, pressure and fluid balance; account for coexisting diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Normal potassium does not exclude secondary adrenal crisis. Replace glucocorticoid before starting or increasing thyroxine in untreated combined pituitary deficiency.
Take-home: Secondary adrenal insufficiency can present without hyperkalaemia; major stress still requires timely glucocorticoid replacement.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

case_bank.title: Adrenal incidentaloma before elective surgery
case_bank.text:
Case: Adrenal incidentaloma before elective surgery (Phaeochromocytoma, Intermediate)
Patient: An adult awaiting elective joint replacement has an adrenal incidentaloma and elevated metanephrines.
Presentation: They report few symptoms and the surgical team asks whether the unrelated operation can proceed.
Stage 1 — Assess hidden risk
  Question: Can an asymptomatic patient still develop crisis?
  Model answer: Yes. Anaesthesia, intubation and surgical stress can trigger catecholamine release.
  Model answer: Review biochemical certainty, imaging and end-organ effects.
  Model answer: Do not equate few symptoms with low perioperative risk.
Stage 2 — Prioritise procedures
  Question: What happens to elective surgery?
  Model answer: Postpone non-urgent surgery for endocrine evaluation and preparation.
  Model answer: Institute alpha blockade and volume restoration before definitive management.
  Model answer: Avoid isolated beta blockade.
Stage 3 — Handle an emergency exception
  Question: What if unrelated surgery cannot wait?
  Model answer: Use senior multidisciplinary planning and invasive arterial monitoring.
  Model answer: Prepare titratable vasodilators, vasopressors and postoperative critical care.
  Model answer: Avoid known catecholamine-provoking drugs where alternatives exist.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: An adrenal incidentaloma with biochemical catecholamine excess creates risk even when symptoms are mild. Elective unrelated surgery can trigger crisis through induction, intubation, surgical stress or interacting drugs.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Postpone non-urgent surgery, confirm biochemistry and imaging, assess end-organ effects and establish alpha blockade with volume restoration. If emergency surgery cannot wait, use an arterial line, senior multidisciplinary input and prepared short-acting vasodilator and vasopressor infusions.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not dismiss an asymptomatic tumour or proceed after simply adding a beta blocker. Explain why the unrelated operation should usually be deferred.
Take-home: Biochemically active phaeochromocytoma makes unrelated elective anaesthesia unsafe until appropriately prepared.
Cited sources: BJA Education: phaeochromocytoma (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkv051)

Optimisation (anaemia, nutrition, fitness — prehabilitation). Carbohydrate loading (maltodextrin drink 2h pre-op). No prolonged fasting (clear fluids 2h, solids 6h). Short-acting anaesthetics. Regional/neuraxial analgesia. GDFT. Normothermia. Minimally invasive surgery. Avoid drains/NG tubes where possible. Antiemetic prophylaxis. Early oral intake (day 0). Early mobilisation (day 0). Why is goal-directed fluid therapy preferred over fixed-volume regimens in ERAS? Stroke-volume optimisation with small balanced crystalloid boluses titrated to dynamic indices reduces postoperative complications and length of stay compared with both liberal and overly restrictive fixed regimens (POM-O, OPTIMISE). Short-acting anaesthetics. Regional/neuraxial analgesia. GDFT. Normothermia. Minimally invasive surgery. Avoid drains/NG tubes where possible. Antiemetic prophylaxis.

# Perioperative Fluid Therapy Crystalloids vs colloids, goal-directed, fluid responsiveness Na⁺ (mmol/L) Cl⁻ (mmol/L) 0.9% NaCl Hyperchloraemic acidosis. Not "normal". Contains lactate 29 mmol/L (metabolised to HCO₃⁻). Balanced. Most physiological. Acetate + gluconate as buffers. 5% Albumin Colloid. Better intravascular expansion. SAFE trial: equivalent to saline in general ICU. Stroke Volume Optimisation Dynamic Parameters PPV, SVV (arterial waveform analysis). Reliable only in sinus rhythm + controlled ventilation + VT ≥8 ml/kg. PLR test for spontaneous breathing. Cross-section of the endothelial surface layer (ESL): proteoglycan / GAG mesh that excludes plasma proteins, and the consequences of its shedding by ANP, inflammation and crystalloid overload. Revised Starling: Fluid filtration occurs across the glycocalyx, not at the capillary level. The sub-glycocalyx oncotic pressure (not interstitial) opposes filtration. There is no venous reabsorption in most tissues — lymphatic drainage returns filtered fluid. Clinical implication: Fluid overload, inflammation, ANP, and surgical stress damage the glycocalyx → increased permeability → oedema. Avoid hypervolaemia — it sheds the glycocalyx via ANP release. Step-by-step reasoning Assess fluid responsiveness using a dynamic index — PPV/SVV from arterial line. PPV >13% suggests responsiveness. Give a 250 ml balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's/Plasmalyte) bolus over <10 min — avoid 0.9% NaCl (SMART: ↑MAKE30). Reassess SV/MAP/lactate after 10–15 min. If SV rises ≥10% → responsive → repeat. If <10% → stop fluids; consider noradrenaline. Aim for cumulative balance avoiding excess (RELIEF: overly restrictive ↑AKI; overly liberal ↑ileus, oedema). Common traps PPV/SVV unreliable in spontaneous breathing, AF, or VT <8 ml/kg — use PLR instead. Repeated 0.9% NaCl boluses → hyperchloraemic acidosis, masking true lactate trend. Chasing CVP — static pressures poorly predict fluid responsiveness. The endothelial glycocalyx is a carbohydrate-rich layer lining the vascular endothelium. It regulates vascular permeability, prevents leucocyte adhesion, and modulates coagulation.

references.excerpt: The endothelial glycocalyx is a 0.5–1 µm thick gel-like layer of membrane-bound proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans covering the luminal surface of every endothelial cell. Its degradation by sepsis, ischaemia–reperfusion, hypervolaemia and atrial natriuretic peptide release is a central mechanism of perioperative capillary leak and interstitial oedema.

case_bank.title: Oliguria on the first postoperative night
case_bank.text:
Case: Oliguria on the first postoperative night (Renal, neuromuscular & autonomic, Foundation)
Patient: After open colorectal surgery, an adult passes 15 mL of urine per hour for three hours. Mean arterial pressure is 65 mmHg, and the chart includes an ACE inhibitor and regular ibuprofen.
Presentation: The nurse asks for a fluid bolus. The patient looks comfortable, warm and peripherally well perfused.
Stage 1 — Explain the renal physiology
  Question: How does the kidney normally protect glomerular filtration?
  Model answer: Autoregulation keeps renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate near constant across a mean arterial pressure of roughly 80–180 mmHg through myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms.
  Model answer: Afferent arteriolar dilation depends partly on prostaglandins; efferent tone depends on angiotensin II.
  Model answer: NSAIDs blunt afferent dilation and ACE inhibitors blunt efferent constriction, so both together strip away autoregulatory reserve at low pressure.
Stage 2 — Assess before infusing
  Question: How do you evaluate this oliguria?
  Model answer: Exclude obstruction first: flush or replace a blocked catheter and examine for retention.
  Model answer: Assess perfusion with capillary refill, lactate, pressure trend against the patient's baseline, and dynamic response to a small measured fluid challenge.
  Model answer: Look for bleeding, sepsis, raised intra-abdominal pressure and drug causes; review nephrotoxins and check creatinine trend against KDIGO criteria.
Stage 3 — Treat proportionately
  Question: What do you do?
  Model answer: Stop the NSAID, withhold the ACE inhibitor and restore mean arterial pressure towards the patient's usual value using fluid where hypovolaemic and vasopressor where vasodilated.
  Model answer: Avoid indiscriminate large-volume fluid loading, which causes venous congestion, oedema and worse outcomes without protecting kidneys.
  Model answer: Recheck urine output, creatinine and electrolytes, and escalate for critical care review if oliguria persists or acidosis, hyperkalaemia or fluid overload develop.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Postoperative oliguria is often an appropriate neuroendocrine response to surgery — antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone conserve water and sodium — but it is also the first sign of hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity. Because autoregulation depends on prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent tone, combining an NSAID and a renin–angiotensin blocker at low perfusion pressure predictably reduces glomerular filtration.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Work through obstruction, perfusion and nephrotoxins in order. Use small, repeated fluid challenges with a defined endpoint rather than open-ended boluses, and add vasopressor where vasodilation rather than hypovolaemia dominates. Track hourly urine output, creatinine, potassium, acid–base status and fluid balance; diuretics treat fluid overload but do not treat acute kidney injury or improve outcome.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not give a reflex 500 mL bolus for every low urine output, and do not forget a blocked catheter. Frame the answer around autoregulation, KDIGO staging and drug review.
Take-home: Assess obstruction, perfusion and nephrotoxins before infusing: NSAIDs plus renin–angiotensin blockade at low pressure remove renal autoregulatory reserve.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: renal physiology (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mku047); KDIGO AKI guideline (https://kdigo.org/guidelines/acute-kidney-injury/)

case_bank.title: High anion gap acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis
case_bank.text:
Case: High anion gap acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis (Acid–base, Intermediate)
Patient: A young adult presents with pH 7.08, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 2.4 kPa, glucose 28 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L.
Presentation: After 4 L of 0.9% sodium chloride and an insulin infusion, ketones fall to 1.0 mmol/L but pH is still 7.20 with bicarbonate 14 mmol/L and chloride 116 mmol/L.
Stage 1 — Interpret the first gas
  Question: Describe the disorder quantitatively.
  Model answer: Severe metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation: expected PaCO₂ is close to the measured value, so there is no additional respiratory disorder.
  Model answer: Anion gap is raised at about 31 mmol/L, consistent with ketoacidosis; the modest lactate rise reflects hypovolaemia and catecholamine-driven glycolysis.
  Model answer: Delta ratio confirms a pure high anion gap picture rather than a mixed acidosis at presentation.
Stage 2 — Explain the second gas
  Question: Why is the patient still acidotic after ketones have cleared?
  Model answer: The anion gap has normalised while a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis has appeared from large-volume 0.9% sodium chloride.
  Model answer: In Stewart terms, the infused fluid has a strong ion difference of zero, so it reduces plasma strong ion difference and lowers pH independently of ketones.
  Model answer: Bicarbonate regeneration also lags behind ketone clearance because ketoanions were excreted rather than metabolised.
Stage 3 — Manage from here
  Question: What do you change?
  Model answer: Switch to a balanced crystalloid, continue fixed-rate insulin with glucose-containing fluid once glucose falls below about 14 mmol/L, and replace potassium aggressively.
  Model answer: Do not give bicarbonate for a resolving ketoacidosis; treat the cause and monitor ketone clearance rather than pH alone.
  Model answer: Look for the precipitant — infection, non-adherence, myocardial infarction, pregnancy — and monitor for cerebral oedema in younger patients.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Two acidoses appear in sequence here: an organic high anion gap acidosis from ketoacid production, then an iatrogenic hyperchloraemic acidosis from resuscitation with saline. Only anion gap and chloride tracking reveals the switch; following pH or bicarbonate alone suggests treatment failure and risks unnecessary bicarbonate or insulin escalation. Ketone measurement, not glucose, defines resolution.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Use fixed-rate weight-based insulin, balanced crystalloid, early and generous potassium replacement, hourly ketone and glucose measurement, and regular electrolyte and gas review. Add glucose-containing fluid to permit continued insulin. Watch for hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypophosphataemia, fluid overload and, especially in adolescents, cerebral oedema. Address the precipitant and involve the diabetes team before discharge.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not attribute persistent acidosis to ongoing ketosis without recalculating the anion gap, and do not reach for bicarbonate. Show the compensation calculation and name hyperchloraemia explicitly.
Take-home: Recalculate the anion gap: persistent acidosis after ketone clearance is usually saline-induced hyperchloraemia, treated by changing fluid, not giving bicarbonate.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: acid–base interpretation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx008); Stewart approach to acid–base (https://doi.org/10.1186/cc3927)

Device Overview Classification Peripheral Cannulae Midline Catheters PICC Lines Multi-lumen CVC Vascath & Haemodialysis Trauma Lines Swan-Ganz & Long-term Devices Dwell Times & Clinical Scenarios Vascular Access Devices FRCA Primary / Final / FFICM — peripheral cannulae, midlines, PICCs, CVCs, vascaths, trauma lines and Swan-Ganz introducer sheaths Devices to scale — length and tip position Lumen geometry & flow Device archetypes — labelled anatomy & dwell times Dwell-time approach — clinically indicated vs scheduled Classification follows tip position: peripheral (vein) → midline (axillary v.) → central (SVC). Vesicants and vasopressors require central tips. Hagen–Poiseuille: flow ∝ r⁴ / length. Short wide single-lumen devices (14 G, RIC, MAC, Swan introducer) outflow long narrow multi-lumen CVCs by an order of magnitude. Midline ≠ central — tip in axillary vein, no SVC. Suitable for ≤ 4 weeks of non-vesicant infusions only. PICCs offer long-term central access with no neck/chest puncture risk but have higher upper-limb DVT rates than tunnelled CVCs. Triple-lumen CVC: distal (16 G) for vasopressors and CVP, medial for TPN, proximal opens later — useful safety margin if catheter migrates. Vascath 12–14 Fr supports 200–400 mL/min for RRT/PLEX. KDIGO 2012 site preference: right IJ > femoral > left IJ > subclavian (subclavian risks central stenosis). RIC converts a peripheral cannula to a wide-bore line; MAC introducer combines a side-port for rapid volume with a central lumen for vasopressors / PAC. Swan-Ganz sheath = introducer, not the PAC. Wide bore doubles as a high-flow resus line; specific complication is PA rupture if a PAC is wedged for too long. All CVC insertions use the NICE TA49 ultrasound-guidance bundle, maximum barrier precautions and 2% chlorhexidine; CXR confirmation of tip position before elective use. Long-term access: Hickman (open-ended, heparin lock), Groshong (slit valve, saline only), Portacath (fully implanted, lowest CRBSI ≈ 0.1/1000 catheter-days), Permcath (tunnelled HD). Dwell times: peripheral cannulae are now removed when clinically indicated (Rickard 2012, Cochrane 2019, epic3) — routine 72–96 h replacement no longer recommended. Site evidence (3SITES, NEJM 2015): subclavian lowest CRBSI & DVT but highest pneumothorax; femoral highest infection & DVT; right IJ is the default compromise. Avoid femoral when possible. A 55-year-old needs 6 months of cyclical chemotherapy with intermittent blood sampling. Compare PICC, tunnelled cuffed Hickman, and a totally implantable port — which is best? >Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Map the requirement: intermittent (not continuous), 6 months, vesicant drug, home discharge
  2. PICC: easy bedside insertion, high thrombosis rate (5–10%), unsuitable for swimming/showering long-term
  3. Tunnelled cuffed Hickman: external lumens, requires regular flushing and dressing; better for continuous infusion (TPN, induction chemo)
  4. Totally implantable port: subcutaneous reservoir accessed by Huber needle, low infection rate (<0.2 per 1000 catheter-days), allows normal activity — best for intermittent long-term therapy
  5. Insert under ultrasound guidance, confirm tip at cavo-atrial junction by fluoroscopy or ECG (P-wave maximal then biphasic)
= [ [ By Hagen–Poiseuille — flow is proportional to the fourth power of internal radius and inversely proportional to length. A short, wide-bore (16G or 14G) cannula delivers far greater flow than a longer central catheter of equivalent gauge. When is a midline preferred over a PICC? For peripherally compatible therapies of 1–4 weeks duration (e.g. antibiotics, fluids, non-irritant chemotherapy). Vesicants, parenteral nutrition or hyperosmolar/extreme-pH drugs require a central-tip device such as a PICC or CVC. What are the key complications of internal jugular CVC insertion? Carotid puncture, pneumothorax (lower than subclavian but not zero), arrhythmias from wire or catheter contact, air embolism, catheter-related bloodstream infection, and late venous stenosis or thrombosis. Ultrasound guidance is mandatory (NICE TA49). workedExamples={VascularAccessDevicesTopicWorkedExamples} quizQuestions={vascularAccessDevicesQuestions} objectives={[ Apply Hagen–Poiseuille flow physics to compare achievable infusion rates of cannulae, CVCs, vascaths and rapid-infusion (trauma) lines. Recognise the indications for, and complications of, peripheral cannulae, midlines, PICCs, multi-lumen CVCs, haemodialysis catheters, RIC/MAC trauma lines and Swan-Ganz introducer sheaths. Describe ultrasound-guided central venous access using ANTT and the Seldinger technique, with strategies to avoid arterial puncture, pneumothorax and CRBSI. Justify a device choice from a typical clinical scenario (e.g. resus, long-term antibiotics, RRT, cardiac surgery). , ], keyPoints: [ > How to classify vascular access

Devices are grouped by where the tip sits, not by where the skin entry is. Tip position drives the safe range of drug osmolarity, pH and vesicant potential.

Peripheral Forearm / hand / ACF vein 20 G–14 G cannula Isotonic, non-vesicant, < 600 mOsm/L; short courses (≤ 96 h) Midline Axillary vein (NOT central) 8–20 cm 3–5 Fr midline catheter Same constraints as peripheral; suits 1–4 weeks of antibiotics Central (CVAD) SVC / cavo-atrial junction PICC, CVC, vascath, tunnelled Hickman/Permcath, port Vesicants, vasopressors, TPN, hyperosmolar drugs; long-term therapy
Peripheral cannulae

Short, wide, parallel-walled plastic catheter over a steel introducer (Seldinger NOT used). ISO gauge colour-codes the hub (orange 14 G → grey 16 G → green 18 G → pink 20 G → blue 22 G → yellow 24 G). Maximum gravity flow is for water at 20 °C — viscous fluid (blood, colloid) flows roughly half as fast.

Indications

  • Induction of anaesthesia, drug administration
  • Maintenance fluids and short-course antibiotics
  • 14 G / 16 G — large-volume resuscitation, blood
Complications

  • Phlebitis (Visual Infusion Phlebitis score ≥ 2 → resite)
  • Extravasation — particularly catastrophic for vasopressors
  • Air embolus, sharps injury, infection (CRBSI rare)
Midline catheters

Inserted by ultrasound-guided Seldinger or modified-Seldinger (accelerated Seldinger technique) into a deep upper-arm vein (basilic, brachial, cephalic), advanced 8–20 cm so the tip sits in the axillary vein. NOT a central line — there is no SVC tip. Designed for 1–4 weeks of non-vesicant therapy when peripheral access fails.

Caveats: still counts as a peripheral device — do not run vasopressors, chemotherapy or TPN; mechanical phlebitis common in the first 48 h; thrombosis risk higher than peripheral cannulae.

PICC lines

Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter — long (40–55 cm) 4–6 Fr silicone or polyurethane catheter inserted under ultrasound into the basilic / brachial vein and advanced so the tip sits at the cavo-atrial junction (confirmed on chest X-ray, ECG-tip location or fluoroscopy). 1–3 lumens; safe for weeks to months.

Strengths

  • Avoids neck/chest puncture (no pneumothorax risk)
  • Bedside insertion — outpatient antibiotic / chemo
  • Easily removed; lower CRBSI than non-tunnelled CVC
Weaknesses

  • Higher upper-limb DVT rate than tunnelled CVCs
  • Narrow lumens — slow flow, easily occluded
  • Tip migration with arm movement — recheck after insertion
 Multi-lumen central venous catheter (CVC)

Non-tunnelled 7 Fr triple-lumen catheter inserted under ultrasound by Seldinger technique into the right internal jugular (preferred), subclavian or femoral vein. 16 cm standard length (RIJ). Provides reliable access for vasopressors, parenteral nutrition, CVP measurement and repeated blood sampling.

Lumen role

  • Distal (16 G, brown) — CVP transduction, vasopressors, blood draw
  • Medial (18 G, blue) — TPN or single drug
  • Proximal (18 G, white) — boluses, sampling — opens 2–3 cm proximal so opens later if catheter migrates
Insertion bundles

  • Hand hygiene, max barrier precautions, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol
  • Real-time ultrasound (NICE TA49)
  • Avoid femoral if avoidable; remove as soon as not needed; aseptic dressing change

Complications — early: arterial puncture, pneumothorax (subclavian), haemothorax, air embolus, arrhythmia, malposition, guidewire loss; late: CRBSI, thrombosis, catheter fracture, fibrin sheath. Confirm tip position on CXR (above the carina, parallel to the SVC) before non-emergency use.

Vascath / haemodialysis catheter

Wide-bore (12–14 Fr) twin-lumen central catheter designed to support extracorporeal blood-flow rates of 200–400 mL/min for renal replacement therapy, plasma exchange or ECCO₂R. The two lumens are staggered (5–10 mm apart at the tip) to minimise recirculation between the return ports.

Sites in order of preference for acute RRT: right internal jugular > femoral > left internal jugular > subclavian (KDIGO 2012 — subclavian last because of the high rate of central venous stenosis that would compromise future AV-fistula formation). Locked between sessions with heparin or 4% citrate; never used for routine drug or fluid administration.

Trauma lines — RIC and MAC

Designed for one job: deliver warmed blood and crystalloid as fast as physically possible.

RIC — Rapid Infusion Catheter

Short (6.4 cm) 8.5 Fr single-lumen catheter exchanged over a wire onto an existing 18 G/20 G peripheral cannula. Achievable flow with a pressure bag > 500 mL/min — comparable to a 14 G but in a vein already cannulated.

MAC — Multi-lumen Access Catheter (introducer)

9 Fr central introducer with a side-port plus a 12 G distal lumen. Typical use: massive transfusion in trauma / obstetric haemorrhage / liver transplant. Side-port for rapid volume; central lumen for vasopressor or PAC passage.

Swan-Ganz introducer sheath

An 8.5–9 Fr percutaneous sheath placed in the right internal jugular or subclavian vein, with a haemostatic valve to allow passage of a 7.5 Fr pulmonary artery catheter (PAC) or transvenous pacing wire while a side-arm permits simultaneous fluid administration. Often misnamed but the sheath is the introducer, not the PAC.

Uses: cardiac surgery (PAC monitoring, pacing wire conduit), unstable ICU patients needing continuous CO measurement, suspected VAE during sitting neurosurgery (aspiration of air). The wide single lumen also doubles as a useful resuscitation line — comparable flow rates to a RIC with the security of central venous position. Specific complications include valve leak, pulmonary artery rupture (if a PAC is wedged forcefully or for too long), arrhythmias on insertion and knotting of the PAC inside the right ventricle.

Long-term (tunnelled & implanted) vascular access devices

When central access is needed for months to years (chemotherapy, long-term parenteral nutrition, chronic haemodialysis, cystic fibrosis antibiotics), tunnelled or fully implanted devices dramatically reduce CRBSI rates compared with non-tunnelled CVCs by separating the skin entry site from the venotomy with a subcutaneous tunnel and a Dacron cuff that fibroses to anchor the line and form a mechanical bacterial barrier.

Hickman / Broviac line

Tunnelled cuffed silicone catheter (Broviac = paediatric, smaller calibre). Open-ended lumen with an external clamp; requires regular heparinised saline locks and meticulous dressing care. 1–3 lumens. Used for chemotherapy, long-term TPN and stem-cell transplantation. Tip at the cavo-atrial junction, skin exit on the anterior chest wall.

Groshong line

Tunnelled silicone catheter with a closed, rounded tip and a three-way slit valve just proximal to it. The valve opens outwards on infusion, inwards on aspiration, and stays closed at rest — eliminating the need for heparin locks and reducing air-embolus and reflux-thrombosis risk. Saline flush only. Otherwise managed like a Hickman.

Portacath (totally implanted port)

Silicone catheter attached to a titanium / plastic reservoir with a self-sealing silicone septum, implanted in a subcutaneous infraclavicular pocket. Accessed transcutaneously with a non-coring (Huber) needle. Lowest CRBSI of any CVAD (≈ 0.1 per 1000 catheter-days), best cosmesis, no external components, can be left in situ for years and flushed only 4–6 weekly when not in use. Best choice for intermittent long-term chemotherapy.

Tunnelled haemodialysis catheter (Permcath)

Cuffed twin-lumen 13–14.5 Fr silicone catheter (e.g. Permcath, Tesio) tunnelled to the anterior chest wall with the tip in the right atrium. Bridge to AV-fistula maturation or definitive access where a fistula is impossible. Lower infection and dysfunction rates than non-tunnelled vascaths beyond ~1–3 weeks of use.

Evidence on safe dwell times by device & site

Historical practice was to resite peripheral cannulae every 72–96 h. The landmark Rickard et al. (Lancet 2012, n = 3283) RCT and the subsequent Cochrane review (Webster 2019) showed no difference in phlebitis or CRBSI between routine replacement and clinically-indicated removal — current{ } is therefore to leave peripheral cannulae in situ until clinically indicated, inspecting at least every shift (VIP score). For all central devices the evidence supports removing the line only when no longer needed; routine elective change does not reduce CRBSI and exposes the patient to mechanical complications.

Peripheral cannula Forearm / hand Clinically indicated (no fixed maximum) Rickard 2012 (Lancet); Cochrane 2019; epic3 2014; RCN 2016 Arterial line Radial > femoral > brachial ~7 days; remove when not needed (no scheduled change) CDC 2011; O >Midline Basilic / brachial → axillary v. 1–4 weeks (manufacturer ≤ 29 days) INS 2021; Adams 2016 (low CRBSI ≈ 0.2/1000 d) Non-tunnelled CVC RIJ > subclavian > femoral Clinically indicated; ideally ≤ 7–14 days 3SITES (Parienti NEJM 2015): subclavian lowest CRBSI & thrombosis, highest pneumothorax; femoral highest infection PICC Basilic / brachial → SVC Weeks–months; clinically indicated MAGIC criteria 2015; Chopra 2013 (PICC DVT > CVC) Non-tunnelled vascath RIJ > femoral > LIJ > subclavian Days–weeks; tunnel if > 1–3 weeks KDIGO 2012; Parienti Cathedia 2008 (femoral non-inferior in BMI < 28) Tunnelled CVC (Hickman / Broviac / Groshong) RIJ → tunnel to chest wall Months–years; remove for infection / dysfunction IDSA 2009; epic3 2014; CDC 2011 Implanted port (Portacath) Subclavian → infraclavicular pocket Years; lowest CRBSI of any CVAD Maki 2006 meta-analysis (≈ 0.1/1000 d vs 2.7 for non-tunnelled CVC) Tunnelled vascath (Permcath / Tesio) RIJ → chest wall, tip in RA Months; bridge or definitive HD access KDOQI 2019; KDIGO 2012

Site effects: femoral CVCs carry the highest CRBSI and DVT risk and should be avoided where possible (3SITES); subclavian has the lowest infection and thrombosis but the highest mechanical (pneumothorax) risk; the right internal jugular remains the default compromise. For arterial lines the femoral site has comparable CRBSI to radial in modern data but higher local-haematoma risk.

How should a pacemaker-dependent patient be managed when monopolar diathermy is required? Reprogramme to an asynchronous mode (DOO/VOO) or apply a clinical magnet, position the diathermy return plate so the current path does not cross the device, use short bipolar bursts where possible, and check the device postoperatively. What are the anaesthetic principles in pulmonary hypertension? Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia and high airway pressures — all increase pulmonary vascular resistance. Maintain RV preload and coronary perfusion pressure, use noradrenaline or vasopressin for systemic hypotension, and have inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (NO, iloprost) available. At what blood pressure should an elective case be cancelled for hypertension? Per the AAGBI/BHS 2016 joint guideline, proceed if pre-assessment BP is <180 mmHg systolic AND <110 mmHg diastolic. Above this, refer back to primary care for optimisation rather than treating acutely on the day — there is no evidence that short-term in-hospital lowering reduces perioperative cardiac risk and rapid drops may cause harm. How should ACE inhibitors and ARBs be managed on the day of surgery? Both ESC/ESA 2022 and the 2024 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline recommend withholding ACE-I/ARB on the morning of surgery when they are prescribed for hypertension, to reduce intra-operative hypotension. POISE-3 (2023) supports this approach with a MAP target ≥80 mmHg. Restart within 48 h once the patient is euvolaemic with stable renal function. How do you manage true hypertensive emergency before urgent surgery? Use an arterial line and titrate IV antihypertensives (labetalol or esmolol for dissection/phaeochromocytoma surge, GTN for ACS/pulmonary oedema, magnesium + labetalol for eclampsia) to lower MAP by no more than 20–25% in the first hour, then to around 160/100 mmHg over 2–6 h. Treat reversible precipitants (pain, hypoxia, hypercarbia, raised ICP) first. Truly time-critical surgery should not be delayed for chronic hypertension alone. > Cardiovascular disease is the leading driver of perioperative morbidity and mortality. This topic covers the conditions most likely to influence anaesthetic planning — ischaemic heart disease, valvular pathology, heart failure, arrhythmias and devices, pulmonary hypertension, and adult congenital heart disease — with a focus on risk stratification, optimisation, and intra-operative goals.

{/* Ischaemic Heart Disease */}
Preoperative Assessment
  • Functional capacity assessment (METs): patients unable to achieve 4 METs (climb one flight of stairs) are at increased risk
  • Revised Cardiac Risk Index (Lee index): IHD, heart failure, CVA/TIA, insulin-dependent DM, creatinine >177 µmol/L, high-risk surgery
  • Recent MI: ideally delay elective surgery ≥6 weeks (bare metal stent) or ≥12 months (drug-eluting stent)
  • Continue aspirin for most surgery; discuss DAPT with cardiologist and surgeon
  • Continue β-blockers and statins — do NOT start high-dose β-blockers de novo (POISE trial)
Anaesthetic Goals
  • Maintain coronary perfusion pressure: CPP = DBP − LVEDP
  • Avoid tachycardia (HR <80 bpm ideal) — increases myocardial oxygen demand and reduces diastolic filling time
  • Maintain normothermia — hypothermia causes catecholamine release, tachycardia, and increased SVR
  • Invasive BP monitoring for major surgery; consider cardiac output monitoring
  • Postoperative troponin surveillance for high-risk patients (VISION study — myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery, MINS)
{/* Valvular Heart Disease */}
Aortic Stenosis
  • Highest perioperative risk of all valvular lesions — fixed cardiac output, concentric LV hypertrophy
  • Severe AS: valve area <1 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg, Vmax >4 m/s
  • Goals: maintain sinus rhythm, normal rate (60–80), adequate preload, and SVR
  • Avoid: tachycardia, hypotension, loss of sinus rhythm, myocardial depression
  • Neuraxial anaesthesia: cautious low-dose spinal or CSE may be considered; epidural preferred (slower onset)
  • Emergency surgery: proceed with invasive monitoring, vasopressin/phenylephrine to maintain SVR
Mitral Regurgitation
  • Regurgitant fraction worsened by: increased SVR, slow heart rate, increased preload
  • Goals: slightly faster rate (80–100), reduced afterload, adequate preload, maintain contractility
  • Regional anaesthesia with sympathetic block may actually be beneficial (reduced afterload)
Aortic Regurgitation
  • Goals: slightly faster rate (80–100), reduced SVR, maintain contractility
  • Avoid: bradycardia (prolongs diastole → more regurgitation), increased afterload
Mitral Stenosis
  • Fixed low cardiac output; dependent on preload and diastolic filling time
  • Goals: slow rate (60–80), maintain sinus rhythm, adequate preload, maintain SVR
  • Avoid: tachycardia, fluid overload (risk of pulmonary oedema), AF, increased PVR
{/* Hypertension */}
Definitions & Staging (NICE NG136, 2023)
  • Stage 1: clinic BP 140/90–159/99 mmHg with ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85
  • Stage 2: clinic BP 160/100–179/119 mmHg with ABPM/HBPM ≥150/95
  • Stage 3 / severe: clinic systolic ≥180 mmHg or diastolic ≥120 mmHg
  • Treatment thresholds and targets (clinic): <140/90 mmHg under 80 y; <150/90 mmHg ≥80 y
Elective Surgery — Thresholds (AAGBI/BHS 2016)
  • Accept primary-care BP <160/100 mmHg documented within the last 12 months without further measurement
  • If no recent reading, measure in pre-assessment using a standardised technique (seated, rested, validated device)
  • Proceed with elective surgery if pre-assessment BP <180 systolic and <110 mmHg diastolic
  • Defer and refer back to primary care only if BP ≥180/110 mmHg — no evidence that short-term in-hospital treatment reduces perioperative cardiac risk, and rapid lowering may cause harm
  • End-organ damage (LVH, retinopathy, renal impairment), not the absolute BP alone, drives true perioperative risk — investigate where suspected
Chronic Antihypertensive Management on the Day
  • Continue β-blockers, calcium-channel blockers and centrally acting agents (clonidine, methyldopa) — abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension/ischaemia
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs: ESC/ESA 2022 and ACC/AHA 2024 both recommend withholding on the morning of surgery in patients taking them for hypertension to reduce intra-operative hypotension; POISE-3 (2023) supports a hypotension-avoidance strategy (omit ACE-I/ARB, target MAP ≥80 mmHg) over continued therapy
  • Restart ACE-I/ARB within 48 h post-op once euvolaemic and renal function stable
  • Diuretics: typically omit on the morning of major surgery to avoid hypovolaemia and electrolyte disturbance
  • SGLT2 inhibitors: withhold for ≥3 days (4 days for ertugliflozin) pre-op (MHRA 2024; ACC/AHA 2024) to reduce euglycaemic DKA risk
  • Continue statins and aspirin per surgical/bleeding risk

references.excerpt: Patients referred for elective surgery from primary care should have documented blood pressures lower than 160 mmHg systolic and 100 mmHg diastolic in the referral letter, which should be considered valid for 12 months. In the absence of such documentation, secondary care providers should measure blood pressure in a standardised manner. Patients with blood pressures of less than 180 mmHg systolic and less than 110 mmHg diastolic measured in secondary care can proceed to elective surgery without referral back to primary care.

case_bank.title: Spinal anaesthesia in severe aortic stenosis
case_bank.text:
Case: Spinal anaesthesia in severe aortic stenosis (Cardiovascular, Intermediate)
Patient: An 82-year-old with severe aortic stenosis (peak gradient 70 mmHg, valve area 0.7 cm²) needs hemiarthroplasty after a hip fracture.
Presentation: A single-shot spinal is proposed. Ten minutes after injection the systolic pressure falls from 150 to 80 mmHg and the patient becomes confused.
Stage 1 — Explain the physiology
  Question: Why is this fall in pressure so dangerous?
  Model answer: The concentrically hypertrophied ventricle is stiff: filling depends on atrial contraction and adequate diastolic time, so tachycardia and loss of sinus rhythm are poorly tolerated.
  Model answer: Stroke volume is relatively fixed across the stenotic valve, so cardiac output cannot rise to compensate for vasodilation.
  Model answer: Coronary perfusion of a hypertrophied ventricle occurs almost entirely in diastole and depends on aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure — hypotension rapidly causes subendocardial ischaemia.
Stage 2 — Treat the hypotension
  Question: What is your immediate management?
  Model answer: Restore afterload early with a vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine or metaraminol rather than relying on fluid alone.
  Model answer: Maintain sinus rhythm and a controlled rate (roughly 60–80 beats per minute); treat new atrial fibrillation urgently.
  Model answer: Give measured fluid to preserve preload, keep the patient in a head-down tilt if needed, and give oxygen while reassessing.
Stage 3 — Reconsider the technique
  Question: How would you plan the anaesthetic for the next such patient?
  Model answer: Either a carefully titrated technique with invasive arterial monitoring and vasopressor infusion prepared before block, or a general anaesthetic with slow induction and the same monitoring.
  Model answer: Avoid rapid-onset sympathectomy and large-dose single-shot spinals in fixed-output lesions; consider incremental epidural or low-dose spinal plus nerve block for hip fracture.
  Model answer: Escalate to senior and cardiology review, and do not delay hip fracture surgery unduly for investigations that will not change management.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Severe aortic stenosis converts a normally compliant, output-adaptable circulation into a fixed-output, pressure-dependent one. The ventricular pressure–volume loop is shifted left and steepened, so small volume changes cause large pressure changes; the transvalvular gradient means systolic ventricular pressure greatly exceeds aortic pressure, increasing wall stress and oxygen demand at the same time as diastolic perfusion pressure falls.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Prepare invasive arterial monitoring and a vasopressor infusion before establishing any sympathectomy. Aim for sinus rhythm, adequate preload, normal-to-high systemic vascular resistance and avoidance of tachycardia. Treat hypotension immediately with a vasoconstrictor; if arrest occurs, resuscitation is often ineffective because cardiac massage cannot generate flow across a critically stenotic valve, so prevention is the whole strategy.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not answer 'give fluid' alone, and do not describe ephedrine as first choice where tachycardia will shorten diastole. State the fixed stroke volume, the diastolic coronary perfusion argument and the rhythm target explicitly.
Take-home: In severe aortic stenosis, output is fixed and coronary perfusion is diastolic: protect afterload, preload and sinus rhythm, and monitor invasively before you block.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: the cardiac cycle (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mki024)

entries.text:
# Respiratory Co-Existing Disease Asthma, COPD, OSA, restrictive lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, respiratory infections Step-by-step reasoning Pre-op: PFTs (FEV1, DLCO), V/Q split function, exercise testing (6MWT or CPET; VO₂ peak <15 mL/kg/min = high risk), optimise bronchodilators, treat infection, smoking cessation Calculate predicted post-op FEV1 (ppoFEV1) and ppoDLCO; <40% predicts increased respiratory failure risk Intra-op: thoracic epidural or paravertebral for analgesia, double-lumen tube with bronchoscopic position check, lung-protective OLV (Vt 4–6 mL/kg ideal body weight, PEEP 5, plateau <25 cmH₂O, permissive hypercapnia) Manage hypoxia on OLV stepwise: FiO₂, recruit dependent lung, CPAP to non-dependent, intermittent re-inflation, surgical pause if persistent Post-op: HDU, regional analgesia, early mobilisation, chest physiotherapy, NIV if hypercapnic respiratory failure develops Common traps Excessive tidal volumes on OLV → acute lung injury (ARDS 4–8% post-pneumonectomy) Volume overload — restrictive fluid strategy (1–2 mL/kg/h crystalloid) Failing to plan analgesia for chest drain pain (intercostal block + opioids) Preoperative Assessment Severity classification: frequency of symptoms, hospitalisations, ICU admissions, ever ventilated Current medications: inhaled corticosteroids, LABAs, oral steroids, biologics (omalizumab) Steroid supplementation if >10 mg prednisolone/day for >3 months (risk of adrenal suppression) PEF or spirometry: FEV₁ <80% predicted suggests suboptimal control — consider postponement and optimisation Continue all asthma medications including on morning of surgery; nebulised salbutamol preoperatively Anaesthetic Management Regional anaesthesia preferred where feasible — avoids airway instrumentation If GA required: deep plane of anaesthesia before intubation; LMA preferred over ETT (less airway stimulation) Induction: propofol (mild bronchodilation); avoid thiopentone (histamine release) Sevoflurane: bronchodilator — preferred volatile agent; desflurane can cause bronchospasm (pungent, airway irritant) Avoid: atracurium/mivacurium (histamine release) — use rocuronium or vecuronium Avoid morphine (histamine release) — use fentanyl or remifentanil Neostigmine may cause bronchospasm — consider sugammadex for reversal Acute intraoperative bronchospasm: deepen anaesthesia, salbutamol MDI/nebuliser, IV salbutamol (250 µg), IV magnesium (2 g), IV hydrocortisone (200 mg) Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Pathophysiology & Assessment Obstructive defect: reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio (<0.7); air trapping, hyperinflation, gas exchange impairment Cor pulmonale: RV failure secondary to chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction GOLD staging (I–IV) based on post-bronchodilator FEV₁ % predicted Risk factors for postop complications: FEV₁ <1 L, current smoker, upper abdominal/thoracic surgery, TLCO <40% Smoking cessation: ≥8 weeks ideally (carboxyhaemoglobin normalises in 48 h; case_bank.title: Confusing gas in acute-on-chronic respiratory failure
case_bank.text:
Case: Confusing gas in acute-on-chronic respiratory failure (Acid–base, Advanced)
Patient: A patient with severe COPD on long-term oxygen presents drowsy after three days of increasing breathlessness. Gas on 60% oxygen: pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 9.8 kPa, PaO₂ 9.0 kPa, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L, lactate 1.2 mmol/L.
Presentation: The referring team says the gas is 'normal for him'.
Stage 1 — Interpret the gas
  Question: Is this chronic or acute?
  Model answer: Bicarbonate of 32 mmol/L indicates established renal compensation for chronic hypercapnia, which takes days.
  Model answer: The pH of 7.22 is far too low for fully compensated chronic retention, so there is an acute rise in PaCO₂ on top of a chronic state.
  Model answer: Uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen has probably worsened hypercapnia by increasing dead space through reversal of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, the Haldane effect and reduced ventilatory drive.
Stage 2 — Treat immediately
  Question: What do you do first?
  Model answer: Titrate oxygen to a target saturation of 88–92% using a controlled delivery device, and repeat the gas within 30–60 minutes.
  Model answer: Give bronchodilators, corticosteroid, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and treat any coexisting heart failure.
  Model answer: Start non-invasive ventilation for persistent respiratory acidosis, with a documented escalation plan.
Stage 3 — Plan escalation
  Question: When would you intubate, and what ventilator settings?
  Model answer: Intubate for failure of non-invasive ventilation, exhaustion, reduced consciousness, inability to protect the airway or haemodynamic instability, taking prior function and patient wishes into account.
  Model answer: Set a long expiratory time with low rate, tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, and permissive hypercapnia targeting pH rather than normal PaCO₂.
  Model answer: Monitor intrinsic PEEP with an expiratory hold and watch for barotrauma and haemodynamic compromise from hyperinflation.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: Chronic hypercapnia with renal bicarbonate retention shifts the baseline, so pH — not PaCO₂ — indicates acuity. A patient in whom pH is markedly reduced with a raised bicarbonate has an acute-on-chronic picture demanding intervention. Excess oxygen contributes through several mechanisms, of which increased physiological dead space is the dominant one, so controlled oxygen therapy is treatment, not restraint.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Controlled oxygen, bronchodilation, steroid, treatment of infection and early non-invasive ventilation form the bundle. Reassess gases serially, monitor conscious level and work of breathing, and agree ceilings of treatment early with the patient and family. If invasive ventilation is needed, prioritise expiratory time, accept hypercapnia, avoid dynamic hyperinflation and check intrinsic PEEP.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: Do not accept 'this is his normal gas' when pH is low, and do not remove oxygen entirely. Quote the 88–92% target and the pH-based interpretation of chronicity.
Take-home: Judge acuity by pH, not PaCO₂: acute-on-chronic hypercapnia needs controlled oxygen at 88–92% and early non-invasive ventilation.
Cited sources: BJA Educ: COPD and ventilation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkr054); BJA Educ: acid–base interpretation (https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx008)

case_bank.title: The overlooked inhaled steroid
case_bank.text:
Case: The overlooked inhaled steroid (Steroid cover, Intermediate)
Patient: A 49-year-old man with severe asthma uses high-dose inhaled fluticasone and has received three oral prednisolone courses this year. He is listed for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Presentation: He denies taking any ‘regular steroid tablets’ and the initial assessment records no risk of adrenal suppression.
Stage 1 — Identify hidden exposure
  Question: Why should the steroid history be revisited?
  Model answer: High-dose inhaled steroids and repeated systemic courses can suppress the HPA axis.
  Model answer: Ask about dose, duration, recent oral courses, steroid emergency card, Cushingoid features and previous perioperative problems.
  Model answer: If uncertainty cannot be resolved before surgery, a safe supplementation plan is preferable to an unrecognised crisis.
Stage 2 — Plan moderate-stress cover
  Question: How would you manage a patient judged at risk?
  Model answer: Continue usual inhaled therapy and optimise asthma control.
  Model answer: For moderate surgical stress, give hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction followed by 25 mg IV eight-hourly for 24 hours.
  Model answer: Monitor glucose, blood pressure, sodium and potassium; resume the normal regimen promptly.
Stage 3 — Differentiate postoperative hypotension
  Question: What features make adrenal crisis more likely?
  Model answer: Hypotension that responds poorly to fluid and vasopressors, especially with hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia.
  Model answer: Treat immediately with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV and fluids while also excluding bleeding, sepsis, anaphylaxis and cardiac causes.
Discussion — Clinical reasoning: HPA suppression depends on cumulative systemic exposure, not whether a patient currently takes tablets. High-dose fluticasone, repeated oral rescue courses, topical preparations and injections all matter. Features such as Cushingoid appearance, a steroid emergency card or recent withdrawal increase concern.
Discussion — Management and monitoring: Continue inhaled therapy and optimise asthma. If moderate-stress surgery proceeds with credible suppression risk, give hydrocortisone 50 mg IV at induction followed by 25 mg eight-hourly for 24 hours, then resume the established regimen. Observe haemodynamics, glucose and electrolytes and treat unexplained shock promptly.
Discussion — Exam pitfall: A normal-looking medication list can conceal recent systemic exposure. Ask specifically about every route, dose, duration and cessation date rather than accepting ‘no steroid tablets’.
Take-home: A steroid history includes inhaled, topical, injected and recently stopped treatment—not just current tablets.
Cited sources: Association of Anaesthetists 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.14963)

  • HbA1c: target <69 mmol/mol (8.5%) for elective surgery; >69 = consider postponement for optimisation

  • DKA: insulin infusion (0.1 U/kg/h), IV fluids, potassium replacement, monitor for cerebral oedema
  • Hypoglycaemia (<4 mmol/L): 75–100 mL of 20% glucose IV; glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV access
  • Euglycaemic DKA: suspect in patients on SGLT2 inhibitors — normal glucose but raised ketones and metabolic acidosis
{/* Thyroid Disease */}
Hyperthyroidism
  • Cardiovascular effects: tachycardia, AF, increased cardiac output, widened pulse pressure
  • Must be euthyroid before elective surgery — carbimazole/propylthiouracil + β-blocker
  • Anaesthetic implications: exaggerated response to catecholamines, increased MAC, risk of thyroid storm
  • Thyroid storm: hyperthermia (>40°C), tachycardia, altered consciousness — mortality >20%
  • Treatment: propranolol, Lugol >Hypothyroidism
    • Cardiovascular: bradycardia, reduced cardiac output, pericardial effusion, diastolic hypertension
    • Increased sensitivity to anaesthetic agents and opioids; reduced MAC
    • Delayed gastric emptying, hypothermia, and impaired drug metabolism
    • Mild/moderate hypothyroidism: safe to proceed with surgery; severe (myxoedema coma) is a contraindication
    • Myxoedema coma: IV T3, hydrocortisone, rewarming, ventilatory support — ICU management
    Thyroidectomy Considerations
    • Airway assessment: retrosternal extension, tracheal deviation/compression, CT thorax if stridor
    • Postoperative complications: recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (hoarseness), bilateral RLN palsy (stridor → reintubation), hypocalcaemia (parathyroid damage), haematoma (surgical emergency — open wound at bedside)
{/* Adrenal Disorders */}
Adrenal Insufficiency & Steroid Supplementation
  • Chronic steroid use (≥5 mg prednisolone/day for ≥3 months) → HPA axis suppression for up to 12 months after cessation
  • Perioperative supplementation (2023 guidelines): minor surgery — usual dose; moderate — hydrocortisone 50 mg at induction + 25 mg q8h for 24 h; major — 100 mg at induction + 50 mg q8h for 48–72 h
  • Addisonian crisis: refractory hypotension, hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia
  • Treatment: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, 0.9% saline bolus, 10% dextrose for hypoglycaemia
  • Features: central obesity, hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, proximal myopathy, thin skin
  • Difficult IV access, fragile tissues; anticipate difficult positioning and pressure area care
  • Continue perioperative steroid cover — risk of adrenal crisis with adrenalectomy
{/* Phaeochromocytoma */}
  • Catecholamine-secreting tumour of adrenal medulla (90%) or extra-adrenal paraganglia
  • Classic triad: headache, sweating, palpitations with paroxysmal hypertension
  • Preoperative preparation (10–14 days): α-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD, titrate up), then β-blockade (propranolol) once α-blocked
  • Never give β-blockers without prior α-blockade → unopposed α-stimulation → hypertensive crisis
  • Volume expansion: patients are chronically vasoconstricted and intravascularly depleted; encourage salt and fluid intake
  • Readiness criteria: BP <130/80 sitting, postural drop present, no ST changes, nasal congestion developing
  • Intraoperative: arterial line + CVP essential; have phentolamine (α-blocker), SNP, GTN, esmolol, and magnesium drawn up
  • Tumour handling → catecholamine surge → hypertension/tachycardia; after venous ligation → risk of profound hypotension
  • Postoperative: risk of hypotension (depleted catecholamines) and hypoglycaemia (rebound insulin secretion)
    • {/* Carcinoid Syndrome */}
  • Neuroendocrine tumour secreting serotonin (5-HT), histamine, kallikrein, and prostaglandins
  • Features: flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis (carcinoid heart disease)
  • Diagnosis: urinary 5-HIAA, serum chromogranin A
  • Perioperative octreotide infusion (50–100 µg/h) — blocks mediator release; have bolus available
  • Avoid histamine-releasing drugs, sympathomimetics, and suxamethonium (may trigger carcinoid crisis)
  • Carcinoid crisis: IV octreotide 100–500 µg bolus; avoid catecholamines (may worsen); use vasopressin for hypotension
